Aura Kingdom is by far one of my, if not the most, favorite f2p MMORPG ever. I began playing this game during beta phase and I fell in love. This game is so easy to pick up and play, definitely new user friendly. The main story is a little boring, but you can get into it. There is so much content in this game and it just came out. If you like SAO or anime theme games and an open world with an awesome community then this is for you. I agree the most with user:
patroklos_ps
PROS :
- It is FREE , you can become great without even spending a single euro/dollar !
- Anime graphics , well designed world and characters !
- New player friendly , anyone can learn all he needs to know from the in-game tutorials which are all implemented in the story-line and are presented at the proper time.
- Nice storyline that will keep you interested (if you are ever read missions and not skip them)
- Clever way to involve pets (named eidolons in the game) in the storyline and awesome system to get them gathering key fragments. (pets and mounts are different)
- A big variety of classes and the abillity to choose a subclass at later levels allows for many different playstyles and combinations !
- Fishing , digging and other extra stuff to keep you busy even when you think you are done leveling up (you ll never actually be :P ).
- Nice and friendly community, you can surely make a lot of in-game friends and have fun in the game !
- Quests offer an autopath for the monsters you have to slain or the things you have to find so you wont need to blindly search for them.
CONS :
- For those who skip missions it will be boring as it doesnt offer anything more in leveling up other than grind and more grind.
- There are not TOO many dungeons , you will have to repeat some of them at certain points which you may find tiring.
- Lags and glitches do exist but they are not unbearable , considering that the game is still young they shouldnt be a problem that will last for long.
- IF you decide to buy something with real money you need to know that things in the store are TOO expensive.
- Still in progress so the game still doesn't offer an ending at it's story line , it will be released at a later date.

Old (old enough to only run at 640x480, in fact,) but not only still good, but in many ways, still unique.
Rebellion gets classified as an "RTS" because it is sort-of real time, and definitely a strategy game, but it's far from a game of Starcraft.  While it is a head-to-head match up between player and AI or two players, with no third faction or side units, and borrows heavily from 4X games, the closest analogue is really a Paradox grand strategy game like Europa Universalis.
What really makes Rebellion unique is how they incorporate asymmetric warfare into the basic gameplay.  The Empire starts stronger than the Rebel Alliance, but lacking in the capacity to really capitalize upon that advantage to do much more than scare the rebels away.  Ships can jump into hyperspace, which makes them functionally invulnerable, preventing any showdown from occurring, at least until mid-game when you research gravity projector ships.  Planets can be bombarded, but that doesn't change the face of battle.  Planets can be conquered, but if you don't get the planet's population on your side through diplomatic missions, they are vulnerable to agents sabotaging the garrison and fomenting revolts that will drop popular support throughout the sector. Early-game, rebels can easily take a whole (10-planet) sector just through a few hero units sabotaging garrisons and fomenting revolt, even when they have no fleets to stand up to the imperial doomfleets.
Also, the player knows nothing about what is going on outside their worlds without sending spies or reconnaisance units out to gather information, which provides "snapshots" of information.  You're perpetually acting off of information several days old, and making assumptions about what your enemy did since then.
Ground forces are vulnerable to bombardments from space, but both space and ground units are vulnerable to heroes and agents performing missions. Heroes and agents, however, are vulnerable to "detection" from concentrated amounts of ground or space forces.  (Faster spaceships like fighters, and special, often weaker, ground forces are better detectors.) The end result is that it's generally better to have a "bastion" in a sector and leave most of the other planets lightly defended or undefended, relying upon a rapid-response team to simply drive off the enemy and take back any enemy gains quickly, rather than protect everything.  It creates a slippery sense of what is "yours" and what is still up in the air.
Ultimately, I'm not sure the pseudo-real-time nature of the game plays too well in multiplayer.  It's extremely difficult to play the game at any speed setting other than the super-slow one if you are managing your own build queues.  Since you basically want to agree on game speed, it's more meant for head-to-head with a friend than pick-up games with strangers you don't talk to the way that a multiplayer FPS pick-up game works.  That said, single-player can rapidly become unsatisfying without you imposing some challenges upon yourself, because as soon as you really start to get used to the rules enough to make smart decisions, you'll find the AI is nowhere near smart enough to manage the complexity of the game as well as a human.  (They'll happily send their giant fleets on wild goose chases after a decoy fleet while your invasion forces hop into the void unopposed.)
For sheer uniqueness, however, I strongly recommend this to any strategy game fan who hasn't played the game yet.  On sale, it's dirt cheap, and the novelty of the asymmetric strategy game will leave you wondering why nobody thought to copy and refine this game's great, but tragically unpolished ideas.

Absolutely enjoyable 4X space experience. If you don't mind the relatively slow game pace, compared to many other real-time strategy games, you'll feel at home in Stellaris. You can, however, turn up the game speed, if you are so inclined, which is a big bonus, should you want to hasten up things.
The lack of a technology tree, as one knows it from similar games, such as Civilization or Endless Space 2, can be seen as a positive or negative aspect. For my part, I believe it adds an exciting twist to the genre, as you never know precisely, how your research path will look like - even though it is somewhat determined by your global actions in the game (your research options adapt to how you play the game in its entirety).

Another drop-in-drop-out F2P shooter, except this one is third person and has a wacky asthetic! Loadout probably had some potential at one point, before the overbearing cash shop came into play. As it is now I find it hard to recommend, despite being F2P because of the cash shop, broken matchmaking, terrible map voting system, and a limit of 4v4 for every game mode.
Even though it claims to be "all about the guns, baby!", the weapon customization is limited to four types of guns that share almost all the same parts. There is little room for creativity because of the tech tree system; more complex upgrades require "previous" unlocks to be bought using the in-game currency, Blutes, which are tallied after every match. Although you can test out upgrades before you buy them, you can only test out what you can unlock on the tech tree currently. Once you unlock a part it is permanently unlocked, but only for that weapon (even though many parts are copied across weapon types). This leaves you struggling to upgrade your weapon parts (which gain exp as you use them) to increase their stats (damage, accuracy, RoF, etc.!) as your fellow players race through upgrades and power up their base damage & accuracy while using cash shop exp boosters.
This all leads to another huge problem: Matchmaking. The "Casual" matchmaking, where the majority of the game modes are held, seems to simply slap together 8 players and split them into teams. It does this so haphazardly that the forums were flooded at launch with complaints about parties joining a lobby only to be broken and split between teams at the start of the match. Matchmaking also doesn't seem to care about player stats or skill level because before the end of match weapon levels were disabled, many times you would see players with level 8+ weapons in a game of level 1-2 weapon players. This is a huge leap in passive stats that would take a non-boosted player dozens of hours to attain and leads me to believe that there simply is no real matchmaking outside of the competitive mode.
Loadout is simply another barebone F2P drop-in-drop-out FPS (in third person this time!) that demands you spend cash if you don't want to be left behind. Some will find this amazing and stick with it for months but many others, like me and the rest of my friends, will play for a dozen or so hours, notice all the problems with the game, and just move on.

My first day with it I tested a few games, with mostly default settings. Fallout 4, Arkham Knight, Shadow of Mordor, etc etc. And began to get used to the controller. I didn't actually have a lot of time to mess with it as I got home at midnight. The next day I had more time to work with it, and since then I have come to love the controller.
1- Customization is key. This is the area where the controller truly shines. The controller has 2 dual stage triggers, 2 bumbers, two grips, trackpads, start and select buttons, and analog stick and 4 xbox style face buttons. Every single input can be customized to work like any input of a mouse, keyboard, or traditional gamepad. One example of customization I have tried out that shows off the versatility of the gamepad was setting the analogs click in Dark Souls to "W+RB", which gave me a simple click to kick an enemy rather than the original control pattern.
2- Trackpads/haptic feedback. The trackpads take some getting used to at first, especially if your using a different configuration than what you may actually want, but once you learn what your doing, they are far more accurate than an analog stick for camera movement. In any game where you can use a mouse and gamepad simultaneously, I would suggest setting the right trackpad as your mouse, this is by far the most accurate option. some games like Assassins creed syndicate I am using the mouselike joystick option, which while not terrible isn't quite as good, and in fallout 4 I now have the buttons mimicking the KB/M with no controller prompts so I can use the mouse mode. The haptic feedback is also a nice addition, without which the trackpads might have felt cheap. whenever a move my analog stick to a differant direction in Fallout 4 ( since it's emulating WASD movement ), I get a slight thump from underneath it, or when I move my thumb over a trackpad I get small clicks that tell me how fast I'm moving and how close I am to the edge. The only way I can describe it at the moment is the difference you feel switching from a rubber dome keyboard to a mechanical keyboard with a click that lets you know that you've actually input a command.
3.Grips/overall feel. The two new buttons on the back of the controllers handles added way more functionality than I thought they would. In fallout 4, I am using the right grip to jump, but the left grip is a modifier that changes my left trackpad from a dpad with my 1,2,3,and 4, hotkeys, to an up and down scrollwheel. They also didn't hamper the feel of the controller as a whole. I've seen lots of criticism on the internet that it feel's cheap or that they didn't like the ergonomics of it, but I disagree. It may be plastic and slightly more lightweight than the xbox one controller, But unlike the IGN review where they said "The first thing you notice is just how cheap it feels", the first thing I noticed is just how much nicer it felt than I thought. The handles on the controller curve out, making the controller have a concave look, that I thought would feel like an nVidia shield portable ( I don't like the way that feels ), however since the analog stick is on the lower half, and your right thumb doesn't have to curve up to meet an analog stick, it helps you curve down and onto the trackpad instead and feels very natural. I also noticed after gaming with it for a few hours the xbox one controller felt small in comparison, despite the fact they are similar sizes.
4.Gyrometer. One of the less talked about features is the gyrometer. so far I've set it do one thing, and that's for it to activate when I aim down sights and have a low sensitivity compared to the trackpad. While I would say I am more accurate with the trackpad than an analog stick, the trackpad alone was not enough for me to have the same accuracy as a mouse, however, with use of the gyrometer I feel I may be more accurate than I was with a mouse. ( I'm also not the best shot in general so take that as you will XD )
Cons- I have one con really. Big Picture Mode. don't get me wrong, I like big picture mode in general, and understand steam is trying to tie big picture mode with the living room, along with this controller, however, I don't like that I have to use big picture mode in order to customize my control scheme and play my games with the controller how I want. If you have a non-steam game you also can't access the community made control schemes for your games, like the witcher for me on gog, or syndicate on uplay for me as well. these are minor problems that have not deterred my use of the controller.
Conclusion- I would give the controller a 9/10, however, I would not recommend anyone purchase this controller hoping it will be an easy transition to use, or that games will work how you want right off the bat. If you are willing to mess with settings and learn how to use the controller, and have games that you either want to play in the living room or games that either don't have controller support (I'm looking at you Mass Effect 2! ( which plays great on the steam controller by the way ) ), or don't work well with traditional controllers than you're the person I would recommend this to. I hope this was helpful.

If I were more cynical, I would call this a moneymaking scheme, leveraging the Steam Trading Card system to get people to pick it up for 19-25 cents during sales and re-sell the cards for a small profit. However, I don't hold the developers responsible for this and I want to give this an honest review.
If I were judging this as a concept demo, or in a game jam, or even on Steam Greenlight, I'd rate it very highly. I'm glad that Steam exists not just for big-budget studios to market games but also as a platform for small indie developers to try out unique concepts and hone their skills. I just feel like this game would work better on something like itch.io or gamejolt, in a pay-what-you-want market. As a finished game, I can't really recommend it.
The core mechanic of Polarity - color swapping - isn't really new. Basically, walls/platforms block things the opposite color as them, lasers destroy things the opposite color as them, and boxes/buttons have to match colors to work. You can swap colors, you can change a box's color by sending it through a color-changing field. Oh, and don't touch green lasers. That's it.

Not every game needs to be super innovative to be good; puzzle games can take simple/already existing ideas and turn them into good puzzles. The problem is, this game doesn't get that far. There's only a handful of very short levels, and they're all super easy, even the 'bonus levels'. In an hour, I completed 75% of the game (I started skipping to later levels once I started finding them easy). You don't really need to explore, or reason/plan solutions to puzzles, or do anything beyond the basic interactions. I'm not sure if this is because of the level design/lack of levels, or if the concept itself doesn't lend itself to difficult/interesting levels.
It's also not polished. Level design is sometimes annoying: lots of wide open rooms without many puzzle elements (and a slow-ish walking speed), and there's really no point to the green lasers apart from making you return to a checkpoint. There's a general awkwardness to the movement (jump boosts and moving platforms are inconsistent, and held boxes get stuck on things really easily). Control setup is weird (it's Unity, so you can remap things, but there's a bunch of controls that aren't used/show up twice). The tutorial is really unnecessary (the game pauses to display button prompts when a simple tooltip saying "WASD, Spacebar, Q, click, have fun" would have been more than enough).
Polarity doesn't really have much else going for it (I guess controller support and local multiplayer are kind of neat considering the suprising number of big-budget games without these features, but again they're auxiliary to the main experience and they don't really affect my overall review).
So ultimately, who would I recommend this to? My friends that already enjoy puzzles would finish it within minutes, and my friends that are new to the genre would probably enjoy something that's more polished/complete.
Despite all that, this game does a few interesting things right: Gameplay elements within the levels have a very clear and consistent visual design. There's subtle hints that players might use without noticing (like a white square/black frame that means 'throw a box at this from far away') and platform placement/wall design actually guides players toward the optional objectives. The system of checkpoints is actually really well done (most games like this make you restart levels completely). Despite my earlier complaints, the level design is pretty good overall, and it's clear that effort and time was put into this experience.
Sadly, as a finished game I can't recommend it.

Having played all prince of Persia games, I think this is one of the better ones, but not the best. And the reason why it isn't is because of how the saving works. A mechanic that is so badly done it destroys the enjoyment of this game.
Despite its age the graphics hold up. Not because of the latest state of the art graphics obviously, but because it fits the game and there is nothing detracting from it. The art style is also superb with interesting locations and beautiful vistas. The only gripe is that there is only a 4:3 ratio and not 16:9. I believe you can mod it, but I think the game breaks slightly if you do. The story is nothing to write home about and often feels very cheesy and videogame-cringeworthy. You know, bad lines and scantily clad women with enormous boobs. It just feels way to forced and out of place.
If you are familiar with the game -series, you'll find great platforming and puzzles in this one as well. This is probably the most challenging game in the whole series. Puzzles are truly difficult at times, and you don't always know where to go. You do have a map, but it is not particularly helpful. I found myself going down the wrong path quite a few times because It is not obvious where you are going next, especially if you have not played the game for a while.
The combat is the best in the series. Lots of variety, "different weapons", many combos, tight controls and fun game-play. You can even use the environment a bit. It works great with mouse and keyboard, but I also found that a controller (a little fiddling to get it working properly) worked quite well.
This is all good. But what eventually makes this game the only one I have never completed(!), is how the saving works, and what happes when you die.
You can only save at certain locations and there is no autosave. So what? That is normal of older games. Well, it takes quite a while to save (first he drinks for quite a while, then you go in to a menu asking if you want to save, then you get asked where to save, and then ok etc - a lot of small steps to save that feels really tedious after a while). Also, these save locations are sparse, especially later in the game. Which means that you might have to go through a bunch of difficult puzzles, beat monsters, and oops 15 minutes later you died and guess what, you have to redo all that again. If you find the boss and/or monsters hard you have to redo that quite a few times. The problem is that you have to redo all of it, not just the part you find difficult.
This is absolutely hair-pullingly frustrating. It is not fun to replay 10-15 minutes of platform puzzles (that sometimes are quite difficult) and then you die to the next section of monsters or bosses. Sometimes the game seems to aknowledge this problem and you don't always start over at your last savepoint, but at a specific points in the game. But this doesn't happen often enough. This really feels unfair when the camera and/or controls can be the fault of your death or you might not know where to go.
And the whole "you died" screen animation... It seems silly to bring up, but the whole experience from pressing the wrong button, or perhaps not seeing what is going on because of bad camera angles, then dying in slowmotion, getting the "you died screen" that is just a tad too long and you can't skip it, then going back to load your game and realizing you just lost a bunch of progress... - it all ads up, and takes too long to be fun.
It is a shame because it really is a good game otherwise, and could have been one of the better ones. But now I would say it is the 3rd or 4th in the series because of this problem, because your overall experience is more frustrating than fun. Otherwise it has it all, great combat, nice platforming, bosses, good puzzles and a great theme and art style.
Also, the music is not the best. They were going for some kind of tough rock-style. While I don't mind that kind of music, it just doesn't fit as well in this game and also feels rather repetitive.
I still reckommend this game, but only for the die-hard fans who enjoys a little torture and no hand-holding.

Notable due to lack of Farah co-op levels. The parkour is AGAIN flawed by the weird camera shifting that makes running hard. Mostly during the Dahaka chase scenes. Speaking of these - apart from the camera they are awesome. They include an epic soundtrack and the game really pumps you up to try to get away from the monster. I guess it balances out the fact that there is MUCH more fighting and less jumping around in WW. The boss fights are cool but very punishing so be prepared. There are secrets which you can unlock and if get all of them a water sword appears and you get a different ending! This I thought to be cool because the final fight is then totally different too. Worth mentioning is that the game runs well but there is a glitch now and then. You can see the main design focus is elsewhere but while I find the previous game to be better I still like this one a lot and recommend it!

The Secret of Monkey Island is without a doubt one of the best point and click adventure games ever made, and one of the rare few in which the sequel can claim to be even better. You are Guybrush Threepwood, newly arrived on Melee Island to follow your dream - to become a pirate. On the way you'll learn how to insult sword fight, fall in love with a beautiful governor and battle an evil ghost pirate while searching for hidden t-shirts, looking for 3 headed monkeys and discovering the secret that is Monkey Island. This re-mastered version is wonderful to play, now with full speech, which include the actors who did the voices for the last couple of Monkey Island games. However, the game does not support surround sound and the action commands are cumbersome at best.

The Secret of Monkey Island is a PC gaming classic of a bygone gaming genre.  Point and click adventures are largely extinct nowadays but playing this game gives you a casual gaming experience focused on solving puzzles and thinking outside the box.  Extremely well done voice-acting and a solid and comedic storyline make this short game worth at least a play through.  Certainly a game that you should play, but its lack of replayability and retro gameplay means you shouldn’t ever pay more than $5 for it.

You know the adventure genre is not dead. Once you play this game you'll probably poke around the Internet for other similar games of the "Adventure" genre. If you've never played an adventure title you owe it to yourself  to try at least one. The Secret of Monkey Island is a great place to start.
Once you finish look on Google for AGS (Stands for Adventure Gaming System), it's a programming language for writing your own adventure games. There are a lot of them online, free to download and enjoy. Some of them are even made by Yahtzee Crowshaw. If you don't know who he is, Google him, he's a fabulous writer and sly whit and cynicisim will leave you in stitches.
(He also writes horror adventures that will freak you the hell out!) Don't miss out on this wonderful genre, get started here ASAP.

The game crashes. A lot. It crashes roughly once every 2-3 hours for me. That may not sound like a lot, but this is a game without auto-save. A lot can happen in 2-3 hours, and a lot that you basically need to redo. Every time the game crashes I feel like giving up because unlike starting a game afresh, it's incredibly boring to execute the same strategies to take the same planets to have the same outcomes again. So... great game. But what a frustrating port.

This WAS true, but as more people have become aware of this problem, more and more TDM and GTC servers are popping up.  The new update also added a new game mode called "Survival", and it's pretty fun, and Survival servers have been replacing free-roam servers.  The loot system has also been improving, especially now that their is a new member of the dev team to make cool skins.  Of course, there are still bugs and balancing issues, but these should be fixed over time, and are largely the results of a whiny community.  In the end, if you were a fan of the original, and you have patience, I would definitely reccomend Primal Carnage: Extinction.

My biggest  complaint however is that the game is long, and slow. Even when you've got the fast forward button on, the game moves at a visible snails pace. I've honestly never managed to reach any of the endgame events because after several  days of playing the game becomes such a repetitive slog that I get bored and quit. No game should move so slowly.
The other issue I take is that ultimately, no matter which path you try and take, it all comes down to an intergalactic arms race. You're going to be forced into massive conflict at some point, and there's no way around it.
Its honestly an interesting game, and I definitely had some fun with it, but for the price, especially with all the DLC, I actually wouldn't recommend buying it. At the very least I'd say don't buy it unless it's 50% off or more, preferably in a bundle.

I was a bit skeptical about this game at first since I read some stuff on the forums about it not receiving updates that often, devs being lazy and so on but I gave it a try nevertheless.
So far I'm loving it. Even if it's like your usual get that / do that type of MMORPG the art-style, graphics and gameplay are what keep me going with it. At the moment, I'm Lv16 and from what I see there are lots of features unlocking at Lv20 and Lv25.
Leveling is fairly easy, as of now I am leveling from like 3 quests which are easy to do, just go collect some things or kill some monsters.
The story is somewhat interesting, I don't usually read quest logs and stuff like that but this game made me read them. There are some cliche things here but still, compared to how other MMOs cough up story it's awesome.
This game has an interesting guild system as well. After you reach Lv10 you can join guilds by simply pressing G and searching for a guild that fits your liking. You instantly join them, no acceptance required. Now I'm not sure if this applies to every guild but still.
Another cool feature that I noticed is the friends system. It has this Intimacy thing which categorizes how close you are to your in-game friends. If you spend a lot of time with them in parties and stuff the Intimacy level goes up.
Skills are fancy, classes are awesome, mounts and the most important thing which I should have mentioned in the beginning, this game is not Pay-2-Win at all. At least from what info I managed to scrape so far.
As of now that's all I can say about this game, I highly recommend it to anyone that loves MMORPGs and doesn't mind anime-like graphics.

Pros and cons of the game so you don't have to read a bunch of opinions!
+ are good factors, - are bad factors, and = are unsure factors, make up your mind about that yourself!
= The game starts out slow and holds your hand a lot so it's perfect for people new to mmos with the battles and quest system.

= Looks childish, but takes skill to play right and is fun.

Some downers so far.
- Healers are not so much necessary early on. (to level 20 experience, will update as i go along)
- No choices to make your character stand out to yourself. (So far to lvl 20)
- Each item sells for 1 - 5 silver until lvl 20. (example.. a 40 silver item sells for 3 silver, horrible exchange rate for shops)
- Cannot use a few basic functions at lower levels like trading.
- bots, bots everywhere, but this is hardly a negative, they are in all mmos, and to be frank, it's not as bad here as it is in Archeage, for example.
- A few things are broken right after release, not too uncommon but it may be unsightly. (Scythe weapon class for example)
---------
Now on to the good stuff!
+ Items are wonderfully easy to come across, but forces you to tidy your inventory very often.
+ I can unsocket stat gems from my equipment for free? Oh look, it does not break anything either!
+ Loyality points for the cash shop, you get loyality points fairly easily by playing the game. Nice!

Polarity is a first person logic puzzle game whose concept is vastly inspired by Portal. It has similar mechanics but at the same time it is full of originality. The companion cubes might not be as cute as in Portal, but they’re still present in this game and needed to complete the puzzles. An innovation consists in the ability of the player to switch between two polarities (red – blue) which allows him to run through gates or to jump on platforms, according to the selected polarity.
The single player part consists of 14 puzzles that are not too hard to solve, with difficulty increasing each level though. However, even the most difficult levels can be solved in less than 5 minutes each. The 10 bonus levels are slightly more difficult to figure out, but they add new fun features to the game.
The coop mode, on the other hand, is quite challenging. The two players must cooperate to solve the puzzles that are much more complex than in single player mode. The levels are bigger, now consisting in multiple rooms. The path to the exit isn’t usually the same for the two players, but nevertheless, they need to work together to reach it. There are places in which timed jumps are needed while trying to grab certain objects at the same time, and these jumps are not easily performed with a controller as compared to a mouse and keyboard setup. Sadly, the game offers only local coop and not online multiplayer, so make sure to invite a friend that can be persuaded to work on those together with you, without him losing his patience. Or even better, maybe you can convince him/her to do those tricky jumps :)
Don’t hesitate to buy it, especially discounted, since it is a very fun game!

I want to like the Steam Controller, but unique hardware is hampered by atrocious software. It only works in Big Picture Mode, which is fine for consoles or Steamboxes on a big TV, but it is ABYSMAL to use on a normal gaming PC. I honestly can't recommend anyone buy a Steam Controller until Valve makes it functional in normal Steam, outside of Big Picture Mode.

As is, the steam controller is awesome. With continued support from valve, and developers considering both controller and keyboard support for games, it could get to the point where there may never be a reason to purchase a console again. I like to shoot with my mouse, but race with a controller. I can now do this easily on one machine. Even for games not designed with controller support in mind, Big Picture Mode will let you assign specific key mappings for games so that you can set them up in a way that works best for you.
I only have a few issues with it. The "Y" and "B" buttons are a bit close to the right side touch pad, and my fat fingers tend to hit that touch pad when I go to press Y or B. This has messed with my view in some games. Also, pushing buttons seems a bit louder with this conroller than say the PS3, PS4, or Xbox controllers. A lot of the functionality for the controller is specific to Big Picture Mode, and controls such as key mappings can only be accessed via Big Picture Mode. I would like to have just as much control over it from the desktop mode. Settings such as key mappings are more easily assigned from the desktop with keyboard and mouse, than with the controller. I wanted to go through and set up key mappings for many of my games. but doing it from Big Picture Mode seemed like more of a chore than it has to be.
Other than that, it's been great. It gets good duration out of the batteries, and the dual touchpads make it pretty easy to do things such as browse web pages with the controller from a distance. It's comfortable to hold, easy to use. and with Valve at the helm, we can expect that their next steam controller will be even better.

The Binding of Isaac is a top-down rouge-like action RPG about a young boy named Isaac, who grew up in a christian household. One day, his mother hears a voice from above, asking her to cleanse Isaac from sin, for he has become corrupted by it. She takes all his toys and drawings. The voice calls to her a second time, telling her that her son is still corrupt, and that he must be locked away from the sinful world. The voice calls to her a third and final time, telling her to sacrifice Isaac's life in order to prove her faith. Isaac sees this through a crack on his door, looks for a hiding place, then he finds a trapdoor under his rug. The exact moment Isaac flings open the hatch her mother barges is with a butcher's knife! Isaac, without hesitation throws himself down into the unknown depths below...
This is probably one of my favorite games of all time. It has a ton of content all well as replayability. The game is full of biblical references and imagery. For 5$ it's way more than worth it. If you like rouge-like dungeon crawlers, an interesting narrative, a lot of replayability, then this is the game for you.

There are menus, sub-menus, scrollable lists, and tabs galore. There's lots of scrolling and hunting around for things, as well as lots of clicking to initiate things you want to do in the game; sending Han Solo and Chewbacca on an abduction mission, aided by a team of rebel infiltrators, to capture Darth Vader on Sullust, for example. The depth of this game and all of the many things you can do can really make it hard to keep track of all that you've got going on around the galaxy. At least the game provides a search tool that lets you find specific planets, personnel, or fleets pretty quickly.
Seriously, if you love Star Wars and strategy on a grand scale, you owe it to yourself to try this oldie-but-goodie. I can't wait to try out playing against someone head-to-head, something I never did way back when.

Great as a 4x game, not so great as a Paradox game.
Pros:
- visually stunning
- most playthroughs feel varied
- lots of tech to research and relatively strong writing on random events
- custom empire creation is a strong point
- combat is beautiful
- a ton of mods
- DLC adds a lot to the game, granted, some of this should have been in the basegame, but fortunately the DLC is cheaper than many other games comparable DLC.
Cons:
- lacks the depth other Paradox games like EU4 or CK2 have, hopefully this will improve as it matures.
- endgame performance is bad even on an Enthusiast level gaming rig, highly cpu bound in this regard.
- warscore is super broken and makes conquering the galaxy through violent means a real chore.
- enemy ship building AI is weird and a many weapons/categories of ships you can create end up being useless (never pick missiles).
- endgame tech - eventually you reach a point where the only research is for 3% empire modifiers and nothing new is being unlocked. Feels like they could add some new things here.
With all of this said, nothing feels as cool as turning your empire into something completely different with ascension perks, or building massive megastructures and becoming your own fallen empire. Its still an amazing game that I will certainly put more hours in, and I can't wait to see what is coming in some updates that are being discussed on the dev blog. The game will certainly be improved for the better within the next months/year.

WARNING : I only recommend this game because it is F2P, and other than cosmetics, there is no real advantage of paying IRL money.
TL;DR : Decent game. Dev team prefers making money over improving game (not by a lot tho, i'd say 60-40 split). F2P. Has interesting heroes. Card system keeps matches fresh. Some heroes have been definitely under/over-powered for AGES.
OK, Paladins is about you and your team picking unique heroes and battling it out with the enemy team.
5 players per team, each player must choose a unique champion and you are locked to that champion until the end of the match. So, bad picks are punished and good picks/counterpicks are rewared.
You can modify how your hero works by "cards". Pick 1 out of 3 big cards that massively modify your playstyle and pick a "deck" of 5 cards that modify it slightly (EG : Viktor. One big card heals you when you use Sprint. One of the small cards increases run speed, another gives you ammo while you sprint. So you can stack those cards to make you heal yourself and run faster AND gain ammo while you sprint.
Then you have temporary cards, bought with in-match credits. These only exist for current match, and once bought, cannot be changed/sold/traded. These will give you a big boost. Eg, a card which makes you run faster, deal more damage to shields, or give you health on a kill.
Matches take anywhere between 5 minutes (complete pubstomp) to 20 (a fair and balanced match) to 30 (a reeeealy drawn out match with lots of overtime).
You initially get 4 heroes (one from each type, Flank, Frontline, Support, Damage; Skye, Fernando, Pip and Viktor, resp).
You unlock more heroes via Gold (ingame currency) or Crystals (premium currency).
Gold is only used to buy heroes and loot boxes, and is earned at a decent rate. One can unlock 2-3 new heroes each week if you play enough.
I RECOMMEND you to unlock a support and a flanker ASAP, since Pip and Skye are considered "weak" and "harder" to master. I'd say unlock Jenos and Lex, or if you're poor, Grohk and Buck.
You can join either casual or competitive mode.
insta-lock a hero of their choice regardless of the map/enemy team composition.
You get some free stuff for playing competitive, PLUS a special portrait frame for your rank.
So, why play Paladins?
1. Its free.
2. Some very interesting heroes. My personal fav are Bomb King and Drogoz.
3. Can run on low end rigs. I am using a Lenovo E49 with an Intel i5-2520M. Runs at 15-30 fps. Not too shabby.
So, why NOT play Paladins?
1. Newer heroes are intentionally unbalanced... live testing ftw.
2. Recently, focus has shifted towards more visual updates rather than gameplay updates.
3. Certain heroes are definitely overpowered/underpowered and nothing has been done for ages... despite lots of feedback/complaints (seriously, just go look at the sub-Reddit).
4. Recent "shady" practices... eg, moving the Radiant chest (this can be bought with gold, very good gold sink for people with all champs unlocked) to the very end of the chest queue... so you have to scroll thru ALL the other chests... have turned me off. YMMV.

With a Steam backlog breaking 1,000 games, I have no excuses for choosing to complete this 50-cent platformer. It captures the mediocrity of the SNES' 3rd-party platformers darn well -- and it's one I would have loved as a kid for simply having dinosaurs, even if it wasn't very good. (It also pays homage to tons of the the SNES' dino games, with my favorite being Joe & Mac references out the wazoo.)
The pixel art is amazing, and the game's best asset. It's simple, but vibrant and full of animated enemies and backgrounds. It can get ugly, too, with drab occasionally drab color choices -- but either way, it's charming. The platforming is solid, and solidly simple. There's (double-)jump, dash, and a single attack, all of which provide a good framework for a platformer, but, in this case, fail under uneven level design. The worst moments force you to take lethal leaps of faith, and there are unfortunately quite a few of these moments. The bosses are incredibly well-designed and fun to figure out: They're predictable, mixing with the controls really well, and the attack patterns are fun to dodge and overcome.
The worst part of this game, however, is the music. The retro soundtrack is nails-on-the-chalkboard bad. It doesn't even sound like music. It's repetitive, nasty loops of dreary boops and bops without any structure or hook or anything appealing at all. It's seriously the worst game soundtrack I've ever heard in my life. I would rather listen to the Buck Bumble theme song on repeat for 24 hours straight than ever hear another one of these dreary boops. Ugh.
Anywho, shows promise for the developer's future games. I felt compelled to play through it, despite it's complete average-ness in everything but pixel art. Pretty dinosaurs.

I'm sorry, fans. This game sucks.
I get it. You like the concept. You like retro platformers like this. You like the love story between the caveman and his dead wife, and you like the challenge. But there's a good way and a bad way to do challenge, and this game does it badly.
Floaty controls, unfair level design, bad hitboxes, and punishing difficulty don't make a game fun. They make it ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I'm not going to cut this game any slack because it's an indie title. This is where the big boys play, and you need to do better than this.
The game is not properly optimized, and that is the failing of the developers. Gamepad support is only partial, and doesn't even work properly on all systems. The entire purpose of x-input is to make gamepad support idiot-proof, and yet somehow, this game manages to screw it up.
People constantly praise how much better games were in the 8- and 16-bit days when they offered actual challenge, but a lot of designers and players don't understand that there was a lot more going on in those games than you realize or remember. It's not just a matter of making a game hard and sending you back to the beginning if you're not perfect. It's a matter of designing levels in a way that makes playing through them enjoyable, even if you're not MLGproswag360noscope. And TWaC doesn't manage to do it right. Take a closer look at games like Spelunky, Binding of Isaac, VVVVVV, Super Meat Boy, and don't dare try tell me that this game is in the same league as them. These games are the end result of spending YEARS making sure that the controls and jumping physics are spot on PERFECT. These games have earned the right to offer players a challenge. Caveman has not.
Fix the controls. Make There Was a Caveman 2 and do it right. I'll happily play it. There's a lot of nice ideas here. Skulls as currency. Diminishing returns as you keep dying. Fine. But the execution is straight up bad.

Imagine a sitation where the auto companies built a cars with the clutch, brake, gas, gearshift, headlights, windshield wipers, and other controls in random positions in the cars they make, and each control has its own peculiarities .   This seems to be the situation that the Steam Controller is wrestling with in the game software industry.
Having used the Steam Controller for several hours, I feel that the controller is a great idea but it won't be of much value until the game companies and/or users develop control configurations for the Steam Controller that move toward a standardization of game controls.  For the games I have tried with the Steam Controller it has mostly been an exercise in frustration just trying to accomplish the most basic tasks in games.  To say it has a steep learning curve is a gross understatement.
To remedy this situation, Steam might start certifying the games it sells that have met some basic standards of control configuration that will work with their controller.  This could assist potential purchasers of their games in knowing how long it might take them to get a basic mastery of the game controls.
In the mean time, unless you have an enormous amount of free time on your hands and a high tolerance for frustration, I would wait a while before purchasing this hardware.

It's a very oldschool game in a way: unique and novel and enigmatic - the antithesis of the simple but highly polished games that thrive in this day and age. The control scheme won't be familiar. It's overly complex, not really intuitive and the game doesn't try very hard to teach it to you. Instead the controls as well as the game mechanics are something you need to figure out by playing with it. But if you're like me then even fumbling around is fun enough that you stick to it. And when you dig into it you'll be rewarded with a constant stream of little insights that help refine your idea of what-the-♥♥♥♥ am I playing here? Next it will kindle your ambition. Winning for the first time doesn't mean you understood everything - there are still more questions then answers. Theories. Annoyances. Ideas for improvements. Rough edges. Elements that you might consider poor designed, or poorly implemented. But maybe... maybe that's the most charming part of the game that it doesn't try too hard for you to like it. This makes the game an even better antagonist, the survival part more genuine and only amplifies the joy you get out of mastering it step by step.

This game made me rage so much that I should rate it negatively. However, it still is a PoP and overall it's still a "solid" game.
My main gripes:
- Combat is pretty decent this time around, much less getting knocked down and not being able to get up again. That being said, fighting multiple opponents can still often be extremely tricky. Single opponents, however, are fodder.
- The bloody camera. I think this is the one thing that caused me the most deaths in this game. It's very difficult to control and does what it wants sometimes, even invert the controls, despite it not being enabled.
- Controls are muddy again, the Prince is often not doing what you want him to do. For example, I used a 360 Pad and bound the time button to the left trigger. Well, guess what, that button does not work for the combat time skills, instead I had to rebind the key to another one (left shoulder). Figuring this out was a pain. Another example: Changing direction on a swing pole is left to chance it seems as the Prince sometimes turns and sometimes not. Gladly there are almost no time sensitive jumps in this fashion. You also still need to hold down the action button for all those things to work. Another example: Holding down the direction button to move the Prince forwards does not always result in him going forward, because the game takes the bloody camera angle into account, so instead of just pushing forward on the stick to move a rotating lever, you have to also rotate your stick to move it...*sigh*
And my main gripe with the game: The god damn back tracking. I needed 15 hours on easy with a guide to complete this one, I visited some areas 3 or 4 times due to story reasons. You'd better memorize all the areas (in the past and present zones nonetheless) or use a guide. I shudder taking a break for a week or a month from this, coming back and realizing that I have no clue whatsoever where to go and how to get there. The game is an enigma. While it does have a "map", it's absolutely useless, as it's just an "overworld map" and offers NO details whatsoever. Infuriating.
Another gripe: The last portion of the game is, again, just back tracking and repetition, but also extremely trivial. There is almost no way to fail at that stage and combat becomes extremely simplistic.
What does it do well then? Well, it's still fun swinging around, the story is interesting and the past/present mechanic is pretty neat. However, the game needed to be streamlined. The last part is for the most part easy to navigate, but the rest? A nightmare. If you want to find all the secrets, prepare to spend even more time with it. Imho it's partially better than Sands of Time, but Forgotten Sands still beats it in terms of accessibility. Warrior Within is hardcore even on easy...

TL;DR: If you like Star Wars and strategy games and are willing to look past its age, buy this game.
Star Wars: Rebellion is an older title, but still one of the best in its class. No other Star Wars game has the level of depth and strategy as this. You have all the forces of the Empire or the Rebellion at your command, and it's up to you to lead them to victory. As its leader, it behooves you to strengthen your faction's military, industrial base, political support, and information networks in order to keep the war machine at full capacity. Few other games will make you feel like a master strategist as Star Wars: Rebellion.
Pros:
+ Broad-scale strategic gameplay that ranges across the entire galaxy
+ Deep mechanics for building, managing, and conquering your faction
+ Control famous characters like Luke Skywalker, Han Solo, Princess Leia, Darth Vader, and Emperor Palpatine
+ Command space battles with iconic Star Wars ships like Star Destroyers, TIE Fighters, X-Wings, and even Death Stars
+ A who's-who look into the Expanded Universe pre-Prequel Trilogy ; almost every unit, hero, planet, and building comes  from the EU
Cons:
- UI is a bit outdated - it's a very menu-based game with little in the way of keyboard shortcuts or other modern concessions
- Some of the mechanics aren't explained well in-game, meaning you will have to consult resources outside the game to understand how everything works
- Tactical depth of battles are lower than you might expect - space conflicts play out a bit slowly with a strange UI, while land battles happen completely behind the scenes without player input after the battle begins
- Little optimization for modern hardware - you may need to do some work to get it to run on your machine. Running the game in compatibility mode helps a lot

If you love really complicated strategy games then this is for you. There's no tutorial so it's up to you to figure out how to do things. Just be aware, there is an extreme learning curve, but the game is a ton of fun once you figure out the mechanics.
I have Windows 7 and it runs just fine on my system at full screen although this does not seem to be the case for everyone. So far I have not encountered any bugs.
Overall it's like coffee. You grow to love it but it's really bitter in the beginning.
If you played Empire At War and wished that it had more depth, then buy this game.

This game is definitely something. I should preface this by stating that I am a huge fan of science fiction, so I may be a little biased given the spin this game takes on the grand strategy genre.
First, some pros. It is epic in scope, appealing to those that genuinely get off on long-term planning coming to fruition. It gives you tonnes of optimization options for your ships, allowing you to create the Navy you want. It includes a huge number of SF tropes and references, tickling the fancy of anyone who loves the SF genre. Genetic and robotic modification allow a huge range of options, the late-game crises dodge the stagnation of well-I'm-the-king-now endings a lot of successful strategy runs contain, and the tech balancing by empire size ensures you can't just run the tech tree by out-populating the other nations.
Then, the cons; don't worry, every game has them. The epic scope means you better be ready to wait to get to that next fancy tech, because you'll be playing a while before it happens. It's fairly easy to come up with a pretty-well-ideal ship outfit based on measuring out shield and hull damage. Wrong turns often only become apparent several hours after the ball was dropped, which can lead to some frustration.
Would I recommend it? Yes, but conditionally. If you're looking for the instant-gratification kind of strategy game, you should avoid Stellaris. If you're looking to have carefully made strategic decisions potentially pay off in unexpected ways, and if you've the patience to see the game through, you will enjoy this game beyond measure.

I purchased this game during a recent sale and paid about 49 cents for it. The game is most definitely worth that price, but I cannot say it is worth the full 2 dollars.
The Good:
1. I always have a soft spot for the pixelated, nostaligic graphics and sounds.
2. The sound track is amazing and does tend to be stuck in ones head after you sit down the controller.
3. The physics and animations were well done, basically perfect.
4. I did like the merger of the side scrollinger shooter and the planetary exploration/platforming. I found them to be very   complimentary to one another in this game.
5.  Personally, I liked having to avoid the enemies, relying heavily on the telportation gun. I liked the puzzle aspect oft his game, though it was a bit easy.
The bad:
1. The game was too short. My first play through, and not in any particular rush to beat the game, took 40 minutes.  this is taking into consideration the time I spent trying to get some of the extra items.
2. The developers said this game was directly inspired by Cave Story and Super Metroid, but I fail to see much of those characteristics in this game. It is possible that I am not looking or thinking hard enough. I expected more weopons, different abilities that would allow you to progress, etc.  This game did not feel as atmospheric or epic as metroid and was not long enough to qualify for any kind of story, like Cave Story.
3. The puzzle aspect of this game, while I love it, is wayyyyy too simple. Once you get the hang of the fact that the teleporation gun conserves momentum, you have beaten the game.
4. Not a whole lot of variety. I disagree with the main character when he says that 3 types of beam obstacles are too many. They are not enough.
5. One could argue that this is trying to turn the game into something its not, but: I wanted to see more than one planet. I wanted more intermmediate shooter levels and more planets to explore. I'm not suggesting a re-write, but the simple addition of more content that is already within the bounds of the game engine.  "I'm sorry, but Grigori is on another planet" would have been an accpetable transition between levels.
Overall:
The game felt less than half completed, like a teaser trailer of itself. Imagine the first mario brothers game, on the NES, if the princess was really in the first castle. That is this game.
I think this game could be great if it just expanded on the content a bit. I am not suggesting anything revolutionary. A few more obstacles and perhaps some variety to the planet (or add more than one planet).  Achievements do not do it for me and did not add to the game.
For < 1 dollar, this game can be recommended. Not for the full price.

There's people who will defend this game because Minecraft and people will oppose it because it's popular and it's a childrens game. My review will cater to those who do not want any of these sides to be taken. And here's what I thought before I played it.
Minecraft IS a popular game, not just a childrens game and certainly did not start off that way. If any of you were there since 2009 this was mostly built around fans who were young adults to teens. Over the years Minecraft has become such a big phenomenon that all walks of life play Minecraft. Now, keeping this in mind TellTale does have a heavy burden to deal with especially since they're making a story mode on Minecraft. As much as I was keeping open eyes for such a big franchise and not buying into the entire negative arrogance to a popular "childrens" game and not being a blind fan I seriously gave it a chance since TellTale is known for their dramaticsm of their games. The verdict?
It is really not that original compared to their other titles. I've played the Walking Dead and it's very similar to the structure of the story. It seemed very corporate and seems like they were playing it safe. I was wishing they would make the story a bit more different since it's literally Minecraft but it just didn't feel like it was being its own thing.
Don't get me wrong, the game is absolutely fun, probably even better if you haven't played any TellTale adventure games. Probably even better if you're a fan. But the story didn't feel original. It was definitely fun and the characters were fun but not original at all so far. Seriously, it's the Walking Dead with Minecraft characters. Without spoiling it too much at one point in the game you're having to run into the middle of a night and there's a section that was literally straight from TWD. Also, sometimes it's so predictable (if you've played enough TellTale games) where basically everything is fine and then SUDDENLY enemy appears and button sequence engages.
I really tried my best to like it, I did but not in the way where the story was original. I guiltily like it and as of this writing I've played Episode 2. I may change this review once I finish it but I do not recommend unless you're a Minecraft fan.
Edit: Whatever, I liked it. You got to me TellTale.

Don't let the bad reviews stop you from getting this game.
Did I buy it? Yes. Was it worth it? Definitely.
While this game was short and quite clearly a Portal-style remake, Polarity is a fun 3D Platform game. The goal is to get to the end of each stage while collecting data fragments along the way (there are 3 for each stage). Using only your intelligence and a few colored cubes placed in specific locations on the map, you run and jump through 11 stages in story, 10 stages of bonus levels and some stages in Co-op (I admit, though, I never tried Co-op). While simplistic, the challenge of collecting the data chips makes it a little more exciting. It's a nice, simple, short game, that is still worth playing.
The only con I would have to say is the ending.. It left me wanting more. A lot more. As for the soundtrack? I actually liked it. It was catchy.
tl;dr short, fun 3D platform game that can be a little challenging, but wish it was longer. The music is now permanently engraved into my brain.

A fun and relatively novel puzzle game. While the puzzles border on trivial in places the game make use of some interesting game play elements. I really like the idea of the switching polarity and I think there is a lot of potential to expand upon the mechanic. The level design is simple but appealing and the soundtrack has a nice ambient, soothing quality that I think really suits the gameplay.
The only real complaints I have are the polish, difficulty, and length of the game.
During gameplay, there wer scattered instances of getting caught on small edges and sequences of accelerators. I don't think it detracts from gameplay too much but with the timing component it seems like this has potential to frustrate speed runners.
The difficulty is obviously subjective and I understand that it can be difficult to strike a balance here. I think the game would benefit from the addition of more challenging puzzles, either by developer addition, or support for community creation.
The campaign and bonus levels felt a bit short overall. Obviously there could be replay value for people wanting to improve time overal but without a leaderboard for friends this might be rather niche.
Overall, I like the game and recommend it for people who like relaxing puzzle games.

Before I begin, I want to make one thing clear:
With that out the way, this game is simple but packs a wallop for it's simplicity. To cut to the chase: This is a rogue-type RTS game that has heavy levels of RNG in it to have you to survive. One of aspects of the game is leveling up your hero which grants more health and stronger hero abilities for each tier you've unlocked. The game requires that you juggle between leveling your character or your base structures through

and Material are the key of the game's mechanics as you're forced to mine out Material and kill monsters for Aether with the game increasing it's difficult each step of the way.
The game, after a few nights, becomes exceedingly difficult if you don't keep on your Hero's Level and the level of your defenses around your Crystal. With some of the RNG events, like nights where Goblins bomb the living hell out you to nights of peace with fire flies flying around, you can either lose that run or exhale that deep breath you were holding onto to let your workers work at night.
Overall, this game is fun and I enjoy it deeply. I hope the devs continue to add new patches/content to this game as I can easily see it becoming a classic for it's fan-base.

Great mixture of Rogue-like RPG and RTS. Controls are easy to remember and overall learning curve is quite simple.
Though, AI could be improved and RTS elements of the game should be expanded and simplified in some ways (A lot of micro control, can't use mini-map to move camera etc.).
Lastly, I wish the developer would implement adjustable difficulty (such as prolonged day time, treat level increment, abundance of resources etc.)
All in all, this game is definitely worth its price + its made by a single developer, who did a great job merging different genres into one (almost!) complete game.

Base game review
The game is good, there is no doubt about that, great production value, great look, depth.
Now there are things that may ruin your experience however or at least hinder it (at least in the base game as I did not get the dlc yet):
- Combat: Doomstacks are the key, there are not a single mechanic in place to try to fix that or diminish its impact, research does not make a big difference enough, the key is number and the game will push you to create a big ball of ships in the middle of your territory which you'll be using everytime it's required.
- Research: they went away from a tech tree and instead propose you 3 techs available from which to chose, not only is it annoying for new players who do not know what to expect but it sometimes put you backward compared to your opponents without realising it. Also like said above, definitely not enough impact on combat to stop the stupid snowball thing. Also not enough ways to speed up research (building research stations sure...but no sliders to try to invest more, no events linked to characters)
- IA coverage and expansion: Expansion does not really make you stronger, it's important for resource gathering but it does not provide enough and it's something the IA barely uses in fact, they create their ball until they meet someone, and roll over it if they can, IA is not diplomat enough and there is in fact a low amount of diplomacy available for a pdox title.
Overall the main positive aspect of stellaris is its pace and the way it presents your empire (characters, traits, factions, pops) but it's not the best 4X out there in its vanilla form.

The music sounds randomly generated, and the sound effects click like there's some 30HZ sine wave starting in the middle of its duty cycle. I played through it to the end, but can't really recommend.

I find neoretro platformers to be like pizzas; they have the same basic ingredients and can be found everywhere, but I never tire of them, and would be loath to turn one down unless it lay solidly within the "salted cardboard" zone (or "Cheetahmen" zone, as the case may be).  If I am allowed to indulge in delicious foods in my afterlife (rather than the maggot and feces stew I hear they serve in hell), I will probably eat pizza every day for fifty mortal years.  Some people don't like pizza that much, but I don't care about those people, nor their disgusting tastes.
Now, viewed through my paradigm of platformer-as-pizza,
is a scrumptious artisanal pie with all one would expect from such:  a savory strata of gourmet cheese that strikes a perfect chewy-to-gooey ratio; toppings including locally grown mushrooms, crunchy bell peppers and freshly caught shrimp; organic Genovese basil; tangy, yet not overly salty, sauce that bespeaks of the heirloom tomato that birthed it; and a buttery, hand-kneaded crust that would be delicious bereft of all else.  Undoubtedly, it
a pizza, and you can easily imagine its primary flavors before you bite, but it's a superb specimen of its kind and a true delight for the pizza-lover.
Speaking less obliquely, one might say that the game plays smoothly, has a consistently high framerate on fullscreen, provides intense yet fair challenge, and exhibits finely etched hitboxes (I tested them on the pendulum grubs in the forest -- you can safely stand in the trajectory of their short swing until they actually
you).  I could also talk about the wonderful consistency of the jocular pixel-Prehistoria aesthetic.
But I'd rather just see it as a damned fine pizza, served up by a lovelorn Cro-Magnon.

Platforming sections feel like you are being punished for no reason, with instant death pits in the middle of the room when you could have just made more floor and jump distances that flip a coin as to whether or not you actually stick to the very edge of the platform you are expected to jump on to.
Some gameplay features are never explained. If you had to search how to even begin Level 10, you know what I am talking about.
Overall:
You shouldn't expect anything great. The biggest puzzle of this game is figuring out why the floors and walls of this place are screwing with you. Play this only if you have just played Portal for the millionth time and still want to solve puzzles, but are worried because you now hear Glados talking everywhere you go. And even then, you should only buy it on sale or as a part of a bundle, like I did.

Great game for anyone who loves MMORPG's and/or anime.
Some good things about the game :
-It's 100% free but has an option to buy items in-game w/ AP, generally costing a fair amount of money from your Steam Wallet.
-Amazing storyline
-Animations/Actions are nicely polished.
-Full of life in major areas like Crescent Hill, Helonia Coast, Port Skandia, and Navea (These tend to be the most popular locations for players).
-Classes specialize in a couple specific stats but overall, all classes are balanced.
-Dungeons and bosses in general can be somewhat easy to defeat alone but are more rewarding when fought with friends or in Hell Mode and the Otherworld.
-The Battlefield events are fun to play and generally occur every 1-2 hours. Leveling from 1-40 is simple enough then takes noticeably longer (40-50 isn't too long, 50-60 takes longer, 60-61 takes way longer than both). After finishing the main story, grinding tends to be the main thing to do.
-Guilds are fun to be a part of and are very rewarding when leveled up and active, they also fill the chat if you find a good one.
-Selling items through a stall or the auction are both good ways to make money, as quests don't give out much.
-Archeology is fun, a good way of getting items or money but can be a bit costly for beginners (10 gold for the pickaxe, 5 gold per 100 relics dug up).
-Beautiful locations to visit and unlock with their own unique creatures and story.
-Has more of a unique feel compared to other MMORPG's
-Great camera movement (Zooming in/out and rotating the camera)
Some bad things about the game :
-PvP can take a while to get into because of the mass amount of high level players w/ PvP gear, meaning lower levels (-60) won't stand much of a chance and will most likely die when fighting another player.
-Some enemies seem a bit boring (Some creatures are the same as other creatures but resized to be bigger/smaller)
-Dialog/Cutscenes seem a bit rushed after lvl 55 (Spelling mistakes or no dialog at all)
-Community does not tend to speak much in the chat until you join a guild.
How I'd rate Aura Kingdom :
Gameplay : 8/10
Graphics : 9/10 (For an anime game at least)
Story : 9/10
Community : 6/10 (Unless you're in a guild or in trade chat, the chatbox is quiet)
Overall : 9/10

TL;DR: I recommend buying this controller.
I kept reading bad reviews upon bad reviews and decided that I had to find out how bad this controller really was, so I bought it.
To start things off, the packaging is well done. The controller is very frustrating with the preset bindings that the game may recommend, but if you actually try the profiles that others have been setting up in the community, this controller works great!

Is the steam controller a replacement for KB/M? No is it a replacement for your traditional controller? No again. Then what exactly is the steam controller? It is a highly customizable controller with that is ridiculously versatile. It can function like a traditional controller, KB/M, or even a hybrid of the 2 devices put together. This can be used for pretty much any game. From Sonic generations, to CIV V, to racing games to whatever else including fps games using the gyro (look it up its crazy). I use mine on my desktop from my sofa in my gaming room (usually used for 3ds and the like) to play games such as divinity orinal sin, dragon fin soup, CIV, Portal, Halflife2 and many more in unique and intuitive ways. I generally download somebody elses pre-configured game config and customize it to fit my needs or I use a template and customize from there. This is a unique piece of hardware and admittedly I am a bit of a hardware-nut  but I feel a lot of people will be able to appreciate this piece of hardware so long as they know what they are getting and don't expect it to be what it is not.

This controller has a lot going for it, every bit of it is configurable per game. It has a nice look and feel and a decent weight to it. I thought the small ABXY buttons would be a problem but actually they work well and you can press them very fast. The left and right grip buttons are easy to forget about at first but soon become a lovely thing to have, especially for using mode shifting.
My complaints with it are the left and right bumpers are very dense compared to other controllers and require some force to press, I feel they will loosen with time. The biggest issue I had with it was learning the sensitivity and the overall learning curve with using the right pad for camera controls. I also do not like how this controller is only configurable via Big Picture mode especially since you can use it as a wiresless mouse and keyboard for your standard desktop - so I feel this should be a feature across Steam and Steam Big Picture. Lastly it does not have a rechargable battery but can be used wired so not many complaints.
Overall I really like this controller and it works very well, I feel a lot of any remaining UI bugs will be sorted out over time and it has already replaced my previous controller. I probably wouldn't play a competitive FPS game like Counter Strike: Global Offensive with it but for casual use it's perfect. Just do not let the learning curve push you away, it's worth it.

Warrior Within is a worthy sequel to the great Sands of Time. The story continues seven years after the events in the Sands of Time with the Prince of Persia as he sets out to find the Empress who created the sands... of time. His goal is to stop her and change his fate. In the first game, after stabbing the hourglass with the Dagger of Time, the Prince had released the Sands and changed the timeline. Due to this, he has been constantly hunted down by the Dahaka, an inevitable being of fate which, by killing the Prince, could correct the timeline and the Prince's fate. That is why the Prince embarks to the Island of Time to confront the Empress, to change his fate permanently.
One of the more notable aspects of Warrior Within is how violent it is. The tone is much dark than it's predecessor and even the levels are grimier. But the platforming, bar hopping, ledge jumping, wall running, etc; it's all still there. And still just as fun. But what's even more notable about this game is the element of time travel. The plot gets really interesting about 3/4ths of the way through when various mysteries are uncovered and pieces are put together by the prince. His development and keen insight were a joy to watch throughout.
One last thing, make sure you get all nine life upgrades to get the water sword for the alternate ending, which in reality is the canonical ending that continues into The Two Thrones. Plus it's so much more rewarding than the regular ending.
Anyway, great game, but my only major complaint might be the drastic changes in music, from the Middle-eastern styled orchestral to the guitar driven metal. Not a fan of the metal use in this game. Oh, and I guess more PC options would have been nice. A few bugs. No other complaints really.

Short summary of this review: This game tries to be Portal. It isn't Portal. Not by a long-shot.
Graphics: Mediocre at best. I'm not a stickler for graphics, but what we have here is a few painfully generic primitives and lighting effects. I wouldn't mind this if the game excelled in some other area, but... well. At any rate, 3/10.
Sounds: They don't stand out, but they aren't awful. I somewhat suspect they might be taken from a free sound library somewhere. Nothing wrong with that, but it doesn't really wow me. 5/10.
Music: It doesn't make my ears bleed. 5/10.
Gameplay: Red block goes on red switch. Blue block goes on blue switch. Press Q to change color and pass through certain walls. As I mentioned, this game is trying to be Portal, but the core mechanic is extremely stilted. There's also the data packets which are hidden in each level, which feel like they belong in an entirely different game. About five levels in, I started thinking 'man, how long is this game???' which is never a good sign. 1/10.
Story: An excuse plot, so I won't be taking it into account in the final score. N/A
Other notes: Supposedly, Polarity is made for 'experienced gamers'. Each level is about three minutes long, and the only real challenge is finding the switch that you have to throw the cube at. Right.
Overall score: 3.5/10. Clearly a first attempt at a game by an extremely inexperienced studio. It showed a little promise at first, but doesn't really do anything interesting at any point.

Endless Fables: The Minotaur's Curse is an exceptionally well done hidden object game full of excellent puzzles and ancient Greek mythology. The mythological snippets are present in basically all of the puzzles, just like they are in the story of course, which is about the well-known legend of Theseus, Ariadne and the Minotaur. I happily discovered (from the names in the credits) that the game is made by a Hungarian studio, but of course I'll try to remain objective and write an unbiased review.
We play as Pamela Cavendish, an anthropologist who - after a disturbing encounter with a mysterious hooded figure - interacts with Ariadne's Thread proving that the legend of the Minotaur was/is indeed true. We soon learn that the Minotaur is waiting to be revived and only a descendant of Ariadne can kill him with the combined power of the thread and a magic crystal. That leaves us with only 1 question: who might the descendant of Ariadne be? :)
The special feature of the game is the aforementioned thread with which we can solve puzzles by doing several things: it can melt things, revive creatures and neutralize magic. By collecting crystals can we unlock the powers of the thread.  The melt feature is the one we are going to use most of the time so if we get stuck, we'll probably have to melt something.
(Unfortunately it doesn't function as a normal rope, so at one point where we have to rescue a guy from a well, we are going to have to look for a regular rope.)
Altough the story itself is pretty good (even if it gets a bit dull as we progress) the game's main strength are the lore about Greek mythology and the diverse selection of puzzles. The number of these puzzles outweigh the hidden object scenes, which is good news since puzzles and minigames are generally more enjoyable, than simple hidden object scenes. Even the HO scenes are out of the ordinary and often require a bit og extra attention. As more and more of the story is being revealed the game also tests our knowledge of Greek mythology. Of course we can't get stuck during these storytelling parts, it is a nice touch.
I really liked the fact that after the main story, the bonus chapter continues our adventure right off the bat: we have to escape from the magical island where we fought the Minotaur. Even though the quality of this roughly 30-40 minutes long expansion is lower than of the main game, it's still enjoyable. I particulary liked how some of the collectibles are scattered throughout this bonus chapter as well, so in order to collect them all we have to remain vigilant through this part of the game also (there are all sorts of them: butterflies, dragonflies, fireflies, night butterflies and morphing objects, but surprisingly they aren't that hard to spot).
The graphics, altough generally nice, sometimes isn't as detailed as in other recent HO games. During the cutscenes character animations seem a bit clumsy and due to zooming pixelation may occur. And the vegetation seems strange: it doesn't seem as mediterranean as one would expect from Crete.
On the other hand small things, such as the achievement icons which look like works of art or the design of some puzzles are really well made.
The music unfortunately is totally forgettable.
Endless Fables: The Minotaur's Curse is one of those hidden object games that can be safely recommended for everyone and while it's not the most spectacular looking one, its deep mythological content and great puzzles it deploys make it a must buy for the fans of the genre.
PROS
+ Greek mythology
+ plenty of great puzzles
+ variety in hidden object scenes
+ interesting concept
+ bonus chapter
CONS
- pixelated graphics during certain cutscenes
- some character animations are awkward
- music is mediocre
RATING
8/10

Endless Fables may not sit well with those hidden object game fans that play for the hidden object scenes, but its mythology-based story and wonderful graphics should compensate its shortcomings.
I almost hesitate to call Endless Fables: The Minotaur’s Curse a hidden object game, because most of its hidden object scenes are actually more like single-screen mechanical puzzles. Still, the rest of the usual mechanics are all there: casual point ‘n’ click item hunting, conventional puzzles… everything but the more traditional hidden object parts.
These gameplay parts are held together with a tight story that likes to push forward, omitting almost all backtracking. It follows the adventures of an archaeologist who also happens to be a late-late descendant of Ariadne, the Cretan princess who was involved with the nasty business of a certain Minotaur. While the plot has the usual issues of cramming most of its events in the opening chapter, it never sits down completely, giving plenty of incentive to keep the player on the road from start to finish.
