The night that I first finished NieR: Automata I slept soundly. The night that I actually finished NieR: Automata I hardly slept at all.
I had that high, that nervous energy, that hum in the back of my head that comes from an overtired brain trying to absorb an experience that was so much bigger than it initially seemed.
It’s been a few days, and I’ll admit I’m still humming.
It’s a story I thought I’d heard before. It’s the distant future and the earth is in ruins. Machines have replaced mankind, and therefore they must be destroyed. Cue the ethical dilemmas, the friendly machines. Cue the crisis on a shattered concrete stage, and of course the swelling orchestra. Nier: Automata did give me a lot of what I expected, but it also gave me a lot that I didn’t. Even when I’d seen the twists coming there was always still some surprise, some little (or not so little) knot left for me to unravel.
This premise isn’t the only thing that felt familiar. Mechanically speaking, picking Nier: Automata up for the first time could result in déjà vu. Combat starts on the tried and true foundation of light attacks, heavy attacks, dodges and combo chains. Then there are the flight units, used sparingly for some of the bigger and more bullet hell-ish fights. Bullet hell-style gameplay (which generally involves dodging complex waves and patterns of enemy projectiles while fighting) figures into boss fights and hacking minigames quite heavily too.
As for equipment, weapons from swords to fists to spears can be found or purchased, then upgraded with the requisite materials to increase their damage as well as the length of their combo chains and the stat bonuses they grant when equipped. Player character 2B has multiple weapon sets that she can switch between on the fly, and she can likewise switch between multiple equipped programs for her pod (a sort of support drone that specializes in ranged attacks like missiles and lasers.)
That said, the bulk of your gear is not programs or weapons but chips — which even provide many of your UI functions. The mini-map is a chip, as is the HP gauge, as are items that will boost 2B’s attack power or allow for health regeneration. 2B starts with limited memory space and each chip has a cost, so early on I found myself unequipping non-critical UI elements to squeeze in that last upgrade chip. Memory space can be purchased easily enough, but even when it’s maxed out there will never be enough room to equip everything. I always had to weigh my priorities, though the ability to save different chipsets suited to different situations helped mitigate that.
If it wasn’t obvious, being a newcomer to the series didn’t hinder my appreciation for Nier: Automata’s story in the slightest. It’s true that the deeper you dig into the game’s lore (and even visual symbolism) the more everything from Drakengard to Nier comes into play, but Nier: Automata is self-contained enough that it fills in most of its biggest holes through endings and assorted unlockable bits. Even with a few pieces of the puzzle missing it does something very different, and very interesting.
It helped that I loved being in that world too, not least of all because of its music. Nier: Automata’s score is excellent, but it also adapts — instrumental and vocal mixes of the various songs interwove depending on what I was doing and where I was going. While initiating a hack, strings and drums start to subtly blur into blips and bloops, anticipating the full transition that would come if I succeed. When I ducked out of a crowded area into a calm passageway the vocals might drop out and leave me with a haunting tune that would swell back up once I slipped out again. Sometimes the surreal lyrics would instead shed their backing instruments as I moved between zones, following me like a ghost for a stretch before the next area’s theme would inevitably overtake them.
Nier: Automata does a lot and only seems to suffers for it in a handful of very small ways, the most glaring of which are its many invisible walls. Though you can double jump and mantle your way across the obstacle-riddled environments, there’s little distinction between climbable surfaces and unclimbable barriers even in areas that look like they’re absolutely built to be scaled. Its maps are filled with secretive nooks and crannies which makes the inevitable backtracking more tolerable, but actually accessing those spaces can be deeply frustrating, and the cumbersome 3D world map doesn’t offer much help in that regard. :)

Warning: the following review may contain spoilers.
Warrior Within has quite a mixed opinion among fans of the Prince of Persia franchise. The negative arguments have some rational points such as the ridiculously skimpy outfits of the two major female characters and, at times, impossible to control camera angles. However there are many arguments made as "negatives" despite the fact that they are completely subjective.
The dramatic shift in tone from Sands to WW can definitely be unappealing for those who enjoyed the more colorful and lighter aspects of Sands but this is based on opinion, rather than based on quality. The darker and more pale colored environments in WW are actually done quite well as they enforce a more negative attitude without being outright depressing or boring. This is the reaction that the player is supposed to experience, so saying that the dark environments are "bad" for not being lighter or more pretty seems illogical. There are also plenty of areas to explore, each with their own theme and personality (so to speak) i.e. the hanging gardens and mechanical tower, but always adhering to the theme of appearing pale and unwelcoming.
Another misrepresented point of the game is backtracking - while Sands was a constant adventure that continually sent the prince through various areas and rarely revisiting the same location twice, WW features quite a bit of going back and forth through familiar locations. This is often cited as "lazy" level design or "lack of creativity" but misses the point that the level designers wanted the world to feel real. I admire the idea of constantly finding new areas to explore but half way through Sands I started to wonder if I was still in Azad or not, WW continues to send you to new places for the majority of the game but also tried to combine these newer areas from the later period of the story into the locations previously visited as it makes the game world feel connected. I must also point out the difference between time periods (past and present) as it allowed the level designers to create two distinct environments in the same location; the distopian present and the glorious past. An idea that I very much admire.
Finally we come to one of the biggest issues of WW - the prince. Many fans hated the way his character had changed, going from a young, happy go lucky joker to a more grizzled, vulgar and take no prisoners soldier, stating that they come off as two completely different people. The problem with this argument is that in the game world it has been seven years since Sands. Anyone reading this can look back at their own lives from seven years ago and see differences between their behaviour before and now and they didn't have an invincible beast trying to kill them for all that time. If we also bear in mind the dilemma the prince faces in WW - NO hope, you WILL die, you CANNOT change your fate, it's all very negative and this all rubs off onto the character. He despises the fate he has been handed for a mistake he had no way of forseeing, he aggresively disregards the warnings of failure and is determined to free himself from this living nightmare. To be perfectly honest, the prince comes off as more of an anti-hero; a very selfish individual, willing to step over people he grows to care for (i.e. Kaileena) and takes no consideration of the consequence of his actions should he succeed in removing the Sands of Time from ever existing. It would be very easy to change the story so that the prince is a villain due to just how selfish his actions are, however, I personally like this anti-hero character. Rather than trying to "save the day" like a good generic hero always does, this hero is only interested in saving himself. It's a very interesting concept but, as mentioned before, can be very unappealing for fans who enjoyed the personality displayed in Sands.
Moving over to the more positive elements, or at least the positives that haven't already been mentioned...
Combat has been expanded from the previous game, allowing for the prince to make better use out of two weapons, or opting to use one weapon, as well as adding newer ways to interact with the surrounding areas and enemies during combat. The fighting system has lost it's smoother, more fluid movements from Sands but takes on a more aggressive and in-your-face approach, which is fitting for the mood of the game. I won't go too far into details but players willing to experiment and play around with the various attacks, counter-attacks, vaulting, running and jumping will have a lot of fun finding the various ways to slice their enemies in half or perform decapitations. Or at least I did.
The story has some questionable points if you look closely enough, but, at it's heart, is coherent, consistent with its facts and, while some plot points are more than a little obvious, the overall journey is quite unpredictable and leaves the player questioning if the prince will actually succeed, that is until you realize that it makes for a pretty crappy ending if you ultimately fail your mission.
Final Verdict: Warrior Within is a good game, fans of it's predecessor should at least consider trying it out but bear in mind that the two have very differnt personalities. If you don't like dark, gritty and violent then this is NOT the game for you. Much like its predecessor, this game has aged remarkably well.  It started off rather slow, but once I became familiar with the combat system I found it hard to tear myself away from the computer.  The combat system is a major improvement over the original and places a great deal of freedom at your fingertips.  Moreover, it fosters a blend of action and exploration to keep you interested and to keep the game fast-paced.  When the game is at its best, you'll find yourself catapulting from acrobatic duels into high-adrenaline chase sequences through beautiful Gothic-style ruins.  I recommend it, especially for the price.
There is one caveat worth mentioning.  This game is a significant departure from the original, especially with regard to its ambiance and storyline.  Warrior Within tries too hard to be dark and edgy, often to the point of ridiculousness.  That's a minor critique though, and if you can look past the stylistic flaws, I think you'll find that this game has aged gracefully and serves as a worthy successor to The Sands of Time.

NieR elevates game design. This is one of the finest games to date, technical shortcomings of the PC port notwithstanding (Google: FAR). It does many things, and does them all well. It deliberately subverts expectations, but remains invitingly familiar. It's a polished brawler, danmaku, robotron, role-playing game; its disparate parts cohere surprisingly well. First and foremost, it's consitently rewarding, engaging, and fun to play. It happens to be one of the most intelligent games available, an ostensibly postmodern bricolage (requiring multiple 'playthroughs', each of which is substantially different) undergirded by a shockingly redemptive metanarrative crystalised in what may be games' best and most self-aware synergy of message and medium, during a closing crescendo rivalled only by the phantom button-press of Brothers: a tale of two sons. NieR wears its cultured creativity lightly; this is the opposite of pretentious indie grad-school didacticism. It's brilliant, but doesn't mind if you think it isn't. It just wants you to be happy. Buy this game.

I give this a recommended because I can tell that the developer really cares about the product, and it seems like a tremendous amount of work and love was put into this game. However, there are quite a few blatant problems that hold the game back in some areas. I'll be going in depth on them, but honestly, if you like quirky action platformers, pick it up when it's on sale.
First off, while I'm sure this is rectified with controller support, there are too many buttons to play the game smoothly with a keyboard. I hardly ever used the "dash" move, simply because it felt to unintuitive with the keyboard. I don't have a controller to play with, and it seems like this was designed with controller support in mind, so take this one with a grain of salt.
The music ranges from forgettable to annoying, and it seems like that mainly has to do with the "retro" style of it. If it used synthetic instruments instead, I feel like it would be more bearable at parts. But as it stands, certain areas made me mute the game due to the soundtrack giving me a headache. Another minor nitpick, but it seems to loop at weird areas that make it super noticable.
There are no lives in the game. When you die, you lose one of the extra hearts you may have earned and start back at the beginning of the current screen you're on. While this seems fine at first, there are some parts where the screen goes on for way too long, coupled with one hit kill spikes, which gets old fast. Speaking of the spikes, they appear often in levels, but only some of them actually kill you in one hit, and they don't look any different from the others. I feel if they each had a respective color, it would definitely be better in terms of design.
There are quite a few areas where you swing on vines in the game. While it seems like a fun idea, the vine swings automatically, and you can only jump off of it at the apex of the swing. I've also encountered a glitch several times where  the game auto locks me onto a vine for a split second, and then puts me back to where I was when I was jumping, but having lost all the momentum from the jump, leading to a frustrating death.
In addition, the screen scrolls in a way where you are typically vulnerable to obstacles before you can react to them. There are also places where you are expected you make jumps into areas that you can't fully see, with the OHK spikes on the ground. I feel like a lot of deaths in this game are due to no part by the player. While I tend to be a patient gamer, I feel like this would make quite a few players not pick this game up.
Most basic enemies are simple and easy to work around, which is a shame because if this game was more focused on complex enemy design instead of platforming, I feel like a lot of the problems would be solved. The action parts are truly where this game shines. The bosses, while challenging, are still very fun and interesting. Being able to throw a spear and stick it to a wall to use as a platform is done geniously. The shoot-um-up segment was great.  If this game ever gets a sequel, I hope it takes a more "Metroidvania" style approach. I feel like the combat system and control feel would be greatly suited to a more action-adventure exploration focused environment, instead of a platformed with some action sprinkled in.
Basically, here's what I feel could be improved on
1.) Fix the vines. For comparison, if it was more akin to the rope swinging in The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker, it would feel smoother.
2.) On longer screens, a checkpoint would be nice. Even if it's out of the way, and a challenge to get to itself.
3.) Make it obvious which spikes kill you in one hit and which ones just harm you. A simple palette  swap for one is all it needs.
4.) The screen should scroll faster
5.) The player should be able to hold down to recenter the camera and see what it below. Instead of hitting down to jump off certain platforms, change it to down and jump.
Also, I just want to give the game major props for the atmosphere. It's very subtle, but it works sooooooo well.
Like I said before, this is clearly a well made game, but if I was a teacher, I would put a "Needs Improvement" on the top of this assignment in big red ink. For what it is, $7 seems like a tad too much. I haven't beaten it, but I think that if you can get it on sale for less than five, that's probably about what I'd say to spend on it. Keep in mind that this is all meant to be constructive criticism. I took the time to write this review not out of spite, but because I feel like this is a good game that could be amazing with a little fine tuning.

Generally speaking this is a derivative platformer with excellent, detailed pixel art work. You have seen everything in it before, but that being said, it covers a wide base of platforming ideas and never overuses any of them.
+High quality pixel artwork with lots of care and work.
+Above average movement options - combining the dash and double-jump means the game can through some interesting platforming at you
+Good variety in enemies and bosses - derivative, but there's new stuff in nearly every section
-Game is over-tuned in some sections, some enemies take too many hits and the game's difficulty curve is bizarre
-Music is truly dreadful
-Incredibly, unbelievably pointless upgrade/currency system. It's a small minus since it has no impact on gameplay but it's just baffling. You can save up bones to buy items, but then you die and they're gone. You can search out secrets, but then you die and they're gone. And you WILL die unless you're experienced at the game ... At which point why do you need the items, since you're not dying?
Anyway if you're into somewhat hard "flavor" platformers, I think this one will give you a couple hours of enjoyment.

This is a speed-running, platformer puzzle game.  Each level has some endpoint you must reach by using color-coded switches and platforms.  (The colors are supposed to indicate opposite polarities.)  Each level also has 3 collectibles to find, which are always positioned in some out-of-the-way location to increase your completion time.  Surprisingly, there is no reward nor punishment related to how quickly you finish each level, so there's not really a point to actually try for the speed-running.  The puzzles are okay, but certainly not comparable to Portal as this game's steam page claims.  I found the game moderately enjoyable, but it's very short with less than 1.5 hours playtime (and that includes retrying a most levels for faster times).  The game could certainly use a lot more levels.  In fact, it's perfect for Workshop content, yet there is no level maker.  There are a few bugs with platforms and the small blocks used to activate switches, but nothing game breaking.  I'd like to also play the co-op levels, but the game is sadly local-multiplayer only.
Ultimately, I feel like the game failed at nearly everything it set out to do.  You get a handful of mediocre puzzles that you can complete in one sitting, and that's it.  Not a bad game, but not one I'd recommend.

Pros:
The first month that you'll be playing this game, you'll be nothing but amazed. No other game I've played makes me feel like an adventurer like this one does. The music is engaging and powerful and I find myself many times staying on the main menu just to listen to the Skyrim theme. The game makes you feel like you're needed in this world. There is a quest in every single corner of the game and you can never do them all. If you want an engaging, fun and overall great rpg experience then this game is for you. Here is a list of a few things that are good about this game:
-There is always something to do
-You are presented with a huge world and it is up to you how you want to approach it
-Awesome DLC
-Mods that make the game even bigger or introduce you to entirely new expiriences
-Awesome music
-Improved graphics
-Fun quests and storylines
Cons:
While there are a lot of things that make this game great there are some things you should consider before buying it. First of all,
and it has no problem reminding you with things such as broken quests and glitches. Second of all, the game is a buggy mess. You dont always encounter bugs but when you do, you start questioning your existence. What Bethesda did with the release of this game, was just slightly improve the graphics of the old game (something that could already be done using mods) and leave the rest untouched. These bugs can be fixed using mods that are easily accessible to the player, but it's still a shame. Third of all, in the beginning of this review, I mentioned that in the first month everything will be great. But as you sink your teeth into this game, you start seeing just how repetitive it is. You can't really compare this game to newer rpgs.
But in the end, every single hour I spent in that world was 100% worth it and I'd be lying if I said that it wasn't one of the best games I've ever played.

It may have taken a while for me to come back to writing but between very hard achievements in Moai IV and the freaking Beat All Developer's time in 12 Labours, I may have put some pleasuring hobbies of mine on the side. One of them is playing Artifex Mundi's game.
Even if here, they didn't develop it. However, I already knew about it when I was researching the rest of the series The Secret Order (also published by Artifex here).
When a colleague of yours found a mysterious artifact related to Ariadne, Theseus and The Minotaur, you're thrown into a world of secret sect, Ariadne's lineage and a hidden island.
Given my studies background (archaelogy, main interest in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome), you bet that any Greek myth in a hidden object game is increasing my eagerness to play it. And while I liked the first part of the game, I don't know why but the second part was less... interesting. I suppose that I got a problem with the end which was anti-climatic. No sect member to pursue you, no word on how your friend had his soul captured... And even the bonus chapter is quite strange as I can't understand how it can be included in the story (as an epilogue or as a cut chapter). And I was probably expecting more ruins really related to the Minotaur. Because seriously, when I saw the background of the credits, I was disappointed not to have seen that kind of landscape.
If the gameplay is quite standard (clear hidden objects scenes, use items, find them, solve puzzles), there is a little twist that was for once well-used: the Ariadne's thread. Indeed, there are three powers, which are acquired through time. The first one is present at the beginning: melting golden objects. The second one is ressucitating petrified creatures (by Medusa) and the third one is to dissipate evil illusions.
The hidden objects scenes are varied: shaped, list of words, interactions. But this is not the part of the gameplay I'm disappointed in. It's mainly the fact that you're in front of minigames and some of them aren't explained at all unless you hit a button to show the instructions. I wish it was explained from the beginning: I didn't understand that I was in front of a memory for example.
The graphics are good, though Daniel, a friend of yours, had a weird head. However, the rest is good. And I liked the soundtrack.
I'm going to say that for once, some achievements are quite different from the usual ones. The eight minigames under 60 seconds was quite the dreadful one but I got it normally, as I never realized that indeed, many of them can be done under that time limit. It still doesn't mean that the absence of the explanations was justified.
I've probably put high expectations on this game and I found myself disappointed in the story and in some aspects of it. I don't say that it's a bad game but seriously, Sunward, the developer, did well with the Secret Order and perhaps that they wanted to do something different and lost themselves in the game.
It's not a favorite but it's still decent, so acquire it through a bundle or through a discount.

Before I go any further with this review I’m going to say flat-out that this is a very good game and if you enjoy hidden object games, then buy it.
offers a ton of variety with its gameplay, great graphics and the story isn’t that bad either; it’s a fun experience for new players to the genre as well as old fans. Before knowing anything about the game I was drawn in by its title, as a fan of mythology the prospect of delving into a world of ancient Greek fables fascinated me. In truth, I didn’t know too much about the legend of the Minotaur until playing this game.
The game starts off with a brief and very sanitized version of the Minotaur legend, leaving out anything that may not be family-friendly and also keeping things simple. This overview is narrated by Pamela, the protagonist of the game in a museum showing guest an item called Ariadne’s Thread. Things soon go south as hooded men attack, later revealed to be part of a cult trying to revive the Minotaur. Pamela ends up being the Chosen One, a descendant of Ariadne, who aided the hero Theseus in defeating the Minotaur so she can use the magic of the thread. She ends up traveling to mystical locations on a mission to stop the Minotaur’s revival and save the stolen souls used as sacrifices to him. There is a lot of action here with plenty of magic and mysticism as well, my only real complaint is that Pamela isn’t very well fleshed out as a character and the Minotaur isn’t a very scary threat, the cult is more dangerous and they only show up twice.
What I enjoyed most was the gameplay here, there are plenty of hidden object scenes and I can’t recall many (if any) second visits to the same scene. There are also a good amount of puzzles, most of which aren’t too difficult. What stood out was the variety in terms of hidden item scenes, instead of most of them just giving you a list of items to find each time they switched it up. Some gave you shadows of the objects you had to find, others simply told you to interact with objects to solve a bit of a puzzle, almost. As mentioned before, you also have Ariadne’s Thread and its magic is useful to progress in the story, it lets you melt things and also revive people who have been turned to stone and its final power up breaks through illusions. The game offers three difficulty levels as well as a custom option to tweak the game experience to what you were prefer. You have an in game map that allows you to teleport and a useful inventory system with interactive objects that sometimes require extra steps to be taken before you can use them, like a box that must be opened or a corkscrew you need to put together.
The game has graphics on par with most other titles in this genre. The scenes are well done, colorful backgrounds and well-drawn characters. The animation is smooth, characters walk and talk well in engaging cutscenes. You won’t have to worry about squinting, the items in the hidden object scenes are easy on the eyes and aren’t a chore to search for either. The audio is good, the music fits the story well and the voice acting for the most part is well done. My only issue was with Hephaestus, his audio level was lower than the other characters when he spoke. Also, sometimes the audio quality in general in the game got really low when you went from one area to another.
is a very good game, why are you still reading this, go buy it! With a refreshing amount of variety to its hidden object scenes coupled with lovely aesthetics, this game offers a few hours of entertainment with its main storyline as well as a fun bonus chapter. There are a lot of Steam achievements to hunt after as well as trading cards to collect adding more value to the game. The year is 1888, and archaeologists have discovered an amazing relic - the actual thread Theseus used to find his way back out of the Labyrinth after slaying the minotaur! Naturally, the discovery draws the attention of an evil cult of minotaur-worshippers, and it's up to the player to avoid their schemes, find the hidden isle of the Greek Gods, and prevent the resurrection of a certain bull-headed monster who has already been mentioned twice in this paragraph, and a third would probably be excessive. It's a crash course in mythological monsters packed alongside some great art and solid puzzles.
Now, on to the Hidden Object Criteria!
Criteria 1: To what degree do the puzzle screens look like a thrift store vomited on my monitor?
It's not a problem in the least. Logic and style are the buzzwords underlying the game's HOS design. While the screens themselves aren't the most intricate or beautifully-drawn, they fit perfectly within the game world. Whether the player is exploring ancient ruins or a cluttered blacksmith's shop, every time they're asked to search for hidden object, it's in a place that make perfect sense. The screens are also completely fair. No colour or gravity cheating here - they even go easy on asking players to find images of items rather than the items themselves. The end result are screens that are perhaps a little on the easy side as HOS go, but always a blast to play.
Criteria 2: Are the searches justified by the premise/story?
Almost completely. This is where the game really shines. While a couple of 12:1 screens make an appearance, by and large the player only has mini-puzzles and construction screens to work with, and wonderfully-built ones at that. The mini-puzzles are especially well thought out - the player is told how many 'interactions' are left before they can find the item they're looking for, and then they simply have to figure out which items on the screen can be used to pry open one container to find a secret emblem to open a safe to grab a knife... when these screens are well-done, they encapsulate the whole graphic-adventure experience in tiny slices, and this is a perfect example of developers knowing what they're doing.
Criteria 3: How well do the various puzzles and object searches meld together to form a coherent whole?
There are many familiar puzzles in this one - sliding blocks, chain linking, a maze to run marbles through. They probably make more sense in the context of this game than any other. Set in the millieu of the Greek Pantheon, Endless Legends has the player at one point traverse the labyrinth crafted by the actual Daedalus - so of course there are going to be some elaborate locks lying around. This is where that concept originates from, after all. The game splits up its journey into a series of 3-4 screen areas, each one involving a different mythological creature which needs to be helped or defeated, and this contained design helps keep the player focused on the task at hand, as well as moving the story along at a good clip. There's never a moment for the player to wonder what the dozen items in their inventory for, and it's almost inconceivable that anyone would ever have to check their map to see where to go next.
With great production values, an intriguing story, and wonderful puzzles, The Minotaur's Curse is a great jumping-off point for a potential series. This trip into antiquity feels fresh - while ancient evil returning to bedevil a chosen one may not be the most original premise, the developers manage to find new twists to the story with a surprisingly faithful presentation of Greek mythology, along with some surprising new gameplay mechanics. The game's breakneck pace ensures that players will constantly have new puzzles and HOSs at them, turning it into a thrilling ride which doesn't let up for the whole two-hour playtime.

When I bought this game way back in '09 my first impression was pretty negative. Here I was playing my GTA's and Left 4 Deads, and this game found it's way into my library. It certainly wasn't pretty, the story was ridiculous and the voice acting was cheesy. GTA IV had made me expect gritty realism and graphics.
But the more I played the more I realised just how brilliant this game is. The story finds a perfect balance between humour and seriousness, something later games in the series failed to do. It's humour is more subtle than the stupidity of 3 and 4. And the voice acting I once thought was cheesy is just perfect and includes such talents as Michael Dorn (Worf), Yuri Lowenthal, Keith David (!), Phil La Marr, Eliza Dushku, Neil Patrick Harris and Jaime Pressly. The 'cockney' voice acting by Charles Shaughnessy (5th Baron Shaughnessy I should say) is sublime and adds a whole new comedic twist to the game. Charles Shaughnessy was replaced for 3 and 4 and whilst the replacement does a good job, he just doesn't get it the same way Charlie does.
The gameplay is crisp and shooting feels amazing, no auto aim here. The driving is very arcade and might not be to some peoples tastes but you get used to it. The missions are varied and range from stealing radioactive goo for it to be tatooed on to a rival gang boss, to defending your HQ after being spiked with something potent, to just a good old katana battle.
Where this game truly shines is it's exploration. Whilst the map is obviously not as big as games these days, it is choc full of things to do, side missions, assasinations, bodyguarding, shopping, drug dealing, gang wars, Fuzz (where you are basically filming an episode of COPS), ho-ing minigames, stick ups and the list goes on. Even after hundreds of hours I was still finding secret locations and things I didn't know were there, the first time since San Andreas a game could still suprise me after that much time.
This game is still one of my all time favourites and deserves more recognition, when people think of Saints Row they usually refer to 3 and 4. This is the one they should be playing.

I believe Saints Row 2 to the the pinnacle of the SR series, and there's many things in which games these days, especially the proceeding games, should strive to contain.
The open form of how you can tackle all the different factions, which diminished somewhat in SR3, allows you to play the game at your own pace, and progress all parts of the story equally if you so wish, or power through each story individually.

Special bonuses for performing feats in the game, and getting bonuses for completing the side quests makes you want to do all the challenges and missions. SR3 took this away and made the majority of these bonuses buyable after certain levels.
Another thing which I love about this game, which irks me in SR3 and SR4, is the car customisation, more specifically, the colours for the cars.
SR3 and 4, all the colours are generic. Orange 3, Blue 7, etc.
SR2, all the colours have names, all the colours stand out. And the gold in the game actually looks gold, not bright yellow like in it's successors.
The game does have some bugs, many of which are to do with cars (most crashes were from trying to enter cars), but overall, the bugs aren't that numerous or bad,
I highly recommend Saints Row 2 for anyone looking to play a fun Sandbox "Crime sim" that isn't afraid to make fun of itself and it's genre.

My favorite Star Wars game ever (despite it being reviled by many critics as one of the worst SW games ever), haven't played the Steam version yet, but I've had the physical version since I was like 15. Get it while you can in the Humble Star Wars Bundle 2. Admittedly, though, it is one of those games you will either love or hate. It is basically a grand, realtime 4X strategy game set after the destruction of the first death star. You have the whole galaxy and all the powers of either the Rebellion or Empire at your fingertips. It is a blast managing your agents (there are dozens and dozens of named major and minor characters for each faction) and sending them on missions, deploying fleets and armies, managing production, exploring new worlds, balancing diplomacy, research the list goes on. The interface is a bit archaic, but once you get the hang of it, it really is easy and makes a lot of sense, unfortunately, the real time 3D space battles never had good graphics even when the game came out, still they are satisfying and were way ahead of their time.
The game features tons of Stars Wars lore nods, including
legends content and characters. The game is relatively slow paced (compared to other SW RTS like Empire at War), but really focuses on large scale strategy and learning the various intricate systems (economics, military, diplomacy, production, espionage, research, etc). So, if you want to try this game, be ready to learn (I recommend reading the manual or a quick guide on the internet before jumping in). If the game has some weak points, they are largely the failures of the AI (which is nonetheless fun to play against, but can be easily exploited if you discover its weaknesses), and a few minor stupid rules that you can fairly easily avoid (such as sending a character on a mission that fails will send them retreating back to their point of origin and not to the nearest friendly system).
My favorite part of the game definitely has to be how all the systems interact and how interesting situations emerge regularly. Bombarding a system here might hamper diplomatic relations in the sector if your moron admiral causes some collateral damage, maybe even causing an uprising on a garrisoned world. Perhaps your stormtroopers capture a rebel spy who provides the location of Leia Organa on a diplomatic mission to a neutral world, time to send Darth Vader and a few cronies to capture her, or send out the Star Destroyers and hope to catch her in the net of a blockade? Imperial probe droid locates the hidden rebel base in the outer rim, time to evacuate it in fear of an Imperial task force to follow, or stand and fight? Form a plot to kidnap the Emporeror? Don't care about capturing a planet but want to deny your enemy use of it, time for a base delta zero (or maybe send your newly armed and operational Death Star)? Luke Skywalker finds one of your characters to be force sensitive, time to send them to a secluded world for Jedi training? The staggering amount of emergentant possibilities are just awesome in this game.
Overall, like I said, this is either a game you will love or hate. If it sounds enticing, give it a try, I think you'll be glad you did. If dealing with an archaic interface and learning some intricate systems that will require reading a manual sounds like a slog, just run the other way.

Front loaded TL;DR:
Verdict: Wait before buying. Lots of potential, needs polish. While the game can be a lot of fun, that fun is weighted pretty heavily toward the early game. Once the thrill of exploration and expansion wear off, the other two X's get kinda sloggy. Some of the core systems are kinda opaque, and others just make no damn sense.
To collect and expand on what a lot of people have been saying in the reviews, much of which I've observed for myself:
There is very little nuance or strategy in exploiting the territory you've already grabbed, and static fortifications are too weak to be meaningfull. As a result, your choices on how to manage your non-colonized worlds are very narrow. Build whatever extractor the game lets you build, slap a defense station around the star so that an invading AI wastes time poping it (it'll put up no meaningfull resistance, but will pull them out of position to move to the next system, buying you time to gather your blob of doom), and move on. Most of the time they'll just skip straight to your inhabited systems anyway, so defense in depth isn't really a defense. Honestly, the only way I've found to add more strategic depth to this is to force everyone to use old school hyper lanes, such as in the Space Empires series. Having actual choke points means that geography *matters*.
Even your colonized worlds get a simple optimization based on natural resources and such: because of the communal nature of food and mineral supplies, there is absolutely no need for any planet to look after itself. Exploit the natural tile resources as you have the population to do so. Speaking of which...
Unbalanced racial/societal traits. Seriously, population growth speed is king. Your planets only produce on tiles that are inhabited, so get that population up there as quick as you can. Oh, you swung all your points to get a cumulative 35% bonus to mineral production? That's nice, I have twice as much population by year 20, so I get twice as much EVERYTHING. You have a 50% bonus to ground combat? Great, i just bombarded your army out of existance from orbit with my ENORMOUS FLEET. Seriously, having more pop means expanding faster, being able to exploit more, and having a bigger fleet to go exterminate with. That's three of the 4 "X's" right there. The rest of the bonuses to everything else are too small to make a real difference. The only real exceptions are bonuses to leaders (especially longevity, you spend less political influence on leaders, meaning more for politics) and core sector systems (which let you directly control X number of systems without having to let the AI manage it). Oh, there are no more planets to colonize/terraform, and I'm at max population for the rest? Guess what, I've got techs that let me edit my species' traits! Let's remove that no longer needed pop growth and spend the points on something else instead. There is literally no downside to this.
Combat is basically Blob vs Blob. Your weapon selection is meaningfull, in that you can observe how your opponent builds their ships and retrofit yours to rock-paper-scissors them to death. On the other hand, your control over actual combat is obtuse, arcane, and basically breaks down to the fact that how many of which ships you build determine how the blob behaves. War goals is another problem. No explanation for how it works, but i've had some weird♥♥♥♥♥♥happen. Landed troops on an enemy's homeworld and officially occupied it, only to have them turn around and surrender it to another nation's control as part of their peace agreement. Seriously, my fleet darkens your sky, my soldiers patrol your streets, and my merchant marine is feeding your population: It's not your planet anymore.
Diplomacy is basically pre-determined. Other race's opinion of you is measured on a +/-1000 scale, and the ethics and form of your government are overriding concerns. I've had other races start off at -1000 opinion of me because of this. That's not recoverable. Even a -100, which happens fairly often, is beyond your ability to fix. Your ability to get others to trust you is soft capped at +50 points, iirc, with a hard cap of +100. Getting it up that high takes decades, and you *START* with a -10 to -20 handicap (that wears off slowly) when you first make contact. You had better hope to whatever God your people worship that you have something in common with your neighbors. What makes it worse is that there seems, in my observation, to be a weight to the selection of ethics. The AI likes to pick ethics that have high opinion modifies like spiritualist which HATE materialists (and to a lesser extent, anyone who is not also spiritual) or xenophobes, who hate everyone. I very rarely meet any pacifistic xenophiles, but i've met oodles of militaristic xenophobic dictatorships.
The game positively oozes charm and style, and is leaking atmosphere from every seam (sorry, sci-fi joke). The problem is that there are so many places where you simply have no control, either from a lack of understanding of the system involved, or simply because there are no meaningful choices to make.

This game has given, and is still giving me countless hours of fun. The different government types, and their respective ascension perks. Help make each of them feel and play different. Add to that the fact that Paradox is constantly updating, and expanding on their game, and the replayability is exceptional. It's really easy to get into as well. And the tutorial (Unless you play a Gestalt Consciousness, in which there is no tutorial) is really helpful, as later on in the game, many new things seem to come at you at once. And the tutorials genuinely help.
There is no campaign, something you should be aware of. There is no real "race" either, as you design your own, completely from scratch (it's a very easy, and intuitive process) You can adjust almost everything. You can even write a short bio for your species (Hooray roleplay!)
The only downside is, I quite often lose track of time, making me grumpy and sleepy in the morning.
I definitely recommend this game.

When i first saw Stellaris advertised on various different media platforms whether it was on let's plays from YouTube to actually seeing the game while browsing through the steam store i never battered so much as an eye lid. Nearly 500 hours of play time later here i am writing this review on what i personally think about the game. This is the first 4X game i have ever played and i have to say it is one of my all time favorites.
Stellaris has both a sandbox feel to it combined with a deep story element built to it's core. Starting a new game from creating your own alien civilization, empire type, ship designs, language, everything to make your species unique is there. However what differs from most other games is the way you write your own story while playing.
What ever direction you take with your empire can drastically change the outcome towards the end such as, driving other alien races to extinction, subjugating empires to building a mighty federation to ensure the survival of your own species. I love how paradox has implemented the various anomalies, precursor events, leviathans and ancient fallen empires, one word i can only describe these is enigmatic.
Ofcourse like many games there are bugs, unbalancing issues etc but it is to be expected with most games and Paradox has always tried to release patches to fix them as quickly as possible but it has never put me off from playing. This is the first review i have ever written out of the many games i have played over the years and look forward to seeing what the future brings for it.

Here are some pros and cons I've encountered before I get into a written review.
Pros: Amazing for couch use, but I've found it also functions well at a desk.
Semi-good battery life.
Good button layout, although console users will say the button pad should be above the right analogue (or in this case trackpad)
The paddles were amazing
Community templates allow you to just take the lazy route and use other people's configurations.
Customizability and per-game customizability is unfathomably good
Very ergonomic design
Trackpads are very precise
Haptic feedback feels good
The weight is really well balanced.
It's durable.
Plug-and-play ease of use. Seriously. Plug it in, click Ok, wait a little, and get started.
It powers up and connects with a push of a button, and almost no delay.
The (completly optional) wire for the controller is nice and long for most situations.
Price is only 50 USD
Triggers feel AMAZING to pull, and duel stage triggers makes it much better for racing.
And now, regrettably, some cons.
Bad choice of plastic used, feels cheap.
Haptic feedback is surprisingly loud. Sounds like a giga counter, I normally just turn it off.
the gyro is.... working but not exactly the best.
Paddles are massive and are right in the spot everyone grips down on during intense fights, which can cost you a victory if you accidentally squeeze and throw a grenade.
Wireless range can be a pro or a con, I'd say it's a con for shortness. This won't be an issue for most people, but I have a massive home theater setup.
I'm not trying to at all judge the product by it's box but it was a slightly underwhelming box.
I mean, they've been hyping this thing up for over a year, and the box is paperboard with ink on it.
For some people with particularly shaped hands, the controller's far bottom part of the handle sticks into the ball of their hand and hurts them. I never had this issue but I've heard about it.
Now that those are out of the way, let me get onto my "wall of text" review.
The Steam Controller has been an all-in-all good experience for me. Though I have encountered some issues with things like Portal 2 or Half Life where walk controls don't work properly.
My favorite game to play with the Steam Controller is probably One Finger Death Punch, because of the simple controls (I recommend binding triggers both soft and full pull to x and b so you don't have to use the x and b buttons)
It's one of the easiest controllers to setup i've ever used. You just plug it in, get a prompt to install some software, you get recommended to launch big pictue mode, and you're done.
If you're playing a certain game which you want to control a certain way, you can easily rebind EEEVERYTHING on a per-game basis.
The trackpads.... definitely took some getting used to.
By the way, both of the big black round things are trackpads, even the "D-pad" as it may look. It's still a trackpad, but with D-Pad shaped lines in it.
I'll go ahead and say this, web browsing is mediocre at best.
Typing experience was surprisingly good, after only someodd 20 minutes of typing I was already able to type at a reasonable speed, without too many typos.
I've come to using the box it came in as a carrying case because as of current, I am travelling a lot and I normally do bring things like this with me.
I got my Steam Controller on Nov. 10, have been using it plenty and on a daily basis and surprisingly the batteries are still going strong, which I found rather surprising.
A good way to save power in the long run is to turn off all haptic feedback. I just don't like it at all, so I don't care.
The Haptic Feedback is one of my main complaints, basically, if it's on low you just hear a mind numbing ticking, like a giga counter, every time you move your trackpad.
on Medium, it's just louder, more intrusive, and I still can't feel anything
And then there's the high setting. High means its very loud but at least you can feel it. too bad you'll be deaf and poor after spending all that money on really nice noise cancelling headphones to avoid losing your mind.
the gyro is pretty good, but not the best.
it CAN be used as a racing wheel, but I would recommend investing a good 70-100 dollars in an actual racing wheel if you intend to need one.
You can also aim with it in first person shooter games which I quite like.
The buttons are apparently slightly smaller than normal for console users, but I completely love the size.
The dongle is semi-compact and durable.
And again, the price point is a massive reason to buy.
50 dollars, incase you've forgotten.
In short, Yes, I recommend this piece of hardware to most people, but it's NOT meant to replace your mouse and keyboard for competetive play. You're going to be at a severe disadvantage in things like CS:GO. I've found it functions best in casual, or at least singleplayer games.

This is a positive review of the Steam Controller (SC). Console gamers are couch gamers. They want to be comfortable when they play, and they just want to get into the game asap. PC gamers don't mind sitting at a desk in order to tweak the game so that they have the best graphics, and the best control setup via mouse and keyboard. The SC is for PC gamers that strive to be couch gamers. The SC is the most customizable controller in existance today. Every button, every touchpad, can be customized to any keyboard or mouse button. It has an acelleromiter that lets you use the SC like a Wii-mote, and there are deeper options to have multiple controller layouts pre-mapped to switch at the touch or hold of a button. This customizability is the SC's greatest draw, and drawback. Every single game needs to be remapped from scratch. However, the interface to do so is very intuitive and easy. There is no tutorial, but many reviewers have good tips on youtube, and you can also download other people's layouts. The learning curve is steep, but if you can PC game with a thumb operated trackball, you can use the SC.

The hacking mechanic though can get really stale and repetitive after a while but does sometimes offer some insane easter eggs and visuals!!

Port: DO NOT USE MOUSE AND KEYBOARD!!!! Like the dark souls series and most other games that come out of Japan PC doesnt really get the best support when it comes to controls. Please ignore the low playtime. I own this game for the Playstation 2, & from what I've seen, this version is reletively unchanged.
So yeah. 2nd game in the prince of persia trilogy, & considered the worst of the 3 for being buggy, having the game being more combat focused, & turning prince into a gruff ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. But, I like these changes. I like the darker tone, I prefer the game being more focused on combat, & I like princes new personality.
Story: 7/10
The first game had you trying to undo what the prince did: Opening the sands of time with the dagger of time. In this game: the prince is being chased by the unstoppable guardian of time: The Dahaka. The prince is being chased by this creature, because when he opened the sands, he should've died, he however, did not. Because of this, he has disrupted the timeline & must be killed to restore it. The princes job is to somehow change his fate. Okay, pretty interesting. Its not 10/10 5 STARZ, but its not too shabby.
Music: 9/10
HOLLY SHEET METUL!! Most of this games soundtrack is heavy metal, which I really like! It fits this games darker tone, & they all sound fantastic. The main song of the game is "I stand alone" by Godsmack. an instrumental version of the song plays during certain parts of the game, & the regular version during a few of the games trailers.
Gameplay: 6/10
I like the fact that this is more combat focused than the previous game. In sands of time, you didn't have much in the way of combos, you could stab with the dagger, vault over an enemy, or do a 6 hit sword combo. thats it. this game changes that by letting you take enemy weapons & do several flashy looking combo attacks, ranging from simple spinning, to breakdancing & handstands. But the game isn't just combat. Like the previous game, it still has plenty of parkour-esque platforming sequences, & puzzle solving. some puzzles in this game are actually pretty tricky. however, like I mentioned earlier, this game is buggy. like, REALLY. buggy. there are a few that might be patched, but on the ps2, I'd vault over some enemies & teleport across the map, or I'd dodge back & start dancing on a rail (It does look pretty hilarious though.), but most of the time, I'd kill an enemy, as in, theur death animation would play, but they'd still be attacking, I couldn't kill this ghost, it just kept attacking, & as I was in a situation where I had to kill every enemy in the room, I had to reset. Thats another thing: this game uses save points. but at least they're evenly spaced apart, like after a long section, just after a key plot element, or after a Dahaka chase. Speaking of which, thats another element. The Dahaka isn't just a background character, there are certain points in the game where you will have to run from the large black monster as he tries to disintegrate you with his... tentacles...? Uh... Anyway, Running from the dahaka requires you to do a lot of platforming & fleeing, as if you are hit by the Dahaka, its a one hit kill.
Controls (Keyboard): 5/10
I had to spend quite a while re-configuring controls to find something I was comftable with, & I'm STILL not comftable with my setup. Its kinda annoying.
Controls (Gamepad): 5/10
To play with a gamepad, you also have to do a LOT of control re-configuration, but it doesn't feel awkward with a gamepad. Unfortunately, you can only use a PS3 gamepad. So if you have no gamepad, or an Xbox gamepad, you're not gonna have a fun time with this game.
Overall: 8/10
Great gameplay, more combat focused yes, but its something I prefer. Dahaka chases spice things up, & the soundtrack is PHENOMENAL. I would recommend this if you don't mind the platforming to combat change, or if you can get past glitches. If not, at least listen to this game's OST.

Star Wars: Rebellion is a classic grand strategy game that's almost as old as I am, and it shows. A word of warning; many of the negative reviews here (rightfully) deal with issues regarding graphics and loading the game, which can be resolved with a bit of tweaking.
I played this game to death as a kid, even though a lot of my success in it was the result of endless hours of trial and error; the learning curve is perhaps the steepest in video game history, there's no tutorial, and everything that's thrown at you can be overwhelming even for people who are familiar with grand strategy titles (a PDF scan of the old instruction booklet can be found in the folders, though). Likewise, while the graphics might have been cutting-edge in 1998, they're... lackluster nowadays.
But don't let either of those disuade you; Rebellion is one of the greatest strategy games ever made, and could easily give most games nowadays a run for their money. You can play as either the Rebellion or Empire with the ultimate goal of defeating the other faction and liberating/dominating the (size adjustable) galaxy.
At your disposal to accomplish this monumental and occasionally grindy goal will be a near-endless array of space ships that you can command in glorius 32-bit space combat (the spiritual successor to this game; Empire at War, would refine this aspect greatly), dozens of characters from the period ranging from everyone between Luke Skywalker to Thrawn, agents who you can send on missions to subvert the enemy or strengthen yourself, and as many armies, shield generators and Death Stars as your infastructure and technology can support. And as everything takes place in real time, you will rarely find youself without something to do if you play proactively - and the AI won't sit back on its laurels, either.
In addition to everything else this game has to offer in terms of gameplay and replayability, the game also comes complete with an encyclopedia that gives a treasure trove of information about all the units, ships, planets and characters that appear in game, all drawn from the across the entire extended universe lore available at the time. So if you also want to explore the old Star Wars EU, or just dislike Disney's, this is also the game for you.
You can also train Chewbacca as a Jedi if the game smiles on you, so there's that.
Rebellion is well worth the $6 and initial headache, and can be immensly fun, immersive and addicting if you have the patience to learn its ins and outs, and I highly recommend it for any fan of Star Wars or grand strategy.

One of my favourite games on PC; I played this for hundreds of hours when it came out, and am very glad that this version is out, working absolutely fine on my modern PC. It is dated and lacking in some respects - especially the way research works - but it is a hugely addictive grand strategy game, especially so for Star Wars fans.
Taking place just after the events of Episode IV, you command either the Rebel Alliance or Galactic Empire, seeking to defeat the opposing faction (yes, this does mean you get to tell characters such as Emperor Palpatine, Han Solo, and Darth Vader exactly what to do, as well as a host of more minor characters, such as Admiral Ackbar). Through diplomacy and military efforts you have to sway neutral planets to your cause, as well as taking them from the enemy, and exploring the outer edges of the galaxy. There's a few differences between how each side plays, with their own strengths and weaknesses, but the basics are very similar.
It's disappointing though that there aren't a few more modern updates, such as Steam overlay or a nice easy way to play in Windowed mode (if there is one, please let me know!), but I'm yet to run in to any of the problems people reported on the GOG version. But, the sheer joy of being able to play this game again after so many years without any problems more than makes up for that - it holds up surprisingly well. There's not much else like commanding a Death Star as you go around destroying half the known planets in the galaxy.

In my experience this game is actually pretty good. The characters are cute, the combat system is straight forward, and the quests and auto-routing makes this game, basically play itself.
Now I'm not new to mmos, and I have played countless types of various styles and this one really caught my attention. What I like the most is that it's super easy to level up on your own, and you don't really have to rely on others. I've played other MMOs, where I simply couldn't progress on my own cause well, the character I made just wasn't fast/strong enough to gain the exp. Clerics suck, just saying but, I also can't play non-clerics/squishy characters.
I also like how, you don't have to work as hard to level up to get those cooler looking skills, or in other words, you get to get those cool skills at the get go. Cause that's a major selling point for me, I'm all about the graphics and how flashy and cool you get to make your character.
The edioleons are super cool, wish there was more of a way to pick which ones you get, or at least raise the chances of getting the one you want. If there is, well... I guess I haven't looked into it enough. But I'm also not the type to like grind for hours in the same dungeon to get something super rare however what I noticed from dungeoning it probably won't take too much time to get that shiny armour you want. Anyone willing to do that, super props to you. I never know how you do it.
Other cool features are the gliding, the duel class option at level 40, dungeons and auto-loot pick up are super useful and that there is a pretty extensive fishing option. Armour and Weapon fortification is pretty simple too, making anyone able to upgrade their stuff; takes a lot of resources, but it's still fun and you're not likely going to loose your stuff if it fails. All of these I find super awesome cause these are stuff I wish was found in other games.

super easy to play on your own, has everything you can want in a game that you probably wouldn't have thought of. I barely scratched the surface of this game, and I bet it's even better when you dig deeper.
Now what I don't like, and I don't know if this is just me, but I have played this game with a friend, and even though we were both playing the game, it didn't really feel like we played together. We were both just running about on our own, and talking in between when we were stuck. I'm super social when it comes to mmo games, but the fact that there isn't the shared loot pickup for quests, or that exp isn't shared between us, it really feels like a solo game. The best you can do is just stand around and kill stuff while waiting for your friend. And a lot of the quests are specifically solo anyways.
What also bothered me is the mouse controls. You get used to them as you play (not really) but the two camera functions can really hinder you in a bind. Like one camera simply rotates around your character, and the other one actually makes your character turn with it. So like I know during boss fights, I turn my camera a lot to look at different angles, but I don't nessecarily need my character to be turnt around too cause some skills require them to be facing a monster. So with that, sometimes I would need to run away to get out of a red zone, and I find myself using the wrong camera move, and I just have my character running backwards super slowly, and usually on the verge of death now. (I'm not the type to click-to-move) And some mobs jump around a lot so you need that camera moving.
And another is the skill keys hot-bar. There are waaaay too many skills to fit on one hot bar and it's inconvient how they only go up to 8. I used to it going up to the "=" key. Plus with the eidoleon skills, mounts, glide features and other stuff I can't remember, you are't left with a lot of space, especially when the second class comes into play. So you're left with like maybe 4 of your favourite skills from each class.
It doesn't feel as social of a game going by my standards. There isn't that sense of playing with friends, but just having them on the side (but thats not too bad). The mouse controls are super annoying and the hot-bars don't have enough space and can get pretty cluttered.
I would totally recommend. There's a lot I complained about, but really they don't affect gameplay that much. If you know what you're doing it's pretty meaningless.

Ok so after committing 200+hours over the last 2 weeks that I have bought the game I can happily say a few things positive  and a couple negatives.
Let's start with the negatives. Now truly if you were too buy the base game of Stellaris and expect a fully fleshed out 4X gameplay and beautiful environments you really would be half satisfied. With all the content that is added through dlc the base game looks sorely lacking in numerous areas. The only other think that truly irks me is being locked basically too 4 maps that get truly boring after your 200 hundredth playthrough. The last thing is it seems the modding community is struggling to either adapt or keep pace with the changes that the developer makes. Now I mean no slight towards anyone who devotes their time to making a game better through their own works. It just seems that the tools given to mod the game are still almost the same ones as what they gave the community on a few months after releasing Stellaris.
So now we come to the part where I simply scream at the top of my lungs "I LOVE THIS GAME!!!!". Now to even basically address the very issues I brought up myself thanks to user generated content in the Steam Workshop most of my severe drawbacks were immediately cured. Then to top it all of the content added through the dlc truly polishes off a fine piece of work.
If they keep going in the direction of getting feedback from the community and implementing chages while at the same time continually adding new content this will be a supreme 4X game.

This is a positive review of the Steam Controller (SC). Console gamers are couch gamers. They want to be comfortable when they play, and they just want to get into the game asap. PC gamers don't mind sitting at a desk in order to tweak the game so that they have the best graphics, and the best control setup via mouse and keyboard. The SC is for PC gamers that strive to be couch gamers. The SC is the most customizable controller in existance today. Every button, every touchpad, can be customized to any keyboard or mouse button. It has an acelleromiter that lets you use the SC like a Wii-mote, and there are deeper options to have multiple controller layouts pre-mapped to switch at the touch or hold of a button. This customizability is the SC's greatest draw, and drawback. Every single game needs to be remapped from scratch. However, the interface to do so is very intuitive and easy. There is no tutorial, but many reviewers have good tips on youtube, and you can also download other people's layouts. The learning curve is steep, but if you can PC game with a thumb operated trackball, you can use the SC.

Right Track: I think Valve is definitely on the right track, great concept ideas. Do I think that the egronomics of the control are great? No. The layout is terrible in my opnion which caused me to get a massive hand cramp. The sticks being "up" wasn't terrible but the grade was too high and needed to be lowered. I say the paddles were AMAZING though. If Valve can figure out where to place the buttons without making my thumb stretch for them, I would by V2 as it stands V1 needs a lot of work.

It was weird at first but at this point I wouldn't want to go back to the old xbox controller.  It also works pretty well just for cruising around Windows.  I just wish you didn't have to go to Big Picture for it to work properly for games (I don't like big picture at all, really).  The track ball emulation is the best part of it; didn't expect to like that so much.

There are many games that it doesn't work with and few that it does (it actually has not worked well for any game I've tried).  For me it's not worth screwing around with it.

I have been putting off forming an opinion on this controller for a week or two. It definitely takes a learning curve if you're used to a controller but it's similar to the learning curve i had with the keyboard and mouse when i first started gaming on PC. One of the hardest things for me in the learning curve was getting used to the placement of the ABXY buttons. I kept thinking B was A because i was so used to an xbox controller. It is definitely more versatile than an XBO or PS4 controller once you get over the learning curve.
I suppose it would be best to list my pros and cons and elaborate if necessary
Pros:
-Ability to customize controles specific to each game. This includes one command for a half pull on the triggers and a different for pulling it all the way. I find this application great for Rocket League. partal pull on the right trigger hits the gas and a full pull activates boost. There are also gyro controles but i haven't found an application for it yet. (Edit: I have since experimented with the gyro and included it down below)
-The track pad is great for games like fallout or skyrim for aiming. It's not as good as a keyboard and mouse for action shooters like COD or Counter Strike but it could still suffice if you got skilled enough with it.
-Think the track pad isn't accurate enough? add the Gyroscope to your mouse binding and you'll have instant near-mouse accuracy. Personally I use both the trackpad and gyroscope binded to the mouse. I use the trackpad to get the curser in the general facinity and then the gyroscope for accuracy. Teaming these two togeather works phenomenally! Mouse and keyboard may still have a slight advantage in FPS games but this method seems to close the gap substantially
-Back paddle buttons that create another options under the triggers
Cons:
-Trouble with games not native to steam. This is my biggest complaint so far. It would be nice if it were at least recognized as a standard controller by non-steam games like FIFA. tested it out with FIFA 15 and it is completely unresponsive. I'm sure this could be fixed with a firmware update but for now, it's really the only thing that i truely dislike about it. Sure i can just pull out my xbox one controller to play these games but it would be nice if i didn't have to.
-The left track pad also has D Pad marks etched in it and is usually used for this. It is a little more of a hassle to use this instead of a traditional D pad but isn't too bad once you get used to it.
-Many times customization is required for the controller to work properly with some games taking away from the "just jump in and play" aspect. not really a turnoff for me but i can see some people having a problem with this.
-Steam is very open about warning you about this last one and is really a problem on a game developers side, which i'm sure will be fixed with new games coming out. However, be warned that customization, especially when binded to keyboard and mouse controls, in-game prompts still show up as their original buttons. It would be nice in the future if developers are able to detect what you're controls are set to and provide those as in-game prompts instead.
I understand I have one more "con" than "pro" but in all fairness the cons that I could come up with didn't really carry as much weight with me as the Pros and advantages the controller offers. If an update can be released that will allow me to use the controller outside of steam, i'll be perfectly happy with the controller.

It has a bit of a charm to it and it does do some things right but there is also a fair amount that needs improvement. I'd recommend this to you if you are prepared to deal with a bit of frustration.
The game does a good job of trying to mix things up, it does all the platformy gimmicks like a level where you have to stay on a moving platform and dodge things coming from underneath, or a boss that gets a stronger attack when you've almost killed him (I'm at the final area right now and only one boss seems to have done that), and overall has a lot of elements that could make it a great game, including a level that is essentially a side-scrolling shmup like that old alien shooting game on nokia phones.
Unfortunately a lot of little issues come together to make the experience less than ideal.
First off, the way that jumping handles in this game is a bit jenky. The first jump works fine but the second jump throws your character in whatever direction he is facing which can sometimes cause your character to get tossed into spikes or other things when you are doing jumps in certain areas that require you to double jump and probably get hit by said spikes.
Another issue is hitboxes. Your character's hitbox is a bit weird, sometimes you will get hurt by things that are clearly not touching you and when you jump you have to get much higher than it looks in order to get onto platforms. There have been platforms where the character very clearly is able to jump higher than the platform yet is unable to land on it because the hitbox is a bit off so you are required to take a different path there.  This problem is at it worst during one of the earlier levels where you have to swing across vines in certain areas. You are only allowed to catch onto the vine if you hit it right at the tip which is weird in and of itself but when added with your character's slightly off hitbox it can mean a lot of dropping into an instant death when, visually, your character should have been perfectly fine,
A lot of the difficulty in this game actually stems from little issues like this and not actual hard platforming. In the aforementioned section, where you do the whole moving platform across a river of acid or toxic water or whatever, you basically have to stand on the platform and dodge the balls coming from underneath. The big issue with this is that there is neither an animation prior to the balls launching up at you or a consistent timing for the balls. One or the other would have been fine but without both it means your character is at the mercy of the random intervals since you can't actually use timing or visual cues. You can help this to some degree by standing all the way at the back of the short platform and running past the ball the instant it launches then running back (provided you aren't in a bit with 2 balls launching which can seriously screw you over if one decides it's going to resurface in half the time it generally takes). But this strategy gets compromised by flying enemies going at your head that you will have to attack, this wouldn't be an issue at all but when your character attacks he mysteriously stops where he is on the screen while the plaform keeps going so you may end up falling into the acid which is an instant death because your character does something illogical only on that bit.
The game attempts to make boss fights easier by letting you find golden hearts that increase your max hp (you start with 3). The issue with this is if you die you will lose the extra hearts. With the combination of most deaths being instant and there being next to no regular hearts for you to pickup (enemies don't drop them and on some levels they seem rarer than golden hearts) the odds of you making it to the boss with the extra hearts is very unlikely. Now let's say you do make it to the boss with the extra hearts, it's gonna come at you and with how easily your character dies you will likely have to fight it a couple times in order to get the patterns down. That is standard with these games but it also makes the extra hearts you might have had when you first encounter the boss virtually worthless and is furthered by certain points which are clearly designed to kill you the first time you enter them because of the surprise which makes anything you picked up (or even purchased immediately before that screen) pointless.
Artstyle is pretty basic, wouldn't say it's good or bad. The music ranges from certain tracks being very good to one that is  actually quite annoying given some time.  The main issue pretty much all the music tracks have however is that they weren't designed to loop. There is a very obvious start to the tracks and since it loops right back to the beginning when a track ends it creates very abrupt transitions which does break the mood quite a bit.
There are probably about half a dozen other issues that I won't get into yet but yeah, this game has potential but it definitely feels clunky as hell.

There Was A Caveman is a fun throwback to old platformers, where you attempt to save Cavekind!
First, you'll notice that the game has quite an authentic look and feel to the era it's trying to portray.
The controls are quite simple. You can double jump, swing your weapon, dash, and throw different projectiles that you find.
I found that the game did a very good job at shaking things up throughout. Different enemies force you to react accordingly, as well as the levels themselves having different ways of playing. Underwater levels, dark levels, or even flying on a pterodactyl all keep the game from feeling stale. As well as changing up the obstacles, you can use a variety of projectiles, which all act differently and can be used in different situations.
Although, I'm very happy with the difficulty of the game, it's worth noting that I haven't found a way to get a game over screen. You just respawn from the latest checkpoint, which keeps the game from getting frustrating. You have a limited amount of health, however, if you find secret health upgrades or purchase some from the store, you can increase that limit. Once you die though, they're gone. Which drives you to play very carefully.
Overall, I really liked the game! It takes a lot of elements from the good old games we enjoyed, and leaves behind the frustrating elements from some of the others.
