Loadout is an arena based Third person Multiplayer shooter that is free to play with microtransactions... Hey! come back! This one's good! I promise!
The arena-based combat centers around custom guns. I don't mean custom-IZABLE guns. You know, like in COD where you can stick things on your gun which allows you to do different things. Loadout allows you to BUILD YOUR OWN WEAPON FROM THE GROUND UP. In fact, you pick:
The type of projectile,
The barrel
The reloading mechanism,
The fire rate,
The aerodynamics of the projectile,
and a whole bunch of other options specific to that type. The different options have to be unlocked with Blutes, the you-can't-pay-real-money-for-this currency that you get from playing the game. (more on that later.)
After you finish creating your own gun, you end up with a gun that seems custom made just for you! (That's because it was.)
This wide amount of versatility for different play styles makes the game much more fun no matter how♥♥♥♥♥♥you are at shooters! You can even modify your gun to heal players instead of hurting them! (Want to heal with a rocket launcher? go ahead!)
This seems like this would make for an insanely difficult game to balance, but the Devs have an elegant solution:
Every weapon part has a Yin-Yang effect that buffs your gun in one specific way at the cost of nerfing it in another. This means that every gun you could possibily ever make has been balanced before you could even think of making it!
There's also a really interesting art style going on here: It's kind of like a Rated-R version of Ed, Edd, and Eddy. Slapstick and gore in equal measure. You can blow limbs off without killing them, and if you get a headshot and manage to not kill them, you see their head come off, but their brain still undamaged. You can even blow a hole through their stomach!
Now to that Free-to-play thing i mentioned earlier. There's two types of currency in this game: Blutes and Spacebux.

Blutes are what you spend to advance in the tech tree to customize your gun and generally progress in the game at all.
You can ONLY get blutes by playing . You can't buy any amount of them with real money or spacebux.
Spacebux are what you spend on things you DON'T need to progress, like clothing, Blute & XP multipliers, Extra loadout slots, and extra weapon presets.
You really don't need anything you can buy with spacebux. You get 3 weapon slots and one loadout slot just for downloading the game, and you can unlock 2 more loadout slots and 3 more weapon slots for reaching certain character levels. It is possible to increase the amount of Blutes that you earn for a day, but even then you still need to play the game to take advantage of that in the first place.
Loadout is not Pay-to-win. In fact, it's the least pay-to-win game with microtransactions since TF2. This is the case because TF2 allows you to buy the special weapons instead of crafting them, completing the achievements, or waiting for them to drop randomly.
Loadout, conversly, doesn't allow any purchasting any of the weapon parts with any real money whatsoever.

Gonna be totally honest, most of the reviews I saw when I looked down where thumbs down, but they were complaining about bugs and shuttery frame rates. I'm going to tell you why even if the game is working perfectly it's still awful.
At it's core if you loved the first 2 dead risings like I did you won't find much here. The game feels totally differnent and in all the wrong ways. 6 hours in and...
1. I've only fought 2 psychopaths and have no hints on how to find any others. Survivors escorts have been replaced with either fetch quests or eliminate small horde of zombies. In between each "Chapter" of the story you will get three calls from your radio, pointing you towards 3 survivors (and in 1 case one COUNT THEM one psychopath). That's where those fetch quests I mentioned come in.
2. Los perdios compared to Fortune city and Willamete is a cluster♥♥♥♥ of confusion. Prepare to spend hours wandering around in circles. The map has a minimum of information, stores and buildings are not labeled and verticle pathfinding is a nightmare.
3. Combat is totally shot, What made the pasts 2 games fun in combat was a certain scarcity of good weapons, your movements through were hopping between good spawns while occasionally making do with lesser weapons. In this game it is totally possible and not in anyway a challenge to just use ar 15's and m60's. In fact ranged combat seems to be the focus of the game, in the apocalypse edition once you unlock the weapons locker early on you'll have access to fire cannons, miniguns, smgs, rifles, lmgs, and shotguns. For the 12 dollars I got this game for, you really can't go wrong. It's a really solid game that does many many things right. It's more tacticle and punishing than say, Battlefield, but it's mechanics and controls aren't so complicated and complex in simulator type games such as Arma.
The gun mechanics feel really nice, damage dealt is accurate. You really cannot run and gun, or run into a field and expect to stand a decent chance. You will be mowed down, and you will die before you even realized what happened. Instead, you need to take advantage of cover, go prone and crawl through that field instead. You won't be running for 5 minutes to get back to the battlefront, and spawn times are pretty short so you don't feel like you're being punished for dying. Controls feel very flueqent and direct, you don't feel like there's a buffer on everything you do. Your character moves or does an action the moment you want him to, which really helps the game feel smooth. The graphics are nothing to write home about, but the game is very well optimized. I'm able to get 144FPS with my 390X with everything on High in 2K. I can barely get 60 in PUBG everything on low.
Ultimately, Rising Storm 2: Vietnam is really a great example of what modern shooters (and PC games in general) should strive to be. Tacticle, realistic within reason, yet leaving you saying at the end of each round, "Wow. That was honestly really fun."

My review:
Anyone who DOES NOT LIKE ANIMEE or is coming to this from World Of Warcraft, then DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME!...
Your still here? Good, then let's discuss this great game.
The Good Points:
(Please note, if i need to explain something indepth, i will do at the bottom of the review... You will tell if i am explaining something in depth because it will be bracketed with [.])
It's animee (I lOVE animee)

Eidlons [Battle companions]
[Quick access to mount]
[Auto Route]

Now the explinations...
Why have i listed ever good point as a bad point? Because this game nis like *marmite* (literally)
[Fast leveling explained]: Ok, someone coming from WoW or another famous MMO will play this game for 10-15 minutes and already be level 12 and feel over-powered... That all changes from level 20+... you will start to realise that it becomes a heavy grind after 25 (taking up to 45 minutes just to gain a single level... unless you have an exp booster, or exp heay gear) Where some might love the fast levels, other people wont... where some will love the long levels, other people wont.
Eidlons [Battle companions]: ok, once you get to about level 4-5 you will have a blue orb follow you, this eventually turns into your battle companion (the one you chose to team up with at character creation)... This is good because depending on your class choice your Eidlon will complement it (THATS WHAT THEY ARE FOR so choose wisely... example: If your class doesn't have any stars (or very minimal stars) in health then choose the pink flying eidlon, as she will heal you over time... The bad points with eidlons is you HAVE TO LEVEL THEM UP (it wont do it for you).... some people think they are over-powered when they get to high levels (you fight a mob... you only get a single hit in before your eidlon does a *Smack-down* on it...), you have to interact with your eidlon (ask it things) for *Link Points*, (liks are good), if you link with your eidlon you have a % of recieveing eidlon food or upgradeable *stones* (please play the game for more info ;)
[Quick access tgo mount]: THIS IS NOT WoW!!!!
Ok... this is a double edged sword... you get your mount (every one in the game does) at about level 3-4... its an osterich!!! (lolz) the bad thing about this is the fact that its universal (everyone in the game gets it at the same level... you dont even have to work for it!(you get it from a quest)) Its also slow as hell!!! (maybe 5% faster than walking IMHO)... Good points? Its FREE and... it's a MOUNT :D
[Auto Route]:
Why is ths bad?/Why is this good?
Ok its good for these reasons... You have a quest? You're lost in the wilderness/you have to go to the other side of the world to do it? WHY THE HELL ARE YOU COMPLAINING? just left click the quest you want on you quest list and ZING... Auto piolet!!!.. this means you can chat... roll a ciggy... look on google, download more games etc while you get to where you need to be.
Why is this bad?
Ok... i will list the reasons I think its bad:
Its bad because it will speed you through tonnes of mobs that could give you exp... you can't explore on your own with it enabled, there is no option to turn it off (however, independant movement will cancel this feature... all you have to do is click the quest again and.... ZING!!!)
[Skill and stat Heavy]:
Not everyone's *Cup of tea*
ok, let's say your a duelist... you need crit and speed/evasion above anything else?... That's ok, because every piece of armor that drops is 95% class apparent (most of the quests will only give you armour/weapons for your class) Go figure...
When using the stat/power system you have to make sure that you spend 99% of it on crit/speed/evasion (in THAT ORDER) or you will fail as a duelist (that's my personal oppinion)
Auto Leveling Sytem [If you wish]:
This will not be for everyone!
at least its a choice... when you are leveling up your stats you have a choice for it to do all the hard work for you (it will auto allocate stat points if you ask it to) or whether or not you want to be a confused *Nab* and fail with your class (you will only use this feature for about 5 levels, and then you will get the idea)
My reveiew is almost done:
Me personally, i got this game when i couldn't afford to pay for WoW once, and it got me hooked.
I feel that almost everyone is on an even footing in this game (ofc there is going to be someone bigger/faster/stronger/betetr than you, its an MMO! But it doesn't penalize you for being a noob as much as WoW or any similar game would.
I know my reveiw is very mixed, but thats the point... i am not telling you to * Buy/not buy* this game based on a one-sided/biased *This game is rubbish don't get it/ This game is amazing, get it now!!!* you deserve to know the truth when thinking about playing a game :D
All i will say in endorsing this game :D :D.... It's free to play!!! (but its also P2W... NOT HEAVILY btw!!!! But it is P2W... although you can do it as F2P but it is a grind... and that... IS THE POINT!)

Devs have strange practices and their game is buggy as all hell
Let me first give you a warning of the shady marketing/advertising this company practices. This game is around 2 years old, but the release date has changed multiple times. The developers claim this is a steam bug, but it has happened too often for it to not be suspicious and the developers try to dismiss the claim too much without providing any reasonable evidence.
If those business practices haven't put you off the game, then maybe the actual game will.
First off, I will talk about the general gameplay and what you do in this game. This game is a first person puzzle game. There are 12 regular levels; 10 bonus levels and 15 co-op levels (NOTE: The co-op levels are local co-op and use 1 keyboard and 1 controller, so don't think about playing with friends online). This game has
mouse acceleration. There is no way I, or my other friends who have put more hours into this game than I have, have found a way to turn it off. The developers are also lazy, and do not bother to connect planes of the levels, as seen
in level 9 where the walls and floor are not connected.
The aim of the game is to solve puzzles in order to get to the end of the level. Most of this is done through picking up cubes and throwing them in receptors in order to activate certain things. There is also the 'polarity' aspect of this game in which you can change your 'polarity' from blue to red. For example, with blue polarity you can walk on red platforms and safely go through blue lasers. The opposite is true for red polarity. Some puzzles in this game are pretty fun to figure out, but most of them are incredibly easy.
Now, the meat of the review: bugs.
This game is
with bugs. To demonstrate most of the found ones, Siglamii and I have created some videos showing them. For some bugs, there is more info in the video description about the bugs:
There are also strange framerate bugs that exist. On any frame rates other than 60, jumping might not register, and framerate also dictates momentum and jump height to some extent. For example, higher framerates make you jump lower and make your momentum more sensitive. Setting the graphics to simple will limit the framerate to 60; setting the graphics to medium will limit the framerate to 30 (if in windowed mode) and setting the graphics to gorgeous will cap the framerate to your monitors refresh rate. There is no reason for this.
I hope reading this review has persuaded you not to support the developers with their questionable practices by purchasing their shambles of a game.
Thanks to Buttravage, MHFSilver, Dungeonfire, Avetixz and Siglamii for helping the speedrun community and I find these bugs and thanks to Siglamii for helping me with the review and demonstrating the bugs.

NieR elevates game design. This is one of the finest games to date, technical shortcomings of the PC port notwithstanding (Google: FAR). It does many things, and does them all well. It deliberately subverts expectations, but remains invitingly familiar. It's a polished brawler, danmaku, robotron, role-playing game; its disparate parts cohere surprisingly well. First and foremost, it's consitently rewarding, engaging, and fun to play. It happens to be one of the most intelligent games available, an ostensibly postmodern bricolage (requiring multiple 'playthroughs', each of which is substantially different) undergirded by a shockingly redemptive metanarrative crystalised in what may be games' best and most self-aware synergy of message and medium, during a closing crescendo rivalled only by the phantom button-press of Brothers: a tale of two sons. NieR wears its cultured creativity lightly; this is the opposite of pretentious indie grad-school didacticism. It's brilliant, but doesn't mind if you think it isn't. It just wants you to be happy. Buy this game.

This is my favorite multiplayer strategy game for the PC, hands down. Back in the day, I played a lot of strategy games, and I did pretty well at most of them. I was in the top 50 at StarCraft in the late 90s, top 5 at Red Alert 2, #1 at Empire at War, and I took the top 10 spots in other games. Needless to say, I'm a strategy gaming fanatic. I was even interviewed by GameSpy at one point. Yet, this is the game I ALWAYS go back to playing, even after so many years. I prefer this game over StarCraft and other games. It is THAT GOOD. The multiplayer is absolutely phenomenal and incredibly addictive. Every game is unique and different. You get different starting conditions each time and you really have to be smart about how you use your personnel, facilities, and ships. There are so many strategies and counter strategies.
In multiplayer, the game is played at variable speeds, it automatically adjusts to the slowest player. If one of the players selects the medium pace, and the other player selects the fast pace, the game is played at the medium pace. You can change the speed of the game while you play, so you're not locked in at one particular speed for the entire game.
Multiplayer is where this game shines. It has the best multiplayer out of any other strategy game I've ever played. It's so incredibly interesting, especially once you understand the mechanics of the game and how everything works. If you've never played this game before, or if it has been a while, definitely get this game. Then, get online and start playing some multiplayer games. Currently, the most popular way to play this game online is via Game Ranger or Direct IP.

Back in 1998 I had the pleasure of experiencing my first Star Wars strategy game. It was Rebellion, I still have the original box, but the old disc and newer operating systems wouldn't allow me to reinstall it and play it properly.
Now this version turns out to work flawlessly. I'm running the game on Windows 7 64-bit and it even passed the utmost test of all with flying colors... Alt tabbing. The game shows its age with all the pixelated cinematics due to the poor encoding of the time, but it also runs on my 1080p monitor with a 480p quality without compromising gameplay. I believe this is the same build used by Good Old Games with just a few tweaks to make sure it wouldn't fail.
This is particularly great for me because at the time my English wasn't nearly as good as it is now, so I finally understood the garrison requirements to avoid uprisings. I'm also glad to know that I got most of the rules at that time and the nostalgia is fitting. People hardly get to live the glory of certain games after a given amount of time has passed, but it seems to me that Star Wars Rebellion was meant to be a great game no matter how old. Coolhand managed to fit so much of the expanded universe lore in there that I was able to picture the faces of many cherished characters I hadn't even read about by then.
You should definitely give it a try if you're ok with a 32-bit color game featuring some of the most repetitive advisors on the history of gaming.
edit: I forgot to mention that this version does not include multiplayer at the moment. Also, it doesnt support steam overlay so there's no way to upload screenshots at the moment.

Review Edited post patch:
Now that the game works properly, a review can commence without ire.
Overall the game was, for its time, a nice semi-real time Civ-like strategy set in the Star Wars universe, with the now defunct "Legends" EU content mixed in. Its not a game one can play a few casual hours in, but one could definitely find themselves saying "Another hour then I'll do something else..." only to find a day has passed realtime.
There's a lot of resource management and strengths/weaknesses to each system/world owned. Its a case of complexity vs. depth, whereas some parts of the game are deep and others just overly complex. I could write a review on the mechanics alone but that would be an essay rather than a snapshot review, suffice to say there's a lot going on here and not all of it is great.
My recommendation is, if you can get past the Windows 95 era graphics, you have a solid strategy/galactic management Star Wars game. Empire at War seems to have taken *some* notes from this game, and the similarities can be seen after a few hours of play (especially if one uses the Thrawn's Revenge mod for EaW).
So 7.5/10 is the numbered score I'll rate it, very replayable but heavy on complexity. Not really for casual players due to the number of hours one would have to sink into the game per playthrough.

Of the Sands of Time trilogy, Warrior Within is easily the most controversial of the bunch. Forgoing the whimsical
theme of the much beloved Sands of Time, Warrior Within employs a much darker tone, replacing melodic instrumentals with blood pumping metal music, and an emperor’s majestic castle with that of some dreadful thing from a metal album cover. Gone, too, is the storybook hero known only as the Prince, who is now a curse spewing, murder loving psychopath, easy to anger and eager to slice open stomachs. Understandably, not all took a liking to the new Prince of Persia, and many either wrote it off or gave up after dying in the first 10 minutes, all while cursing the monsters at Ubisoft who would dare slight their beloved franchise so vehemently. I am ashamed to admit that while I did not join in the publisher bashing those many years prior, I
assume the many fans’ angers as legitimate. After having neglected the franchise for many years since the original, I have finally played through the trilogy’s entirety. Lo and behold, my judgment is thus: Warrior Within is the best of the Prince of Persia trilogy, and one of the most challenging and equally frustrating and rewarding titles I have ever had the pleasure of besting.
Where its predecessor, The Sands of Time, relied on linear level progression, a typically gradually increasing difficulty, and relatively basic (and easy) combat, Warrior Within features a (sort of) open world, varied weapons of combat, and enemies that will break your face if you’re not perfect. It also features a higher emphasis on combat than its predecessor,
some of the most frustrating puzzle and enemy design than any other game I’ve played in years. But understand what I mean by that. Warrior Within, for the entire duration, never held my hand. The moment I felt I had a handle on how to deal with an enemy type, a brand new exploding, near unavoidable dog animal thing would be introduced. Obviously, it wasn’t always an exploding dog thing, but you get the point. WW is never easy or gradual in its difficulty. It’s not typically fair, either, but it also never felt impossible, and that’s what made it fantastic. For comparison, while playing Demon’s Souls, I always felt in control of what I was doing, and typically only died if I was quick to run into a room before checking for barriers to hide behind, traps or tricky enemies in the shadows. WW will put you in a room and deal death unto you until you learn to deal with it, and the experience became infinitely rewarding upon besting said situations.
Puzzles don’t quite follow the same degree of difficulty that the combat does, but the challenge comes in unintended traversal. By puzzles, I refer to the Prince of Persia’s method of travel; running along walls, sliding down ropes and hanging banners, and avoiding the many, many spikes and saw blades inexplicably sticking out of walls. The open world aspect of Warrior Within allows you to re-visit any portion of the island that you’ve previously visited, and you don’t necessarily have to follow the same paths. However, the design of these pathways are sometimes altered by the game’s events, and even when they aren’t, traversal in any way different from the standard is a challenge in and of itself, as the developers clearly did not design these paths to be easily followed backwards (or forwards, for that matter), as you will have to do. Worse yet, enemy spawns remain, especially those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dogs I mentioned previously, the ones that can take half of your health. If this sounds frustrating to you, it should. But by the point you should even be considering doing anything like this, you will have already become invested in beating down this seemingly personal hell that the developers have created just for you.
I won’t divulge any of my secrets for passing through Warrior Within, and quite frankly, I would recommend any and all to refrain from guides as much as possible throughout (except for the collectibles, you’ll need a guide for those). Warrior Within is a truly brutal and often unfair achievement in sadistic game design. It’s also one of my most satisfying completions in the entirety of my gaming career. Nearly every instance of combat in this title will chew on your face and kick you in your♥♥♥♥♥until you
learn to play it. The learning curve can be steep and unfair, and you will want to quit. Don’t. There are no tricks to Warrior Within, and only your skill, and hopefully a share of dumb luck, will see you succeed. What faults it has, of which there are plenty, only add to the experience..

This is a pretty serious departure from your conventional controller, so it can take some getting used to, especially for those who are accustomed to another controller. I'm used to changing up my peripherals every so often, so the transition was not too difficult for me.

A very real concern was using a touchpad as a joystick. I have to say, it does OK from a functionality standpoint. I won't tell you it's magical and feels like a real joystick, that would be nonesense. I think it requires some configuration tweaking on my end to feel "right" so I'm not going to hold the controller at fault. I'm not actually a fan of joysticks for aiming anyway, so the trackball emulation is more than acceptable. Speaking of, the trackball emulation is amazing. That part IS magical. And yes, it also works very well as a mouse.
The cool thing is, it will only get better over time as they update the software. :)

I was already a fan of the Europa Universalis and Crusader Kings series when I heard Paradox was making a space game in the same style.  I was totally pumped straight up until its release, and it lived up to most of my expectations.  Of course, in those months I was waiting, I was painting a picture of this game in my head that was almost impossible to live up to, so I give it some slack.  It is by far the closest thing to a truly epic galaxy-spanning 4x game I've played, and I've played them all.  It has some great story-telling attached to it in the form of random events that help to immerse you into the game, making it so much more than what most similar games that came before it offered.  It has excellant customization options, and the modding community has put out some real gems that can improve some of the weak spots the game has.  There are even total conversion mods that completely alter the game, which can add tons of replayability to the game if it ever gets boring to you.
It isn't perfect, by any means; and different people may love one or more features that another person hates, and vice versa.  The strategy part of the game doesn't really involve a lot of strategy at the moment; it's more of a resource, tech, and brute force kind of system.  But it works... as long as you aren't the one on the recieving end of superior brute force (it'll happen more often that you might think, if you don't keep up).  The strategy thing is probably the thing most people have problems with, but I really don't.  It may not make for the most epic of strategy, but it actually makes sense... in the huge expanse of outer space, meeting your enemy head-on for an epic showdown with everything you've got is the way to go - whether on the offense or defense.  Something I do feel needs work is the fact that every victory condition depends on controlling a certain % of the galaxy, either independantly or in a federation, or through conquest.  It could really use some variety in that area.  As is, if those aren't personal goals of yours, then you're just playing for fun.  No problem with that, but having goals to strive for with every playstyle would encourage people to play different ways.
The cool thing, though it's a double-edged sword, is that Paradox is constantly working to make their games better.  A lot of their financial strategy comes from doing rather frequent dlc expansions for their major games, which helps to keep them feeling fresh, even years after release.  Even if you don't buy the dlc, there's usually free updates that accompany them that add elements to the game, or sometimes, change it dramatically.  This is where the double-edged sword comes into play.  If you've played EU4 or CK2, then you already know that sometimes the expansions are priced well above their worth, and sometimes the version updates that accompany the dlc drastically mutate parts of the game that worked perfectly fine before.  Sometimes it plays with the dlc, bringing "depth" to previously basic features.  Sometimes these newly enhanced features make previous playstyles more difficult or even impossible to play.  Sometimes they directly benefit a certain playstyle, and offer no benefit whatsoever to any other.  This is likely going to be the case eventually with Stellaris.  Paradox is completely unaffraid to risk ruining their games to make changes that they want made.  Not necessarily anything that's been requested by players of the games, not necessarily to a system that was exploitive or over/under-powered, etc.  Sometimes, they will just change things for the sake of selling you an expansion to make the version update sting a little less.  Go and read reviews for the EU4 and CK2 expansions for details.
The point I'm trying to make is that the game is good, and the game will change.  Will it get better?  Will it get worse?  While only time will tell for sure, I'd say the answer is yes, to both questions.  Anything they change will be applauded by some and despised by others.  My fear is that they will take this wonderfully diverse sci-fi strategy lovefest and narrow it down trying to cater to a select few.  So if it sounds good to you, as it is right now, go on and give it a try.

I played many hours of this game before it came to Steam. It's not the perfect MMO and it caters to a specific demo, I would recommend it based on the fact that is is free to try and worth a look.
Pros
- Beautiful world. The enviroments and the animals look like hand drawn anime.. the good kind. Not the cheesy cliche kind
- Very populated with a (usually) friendly player base.
- I thought I had to pay for the scarf around level 20 to continue the main quest line but apparently I did not need to. I think they make that a bit confusing on purpose. Other than that the F2P model is pretty good.
- Very easy to understand and pick up and play. Nothing is overly complex and the UI and all other things surrounding gameplay make sense.
Cons
- The million dollar MMORPG word.. grindy. The game is VERY kill 10 of these and collect 8 of these. They throw some curveballs in there occasionally but this is what ultimately had me stop playing in the 40s. It just stopped being fun.
- Dungeons are repetitive cut and paste. Nothing special there for sure.
- Didn't care for the music so I put my own ambient soundtrack to it.
- Easy. This could go under pro or con. I didn't mind it but some will.
Aside from dueling I never got too much into PvP in this game so I can't really speak on that. Each class seems pretty cool and you get to pick a secondary skill along the way which helps keep combat fresh. The battle companions are cool but can get annoying with the constant dialogue thing.
Overall I'm happy with the time I put into it. I'm sure it gets more fun when you are at or close to cap but I could not continue any longer. You can check out my video review in my First Impression/Final Impression videos below. Enjoy!

And before you start going ballistic, I'M NOT HATING ON THIS GAME IN ANY WAY. There's just some critizations I must make.
I am a big fan of the original Primal Carnage, over 200 hours into that game. However, this "release" of the game is an EVEN BUGGIER and more unbalanced version of the original Primal Carnage. This game was in no way ready to get out of Early Access.
8/10 Dinosaurs will most likely win, due the lack of organization possible with humans. This is a nasty, boneheaded sequel to a great classic game and its sins are many.  For one, it emphasizes combat far more than the first game while utilizing a fighting system that is more busted than ever; this time the Prince flails around like a stoned acrobat who also happens to be a dead swan, flopping his lanky limbs at everything BUT that which you intend.
The combat is not the greatest offender, however.  That honor goes to the level design!  Whereas in the first game you joyfully somersaulted once through each well-designed obstacle course before assailing the next unique level, Warrior sees you slogging repeatedly through the same murky, uninspired switch and saw and pole courses, interminably back and forth, back and forth, until either your sanity departs or you do a rage uninstall, which is what I SHOULD have done.
And for the crap-flavored icing on the carrion cake, the tone has shifted from cool and easy Arabian Nights-style to grunty grimdark BS.  No longer is the Prince a tough yet somewhat sensitive sort (which jived with his incredible acrobatic ability); now he's just some turd with tribal tats who gruffly tells everyone and everything, including ****ing bats, that he will bloodily DESTROY any and all who stand in the way of his legendary sword arm!  Uhhgh!
This is garbage, this is trash, this is a poopy old relic that deserves to stay buried forever.  Why did I bother to play through this endless torturefest, acquiring all the life upgrades and getting the "good" ending no less?  Chock it up to a bout of extreme self-loathing.  But never again, never again will I waste life and time on something so worthless as this . . . so perhaps I learned something from the experience.

I’m never going to not recommend Skyrim. It was the first major game that I got into back in high school and is still a game I play today. Over my three copies of this game, I have put in well over a thousand hours, and I feel at least a little qualified to throw in my two cents.
If you’re coming from Oblivion or Morrowind, things will be pretty different. Skyrim is a lot more streamlined than previous Elder Scrolls games, especially in the levelling and skills systems. Classes and signs are also a thing of the past, replaced with a perk system that allows for more individualized character building. Whether or not these changes make the experience better or worse is pretty subjective, and an entirely different can of worms.
The Special Edition is a remaster of the 2011 release. In my opinion, Skyrim was the TES game that needed a remastered version the least, because it is still a pretty new game, with the Legendary (Collector’s) Edition coming out only three years earlier. The only real difference between 2011 and the Special Edition is that this one is on a new engine with more dynamic graphics and lighting. Skyrim Special Edition is by all reasoning just a better version of the game, however if you have the choice, I recommend getting the older version instead. I have a decent computer, and I honestly can’t tell the difference graphically between the two, just that the Special Edition runs substantially slower for the same setting. The original also has access the Steam Workshop for mods, which make the game a lot more fun and can be used to get better graphics than the Special Edition, unlike the Creation Club paid mod bs that disables achievements. Steam and Bethesda are hiding the page for the original game, but there are links scattered throughout the reviews.
In short: this is a good game and definitely worth playing if you haven't already, but if you’ve got the extra cash, spring for the original version of the game instead.

TL;DR: I recommend this game, but not at this price.
To get it out of the way: There have been some accusations of shady behavior. First: the release date of the game changed several times, putting it back on the new releases list. The dev claims this was due to a bug, many claim it was done intentionally to get the new releases publicity. I follow the axiom of "never ascribe to malice what can be explained by incompetence" and so I'm willing to give them the benefit of the doubt.
The other thing is that the price of this game has changed several times. This is fully within a game dev's rights, and the dev's claim that when the price has changed it has stayed that way for a decent length of time rather than quick changes to game the sales seems to hold (mostly) true. You can see the sale data at
the July 15, 2016 spike is the only part that does seem a little shady. At the end of the day, the pricing data is available, and as a consumer you should be doing your research about purchases rather than getting sucked in by sale percentages.
So the game itself. Worth $10? no, sorry. Thing is, the game has gone on sale many times, for as low as 19 cents. Wait until it's less than a dollar, or part of a cheap bundle to pick it up. Alternatively, you can get this game for actually free if you have "Out There Somewhere", another game by the same dev, and give them your email in the launcher.
The game itself is pretty solid FOR DIRT CHEAP. It's not a great game by any means. It's pretty short. At no point in the main or bonus stages (didn't play the co-op) did I ever feel like a puzzle was challenging. The game introduces a lot of mechanics that could have been explored in more depth with much more complicated puzzles, but just weren't, such as the rotatable launchers that you almost never have to rotate. The game also has its fair share of bugs, for instance I was able to clip cubes through floors a few times, I managed to bypass an entire puzzle just by jumping to the exit, and I also managed to get in a configuration that soft locked a level, forcing me to restart from the beginning.
Other than that, I did enjoy my short time with the game. The puzzles generally took a little bit of tinkering with to get all the data, even though they're completely straightforward. I originally started this as a positive review, but I realized that the only way I could recommend the game was with the thought "what can you expect for less than a dollar?" But it isn't less than a dollar, it's currently 10, and as a 10 dollar game it's garbage.

*Updated to recommed*
Ergonomics:
The controller is big I guess? I keep hearing that but the dimensions are almost the same as the Logitech F310, though it is a little bit bigger. As long as you hold the controller relaxed its fine, I’m 5’ 11” and my wife is 5’ 4” and neither of us have a problem with the size.
A lot of reviews have complained about the “wings” on the side of the controller and how low the buttons are but I think they simply didn’t adjust to the new controller. Relax your grip a bit, and try to fight the years of muscle memory from using an Xbox/PS controller. There is nothing physically wrong with the button placement, though I admit they could be bigger.
Function:
The touchpads work well form FPS to 4X strategy’s games and the bottom paddle/grip buttons are very useful. The hardest part is being creative about the bindings and seeing what works for you. The controller is incredibly customizable so it may take an hour or two of adjustment (at the very least) to get everything just right. This sounds like a long time, but the community bindings are helping to mitigate this issue.
The d-pad is likely the worst I’ve ever used. This is because of the concave shape of the touchpad and the slightly upwards slant. The grooves are hardly noticeable when your using it as a d-pad so it's hard to press the "directional buttons", but too noticeable when you want to use it as a touchpad. I could hardly use it when I was playing Towerfall, but luckily there aren’t many games that I play that a d-pad is needed. Most of the time the joystick takes up that role. But for those of you who own a lot of arcade games and rely on the d-pad, you will need more time to adjust then someone who plays RTS games or FPS (which is very surprising).
The controller honestly works with most games when an update doesn't break regularly used features. Most of the time, games I had a hard time getting it to work with were very surprising as I figured they would have been easy to do. I haven’t found an Elite: Dangerous binding that I liked, but this game is better played with a joystick anyways. Also Space Engineers and Arma III have also given me a lot of trouble.
Build Quality:
A lot of people have said that the controller feels cheap. I can’t understand why though. The entire thing is made of plastic, but it doesn’t feel flimsy. Most gamepads are plastic. I’m not sure what these people were expecting. One noteworthy issue with the full plastic construction is the touchpad wear. Like with a cheap laptop touchpad, after a bit of use the touchpad becomes “polished” and worn. Glass or metal touchpads would have been nice but that would likely have driven the price up.
Problems:
It seems you actually have to play the game with a mouse and keyboard to know what bindings are most important and frequently used, before you can make a binding for a complex game. This means you can’t just buy a game and then make a binding for it on the fly, unless you want to spend hours making a binding. (For example: I was playing Wolfenstein New Order with the controller set to xbox with joystick-mouse mode having a good time, until I found out you can't use the joystick-mouse mode to pick locks in doors, which is neccessary to advance in some parts of the game. I had to stop everything and rework the bindings, for something that hadn't effected the game at all up to the hour I had been playing).
There isn’t an easy way to look through the community bindings. It’s just a list of bindings with no preview or ranking. You won’t know when one is complete or not because it doesn’t preview the bindings until you select it. Then whatever binding you had before is now gone, and replaced by what could be a completely broken binding. Now you have to go back to the list and look for a functioning one. (Update: Now the system will save your old binding so we can switch back to your custom binding. This still does not make it easier to look through community bindings) Why can’t you up-vote or down-vote bindings? I couldn’t say. Why can’t you search for bindings by name? I don’t know.
There are a couple of caveats with the big picture interface (which is NOT completely mandatory now). The controller works as a mouse with the normal steam desktop window and becomes a gamepad with big picture open. This means that neither touchpad is functional in big picture mode (not even the d-pad) and you can only navigate with the joystick. This is especially frustrating when you sometimes have to navigate a certain part of the menu with a keyboard and mouse. It’s really inconsistent with how you interact with the controller in browsers and there is no way to change that yet. I don’t know why the right touchpad doesn’t control the mouse and the left touchpad works as a scroll wheel or D-pad.
Take away:
To be honest, it feels like this hardware is early access. Frequent updates that make major changes without any notice or instructions on what the functions of the new interface or how to access features from the old interface.
I like the controller, and I enjoy using it when I can get it to work. It’s become my primary tool for playing games. I recently showed it to a few of my friends (some of them non-gamers) and they picked it up very quickly. This was likely because I had gotten the perfect bindings set up ahead of time, so it was pretty easy for them to pick up and start playing equal or better to a regular controller. I was really impressed.
It's not as accurate as a mouse and keyboard, but this is the most accurate gamepad available on the market. The additional buttons along with the accuracy make it a must buy for any PC Gamer.

I am absolutely in love with this thing. In this review, I will be breaking it down to four different categories:
-Community / Playerbase
-Gameplay
-Money System
-Overall thoughts/experience
Oh, and there will be a TL;DR at the bottom as well.
Aura Kingdom's community throughout my experience was not exceptionally bad, although it isn't what I would consider good either. In AK, the majority of players are quiet, there are very few conversations going on in even the main cities/zones in the game unless it is due to a quest and/or event where partying is required. This issue may be due to the fact that Aeria Games, or rather, Aura Kingdom specifically is having a 'bot' problem making players (including me) feel less engaged into the world.
Even though Aura Kingdom uses the standard MMORPG controls (who some may not prefer), the game itself was very enjoyable, the animation in each classes abilities were stunning and beautiful. Mobs and monsters in this game were each unique but some displayed the same attack patterns making it feel slightly repetititve. Also take note that AK is a extremely easy game until near endgame (lvl 60+) as well as the fact that once you DO reach endgame it is extremely slow to level which may make it feel boring due to lack of effort needed or fatigue. Overall, it uses a nicely executed combat system but Aeria Games may want to take a step up on the early difficulty.
So, is Aura Kingdom Pay to win or not? The answer is no, heres why;
Although Aeria Games advertise themselves quite heavily as you play through, all you can really buy with the real money content are rare items or ruby coins which can be used to sell for in-game currency, gold. The rare items (such as costumes) changes your stats very insignificantly and is not different to those stats of a free costume that is earned through questing. Sure, you can buy gear with that gold you earned from spending your real money but in the end, most gear in Aura Kingdom isn't very expensive and can be earned fairly fast without even having to spend a penny on the game. I have experience on both my characters, one which I spent money on and the other I didn't, although they are different classes there aren't much difference in strength, at least not enough for me to consider Aura Kingdom pay to win.
Aura Kingdom is a fun and entertaining game, it may not suit everyone but it definitely kept me satisfied with everything it is and will continue to for a long while, I have shared a lot of fun memories with my friends and people I have met on this game and although the community is fairly quiet once you find the right people, it will make the game feel so much more engaging and lively. If I were to give Aura Kingdom a rating, it would be a 8/10.
TL;DR: Aura Kingdom is a fun and entertaining game to play but has its own fair share of problems such as bots and being too easy. It is not pay to win.

This game is very interesting.
The story is about a space cop who is hunting a villain named Grigori. But after a fight with him, his space ship gets badly damaged and both land on a same planet. Main gameplay begins here and you have to find a light orb to fix your ship and defeat Grigori for good.
Gameplay is really nice. you have a teleport gun which is frequently used in the game and nearly all of the puzzles must be solved with it and a gauss gun to kill enemies. After progressing further in the game, you will encounter new enemies, three types of lightbeams, mirrors, breakable objects and moving platforms which add to the challenge.
PROS:
- Nice gameplay
- Great soundtrack
- Collectables affect how much hard the last fight will be
- Can 100% the game easily with a little skill and patience
CONS:
- Short (Can be completed in 14 mins to 75 mins on first playthrough)
- You HAVE to lose in the first encounter with Grigori and you can even lose at the beginning; but it's not clear. So you do your best to take him down and after a lot of minutes you find out it was a complete waste of time.
- Some rare achivement problems: One of the achievement did not unlock until I did it's required action for the third time.
VERDICT:
This game is really nice and definitely worths trying but it's short and after you unlock every achievement, you may not want to play it anymore.

GYAHHHHHHH!   I have been playing this for the last 3 nights, and I must say it feels weird to say the best thing about this game IS THE TITLE MUSIC!

Then there's the fact that there's no world map travelling and towns are highly condensed.  Everything feels cramped, and you don't get a sense you are exploring a world.
Then you have the gem system in which your characters gain abilities through, however it also sucks since Alphadia Genesis also had a gem system like this but there it worked 10 times better!
And then the entire story is done like a visual novel, however none of the characters emote, like AT ALL.  It makes everyone feel bland, not to mention there's even less backstory here than in other KT games.  Not to mention that even with some time looking over the antagonists, nothing they say makes any bloody sense even at the big reveals near the end of the game!

Yet again, I wish for a more nuanced review option from Steam than a mere "thumbs up" or "thumbs down"...  I'll ultimately err on the positive mostly because it is not a bad game for what it sets out to do, it's just lacking in much ambition.
Tears Revolude is a Japanese-made mobile game ported over to Steam.  It can be played entirely with the mouse using only the left button (right button does nothing "cancel" involves hitting a "back" button), using the keyboard, or a gamepad.
The game has four difficulty modes, and since, in a game like this, that basically is asking "how much do you want to grind", I picked the "Normal" mode.  I shouldn't have bothered, however, as you need to grind a bit, anyway, to level up your skills, which gain levels through a set number of uses, regardless of what they are used upon.  Hence, you gain better healing spells by having the healer drop heals regardless of actually having taken damage, and hover around the healing points or edge of the map.  The game suggests I reforge my weapon levels every 10 character levels, but there's literally nothing better to spend your money upon, so I wound up reforging every time I came back to town, and being even more massively overpowered every trip.
Dungeons are basically just unadorned hallways.  Fights are represented by purple clouds you walk into, and because most passages are so narrow, they're basically unavoidable.  There are treasures that disappear after being opened, which also appear on the map.  Dungeons are generally rather short and far from complicated, at least so far as I've gotten into the game, but you also have very little MP. (Granted, MP restoration items are also cheap, though...)
On Normal Mode in the early game, your characters will take about 60 damage (100 on a crit) from enemies while having several hundred to a thousand HP, and then bosses will suddenly be dealing ten times that, while having a hundred times the HP.  (There is no "defense" stat, you have to equip physical/magical damage % reduction gems to reduce damage.) There are health restoration points (basically like save points, but you can save anywhere, anyway,) right before every boss.
This doesn't make the bosses hard, however, as there's also a special ("Limit Break") system.  If you make a character who has an offensive special use this with everyone else joining in, you are asked to connect the dots as quickly as possible to increase damage... or just use a gamepad and spin the stick to gain power five times faster, since there's no penalty for a wrong imput, and you just need to tilt the stick in a direction corresponding to one of the arrows.  Doing this super-charges the special such that you deal roughly 50 times as much damage as your skills, and insta-gib bosses.
Equipment consists of a weapon, two accessories, and multiple "gem" slots, the last of which you have to pay to unlock over the course of the adventure.  The "four weapon types" are basically a way to alter what stats your weapon focuses upon, so the main character (who is a mixed physical/magic character) can have the standard sword; the more physical attack, less magical attack sword; the more magic attack, less physical attack sword; and a more HP/MP, less attack sword.  Swapping out is free, but this basically just amounts to asking whether you want a specialized or generalized character, and it rarely makes a huge difference.
Gems can give things like simple +10 ATK, or give multiple benefits like regneration plus +200 HP plus bonus ATK while in critical health, all fitting into a single gem slot.  Obviously, this makes the gems that have tons of benefits far more valuable and desirable, and the bait used as rewards for the mini-quests or bonus dungeons.
The game also features a "TRP" or *sigh* "Tears Revolude Points", which are gained per 5 fights (regardless of relative power of the enemies) or from accomplishing certain (in-game only) achievements.  These points are shared across saves, but spent in specific save files.  These seem like they may have been how microtransactions were shoehorned in, but they just replaced it with a "fight more to get more points" system.  In the world map, these points can be spent in a shop to get things like more money or some of the better gems.
The story is also nothing to really write home about.
You play as a guy named Sion who's in a cave that they call a "hidden lab" for unexplained reasons, looking for... something unexplained from some famous artist.  He's accompanied by a woman who dresses in nothing but a leather bustier and thong that fights with a whip for unexplained reasons.  (I mean the reason why she's in the party is never explained, not the reason why a woman who wears nothing but leather enjoys hanging out in dungeons and whipping people... I mean, they don't explain that either, but I figure her motivations for that one are pretty self-explanatory.)  Instead of finding whatever it was they were looking for that clearly wasn't important if they're willing to totally forget it as soon as the plot starts, they find a deadpan snarker girl who's pretty much the only character who breathes any kind of interesting dialogue into the whole game.
You then proceed to go to more dungeons that are supposed "labs" of this artist, only to find out the evil... "The Guild"... by which they mean "The Empire", wants this mysterious humanoid MacGuffin with no memories.  We're informed of their villainy primarily through their fashion choices, since they seem to get their outfits from the same catalgues as 80's anime "evil empress of the moon" characters.
The heroes, after defeating some of The Empi- The Guild's top captains handily decides they need help for some reason, and so turns to the resistance movement against The Guild, called... "The Resistance".  Yeah, they stayed up late thinking of these names...
What mysterious secrets does the humanoid MacGuffin who seems to maybe not be human after all hold?  There couldn't possibly be some doomsday secret where only the mysterious waif the main character rescues in the first ten minutes turns out to be able to decide the fate of the world, could there?  I won't spoil the ending because I haven't finished it, anyway, but the game is not exactly A-game storytelling, as you can probably tell.  It's pretty paint-by-numbers JRPG fare...
So, why do I recommend it, anyway?  Well, sometimes you just enjoy something mindless and comfortable.  I got this game in a bundle deal, and I definitely recommend people interested wait for a sale, but it's basically a simple, familiar comfort food for someone who grew up on playing JRPGs on the SNES and PS1, and who plays free amateur RPG Maker games for a lark.  It has the same sort of feeling as an amateur developer's 3rd try, where it has at least some polish, but not the skill to make anything great, and the plot is at least MST3K treatment-worthy.  In that sense, it's a Good-Bad Game, and if you're of that particular mindset, it's enjoyable... I'd just recommend not playing on the harder modes, since this game wouldn't be any fun if it were more of a grind.

Should you buy a Steam Controller?  Maybe, if you're an early adopter who is interested in testing Valve’s living room dreams (to include BPM) and are willing to put lots of time in making the controller work the way you want,  but for everyone else, no.
Construction:
Overall, I would say that the construction of the controller is pretty good.  When getting it out of the box, I do admit it feels like a cheap piece of plastic.  But once you put the batteries in, it gives it enough heft to feel solid.  I think the construction is sturdier than the Xbox one controller that I normally use.  I do not like the reflective black plastic though, it's shiny and attracts fingerprints.
Layout:
My first big gripe.  All but the Face buttons (Y,X,B,A) are located fine, but those face buttons are located too far away from the right touch pad to be convenient.  Part of it, I think, is that I am used to a controller layout from the Xbox controllers.  So there is so muscle memory trying to tap buttons that are not where I would normally expect them.  Personally, I think ditching the familiar layout all together would have made more sense.  Perhaps the buttons laid out in a crescent, so all the buttons would right next to the right touch pad would be better.  The layout of the other buttons are fine for me.  It takes some getting used to the left touchpad as a DPAD because it is up rather than down, but it seems to work fine for me.  On the positive side, the rear paddles are kind of amazing, and I like them so much that I would like to see all controllers utilize these.
Using the controller:
To the meat of the issue, because it's not so much just a controller issue as it is game issue.  My intent using this controller was not so much to replace my mouse and keyboard, or even my xbox one controller but to allow me to use games that are strictly mouse and keyboard on the couch.  I am thinking of games like Pillars of Eternity, Civilization V, Europa Universalis 4, Tropico 4.  So I will leave my comments to the controls for those kind of games.
By in large, it works.  Pillars of Eternity, for example, plays like a dream with the controller.  Everything is easily bindable to the controller and being that combat is turn based, I feel like I am always in control without things getting unmanageable.  When Valve enabled the Touch Menu for the left touch pad, it made the controller much more useful for these types of games.  All my hot keys go to the left Touch pad, camera movement to the lone thumbstick, and mouse movement to the right touch pad.  It plays like the game is meant to be controlled with the Steam Controller.  Likewise Civilization V works perfectly as well, as did Torchlight 2.
Games like Europa Universalis which controls well with the Steam Controller (again I use the touch menu heavily) have a different issue.  If you try to play that game on the Big Screen, you are going to have a hell of hard time reading anything.  If anything, this is the biggest problem I think Valve and Big Picture mode in general are going to have with these sort of games.  If things are so small on the big screen that I am forced to use my regular monitor, then why would I use the controller over the mouse and keyboard?  Most of the strategy games that I went to play on the big screen, were more than functional with the controller but I always ended up going back to the mouse and keyboard cause the experience was meant for a smaller screen.
When it comes to FPS, and 3rd person games….  Well, your mileage is going to vary.  It useable and with practice it works very well.  Not as good as mouse and keyboard but functional, at least as good as a regular controller just with some practice.  Although out of the two types it is third person games there are much harder to get used to.
RTS games… I really wouldn’t bother.  Maybe with something like the Game banished, but Starcraft, Age of Empires.  You are going to want a  mouse and keyboard, it's faster and more efficient.
Configuration:
The amount of customization on this controller is crazy, it rivals high end keyboard customizations.  This is both a negative and positive.  I spent 45 minutes getting Pillars of Eternity (a GOG game btw), to work the way I want, same with EU4.  I picked a profile from the community and tweaked from there.  But that is the thing, you are going to have to tweak it and customize it.  It is time consuming, and if you are willing to work on getting the controls just right then there is no point in getting the controller.  To be honest, some of the big gaming review sites that have reviewed the Steam Controller sound like they didn’t do any customizing at all, hence why they couldn’t get them to work the way the wanted.  You have to sit down and make it work, cause the default controls are almost always need to be tweaked.  Using the communities templates help, but you will still end up making it the way you want.  So if you are looking for something plug and play, just look somewhere else.
Conclusion:
I like the Steam Controller, as I am willing to put the time and effort in to make it work, but I get the feeling most people won’t.  More importantly, the biggest single reason I am giving it a negative review is that the games that would benefit the most from the controller (strategy games) aren’t really meant to be played on a big screen.  In which case, use your mouse.  Its easier.

I bought the original Primal Carnage a few years ago on sale and enjoyed it immensely. I bought Primal Carnage: Extinction at the start of January and boy was it a broken mess. The balance was terrible, a lot of bugs, and everyone moved at 1000 miles per hour. When I saw the game was finally released, I expected to play it and it still be a broken mess, however I was shockingly surprised that it was actually playable now and it was superior to the original Primal Carnage.
For anyone unfamiliar with the series, this game is basically a FPS/TPS where one team plays as dinosaurs in third-person and the other team plays as humans in first-person. Each side has different classes. Humans have classes like a sniper, a trapper, and a pyro. Dinosaurs have classes like the T-Rex, those spitting dinosaurs from Jurassic Park, and the raptor. This of course is to just name a few.
There are several gamemodes like Team Deathmatch (the main gamemode) and Get to the Chopper (a Def/Atk type gamemode), and with Extinction you now have Dino Deathmatch and Roleplay (ughh). Most servers you'll see will be running team deathmatch or roleplay, with a few rarely playing the other gamemodes.
First off, this game is pretty well balanced. Both sides are fun to play, so you won't dread switching teams. There are a few balance problems here an there like Pathfinder still being overpowered as hell. Other than that, it's the most balanced the series has ever been. The graphics are really good looking now, and much improved upon since the original.
One of my main problems with Extinction is the changes to human outfits. In the previous game, all the classes wore different outfits and were easy to tell apart. For some reason they decided to give the Scientist, Commando, and Pathfinder all green outfits this time, so they can sometimes be hard to tell apart. This also brings us to the next problem.
The developers decided to take a page out of TF2's book and have hats and random drop skins and outfits. If you think it's hard to tell apart classes now, wait till you see someone running around dressed up like Santa Claus (yes this seriously exists), or wearing completely different items than the default model. This also takes away the style of the game especially when you see a dinosaur wearing earmuffs. As you'd expect this leads to an extremely toxic community and speaking of which...
The community isn't the best in the world. You have people focused on getting drops, others forcibly dieing, and let's not forget the roleplay servers. This isn't RP like's Garry's Mod. There's literally nothing to really do in these servers except walk around yet half the servers (and just to let you know there's probably 20 servers max) are roleplay and another 1/2 are dominated by 24/7 single map servers. The previous Primal Carnage game got to the point where the only active servers at certain times were roleplay servers. Right now there's a lot of active people, but there's a chance that once the newness wears off from the game, it could become impossible to find a server.
There are a few bugs here in there like spawning above water thus dieing and the infamous crazy legs. The biggest bugs right now are related to the netcode. If you have a tiny bit of lag you'll be unable to pounce as the raptor even after the lag ends, also there's extreme amounts of rubberbanding. You can swoop down as a pteranodon, kill someone, then half a second later be at the top of the skybox even though you did just kill someone on the ground. Not uncommon to be walking on a 2nd story platform for several minutes then to randomly rubberband to the ground floor. Although these bugs shouldn't take too long to fix, and not a huge deterrent from playing.
I recommend buying the game, you'll defiantly get your moneys worth of enjoyment out of it.

The second part of the amazing Prince of Persia trilogy. This time it's a whole lot different kind of adventure. No more fancy palace and no more romance in the air. This game tells you a different story.
Prince of Persia: Warrior Within is an excellent game that reveals its greatness as you progress. It starts off a bit run of mill with our moody hero slicing up bad guys, but things take a turn for the best when you get to the island. From here on it's a mind bending challenge after mind bending challenge - each more well thought out and engrossing than the last.
The graphics are very dark and atmospheric and the gameplay is great too. The Prince feels nice to control as he runs across walls, swings on poles and does tons of cool acrobatic tricks.
They made some huge changes to the fighting system. Now there are lots of combos and even enviormental kills. Now you can grab and throw enemies off ledges and over them.
The voice acting seems worse to me.
The music is very different from the first game. This time it's all rock and metal, which I didn't really like. Because I'm not a fan of such. But it was necessary. The game forces you to run away from an dark, terrifying guardian of time named Dahaka. And the music is chosen well for this part of the game.
The game looks and feels awesome. The plot is a sick sticky web that makes you think fast and act faster. New powers and weapons are always nice to see in a game. And trust me, there are a lot of weapons here. Especially because the Prince can now Dual Wield.
Lots of secret areas, just like the first game. And some awesome hidden weapons too. You'll have to stray off course in order to find them.
Prince of Persia: Warrior Within is a challenging and fun game. It requires brawn, brains and an appreciation of wicked looking island. It doesn't beat the first game, but still...

Do you dream of purging the xeno filth from the galaxy?  Of asserting man's rightful place as the sole masters of the universe?  Then look no further, for Stellaris has heard your pleas of genocide, and it has answered.
Become the most powerful empire in the galaxy or join a federation and eradicate the rest of the indepedant empires.

Paradox struck gold.
Just look at he amount of hours reviewers have spent in this game. What kind of game can give you hundreds of hours of gameplay? this kind.
This is the definitive space 4X. They took the sheer complexity of Europa Universalis and added it to Master of Orion. A single campaign can last weeks of your life, about 400 years of game-time. You start with a single system and must attempt to expand across the stars. A single galaxy can contain 800 stars (In huge galaxies), and over a dozen different empires, ranging from peaceful diplomats to genocidal space ISIS, from bronze age primitives to millennary Fallen Empires. The scale of the map is overwhelming. Here you must make your stand. Join a federation to protect yourself? Enslave those meatbags? Sterilize the galaxy from all organic life? It is all possible.
DOMESTIC POLICY: Your empire is composed of "pops". Which represent (roughly) 1 Billion sentients. Each pop has it's own species, ideology, opinion and happiness levels. If you conquer a planet you will immediately face the 13 pops that inhabit it. Integrate them into your democracy? Enslave? Purge? your choice. Each pop works a tile on each planet, like in CIvilization. Each pop grows on it's own, and can have it's own attributes and perks. Maybe they support your democracy, or maybe they are slaves rebelling against your grip. Maybe they are wasteful mammals, or or industrious space slugs. Multiply this by hundreds of planets. Are you Star Trek's Federation? Star Wars' Empire? Warhammer 40K's Tyranids? Skynet? All have different mechanics, and the population in your empire grows accordingly.
EXPLORATION: The galaxies are huge, filled with anomalies, aliens and danger. Even the empires behaviors are distinct. Are you neighboring a Fallen Empire? prepare to bow to your new overlords. Close to a Fanatic Purifier? better find some allies quickly, or you will be exterminated. You will have to fight for each single sistem in the early game, while your rivals (and allies) fight to expand into your terrain. Monsters also roam the stars, from Space Dragons to ancient abandoned citadels, from pirates to Space Byzantium. But from danger comes opportunity. A fertile gaia protected by that pirate fleet.
DIPLOMACY: Dozens of empires inhabit the galaxy, and diplomacy against them is a very important tool in your arsenal. Alliances, vassals, thralls, federations, all kinds of different diplomatic relations with your neighbors. If your missiles don't do them any harm, maybe your federation allies will?
WARFARE: right now is the weakest part of the game. It consists of concentrating your fleet in a single group and facing off against the enemy Doomstack. Whoever has the bigger fleet wins always after just one battle. Defense stations are worthless. (This balacing is currently being fixed, see disclaimer below).
EVENTS: Hundreds of scripted elements and stories, from simple fluff to galaxy-wide cataclysms. Incredible emergent storytelling. Interdimensional visitors? Underground civilizations? Comedy worthy of Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy? They really made an effort in bringing al kinds of disparate Sci-Fi franchises into life.
ENDGAME CRISIS: around the 400-year mark stuff... happens. A crisis is very likely to explode. A crisis that will consume the galaxy and kill billions. And you are suddenly in the front seat in the fight for your own survival. I won't go into spoilers, but think of the REALLY bad things that happen in Warhammer 40K or Babylon 5 or Battlestar Galactica or Mass Effect or Starcraft; after weeks in real life of role-playing all your efforts are suddenly in threat. Can you save the galaxy?
CONCLUSION: The best space chancellor/tyrant/overmind simulator ever. Shame the war system does not do justice to this package of meaty sci-fi. The God-Emperor approves.
[h2]DISCLAIMER[/h2]: big update incoming (called Cherryh), which feels like a sequel aleady. The war system will very likely be fixed, at the cost of removing all FTL methods save Hyperlanes. I am very optimistic, but will reserve judgement until release.

This game is, quite literally, what I've always wanted in a space empire game. To even begin to describe it would take ages, so I'll be succinct: it let's you roleplay as a galactic empire unlike any other game before it. Even the aspects the game is limited in -- such as a lack of micromanaging space battles -- make it even better by letting you focus on what's truly important: galactic politics. Yes, you heard me right. Politics.
Sure, it's not too complex; and sure, the AI is exactly as stupid as you'd expect given our current technology; but what other game can you conquer another empire only to turn them into literal livestock for your consuptiuon? What other game has a victory condition where LITERALLY the entire galaxy can win by joining the same federation? And what other game can a rogue scientist escape to a primitive world, and unite it under his rule using advanced technology?
In short, I love this game and what I've talked about only scratches the surface. It's not for everyone, as it can be quite overwhelming to some people, but if you love the thought of expanding your empire across the galaxy with immense freedom, then this is the game for you!

*****Below remains true but read the edit after the review as well****** IMPORTANT
So a lot of people have reviewed this game. Most with positive feedback. But the reviews, while lengthy and detailed, are often overlooked for that very reason. I encourage you to read more detailed reviews below; but here is what I see as the driving forces behind the game in as little embelishment as possible:
Firstly, the graphics and over all Anime-like art style is stunning, colorful, and fun. 10/10
Secondly, the beauty of the game is it's simplicity and pace. It is the type of game that you can log on to, play for twenty to thirty minutes, and log out feeling like you really accomplished something in game. Fast paced enough and simple enough for the casual gamer, yet the various systems and options available for adventuring in game allow for a veteran to get their kicks as well. 9/10
Finally, like any MMO the quests are important. Understatement I know, however, while it is true that Aura Kingdom subscribes to the whole kill this many this and gather that many that, it is also true that these quests are quickly achieved and the combat is incredibly enjoyable. In that light, kill this many of these becomes, lets kill some more. In addition, there are multiple side quests that are more of a find and seek kind of variety or mystery type quest that can add variety to the overall experience. 8/10
To conclude, due to its gorgeous characters and world, balanced fast paced gameplay, and fun and dazzling combat I would highly recommend Aura Kingdom to any Anime/Manga lover and would encourage everyone else to give it a go as well.

I am a big fan of Saints Row and I say - do not believe all those hipsters online who keep saying that this old game is "the♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; because it is not - apart from being a blatant GTA clone with no individuality, thus game suffers from more than just that...
The whole bundle of Saints Row is definitely worth it - Saints Row III, Saints Row IV and Gat out of Hell are all amazing and innovative games - the series have massively improved since then, just this game automatically comes with them, yet it's still cheaper than buying those three seperately. Nobody should buy SR 2 by itself. Why?
1. Graphics are godawful even for its release year, they look simply cheap and severly lacking detail, also they are not optimized for PC, the performance for PCs MULTIPLE TIMES exceeding the requirements is still horrible - the experience in that aspect is similar to that of GTA 4, it is a bad port, which leads to the next point...
2. It is essentially a console game with rushed port - even the UI is screwed, you don't use "up" and "down" but something like "Shift" and "control" to move forth and back in options, etc. also when you switch through weapons and collectibles, it shows on the screen a CONSOLE BUTTON - even that was not changed... check it out -
- holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ how lazy is that?!
3. Even the movement is laughably bad - when you walk, it looks like that your character is something like a toy soldier which is erratically moved around by a baby who plays with it.
4. Vehicle controls require A MOD to be somewhat playable, the sensitivity of turns is off the charts, it is unnecesserely difficult just to keep the car on the road... I have to add - vehicle controls in Saints Row III are absolutely amazing, and it was one of the first things which surprised me, yes, the company did take note of it and made a change for good in their upcoming releases after this failure.
5. To be able to move forth to the next missions of the main story, you are required to do a certain amount of side activities, which by themselves are not bad, however such system is unnecesserely restrictive and can feel like a chore instead of an entertainment.
To sum up: Saints Row II is low-quality game which is highly overrated by some individuals with very questionable common sense, it does not stand out by anything, it is cliché, without identity, very cheap in value and suffering from a lot of technical and performance issues.
The only reason why you happen to have this game is if you, just like me, bought the whole Saints Row bundle and if you also happen to be more curious about the story of the series.
Forget about this old garbage and move forth to Saints Row III and newer games - Saints Row II is like a dirt and Saints Row III is like the stars - the ascendance which the creators of these series have made is spectacular!
