Finishing this game was in some moments just a pure pain.In this review I will point out advantages and disadvantages of the Saints Row 2.
What's bad:
-Firstly the quality of the port is just horrible.My FPS counter showed that the frames per second barely slightly exceeded 60 on the highest settings and there were some horrible drops during the gameplay even to 20 fps...8 years after the release on i7 and GTX980...
-The second biggest sin of this production is the AI...the developers clearly were not able to create any good algorithms for the non-player characters so they invented a "great"(not really,it's horrible) way to lift the
There are unlimited waves of enemies,besieging you during missions.They simply come out of nowhere.Additionally the devs equipped some of them with the rocket launchers,because otherwise they wouldn't be any threat for you.
-Also the game is not free of bugs.Unfortunately this looks like it was just released - there's a huge amount of unpatched things.Excluding some random crashes,the biggest disaster was the cutscenes,during which items that the characters were interacting with were flying,the NPCs had robotic moves and were disappearing from the frames.But the most hilarious were scenes in the vehicles where the characters were just simply sliding out from them and left empty.
-Some weapons(including the rocket launchers) feel like you were shooting a water gun...
-The SR series is well-know for being crazy,but this part tried to be more mature and it turned out bad.The plot is not interesting at all,it has some funny moments,but it's nothing splendid.
-The graphics also aren't the strong point of this title,even considering they year of release.The most of the textures are average,some are really bad and blurry,even on the highest settings, and the ones in the background,which as I assume were meant to be blurred are pixelated.Additional minus for me is a colour palette,which looks faded.
What's good:
-The customization is a strong point of this game.You can create your own,male or female character,choose the voice,the hair,the way he/she threatens and cheers,later add some tatoos,change the combat style,buy clothes etc. ,etc. But that's not the end! You can modify your cribs,adjust what the gang members should wear and what cars they should drive.There's also a car tuning included.
-The driving system isn't as bad as in the other GTA-wannabe games.It's still as stiff as the corpse in the trunk of the protagonist's car,but it's pretty easy to learn and doesn't cause any problems during the gameplay.
-The side missions diversity is also worthy highlighting.There's a lot of side activities to do.From protecting your hommies to insurance frauds.Unfortunately even if you're not interested with them,you gotta be probably forced to do some,because you need a respect to do the main missions and the side activities are a good source of it.(Better invest in your style by buying cars,clothes etc. it boost the respect).
-A big choice of vehicles.
-Destroyable elements of the environment(especially in the missions taking place in the buildings).
-I gotta also admit that the soundtrack is great.There isn't as many songs as in the GTA,but the seleced ones are very good.
Better spare your nerves and money  and buy SR3 or SR4...or simply any game from the GTA series.

So I'm probably gonna sound like I'm jumping on the bandwagon here, but this really is the best Saints Row game they made if you're into just straight up shooting and gangster♥♥♥♥♥♥ Compared to the first Saints Row game, the basics are pretty much the same: you decide which gang you want to take missions against, but each mission you take means you lose a bit of respect, meaning that you have to do side quests in order to earn enough respect to do subsequent missions. But they basically just improved this game in every way you can think of: making Stillwater bigger and more diverse than it was before; adding different types of vehicles other than cars, vans and HGVs to let you get across the city in new ways; adding in autosave and checkpoints so you're not constantly having to save the game in case you lose at a side game, that sort of thing. And there are also a lot of really minor but appreciated improvements like having to hold the reload button down before you pick up a different weapon rather than just pressing it, so you don't accidentaly replace your fully-loaded Desert Eagle with some crappy 9mm because you were trying to reload your SMG.
But by far the best improvement of this game over the original is that it's no longer a 360 exclusive. I mean, the original game just ran like absolute crap on the Xbox 360, like it would be lucky to get 30FPS at 720p, more like 15 to 20. But by far the biggest joke was the absolutely ridiculous looking alpha channel rendering, which looked like the sort of blocky♥♥♥♥♥♥I used to see on the original Sims game or something. As far as the PC version of SR2 does performance-wise, it runs ok, but unfortunately with it being a late 32-bit game, you're not going to get fantastic framerates unless you have some serious GPU clock speeds that can just bruteforce their way to it. With my setup, I managed to get consistently between 30 and 60 FPS on the maximum settings @1080p.
As far as the series of games goes, as I've said, I think this is about as good as it gets. Why they decided to go in the direction they did for the subsequent games, I really don't know, but I think they felt like they were being criticized for being too much like GTA's poor relation, so they decided to go in completely the opposite direction and just make the games as "out there" as possible, which personally I just think completely backfired on the whole series. I mean I thought SR3 was pretty good apart from the whole sci-fi lazerguns♥♥♥♥♥♥ but SR4 with these aliens blowing up earth and trapping you inside the matrix I just thought was ♥♥♥♥ing stupid. I know the publishers were pretty much going under after they made SR2, but I think their attempt to compensate for it just made things worse rather than better. My only criticisms with SR2 are that the story does lack depth, the AI of the vehicles is annoyingly stupid, the controls when it comes to aiming are a bit "unorthodox", and the mouse controls are overly sensitive. Also, there is a technical glitch where the game tends to crash after a while if you've got a controller plugged in. But apart from that, this is really a fantastic game if you're looking for a fun 3rd person open-world shooter with a fair share of humour thrown in, and IMO is definitely not a "poor relation" of GTA at all, but rather encapsulates a lot of the stuff you wish you could do in GTA.

Okay, here's an honest and unbiased critique (not a review) of Dead Rising 3 on PC.  My PC's specs meet and exceed the minimum requirements - so the game should be able to run on mid to high settings.  For a list of my specs check near the bottom of this "review".  This critique is not about the Dead Rising 3 story or any of the other games in the series.  There are no spoilers!
First off, Dead Rising 3 is playable but only due to sacrificing its entertainment value.  The gameplay would probably be fun and entertaining if the game had at least been optimized properly.  Unfortunately, Dead Rising 3 fails in most aspects due to it's glaring technical problems and severe lack of proper optimization.  Now, nevermind the fact that DR3 is only 30FPS (if you want a somewhat more stable experience), but the fact that the framerate drops are still noticeable when locked at 30FPS is more than a little annoying.  Worst of all, the pre-rendered cutcenes are hit even harder than actual gameplay (the cutscenes appear to use the in-engine graphics so I don't know WTF the problem is).  In other words, the cutscenes are choppy and the actual gameplay suffers less than the cutscenes do, even with a couple of hundred zombies on the screen at one time.   This makes the entire experience jarring and unenjoyable.  I was able to hit, hack, slash, and chop up zombies, after doing some serious playing around with the games advanced graphics settings.  However, I could not find a way to properly fix the god-awful pre-rendered cutscenes.
I played the actual game for a little over an hour, and quite honestly, I don't want to continue until this mess is cleaned up.  I spent about an hour trying out the actual gameplay and about another hour attempting to adjust every individual setting to see what sort of impact they would have on the graphics and gameplay.  Unfortunately, due to the lack of proper optimization, Dead Rising 3 does not reach the level of potential, in terms of it's gameplay fluidity, that actually makes me want to keep playing the game.  It's quite a shame since my PC exceeds the minimum requirements by more than enough to merit a decent and enjoyable experience even at mid-level graphics settings - but the game unfortunately doesn't pull it off.
Here are my specs:
OS: Windows 8.1 64-bit edition
Processor: Intel Core i7-4770 @ 4.00GHz
Memory: 12 GB RAM
Graphics: NVIDIA® GeForce® GTX 650 1GB / and 1 GB VRAM
DirectX: Version 11
Network: Broadband Internet connection
Sound Card: DirectX 11 Compatible sound card
I didn't bother trying the co-op mode because if the game is so badly ported that the Single Player mode is messed up, then the co-op mode can only be worse in terms of framerate drops and choppiness.
So, to conclude this brief but informative critique, if your PC surpasses the minimum specification requirements, and it doesn't exceed the recommened specification requirements, then you probably want to avoid this port until the game is heavily optimized, modified, and updated!  Save your money and be patient.  There are plenty of other games coming out over the coming weeks and months.
NOTE:  This "review" will be editied if / when Capcom adds, removes, or fixes (hopefully) Dead Rising 3.
EDIT:  For reference, here's a list of games that I can play in 1080p using high - ultra settings with my current PC specs:
- Titanfall
- Battlefield 3
- Batman: Arkham Origins
- Saints Row IV
- Max Payne 3
- Hitman Absolution
- Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag
- Dead Island

That's just to name a few.  Now if I can run those in 1080p using Ultra or High settings usually getting 60fps (the ones that don't have their framerate capped) then, I should have nowhere near the amount of choppiness or the annoying framerate dips that litter Dead Rising 3 on high or even medium settings.  Definitely one of Capcom's worst PC titles thus far.

I'm going to come in from a view that is mostly unbiased.
As I have only played the first game for half a year.
This new one, I was on and off since before the official release.
This game and the one that came before it has always had it's ups and downs.
But the same will be said of any game. The importance is in the developer's willingness to expand based on what the players want, or what they are talking about.
As a player, nothing is more thrilling than the concept that you and the community have daydreamed of something until nights end, only to find out it's going to become a feature in an update or new game! Extinction brought a lot to the table, they offer many graphic features that you can tinker with as well. Many may complain about the lag this causes right off the bat. However the common case is that the system has put the settings at the max that your computer CAN handle, but not always what it will run smoothly on. I suggest playing with these options and lowering settings here and there for those experiencing choppiness.
But besides the look of the textures and models themselves, a fresh perspective was clearly taken on the environments and the level of detail in realism. I can't exactly count how many times I've stopped to see rain trickling down a metal sheet or became enthralled by sand blowing off the edge of a cliff, only to be shot down as a result of my appreciation for such features. Which brings me to my next point.
This game is not just for PVPers. PC may have begun with this concept in mind and the main theme of the game is still PVP. It's entire structure is crafted to support the needs of players fighting other players. However there are little tid bits that suggest the developers have noticed and even supported their more artistically inclined audience. Not just the environments, but the addition of features that allow you to set up a functioning role player server. Such as allowing an endless number of folks to be dinosaurs or humans, picking out maps that were made with tons of little hidey holes and good story telling scenes, and even turning off PVP completely so that no one can be ripped from their scene by a trigger happy trapper or that one rex who is just having a majorly bad day and only the feeling of something squished between his toes is going to change that. It's very humbling that the developers are willing to listen to and welcome all of their players, even ones they might not have expected to have. Many young and old dinosaur lovers have flocked to the game. And they were not met with failure to take their passions seriously. The makers have stepped up, revving the diversity of the species and the correction of their anatomy to please the hardcore dino-fan.
Such aspects may seem small in comparison to what one might expect from a game about 'I shoot you, you chomp me.' But it's proof that Primal Carnage is a game run by folk that can and will always evolve. The fact that we can put faith in how much our opinions mean to the developers is something many more games need today. I hope that in the future it becomes a MUST to please your players.
And before anyone thinks I forgot, yes I will remark about the game-play itself because even as an .. obvious role-player myself.. I too partake in the -carnage- on and off. I'm not satisfied with only one aspect of the game and if I try to go too long without either, it becomes boring fast. Sometimes the intricate tales of monsters lurking in the forest makes me restless to go unleash those skills against others in PVP, and as previously stated, the game is built upon the idea of PVP. You can choose your class of human or dinosaur. And though a majority of us obviously enjoys hurling ourselves on a human, turns are taken to make it fair for everyone. The human classes are nothing to sneeze at either. While I always feel a bit dull in comparison to the beast I was moments before, I quickly get over it and focus on fighting again.  It's equally as satisfying to group up as humans and gun down a pack of raptor. Depending on what game-style you're best at, it's very important to find the class for you and start practicing it right away. (The community itself has made MANY guides on the tactics of these classes.)
All of that sounds like too many good points right? Well that's not even all of it, I just knew that no one would read a review this long without being paid generously. But for those who only feel safe purchasing a game after they have seen the flaws they are dealing with, well I'm here to deliver that unbiased opinion just as I promised. Like almost any PVP game, the community itself is fast paced, a lot of them are very young players as well. You may find an army waiting in a server to CAPSLOCK at you about your tactic verses theirs. However you may also find a community of well rounded adults who simply play the game and don't need to make remarks on others to validate themselves. My advice for those bouts of sour saps is to ignore them. Even if they call you or your game-play some ridiculous names, you just keep being you and have fun!
Another issue would be a pickle of bugs here and there this early on. Please make note of the DATE of this rating because the game is practically  brand spanking new of this year, you simply cannot expect everyone to have found every bug yet. When they are found, they are fixed. But they do exist and when you find them you are encouraged to report them instead of quit the game. Be a contribution to the betterment of the game!
The last topic I can offer is .. one I don't fully understand but have heard of among the other players. General issues running the game or lag or bugs that no one else seems to be experiencing. All I can say is that I have never personally experienced any issues like this on PC: extinction. These problems may be to do with something on the players end that can easily be searched up on a forum and fixed.

This game is okay, the gameplay is fun at times but it's really consistent. That's not exactly a good or a bad thing. The whole problem is that it's always that the human team spawn in a random place and the whole team is huddled up somewhere. But the spawns are random and you get separated from everyone if you die. Then there are the straggler dinosaurs that just kill you on the spot because there's no one to help you.
What I would like to see is being allowed to spawn on a teammate or spawn on like flares, mines, or health packs which can be dropped by your teammates. That would allow more teamwork involved and not just have pyros holding down m1 whenever a dinosaur shows up and you die anyways.
Playing as a dinosaur, it can be really frustrating. You are very limited but yet overpowered. It seems that it's always in one favor of a single team. Wow, is this game overhyped. I'll be the most cynical person ever, and post a negative review purely to try and add SOME balance to the plethora of positive reviews. That, and I simply think the game isn't worth the 60EUR asking price.
Here's the thing - the game is by no means BAD. Heck, if we had a more varied score system I'd easily rate it "above average". But it by no means lives up to the "grand masterpiece GOTY you must get it" reviews people seem to be writing.
So let's break it down into the typical sections.
Visually the game is good - there's definitely a few moments that are a pleasure to look at (and no, I don't just mean the main characters bum / thighs). The game makes a pretty clever use of colours - while most of the time the colours are muted, this seems to be deliberate, so that when the colour does show up, it's emphasised. The various characters that show up all have a nice (if sometimes really weird) design. But the quality of environmental visuals occasionally dips into "meh" territory, with certain areas looking like a bland, cheap Korean MMO. Additionally, while the game has these smooth transitions from 3D to 2.5D, this sometimes feels really cheap when the background becomes a meaningless backdrop, rather than something real. This is mostly visible in the "flying" sections of the game.
Sound is where the game shines. Well, music, really. The music is REALLY good. Like, REALLY REALLY good. So credit where credit's due - if I were to rate the game on music alone, then hell yea, I'd say it's GOTY material. As for the other sounds? They're OK. They do the job. The voice acting, however, leaves a lot to be desired. Not the quality of voice acting itself, perhaps, but rather the fact that there's so little of it. It's jarring. On one hand you have a massive game like The Witcher 3, with tons of dialogue (all voiced)... and then you have a game like Nier: Automata, which feels like it has far far less dialogue and they couldn't even bother to voice it all. Additionally, it almost feels half-finished, with voice-overs missing almost at random for certain dialogues, which creates this really strange experience. I almost thought my game was bugged and was simply not playing the voice-overs sometimes... So while the music is awesome and the sound neutral, the missing voice-overs bring everything down.
Gameplay and story is where the biggest let-down is, I believe. While the combat is solid (or should be - I'm not an expert at these types of games), the gameplay often revolves around terribly boring and lazy quests. Go there, kill some dudes, come back. This is repeated over and over and over again and is made even more aggravating because for quite a long while you don't have access to any sort of fast-travel method. Add to this large, MMO-like open spaces and you have a really boring experience.
But I need to give credit where credit is due - the boss battles are interesting and well designed, with bosses themselves having interesting designs and abilities. Still, getting to them is a slog.
Story-wise the game gets a ton of praise... for not really doing anything really special. So, rather than having something akin to chapters, the game "fakes" endings, where it suggests you play again... except this subsequent play-through isn't REALLY a "new game +" as it would be in other games. It is, in fact, the next chapter. In total, there are 3 such "chapters" (and the last one has two endings). And while the last one is sufficiently different to be somewhat interesting in terms of contents, the second one is a major bore as is repeats LARGE sections of the first chapter almost verbatim. And since I wanted to slap the stupid out of the characters on more than one occasion, having to experience the same stupidity multiple times isn't helping things.
Finally people have praised the philosophical aspects of the game, to the point where some "have questioned their own existence"... to this I can only reply "WTF?!". This is philosophy 101, really. The ideas presented aren't in any way original or groundbreaking, and if you ever took a philosophy course / lesson or simply had a few evenings of existential thought then you're way WAY past the questions posed. And the philosophical ideas the game presents are left there, unexplored, as the story does basically nothing with them. It just asks a few, basic questions about existence, and then sends you to kill more robots, which really undermines the whole thing.
The game isn't bad. It really isn't. It's OK. It's decent. I could mention the pretty well designed skill-system, or how heart-warming the final ending is (there's a certain charm to it even my cynical self cannot deny). But none of that changes the fact that the game is by no means perfect, it's not GOTY, it's not without flaws (plenty of which I also didn't list, BTW) and that at the end of the day the game is overpriced and overrated.
If you manage to find this game on sale (40%+ at least) then you'll get yourself a great deal. Otherwise I wouldn't bother. Just make sure to look up the OST somewhere online.

I found myself very confused with the choices of keybinds the game gives you for default;"R to glide" "Double tapping S to suddenly stop gliding". Those are 2 early examples and while the keybinds aren't the best; The glide ability is very appreciated, a neat way to get to places faster; although unrealistic for the most part.
Back to movement, Click to move or WASD or Arrows; Your only source of camera  movement is by means of your mouse which means Arrows are a definite "No". When entering battle which contains elements of "move out of red or be hit by massive damage" it can be tricky for people new to computer gaming or those who aren't used to juggling mouse and keyboard, going from mouse to arrows or WASD while keeping your fingers on Tab for target and 1234 while keeping track of the enemy cast bar..... can be irritating and complicated at times. Especially if you play in a restricted place IE: A small desk.
Apart from the clunky camera and movement controls the games runs great, it has a decent amount of classes but kind of lacking on the "Character customization" front. A bit sad since the art style is absolutely beautiful! Monster's are fairly diversified which is a welcome addition, since newly MMORPGs kind of stopped caring about the amount of different monsters and decided to start throwing in the same monsters with a different names and sizes (Cough cough FF14 cough cough Destiny cough cough)
Skill system is neat so far you have your basic "Spam" attack, your core special attack on a low cooldown and a weird "Ultimate" attack which does INSANE amounts of damage even at low levels. Did I mention there's no mana, that's a damn great change, more games should take that route, basically means no waiting for Mana... Ever.
Health regen is a bit of a complaint for me so far. Your health regens "VERY SLOW" outside of combat and since your potions are auto used in combat when you come close to death, it gets very tiresome to wait around for your health between engagements, a shame since Mana here isn't an issue.
The story is quite "RPG cliche" and the quest are very repetitive, IE: Kill X number of Y to collect Z; Kill X mobs Y times or pick up X amount of Z resources off the ground.
In conclusion; The game is great, runs smoothly even on a subpar gaming PC and the major variety of terrains/land/mobs/pets are welcomed. The community is generally friendly and enjoyable, the F2P doesn't seem to kill the game at lower levels (not sure about endgame). Quests will eventually be very grindy and repetitive but can be a nice alternative while relaxing and doing mindless tasks such as listening to music or a podcast of sort especially since the health regen times can be dreadful. Camera and movement controls are very clunky and I think that might be the biggest flaw, keeping the game from reaching it's full potential. The combat system is a very nice change of paste from most MMORPGs and is a welcome addition mixing in a bit of twist by removing mana and incorporating cool "Ultimate" abilities.
In my honest opinion, I would rate this game a 7/10. Not a must play but a very decent title which is sadly held back by poor design decisions.

Okay, here's an honest and unbiased critique (not a review) of Dead Rising 3 on PC.  My PC's specs meet and exceed the minimum requirements - so the game should be able to run on mid to high settings.  For a list of my specs check near the bottom of this "review".  This critique is not about the Dead Rising 3 story or any of the other games in the series.  There are no spoilers!
First off, Dead Rising 3 is playable but only due to sacrificing its entertainment value.  The gameplay would probably be fun and entertaining if the game had at least been optimized properly.  Unfortunately, Dead Rising 3 fails in most aspects due to it's glaring technical problems and severe lack of proper optimization.  Now, nevermind the fact that DR3 is only 30FPS (if you want a somewhat more stable experience), but the fact that the framerate drops are still noticeable when locked at 30FPS is more than a little annoying.  Worst of all, the pre-rendered cutcenes are hit even harder than actual gameplay (the cutscenes appear to use the in-engine graphics so I don't know WTF the problem is).  In other words, the cutscenes are choppy and the actual gameplay suffers less than the cutscenes do, even with a couple of hundred zombies on the screen at one time.   This makes the entire experience jarring and unenjoyable.  I was able to hit, hack, slash, and chop up zombies, after doing some serious playing around with the games advanced graphics settings.  However, I could not find a way to properly fix the god-awful pre-rendered cutscenes.
I played the actual game for a little over an hour, and quite honestly, I don't want to continue until this mess is cleaned up.  I spent about an hour trying out the actual gameplay and about another hour attempting to adjust every individual setting to see what sort of impact they would have on the graphics and gameplay.  Unfortunately, due to the lack of proper optimization, Dead Rising 3 does not reach the level of potential, in terms of it's gameplay fluidity, that actually makes me want to keep playing the game.  It's quite a shame since my PC exceeds the minimum requirements by more than enough to merit a decent and enjoyable experience even at mid-level graphics settings - but the game unfortunately doesn't pull it off.
Here are my specs:
OS: Windows 8.1 64-bit edition
Processor: Intel Core i7-4770 @ 4.00GHz
Memory: 12 GB RAM
Graphics: NVIDIA® GeForce® GTX 650 1GB / and 1 GB VRAM
DirectX: Version 11
Network: Broadband Internet connection
Sound Card: DirectX 11 Compatible sound card
I didn't bother trying the co-op mode because if the game is so badly ported that the Single Player mode is messed up, then the co-op mode can only be worse in terms of framerate drops and choppiness.
So, to conclude this brief but informative critique, if your PC surpasses the minimum specification requirements, and it doesn't exceed the recommened specification requirements, then you probably want to avoid this port until the game is heavily optimized, modified, and updated!  Save your money and be patient.  There are plenty of other games coming out over the coming weeks and months.
NOTE:  This "review" will be editied if / when Capcom adds, removes, or fixes (hopefully) Dead Rising 3.

Looking through the very mixed bag of reviews for Dead Rising 3 it may be hard to get an idea of whether or not this game is actually worth your time. So I figured I'd come up with a quick list of Pros and Cons of things that I've noticed from my experience with Dead Rising 3 on steam to help those considering the purchase.
Pros:
*There are an acceptable amount of graphics options to configure
*All keyboard and mouse controls are fairly intuitive and can all be changed to suit your liking
*The crafting system is far better than the previous Dead Rising and can be accessed anywhere on the fly
*Most animations and models are all fairly high quality
*The Characters are believable and seem more diverse then in the previous Dead Rising games
*The Main Character is likeable and not a total♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(however this may be a con for some people who liked Chuck Greene or Frank West)
*With the new AI more zombies can be on the screen at one time
*Vehicles handle surprisingly well
*Inventory management isn’t required, which was kind of a fault in Dead Rising 2
*Online Co-op is easy to start with little hassle at all
*...Annnd Killing zombies is just as satisfying if not more satisfying than ever
...I could probably come up with a few more but these are just the things that stuck out to me the most and what I thought was worth mentioning.
Cons:
*Frame Rate is locked at 30fps out of the box (Can be unlocked with a simple edit to the games files)
*The game is poorly optimized overall (just to give you a perspective, Dead Rising 3 unlocked with maxed settings on my GTX 780ti will get anywhere from 80fps all the way down to 30 fps and on rare occasions dipping below 30)
*Texture quality isn't that great, nor is it good enough to justify the extremely variable frame rates
*It's very easy to craft and obtain extremely powerful weapons very early on which kind of unbalances the game overall
*The game is still kinda buggy in places and some people are claiming they are having issues with crashing still (luckly I haven't had a single crash since the new Nvidia 344.11 drivers came out which seems to have fixed the majority of crashes for nvidia users)
...All I can really think of at the moment. So far these are the only issues that I've ran into, your mileage may vary. Would I recommend the game even with these issues? All and all the gameplay and mechanics are what make Dead Rising 3 really shine, so I think I can safely say I would. I will definitely be able to give a more in-depth review once I finsih the game and have a better idea of the game as a whole.

So, if you ever played Fighting Fantasy and you don't buy this game, then you are missing out on some hardcore nostalgia.

A challenging, faithful adaptation to three classic Fighting Fantasy Adventure gamebooks. I've seen it referred to as a "card game", but the main combat and luck mechanics are dice based. Knowledge and items gained from exploring the many different options presented to you will provide the most efficient and safest paths to success, but it will take you a few goes to learn them!
Fantastic journey back to my formative years while I wait for the relaunched paperback versions to arrive :)
Absolutely looking forward to some DLC!
Great game, loyal in many ways to the original Fighting Fantasy game books. Plenty of replayability and potential for future expansions.

Like many, I grew up reading the Fighting Fantasy series. Each book taking you on an adventure where you would battle ferocious monsters and try to defeat villainous tyrants. You might not always win but that was the point. The next time you read the book you could make different choices and learn from your previous mistakes.
Playing Fight Fantasy Legends evokes exactly that same feeling, except this time, you are on a huge adventure to defeat three of the Fighting Fantasy series' greatest villains. You get three books for the price of one.
Playing the game and reading the text took me right back to how it felt to read the gamebooks. Nomad have done a terrific job in capturing the feeling of the Fighting Fantasy series.
It is beautifully designed too. As you play you'll notice lots of detail in the landscape and locations. The textures and animations make it very pretty to look at. Sound and music again are top-notch. I appreciated the individual character walk cycles too. You can see the weight and slight waddle to the dwarf as he walks and the sprightly strides of the long legged elf. There's lots of attention to detail here.
As I played I was continually surprised by game mechanics and the way that specific choices and actions would have consequences later in the game. Again, it echoed playing the original game book series perfectly.
As has been said, this is the closest you will get to playing a Fighting Fantasy book. Nomad have designed and produced a brilliant game. New players can look forward to a really fun fantasy based RPG taking them on a fantastic adventure where YOU are the hero!.

Wow, what a great product.
The steam controller was obviously made to combat the common "But I like to play games from the couch with a controller!" argument from console gamers. The Steam controller, in Big Picture mode, lets you seamlessly switch between games, the steam overlay and a web browser configurable with default favorites. Not only that, but it automatically configures to common games, and gives you the option to custom config with your preferred settings. It's a plug-and-play solution to let you game from a kicked-back seat rather than hunched at your battle station.
Outside of Big Picture mode, this controller will let you interact with Windows, as well. The right trackpad has haptic feedback and a precise amount of control. The left trackpad works like a scroll wheel a la iPod Classic. The combination lets you scroll smoothly while having the precision to select links, click small buttons, and perform other actions you might need in a setting such as playing music or watching YouTube or Netflix.
The design is very well thought out and effective. Like a now-standard Xbox 360-style PC controller, you get the usual joystick and directional control options, but the highly responsive haptic feedback in these inputs along with the trackpad gives a lot more confidence than a standard joystick-based controller. The triggers and bumpers are large and let the hand remain relaxed for extended gameplay and input sessions. The addition of two more rear triggers for the ring fingers/pinkies adds more input options PC gamers will probably find themselves needing. They are set to jump and duck by default for TF2, allowing you to jump and duck without taking your fingers off of movement(joystick), look(trackpad), or reload/weapon change buttons(bumpers). This was a big fallback of using standard controllers for PC gaming in the past, and is just one example of many in how this controller's design puts it far ahead of anything before it.
I see the steam controller being effective for all but the most competetive shooters (CS will always be a M+KB game). Call of Duty, Team Fortress 2, Fallout etc. will all be casually enjoyable. This controller has enough sensitivity and precision to be used in RTS/City Builder type games. Third person games should shine with the highly accurate trackpad sensors. The best use, of course, will be Indie Platform/Adventure/Racing
I look forward to continuing to explore the possibilities of this hardware. I believe it will open up my gaming possibilities in the direction I was hoping, switching to a TV and couch setup for many of my games.

Ok, I've never heard of 'Fighting Fantasy' before I picked up this game, but watching some pre-release video of the game made it look interesting. It's a fun time-burner at a $10 price point, but after about 20 hours or so sunk into the game there's nothing left to do.
Basically I'd describe it by calling it a Choose-your-own-adventure book meets an RPG. The combat system is dice-based, but encounters are card drawn. As you progress in the game, you earn more faces for your die, improving your odds of overcoming combat or luck resolutions.
Once you complete all three level of difficulty there's not much replay left, aside from hunting down achievements. The developer, Nomad Games, is good about listening to player feedback and bug reports, and so far has been fast on the hot fixes.
If you have a household where more than one person will be playing, I'd definately reccomend it. A couple of kids who want to play it when you're done makes the purchase more than worthwhile.
If the game has any other major downside though, it's that you can't have multiple save games at a given time. You only have one save slot available to you.

Fighting Fantasy has seen something of a rebirth over the past three years in the form of comics, new book releases and a video game. Each have been very hit and miss among the old school fans of this brand but NomadGames have sailed through creating not one but three adventure games with an ariel view of the world of Titan reminiscent of the good old 80s computer games such as Gauntlet or Druid. Not only have they padded areas such as Port Blacksand and Firetop Mountain out with multiple nods to the original books, they have added a whole lot more of their own stuff without breaking the consistancy of the Allansian feel.

Hello everybody, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for The Journey Down: Chapter 2 by SkyGoblin.
The Journey Down Chapter 2 is a point and click adventure game that continues the story of Bwana, Kito and Lina after their airplane crashes into the mist. The game begins with our heroes being rescued by a small eel fishing vessel that’s been lost at sea. The majority of the game takes place in the city of Port Artue which is only mentioned in Chapter 1.
Port Artue is a place full of corruption. Where the rich spend all their time at Club Temba and the poor (Misters) are left doing the work. Upon arrival in Port Artue they’re confronted by the police chief, Barlow. Bwana and Kito are arrested and Lina and her book are taken elsewhere.
In this chapter, the game engine has seen an upgrade and it renders Port Artue in beautiful fashion. The city is beautifully detailed and it still utilizes it’s hand drawn 2D/3D mixture to winning effect. The game also features a section with rain effects and the puddles of water shining on the ground are quite impressive. The lighting effects have also seen an upgrade and they really add to the atmosphere in many areas. The cinema’s lights are the most impressive I felt.
Much like the first game, this game features a superb soundtrack. This time it uses a more jazz oriented theme and it sounds amazing. It fits the city of Port Artue perfectly and it really adds to the atmosphere. There were quite a few really catchy songs in this game, including the main menu theme once it got going.
This chapter is also an hour longer than chapter 1 as well. I clocked in at 4.3 hours to completion. I completed Chapter 1 in 3.3 hours by comparison. The chapter features a large variety of puzzles and they’re always fun to solve.
Overall, The Journey Down Chapter 2 was a superb continuation to Bwana’s journey and I can’t recommend it highly enough. The game features a great story, an excellent soundtrack, gorgeous artwork, and a great cast of interesting characters. It’s a great game all around and it makes me excited to see how Bwana’s story will end in the final chapter.

With only the tease of an adventure after leaving Kingsport Bay, we continue a little bit after Chapter One ended. We left Brawna, Kito, and Lina just as they flew away from Kingsport Bay, but with forgetting gas they were left to drift around in the water. Till a boat happened to catch them in their net. Without a lighthouse to guide and a thick fog surrounding them, arriving at land may be difficult to do. At this time, you can also go to Kito for a story recap.
Eventually, you will get back on land after getting a few objects to help in navigating through dense fog. We can’t have a part of the story based on being on a boat the whole time after all. After docking, we find out that the mysterious place plagued with thick fog is Port Artue. Port Artue is not like Kingsport Bay, corruption runs rampant throughout the higher ups. With St. Armando Power Company possibly being the main link to why corruption has taken Port Artue, leaving those doing the work to keep the town running wallowing in a bar. So when a police officer takes the Journal of the Journey Down by force, well, it may not be a surprise to the residents but a surprise to us.
Instead of grabbing some parts of an airplane, here we deal with the corruption of Port Artue as well as helping the town get back on it’s feet. All leading towards getting the Journal of the Journey Down back and hopefully get to the Underland safely. A lot of questions that were brought up in Chapter One gains some more development in this installment, having played out in this very town.
The puzzles take up the same mantle to solve them. A lot of them are really easy to figure out, with the hints portrayed by dialogue or by other objects needing items that will lead to the puzzle being solved. At times you will get to points where you have to get something, which can stem into a few other puzzles to solve to gain that particular item to advance. However, the last puzzle of the game does hike in difficulty as only half of it is hinted at.
As we left Kingsport Bay and arrived at Port Artue, we are able to see a whole new area meant to be a town rather than a few places meant to service those visiting. In terms of art style, you still get hand drawn backgrounds and modeled characters based on African tribal masks. With being in more of a town, you do get the sense of people living here and the possible scope of it. With a few interesting ways they show traveling as they focus on colors rather than detailed line art. The sense of Port Artue being a port is also shown by the differing face shapes and accents the new characters possess.
The sound quality has gone up but not quite there. I often found that some characters had a higher volume than Brawna or the other way around. There were instances where you did expect their voices to go lower, whispering to themselves a realization they had, but there were some instances where Brawna’s voice was lower than the background music and became harder to hear him.
Unsurprisingly, the soundtrack still holds the same quality as the last chapter. Unlike before, two different composers worked to give Port Artue a unique powerful jazz feel. Even if you never found out that there were different composers, it is hard to tell as both blend in together nicely that it may as well of been done by one person.
+ Soundtrack
+ Visuals
+ Sense of Port Artue being a popular spot to dock/live
+ Character design
+ Logical puzzles
- Dialogue volume differs between characters and can cause some lines to be lower than the music

This game gives you the opportunity to choose not only one class over a high number of available classes, but also to combine two of them into one. This kind of feature is almost non-existant in the world of MMORPG's. There was once Runes of Magic, which was (I have to say) more deeper in terms of primary and secondary jobclass, because no matter which classes you took, you could always create some hybrid skills only available to the combination class. In Aura Kingdom, you get for one class about 2-3 recommended classes in the passive skill tree. Once you have that recommend class, you can unlock some specific skills only available to the combination. If you take a different non-recommended class, you won't have such a special skill, but you surely will have fun nonetheless.
Why? You ask? Because Aura Kingdom doesn't punish you for taking different classes. Furthermore, your choices have impact on your character. For example, I've chosen for my first character the class 'Tachi' (The name is kind of ironic, because a Tachi is a saber-like katana, but in fact the class Tachi uses a extremely long version of a Katana which is called Odachi/Otachi/Nodachi). The class Tachi is a great mid to close combat class that excels in bursts, fast attacks and AoE. For my secondary class, I didn't use the recommended classes (Wizard/Katar/Necromancer) because all three of them are not my style, atleast not in the style I wanted the character to be. So I used the Gunslinger. Why? The Gunslinger class is a great sub-class because he generates up to 5 different ammunition that can heal, reduce enemy target's damage, deal damage over time or reduce the target's armor and more. The Gunslinger class is also a great single-target focused class, with a few skills that can deal damage in a line of path. He also has some traps that can snare the target, which is great for the Tachi to set up his special skills. On top of that, the Tachi can dash multiple times, appear at the target and yet has only one ranged attack. With the Gunslinger, the Tachi becomes fearless in both close and ranged attack and I have met many situations where I couldn't go head-first into the fight and had to attack from afar.
There's another example. I've chosen for my secondary character Ravager. The Ravager is a beast, with a ramping damage amplifier, he can deal tons of damage in short time. He also has two ranged skills, but the best thing on him is his durability. However, he has no real sustain and can be bested with damage over time and crowd control. So I've chosen as a secondary class the Sorcerer. The Sorcerer has great range capabilities and is similar to the Gunslinger, a great secondary class to build its special resource in the course of time. The Sorcerer can leech, heal and inflict a formidable stun. On top of that, he has a great AoE sleep skill and contributes very well with a debuff that he inflicts on the target, which heals the attacker everytime when the enemy target is hit.
Aura Kingdom also offers a variety of dungeons, which can be attended fast with a dungeon finder plus teleport. Like in many MMORPG's, you find out that there is no connection between high level players and low level players. Mostly you'll encounter them only if you're a high levler yourself - Not in Aura Kingdom. You can encounter and fight with them already with level 45 and play with them in dungeons, because there are so many things you can do in this game and everything contributes to a goal.
This is my review. Most people wouldn't agree, as they see to many negative things in Aura Kingdom.
Yes, I've played 111 hours. Yes, I've tried to get a Eidolon (battle pet) about 50 times in the temple and only fragments of keys dropped. Yes, I know that you have only three character slots which can be unlocked with loyalty (obtained through questing and so on) or with real money.
The focus on Aura Kingdom is to have fun, and for a long time I can agree with that. Since AION 2.1, Tera CBT, RoM GameForge and WoWotLK I didn't had so much fun and was so addicted to a MMORPG. I know this won't last forever, but I'll try to enjoy the game until it's dawnfall. And I hope you will find great joy in this game as well.

It has been nearly two months since I played NieR: Automata. It was the first 4K game that I played on my new Rig which in fully 4K ready so that I was able to play on optimal settings for the best visual effects. I read a number of very positive reviews about the game and that's why I purchased and summarily played it. I even disseminated some information at its respective wiki for the edification of fellow players. It is true that the game has a well refined synergy between visual, auditory (sound effects, vocals, music, etc.) which melds in a seamless confluence, transporting one into an experience that is simultaneously rare and remarkably unique. It is also true that the adventure is wondrous and one is drawn in wholly so that moving through the game is a sublime compulsion. One becomes so familiar with the protagonists and so fond of them that they feel quite like family. That is where the problem lies, in my assessment, because the developers made a singular but significant error, or at least a major miscalculation.
There are no "good endings" but many endings, the majority of which are not only bad but fraught with sorrow, many with hopelessness, some that are just poor jokes. All of these possible endings I could discount if there were but one clearly "happy" ending where there is some manifest hope and redemption, a definitive reward for having made wise choices. It seems apparent to me that Square Enix wished to make a statement against war and perhaps an illustration of the violence in and the futility of life rather that making a game that people would love to experience again and again. I have learned in life that the human creature can tolerate only so much of death. Death which occurs close to one, especially that of friends and loved ones fills said capacity much more rapidly. Perhaps it was by design to force gamers to go on to buy their next game. I, for one, feel betrayed. A game should, in my opinion, not make one regret playing it over and over trying to make things turn out "right" without that being a possibility. A work of art is defined by its ability to create emotion and NieR:Automata achieves this in so many ways. Howevrer, the game should not have ended with clearly defined negative emotions. Rather, the developers had the opportunity to transform its players so they would experience the joy and the hope in learning the inner reward for overcoming adversity and doing in the end what is noble, right, and just. Such is life's greatest lesson. I will now more carefully choose my next game and certainly before I decide to be a patron of Square Enix.

Ok. This probably sounds contradicting.
Yes, I have spent hours playing this game. I completed it once. Still, I cannot recommend it.
Why? Because it is frustratingly random. The mechanics, the story - everything is bizarre. I walk into a tavern and approach the barkeeper. He draws his dagger shouting he doesn't serve strangers. I attack. He opens a trapdoor behind the bar and a troll jumps out. I kill the troll. The barkeeper apologizes and offers me a free drink.
Seriously?
Very few options, some with absolutely bizarre outcomes. "Do you want to be pleasant or demand answers forcefully?" - Be pleasant. - "He is enraged by your pleasantries!"
Most annoying is the fact that most of the time you cannot go back. E.g. there are multiple, always linear ways to cross a city. You have to do this multiple times, leaving and entering the city again, to get to all the points of interest. With no map to help you! Very frustrating. Oh - and do not hesitate to attack and kill every shopkeeper you come across and break into every house that sparks your interest. Sometimes it's an easy and cheap way to get the items you need. And no worries, you will be forgiven all atrocities and become the cheered hero nonetheless.
In the end I kept at it just to see what kind of bizarre ideas I would come across. Like the golden flower that turns into gold coins when it touches dog blood.

Firstly, there is relatively little text in this game, so in that sense it is not like a Fighting Fantasy book.
It does faithfully recreate the events of City of Thieves in the  Port Blacksand section, but the way it works seems very much a grind. There is no way to save game or retrace steps, which means if you wish to try turning left rather than right at a given intersection you must return to the start of the city and complete the earlier section again.
There seems to be no way of scrolling around to look at the city and check where you have been before. This makes it tempting to get out a pen and paper to make sure you don't take a wrong turn, and have to start the city yet again. It seems like a time wasting mechanism, rather than good game design.
If you happen to die you receive penalties to two of your dice. To cut a long story short, this makes your slim chances almost impossible, unless you spend 20 gold to remove these penalties. 20 gold is a lot, so to get it you will have to grind random encounters. The other alternative is to fight random monsters until you increase experience and become unbeatable, aslo by grinding random encounters.
In short, the game felt too random and repetitive to be fun.

Short review:
The controller itself is great. It does need a rethink on how one uses a controller (a lot more finger action for a lot of games....stop laugh down back!) and its dpad is not good for critical stuff. But overall an excellent controller.
The software side....well its a work in progress.
Long review: the controller:
It's a nice controller to hold and use. The right touchpad is a much better substitute for a mouse than an analogue stick (though still not as good as a mouse).
The haptic feedback is a great idea that really gives the player information on what the controller is doing.
The paddles at the bottom of the controller are also a great addition.
The face buttons are very small and kinda awkward to get at but I think thats kinf od the point. Critical actions in games should be mapped to one of the shoulder buttons instead and those face buttons should be for just basic things like bringing up the map or inventory.
The build quality is very good. It feels sturdy and well put together.
Hardware wise the only things I would change are make the left pad a bit smaller and maybe a bit more shaped so it can be a better dpad also. I would als make the L and R buttons a bit easier to click (if they were a bit more like the vitas shoulder buttons that would be great). Other than that its brilliant.
The software:
This needs work.
I suppose the first surprise is that the steam controller really relys on steam. I know this probably sounds a bit "DUH" but usually when i buy a controller for my PC its a case of plug it in, maybe install and driver and/or utility and tweak as needed. But this needs steam. if you want to use it with games you dont have on steam then you need to add those as external games.
More specifically it needs big picture mode and that needs a lot of fixing. It leaks memory and hampers performance. I though it was my PC but exit/relaunch steam and play the same game with no BPM and all is well.
It also shouldnt require BPM at all. Why cant I configure it from the standard steam interface?
The description of some of the configurations also needs work. They need a technical writer in there to shorten the descriptions down and clear it up.
On the positive side i have had no connection issues. It was a bit of a faf getting it connected initially (a combination of needing to tweak linux (not valves fault) and not sure how to get it connected (valves fault) but once connected its been bullet proof.
Using the steam controller for typing is also a neat setup that should prove effective with practice.
The scope of configuration is also excellent. It would be nice if we could see actions that need to be mapped for games while on the config screen (that probably needs to be organised with developers though) but overall the configuration system makes the steam controller a very powerful tool.
Ideally i would like to see all the configuration seperated from BPM (perhaps even steam itself..just have it as an external tool that you need to run to use the controller) and i would like the configuration to be a bit more intuitive (is there a way to dig the control mapping out for games?). Also there be big that need squishing.
So would i recommend it? Yes but you will need to be patient with the software for now. Valve do seem to be listening to feedback so maybe in even a months time the software side could be much better. You will also need to take what you know about 360/PS3 controllers or mouse and keyboard and park it....this is a different animal.
But it is a very flexible and powerful controller.

After the first time you use this device, you'll likely hate it. And maybe want to return it.
But the second, and third time, once you've adjusted to the pads, and once you've started figuring out what sensitivity and drag you like, it'll click. And once it does, it'll become the best controller you've ever used. Will you be playing competitive CS:GO from your couch? Likely not. But Fallout, or XCOM, or Baldur's Gate-style RPGs, or World of Goo, or Rocket League or Grand Theft Auto? Hell yeah.
So first things first: this is a new type of controller. It'll take some time to adjust. Think back to the veeery first time you used a controller, or analog sticks, or the Wii. It took a bit to get going.
While many may write it off, I recommend checking it out for two major reasons (that, to me, trounce any other controller):
1.) You can download control schemes from others, from the developer or create your own. And they can map controller input, mouse-and-keyboard or any other combination you can dream up.
2.) The level of customization, especially regarding the oft-detested pads, is unmatched. Sensitivity, trackball-style, friction, acceleration, click. It's awesome.
Give it a try. Play a few types of games. And then buckle down with an RPG, or an FPS that's not too hectic. Try a few control schemes. Tinker with the sensitivity. And once it "clicks", no pun intended, you won't go back.
Also worth noting: with two pairs of rechargeable batteries, the battery life and connectivity is fantastic. And I'm not typically a battery person.
Love it, and can't wait to see firmware just make it better with time.

I will admit, I am a previous console gamer. I have played on just about every console there has been since Atari 2600. While my opinion may seem biased to console games and controllers, I love my PC in every way and haven't touched my PS4 in a few months now that I have built a pretty decent gaming PC.
As far as this controller is concerned, alot of people saying you need to "get used to it" first. I feel like first impressions tend to stick with these type of things. I honestly tried to give this controller a fair shot but I just couldn't get a feel for it. It's not like this was a terrible design in theory but it seemed to fall short by trying to accomplish too much (combining a kb/m with a console-like controller).
For older games that are PC-based that have no controller support, this might be an alternative, depending on the tiltle, of course. Expect to bind a few buttons  here and there for just about every game you play, as the default settings only partially work. Maybe just a minor annoyance, but it still takes up time that you could be playing. A mouse is still going to be superior in many cases with these types of games, in my opinion.
Button placement took some time to get used to. Valve felt the need to be different and that's okay. I initially found myself pressing the wrong buttons but after a few hours, I got the hang of it. They could have been a little bigger but not really a big deal.
The right touch pad on the Steam controller is somewhat "twitchy" and takes away from the smoothness of camera panning. Sure, you can adjust sensitivity, dead zones and all that jazz, but it still doesn't move smoothly or accurately with your thumb as it should, especially in FPS games. With sights drawn, it seems to stick in places, requiring you to lift your thumb and scroll a little to keep the camera and sights centered on your enemies. With all the over and under-compensating with the camera going on, it makes the entire game look "shakey" for lack of a better word. While moving around open world, it does a fair enough job but when the sights are drawn it's a constant struggle. Forget about multiplayer shooting, by the time you get the camera where you need it ....you're dead!

While there are alot of community profiles or "templates" you can choose from while in Big Picture mode, none of them felt quite right to me. It only seemed to affect total travel distance and sensitivity of the right touchpad, not really helping the "sticking" isssues that seem to plague this control.  It seems like a hardware limitation instead of software. I don't foresee firmware upgrades/drivers being able to fix this. This is  the biggest flaw of the controller and a significant one at that.
I was a bit confused by the many reviewers who are claiming that this touchpad is more accurate than a joystick could ever be. I thought the problem must be with me, due to all the positive reviews. I tried different games like Portal 2, Tomb Raider (2013), Star Wars Battlefront, Witcher 3, Rocket League, Shadow of Mordor, Fallout 4, and Mad Max. Each game had it's own issues with the touchpad. I spent enough time where I should have gotten "used to it". Bottom line, it's a flawed design. If touchpads are the future and are so much more accurate, I wonder why they aren't making r/c helicopter transmitters with touchpads instead of joysticks?. They require precision and accuracy too, yet they rely on joystick-like controls. I sure as heck wouldn't trust a 5 lb. r/c helicopter spinning at 5000 rpm being operated by someone with a couple of touchpads, would you? Okay, maybe that is an extreme point but you get the idea. Touchpads are great for laptops and that's about it.
Sure, it's new and different and even somewhat fun to play around with, but if you are looking to improve your performance in games that were designed to be used with a controller, especially newer FPS, you will more than likely be disappointed. There is a reason why the dual joysticks have been around since the PS2/Xbox days. They work. You are in full control of the movements. This is where a real gaming controller excels in many of the newer games that are ported for both console and PC.
It really is a shame because I wanted to like this controller. It looks sharp and feels good in my hands. Well made, just not well designed.

I'm a lifelong console player, and I've been using dual analog for probably around 14 years. I figured, hey, I'll go ahead and try this. If I don't like it, I'll just use it for KB+M only games and use my Xbone controller for others. So I turn on Fallout 4 and after playing with settings, find a config that really works. Honestly, about 7 hours into using the Steam Controller, and I'm already better with it than I was with the Xbone controller, which is almost exactly the layout I've been using for damn near a decade (360 controller, anyone?). Needless to say, it works, and it works well. Gyro aiming is also nice for fine tuning your shots, as it works remarkably well. One of the features I expected to be a gimmick is actually very useful. Very pleasantly surprising.
Hardware quality is solid. It's plastic, but it doesn't feel cheap. The only cheap plastic that's used is on the grips, and on the part that you aren't actually touching. It's definitely a quality plastic throughout the controller, and it feels nice in the hand. The upward arches of the grips may feel a little odd at first, but it's quite comfortable. The thumbstick is nice, the buttons work, though I would prefer it if they were clicky instead of squishy, the d-pad is... odd, and the right pad works great. The hyped-up haptic feedback is present, and as a skeptic, I have to say that it works really well. I can tell where my thumb is, what direction I'm moving, and how fast I'm moving. For some reason, the haptic feedback sounds like a geiger counter. Not sure why, but it's not actually distracting. There are 6 buttons on the back; two bumpers, two triggers, and two paddles. It all works very well. The only questionable part is the d-pad. Honestly, Valve should've just put in a physical pad, but I can understand if they were trying to give left-handed users the option to play southpaw like the weirdos they are.
TL;DR: Within 7 hours, I'm doing better at FPS games with this than I was with an Xbone controller, which is a layout I've been using religiously for 10 years, not even mentioning the various dual-analog layouts I used before the famous 360/Xbone layout. It's comfy, the trackpad works well, the haptic feedback is amazing, gyroscopic controls are surprisingly good, and plenty of buttons on the back. All buttons are also customizable, which is a huge advantage over other controllers. Literally the only questionable part about this controller is the d-pad. Unless they decided on a touch d-pad for the lefties, it was a poor design choice. That said, it works well enough. I can't imagine myself playing a platformer or a fighting game with it though.

I have seen a fair number of reviews that roast this game for its combat system, which is, in fairness, not the most tactically interesting one ever conceived. However, Civ IV had a combat system that was (for myself, at least) equally if not more confusing and shallow to Stellaris. People still enjoy playing it. The point is that Stellaris is at its core about exploration, not combat, and thus that its core mechanics, even in the original version without dlc, are engaging enough for me.

As far as Sci-Fi grand strategy games go, this one basically takes the cake.
The DLC practice with Paradox isn't the best, and sometimes I feel as if they're exploiting a niche market/genre given that grand strategy isn't as widely acclaimed as say, RTS or FPS games.
That said, there is a formula they tend to go by. The earlier you get your hands on one of their titles, the easier it is to fork out over a hundred dollars for it overtime through paid DLC and what not.
Businesses practices aside, however, Stellaris is definitely a great game.
It isn't perfect by any means, there are a number of different small bugs I often encounter, and the balancing definitely is subpar in comparison to other Paradox titles and such, but what's most important to me regarding this is that the dev team is contantly working on the game. Every Thursday theres another developer diary/update that explains changes they're looking to make and how they plan to make them, not to mention that they do their best to not only:
A. Listen to community feedback regarding not only additional features but also shady business practices (i.e. they're making a previously paid feature free to accomodate players and their newest update).
but also B. consitently balance, tweak, fix, enhance, or update the game so that it's that much closer to that perfect score it has the potential for.
Don't be mistaken, this is definitely still a work in progress, but a work in progress that can still play well and has a very promising future ahead of it.
Worth picking up if you like Paradox, grand strategy, or in my case, Sci-Fi strategy beyond the RTS scene.

I'm a huge MMORPG fan, and had the luck (and time!) to play different games from different developers.
Aura Kingdom is catchy, challenging, original and most of all FUN!
I'd like to highlight this last adjective for one simple reason.
Most MMORPG can be stressful and frustrating, the path to improvement can be tiring and repetitive.
In my opinion this is not the case of Aura Kingdom.
There is no real better player, better class or better build. You can literally create the character you love!
Moreover, another point I'd like to stress, is the complete absence of "Pay to win" factor. Even though there is a cash shop, the items aren't meant to give a great advantage in the game, and for those who aren't willing to spend a single $ there is the Loyalty Point Mall, which is the in-game currency version of the Cash Shop mall (Loyalty Points aren't even hard to obtain).
Someone complained about the repetitiveness of the game at a certain point, dungeons following the same scheme, grinding quests over and over etc. I'd say that this is a typical feature of every MMORPG, and if you can't deal with it, then you better change genre, not game.
I'll briefly list some PRO and CON of the game.
PRO
- Anime Style: I believe this is one of the first reason why players enjoy AK. It's really entertaining to feel like being within an anime (Sword Art Online fans will surely love this game).
- Class and Sub Class System: There is a godo amount of classes that are beign constantly udpated with every expansion (Necromancer has just been released). Plus, at level 40 you can choose a secondary class.
- Solo and Party: Everyone can enjoy the game, wether you are a party player or a lone wolf you can still earn your rewards and do istances.
- A real Free To Play: as stated above, this is not a Pay To Win game
- Lots of events: there is something to do everyday, from special events made for specific occasions (like Christmas, Halloween etc) to sudden ones (like hide and seek organised by Game Masters)
CON
- Steam account issues: as far as I know, it is not possible to register to Aeria Games website with Steam account information. Aeria Game website allows you to earn AP (used for the cash shop mall) as well as winning prizes. If there is a method to log in via Steam please let me knwo via comment :)

I've played quite a bit of this game. Only 51 hours on Steam so far, but I began in Closed Beta and long before it reached Steam in the first place.
This is the first MMO in a long time, which I've enjoyed so much, that I want to play through the game with every class it has available.
Class variety is great and they are adding new classes often.
Eidolon System is also interesting. It's like Pokémon, but you can combo them with yourself (There's an ability, which lets you do that). So far every Eidolon I have has had a different personality and the way they interact with the player.
It has an anime-inspired artstyle, which is also really well drawn. Texture quality is really good (Almost as good as World of Warcraft's high level gear textures)
The game also has a dual-class system as in, when you reach lvl 40, you can choose a second class for your character to increase its dynamic. Gameplay is a hybrid between an action and hotkey MMO with a focus on the hotkey side.
As of writing this "review" or "opinion piece" I have three characters: Level 55 Wizard-Sorcerer, Level 25 Duelist and Level 29 Ranger/Battle Bow.
That's another thing I'd like to add: The game's pacing is great. It doesn't drag out like most MMORPGs. Instead, it goes by really quickly even though there's so much story to be read and experienced.
That brings me to the conclusion. If you like anime-inspired artstyles and would like a more fast-paced MMO to play together with people, then this might very well be a game for you. While the story isn't the best in gaming, it's still good enough to be worth a read or two. Especially since we're dealing with a completely free-to-play game, which funnily enough doesn't have a bad cash shop at all.

Ridiculously tight, well implemented 2D platformer that runs with the idea of a teleporter gun & mashes it with near perfect controls, puzzle design, and learning curve. You'll die, sure, but it's because you suck, rather than the game wanting to make you feel like you suck.
What makes this is inspired is how well its gimmick, the teleporter gun, is implemented - you fire it, a bullet goes off traveling, and when that bullet hits something, you'll be instantly transported to that point - continuing your current momentum. That's what's key.
You get eased into these simple 'jump up & shoot towards this platform you can't jump across to' puzzles & then suddenly you're jumping up, firing it off across to a wall, landing & jumping again in a different direction just as it hits, then repeating all that immediately in a different direction, but with none of the stress of a lot of these dumb modern-retro platformers.

This is a card game version of three gamebooks with a top down 3D environment simply for illustration.
There are many FF games on Steam, from book ports, to game versions like this. FF Legends is based on the books City of Thieves, The Warlock of Firetop Mountain and Citadel of Chaos. Firetop already has a game version on Steam, the game mechanic here is different, you're not making any movement choices in combat, it's your card vs. the opponent card and you roll against each other for the outcome.
Originally these are dice and choice books, FF Legends keeps these elements, so when you decide to go one path, that's it, you might be able to circle back the other way later, particularly if you die, but it's still a version of turn to page X for this or to page Y for that. And the cards are the enemies you fight and items and spells you pick up.
Unlike the four part version of Sorcery on Steam, you don't get constant access to the world map, or any rewinds to undo poor decisions (you can avoid perma-death though through game options here). On the other hand, here you build up your dice the whole time to increase your chances when it comes to fights and tests of luck. So once you become more powerful, you're less likely to be dying at the hands of common criminals in the port, for example.
If you are happy with that mechanic, then this is a fun way to open out the text. My only personal preference would have been to retain the original book art for the relevant cards, as many of the other game adaptations on Steam have in one way or another - but if you're not attached to those, then you won't miss them.
BOTTOM LINE: as others have said, it's fun to play and attractively priced - you will only be let down if you don't know what to expect and think this is something other than a card based version of gamebooks played with dice.

It has been nearly two months since I played NieR: Automata. It was the first 4K game that I played on my new Rig which in fully 4K ready so that I was able to play on optimal settings for the best visual effects. I read a number of very positive reviews about the game and that's why I purchased and summarily played it. I even disseminated some information at its respective wiki for the edification of fellow players. It is true that the game has a well refined synergy between visual, auditory (sound effects, vocals, music, etc.) which melds in a seamless confluence, transporting one into an experience that is simultaneously rare and remarkably unique. It is also true that the adventure is wondrous and one is drawn in wholly so that moving through the game is a sublime compulsion. One becomes so familiar with the protagonists and so fond of them that they feel quite like family. That is where the problem lies, in my assessment, because the developers made a singular but significant error, or at least a major miscalculation.
There are no "good endings" but many endings, the majority of which are not only bad but fraught with sorrow, many with hopelessness, some that are just poor jokes. All of these possible endings I could discount if there were but one clearly "happy" ending where there is some manifest hope and redemption, a definitive reward for having made wise choices. It seems apparent to me that Square Enix wished to make a statement against war and perhaps an illustration of the violence in and the futility of life rather that making a game that people would love to experience again and again. I have learned in life that the human creature can tolerate only so much of death. Death which occurs close to one, especially that of friends and loved ones fills said capacity much more rapidly. Perhaps it was by design to force gamers to go on to buy their next game. I, for one, feel betrayed. A game should, in my opinion, not make one regret playing it over and over trying to make things turn out "right" without that being a possibility. A work of art is defined by its ability to create emotion and NieR:Automata achieves this in so many ways. Howevrer, the game should not have ended with clearly defined negative emotions. Rather, the developers had the opportunity to transform its players so they would experience the joy and the hope in learning the inner reward for overcoming adversity and doing in the end what is noble, right, and just. Such is life's greatest lesson. I will now more carefully choose my next game and certainly before I decide to be a patron of Square Enix.
