The game is not meant for everyone.
I loved minecraft when I was 11 and 12. At first I was confused when I didn't see a campaign mode. I realized it was a sandbox game and I liked even more for that. However, I've always wanted to see a minecraft solo mission, a campaign, or even a: Story Mode.  So, when I saw Telltale making a minecraft story mode I got super hyped. I loved the telltale games, and I loved minecraft, so I thought this was going to be awesome. When I finished the first episode I wanted more, so I played it a second time. Although, I could easily tell the game was targeted for the younger kids from around 12 or under, which I thought was great. At the same time, I would have loved to have the game intense like the other telltale games. If there were more intense situations, blood, and more violence I would pay more for this game. But the game is MINECRAFT which is a game for everyone of all ages, so they couldn't do that. I would have liked it if there was a kids version which is the game that's out now, and a more teen/adult version that was as suspenseful as a real telltale game. Now, I'm not saying that this isn't a telltale game, because it is. It just so happens this isn't our regular drama suspense violence packed telltale game. Another thing is the plot. Yes, it is cliched, corny, and cheesy as it can be. But if it's targeted towards children, then I'm not going to complain, and neither should you. I actually like the game for its cheesiness and corniness, because it reminds me of a lot of games I played in my early childhood. The only other complaint I have is the lip sync animation. That is the only thing in the game I think should have been improved/perfected. I can't wait for episode 3, I hope the story goes a little more original and doesn't become too unpredictable, but I am still excited for the next coming.

A lot of the 'most helpful' reviews seem to make one of two mistakes: They've either never seen a Telltale game before, or they expected Minecraft 2.0. If you come into this with either of these misconceptions, you could easily be sorely disappointed. So, before you buy this game, understand that Telltale games are interactive stories. You're going to be given choices and quicktime events, not a lot of free rein to wander around an expansive world. A lot of the choices at this stage will seem like they're not important, but some of them really will be in the later chapters. You will not be able to do all the same things you can do in minecraft, but you will play a game set in the minecraft world, with minecraft graphics, using many of the aspects and mechancs of the game. And, most importantly, so far you have one chapter of the game, not the entire thing. If you understand all of that, and you like playing interactive story games, then I'd recommend this game to you.

VC is definitely more imperative in WWE 2K18, as it is found to be somewhat difficult to earn, but easy to lose quickly on 'Loot Crates' or increasing your attributes. Word of advice: BE VERY WISE WITH YOUR VC!!! IT WILL COME TO BITE YOU WHEN YOU TRY TO UPGRADE YOUR PLAYER IN MY CAREER!
Anyways...
I've heard a lot of people complain that the game isn't well optimised and lags regularly when they play, even when they have a PC that fits in the Spec Requirements. I had to go to the extent of going into the NVIDIA Control Panel and turning many settings to 'off', and adjusting the resolution to something that my monitor doesn't support properly! Oh well, at least I get a capped 60fps now instead of 30! *Sigh*. No matter how good or high range your PC may be, you will experience stuttering, even if you lower the settings to 'low'.

So, I've played the hell out of this one on PS4 and decided to pick it up on PC because I want to play it in 4K.  Let's talk about the game first.
Great story even if a little confusing.  Let's put it this way; do you loathe anime?  Then pass on this game.  If you don't mind anime then game is worth a shot.  Love anime?  I'll bet you'll love NieR Automata.
Combat is fun and you can customize your character very well and keep three different customizations available to swap between.  This can come in handy for different fights and scenarios.  Combat is fast action.  Reminds me of DMC and old Ninja Gaiden 3rd person combat.  Definitely not near as hard as Gaiden though.
Art direction and music are ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic.  That was one of the things that really drew me into the world of NieR Automata.  Characters may not be the most thought out and plot might not be the deepest ever, but the gameplay will keep you going as you get better at dodging, attack, and learning your abilities and mechanics.  It's satisfying.
Now, let's talk about the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that is the PC port.  Game is NOT OPTIMIZED FOR PC.  No way should a single MSI GTX 1080Ti coupled with an i7-4790K OC'd to almost 4.6 per core not be able to roast this game at max settings in 4K.  And while it does keep frames over 50FPS at all times, that's not good enough.  Also fullscreen is still not working correctly last time I checked.  It will try to stretch beyond your 4K monitor into your other monitor(s) if you have more than one.  It doesn't stretch the picture, but the fact that you're seeing edges in your other monitors is unacceptable, especially this far into launch.
And finally, if you have a controller hooked up to your PC, there is a good chance the mouse pointer will pop up in the middle of your screen often.  I am assuming this is something to do with the game thinking for a second that you're using your mouse and keyboard instead of your controller.  90% of the time the mouse pointer will vanish quickly, but it's still annoying.  The other 10% of the time it gets stuck there which causes me to restart the game.  Can't stand seeing a mouse pointer in the middle of my game while I'm playing.  MY IMMERSION, DAMMIT!
Overall, I recommend the game...but know that it's not optimized and likely will not be for quite some time if at all.  It's clear that the developer or something SquareEnix hired to port the title isn't too concerned about optimization.  I'm sure they'll blame nvidia or amd for "poor driver support" but I'm not buying it.  Requires a beefy PC just to get decent frames on max detail at 1080p and up.  Just be advised of this.

Having been a avid player of "World of Warcraft", I eventually got tired of having to pay a subscription to play a game, so I quit. Upon quitting, I looked up and down for free mmo's that would keep my attention. Some fell flat, some were pay to win, some were just not able to run on my computer.
Then I found this game. At first, I shrugged it off, and kept looking for something different. I'm a big fan of anime style art, so I kept this open as sort of a "last resort" if you will.
After searching and searching, I took one last look at this game, my finger resting on the X (close) button. I decided to google some game play and character design. After looking through that, I thought to myself "You know what.. this seems like a game that I'd pass up just because it doesn't look like something my fiance' and I can play together, but I'm going to give it a shot, merely based on the fact that it IS something that I probably wouldn't think to try or download."
So, I went ahead and downloaded it and got to the character customization screen. I panicked because loading INTO the CAC screen, I was lagging hard core. I started to lose hope. I looked through the (limited) but cute customizations for your character, eventually found one that I liked and joined the world.
Fortunately, the lag was no more, yay!! That would have been the kicker if it lagged during game play.  I played the introduction scenario and was hooked after that. The big test was...would my fiance like it?
The answer was yes! He really enjoys it. He was a bit hesitent at first, but after playing he really enjoyed the art style, the vivid, bright colors of the game, and he REALLY enjoyed the fact that the armor didn't look like your typical, boring earth tone peasant armor that most mmo games give you as a "noob".
There are a lot of features I could name off that are really cool, and a couple of things I don't really care for but I'll just name a few as to not make this longer than it already is, so here it goes!
PROS:  Great art style, enjoyable fighting style, pretty spells (especially the bard with her rainbow magic powers!!), the random "hidden quests" you can find through out the land, recieving really pretty costumes instead of having to decide "do I want to look stupid, or spend money on overpriced costumes?" (That is also an option though, if you're interested in that kind of thing!)  Character designs are adorable as heck, and the ability to have a shared slot in your bank is GREAT!  Also, getting bags from quest is a nice feature. There are a lot of different classes to choose from as well which is great because I tend to get picky on classes. I believe there are 11 classes to choose from thus far, with another one on the way. You're pretty much bound to find a class you enjoy playing!
CONS: BOTS! Ugh!! I really hope the bots die down, but they're everywhere! Since the game has an "auto run to quest" feature (which is great when you are on the phone or need to get up and do something :P) bots use that to their fullest potential and run around leveling up so they can make it to the first big city to spam you with mail for cheap gold. It's very unfortunate, but luckily the bots don't hinder the grinding because the enemies spawn back fairly fast.  Aside from the bots, I'd have to say I'd LOVE the feature to turn on and off the "spell description" where you hover over your spells and it pops up a huuugeeee box saying what the spell does. It's possible that this feature does in fact exist, and I just overlooked it during the 10 minutes that I searched for it, but if it does exist then it's called something else and I overlooked it. I am used to being what most people would call "a clicker" so the boxes covering my entire screen were kind of an eye sore. I don't click anymore in this game, but I kind of feel bad for people who do click because then it covers their character's while they fight and really takes away from the awesomeness of the epic monster battles.
I'd have to say that I'd give this game at LEAST a 7/10. It's really, really fun and I enjoy the heck out of it, but it could definitely do without those bots.  I'd recommend this to anyone who enjoys mmos, and anime art.  That, and some of the purchasable costumes are soooooooooooo cuuuuuttteeeee!!!! <3 <3 <3 I don't normally do this, but when I get some extra cash on hand I definitely want to buy a pair of glasses for my adorable bard! Keep up the great work with this game, Aura Kingdom devs. I appreciate the fun this game brings to my fiance and I :)

I loooooove, love, love my steam controller.  I pre-ordered a while back and got it when they shipped the first wave to pre-order beta testers.
I did not like it at first, but that was before I realized how HEAVILY it relies on user customization.  You probably won't find any of the recommended or default templates to your liking (except for something simple like Rocket League) , nor will you think any of the user made templates are perfect for you.
However, they all make great starting points.  Once you start figuring out the configuration tool, expect to spend around 15 to 30 minutes configuring the controls for each game.  I know it sounds like a pain, but once you get comfortable with it, you can personalize the controller to be exactly natural for you and your body/mind.
Now that I've done it so much, it takes me less than 10 minutes to perfectly set it up for any game.  Once I do, it feels completely natural, as if I'm not even using some input device and am communicating with my computer directly and telepathically.  It is totally worth the effort and time.
I am an avid M&KB user and have spent over $250 on a high-end mechanical keyboard and gaming mouse.  I fully expected to only use the steam controller for more causual/console-y games or when I was playing on the TV and not sitting at my desk.  Instead what I discovered was that I prefer using the Controller even at my desk.  It's just much more comfortable to hold a controller and analogue movement is a huge plus, especially for immersive role-playing games like Fallout 4, where I may want to walk places at times, but think the keyboard walking speed is too slow.  It just feels right.
The only major downside is that I can lose accuracy when the game doesn't support simultaneous use of a mouse and controller, requiring me to use "Joystick Mouse" as my input method.  I lose a considerable amount of DPI (affects "smoothness") this way and it is no where near as accurate as the true mouse mode on the controller.  Albeit, I still end up playing with the controller and dealing with it, as all the positives are just too . . . positive.
The other problems are related to Big Picture mode and other software/firmware quirks.  They are fixing them rapidly and I expect the services to be top notch by the end of the year.
I would like to add that I think a lot of people find the shape awkward and uncomfortable because they're holding it like a 360 controller, with a tight grip.  I find it much more ergonomic to cradle the controller with your last three fingers and hold it low, allowing you to point your thumbs straight down at the controller and not as parallel as you otherwise would. Point and click adventure game with fun characters, good music, good looking locations, and puzzles that don't drive you too nuts trying to solve them.
The first game had an issue where you might notice an item for a later puzzle, but as you had no need for it at the time, you wouldn't pick it up (which was amusing banter until you needed it) and in some cases it was hidden inside another item, so good luck remembering about it if you didn't play it all in a single session and even if you did.

At the time I wrote this review, I had 6 hours logged on Saints Row 2. (And almost all of it was troubleshooting and trying to get it to work.)
Before I say anything, you have to understand that the PC port of Saints Row 2 was broken from the start. It was never intended to be ported over and was done as an afterthought after the success of 3. Due to the nature of the port, and the fact that it honestly is almost impossible to play, this review sadly isn't going to be able to list many pros so I'll just focus on why you should NOT get the PC port.
Controls were poorly optimized and difficult to work with on a keyboard.
Cutscenes are horribly out of sync with audio, and if you're using subtitles those are a train wreck also. (Although, to be fair I believe subtitles were a train wreck in the console version as well.)
The game lags at the most inoppurtune of times, and adjusting the settings has no effect on it.
The games run speed. When I first started the game, before I realized the Hell I had managed to land in, Steam told me I was running the game at a stable 30FPS. However, despite this optimal framerate, it seemed like the game was running at least three times faster than it should've been. (This coming from someone who has played the console version for 20+ hours before this.) There seemed to be no way to correct this issue, and is a key reason in why the game is unplayable. Simply instructing the character to walk a few feet forward results in them suddenly zooming forward at speeds that would put Sonic the Hedgehog to shame and slamming their body against any solid object. (Assuming they don't clip through it first.) Heaven forbid you decide to RUN while attempting to control the player and engage Warp Factor 9. Following this pattern, I'm sure you can come up with your own witty analogy for what happens when you attempt to control a vehicle.
Swapping weapons is a chore as well. The numbered keys work for changing weapons, but hitting them can often be more trouble than it's worth (particularly when in the middle of a nearly impossible fire fight.) and using the mouse and buttons to change weapons rarely works because the game doesn't like to register diagonal mouse movement.
IF YOU ARE HELL BENT ON PLAYING THIS ON PC, LISTEN UP.
Supposedly there are four things you can do that will make the game playable:
1. Installing the 'Gentlemen of the Row' patch.
This patch is made by IdolNinja (and friends), now an actual member of Volition who has done work on later Saints Row titles. I've used several mods and patches made by IdolNinja, and they all enhance gameplay experience and work like a charm. The patch is supposed to have several built in goodies that make playing the game on PC more enjoyable, however for me the patch has not worked. (This is likely due to me having an OS that has been proven to not get along well with the game.)
2. Using Powertools.
Honestly, I have no idea what Powertools was until I read about it while frantically searching the internet in my rage. I STILL don't know what it does, but it's supposed to slow down the running rate of the game and allow it to be played. It does this based on a percentage that can be adjusted from a text document contained within the Powertools file. There's no set number to use, it's a lot of guessing and checking. The closest I've been able to get to "working" was with a value somewhere between .6 and .4 percent speed. (Even then, driving a car was almost impossible and may lead to difficulties with later missions.)
3. Switching to Windows XP OS.
I'm running Windows 10 right now, and from what I've gathered lurkig forums and Reddit, everything Windows 7 and above does not play well with the port. I haven't read/heard anything about Windows XP having trouble. The only thing stopping me from doing this myself and testing it is because I don't know how to do this? Is that even possible really? I wouldn't recommend it unless you have a lot of computer knowledge.
4. Running as Administrator/Safe Mode/Compatibility Mode
Again, this is just something I read/heard while lurking online. I haven't tried this method because for whatever reason my computer doesn't want to launch games unless I'm using the Steam interface and there is no such option SO. But hey, it's worth a shot?
Well, that's my two cents on the game. I'm a stubborn SOB so I doubt I'll give up on getting it to work, and I'll update my review with any good information I find.
One final thing I would like to say: The game is worth playing on 360. If you can find a copy of it somewhere, GO GET IT. I'm almost to the end of the game on the console version, and there's been like three times tops where the game has been just utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and unfair.

Most complaints I'm seeing are completely unfounded... by that I mean they're false. No RPG elements? No progression? They either didn't play the game or they're abysmal at it:
- Characters gain permanent XP that translates into levels/abilities
- Characters collect temporary gold, items and buffs
- New characters can be discovered and unlocked
- Each world has a set number of randomized encounters before its respective boss.
- Defeating each world permanently unlocks the next world
- When you lose a run, you lose the items/buffs you've gathered along with that run's progression, but not the XP or unlockables.
- The game clearly explains everything I just typed.
There's only one instance wherein you encounter extremely obscure/complex words: during Last Stands. When a character hits 0 HP, you get one chance to save them by solving a (keyword:) difficult anagram. Depending on your input, you might damage the enemy, survive with a little health, or (if you solve the full anagram) return with 100% HP. Those words are
esoteric. You're not supposed to recognize them regularly, if ever. Last Stand is there to teach you new words and give you the chance to feel awesome if you can solve them. Complaining about the mechanic is asinine. If Last Stands were easy, you would never lose and the game would be boring. The alternative is having the character die when they die.
Words for Evil is a vocabulary game. If you don't appreciate language, why buy it?
The game has one major in my opinion: The letters should be in circles, not squares. Making them squared means they fight you tooth and nail when attempting to connect letters diagonally. It's difficult to drag the cursor through the tiny space between two corners, often resulting in frustration and lost time. Were they circular, your intentions would be equally executable from any direction. If this extra "difficulty" was by design, it was a
design choice.

Loadout is a painful thing to see, as it, like many other complete faliures, had a good idea but took it in the complete wrong direction. I will start with the game's weapon customisation options, as these are supposed to be the game's most original feature.
Upon coming into the menu, my first question was "Where is the customisation?" Sure, you can change what muzzle your weapon has, what stock you use, how its rounds are loaded etc. but what purpose does it all serve? These options barely change anything visually, but just going from the stats means that you are always going to be sticking with a particular setup because it is the best one for that weapon type. The types of weapon may be balanced between each other, but there are really no sidegrades in the attachments and options, only upgrades and downgrades. Some options are so impractical (and yet offer no other benefits) that I wonder if they are even meant to be there. Why the hell do I want a two-round burst on a beam weapon? It isn't comical or special in any way, it just does exactly what it says and doesn't look good or work well. I sound like a tryhard here, but if your aim is to mess about and do random, original things, you're going to end up disappointed.
Now on to the gameplay of Loadout. The gamemodes seem relatively team-based from what I can tell, having only played two matches due to server issues involving me being disconnected at random points. There is a mode in which one person from each team is allocated the role of Collector, and they must grab stacks of "Blutonium" (Crystal things) and carry them to a hopper to score points for their team. I assume it was intended that the rest of the team defend the Collector while he is carrying the Blutonium (as his weapons are disabled while doing so) however this does not seem to be the case in-game. Nontheless, the gamemode still works pretty well.
The other gamemode I played (although I assume there are more) was a control points type of thing, where multiple team members had to stand next to flags to gain control of that area. I did not get to see much of this mode, however, due to the aforementioned problems I was getting with the game.
The game was laggy. I turned the graphics down to medium (using the slider that gives you no other/advanced options for changing graphics settings) and although the game then looked quite poor, the framerate was barely improved at all. As a comparison, my computer can comfortably (at least 40+ FPS) run Assassin's Creed 3 and Just Cause 2 at high graphics settings, two games that are arguably better looking than Loadout.
In conclusion, Loadout is a good concept made into a poor game. I will play the game some more and maybe turn the settings down to low to see if that changes anything. Despite the game feeling slightly bland like I mentioned, it was fun enough that I am prepared to give it a second chance to see if I can enjoy it.
EDIT 4/1/2015: I have played the game a bit more. The server issues and lag have been completely fixed, but the weapon customisation hasn't had anything changed or added which disappoints me. My verdict is still the same. But I suppose as long as you don't spend any real money, Loadout is still a bit of fun.

Alright guys so the main thing I want to talk about in this review is all those really annoying people crying about MicroTransactions.  WHO CARES?! There are literally about 5 different things you can buy with microtransactions and not one of them is whatsoever necessary to play the game of Skyrim.  It's just little add ons that barely have any effect on gameplay.  The only major one is survival mode, and thats not even that much.  The microtransactions aren't advertised in the middle of the game or anything either.  It's literally just a little side tab on the home screen.  So, to sum it up, this game is just as great as it was without Creation Club as it doesn't matter whatsoever if you decide to buy stuff in Creation Club.  I don't see why people think Microtransactions ruin this game, it has zero effect on your game if you decide to buy nothing.  You still get every DLC and the full game.  End of story.

Let me start off by saying that Paladins is a good game. It's fun, it's fast-paced, it's vibrant and colorful and much better than you'd expect from an Overwatch-clone. With that being said, this game is nigh unplayable (at least for me) at the moment, for one reason and one reason alone: The matchmaking.
The matchmaking in this game is ATROCIOUS. Whenever you join a casual game, you can expect to play against - and sometimes, if you're lucky, with - players who are much better and higher ranked than you. Now, this may sound like whining, but consider this: You're playing a casual match to have some fun, and your enemy team is comprised solely of Platinum and abouve players. That's just a fluke, you might think. Then consider this scenario happening over and over and over again, and you have an environment with no place to learn and grow. I'm all for tough gameplay and "earning your stripes", but this is just unfair. And don't even get me started on ranked.
Couple this with Hi-Rez making some frankly outlandish decisions regarding the direction of the game, and you have a stinker. I really want to enjoy this game, but I just don't anymore. If they fix the matchmaking, I'll gladly return, but for now I've uninstalled the game.

I'll review chapter 1 & 2 together, as if they were one single game since their mechanics are exactly the same and the chapter two continues the story from the point where the first chapter ends. Also their play times are very short individually. Even though i like to explore every detail in such games, it took me about 7.5 hours in total to complete both chapters.
TL;DR: Get it if you like pointing, clicking, humor, a bit noir style, a bit mystery, the good old jazz and Bob Marley. :)
The Journey Down is a very nice point & click style adventure game with humor that i would recommend to anybody who likes the genre. If you decide to buy, get the both chapters together. The game doesn't have tedious parts like some members of this genre does. You don't have to watch your character walk for ages, it skips to the place if you double click.
The story is not the most amazing one i've seen in a point & click style game but it's decent enough. It has some mystery elements and can make you curious at some points. In short, not amazing but good enough to keep you playing.
Most of the time the puzzles are pretty easy. You usually know what you need to do when you first see an item ,if not, you can figure out quickly. The game is rather relaxing than pushing you hard to solve a puzzle.
The characters are cool and their accents are really fun. Their heads are inspired by african tribal masks. You play as a young guy named Bwana. There are two other main characters named Kito and Lina. I liked all of the characters in the game especially our guy Bwana.
The art design is very charming. The game has a nice carribean and also noir atmosphere. The hand drawn places look wonderful.
One of the best things about the game ,besides its art design, is it's soundtracks. It includes some reggae and jazz tunes and the soundtracks become more jazzy in second chapter. The music fits well with the atmosphere of the game.

Chapter Two of the Journey Down was very satisfying after completing Chapter One. The plot develops well, the music and artwork is even more incredible, and you get introduced to many new people and places. There were a couple of times where I acquired items or seemed to have a task to obtain an item without clearly knowing the reason for it. This isn't uncommon in PAC games and perhaps it's because I talked to people out of order, but I found this detracted a bit from the story. The other thing I found was that Bwana's voice was consistently quieter than everyone else's, and I had to adjust my volume a bit to avoid other characters sounding like they were shouting - just a sound-mixing issue.
Looking forward to Chapter 3!

What can I say that already hasn't been said? Not anything you haven't heard really. All I can actually explain is that if you are like me and you are interested in breaking out of the humble controllers boundaries, this is it. I was pretty amazed a couple years ago with the Razer Hydra. Had a lot of potential but just did not work for the simple reason in required a lot of tiring wrist action and steady hands. Its software to make it useful was never really easy to use or refined enough for any but the hardcore entusiast gadget man. Not a good combination that buried it deep and fast. The only game that was actually fun to use it with was Portal 2.
Moving away from mechanical sticks to touch pads to control games is a promising idea that will only get better with time. Valve didn't mess with a controllers general design, they just make it technically enhanced using something simple and modifiable; a touch interface. Although the buttons are a bit noisy, some a little bit stiff and some buttons aren't very well placed for easy access, overall its not a deal breaker.
Think of it like VR. Does it work for everything all the time? No. Does it give you an edge in the things you want it to work with? Hell Yes. You wouldn't walk around with a VR headset for everything that requires a screen to look at, so why would you always want a touch controller for every gaming situation? Maybe a touch controller will become the only controller one day. Maybe one day my fingers and hands won't sweat at all, or they'll invent a touch interface that works even with puddles of water on the surface. Maybe one day I'll be connecting my Cyberbrain directly into a game and won't have to move any part of my actual body whatsoever.
The Steam Controller is not the best controller in the world for every gaming situation, yet. It does require patience and time to really use it effectively. A learning curve. You can't just plug and play all your games, you need to know how to program it occasionally to use it for you as an individual. Some games just work with it as is thankfully, and the compatibility of games will certainly get better if this controller becomes a new standard. Only time, updates and version upgrades will truly tell if this device has a future. The software is the true backbone of this device, so I can only hope it doesn't get ignored like the Razer Hydra. Words of Evil is a nice little time waster when you need to kill 5-10 minutes, but it's also extremely repetitive. It is simply a rapid fire word search game where you're on a clock to outmatch the monsters. Time limits lead to rushing, which in turn leads you to look for the first match you can find. Spamming matches, even short words, works effectively. The monsters are all pushovers. Just keep your party healed.
I would recommend fans of word games to try it for themselves. I put 2 hours into it, which I think is fine for the price. I'd imagine to collect all the heroes and monsters, you'd have to put maybe 6-8 hours at the rate my logs were filling up, but it never changes the game any. I didn't really feel it mattered which characters I was playing with. If you have a short attention span when it comes to repetitive tasks, this might not be a good selection.

I have no clue, because when I reopen the game, it'll look exactly the same.
This dictionary is also ridiculous. Some of the words in anagram sections are so obscure that when I look up definitions online, google shrugs and asks if I meant something else.
The actual mechanics are lacking. Whenever I try to connect letters diagonally, it more often than not will skip horizontally or vertically instead of where I want to drag it.
Overall, I paid about $1 for this game and I barely feel like I got my money's worth.

I write this review without having finished the game, but since I find no indication that there is a 'finish', I think it's fair.
You play as a party of adventurers completing "quests"(let's call them that)... for some reason. In fact the quests are scarcely explained so I'm not exactly sure what I'm doing except typing random letters and seeing if LJCQUES is a word that the game will accept. As you travel from scene to scene, occasionally people will request to join your party to which you have only two responses. "Absolutely" and "No". Quite a jarring contrast of responses.
RPG elements are introduced in the form of character classes and upgrades. Every class gets three types of attacks and each can be upgraded three times (max level of 10 for each character). You can upgrade stats at blacksmiths through purchasing equipment and equipping them to your characters. There's no equipment screen and there doesn't seem to be a limit to how many things you can equip to a character so I like to imagine my archer had like a sword (not even a bow, a sword) for every finger and was wearing 4 types of chest armor. Lord knows how he did it, but he did it.
You type words at the screen for like an hour and then you get to the end of your map. Along the way you'll find treasure or evade traps. Then you will be presented with some text "Book Found" or something like that and you'll be told to move to next zone or to stay in your current zone. Very immersive.
I don't really have any complaints about execution. Everything is done quite well. The artwork is nice, and consistent. It has that old 16-bit feel. The fights are... well, typing. If you manage to screw up so much that your heroes drop to 0 HP (maybe you were alt-tabbed) you are offered a chance to keep them alive by typing a 6 or 7-letter word.
Did I phone this one in? I know it's short but it's really not a complex game. You type words. Kinda missing where the 'Evil' is. I don't think there's enough in this game to really extend beyond "type words until done". I'm going to say no on this one.

Primal Carnage Extinction is a spinoff the original Primal Carnage that is no longer being developed. While the concept of this game is great, it does only appeal to a small niche market of players. Over the last several months I have done my best to support this game as much as I can. Alas it has gotten to a point where I have pretty much lost faith in Circle 5 to deliver a game worthy of the name.
Game is in PEA and will be there for some time. PEA = Perpetual Early Access. C5 consistently miss all their marks for a timeline they setup for completion. When game was originally released as EA, it was slated to take about 45-60 days  reach completion and be a full release. This time has long come and gone and game really looks no closer to being completed. As such, I am now referring to the game state as PEA.
Pros:
• Fun game and great concept (Humans vs Dinosaurs)
• Good price point for a game of this caliber
Cons:
• Game is still VERY buggy as dev's try to figure out the version of Unreal they are using
• Game is a massive headache for host
• A pain to update - Each update you have to re-edit your server config
• Server will not run as a service
• Steam is required to be running for a server to appear in browser

• MOTD is a joke
• Loot system and cosmetic items that have ruined the game
• Most of community is toxic and only care about loot and not playing game
• Q&A department fail miserably and do not properly test updates being released
I could easily continue on. Bottom line the cons far out weigh the pros for this game, and I honestly do not see it getting better in the near future. For this reason I honestly can not recommend buying this game at this time.

I bought Out There Somewhere on a whim. It had good reviews on Steam, cost less than a dollar (was on sale for 49 cents) and was reported to be a short game. I didn’t have much to lose. Either I lose a few hours of my time or have a brief but enjoyable experience, fortunately it was the latter.
Out There Somewhere is advertised as “inspired by Cave Story, Super Metroid and Portal”. Great! I love all three of those games and I would consider Super Metroid to be my top games of all time. The bad news is that the game doesn’t really fit two of the games. It doesn’t have the multiple guns, boss battles and exploration elements in Cave Story and Super Metroid. The only game that is an apt description is Portal. Buyer be warned!
The primary mechanic of the game is the teleport gun similar to the portal gun in Portal. The only difference is that instead of summoning two portals, the teleport gun instantly teleports our hero when the projectile makes contact with a wall. The teleport gun makes way for some very interesting puzzles. One common scenario is where you would need to shoot at a wall and quickly jump to maintain momentum after you teleport.
Aside from the teleport gun, there is a blaster gun that you can use. Not much to say about it other than it takes a few shots to kill anything and doesn’t feel like it has a lot of impact to it.
There’s nothing to the story. In fact, I can sum it up in one sentence. Generic space hero gets his ship shot down, lands on a planet, explores the planet to find parts to repair his ship and once his ship is repaired he kills the bad guy.
I finished Out There Somewhere in an hour. I could have spent more time exploring and searching for hidden secrets but the game never compelled me to. After finding the parts necessary to get the ship up and running, I wanted to explore the world more. Oddly when I walked to the next screen I was abruptly placed back into the ship and fighting a boss.
Overall I had fun with Out There Somewhere. The game is appropriately paced and the puzzles had a nice even ramp in difficulty. The lack of content is concerning, but given the price there isn’t much to complain about. Out There Somewhere shines well especially when compared to other games of the same price.

Out There Somewhere claims to have been inspired by Cave Story and Super Metroid, but those games raise expectations in my mind that I feel the game did not meet.
The game is far shorter than expected, my first playthrough lasting little more than an hour. It is also not nearly as varied as Cave Story and other Metroidvania-style games; you will spend the majority of the game with just your teleport gun and a normal gun. And while the puzzles involving the aforementioned teleport gun are definitely interesting, the claimed inspiritations led me to believe I would have a bigger arsenal at my disposal.
Another issue I have with the game is the use of bullet hell-like portions of the game. These sections feel very out of place in a game that is otherwise essentially a 2D version of Portal.
Out There Somewhere is a decent game, considering the price, but the tauted inspirations to me implied a set of standards that the game did not deliver. Like I said above, this is 2D Portal. If that is what you want, then this game will do. But if you're looking for something Metroidvania-esque, look elsewhere.

picks up exactly where the first installment left off, and it expects you to have fully played it as it wastes no time with lengthy re-introductions, save for a quick recap conversation with your trusted friend Kito.
For its intermediate chapter, the series traded its positively laid-back vibe for a resolutely noir ambiance. This is in part due to the nature of Port Artue, the game's main location, set in the confines of a dark mist. Consequently, pitch black darkness and haze envelops most scenes' skylines instead of the warm hues of dusk, city lights and waterfront of the first game.
The visuals look great as a general rule, though some of the art panels are manifestly sketchier. It is never too distracting but it feels lightly inconsistent with the other fully realized backgrounds. Many scenes feel monochromatic, whereas the first game was resolutely more lively. The music is also somewhat less festive but just as effective most of the time.
Regardless of the change in tone, the game hasn't really lost much of its charm. Its characters and situations are truly enjoyable. The first half of the game features less of the cinematic moments and animated transitions. Whereas Chapter One felt more immediate, Chapter Two takes some time to build up into a genuinely fun experience. It picks up tremendous momentum about halfway through, and ultimately reaches the simple greatness of its shorter debut episode.
Bwana remains one of the most original and charismatic characters I've played in point-and-click adventure games. While a lot of his success resides on pure luck, he's delightedly never portrayed as an idiot or incompetent. Puzzles are generally fairly obvious and pleasant to solve, focusing more on the story than on challenging enigmas.
The story unmistakably sets the stage for the third and final chapter but is still satisfyingly conclusive on its own. Chapter Two is nearly twice as long as Chapter One. If you have any interest in this game, and you should, you owe it to yourself to start with the first episode, for which I also wrote a
.
Chapter Three can't come soon enough!

More or less the same as the Chapter One, only bigger, longer and probably just better.

I've had a few hours to play around with the Steam controller, and I am pleasantly surprised.
+:
The setup was relatively simple and allows deep customization for every game you play.  Any controller game you can hop right in and use Xbox-style controls.  For other games, you can pick between 3 basic profiles to start and customize from there.  Other players can share their profiles on Steam, so if someone else has already made a controller layout you can borrow it and save yourself some time.  The haptic feedback felt natural and made adapting to a foreign input device easier.
-:
The right touchpad as mouse takes a bit of getting used to, and the default settings were not appropriate for a 1440p monitor.  It took some tweaking to make the controller function well in desktop mode, and since the settings must be editted from Big Picture Mode yet not applied until Desktop mode, it's tiresome to switch back and forth and tweak them to feel right. The controller build quality could be better - though I found no specific flaws it feels a bit flimsy in the hands.
Overall:  Recommended, software tweaks will likely make this controller better in the future.

For nearly a week I couldn't get it to work properly. I tried the udev thing, I tried multiple walk throughs, workarounds, etc. Lord knows how much crap I have installed and edited that was unneccessary now. I found out what my issue was: my PC was confusing my USB mechanical keyboard and the controller - it didn't know which was which, so it was giving me a really strange mix of the two. I unplugged my mech while using the controller and presto, flawless. I hope this is fixed eventaually.
My actual review: Fantastic. I don't know yet if it can replace a regular controller with actual joysticks, as this isn't "a new controller", but rather an entirely new HID (human interface device) that happens to be shaped like a controller nad used like one. The Steam Controller emulates a keyboard and mouse perfectly in games with no gamepad support. It feels absolutely alien playing Unturned with this thing, yet so right at the same time, because it works perfectly where it shouldn't work at all. I haven't tried using it in a game that requires twitch precision yet, as I want to get a good feel for it before I subject myself to a potentially infuriating experience, but aside from action FPS games, it's fantastic and I couldn't be happier.
In gamepad supported games, it also seems to be a great controller. I mostly play Broforce the past few days/weeks, I really like the ABXY buttons. I thought at first that being so small and so close was a huge mistake, but after a couple hours I had forgotten such resevations and came to love it. Your entire thumb (well, mine anyway, I have large hands) rests on all the buttons at once, and a simple "roll" of your thumb allows you to press whichever button desired, no lateral movement required.
The triggers and shoulder buttons are nice too. They are large, and deviate in shape and size a bit from most controllers, and that's a good thing. The triggers have a bit of travel before the "click" for sensitive actions (like throttle in a car), and the click is very easy but distinct. The shoulder buttons have a nice tactile click to them as well.
The joystick is good too, for a controller. Nothing to complain about, as it's basically the same performace-wise as the 360 controller we are all familiar with. The only notable difference (that I have noticed) being that the head of the stick is convex (dualshock) instead of concave (360 controller), which I prefer personally.
The D-Pad is...new. I'm going to have to use it a lot more before I pass any type of judgement.
The "start" and "back" buttons are in the standard locations, nothing to say really. They flank the "home" button, which is pretty neat. One push turns the controller on, a second brings steam up, and a third will launch Big Picture. From there, it behaves just as the "home" buttons do on the consoles - click for BP menu, hold for more options.
Overall, and objectively, I'd rate it an 8.5/10 as a gaming controller, but then you have the fact that you can control your entire PC with it. It works on the desktop as well as in steam/in game. The right touchpad is *very* accurate for such a relatively small touchpad. I play Unturned exclusively with the Steam Controller now, it's so fun to be able to sit back and be a lazy sh**. I don't play many twitch based FPS games, but for everything else this is great. It may even work for those with some sensitivity tuning, but I prefer a mouse for those anyway, just too used to it to change.
If you use a 360 controller, I highly recommend this controller. It truly is awesome.

This may be a long review. It is needed to make all the points clear.
If you don't want to read it all, or already know how the main Telltale's games are, you can jump to the 4th point.
This game raised a lot of questions. Two of them are: "What is it about?", and "Is it like “the original” Minecraft?"
This game is about a group of friends which started by participating in a build competition. And after that competition, the whole mess started because of a bad deal. And I’m not spoiling any more of the game. See some walkthroughs on YouTube if you want to know its story without buying it.
The short answer is: No it isn’t. You won’t have a “large” world to explore or build whatever you want when you want and where you want. This only has Minecraft environment, ambience and esthetics.
The answers for this is kinda long but simple.
This is like any other Telltale's game which tries to tell a story. It’s all about people’s tastes though. Not everyone likes this type of games.
If you played “The Game of Thrones” or “The Walking Dead” or “Tales from the Borderlands” (all by Telltale games) you already know what to expect from this game in terms of mechanics and such things. If you never played any of their games read this next explanation: this game is
.
Imagine watching a movie where you can control the main character, choosing what he says at some moments and control his decisions in important moments. And those decisions will have impact in future episodes. Speaking in episodes, this game will have 8 (the inicial 5 and 3 more later) and you can finish each one in 2 to 4 hours.
And now you ask: Episodes? The answer is: yes. This type of games is released in parts, called episodes. Each episode is released at a date chosen by Telltale and comes to your game in the form of updates without the need of paying anything more. When you buy a Telltale game you already pay for the whole game.
So, answering to a question raised by a lot of people,
(that's a Portuguese expression).

Let me talk a little about the reviews on Steam. I always laugh my f****** a** off when I read negative reviews with less than 1 hour of gameplay (that's just the time for opening the game and change the settings) and call it a "cash grab". And this game has lots of negative reviews like that. (now they can ask for a refund, btw)
The second most important reason for all negative reviews in this game's page is: bugs. Every game has bugs now, but this game has some too: bugs with animations, bugs with the subtitles (the character says one thing, and in the subtitle says something similar and way longer with more things sometimes). Those were the bugs I’ve found in my gameplay time.
But people can’t stand bugs, but they still play DayZ or Ubisoft games (*cough* Assassin’s Creed *cough*). ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)
Moving on, the main reason for all the negative reviews here is: people were expecting something like a mod for Minecraft, with quests, story and all that fun stuff. It happens that this is just a regular Telltale's game (I already explained what these games are in the previous question).
.
In this game you only follow the story and interact with the other characters, picking some dialogues, making important decisions that will have impact in future episodes (or in the same where they were made), some QTEs (Quick Time Events) where you need to press a sequence of keys to do a pre-determined action (normally Up, Down, Left, Right, Q and E), biuld some pre-determined stuff (like, bow, sword... just small things), and it’s all. It sounds almost like nothing but you can still have a lot of fun. This game has drama, action and comedy. But don’t expect all that in “too high” levels. Keep in mind that, differently from the other Telltale games,
(just like Minecraft is intended for kids only but a lot of “grownups” play it too).
So, I’ve played this game exhaustively (look at my total gameplay time), finishing the already released episodes like 5 or 6 times or more, testing almost all the differente chices and decisions, and had a lot of fun (the third episode was the best, in my opinion, even with the cut off dialog bug). This depends more on people’s tastes than on random negative reviews here on steam.
So, if you like Minecraft esthetics or ambience and like the style of Telltale games that I mentioned before in this review, go ahead and don’t be afraid to buy this.

This game is a great way to pass several hours of waiting time (or to play in small batches just for fun). It's about 85% word-game, 15% RPG, so if you're looking for anything other than a quirky word game, don't buy it.
If you do love word games, definitely buy it. Buy it right now. This will be a nice change from the usual. The characters and art are simple, but consistently nice, while the designs and worlds are quite varied. There are Shops (potions and armor), Treasure Chests, Traps, Healing Springs (and medicine makers who heal for a fee), run-ins with new potential party members, mysterious otherworldly callings... Aside from weak to strong enemy encounters, a great number of things can happen each time you press on, created by a random generator. I've personally found about 6 hours of unique content so far, though I've never finished a journey or completed the character/enemy index.
There are also lots of different ways the game executes its status as a word game. For instance, if death comes for any of your characters, they have one last chance to fight back - Just solve a difficult anagram for one of two effects: a full solve for healed revival, and a partial solve for a last resort counter-attack (I've never gotten the full solve...).
You can also start a new game with characters you've leveled up in previous runs. (Personal faves are Frost Wizard, River Spirit, and Pope IX. Storm Jarl gets honorable mention.)
The music is light, but pleasant, and the sound design is pretty average.
All in all, it's definitely worth the $3, and I highly recommend giving it a try.

I want to like Barter Empire as it has all the elements of a great game. It has nice mapping, a large range of equipable items and a robust gathering/mining and crafting system. Unfortunately, the game is let down by some questionable design decisions that make it unplayable.
The first and by far the most detrimental would be the enemy battlers. They are google images of animals that are three times the size of the heroes and come as quite a shock after seeing the level of detail in the mapping. If you were to change them to the RTP battlers I would immediately recommend the title. It is that bad and interestingly there are no screenshots of them on the store page. I wonder why?
The next would be the style of the portraits. The realistic facesets clash with the rest of the assests and just look unprofessional. I want to focus on the story and dialogue, but I'm just distracted by these ugly pictures. The RTP facesets are far better.
The last would be the gathering animations. In general all of the resource gathering wastes your time. The huge "Ore Mined" picture is nice, the first time. When collecting a resource takes 10 seconds it becomes tiring. I would recommend three sound effects followed by a dialogue box. That's all the player wants and expects. By all means put the fancy pictures up for the first time the player performs them, but they add nothing to the game after that.
I want to play more as I enjoy resource gathering and crafting. I can look past the early combat being boring (standard attack to win) and some of the dialogue falling flat. There are also some troll moves by the developer (sword guy) that annoyed me but they add character and charm. The enemy battlers are terrible and are the weirdest design choice I have ever seen in an RPGMaker game. I just don't understand...

I'd like to say beforehand that I do think the game has potential, yet Barter Empire has several major flaws that impact game enjoyment quite negatively.
Firstly, the story starts off rather generically: you are a girl dropped off by blue people, recued by an old man and his dog and awake to find you've lost your memories. He sends you off to a nearby town to meet up with Maxie and the pooch comes along to help. Lets skip the rest of the story for now.
Along the way you'll run into several characters  with a ! mark over their heads, these generally have something to say that is relevant to main- or subquests, or to one of the various 'foraging and crafting' spots. The latter essentially boils down to getting a tool, going to a spot and then pressing a button that will let a little script run its course to determine if you get goodies or not.
There are many scripts in the game and some of them might be considered the good points of it. Sadly there is a lot more in terms of bad points: character portraits vary between (bizarre) GCH made portraits and handdrawn ones in a different style that 9/10 times do not match the sprite they nominally represent. Generic RM graphics are mixed with some selfcrafted ones on small maps, titanic enemy sprites are effortlessly slain by tiny character sprites and so on.
Worse though are the graphic mistakes concerning event sprites, if you activate a chest, button, sparkle or whatever there's a chance it will morph into a different part of the spriteset from which it came. Music is a bit bland, and drowned out almost by the looping sound-effects. And dialogue... For crying out loud, what dialogue is in the game is not just corny enough to provide popcorn for three movie theaters for a year, but contains so many typo's and grammar mistakes its painful to watch.
In conclusion, do not buy this game unless its discounted heavily. It has some potential, but the current build (from 2013!) is so unpolished as to be a concept rather than a pre-alpha release and should not have been released on Steam as such.

The trackpads are an interesting new feature for USB (or wireless) gamepads. They provide a bit of extra accuracy in common FPS games when aiming.
The "Dual Stage Triggers" are pretty much the same kind of triggers on the Nintendo Gamecube controllers, as you can hold them down halfway for an analog-based input, and hold it down completely until it "clicks" for a second digital input.
The only thing I dislike about the controller is the Haptic Feedback on the touchpads. For some reason, even the "low" setting seems a bit too much...
The controller overall will take a while to hold naturally in your hands, as the design almost kills your muscle memory for gamepads you use to use, like the PS3/4 or Xbox360/One controllers. If your willing to try something new, or have never used a controller for PC gaming, this may be a nice entry for you.

So if you want to try and play your games from a new angle. To get a fresh perspective (which you will initially suck at using) on playing your games. The Steam Controller is Great.

Not too many games hit the magic mark between two genres quite as well as Words for Evil.
I am a long time RPG player, and every game I have tried before this has tried to put a new spin on the Hack n' Slash or Turn Based Strategy mode of combat. Words for Evil succeeds in creating a unique way to cast your spells and swing your battle-axe. The word variety available is extensive, and I have yet to find a word I know (of three or more letters) that won't kill the bad guy.
The RPG elements here are slightly shallow, and often devolve into a shopping spree of stat boosting gear, potions, and skill points. There are some fun team compositions to explore with the array of playable classes.  And if you want to unlock all of them, you'll get an eight hour experience out of this game easy.
I highly recommend Words for Evil for any fan of word games who doesn't shy away from the grind of a RPG. Now if you'll excuse me, I need to find a seven letter word for "this kills a dragon".
I recommend this Legendary game to any who come across it's path.

Phenomenal.
It's just lightning round Boggle with some alternate rules and mini-challenges.  I played it typing with a keyboard, so I could jam out words pretty quickly, which helped immensely over dragging out words
Summary:
fighting monsters = traditional boggle style, 'used' tiles are replaced after submitting, so it has a constant, albeit partial, board replacement
disarming traps = here are 15 letters, using each only once, form some words.  Any letters left over hurt you.
unlocking treasure chests = form a 5 letter word from a given set of possible letters.  Each index of the 5 letter word has 2 options.  Passable words open the chest.
Last Stand = given 7 letters, form a 7-letter word out of them.  3,4,5 letter words earn an extra hit before the character dies.  6 letter words regenerate 50% of the character's health.
It's omega fun if you like word games.

Please note this review was written during the game's early access. (which means free Volcanic Spino, yay!)
Primal Carnage was a game I had a lot of fun on a few years ago but also I got pretty bored of it. There were only 3 game modes and only one that you could ever really find a match in, Team Deathmatch. I got pretty excited when I saw the developers were re-building the game, and the screenshots they were releasing were so good looking. I got pretty annoyed when I found out that they had decided to turn all this awesome new content into a semi-sequel game. So here it is at last, Primal Carnage: Extinction. Upon first starting up the game its immediatley obvious how much nicer the UI and graphics are. However you immediatley run into the same problems with only being able to find team deathmatch games. However, this time the developers have added loot into the game. This may sound very cool, however it is annoying as less and less players are playing on proper game servers and are instead farming the loot system on 2:00 long match, loot servers, This sucks. It means there is only ever about one fully populated server so it can be hard sometimes to find a good game. However, the core gameplay has been refined, so if you can put up with the small amount of players then extinction is a very enjoyable experience.
+ Graphics
+ Gameplay
+ Skins
- Loot Servers
- Lack of Players
Primal Carnage: Extinction is a very enjoyable game and one that I will continue to play, however it is brought down by how common the loot servers are, balancing issues and the lack of players, especially those playing other game modes.

Okay, lets just get into this. Primal Carnage: Extinction is basically just a rehash of the Original Primal Carnage (That basically declined so bad that the former devs abandoned it) and is suppose to be the "Improved" version. Never mind that this was suppose to essentially be a free update for those who purchased the Original, but that doesnt matter that much. What really matters is the gameplay, now while this game is technically in "Early Access" it's fair game to judge since the original Primal Carnage released to the public about three years ago, but the gameplay is still utterly terrible. You would think that over the course of years that the dev team would have learned already how to balance out the classes (Yes I know this is a new dev team, but this new team can learn from what the old team was doing), but they have not. Now, do you really want to buy a game that after years and years, the dev team simply cannot figure out how to make their own game work? Next up is content, there isn't much of it.....at all (Unless you want to count all the items you can BUY from the market to customize horribly optimized playable characters). Theres the same old boring maps that got a "graphical update", which is nice, but other than that they have not delivered any new content aside from BUYABLE skins. There are two entirely new maps, one of which is actually pretty cool (Consistency), but the rate they churn them out is horrific. For a game that is entirely based around Online Multiplayer, the devs need to try their hardest to update content frequently so it doesn't become stale.
There are only two game modes currently, Get To The Chopper and regular Team Deathmatch. There was a new game mode on the Original PC called Capture the Egg but that hasn't been heard of since last year. Now In Primal Carnage Exitinction, you won't find anyone playing GTTC and if you find a server packed and dedicated to just Team Deathmatch then you are lucky, and all because of this thing called Loot. A good portion of servers for this game are two minute rounds of team deathmatch dedicated to getting loot, which is digital content for the different classes that randomly drops to one or two players at the end of the match.  The devs have worked an awful lot on establishing a Market Place to buy their skins and content to fill their market while ignoring real issues, like bugs and gameplay, funny aye? Basically, this game boils down to this, theres micro-transactions glaore, lack or any real substance content, the community doesn't helps since most of them are dino thumpers who want a re-hashed skin, and theres no definite direction on where this game will go based on past track record. Most of the people who bought this game only purchased it because there was a discount that brought the game down to $3 if you owned the original. For the regular price, I cannot recommend buying it or supporting this game currently. I'd suggest purchasing another game and come back to this one in a year or two to see how it's changed. But If you're the do-gooder type like me who enjoy buying Early Access games to support the dev team and to have a hand in producing some amazing game, then I actually recommend you buy a game called Subnautica, now thats an example of how to really handle Early Access, unlike this game.

Barter Empire is a pretty grand idea for a game company I've never heard of. Crafting, Farming, Economy, Adventuring, Marriage, Adoption, Open-World, etc. are a few of the things this game tries to tackle and in my opinion doesn't do very well.
Let's begin with Crafting. Crafting is partially wonderful, partially. In order to craft new items you must level your crafting ability. That is something you see in a lot of games and is not an issue. The problem is that some levels take a ridiculous amount of items to get enough experience to level, and you must craft every item individually. No mass-production here, if you need to craft 40 of X to level, you have to sit there for 5 - 10 minutes playing the crafting minigame to craft each one. Mainly this is monotonous and gets old really fast.
Farming is SUPER EASY. If you imagined any form of difficulty with it then go back to Harvest Moon. In this, you plant a seed and just wait. No watering for multiple days cultivating your plant, just wait. Approx. 2 minutes after planting your seed it is harvestable. I swear I got a free farming game app for my smartphone instead of an $8 game.
Graphically (Not talking about the RPGMaker stuff) the game is garbage. The NPC potraits (while some a little creepy) are leaps and bounds above the player potraits. Player portraits remind me of someone taking a picture of their friend with a smartphone and then using a free app to cartoonify (is that a word?) them. The portaits in no way match the art-style of NPC portraits so it just looks poorly made. One or the other would have been fine (NPC Style is better IMO), consistency in art is way better than whatever they were trying. Landscapes use the typical RPGMaker textures, which is not bad at all.... UNTIL.... You find an area that tries to mix two VERY different ecosystems together. The game maker does not even attempt to create some sort of beffer between areas or redraw the texture to fit better. They simply put the textures side by side, creating a very obvious line down the center of the map (It looks horrible)
Please do not buy this... Unless you are punishing yourself for something...

There is the good and the bad about Barter Empire.
The Good:
-The Story seems to be pretty decent especially for a RPG maker game at this price.
-There is a whole lot of things that you can do.
-Enemies level with you - Good and Bad - this keeps all battles on a fairly level playing field as far as challange goes, but it also means that bosses or dragons are about the same as lower tier creatures.
The Bad:
-The organization of items and inventory is really very bad.  If you need to use several items at the bottom of a list you have to open the item menu each time and scroll down to the bottom.  The mouse also interferes with scrolling.
-Game ballance is very poor.  Early on, before you get a full party the battles can be challanging.  Once you have a full party then as long as you use a potion when your health gets low then every battle is pretty much the same.
-Battle mechanics  seem to be poorly designed and ballanced.  There are several skills that I have never used as the battles do not last long enough for me to build up enough vengence.
-Enemies level with you - Both good and Bad - See above.
-OP damage on both sides.  This makes battles go  quickly but almost all battles can be won just by using the basic fight command as long as your party is healed up before it starts.
-Too easy to break the difficulty of the game.  There are many items in the game that become quickly availible early on that mean your game is very easy.
-The minigames such as owning a farm have been made to require to much micromanagement.  The shop has not put out any cash for me after the initial 103 gold.
-The crafting mini-game is basically the same for all the different crafting types as well as being very repetitive.
-several bugs found, Items not named.  Getting stuck when an NPC's pathing stops in your only path out.
-Fishing and hunting seems to be totally random without any real use for them.
Overall if you are looking for a cheap game to entertain you for several hours when you are bored then this one is fairly ok.  If you are looking for something well constructed and ballanced then avoid this one.  The story seems to be fairly ok, but the bad overall gameplay makes it difficult to really find value.  I am certain that I am forgetting several points that I should also be placing in the Bad catagory, but I really do not have any intention of going back through and figuring them out.
Side Note:  On the issue of the Tiny screen press F1 to open up the menu, then highlight 'launch in full screen' and then press space bar to select it.  Restart your game and you have full screen mode.
Alternatively you can play this windowed in 800 X 600 resolution and it looks quite good without the full screen stretching.

This game has a nice, unique graphical style with likable characters and a good soundtrack.
However there are a few key components of a point-and-click game where the game unfortunately falls short:
1. Storyline:
The story-line is very linear. A P&C game has to be linear to some degree by necessity, and I have no problem with this, but this is taken to the extreme here. Commonly you have some degree of choice in which order you want to accomplish certain tasks, e.g. some tasks that require completions of several puzzles could be done in your order of choice. In this game the path is set and it is pretty clear what is required as the next step at every moment decreasing the illusion of having an influence on the storyline...
Also, it feels like there is a lot of the story that was lost on the way, like the release was somewhat rushed before the game was finished. E.g. there is a map that you find early in the game indicating many places that are not available in the game. The game design with the taxi makes me think there were bigger plans from start...
2. Difficulty/challenge:
I guess this is the most difficult aspect to get right with a P&C game. If puzzles are too hard you get stuck all the time, feel stupid, and the gameplay is not very enjoyable. If too easy, the game feels less meaningful and you do not get the nice feeling of accomplishment. This game was on the "too easy" part of the scale. Puzzles were very easy and combined with the linerar storyline, there was no point in the game where I had to stop and think. On the plus-side, although not very challenging, puzzles were generally logical and did not rely on pixel hunting...
3. Length:
Perhaps as a product of the two points above, the game felt very short. Being decently affordable and presented as an episode of a game rather tha a full game, perhaps this is to be expected. I guess that the unfinished feeling of lost intrigue/parts of the game, emphasize this feeling even more though...
Verdict:
Despite its shortcomings, the game has a certain charm to it and it was generally enjoyable. I will likely pick up part 3 when available. Although there are many other P&C games I would recommend before this one, there are also many that are worse...

Steam's time played counter stands at 3 hours for this game for me, 3 hours something likely, and despite that, I don't mind. I don't mind at all. Chapter Two of The Journey Down series is an experience pretty much any point and click fan should play through. It pulls of a pleasant balance of noir and infectious positivity, optimism, backed with undeniable visual stylishness and a superb soundtrack that couldn't be more fitting than it is. Now, I might not like all the aspects of the graphics - something about the main character just doesn't sit with me for example - and he's not the only one, but, face it, pulling off a genuinely atmospheric blend of jazzy noir with African tribal art and a mild dash of rasta culture, perhaps, is worthy of respect. The chapter functions well on its own - my memories of the first chapter are beyond fuzzy, but the game does well to explain the background and add and expand the, again, quite original and interesting lore. It does get silly, beyond silly at times, but that grates far less than it does in some other games. The cast of characters is more or less interesting, tropes or not too, some of them memorable, with some obvious hat-tipping going on around. The game is, as can be seen from my playing time, short, and I'll add easy. I AM a seasoned p&c player, but I've played through most of it @ 4AM with half my brain working likely, and the rest, including the final puzzle(s) did not pose much of a problem. You won't or at least shouldn't be wandering around aimlessly, you can't make a mistake really, everything is more or less dead obvious if you listen/read and remember what's there. Only one puzzle, with a car, had me wandering around pixelhunting (not needed in the game really) until I used an item that's really not THAT obvious or hinted at. But hey, as the old p&c adage goes... "when stuck, use everything on everything", right? Eh. Another plus is that, despite it being short, it doesn't feel as short as it is. All in all, a sequel superior to the original that left me wanting more. Will definitely get the third chapter once it's out. Good job!

I tried this game out, liking RO2 and really liking Rising Storm, and thinking that maybe a Vietnam-flavoured variant of the gameplay would be great.
I was wrong, it was awful.
Unlike RO2/RS, most of the key gameplay is hidden behind a connection and SSD-heavy "whoever loads first wins" system where the guy who lives in the same city as the server and has the game installed on an SSD gets to pick being the helo-flyer or the commander or the guy with a weapon more complicated than an M16. Most of the gameplay showcased in the trailers and screenshots is locked away.
Then there's the muddy graphics which get worse the higher you set them. It's an outright advantage to have potato-tier graphics because there's less mixup between an enemy and an oddly-shaped rock. There's something to be said about being afraid of cabbage rocks but when the guy who just killed you is running on potato-mode it's not exactly fun.
I refunded this game just after two hours of playing it, knowing it wasn't for me.
Avoid if you liked the RO2/RS style gameplay and expected it to carry over to Vietnam.

I've had the steam controller for about two weeks now, and I haven't used it for a week or so. I want to love the controller, but right now I can't recommend it.
The hardware itself is great. The comfort of holding it is Nintendo level, and I enjoy the trackpads a lot.
Where this controller falls down is the fact you MUST use the clunky big picture mode to change or customize anything about it. For every new game I used it for, it takes about an hour switching back and forth between the game and big picture mode to tweak the settings. After a while I find myself saying "♥♥♥♥ it, I'm just gonna use KB + M or my Xbox controller".
Lastly, quite often I'll load a game I've already configered and big picture mode has forgetten the configeration that took me an hour. Sometimes when trying to save a configeration I get an error message.
Until Valve either makes big picture mode easier to use, or allow the controller be adjusted with the regular steam overly + the bugs , I can't recommend it.

Where the controller shines is when doing things that usually require a mouse. For playing classic games with controller support, it's savagely missing a right thumbstick.  I'm sure some amount of practice can make you better, but hey, with practice you can probably also learn to play with your toes instead of fingers...  but why would you?  I failed my first Telltale quicktime event 4 times, plugged in a regular xbox controlled, and succeeded on 1st try.  So yeah, for games, it's bad.
So you end up with this middle of the road device that does everything a little but none of them sufficiently.  As much as I like valve and their products, they really missed the mark on this one.  I do enjoy the paddles at the back, but those are novelty items more than anything else.
