It was hard to decide whether or not to recommend this one. After all, the best version of it is quite expensive and 2K never bothered to work out even the most glaring bugs from last year's version. Finally, the changes this year did not help make it so much better. Still, if you are a WWE fan that wants to play a wrestling game, this one does deliver.
I am writing this because I'm NOT playing the game. It just crashed on me going into a big Pay Per View match I was all excited to win.
There are several modes. I tried the Universe mode where you play or watch every single match on the various weekly shows and Pay-Per-View events. I also played the MyPlayer mode where you are roleplaying one wrestler starting out a career. There are also multiplayer options that I have not yet tried.
Okay, so the game looks nice. It also plays a decent wrestling match. You have several moves to use, there's a crowd, elaborate entrances with unique music for each superstar and a challenge. There's play-by-play as if your matches were being broadcast. The events take place in different arenas and cities, some of which even look unique from each other. Even the crowds are diverse.
In the Universe mode you can add wrestlers, both ones you create yourself as well as the ones you download (there is a limited of 20 dls every 24 hours). I enjoyed adding historical wrestlers that were left out (Hulk Hogan, King Kong Bundy, Chyna) and adding celebrities that I'd like to see in the mix (Donald Trump, Batman, my girlfriend). You can create your own weekly shows as well as PPVs adding your new stars to any roster. This part is a LOT of fun.
The MyWrestler part is more of a mixed bag. No matter how long I spent, I really couldn't get my player to look very unique. I bought the game in order to roleplay trying to make it as a wrestler. Most of this mode, instead of being in the ring, my time is spent walking around backstage, talking to people, getting stuck behind others, trying to find quest givers, and doing a lot of other things that were boring from the start and worse when they had to be repeated so many times. It's all the more frustrating because I was asked to make choices but playing the same mode again and again as different wrestlers I learned that my choices did not effect the story in the least. And, just like in the previous year's versions, most of the bugs I encountered were in the myplayer mode, including CTDs, or worse, crashes at crtical points where restarting the game did not help. The entire character had to be deleted and a new one had to be started in order to play the myPlayer portion of the game! This was on the so-called patched version. There were also a lot of graphic glitches, the screen shaking and other bugs carried over from the previous years. Genereally there is no easy and fast efficient way in myPlayer mode to go from one wrestling match to the next. I was always tasked with going around and talking to people. And, after each week's tasks which quickly became mindless chores, I was instructed to walk out to the parking area and talk to a certain NPC to ask for my car. Why didn't they include a simple button to push to end your week rather than have you walk so far out of your way to talk to another NPC?
Oh, and that's another thing. The NPCs don't really talk. Their speech shows up in text, but not by voice. You have to read it. Think about that. This is 2017 and the game's most expensive version costs $89.99, yet they were too cheap to include voice files! I have to read more than half the game as if it were a text adventure!
Where there is talking out loud, it's the commentating, which gets old fast. They only have a few things to say and they say them often. They usually repeat the same tired old phrases again and again if a match goes long, taking away some of the incentive to stretch out a performance and get earn more stars for the gig.
I have been playing this game most waking hours since I bought it. My rig greatly exceeds the requirements and yet WWE 2K freezes and crashes to the desktop fairly frequently no matter what mode I'm playing. I do like it when I'm in the ring, but I'm not in there enough. In myPlayer, they have me walking around looking for people and then having inane scripted text-only conversations with them, making choices that have no effect on the story itself.
It is "playable" to a certain point IF you have the patience, but I don't have the faith it takes to believe that I'll EVER be able to play a myPlayer character all the way through from the start of his career and into the Hall of Fame if they still have one. There are just too many bugs that have forced me to start new characters and scrap rthe promising ones I had been playing. I have every WWE game that has ever been released on the PC, so I know all too well the bugs that 2K did not fix in years gone by. Why should I trust they will fix them this time around?
Still, I HAVE been playing this game for several days in a row ever since I bought it. There are many fun aspects of it. When it works, it works well. The Universe mode is better than trying out your own personal career. You can even create your own special kind of matches. I like creating a tag team of Teddy Roosevelt and Donald Trump to take on the historic greats of the eighties. It's fun having my own perrsonal girlfriend as a diva and my own enemies as the trash I can fight in the ring.  Who doesn't want to see D-X take on the Mega Powers?
I did wait for a sale to get this because, really 90 bux for a game I knew would feature so many glitches seemed a bit much. Still, none of the bugs so firmly intact are game-ending in Universe mode (that I have found), although they can end your hard-fought career in myPlayer mode. Casual players may want to pass on this one, wait for next year's batch of bugs, or at least wait for a deep discount.
So, overall I enjoy the game, but I am a specific kind of player. I subscribe to the WWE Network. I watch their Pay Per Views. I play a LOT of games. I start a PPV with Doink the Clown taking on Ronald McDonald for Clown Suprememacy of the show and follow it up with Batman and Robin versus Demolition. If you are like me, you'll probably find enough in this game to like it, but surely you'll wish they got rid of all the time-consuming walking around, the dialogue that has to be read, and the career-ending bugs.
It's good but wait until it's on sale to buy it or the DLC

I really love this game, I beg the developers to fix the bugs. It's killing an amazing game!
I am not a huge WWE fan. I was a pretty big "WWF" fan back in the day and slowly grew out of it mainly because everything is on cable and I don't have cable anymore. But this is an awesome game to bring back that nostalgia and its also just a really fun game outright although hampered by some bugs, glitches, quirks, and some questionable design decisions.
The most exciting thing and where I have clocked 99% of my hours with this game is the MyPlayer mode. Something about making your own wrassler and working your way up the chain is so satisfying and all of the new options of things you can customize have lead me to spending hours fussing over every detail of my character. While probably not new to some, I was absolutely amazed when I saw that I could take my ugly mug, import the face, and actually have an almost exact replica within the game. WOW!
The storyline, which I will avoid any spoilers, is very entertaining although sort of whacked at certain points. The developers have crafted an overarching story, but also allowed you some flexibility within it. Unfortunately, a lot of times your flexibility leads you down a path you are taking but then the game abruptly ends that to put you back on its own path. I'll explain later on. Suffice it to say, the MyPlayer mode is definitely the reason to get this game.
Now, that said, there are definitely a lot of glitches. Again, I have only really played MyPlayer so I cannot speak outside of it. On my computer, many characters vibrate rapidly. Particularly, the production manager character. I have changed every graphic setting I could, but this particular character is always vibrating rapidly and flashing black and invisible whenever I talk to them. It's almost like some sort of physics glitch.
In the storyline, I was given a brief break where I was allowed to do things on my own. I took this time to go after the US Championship. However, the game had other plans. I won the title, but the game wanted me to get into tag matches. It's almost as if it forgot that I had the US title and instead built up a little arc with a specific person as my tag partner. But then, the storyline started pushing me towards the WWE Championship and the character I was tag partners with was all but forgotten as it focused on some other person I was in a one-off match with. The storyline made it out like me and him had been tag partners all that time even though we weren't.
There's lots of inconsistencies like that. I have been jumped before matches and came back to win the struggle and the managers and backstage characters still talk as if I lost. Doing sidequests for characters is often glitchy and they yell at me for not jumping people right after I have already done so. I have also had parts where it pulled in the wrong "string" for the characters' name so out of nowhere it will mention a completely different superstar.
I wish the game did a better job of telling me if I can't do something. I'm fine with that, but tell the player that is the case so I don't think there are more glitches than there are. For example right now I am in a feud with 2 other superstars and I have found them backstage but despite unlocking the ability to do so, it will not let me brawl anyone or interrupt their promos. Same with setting allies or rivals, it just never seems to let me do it.
As far as other questionable design decisions, your MyPlayer seems to be locked into that mode. So I can't do an exhibition match of my choosing with him. It would be great if I could "copy" him out of there even if I couldn't affect the exact same character but the game doesn't let you do so. I can't use my own music in the game. I get they don't want people online with copyrighted music but in my custom MyPlayer and my own local games, there is no reason I shouldn't be able to utilize my own favorite song as an entrance music. Unlocking things is fine, but you essentially have to unlock them twice. Once to get the ability to use something and then again to purchase the ability. Same with moves, invest thousands of in-game currency into loot crates and then pay again to unlock the move. Why? And also why is it so expensive?
In conclusion, I would recommend this game if you can be understanding of its quirks. WWE fan or not, with the online features, selection of match types, amazingly realistic graphics, extreme customizability, the make-your-own-show Universe mode, and that other than some DLC characters everything is attainable in-game with a bit of elbow grease, there is no reason not to get this game. There's so many characters in the game and many legends that will be available the more I play (I can see some of them but they are locked until I have progressed) and for my old favorites, I can download them or make them myself. The series has really come a long way since my last game on Wii which was Smackdown vs Raw 2k8 and even more so since WWF No Mercy a game I played the hell out of.
There are some definite things to improve on. The developers have stated that next year's title will feature microtransactions. That's quite disappointing but almost all developers are doing that now. As long as you can still play for free it might be annoying but a necessary evil. That said, for the extra money they better work on the presentation and making the next game a lot better. People are finally getting sick of Madden releasing without any improvements year after year. I hope this game doesn't go down that path. It will also be dishearting if they abandon this game "as-is" I don't think people will purchase next year's after getting burned on this one, I know I won't. Fix the glitches, add some new features through a patch, and support this game that is really quite broken in many ways. If you can't do that the next game is doomed form the start. Especially if they build off of the last generation game year after year.

Pros:

A lot of people hate this, and for good reason.  The company is slime, but the product is decent.
Now, I've been playing wrestling games since I could move my hands, at about 3 years.  So I've got nearly 30 years of experience with almost every wrestling game that's ever been out.  Like this stuff was my life back in the day.
Some things I like about the game, some decisions are pourly made.
The universe mode surpasses everything out there right now.  MDickie's Title (as much as I love it, falls short because it's based on such an older engine and lacks many of the features that his older wrestling games had), Fire Pro (While wonderful for Simulation, still has a LONG way to go before it adds in convinences that most people want), and the other one that is on steam is just way too alpha to even begin.
But I'll be reviewing this solely on the Universe mode as that's what I'm using it for, for Twitch.  I was in E-Feds back in the day as a roleplaying wrestler/owner (those of you who are dinosaur age as me remember posting roleplays on forums and waiting for match results).  This helps me relive that.
Not only can I create just about anything for custom wrestlers (would REALLY love to see a randomization option) but they add so much to the universe that it's very intriguing.  The customization options are out of this world.  Match (which is more of an "edit" feature as opposed to creation), wrestlers, arenas, entrances, titles, etc.  This is what I've always wanted.  I can create my own show, my own arena, my own titles, and use my own wrestlers and sim the matches as I announce.
This is what I grew up doing.  I grew up doing this on No Mercy, and all of the games that we loved as kids.  I grew up doing the management side on e-feds on Maxpages, Geocities, and Angelfire.  This adds that to a degree and takes out the need for the roleplay element.
Twitch + Universe mode is the new e-fed of this generation, and I'm right there with it.  While I have stopped watching wrestling for the past 10 years, I still love the showmanship and ideal behind it.  It's a soap opera for fighting, let's be honest, but it can be a darn good one if done right.

That being said, Online was stupid as FLUFF with it's desync on 17, and I doubt they did anything to fix it because...  Well because they're almost like a tiny EA.
But picking the game up on sale and using it as a simulation game?  A+.

If you're looking for fun dino vs human gameplay, you will need to look elsewhere. Aside from numerous balance issues, bugs, exploits, and unfinished maps, the game has become nothing more than an economy simulator/fashion show. Most people only play this game to get skins and show them off, or sell them on the marketplace for money. Alone, this is not a bad thing, but that is the ONLY purpose for this game now. Most normal play servers are empty. What you're left with are no kill RP servers, freeroam servers where you can have people who are upset that you're killing each other on it, servers that put limits on elements of gameplay (like no rexes, raptor pounces, etc), and loot servers specifically designed for people to gind for drops. the way the drop system works is that, at the end of a match, everyone has a chance to get somethng. the longer you play, the greater your chances. Problem is, you don't have to "play" to get something. You can sit idle on a server for long periods and still have a chance to get something. To top that off, there is a persistent bug that prevents some people from getting drops in the first place. In my opinion, the drops aren't worth the time or money people put into them. the rediculously rare alpha skins are "OK", but everything else is more like an existing skin with different saturation levels. It just screams "lazy" on the developer's part. Aside from skins for the dinos, you can also get recolored weapons for the humans which you can barely see most of the time. The most common drop appears to be dino/human crates. To open these you have to buy keys from the game's store. The amount you pay varies on your region and currency, but still feel too expensive. Worst part is, it's all a gamble. You will more than likely get duplicates of a common skin before you get anything remotely interesting. People have reported spending upwards to $200 on keys only to not have a single rare drop. I do not recommend this game. Maybe things will change, but I highly doubt it.

Copying my review from Amazon:
I'm an odd person in that I prefer playing with controllers whenever I can, even when sitting at my desk. Up until now I've used a Dualshock 4 controller with an XInput emulator, which has worked very well for most cases. However, I have a lot of games that are not controller-friendly, and not even the emulator I'm using can perfectly adapt to keyboard+mouse controls. This is where the Steam Controller shines.
The controller has two touchpads with a button in each one, two bumpers, two dual-stage triggers (analog with digital switches at the bottom of actuation), two grip levers, four action buttons, one joystick with click, two start/select buttons, and the steam/power button. Not counting the last one, that's 20 inputs on one controller. Compare that with the Dualshock 4's 18 and the Xbox One controller's 16, and those aren't even remotely as customizable as the Steam Controller. If you count the different touchpad modes as separate input methods then the number increases to 28(!!!).
I tested it with a lot of games (The Witcher 3, Bioshock Infinite, Fallout 4, Cities: Skylines, Civilization V, Half-Life 2, Hearthstone, Faster Than Light, The Sims 4) and had absolutely no trouble setting up each and every one to work flawlessly, even those that don't support controller input. Anything from complex controller setups to simple click-and-drag is supported. The touchpads can act as a mouse, giving you the 1:1 accuracy of a mouse with the same practicality as a joystick, or you can set to work as a normal joystick if you prefer that type of input. all the buttons can emulate any button you might find on a mouse, keyboard, or controller.
The biggest issue with touchpads is the lack of physical feedback. Valve's brilliant solution to this is two linear actuators, similar to the Haptic engine in iPhone 6s, under each touchpad which can click and rumble with different intensities based on what you are doing and of course how you've set it up yourself. When using a touchpad as a mouse, the cursor is given (customizable) momentum as if you're using a trackball, and the actuator underneath makes a slight rumble that you'd expect when using a proper trackball. While using one touchpad as a mouse, you might use the other as a scroll wheel. The actuator on that side will make heavier, more satisfying clicks like a proper scroll wheel on a mouse would. Both actuators might give you feedback when using the triggers as well, clicking when you reach the hair trigger threshold.
But the absolutely amazing thing is the battery life. I've been using it intensively for soon 50 hours, testing every bell and whistle the controller provides and it's still at 100%. The whole thing runs on a couple of (included) AA batteries, and installation is stupid simple - just pop off the back cover and pop the batteries in in the right orientation.
Be prepared to spend a lot of time tweaking every little option to get the most out of your controller. You'll survive with default setups if you're not the fiddling type, but the controller truly shines only when you've set it up _exactly_ how you want it.
Overall, this is a fantastic piece of technology that perfectly suits my needs as an avid controller user. It's pretty much a keyboard and mouse condensed into a controller shape, retaining the configurability of the former and the practicality and comfort of the latter. It's probably not for everyone, but if this concept intrigues you then I will absolutely recommend it to you.

Take the time to configure it for the games you prefer to play, grab a preset for games you just want to try. 100% worth it. Once you have a solid configuration it truly is a superior remote. I was only frustrated when I tried to wing it, and now feel silly for doing so. With so much customization available my old gaming remotes pale in comparison. I'll be picking up a second controller for sure.

This controller is definitely different but it's not that hard to get used to. However, this would be based on what you used before considering getting one.
For instance, I used a Logitech M570 trackball and only trackballs throughout my life and I can say that at first the controller we unnerving to use because of the trackpads which I despise on laptops. However after playing a few hours on Rocket League and Tomb Raider, Rocket League became easier to master due to no need of using the trackpad.
When it came to playing Tomb Raider however, my aim was completely off and I kept playing with the sensitivity in the hopes of getting that "sweet spot". Thankfully, by perusing the community templates and picking the highest ranked(for obvious reasons) the game because easier to maneuver.
That isn't to say I've master 3rd person shooters, however it's because alot more easier and more relaxing to use rather to sit upright to use the keyboard and mouse.
To those thinking that because of the shape of the controller, it will cause being uncomfortable, this definitely isn't the case. Yes you do have to orient your hands in a different position, however it's a more relaxed position and using the trackpads can either require you to use the tip of your thumb or just the surface depending on your settings and if you're aiming for precision.
All in all, the controller is greatly recommended for the everyday PC gamer who just wants to relax on those nights where they have no work and just want to game.

I spent about 12 hours with this controller trying to get used to it, but it's very difficult and tedious. However, I wanted to give it a fair chance, and since it's a bit out there and new in controller designs, I knew I would need time to get accustomed to it. The software feels like it's in beta, crashing on occasion in Big Picture Mode, the touchpads not responding or responding too wildly, and the buttons needing to be clicked on several times to work. You not only have to map every button on the controller to a specific key on the keyboard (and if you haven't played the game in a while and don't remember what every button does off the top of the head, you're out of luck) but you also have to name them. While typing on the Steam controller was quite enjoyable, it's a little nonresponsive. Alternatively, you can accept someone else's button mapping, but I've found that a lot of people play with very strange button mappings. There also aren't a lot to choose from at the time of this review, because the controller has just come out; it does not work well with non-steam games even though I was assured that if I added it to my library, it would work. In fact, most of the games I linked it up to did not even recognize it as a controller which only added to my iritation.
Oddly, about 6 hours into my use of the controller, the left touchpad started making a terrible whirring noise whenever I touched it, like something rolling beneath the surface; it was distracting and worrying, and it was after that I decided to take it back to Gamestop. The design itself is quirky but difficult. The buttons are too far away from the thumb, and you have to mess around with the touchpad response to make it functional. The concave tilt is nice for your hands, but it started hurting after a while of holding it. I also accidently hit the back triggers about fifty times in every game I played, because it is so easy to squeeze the controller.
Would I recommend trying it? Not really. At least, not now. Give it some time for more people to recommend button mappings, for games themselves to do it, and to let them fix some bugs in Big Picture Mode. I was very disappointed in the product, and I was so looking forward to this controller.

>Go to your deadrising3 folder. Default should be (C: Program Files (x86) \ Steam \ Steam Apps \ Common \ deadrising3)
>create new text file in the folder
>name it "user.ini" (make sure you change the file type from txt to ini)
>open the new text file and type in “gmpcr_unlock_frame_rate = True”
>save the document
>start the game
>enjoy!!

First, I'll say I already completed the game on a different account with 45 hours in it. I’m currently playing through it again on this account.
Aside from its common technical issues, this is truly a great game. I didn’t think much of the game going into it, but by the time I was done, I was blown away just how good it was. For those that are unfamiliar with NieR Automata, you need to play through the game 3 times in order to experience the full game. The 3rd play through unlocks the 2nd half of the story. So, don’t stop when you finish it the first time.
As already complained by others, the only thing that drags this game down on PC are the known technical issues. On my first completion, I played with ReShade and crashed maybe 10-12 times out of the entire 45 hours. Playing through it again on this account, I’m using Reshade + FAR mod and I have noticed a significant reduction in crashes with the FAR mod. So, the FAR mod does appear to help and I recommend installing it before you start playing.
Overall, I did not find the crashes to be game breaking, just mildly annoying. If you make a habit of quick saving every time you fast travel, the crashes will only really have a minor impact when they occur. I do hope that they patch these known crash issues at some point though so more can enjoy the game to its full extent.
Despite the technical issues, I still recommend this game as it is one of those rare gems that everyone should play at some point. This game is easily my game of the year and I don’t hand that title down easily.

This is the first game I got just to analyze the game design, because I have heard so many "experts" on Youtube wax poetic about the procedural generation. The reviews here are outstanding. Here are my initial observations:
The Good
1) It gets better as you keep playing. So it is a learning experience and it is easy to restart. I don't feel like I lost much. The boss randomization was a good touch.
2) Some items increase your range and strength, thus making it easier to actually shoot accurately with power.
3) The logical random rooms, monsters, layout, items, and unlockables = great replay value.
4) Theme feels unique- a twisted version of the original NES Zelda.
5) Monster paths seem smarter than other 2D platformers.
The Bad
1) For a game that requires pinpoint control, it is a huge black mark to have such frustrating controls. The default AWSD to move, arrows to fire, Space to use item, Shift to drop bombs is too cumbersome. The mouse option is better, but it is still non-intuititive to fire. Not having easy diagonal is baffling.. Being told to Google Joy2Pad in the actual game was just plain insulting.
The Weird
1) The theme is post-modern or just plain teenage potty humor, depending on your POV.
2) The music fits atmospherically, but the melodies aren't as good as I expected based on the hype.
3) The artwork is also post-modern or done by someone who can't really draw like an adult yet.
4) Although learning what the items do is part of the "fun", negative consquences seem spiteful.

This might honestly be one of the most important games in recent years. The main game consists of three different playthroughs, each one approaching the same story from a different point of view. Just when you think you understand all the motives and events in one playthrough, you learn something earth shattering in the next playthrough that recontextualizes all those things you thought you knew, to a point where it almost feels like, after the cold opening of the third playthrough, the developers are finally letting you look at the bigger picture of the narrative, which in any other game might have come across as contrived, or just as a means to drag out the game length, but Platinum Games really made this feel powerful and rewarding.
A great action RPG with an absolutely mesmerizing soundtrack to boot, Nier Automata is easily one of my favorite games. Very intuitive controls and some interesting mechanics, combined with challenging enemy types and incredibly intense boss fights makes every successful encounter feel fresh and rewarding, which helps considering a lot of the missions can boil down to one of a few formulas, either clearing out an area of enemies, escorting a character to an objective, etc.
HOWEVER, this game is a perfect example of a PC port being done as a complete afterthought, and it performs absolutely abysmally. I've tried every graphical preset in the settings, and no matter how I configure the graphical settings I get a consistent framerate of 24-32 which is absolutely inexcusable. I've also noticed weird things such as how I have my resolution set to 1920x1080, yet it looks as if it were set to something slightly lower.
All in all, an incredible game but a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor excuse for a port. I'd absolutely recommend playing the game, but make sure to get it on sale, because $60 for a game that the publishers/developers have no intention of patching is ridiculous.

The Journey Down: Chapter 2 is a *huge leap* from Chapter 1.
If you have played the first and are nostalgic of classic games such as Monkey Island, I would recommend this for you.
I smiled, giggled, and quite enjoyed it a lot!  :)
The soundtrack is relaxing and amazing. The characters are just as charismatic as in Chapter 1 and the dialogue / story-line have an even greater sense of humour.
Additionally, this game's VOICE actors are talented - which makes the game much more immersive.  They did an incredible job for you to relate to the characters even though they are quite simplistic visually; in a sense that their faces are all based on "African" or "Caribbean" wooden face masks but which were carefully chosen by design to portray their basic personality traits.
Needless to say, graphically, it's well-done. A mix of simple and complex imagery. The cut-scenes are breathtaking.  The feel of the art-style is quite fitting with the entire story / mood.
The puzzles increase in difficulty as the game progresses... I got stuck maybe 2-3 times for a while but it was never frustrating -  I persevered until I figured it out.  Very much satisfying! :)
In summary:  Underrated humorous point & click adventure.  I recommend that you play Chapter 1 if interested, as there is a progression to the story (**even though I noticed that they made sure via the dialogues that you would not feel lost if you hadn't played Chapter 1, so maybe not necessary?**).  The length of the game was satisfying as well, considering it took me so long to figure out the last puzzle.  Ya' mon! :)
I'm looking forward to Chapter 3!

In the second chapter of The Journey Down you will once again be playing the part of Bwana, sorry to spoil it for those who haven't played the first chapter, but the game picks up with the plane crash. You will get to spend the vast majority of this chapter in Port Artue, a city below the previous city that you played the first chapter in. The biggest difference between this chapter and the previous, though, is the fact that the pace has picked up. There's definitely some urgency, and some large obstacles standing in your way. Remember you are still trying to get to the final destination, but there's going to be people who will do anything to stop you.
Graphically you are still looking at the same type and feel as the first chapter. I did like the locations of the game a bit more than the first chapter. You are in a city where it is perpetually night, but there's definitely different levels of feel and look to this chapter. You are going to see the Club Temba, you are going to see a light house, back alleys, some places you don't even want to be in, but you are going to be in. I felt like this game just looked crisper than the first. I know that sounds weird seeing as this is the same engine that powered the first, but it looked like there was more flexing of the muscles in the engine this time around.
Once again the voice acting seemed to fit the tribal masks that were put to the faces of the characters that you are going to interact with. There's also going to be a bigger cast of characters to interact with, and impressively enough all of them will be voiced. What can I say there's just something about hearing voices put to faces and characters.
The controls once again are going to be point and click. Always be on the look out for an object that just stands out, chances are you are going to need to use it, or take it in order to get through this game.
Alright, so here we are, chapter 2. I really wish I could write it without doing spoilers, but there's just some that are just going to have to be said. First off you are in Port Artue. A city in that lives in a permanent night time, but seems to sparkle all the more for it. You are going to find yourself immediately on a boat that is lost at sea. Now I know its not really hard to figure out that you make it into port, but there you have it. You will then have an immediate obstacle put in your path and you are going to find that your crew of characters from the first chapter are going to be torn apart, and it is through the majority of this chapter that you are going to be trying to get them back together. There's definitely another round of puzzles, and utilization of objects in order to reach your goal. I'm going to be honest, there's going to be some head scratching at a couple of points, but if you trust in your inventory, and you are paying attention to the objects you can pick up, you should always have some sort of solution at hand.
This was definitely a stronger chapter than the first, and it definitely shows itself as giving you a hell of a lot of story, and action packed into over 3 hours of game play. Now I know that this seems like a small number for some, but you have to realize that this is a chapter, and that, in my opinion, is a good amount to play with in a chapter. Now that being said, you are definitely going to need to play the first chapter to figure out all the characters, and story, but this is definitely a chapter you don't want to miss out on. So with that I have to give this game a 9.3 out of 10.

This is the first game I got just to analyze the game design, because I have heard so many "experts" on Youtube wax poetic about the procedural generation. The reviews here are outstanding. Here are my initial observations:
The Good
1) It gets better as you keep playing. So it is a learning experience and it is easy to restart. I don't feel like I lost much. The boss randomization was a good touch.
2) Some items increase your range and strength, thus making it easier to actually shoot accurately with power.
3) The logical random rooms, monsters, layout, items, and unlockables = great replay value.
4) Theme feels unique- a twisted version of the original NES Zelda.
5) Monster paths seem smarter than other 2D platformers.
The Bad
1) For a game that requires pinpoint control, it is a huge black mark to have such frustrating controls. The default AWSD to move, arrows to fire, Space to use item, Shift to drop bombs is too cumbersome. The mouse option is better, but it is still non-intuititive to fire. Not having easy diagonal is baffling.. Being told to Google Joy2Pad in the actual game was just plain insulting.
The Weird
1) The theme is post-modern or just plain teenage potty humor, depending on your POV.
2) The music fits atmospherically, but the melodies aren't as good as I expected based on the hype.
3) The artwork is also post-modern or done by someone who can't really draw like an adult yet.
4) Although learning what the items do is part of the "fun", negative consquences seem spiteful.

I spent about 12 hours with this controller trying to get used to it, but it's very difficult and tedious. However, I wanted to give it a fair chance, and since it's a bit out there and new in controller designs, I knew I would need time to get accustomed to it. The software feels like it's in beta, crashing on occasion in Big Picture Mode, the touchpads not responding or responding too wildly, and the buttons needing to be clicked on several times to work. You not only have to map every button on the controller to a specific key on the keyboard (and if you haven't played the game in a while and don't remember what every button does off the top of the head, you're out of luck) but you also have to name them. While typing on the Steam controller was quite enjoyable, it's a little nonresponsive. Alternatively, you can accept someone else's button mapping, but I've found that a lot of people play with very strange button mappings. There also aren't a lot to choose from at the time of this review, because the controller has just come out; it does not work well with non-steam games even though I was assured that if I added it to my library, it would work. In fact, most of the games I linked it up to did not even recognize it as a controller which only added to my iritation.
Oddly, about 6 hours into my use of the controller, the left touchpad started making a terrible whirring noise whenever I touched it, like something rolling beneath the surface; it was distracting and worrying, and it was after that I decided to take it back to Gamestop. The design itself is quirky but difficult. The buttons are too far away from the thumb, and you have to mess around with the touchpad response to make it functional. The concave tilt is nice for your hands, but it started hurting after a while of holding it. I also accidently hit the back triggers about fifty times in every game I played, because it is so easy to squeeze the controller.
Would I recommend trying it? Not really. At least, not now. Give it some time for more people to recommend button mappings, for games themselves to do it, and to let them fix some bugs in Big Picture Mode. I was very disappointed in the product, and I was so looking forward to this controller.

The Steam Controller (1st Retail Generation - November 2015)
Let’s get this out of the way, right from the start. The Steam controller is not and will not be for everyone. For those of us tied to keyboard and mouse setups, then the steam controller will feel limited, mainly because you no longer have a gazillion buttons at your disposal and mouse and keyboard ‘people’ tend to hate any other controller type. For those of us who come from a console generation, this will be the first time you have had a challenge learning a controller since the Xbox Controller onwards. Why? because this controller is radically different and houses an impressive amount of tech, which (frankly) controller’s haven’t really done since the Wii Controller.
So let’s talk about what tech is onboard. First let's talk about the two big owl eyes on the controller face. Both of these are touch sensitive pads that can be configured to work as a trackball mouse or a thumb pad. The touchpad on the left has a cross in the centre to help you feel around and is most often found to be configured as a d-pad alternative, however it too can be configured to work as a trackball mouse or thumb pad. Under each pad is a motor which provides haptic feedback independant of each pad, therefore you have have haptic feedback work differently on each pad, thereby giving you different ‘feel’ feedback under each thumb.
Within the device is a Gyro and Accelerometer - the same tech you find in mobile phones so they can sense what direction they are being moved in. This tech is not dissimilar to the Wii Controller and when activated you can map the gyro to a mouse like interface. This is especially useful in FPS games where you can map pressing down a button (I use the right thumb touchpad) and then you can map to look down sights and move the controller as if it were a real gun before hitting a trigger to unleash hell. On the underside there are two flipper buttons, which I found to be really great at gear shifting in racing games, as well as being used as an intuitive button set to crouch (hide) and run in Fallout 4. Other than that the ubiquitous four button ‘Xbox’ style button layout is there. The buttons are much smaller than even the 360 controller, which initially meant that my thumbs muscle memory would often hit B rather than A. But after a few hours practice the muscle memory now knows where the four buttons are.
Ok so that’s roughly all the tech inside. If you ask me, that's pretty impressive since we have in essence the tech from a Wii Controller, the tech from a Mobile Phone, the Tech from an Xbox Controller, the tech from driving controllers and the tech from ultra sensitive touch pads AND amazing software that allows you to fine tune the setup to match any and all games that can be played using the steam platform.
So, how does it play?
OK, so as I said there is a learning curve you will have to go through, this controller is not a Xbox/PS4 derivative, it is its own master and for that reason you are going to have to take sometime to re-learn what you (think) you already know. But this is time well spent. In FPS games and RPGs (this controller is just the business in Fallout 4), you will need to either select a decent community made layout or create your own. Perseverance is the key here, tweak and tweak some more and you will be ultimately rewarded with (what I believe to be) a far superior controller to either traditional gamepads OR mouse and keyboard. In Driving games, there is little to write home about, this plays (almost) like a traditional controller, however those flippers on the back mean that manual gearbox shifting is intuitive and gives you an edge over players using traditional controllers or keyboard and mice. Where the real standout moment is, is in PC games that were made for mouse and keyboard. Civilization V and Beyond Earth became sofa games the moment I started using the controller for them. Even the ‘recommended’ controller layout worked beautifully on these titles.
Verdict
I took 7 calendar days before posting my review up regarding the controller, I wanted to take time to get used to it and play it on a number of different games and game types. I decided to publish when I accidentally dropped the controller on the floor and was seriously worried I had damaged it, not because it cost £50 but because I really now value this controller over the Xbox360 controllers I have gathering dust (now) next to my gaming rig. For me, this controller does everything exceptionally well, but it's going to take you time to relearn and to tweak.
In many ways this is exactly what we SHOULD expect from a PC controller, it is massively configurable across every game and game type, it gives you choices and options that you didn’t have before. And it isn’t tied to a single configuration across every game type. In Fallout 4 and GTA V, this controller really is allowed to shine, because you can setup different control options for different situations and change between them seamlessly. In GTA V, I can now drive with the feel of a Xbox gamepad, leave the car and aim and take down opponents with the feel of a mouse and keyboard - no other controller can do that.
I often hear people saying the build quality isn’t all that.. I tend to disagree, this controller has alot of tech under the bonnet, and to keep the price down sure there clearly have been compromises made with thinner plastics being used in some places. But once you have the two AA batteries installed the much needed weight is there and I think it holds up well in against other controllers on the marketplace.
I’ve also heard that the controller feels to big, personally I have very large hands so it was nice to finally pick up a controller that seemed to have been designed  adult sized hands.
For me, this controller has become my control mechanism of choice. I don’t want or need to go back to the Xbox controllers, and I can now access games that used to require mouse and keyboard on my TV downstairs whilst sitting on my Sofa.
A clear 9/10 from me - it loses 1 mark only because of those ABXY buttons being a little on the smaller side of optimal, but honestly I’m being really picky here, it's the best controller I have ever purchased (I love it even more than my X55 Rhino!), to the point where I get concerned if it gets damaged and I won't be able to use it.

WWE 2k18 is a typical 2k-game: One step in the right direction, two steps back, one random hop somewhere else and please, if you don't like where you land, you gotta pay to move again.
On one hand, they really did try their best with some of the actual gameplay. Aleister Black, Bobby Roode, Triple H, Ambrose, Nakamura - they all look incredibly good and you can feel that somebody put not just good work, but actual heartblood in there.
However, the game lacks so much else and throws away sooo much potential, it's almost funny if it wasn't so sad.
Yes, the backstage area is a bit bigger - but it's still just the same corridor, and still a smaller era than back in PS2-days.
Yes, we got the biggest roster again - but who needs 5 Stings instead of several of the actual interesting stars (Heavy Machinery? Street Prophets? Velveteen Dream? Liv Morgan? The Singh-brothers? Even Ellsworth? Nah screw 'em all, but hey, who doesn't want to play as the Van Erichs or the Natural Disasters?).
Yes, we get 8-man-matches. Now, Survivor Series Matches are 10-Man-Matches, and we still miss several other types of matches, but at least now we can replay all those great directionless 4-on-4-tagteam-matches that we all love so dearly, Playah!
Yes, career-mode is back - but you don't really "choose" anything resembling a career. In fact, the game is so broken, they even screw up the little "stories" you try to create for yourself. Example? Ok, here we go, a little excerpt from my actual gameplay:
You go to call out the Big Show (why? Because your character decides so on his own, for whatever reason). While doing the promo, Roman Reigns comes out. Why, because he's the Big Show with a wig, obviously. After the promo, which you friggin RULE (by restarting the promo again and again ... not by using simple logic, because the promo is an incoherent mess of barely connected thoughts and cookie-cutter-insults anyway), people comment how you totally OWNED Samoa Joe (why, because he ate Roman "the Big Dog Show" Reigns, obviously). Then, the next week, you face Konnor 1 on 1 - but before your match, you get ambushed by Seth Rollins, because he's p***ed at your promo from last week (... obviously!). This will culminate at the next PPV, where you face Finn Balor, because, at this point, why the f*** not?
The actual worst part about this? The game loads the Backstage Era. You move from the parking lot to the production era. On the way you can talk with random people. It doesn't matter if you do or don't, because they say random BS anyway (yes Asuka, you could eat several Pizzas right now. How cool is that? Yes Brock, i'm really ready for tonight. Yes Bayley, you SHOULD take note at my promos, because yours kinda suck, ... and so on..). Anyway, some production-guy spouts a two liner at you ala "go show em what you got!". Then the game looaads. You cut a nonsense-promo. The game loooaaads the backstage era. Again. You talk to the production guy, again. He wants you to go see Renee. Ok. You go to Renee (who at least looks human now. Yay!). The game looooaaaads, because obviously giving Renee one out of two answers (non consequential answers that is) is load-heavy. Then the game loooooaaaaads the backstage era. AGAIN. You go to the parking lot and get your car. You're finished for this week. The game looooooaaaaaads and you are in the parking lot again. You walk'n'talk with the production guy again, have a very short loooooooaaaaaaading-screen, cut a promo and then ....... repeat ad infinitum. It's LoadingScreen 2k18! And you sit there, wondering if anybody from game-design actually played that mess and why these people hate fun.
Now, all of that would still be entertaining in a trainwreck-kind of manner ... if it wasn't for the incredible individuality the game promises you. BE LIKE NO ONE! is the title. It's in the add, it's in the game. So naturally, when you create a wrestler, you choose a pre-made class, which decides which moves you can or can't use, and what abilities/skills you can buy. Huh. High flyer able to do a piledriver, powerslam or omega driver? Nope. Giant who can do Coast2Coast? Ha! Powerhouse who can just even climb the turnbuckle? Forget it, no powerhouse EVER does that! (to clarify: That means that you can't even recreate several of the REAL and ACTUAL wrestlers on the roster!). These classes and your weight also determine your attributes. You will not exceed 91 points and will always lack in at least one fundamental field, no matter what (because f*** you, that's why).
Anyway, then you get to create your guy - and you can't. Because it's locked. Because you need to buy lootboxes to unlock EVERYTHING, including basic content, fun and your will to live.
Want that facepaint of Sting because 5 Stings are just not enough for you? Or a specific move that is totally cool and exotic like ... chokeslam02 (oh comon...) ? Or want to wear Darren Youngs underwear because you are really really weird and random, almost ... LIKE NO ONE? Well, tough sh!t son. You are not like no one, you are a nobody.
For every match, you get 200 to 400 credits. For 2500, 5000 or 10.000 credits, you can buy lootboxes. And then you pray that there's finally something else inside than just Chris Jericho's boots 01 for the 12th time.
And it is.... a booster for your next match (only for online-gaming. Because of course, who doesn't want to play this mess online?), Titus O'Neal underwear (... i don't even .. just why?), Powermove 18 (..ok), mustaches06 (... finally i can look like my favourite stupid anime character. Hooray. *sigh*) aaaand ... no, not Chris Jericho's boots01, but 800 credits! Ha! Sweeerved!
It's a grind beyond stupid. It's not even next level stupid. It's typical WWE-stupid. And no fun whatsoever.
Personally, i went ahead and edited a few numbers and gave myself a metric f***ton of credits. Opened ca. 80 lootboxes - and still didn't get the stuff i wanted (but hey, they repay me 200 credits in return whenever i get Chris Jericho's boots01 now .. so that's something, right?). It's mind numbingly boring and idiotic. And the worst?
It's so goddamn obvious that they want to 'ease' us into next year's release featuring lootboxes you can buy for real money .. it's so glaringly obvious, Roman Reign's push was subtle in comparison.
Here's to hope that Belgium pushes the ban on this loot-system and the EU follows suit. Maybe then they will remember that fun content is more important than a cash grab.
Last but not least, i want to personally vote for the guy who chooses the Soundtrack for WWE games to be fired. Kanye, Rap and HipHop, is one thing. Country music (who would even listed to this sh!t?!?) is a whole different beast. But who in their right mind decided that Kid Rock singing about being high would be a good fit for a WWE game? Or any game that's not GTA, Saint Rows or the like? At least we got the old classic by Disturbed (censored, of course, because America is totally the land of the free... hah), but you're still better of just muting the music completely.
All in all, i see barely any improvement to last year, a slightly updated roster aside - but several wrong directions this series is taking all at once. In this incarnation, the only fitting description is "wasted potential and bad decisions". So in a way, this is the perfect game for you, if you want that special WWE feeling....

I really like this game. Recently i've been playing heaps of online scrabble and when i stumbled across Words for Evil i thought it sounded interesting and unique, plus the art is really nostalgic of a lot of older games with pretty simple and repeditive adventuring style gameplay.
So in saying that, it definetly is interesting and unique. I haven't played a game like this before. The adventuring style is basically constant sidescroll running across (what seems to be) a totally randomised landscape with different kinds of actions available that you interact with using words. There's monster battles, traps, treasure chests you unlock, blacksmith, potion man, a healing well, and new party members to be found (including santa)
The music and sounds are also pretty nice and relaxing.
HOWEVER- one thing i do not like about this game and keeps causing me to close it in anger is the obscurity of the words sometimes used, (that you have to unscramble to make an anagram and save yourself for example).
I can understand having trickier words for more dire situations but it kind of feels like the people who made this game just found an online dictionary and added the whole lot into the game, including some of the most unfair words no one would really know unless you were specifically looking up the names of certain dog muscles or what the leader of a remote african tribe is called etc.
If the game was a bit less challenging i would definetly say to keep the complex words in, because who likes it when it's not a challenge right? Monster battles would be pretty easy to anybody, you just need to include the "special" letters to do attacks, and that means 3 letter words are OK. However sometimes because of the randomising of encounters, you really need to get into a chest to save yourself because a well just does not seem to be coming around anytime soon, and you can only carry 3 potions maximum.
Also another problem i find is that i can't understand the weapons/armour system. there is no way to tell what weapon you are weilding and im not sure if your weapons replace when you buy them or just add to your attk stat. there is also no way at all to check your armour rating apparently.
So all in all, i would say i reccomend this game to friends because it's simple, can be pretty relaxing, and fun to play when you dont have much time to commit. Just make sure you change the difficult to Zen if you're prone to frustration easily or dont have an extensive vocabulary. I also hope the developers fix the armor and weapon issue soon.

I really wanted to like this game. But, one of the main reasons I play adventure games is that I don't want to have to deal with the pressure of fast action or quick reflexes. However, not long into the game, you suddenly realize that it's getting a bit difficult to breathe, and a timer starts for you to figure out how to increase the oxygen level in your little capsule. Inevitably, the timer runs out before you find the right action, and your tragic death is announced. Of course, the timer resets, and you have another go at it, until you meet your second untimely death, then your third, or however many tries it takes before you discover (or look up) how to get past the barrier.
Then, when you get to the moon, there are these large crevasses to cross by jumping just the right amount in the moon's low gravity. Now, "just the right amount" is determined by a needle that is moving up and down. If you hit the key when the needle is in the green region, you make it across. If not, the announcer is back with another enthusiastic heralding of your untimely death. It's terribly demoralizing.
What's worse, there is some bug that prevents the menu from displaying properly so that you can't always save (or exit!) the game reliably once you've crossed some annoying hurdle.
After a couple of hours, I found the game too frustrating to continue, which is a shame, because the story and graphics seemed promising.

I recently played(and reviewed) a similar puzzle platformer, VVVVV or some nonsense, which I didn't find was to my liking.  As such I had some apprehension about Out There Somewhere.
I'll tell you that was some misplaced anxiety.  This game has a teleport mechnic that allows it to progress beyond simple muscle reflex puzzles and actually assess all the factors on a screen before proceeding with a solution.  After I completed the game, I felt satisfied.  I felt like I had accomplished some pretty interesting puzzle platforming, and I felt like I kind of wanted to play it through again.
All that being said, this game isn't very long.  I don't know how much time I spent playing it, currently, but I think it was about an hour(Edit: 54 mins...)  which was actually perfect since I was on a flight and after I finished we were close to landing.  I see myself playing this again on my return trip and probably enjoying it just as much.
One interesting thing I noticed in the options was the feature to turn on a timer, which seems an interesting little contraption to let you time your runs.  There's also a few areas I can think of where I may have been able to explore but they were early in the game before I really learned the capabilities of the teleporter gun.
That's another bit that's interesting.  They don't throw new items at you through the game to make places accessible, with the exception of a gun near the beginning.  Anything you are able to accomplish late game with the teleporter you can do at the start... provided you grasp the concept fast enough.  The gun you obtain later is really only to destroy blocks and enemies, but it seemed to me (nearly) every screen could potentially be accomplished without killing a single enemy.
The last bit I'll mention is that I played this game entirely on the Steam Controller, I've yet to find a platformer that doesn't work well with it, but I'll say playing a game on the plane was MUCH more comfortable with a controller in hand, rather than playing the part of a contortionist to access the keyboard wedged in front of me, though this is just commentary and doesn't affect my review of the game.
Addition: OK, so since I was in an airplane and didn't pay for wifi, steam didn't register the time I'd played the game and wouldn't let me post a review with 0 minutes logged.  I started up a new game and can confirm in the 12 minutes of extra play time I found 3 screens I didn't even register existed on my first play through within the 'tutorial' section of the game.  So if you happen to be an achievement collector, or just like the game you can easily double that hour play time going through with a replay.
Its worth the standard price(which is cheap as it is,) but if you find this game on sale, don't hesitate to nab it if you enjoy puzzle games or plaformers.  It's got some interesting mechanics.

What can i say about Nier that hasn't been said already?
Gameplay wise, it's good: the player is presented with a good variety of weapons (both melee and ranged), special moves, upgrade chips to customize your characters stats and moves and much more. You feel like a badass chopping away at 10, 20 robots at the same time with some flashy moves. There is also a hacking mini game and shooting sections to spice up the gameplay even more, with cool camera changes and fun bosses.
Great soundtrack with some epic and memorable musics (the village song comes to mind).
But above all, this game has an AMAZING story: you'll follow the actions of 2B and 9S, two androids fighting to reclaim earth for humanity against robots that are more intelligent and alive than one might think. The story is told on multiple perspectives through multiple paths: on one path, you're playing as 2B, on the other you're playing as 9S. The game has a total of 26 endings (21 of them are joke endings, the real ones are endings A, B, C, D and E) that you get by making certain choices or actions during the course of the game. To get all the main endings, the player must finish three main paths: A, B and C, but it never gets boring, far from it: the games gets better and better the further you play and the more you invest in the world and story.
Is it the best game of the world? No: the sidequests are average with only a few that could be considered great and the gameplay could use some more variation, perhaps with a combo system of sorts and some different types of hacking mini games. But the amazing story and great soundtrack more than make up for it.
Seriously, buy the game.

I love mine. I've been a PC gamer for years and play pretty decent with keyboard and mouse, but this controller is just fun to use and very accurate. Will take some getting used to, but I also have a 360 controller and could never get the hang of it no matter how hard I tried, it just wasn't quick enough for my brain to register like it like a mouse. Buy it only if you are not already good with the other controllers and want a device that you could possibly make it a extension of your hands, like console gamers. I wanted to add that my hands don't get tired like on the 360 and after awhile, the controller feels like just an extension of your hand. It does take time to get the correct amount of sensitivity and acceleration on controller and game, but man it is worth it. If you are use to a Xbone controller than you probably would not feel comfortable, but if you like the accuracy of the controller and gyro, but it now.

EDIT: So since the time i have written this review they have fixed 90% of the bugs that i have expirenced every so often and on top of that they have released new features within the software. Couldn't be more impressed with the team at valve working on fixes/updates with the controller. 10/10 Never going back to a "standard" controller again.
Pros:
- makes fps games enjoyable / playable while using a controller and not kb/m.
- fully customizable (im serious, i was suprised to see how many options there were)
- dual stage triggers / grip buttons are jesus
- dual trackpads that can emulate dpads, joystick, buttons, trackball, and more with full customizability is jesus
- comfortable
- it looks sick and you can show off to your friends
- makes a subtle boo-beep and a bee-boop sound when you turn it on and off respectibly
cons:
- big picture mode needs to run in the background for controller support
- big picture mode is kinda buggy
- learning curve, i personally needed 20 hours of handling the controller to feel 100% comfortable with it
Conclusion:
- As long as valve keeps pumping out bug fixes for big picture mode (like they did today which fixed a bunch of the annoying bugs i have been expirencing), there is no reason for it to not replace your current controller. With that said, i would reccomend this product to anyone who plays with a controller already or someone who would like to play casually while chilling on the couch or reclining in their chair.

This might honestly be one of the most important games in recent years. The main game consists of three different playthroughs, each one approaching the same story from a different point of view. Just when you think you understand all the motives and events in one playthrough, you learn something earth shattering in the next playthrough that recontextualizes all those things you thought you knew, to a point where it almost feels like, after the cold opening of the third playthrough, the developers are finally letting you look at the bigger picture of the narrative, which in any other game might have come across as contrived, or just as a means to drag out the game length, but Platinum Games really made this feel powerful and rewarding.
A great action RPG with an absolutely mesmerizing soundtrack to boot, Nier Automata is easily one of my favorite games. Very intuitive controls and some interesting mechanics, combined with challenging enemy types and incredibly intense boss fights makes every successful encounter feel fresh and rewarding, which helps considering a lot of the missions can boil down to one of a few formulas, either clearing out an area of enemies, escorting a character to an objective, etc.
HOWEVER, this game is a perfect example of a PC port being done as a complete afterthought, and it performs absolutely abysmally. I've tried every graphical preset in the settings, and no matter how I configure the graphical settings I get a consistent framerate of 24-32 which is absolutely inexcusable. I've also noticed weird things such as how I have my resolution set to 1920x1080, yet it looks as if it were set to something slightly lower.
All in all, an incredible game but a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor excuse for a port. I'd absolutely recommend playing the game, but make sure to get it on sale, because $60 for a game that the publishers/developers have no intention of patching is ridiculous.

This controller takes some getting used to as it uses a very different control method, so don't expect to be good and comfortable with it from just a few hours of use(or even a few days in some cases). Pros:
+Steam has the best controller configuration functionality I've seen yet, the controller is easy to configure yet has many options.
+The trackpads are great to use once you get used to it.
+Comfortable to hold(similar size and weight to existing console controllers).
+Allows you to play more KB+M games easily with a controller.
+Added inputs(grips, dual-stage triggers) are a welcome addition.
+Convex thumbstick is more comfortable to use than concave ones(at least for me).
+Haptics provide interesting feedback.
+Replacable batteries and amazing battery life(been only using this controller with games for about a week and the included batteries are still going).
Neutral:
+/-Controller requires an adjustment period(although it's worth it, in my opinion).
+/-I'm genuinly unsure if I prefer having the control stick over a traditional D-pad in its place.
Cons:
Got used to this. Oddly this took longer to get used to than the touch pads.
-It is a pain to remove some rechargeable batteries from the controller.
Things I'd like to see in the future:
-Write a "desktop mode" profile to the firmware of the controller for use when Steam is not running.
Anyway, I like this controller, it certainly does open up more compatibility and personalization.

Please ignore my time on record, I've played this game at least 12x as long from the website download before it came out on Steam. Now, before I begin let me say that I'm very picky when it comes to MMOs and my original reaction to this game was 'meh' at best, mainly because Aeria Games had picked it up (and we all know how greedy they can be at times). But, instead of being a total ignorant♥♥♥♥♥♥and judging a game before giving it an extensive crash course testing I decided to give it a go. Let me tell you I never expected to play it as much as I previously stated.
Starting off, this is probably and arguably the best Anime MMO out there that's COMPLETELY free. The cash shop is quite balanced, there are no items that'll make a cash player better than a f2p player. If anything, cash shop has more aesthetics and eye candy (not to mention a few items that help boost leveling slightly) than god-mode items. Coming from Aeria, I was highly surprised to see the cash shop as balanced as it is now.
Now, on to the game in itself. There are (I believe, not entirely sure because I never cared to count) about 12 classes to choose from and each class is fairly balanced. The Ravager (which is the most preferred destroyer class) has insane damage and health, but is easily succeptable to speed reduction and DOT, not to mention stuns and other debilitating debuffs. Too many people believe Ravager to be the God class when in reality it's just the sweeper class, designed to deal damage at the cost of speed and defenses. Duelists are highly underrated, which is a shame because they're Somersault ability allows you to completely avoid and negate incoming damage for a second or two and reduces further damage substantially for a few more seconds. With a rather quick cooldown, spamming that move can make you invincible if used often, though the drawback means you won't be able to deal much damage thus making you a skipping punching bag. Every class has its strengths and weaknesses, you just need to sit down and familiarize yourself with their mechanics and purposes.
The combat is pretty cliche, at first. I've seen many so-called 'hardcore MMO brainiacs' pick apart many good MMOs because of little things that quite frankly only adheres to their opinion and not fact. The combat is, yes, tab/click targetting with hotkey spamming. However, that's where the 'easy similarities' dissipate. At level 40 you are given the mandatory quest to choose a secondary school/weapon, which furthers the customization of not only your character but your combat play as well. Want a Sorceror wielding Duel Pistols? Go for it. Though you're targetting mobs and bosses and other players via tab/click targetting, the hotkey spamming isn't exactly a cakewalk. You have literally over two dozen different abilities to spam, and knowing where all your skills are and when to use what at the right time does take more skill than simply hammering 1-9 back and forth. If certain skills are used in certain orders you're able to perform combos or faster hits whereas if you were to spam your quick attack with a slow stun debuff you just wasted a possibility of four other moves you could have chained. That, however, is not the only part that makes combat a challenge. Bosses and even some mobs have what's commonly called in-game as Red Carpets; a red spot or lane laid out on the ground that tells you where a heavy attack is going to land. However, these Red Carpets have no countdown timer like on Wildstar, it will simply pop up and a few seconds later the Boss/Mob's attack will follow, so you have to continue to move around; you can't stand and tank damage (especially on Party/Hell mode Dungeons). If you're able to get behind a Boss or Mob you also deal bonus damage, so anyone that argues the combat is 'bland and cloned' is just butt-hurt because they can't handle it.
The story isn't nothing special in my opinion (I write novels as a hobby since I was 10, so I've read and written many different plot styles), but that can change according to your opinion. Questing is generic (like ALL other MMOs so there's no need to criticize this) with open world quests followed by a Boss instance near the end. You can either click on your quest to auto-run to your objective or free-run, the choice is yours. Leveling is very fast, with 70 being the level cap but questing ending at level 55 (though there are smart ways to avoid the 55-60 grind that I'll be kind enough to inform you about here shortly). Also, the best gear and items are all dropped, so there is no lazy 'pay to win' unless you have a crap ton of gold (which is reasonably difficult to obtain) and continually trade players said gold for items or stalk the auction houses (which requires a lot of gold, which requires a lot of time).
As I just mentioned, from level 55 up to 60 there is no questing and is known as the Hell Grind. That is because once you hit level 40 the speed leveling from questing suddenly stops and leveling becomes more of a challenge than a freebie. However, there are a few tricks I've learned that will reduce the Hell Grind to about level 58 to 60 or even eliminate it depending on your dedication. The first step is to create a test character (don't use the actual name you want to use, because this requires you going past level 6 and all character names are withheld for a month before repeated use after level 6) and level said character to either Level 10 and join a Level 4 or higher Guild or level your test character to level 20 and create your own Guild and recruit a lot of dedicated followers that'll help level your Guild. Now, the reason I'm saying to do this is because the higher your Guild level, the higher the XP and Loot Drop Rate % is. At level 4, you'll have a passive 4% Loot Drop Rate and XP bonus automatically and continually; and yes it applies to XP given from questing as well. Now, once you've completed Step One give a friend the name of your ACTUAL character and go back and create the character that you want. Once you've finished, add your friend to your new character's friend's list and have him/her add you to the Guild. Yes, you can be recruited manually to a Guild by a Guild member regardless of your level. Now you can have the said XP bonus from ground zero, however there's more to the process. Step Two, once you're in a good Guild and have the first step complete, ALWAYS be in a maxed out party with either some Guildmates or friends, because being in a party ALSO grants additional XP and Loot Drop Rate bonuses that increases per additional player added to the party. I forgot what the max % is but I'm thinking it's close to a 20% bonus that stacks WITH the Guild bonus. Right there, if I'm right, you'll have close to 24% non-stop permanetly automatic XP boosts that'll increase your leveling speed and have you at higher levels while completing lower level quests in no time. The final step, yes there is one more step, is to complete Mirabelle's Bulletin Board Quests (the bonuses apply to the XP given to these quests, which are daily and consistent) and to put ALL of your Tokens towards Monster XP books from your Mastery Vendor in Navea (the XP bonus from your Guild and Party ALSO apply to these books, allowing you to essentially 'buy' xp for free). By following these steps you can eliminate or severely reduce the Hell Grind and focus more on having fun and enjoying the game.
Now, the main aspect of this game is actually all about your Eidolons, a.k.a. your companions. This is what makes the game so unique and appealing. You choose a starter Eidolon during Character Creation, and this companion remains with you from the very beginning of the game. As you play you'll be exposed to more Eidolons, 2 of which (Sigrun and Gigas) are given to you in-game for free. There are about 9 other Eidolons that can be crafted, though crafting takes time and patience. The rest are luck drops, but you've got the Loot Drop Rate bonuses.

Beautiful game, fast and easy to learn, with that said I'm just gonna throw some pros and cons:
Pros:
- If you're into anime stuff you will love this game.
- Beautiful scenarios, day/night phase in almost all of them, colorful and cute.
- Easy and fast to learn, with a few hours in game you will catch it pretty fast.
- Most of the community it's pretty friendly, always glad to help low levels (at least an 80% of it).

There's an alternative to real money stuff, the "loyalty points" are currency in-game that you can earn doing daily quest and completing achievements.
- Eidolon system, which in my opinion adds that special thing to the game, there's a long list of 'em, some are easy to get and some take time.
- Weekly maintenance and more content to be added in the future.
- As every other MMORPG, events.
Cons:
- Grindy, once you finish the main quest, you will probably get stuck in the 57-60 level area, where the only thing that you can do it's: well, dungeons, dungeons, daily quests, dungeons, and desperate a bit for that level 60.
- Bots, yes, each of the three servers have a load of bots, also known as "the redhead army". They're just gold farming bots, who usually send you trash mail telling you to buy gold for 4 bucks.
- Can turn boring time to time, and probably in the "57-60 area" previously descrived.
- Lag/delay in some dungeons
- The devs are hmmm how to descrive it, hmmm they're not bad, but they're kinda lazy, and when a problem arise most of the time they will opt for an easy solution. Note* this doesnt happen most of the time.
- Huge risk of a rollback when an imminent issue shows. Ex. a few months ago the item mall started to work wrong, the prices were wrong, and of course people took that chance to get cheap stuff, with that done the devs just did a rollback (if you're not used to that word, a rollback it's just what it sounds) they returned the status of the server to the day before that issue happen, with that done every single player lost the items/gold/exp/levels/progress achieved that day, after that they apologized with the community and gave to every player affected by the rollback a special package and a week of 50% more drop and exp.
