This game is actually pretty good. I like in-game mechanics and graphic stylization. And the music... I love that soundtrack.

Overall: 7.6 / 10
Voyage: Journey to the Moon is a title that deserved more popularity than it had gotten in my opinion.  This is probably one of the reasons the game never received its sequel which is in my opinion a big shame, even although at the end of the game you are given a small teaser for it.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Graphics: 7.5 / 10
- The game does look very beautiful from time to time, whilst other times it looks alright. There we're quite a decent amount of details put into certain parts of both the map and items. It is obvious the game was polished quite a lot considering its current state and the fact it first came out in 2005.
Story: 7.5 / 10
- Scary, fun and intriguing for the most part. Worst part of it was at the very start of the game where there were a few small loopholes as well as the fact that at one point you get into a "react or die" situation without any instructions, which is not that bad really, as the game allows you to lose a life in many different scenarios (including falling into an empty elevator shaft because you forgot to call the elevator first) but without any penalty. After death, you are not brought back to the menu or loaded in from the last save, but rather just a moment before fatal decision was made. However, game gets a lot better once you land on the moon.
On the way you learn about plant and alien life, as well as social organisation of the aliens, their language, writing and technology and their relations with the human kind. You may also reach earth by not doing everything there is to do, and thus skipping something or doing it a different way. I personaly found the story to be quite short, peaking up to 6.8 hours on record from start to completion with all the time taken to solve the puzzles on the way but overall, I loved it.
Puzzles: 8 / 10
- I found puzzles not to be too hard, although they do have a small difficulty curve as you progress, meaning they get harder and harder. This is good because I believe the game would be enjoyable to both a casual gamer and those in for a quick challenge. It is obvious the puzzles are made by a human rather than an inhabitant of the moon and should demand an avarage logic skill to beat. They blend into the story perfectly as no puzzle is there just for the sake of its existence but rather, everything has a meaning. They are not repetative either, so you should not feel bored during the game.
Sound: 7 / 10
- The strong point of the sound is definitely its soundtrack. Main menu music has a really pleasant and suitable vibe for the type of the game. Voice acting is fine and so are other general sounds, although they are nothing to point your finger at.
Fun factor: 8 / 10

Words for Evil is an enjoyable word puzzle with a lightweight RPG system attached to it– if you can type fast enough (or don’t mind cheesing the game). But it can also be one of the most frustrating word games you ever encountered.
Words for Evil doesn’t offer anything unique: it’s a Scramble/Jumble type word game with a large dictionary and a system similar to Puzzle Knight or any other casual puzzle games with simple levelling mechanics: you have your heroes who fight monsters and collect loot by forming words from a pool of randomised letters. Long words and character-specific letters add damage or special effects.
It is simple and working, but not flawless. The monsters are fast and hit hard, so you either cheese the game by alt-tabbing from windowed mode or you really have to be lightning fast. Although your heroes can be revived in a minigame, it requires a level of vocabulary that probably even native speakers lack.
Still, Words for Evil is as good a word game as any other, and you can spend quite some time unlocking everything, so you can get a decent amount of play time for your money.

I really wish I could give this a neutral review, but if I had to pick I'd be negative.
The game's concept is wonderful, the range of letters you can use each time is extensive and the art is quite well done for a word game.
However, it becomes too repetitive with no sense of a goal while you play.
Also, for some reason, it's permanently windowed with no way to make the game full-screen (correct me if I'm wrong) which is a turn-off for me.
There are ingame options to buy weapons/armor but no way to tell how my characters' stats are stacked or whether equips are really useful.  It initially comes across as a turn-based game but the AI is constantly attacking you, which becomes annoying at higher levels.
There is a room for improvement but at this moment in time I will not be returning to play this game again.

If you liked Forsaken World or Perfect World International (PWI) (in some ways even Battle of the Immortals/War of the Immortals) then you will like this game, it plays a lot like them with various improvements and it may even be the same game engine. Single click auto-pathing for quests, lots of unique little things to participate in, ability to skip quest dialog, full featured minimap will click to move, no need to loot after monster kills, etc. The user interface is refined and has a lot of nice little features not seen in the larger MMOs. The improvements make the game easy to understand and play.
The game is definately targeted for the casual player. It has nice graphics and sound, but a lot of the improvements are focused around making the game fast and easy to play. Unlike so many other MMOs, you get a mount very early on. You should be level 10 and have one toolbar of skills, a mount, and your companion, within an hour or two of starting the game.
You get to choose your companion when you create your character, and there are seven different choices. Each one has different skills and focuses - one may be a healer and another a warrior type. The companion is similar in functionality to SWTOR companions, but you can even have little conversations with them.
You gain new skills (based on the class you choose) as you level automatically, and you have character improvement tileset. You gain one improvement point every three levels. I call it a tileset because its not a tree, your starting point is in the middle of all of the tiles and you can pick improvement tiles moving outward in any direction.
The in game store items seem a little expensive compared to other games. They have plenty of various cheap or expensive items, but just for comparison: 75 cents for a 20% xp boost for 60 minutes, $5 for a 20% xp boost for 24 hours play time (24 hours of played time, not calendar time so it will last multiple days), $50 for a unique mount that is 60% movement speed, if you buy 4 of them you can combine them into a 90% mount. For $15 you can get an item that gives you a 24 hours of 50%/25% monster/quest xp boost. I like the play time versus day time system, because it discourages afks and it is aimed at the casual player who might play one or two days a week. So if you play around 5 or 6 hours a week, the $15 boost will last you about a month.
You can purchase XP books from the store that instantly give amounts of XP, 29 cents for a book that gives the equivalent of 20 monster kills of your level. You can buy the in-game cash shop currency in $5, $10, $25 etc increments. They also have spending "tier" rewards per month, as you reach higher tiers you get greater free rewards. The first two spending tiers are at $5 and $15. Purchases go through the Steam Store so you don't have to visit another website.
Overall it is a very refined game with a lot of features and a better UI that is not found in today's larger MMOs. The cash shop is optional but the enticement to buy XP outright, or buy timed XP boosts will always be tempting - but "free" games are not free to build and run by the companies that make them and they need to make a profit.

After refunding this game on release day due to there being absolutely no fixes to the game after the beta optimization issues, how does the game stack up in November of 2017??
VISUALS: The atmosphere is amazing, feels just like you are in a Vietnam war movie. The game looks pretty dated most of the time, but the way it captures the atmosphere of vietnam makes me forget about it.
Gameplay: The gun play is amazing, one of the most authentic feeling recoil models out there. When it comes to the gamemodes, they are easy to understand, and makes it less challenging for new players to help their team. The one thing I don't like though, is the first person camera. I can't stand how much sway the gun has, makes the game feel as dated as the graphics. I get what they were trying to do, and make it feel more 'organic' or whatever, but this is what almost kept me from buying the game when I first saw it.
VEHICLES: The helicopters are done better than they are in BF3 or BF4. The controls are super similar to the battlefield series, but its less forgiving and harder to master (which is perfect for a game like this)
PERFORMANCE: This section is why I refunded the game back on release day. On this day, the optimization seems way better than it once was (constant microstuttering). However, I still get the very common FPS drops, with a 1070. If this game actually had visuals that looked like they were developed in the last 5 years, I could maybe cut it some slack. I don't understand how my GTX1070 and i5-6500 can handle Squad beautifully, but this game it faces a challenge. Them not being able to fix this issue is probably part of the reason the player numbers are so low.
Save your money and go buy Squad.

This is definitely the best gamepad I have ever used! It has a bit of a learning curve, but really so did every gamepad the first time I used it. The trackpads are incredible and allow for very precise aiming. I can play fps games comfortably and with much more precision than I could any other gamepad. It does sometimes feel as accurate as a mouse and keyboard, and I feel that with more practice I could hold my own against mouse and keyboard players.
The customizability is great too. Not only can you change any button you want, but the trackpads are completely customizable as well. You can change the sensitivity, feedback, and when and how they react along the edge. You can also make modifier buttons that you can hold to change the function of other buttons to make up for additional keyboard commands. Another great feature is the ability to save different controller configs per game and share them with the community easily.
Lastly, this gamepad works well with fighting games so far too. Even though the d-pad is on the left trackpad and feels odd at first, the grooves in the trackpad that outline a d-pad are easy to pick up and I never once from the start had trouble pressing the right direction. I was really surprised at how well it worked for fighting games.
Pros:
+Comfortable.
+Good battery life.
+Amazing precision!
+Customizability.
+Easy to download and share custom configs.
+Good for fighting games.
Cons:
-The only con I can think of is that the customization options can seem overwhelming at first glance. It takes a few minuites to play around with it and then a bit longer to try out the various settings in game and I can see how that could turn some people off, although it really is the controller's strong point and I like how much you can tweak it. That being said you can always download configs from other players with the press of a few buttons and you can see which configs are the most popular and read descriptions of them if they are provided. Also, the default config is usually pretty well setup for most games and after learning all of the settings that is often what I found myself using.

first of all, i just want to say how pleasantly surprised i was to see all of the included materials with the purchase: the required 2 AA batteries, a USB wireless module, a USB cable and a wireless extender
i've logged about 15 hours so far with the steampad across a couple different genres: MMO, FPS, platformer and fighter. i plan on trying RTS next, which i expect to go smoothly based on my experience so far. an important thing to keep in mind is that a keyboard and mouse will always have a competitive advantage over the steampad, so if you are a tryhard, you'll want to stick with K+M for those games. for gamepad games though, it is just as good, unless you really rely on a D-Pad
PRO's:
feels great in your hands and is very responsive and reliable (even over wireless)
the customizabilty is very deep and the (figurative) transperency of the controller is fantastic
i love the idea of the custom profiles and look forward to seeing them develop. in the meantime, the default templates work fine for most games (with a bit of tweaking or rebinding)
the joystick and triggers are as good as 8th-gen console controllers. the grips are a welcome addition to gamepads
i am hugely impressed with the responsiveness and haptic input of the trackpads
CON's:
definitely takes some getting used to at first... and even after that, there is a small learning curve game to game (or at least genre to genre), but that is ok and totally to be expected when using a very different kind of controller
i am a bit disappointed with the two AA baterries that are required, but that's a relatively small gripe
i was also disappointed to see how EASILY the wireless dongle gets stuck in the wireless extender. it is VERY difficult to remove it for some reason
VERDICT:
the next time you buy a new gamepad, make it a steampad

I pre ordered this fine piece of hardware back in august, received it 6 days ago. I'm a lazy gamer, so up until now I have just been playing games with native controller mappings. Just now I created a mapping for one of my all time favorite games, Space Engineers. The game has a lot of buttons to map, so I instead went with a community designed mapping. It worked flawlessly, except for I couldn't get in my ship. I then mapped the T key to one of the grips. I then had no problems, except now I couldn't jump or raise the altitude  of my ship. After I gave up on Space Engineers, I then moved over to rocket league, a game I got when I pre ordered the controller. After playing for about 2 hours, I realized that the controller was basically made for this game. The controls worked a lot better than my crappy laptops keyboard and trackpad. As I mentioned before, I use a laptop for gaming, and as a result, I didn't need to buy a steam link for gaming on my TV. I instead put my laptop on the floor and connected it to my TV and connected my steam controller wirelessly. All of a sudden, I had full 1080p gaming in my living room. Not many games released these days can become a favorite for me, but I would honestly claim NieR:Automata is one of my favorite games ever.
I was beginning to lose hope in video games ever feeling like a medium that can be used to tell a compelling story, as most video games just feel like money machines these days, not to say I havent enjoyed some recent releases. NieR:Automata feels like one of those games that takes advantage of the medium while also providing a game that's fun to play, a game that feels like a game with a good story, not a "Cinematic Blockbuster Experience" that most games aim to be. So much thought and charm has been put into the story and world, and the gameplay is handled by PlatinumGames, so of course it's going to be good.
If you've ever played Bayonetta or Metal Gear Rising, you should feel right at home with NieR. The gameplay feels like a simplified combination of the two. There are no real complex combo moves to buy or memorize, but the combat is satisfying enough for even hard hack-and-slash fans to have fun with it, while also being easy to learn for those who aren't so experienced with the genre. The game also features RPG elements, such as a leveling system and plenty of side things to do in the open world. I like to think the overall gameplay portion is a mixture of Bayonetta and Xenoblade Chronicles.
The story should be experienced yourself from start to finish, so I won't spoil anything. The story is what actually gives you more playtime out of the game, since NieR games kinda make you play the game a few times. You aren't getting anything short of your money with Automata.

Yoko Taro/10
NieR:Automata truly explores the boundaries and possibilites of its medium, and that's what ultimately makes it stand out.

This game... I don't know where to begin. It can be a fun timekiller for a little while, but it's never worth the full asking price of 9,99€. It's on sale right now for 0,99€, and I think that should be the normal price, because clearly there didn't go a lot of work into making the game.
I guess the devs went for a clean and minimalist look, like Portal or Q.U.B.E, and I guess it's ok, but it looks rather dull and like something that everyone could piece together in some game construction kit within a couple of minutes.
All the puzzles are very easy, and not very well designed. If you have ever played user made puzzles for Portal 2, you probably know what I mean. They work, and you had to think a bit about how to solve it, but all in all they seem designed quite badly, compared to the dev-made puzzles. Alle the levels in this game feel the same.
Most of them don't even use that Polarity concept all that much. It's more about taking a blue or red cube to a receptacle of the same colour and activate something that helps you through the level (platform, acceleration ramp, opening a gate etc.). Sometimes you have to throw the cubes at the receptacles, which works reasonably well.
The controls are fine, though the air controls seem a bit off.
The main reason why I think this is worth more like 1€ than 10€ is that the main game consists of 11 (extremely short and easy) levels. There are also 10 bonus levels and a coop campaign, but... come on, really? At about level 8 there suddenly is this new mechanic where you can change the colour of your cube by throwing it through a green force field. This mechanic isn't introduced in any way, and the only reason it's still quite easy to figure out by yourself is because the level design is so bleak that there aren't to much possibilities. It's like "ok, here's this red cube, there's a blue receptacle, and there is nothing else in this room except that green force field over there", so your options are so limited that you soon arrive at the correct solution.
Oh, what I didn't mention so far: you also have to collect 3 green glowing things (aka "Datasets") in every room for no apparent reason. Yes, the story tells you why, but they just feel like this arbitrary thing you also have to do that has nothing to do with solving the room's puzzles. Sometimes they're hidden, but that doesn't really work either, because of the empty level design. If you are at the end of the level and you're missing one of them, it's just like "well, then I'll have to go over there where it's probably hidden and where I didn't go before because I had absolutely no reason to".
TL;DR: Puzzles too easy, just 11 levels in the main campaign, bad level design. It's like the easy first few puzzles of other puzzle games, in length as well as in difficulty.
I wouldn't recommend buying this even at 0,99€ unless you also have someone to play the coop campaign with. I got mine for free, if you can get it free, go for it. It can be entertaining for a short while.

This game won't start from Steam, so I had to gather 5 minutes spamming the Play button to write this.
When I launched it from the exe, the game looked promising.

And that's where it ends.
It's in the name of the game.
The game is called Polarity, for crying out loud.
You're meant to get around by switching your polarity.
Yet, in the first 10 or so levels after the tutorial level (couldn't be bothered to count), I can probably count the number of times the mechanic was used ON ONE HAND.
If that isn't enough, the graphics are lacking and the physics are wonky.
Level design is wanting too; the first few levels were okay, but after that it becomes less of a mind-stretching puzzle per se (which I assume is the basis for it claiming to be the next Portal) but more of "do you spot this tiny thing at the edge that you have to press", which certainly makes the navigation of maps challenging in an annoying way.
Also, attempting to fling cubes across the entire map is just plain disgusting, and takes way too much trial and error. I can only imagine that's the reason for the cube reset button. More disturbingly, it's the most efficient way to place cubes on a receptacle. If randomly spamming cubes at different angles and hoping one gets caught by the receptacle is the best way of putting a cube on the receptacle, I don't see why I should invest any more of my time in this game.
Certainly wouldn't recommend buying for anything more expensive than the 98% off sale price.
(I also wouldn't recommend buying it for the sale price since it's such a terrible game, but you get card drops if you actually manage to start it up.)

I played this game for just under two hours. I found it interesting, but I spent at least half the time being stuck and not knowing what to do.
- It's another old (2005) point and click adventure from this publisher and developer, but the user interface is better than their other similar titles
- Your objectives are vague and it is easy to spend a very long time stuck and unable to make progress just by missing a single small detail
You have a pre-rendered 360 degree panoramic view of your environment. When you move to different locations your perspective will be that of the new location. I haven't played Myst before. But I've been told that this is basically what Myst is like.
-----You interact with the environment in order to solve problems and progress through game. You find many items which can be used with certain objects in the environment. Certain inventory items can be combined with others to create new objects. Not all items appear to be essential to progressing through the game. Some items and actions appear to unlock extras such as information about characters and lore about the alien species.
-----So you start in the very confined space of the shell which has been fired out of giant cannon to take you to the moon. It was an interesting location. But unfortunately I spent over an hour in this tiny little area area. This was because I often became stuck and couldn't figure out what to do.
-----Inside the shell you periodically get to the point where you are running out of oxygen and need to find a way to remedy the situation. Once this happens you have about a minute to get more oxygen otherwise you die. I died at least twenty times or so. When you die you reappear in the shell and you lose no items or progress, nothing in the ship resets to it's originals state. So dying from lack of oxygen didn't really serve any purpose except to be a nuisance. It took me quite me a while to find the solution the first time. The second time also took me a quite a while to discover. I basically found myself scraping the bottom of the barrel. I had to actually look up a walk-through. It turned out that all I needed to do was turn a small wheel. I had no idea about this even though I'd searched through the whole shell again and again. This is what I spent most my two hours stuck on.
-----Finally I arrived on the moon. Which was an interesting place. There were various colorful and animated plants, I came across some alien technology and you had to made great leaps across a chasm in order to navigate the environment.
-----But I soon got a stuck again for a substantial amount of time. Only when I was coming to the end of my two hour play-through did I figure out how to progress some more. Again it was something kind of obvious which I'd just overlooked. Things at that point got a bit more interesting again, but unfortunately I didn't have time to keep playing.
-----I know some people will be against this notion. But sometimes it can be too frustrating to get stuck for so long. It would have been cool if there were more specifics hints. This feature could be optional so that people who want to do it the hard way still can. Hints could have cool-down and only become available once you have been stuck for a certain amount of time in order to prevent over-reliance on them.  But it's probably a bit too much to ask from an old game, and yes I'm sure some people would feel it would ruin the challenge.
-----When I stopped playing I'd found several alien machines. Including a coin operated telescope which was quite amusing. There is also a whole series of 'ideograms', basically alien hieroglyphics. You are able to decipher these in order to understand some of their meanings. I thought that was quite interesting. These ideograms apparently must play a role in understanding the operation of the alien devices and so on. I also caught sight of the aliens but I was unable to get close enough to interact with any of them.
The game looks alright, keep in mind it is an old title. I think the pre-rendered graphics is a better alternative to 3D graphics which probably wouldn't have looked very good at a level that PCs were capable of running back then. Some areas can look a bit plain, such as the interior of the shell especially if you've been stuck in it for over an hour lol
-----Once I'd gotten to the moon, the game reminded me a quite a bit of the another old point and click adventure title, The Dig. That game was by Lucasarts and in it you also travel through space and spend the game on a alien planet solving puzzles to progress.
I like the game, but I'd find it hard to make the time for. Ideally this is a good game if you are prepared to spend a lot of time figuring out what to do and have a lot of patience in case you get stuck for extended periods unable to make progress. Otherwise you could refer to a walk-though to guide you. There is at least one available which is you can find on YouTube.

Words for Evil is a very fun, low stress casual adventure game set in a fantasy world where all attacks are made by creating words with the letters provided. This game is for those of us who love wordplay and typing in particular. I heard about Words for Evil quite a while before it was available on Steam, and bought an entire bundle and downloaded the Desura client just for this game. I have always enjoyed typing and have an average speed of 101 words per minute, and I write for a living, so this game was instantly on my radar. I am constantly intrigued by video games that incorporate wordplay in any form, but typing quickly in this game is also a plus because it directly affects the attack rates of your party members.
Fluency in typing, whether based in speed or accuracy, is not required, however. Words for Evil will be extraordinarily easy for those of us who can type quickly, but it is designed to be accessible for anyone. It also acts as a tool to encourage the player to both properly spell and accurately type because it is in your best interest to attack the enemy at a faster pace than she or he attacks you.
In a nutshell, Words for Evil plays out like a 2D adventure game where the party members you choose move automatically from left to right. Your party will come across enemies, blacksmiths, potion stores, and traps every few seconds. You can purchase goods to outfit your party from the blacksmiths and potion stores. Every time you come across an enemy, you are given a grid full of letters to choose from. Using gameplay mechanics similar to Popcap's classic Bookworm, you can spell out words via typing them if the letters are in order on the grid (connected vertically, horizontally, and diagonally). Each time you finish a word, your characters attack. By leveling up your characters, you gain access to special attacks that are used by utilizing colored letter squares on the grid. Each defeated enemy gives you XP, and each party member can be upgraded many times. In addition, you'll come across new characters every once in awhile that you may choose to add to your party (in an empty slot or as a replacement for another). There are many characters, special attacks, and even worlds to unlock.
Treasure chest mini-games are vaguely similar to fights, but you are offered two rows of letters, and you must choose one letter in each row to come up with a word by the last column. Do this for all five rows within a time frame (for a five letter word), and you unlock the chest. There are also traps that present you with a grid, and you have to try to use all the letters in various words. Once you use up the letters, they disappear and none replace them; however many letters are left over, unused, dictates how much damage your party is subject to by the trap.
Words for Evil is a casual game. Despite being set in a fantasy world (and a beautiful one, at that; the pixel art here is as gorgeous and colorful as it is simplistic), there is really no story to follow or "reason" to traversing the world other than the relaxing joy of it. There is a lot to unlock, there are pages of characters to level up completely, many enemies to come across and beat, worlds to unlock, etc., and the developers update the game fairly often with new content. This is a game that is not selfishly demanding of your time. Between playing games full of deep lore and convoluted storylines, picking up Words for Evil will relax you and may even teach you something. I fell in love with the idea of the game because it was so unique, and it did not disappoint. At $2.99, I recommend it even at full price (I have gotten about 10 hours out of it, including my Desura time before Steam, which far bypasses the $1 per hour of game time rule I follow).
This is a humble little game that is approachable by most. I give Words for Evil a 9/10, and I eagerly await developer Dylan Loney's next game.

So after just under 5 hours totalling a distance of 107.2km covered, my knees are aching because I've been sitting here trying to get to the end of this game. Light and fluffy, it may be but short game play it is not! There's not just a generosity of hero/monsters but an assortment of aspects in this game that'll keep you interested in levelling up every hero you manage to unlock (they're all different and super adorable, btw). Attacks fall under the simplified basic/strong/ultra attacks (length of words) in turn unlocking monsters and working to your advantage depending on what you level up in when you find Fountains (they also heal you 100%). As you progress, in line with any basic RPG, Strength (HP)/Agility (Damage)/ Wisdom (Mana) are your basic stats (you can add Luck (Gold) also), each hero has different strengths/abilities you can hone to your liking.
When you first play, the speed of how quickly you type full words (3 letters+) will "make or break you". Starting off, short words in frantic succession will lay the best results. Don't be embarrassed to type can, man, bat and hat in a row until you're at a moderate level. There are Loot Chests and Deadly Traps to test your word skills and you can buy weapons and potions to aid you in battle. There are very clear instructions in the main menu so check them out. As an on-rails game there is a set route you may not deviate from apart from when you swap between different worlds/levels. Keep in mind that as long as you're good at the word games, you shouldn't need the luck anyway which definitely wasn't an option for my lack of a dictionary. Personally, I found it much easier once I chose heroes whom inflicted more damage to monsters when they inflicted damage on me. In short, the monsters would lose lots of health as they were killing me which was helpful when "lost for words". Once you find your pace, unique words will hit harder and let your relax with the typing.
Though it wasn't too much of a downer for me, I should mention that I'm so busy looking at the word games (the screen is horizontally split in half, upper: RPG and lower: word game) that I have no clue how much my hero is losing health until I finish that game. Another bummer was how at times I'd type something and it would not compute in game. Playing other typing games on Steam, this was never a problem so I found it bothersome. Granted it would actually get me better words at times by mistake though, so yay!
If you've yet to master basic typing skills, it may either teach or frustrate you so proficient keyboard usage will help. If you don't like word games like word search, anagrams and the likes of Boggle, steer clear. As a word maven wannabe and RPG devotee, this game is a bundle of joy!

Aura Kingdom is a fantasy anime-style MMORPG that has the player take on the role of an 'Envoy of Gaia' - a human with abilities far exceeding those of all but other Envoys. Every player is given three Eidolons throughout the story, NPC companions each with their own unique set of abilities, stats, and even personality.
The gameplay of Aura Kingdom is fairly repetitive, with hundreds of kill __ of __ and gather __ of __ quests. There is also very little 'multiplayer' as far as MMOs go. One could potentially complete every quest alongside friends rather easily, but there is little merit to doing so other than the obvious social benefits. Armour grants you stats and costumes grant minor benefits and the visual appeal. While this somewhat stifles players' creativity in creating costumes from inexpensive armours, you will also never have to walk around in a barrel. Everything is stylish and fits someone's tastes.
The level cap set at 65 (correct me if I'm wrong) the grind to 40 goes smoothly enough, with quests being the best source of EXP around. Monsters grant players VERY little EXP, usually below .15% per.
Now here's the catch; this game can be quite addicting when played with friends, and there is always a fresh, shiny new set of armours and weapons waiting for you at every level milestone. Despite being an MMO, this game holds plenty of replayability to try out each class, skillsets, and offensive/defensive point spreads.
I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a casual game to goof around in with friends.

Stellaris isn't quite a perfect game. The AI isn't particularly sophisticated and there are a number of design decisions which are questionable or seem to contradict other mechanics. But there's nothing out there that quite gives me the freedom to build a galactic civilisation to my own vision like Stellaris does. And Paradox has plenty of plans to continue improving the game for a long time to come.
If you love sci-fi and 4X, and aren't put off by an AI that's not too hard to game, I highly recommend giving Stellaris a go. In some ways it feels more like a roleplaying game than a 4X in that I find it more satisfying to set myself constraints or goals and play to those rather than actually worrying about the win conditions. And there's enough content and choices that the game should have plenty of replay value.

I want to recommend this game, I really do. As a huge wrestling fan I play it, I have fun with it. But if I knew in advance about all the issues I would come across, I might've just reconsidered buying this game.
Pro's:
- The game's graphics have improved quite alot.
- WWE 2k18 added a new carry system which I personally enjoy, as it allows for more variety during the match. You can for example hold someone in a powerbomb and then throw them out of the ring.
- The promo system has improved, it atleast doesn't take a game of guessing anymore to get a good promo.
- What especially impresses me is how natural created wrestlers look. In the previous two titles, your created wrestlers felt somewhat out of place. In WWE 2k18, they look far more human, you can truly make them look like they are their own person and part of the roster now.
- Create a wrestler is at its best currently when it comes to customization options.
Cons:
- The game is poorly optimized. I get about 37-40fps, 40-45 before the latest patch (Aside from some entrances and cutscenes which drops to 20-ish) which is playable, fair enough. But if a pc as strong as mine can only run this game so well, I can only imagine how bad the framerate might be for weaker pc's that realistically should be able to run the game.
- Bugs everywhere, especially during universe mode. I could describe them all day but it would take that, all day. The part that works is fun atleast.
- When it comes to created wrestlers, the crowd is absolutely dead. They will make zero sound, if your CAW is face you'll barely get cheered, and if you're a heel well you won't get boo's at all. It's as if everyone decides to fall asleep the moment your CAW's entrance starts. This is a big deal to me because immersion is one of my favourite parts of wrestling games.
I haven't actually played Mycareer mode that much yet. That said, I personally did not come across many bugs and issues just yet, but I lack experience in this area so take these words with a grain of salt. A large amount of the moves and items are also locked behind lootboxes which is unfortunate but not something that bothers me too much in this case.
I like this game, but it could've been so much better than it is if it was more polished and actually worked as it intended.

The Binding of Isaac is the second best roguelike game I have ever played so far, only behind from its remastered-ish game The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth (which I just start playing).
What makes this game so great?, its replayability. It's amazing how every run you make is different from all previous others, thanks to the many, many items you can pick up (passive upgrades, trinkets, on-use items). Believe me, I never get tired of playing it. Every build you manage to make is different (even though it may not be as unique) and it keeps the game refreshing.
But that's not all: enemies can be champions, making them tougher by giving them extra abilities; bosses can also be champions and there are a bunch of them. It will take you quite some runs to see them all and still many more to see their variations.
The map's layout is also random every run and there is much to see, different levels to explore and many hidden rooms to find.
One thing that keeps you going is the progression system: the more successfull runs you're able to achieve, the more content you unlock and the further you'll be able to get, since some areas are locked, requiring you to achieve an objective before unlocking them and be able to go even deep on the levels.
This is a trully fantastic and terrific game. I never expected to have so many hours played and am still not at 100%. Tons of hours of fun through runs, which end up being all different from each other, keeping the game refreshing.
I understand if it may not initially appeal to everyone, it didn't stick to me at first but on a second try, months later, I learned to love the game.
Fantastic roguelike, a must buy if you're on a budget (if you're not, go with The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth - it's the same game but developed for Windows instead of Flash and with much more content).

Like a lot of people, I really dig TellTale's endeavours since The Walking Dead. This time around though I had to request a refund. The game is simply targeted at a much younger audience. Wait! - don't roll your eyes yet reader, it was obvious since the announcement of Story Mode that TellTale would have to change their usual formula and address the millions (billions?) of kids playing Minecraft. Regardless, I expected a game which all ages could enjoy, something along the lines of 'The Lego Movie'. Story Mode however felt like a saturday morning cartoon. Not a bad one I guess, it probably takes a lot of craft to make something enjoyable to kids. The difference is one is aimed 'solely' at kids whilst the other is not. The developers have no obligation to make a game for me, but considering TellTales 'ouvre' some consumer advice is warranted.
Granted, I played this game for less than an hour, so perhaps Story Mode turns around, but this is my general critique.
Everything in this game is very overt, leaving little room for subtlety. This is exceptionally jarring in the characterizations. You notice it in the voice acting almost immedately. The second one of your sullen companions opens his mouth you know exactely which thrope he falls into (big, heart of gold, shy, etc). Incidentely, I stopped playing at the part where your group has to get past a big bouncer who is inexplicately afraid of chickens. This is shown by him cowering in front of a chicken exclaiming his particular phobia all the whilst the camera pans and shows a towering chicken contraption a meter away in the background (Puzzle time!). Not claiming the Tales of the Borderlands was subtle, but that scene was just inane. I can go one listing all the one-dimensional characters but you can watch the trailer and pretty much figure it out from there.
Now, normally you'd think there would be some humor thrown in to please the more adult adience. That didn't happen. There were plenty of opportunities to lampshade certain aspects of Minecraft. The remaining humor is very safe and kids friendly (e.g. a big person gets stuck in a fence for a bit).
This wouldn't all be bad if at least the plot went in interesting places. This could still very well be the case, but judging from what I've seen I am not willing to bet 22.99 on it. All the high notes are being foreshadowed pretty heavily.
Returning to the first paragraph, I am not claiming this is a bad game, just not one fans of TellTale can blindlessly purchase. If you must, please keep tabs on the clock so you don't forfeit the chance to refund this.

This game really impressed me, out of all the free to play mmorpg's on Steam, this one I recommend over all others. This game has a multitude of good aspects, for instance the classes. This game has a large amount of classes available immediately, and in addition at level 40 you can choose a second class. The game has absolutely no need to spend real money in, leveling is fairly well paced throughout the game (I've only had to grind for a level twice) and all items you can spend money on are either customisation, mounts (you get one for free before you even reach level 10), or items you can get by playing the game. The game also has a great guild system, which encourages members to aid their guild so it can level up to provide bonuses to all members of the guild. Graphically the game actually looks pretty good, with an anime inspired art design and some decently creative orginal monster designs. Gameplay is your standard hotkey system mmorpg style, while I have railed on this system multiple times in the past, this game did it well in my opinion. Unlike other games using the hotkey system, Aura Kingdom made it enjoyable by 1. Not requiring me to mash a button for my standard attack (I'm looking at you Star Wars the Old Republic) 2. Having enjoyably flashy ability animations and 3. providing a cool combo system with the second class (which with the correct combinations of weapons can lead to powerful special abilities). The only complaint I have with this game is the story, it's not bad and it's not the game's fault that I don't enjoy it. Due to the previously mentioned Star Wars the Old Republic I have a hard time enjoying mmorpg's that don't at least have voice acting, though as said it's my fault. If you enjoy games with an anime art style, mmorpg's, or mmo's in general, you will love this game and I can't recommend it enough. Other wise definitely give it a shot. Finally though, if you aren't a fan of any of the previously mentioned then admittedly this game won't change your mind on the genre.

Not many games released these days can become a favorite for me, but I would honestly claim NieR:Automata is one of my favorite games ever.
I was beginning to lose hope in video games ever feeling like a medium that can be used to tell a compelling story, as most video games just feel like money machines these days, not to say I havent enjoyed some recent releases. NieR:Automata feels like one of those games that takes advantage of the medium while also providing a game that's fun to play, a game that feels like a game with a good story, not a "Cinematic Blockbuster Experience" that most games aim to be. So much thought and charm has been put into the story and world, and the gameplay is handled by PlatinumGames, so of course it's going to be good.
If you've ever played Bayonetta or Metal Gear Rising, you should feel right at home with NieR. The gameplay feels like a simplified combination of the two. There are no real complex combo moves to buy or memorize, but the combat is satisfying enough for even hard hack-and-slash fans to have fun with it, while also being easy to learn for those who aren't so experienced with the genre. The game also features RPG elements, such as a leveling system and plenty of side things to do in the open world. I like to think the overall gameplay portion is a mixture of Bayonetta and Xenoblade Chronicles.
The story should be experienced yourself from start to finish, so I won't spoil anything. The story is what actually gives you more playtime out of the game, since NieR games kinda make you play the game a few times. You aren't getting anything short of your money with Automata.
Better get good at the hacking minigame.
Yoko Taro/10
NieR:Automata truly explores the boundaries and possibilites of its medium, and that's what ultimately makes it stand out.

I don’t know if anyone else was burning the midnight oil last night, but we knocked this one out pretty quick. Let’s get going shall we?
I – Story [3/10]
Words for Evil is a RPG-like word game from Dylan Loney. WFE doesn’t have much of a story; you (the player) select a hero and slowly gather more heroes as you battle your way through a series of worlds. In each world you must find a shrine to unlock the next and so on and so forth. Pretty basic, but, it’s more of a story than most other word games you’ll probably find out there.
II – UI [10/10]
A good user interface is the heart and soul of any word game and WFE is no exception. Also, WFE had a marvelous UI. Every single command in the game can be issued through the keyboard. You can use a mouse as your primary source of input or in a more supplemental role, but that will become arduous in a hurry. WFE handles like smoother than a fish in water, so bravo to Mr. Loney on his excellent work in this aspect.
III – Gameplay [8/10]
If you’ve played one word game, you’ve practically played them all. WFE has two styles of word games you’ll encounter during play. The first (similar to Boggle or Bookworm) presents you with a table of letters with which you construct words. Once the letters are used, they are removed from the table and new letters take their place. The second style of game is more of a jumble. You are given a series of letters and you must find the word or words hidden within them. Seems familiar right?
Here is where WFE shakes things up. Battle sequences use the first style of play. On the letter table, certain letter tiles will have different colors. These colors correspond to one of you heroes. If you create a long enough word that features one or more tiles of the same (or different) colors, the corresponding heroes will launch an attack on the enemy. In the event that your party of heroes runs up against a trap, a treasure chest, or (Cthulhu forbid) one of them falls in battle, you’ll be presented with a game of the second play style.
My only real complaint with the gameplay was with the jumbles used on treasure chest encounters. Some of the words you are presented with and tasked with unscrambling are either archaic or you’ll never have heard of them before in your entire life. It accounts for some mild annoyance, but the gameplay itself remains solid.
IV – Content [10/10]
Normally, all you’d expect out of a game such as WFE is a dictonary’s worth of words. This, however, is not the case. As I mentioned above, WFE is an RPG-like word game. There are 19 unlockable heroes, 84 different enemies, 6 worlds, and a small collection of items to upgrade your heroes with. At it’s core, WFE is still a word game at the end of the day, but the extra content really breaks up the long-term monotony of the genre.
V – Visual [8/10]
WFE has charming art, but some of the animations happen so incredibly fast, it is almost impossible to see what is happening during the battle. The environments are beautiful and very detailed.
VI – Audio [8/10]
I quite enjoyed the music of WFE. It fit well with the atmosphere of the game and with the theme of each world. You couldn’t ask for more of any game. Some of the sound effects become a bit repetitive after a while though, but, if you get into the zone, you shouldn’t even notice.
VII – Overall [7.8/10]
Overall, Words for Evil is a fun game and a great way to kill some downtime. At only $2.99, it is an absolute steal as well. If you’d like to learn more about the game, you can visit the official website here. If you’d like to go ahead and purchase it, go here instead. A word puzzle game sporting a minimal interface and an RPG feel. Gets a bit repetitive after awhile, but still fun to play.
Starting with a single adventurer, you journey through the land using your vocabulary to power your skills and defeat monsters you encounter on the path. You travel between worlds, encountering different monsters and other adventurers who can join your party. The general game has enemies which attack you in real time, turning your adventurer's health bar into something of a time. You attack by link letters on a grid to form words, using colored tiles associated to power your adventurer's attacks. The game is best played with a keyboard: Typing will not only select the tiles for you, it will change the selection based on the word your type, relinking letters, and prioritizing colored tiles. The only time I even touched the mouse was while selecting adventurers. In addition to the main puzzle, there are a few mini-puzzles used for activities like looting chests and disarming traps.
The RPG aspect of the game has your adventurers gaining experience after every encounter, which can be used to level up their abilities. There is also gold used to purchase potions and items at various shops along the way, which I think is where the game starts to falters. The potions work well, enough, but the equipment doesn't seem to do much. Gear looted from chests is either randomly assigned, or possibly shared between party members; either way, the game doesn't do a very good job of explaining how it works. Gear can be assigned when purchased from a merchant, but there's no way I could find to see what the adventurer's was currently carrying, or compare it to what was being purchased. I'm assuming this means that whatever bonuses given simply stack, even if the old gear is completely replaced.
The only other downside in my opinion is the repetition. Part of this is inherent to the genre: How many letter grids can you look at before it starts to get a little boring? For it's part, the game does a pretty good job mixing up the puzzle types, and the RPG aspect does help a bit. That said, this game feels a bit too easy. The puzzle difficulty feel static, and you can win almost any fight using only three letter words, especially using the keyboard to pound them out. Enemies don't seem to be very powerful. You might lose an adventurer once in awhile, but very rarely will you lose the entire party.

Stellaris is bittersweet in the extreme.
On one hand, it's a great 4X engine.
On the other hand, it's a terrible 4X game.
Mod the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it if you're going to play it past one game; mods make it infinitely better. But remember, you're going to be hampered by the overall simplicity of the game. There's a lot going on, but once you learn the basics, there's almost nothing _interesting_ going on, and the game suffers from being extremely wide, but excessively shallow in terms of all its mechanics.
And I'm not even going to talk about the hot messes that are combat, AI or diplomacy. I wrote about 5 paragraphs dissecting it all, but it all boils down to one thing: the game is NOT finished. It is NOT fully realized. It is NOT a game, in so far as you pop numbers to make other numbers pop bigger. If Paradox can somehow turn it into Crusader Kings 2 in space, instead of a half-baked Europa Universalis 4 with space ships, it'll get way better. But I'm not expecting that to happen until $3k of expansions have been released. What was shall be and all that.
If you're really itching for a 4X, though, Stellaris is probably the best choice on the market in terms of modern games. But I'd highly recommend playing some of the mods after you learn the basics. Star Trek: New Horizons and Alphamod are great, and their developers have good ideas when it comes to making the overall engine of Stellaris into the game it should be, but, like I mentioned, they're hampered by Paradox's pants-on-head choices when it comes to the overarching direction of the game's design.
If you can, wait 3-5 years, and for the inevitable bundle of expansions+DLC to be released. Maybe then the game will have some legs to stand on its own with.

A tough-as-nails, no-nonsense challenge in the same vein as Super Hexagon.  Only one button, but the game requires hair-trigger timing.  It comes down to finding a rhythm for each section.
There are only 4 levels (plus endless mode and drunk mode), but each is fiendishly difficult and brilliantly designed.  The levels are impossibly long, but you don't have to complete them in one shot; the game saves your progress at each checkpoint even if you exit the game.  (I wish I had known this before attempting level 3.  I did it in one sitting because I was afraid I'd lose my precious progress if I took a break!)
Apart from one little detail, nothing is unfair.  It's all about finding a rhythm of button-pressing.
This is a wonderful challenge, so why aren't more people talking about it?  Well, oO is a game about watching a circle spinning around and around inside other circles, which may also be spinning and may contain objects rotating in the opposite direction to your spinning!  It can cause hypnosis and nausea if you stare at it too long.
That little unfair detail: the tiny circles.  You spin so fast inside them it's impossible to see when to push the button to flip into the next circle, meaning it comes down to luck.  Not impossible, but frustrating, and there aren't too many of those moments to break the deal for me.
Highly recommended for those who want something to challenge their reflexes.

The Journey Down is a modern take on the old school point-and-click adventure game, which draws inspiration from the golden era of adventure games (Monkey Island, Grim Fandango, Leisure Suit Larry etc.). The characters are inspired by those creepy traditional African masks (Sort of like how Grim Fandango was inspired by Mexican Día de Muertos masks) and combines it with a noir setting and Rasta accents.
This game heavily relies on the environment, which, in my opinion, is a make it or break it for an adventure game. What the game lacks in story (pretty generic corrupt government tries to cover up a secret-story), the environment and atmosphere makes up for it. The hand drawn backgrounds are gorgeous, the music perfectly complements the drawn art and really adds another dimension to the noir tone of the game.
The dialogue is for the most part fun and clever, while sometimes it can get a little too goofy. The voice actors are doing a perfect job with the material they are given. The puzzles are one of the biggest improvements over the first game. I found the puzzles more creative and challenging in this chapter (dial a number, type in on a computer-type of puzzles).
I was stuck a couple of times, but it never got to the point where I got so frustrated that I wanted to quit the game. The puzzles are always logical, unlike some of the older adventure games where you had to combine completely random items and go pixel hunting). If you are an experienced adventure game player they are still on the easier side, but it's certainly a huge improvement over the first chapter.
The chapter is pretty short, but for a 9 euro game it’s not too bad. You should be able to complete it in one sitting. 3-5 hours.
The ending is pretty anticlimactic. You finally arrive to the destination you have been working towards, and the game ends. Pretty annoying, but it makes me look forward to Chapter 3.
While it’s not as good as the games it draws inspiration from (Notably Grim Fandango), it’s still a great game with a lot of memorable moments. I recommend picking this up for nostalgia value (If you like me grew up with The Curse of Monkey Island and Grim Fandango), if you just enjoy Lucasarts-type adventure games, or if you more recently picked up Broken Age and enjoyed it.

oO seems like a really easily game that won't last, but it is much more. It may be only a dot, circles, and spikes but a lot of complexity was put into making this. You're just a dot going through circles, trying to get to the end and escape. However, spikes come in your way along your way as you try to not die by missing the entry to another circle. Through four levels, this changes up, causing you to not only rely on how fast you can go but how you analyze the situation. Is it now or the next rotation that allows you to safely get past spikes?
oO can be frusturating at times, but trial and error becomes key towards the later levels. A death count is constantly up, beign a score that you can try to lower as you gain experience with the game. Want a more difficult level? Or just bored of seeing the same circles over and over? An extra "drunk" level comes with each level, not needed to complete the game but if the player wants to. With an addition of an endless mode, oO can last for a long time.
I appreciate how the developer didn't make achievements for not dying in each level. Normally this would be the case, but it's great seeing a game without this asthe levels are truely hard to beat without dying. For the low price it is now, I highly recommend oO.

I've played a fair amount of mmo's that seem just like Aura at a first glance. What sets Aura apart from those games, however, is that skills don't cost mana. It takes a massive load off of the player (Mainly the healer) now that you don't have to worry about spending sometimes up to 10k in game currency for 30 billion mana pots to handle a half hour of dungeon or grinding or whatever you might be doing at the time. As well as not having to deal with mana, you have companions from a little after the start that fight with you, (or for you depending on your class, as a bard I needed mine to tank sometimes) give you items, and level up almost as you go. (You have to feed them crystals, which you can get by sending them to Gaia to retrieve items, and also as drops from mobs and chests) There is one problem that I have found with Aura, which is almost game breaking. The massive amounts of bots are enough so that if they could fly, they would blot out the sun for years. Reporting them does almost nothing, they steal drops occasionally, and spam your mail box with offers for "The cheapest, most trustworthy gold selling site on the internet." I'll leave it up to you whether or not that baggage is too much. Try it, and if you like it and can get past the bot trains, have fun, you found a jewel among mmorpgs. If not, then okay I guess.

Review UPDATED. Also, apparently you can find your own reviews helpful and funny? I guess it's good to shamelessly promo yourself sometimes.
Don't get trolled by the positive reviews. This game is getting better, though it still has a ways to go. The concept is good and the game has potential to be fun, though I'm mostly here to get loot and sell it. Already made my three bucks back. Went and bought Hatoful Boyfriend. It's apparently my happy game now. And trust me, you'll need a happy game if you decide to buy this.
The T-Rex and the Spino's vacuums have been adjusted, but they're still there and they're still a problem.
Next we got Pterasaurs. Pterasaurs are good, in my opinion. they require more skill to use now.
The Dilosaurs and Raptors received a damage buff and are good now. Perhaps humans and dinos do a little too much damage now, but that will be sorted out.
Carno paragraphs left intact, because the devs left them intact in the game.
Then there's the Carnosaur, or however you say that name. The Carnotaur is often overlooked because of all the other broken stuff in the game. People claim the Centaur is the most balanced class, but it is, in fact, not. Anytime the humans group up, these Carnatosaurs will rush in and kill everything. And that's exactly what they're supposed to do, is break up groups of humans. However, when the Carne Asadas manage to get humans in cramped locations, they can devastate the entire group faster than a person can react. You see, when a Carne con chile is rushing, it also has the ability to bite, thereby doing double damage. To a human, this is known as the Half-Life. It only takes two hits like this to kill a human.
Now you might assume, correctly, that if a moving object hits a wall, it'll stop. Well not in this game! If you were to approach a Carnosaurataurus running blindly into a wall and not moving, and make contact with it, you would take full damage and be sent flying. It really is incredible how the devs have implemented the ability for dinos to use voodoo magic.
Finally, the last piece wrong with the Carnos. Normally, if they hit a human with their ram, they can't hit them again for another five seconds or so. Well if they were to restart a sprint by, oh I don't know, pressing Shift again multiple times, they can hit the human multiple times within a second. This is known as Obliteration because no human standing against a wall ever survives.
Now on to the humans. The humans do more damage now.
Nademando was nerfed, though Commando still good because human damage buff.
I still avoid using Pathfinder, though Pyro is certainly getting better.
The trapper is excellent at taking down Pteras, Dilos, and Raptors. The problem is, their nets sometimes bug out and just fizzle away, not affecting anything. There's something about projectiles in this game that just goes wonky because it happens to the Commando's grenades, too. Mines still do team damage, makes me laugh every time.
The scientist has the strongest damage of any human in the game. People have the nerve to get mad when the Scientist no-scopes them when they're close. Are you kidding me? They're actually calling for the scientist to only be able to fire the rifle when scoped in. Some people man... smh. They need to reduce that zoom on the scope if they want to take away the ability to pull a trigger.
Also, aiming down the scope is horrendous. The Scientist is apparently a Black Ops trained sniper because she doesn't breathe, at all, when aiming. It really throws me off. Not to mention, even if you've got your shot lined up and everything. Even if you've accounted for wind speed and all this other Call of Duty stuff, the shot just misses. The trail from the bullet, lmao, even if the trail of the bullet passes through the dino's character model, the shot might not register. Where did the bullet go? Who knows. It's like we're working with Magic Bullets used to assassinate JFK or something.
There's also a ridiculous amount of friendly collision in this game that screws people over. You can't shoot nets, grenades, anything through allies so grouping up gets counter productive.
There's still a lot of people who can't connect to the economy server and therefore can't earn loot. Score.
As of now, I can't recommend this game. It's better, but not best enough.

FOREWARNING: If you aren't ludicrously good at tactical shooters or shooters, you're ♥♥♥♥ed. You'll only be able to play dinosaurs. I put in a good amount of time into Primal Carnage and a bit into extiction. Currently I'd suggest you get the original, but this might change.
Assuming you get the basic concept, here are pros and cons as of early access of this game to extinction:
+More dinos
+More content in the form of maps
+Very basic market economy
+Humans buffed in damage and speed, making them much more potent
-Melee removed from humans except for Pyro's chainsaw
-Pyro buffed in the wrong places leading players to misuse him (He's actually back-line supression and used for chucking super-high damage fire nades)
-TREX AND SPINOSAURUS DRAMATICALLY BUFFED (This is a huge issue and the only big con in this entire review. Trex and spino need to be strong to serve their role, but they've been buffed to an impossible level. A competent human can 1v1 a bad trex/spino, but a competent Trex/spino can slaughter waves of humans without ever dying. That's not how a high risk, high reward class works, and it's not even how a low risk, high reward class works, because 'low risk' is actually 'no risk'.)
-TREX AND SPINOSAURUS ARE AUTOMATICALLY LIMITED TO 2 INSTEAD OF BASED ON ENEMY TEAM (This is a step backwards and I have no idea why they did this. It should be at most 1 per 6 humans, but instead you can see 2 trex/spinos versus 6 humans frequently, or even when dinos outnumber humans. This wouldn't be as much of an issue, but they buffed both so hard compared to the original.)
-Some things have no sounds, seen most often with other human players. Bug?
In summary, basic early access balancing needs to be done, and a few bugfixes. More content needs to be added. The finished product should be worth it, and I still recommend it to new players. Just know that you're getting into an asymmetric team based game that isn't as well polished as would be nice.
If you want a DM game similar to this that is well balanced and polished, check out Natural Selection 2. The interesting 'team' is actually harder to play with higher reward.
My final note is that I hope the devs don't focus on the market profits over the game's quality. No one will buy skins if the game isn't good enough, or if they do, they wont use market to do it, but instead 3rd party traders.
Best of luck to the game.

This game needs work and a lot of it.
I am aware that this game is still in the "early access" or "beta" stage, so I will write this review based on what this game currently is right now. When it becomes polished I will probably write a second review based on the game's standing at that point in time.
Visually it is leaps ahead of PC by a great amount. Mechanically PCE has a lot to fix.
Pros:
Extra abilities: Its nice to see that humans (as well as dinos) are getting different abilities now (e.g. health kit, ammo kits, etc). I much needed feature to help create a balance. (balance has yet to be achieved, but its a step in the right direction).
Speed of Gameplay: Although the human stamina needs signifigant improvements, the overall speed of the game I feel has helped to better increase the fluidity of combat (once they polish the game).
Improved textures and lighting (though still needs work) is nice.
Revamped PC maps (like the Dock), its a step in the right direction in draweing in fans of the first PC.
3D scope will be a very nice feature once polished.
New maps are always good, especially dynamic maps (like the one that electrocutes all players outside of the main complex)
Making the Raptor more challenging to use. In the first PC, it was painfully easy to just spam jump and take people down. now you have to work for it.
Cons:
For starters, twitchy dinosaurs. I'll use the Pteranadon for example. They've made it in PC:E where picking players up as a Pteranadon is way too easy, combine that with break neck 90 degree pin turns and a you virtually can't miss. Takes away the skill factor of picking up humans and dropping them to their doom, as well as creating a painstaking disatvantage for trying to shoot it (hit box issues, but I'll get to that later). In short, the Pteranadon should never be simple to use, just like the scientist being tricky to use since it only has ONE weapon that does damage and it is a weapon based on percision and timing, aka requiring some skill to use.
Side stepping raptors. (before you make assumptions, I have a very powerful gaming/work PC and excellent net service).
Back to the twitching raptors, with the hitbox being as poor as it is, all you have to really do to avoid getting hit half the time(not all the time) is tap A and D really fast and the hit box follows the character animation.
T-Rex and Spinos doing 360s to get ya with a "flick"shot movement. Im sorry, nothing that big moves that fast.
Hit Boxes. If you have this game and played as the scientist you know exactly what I mean. The rounds don't always hit their mark, which means either the bullet deviates (which as the scientist it shouldn't), the hit box for the dino isn't complete, or it has something to do with the overall animation.
Spawn points: The games spawning system as it stands (especially for humans) is absolutely attrocious. A personal example would be my character spawning directly beneath a spino 4 times in a row. Also now with the Pteranadon being so painfully easy to use, often times when you spawn out in the open, in 2-5 seconds you're bound to be picked up by a Pteranadon.
General Lighting and texture bugs, examples being shadows from characters a floor above you being visible in the floor below, motion causing render issues, etc. The lighting gets buggy at times, especially if you're using the 3D sniper scope.
Overall motion: It has the potential to be smooth, but as it stands it still gets pretty clunky in verious spots on the map.
Overall, do I recommend this game for the casual player? Absolutely not. Wait for the game to be complete and polished before making your purchase.

Best controller.
A lot of professional reviews have stated that they aren't sure about the steam controller yet.
I think this is because they simply arent spending enough time with it.
However, after a week of use I can say comfortably that I'll never buy another style of controller again if I don't have to.
The ability to remap controls as I see fit is worth it almost all by itself, making several games like Realms of the Haunting playable again without in depth .ini edits.
The fact that I'm able to cite a DoS Box game as one of my examples should give you a hint of how versitile the controller really is, too.

Honestly I wish there was a "meh" button instead of a like dislike as I don't mind having the controller, and won't return it, but probably wouldn't buy it again.  Either way, the positives I found were far outweighed by the negatives in my mind.
To start out, this is the first controller I've owned other than playstation style ones, and a lot of my disatisfaction is in relation to those. So:
Positives:
- The Haptic feedback is great
- I find the left touch pad very convenient for menu navigation and such
- LOTS of programmable buttons
Negatives:
- The decision to inset the "directional pad" instead of raises occasionally leads to your place on it.
- Both the joystick and face buttons are set to far inward, making it akward to hit them with thumbs (and I have big hands).
- Similiarly the center arrow buttons are all but impossible to hit without a really weird reach across.
- Overall I found that my PS3 controller felt overall more comforatble and more solid (part of this is the buttons tied into the battery cover which makes the whole back feel very loose.
- The game capatabiltiy is a bit disappointing, I picked this up specifically for some fighting games, and it turns out they had no native support, while plugging my PS3 controller in and running a simple detection program worked like a charm with far fewer hassles.  Even for games that support the controller natively, the default control schemes are a bit odd, and changing them not only takes time, but the remote will occassionally go back to default when changing between games instead of auto switching to your chosen configuration.
Random Thought:
- Still no match for a Keyboard and Mouse in FPS games.
Overall, my recommendation would be to try to borrow one from a friend, or at least get some hands on time with one at a Game Stop before buying it to see if it meets your needs.  I will give a breif shoutout to Game Stop since that is where I bought mine, and got 10% off Steam Wallet credit, which was more useful to me than the games available with preorder.
Cheers!

I don't know where to start. The Steam Controller is so different and at first this controller might feel worse on controller optimized games compared to the competitors, but with this controller Valve just made a large amount of the entire Steam Library playable on a controller on your couch.
The amount of customization you can apply through the software is insane, and for all the people that don't like tinkering you can easily download popular templates for each game.
Getting used to this controller will take some time and I can see that many people still prefer other controllers for games that support it, because learning something new when you're so familiar with the way it has been done until now can be quite off-putting, however I see a huge potential in this product and the community is so creative in creating templates for the Steam Controller it's really great.
In the end I am very happy about the Steam Controller. If I want to lean back and play some games I don't have to worry about controller compatibility anymore, because this controller is compatible with all games, not the other way around.

Played mostly Cave Story and Brawlhalla so far.
Good size. Good weight. A ton of inputs (shoulder buttons out the wazoo), Clicks feel sufficiently clicky. No silly uncomfortable hand formations to reach any of the buttons. Games that don't outright provide controller support (Cave Story) have user-uploaded bindings so you don't have to spend any time setting up.
It is, however, not a Nintendo controller that can survive being dropped 20 stories while on fire and then run over by a bulldozer coated in acid. It is a dainty lady. The track-pad simulating mouse movement is super sensitive. The plastic holding in the batteries is also a trigger/shoulder button and doesn't seal. I feel like a need to put on velvet gloves and delicately cradle it for it to get the lifespan I expect out of a controller, but only time will tell.
Overall positive: it feels great. Just worried it will turn out to be not as durable as standard console controllers.

After a few hours of play with it the first time round I was perplexed by how one goes about programming the controller for each game, however the challange was quickly tackled. Several days in, I've created builds that are optimized in my mind & one I've published. As my time with the crontroller pass things will only get better as I learn better way to program it for each task in whatever game I set my eyes upon.
Wether the game be fast pasted shooter, puzzle game, platformer, action adventure, or action rpg one can figure out ways to programe their needs into something comfortable to their hand. However the only games I wouldn't suggest any controller for are turn based mmo where you have to use your number keys to attack or perform any action. Despite my doubts, I am sure some one either will or has already taken up the challange & managed to make workable bindings for their games of choice in the genera.
As far as the controllers feel in my hand, I find that it is most comfortable to use a lose grip unlike the grips I tend to have with other controllers with more triditional handels. I don't find my fingers becoming stiff or sore after long hours of play regardless of the game I've played thus far. I also never onces feard it falling from my hands due to sweety palms.
It's looks are, outlandish to say the least, however I didn't buy it for it's looks.
The only con I have for this controller thus far is that some games just wont work with it. However I've only came across two games in my lybrary that appear to ignore the controller, mayhaps with time even they will recognize it as well.
Edit: After a long time playing with the controller & having the replace it only once It seems that the left & right bumber's inner arms that make contact with the actual buttons within are the weak link in this controllers design. For the second time one of the arms have broken inside leaving me unable to activate commands programed for the bumper. I may have found a work around.
Despite that I still find this controller a good buy, the warranty doesn't hurt either.
