This game needs work and a lot of it.
I am aware that this game is still in the "early access" or "beta" stage, so I will write this review based on what this game currently is right now. When it becomes polished I will probably write a second review based on the game's standing at that point in time.
Visually it is leaps ahead of PC by a great amount. Mechanically PCE has a lot to fix.
Pros:
Extra abilities: Its nice to see that humans (as well as dinos) are getting different abilities now (e.g. health kit, ammo kits, etc). I much needed feature to help create a balance. (balance has yet to be achieved, but its a step in the right direction).
Speed of Gameplay: Although the human stamina needs signifigant improvements, the overall speed of the game I feel has helped to better increase the fluidity of combat (once they polish the game).
Improved textures and lighting (though still needs work) is nice.
Revamped PC maps (like the Dock), its a step in the right direction in draweing in fans of the first PC.
3D scope will be a very nice feature once polished.
New maps are always good, especially dynamic maps (like the one that electrocutes all players outside of the main complex)
Making the Raptor more challenging to use. In the first PC, it was painfully easy to just spam jump and take people down. now you have to work for it.
Cons:
For starters, twitchy dinosaurs. I'll use the Pteranadon for example. They've made it in PC:E where picking players up as a Pteranadon is way too easy, combine that with break neck 90 degree pin turns and a you virtually can't miss. Takes away the skill factor of picking up humans and dropping them to their doom, as well as creating a painstaking disatvantage for trying to shoot it (hit box issues, but I'll get to that later). In short, the Pteranadon should never be simple to use, just like the scientist being tricky to use since it only has ONE weapon that does damage and it is a weapon based on percision and timing, aka requiring some skill to use.
Side stepping raptors. (before you make assumptions, I have a very powerful gaming/work PC and excellent net service).
Back to the twitching raptors, with the hitbox being as poor as it is, all you have to really do to avoid getting hit half the time(not all the time) is tap A and D really fast and the hit box follows the character animation.
T-Rex and Spinos doing 360s to get ya with a "flick"shot movement. Im sorry, nothing that big moves that fast.
Hit Boxes. If you have this game and played as the scientist you know exactly what I mean. The rounds don't always hit their mark, which means either the bullet deviates (which as the scientist it shouldn't), the hit box for the dino isn't complete, or it has something to do with the overall animation.
Spawn points: The games spawning system as it stands (especially for humans) is absolutely attrocious. A personal example would be my character spawning directly beneath a spino 4 times in a row. Also now with the Pteranadon being so painfully easy to use, often times when you spawn out in the open, in 2-5 seconds you're bound to be picked up by a Pteranadon.
General Lighting and texture bugs, examples being shadows from characters a floor above you being visible in the floor below, motion causing render issues, etc. The lighting gets buggy at times, especially if you're using the 3D sniper scope.
Overall motion: It has the potential to be smooth, but as it stands it still gets pretty clunky in verious spots on the map.
Overall, do I recommend this game for the casual player? Absolutely not. Wait for the game to be complete and polished before making your purchase.

The following are opinions collected from several players and former members of Primal Carnage's QA testing team:
"The animations [in PC:E] are somehow even worse [than the original] and harder to follow. Rex and carno animations move way too fast as they're getting up to speed, making their legs look like they're going much faster than they should be. Also, once freed from a raptor pounce, I was bugged by the fact that there is no accompanying animation. The player simply goes back to the first-person HUD, but is forced to stare, unmoving, as they "stand back up". So that's just a few issues with the ungodly animations."
In regards to PC:E's flight mechanics versus the original Primal Carnage's:
"The forced turn radius, the inability to fly up or down, the delayed peck damage, the disgustingly-pitiful range AND cooldown of the ptera's roar... All things that have angered me to the point of swearing to never play PC:E, again."
..."On another note, the introduction of sidearms to the human classes. Pisses me off." ..."they add a feeling of cliche dullness to the game. They just plain aren't needed in the scope of gameplay.
Some human classes were just plain ineffective against certain dino classes, as it should be. Like the pyro was♥♥♥♥♥♥against rexes because they couldn't get close. Now, a pyro can simply stand inside a building and take potshots at the rex with his handgun. This also goes with pyros, commandos, and pathfinders, who used to not be able to shoot pteras for♥♥♥♥♥♥until they came close. Now, every god damn class can just whip out their sidearm and take relatively-accurate potshots at a flying ptera. That, combined with the artificial difficulty of ptera controls, makes me not want to play pteranodon."
"I had to set mouse sensitivity to the highest setting just to get some decent movement on-screen, but it still wasn't enough. Even on its highest, mouse sensitivity is still sluggish and I find myself having to whip my mouse from left edge to right edge of my mouse pad, just to turn part of the way around. Rinse and repeat to turn -all- the way around."
"Probably my biggest complaint about PC:E, at this point in time... Is the shamble of a dev team that's behind the whole thing. It's the dishonesty of the studio that bugs me the most. According to previous QA testers, Lukewarm Media had begun production on PC:E almost a year ago, spring of 2014. The community was told that this "re-code" would be a free update to the base game ALL THE WAY UNTIL LATE OCTOBER. According to the PC forums and Apoc's announcement, PC:E as a standalone game wasn't actually revealed until October 27, 2014. That's at least six months of misleading information.
Then there was the underhanded PR stunt where Circle 5 requested extra payment from existing players for what was basically an updated version of Primal Carnage. I don't fully fault them for that, anymore, since the price they asked was negligible. Still a dirty trick, though.
Lastly, the fact that they departed so heavily from the original PC's gameplay mechanics. I loved Primal Carnage because of exactly how it was. I enjoyed the mechanics. Though broken and in dire need of balancing, I still prefer them over these "new and improved" mechanics. Speaking of which...
I thought that PC:E was supposed to fix all of the bugs and glitches and graphical issues that the original had. Well, they made the decision to release PC:E in Early Access and that all went to♥♥♥♥♥♥ Extinction somehow manages to contain bugs never-before-seen in other video games of its kind. Most memorable being the "two dinos get stuck on each other and one floats endlessly upward through the ceiling" glitch. With so many glaring issues in Extinction's presentation, I can't be sure if Circle 5 doesn't know how to properly code a game, or if they just truly don't care about their playerbase, anymore. Extinction is even buggier and harder to play than the original Primal Carnage."
In summary, don't waste your time or money.

Pros:
- Unique concept
- nice challenge
- pixel art
- zen difficulty option
- many characters and monsters to unlock
- level select at new game, keeping character level-ups
Cons:
- too fast, so you have to write short words to deal damage fast
- you do not enjoy the fights, as you focus your eyes on the letters
- many obscure words, so you need to be creative
- no ending (and the game tells you that in a very subtle way)
- armor and weapons just add skill points, they do not behave as in-game objects
- no fullscreen support (you can make the edges larger in the options screen, but you cannot make it go fullscreen) because the author decided this was the only option  he had (see Discussions for this game on Steam).
So yeah, I recommend getting this game, it is fun if you enjoy word games, even if it is flawed. And, if you can wait, get it in a bundle like me or wait for a very good deal. No reason to pay full price on Steam, anyways :)

This might honestly be one of the most important games in recent years. The main game consists of three different playthroughs, each one approaching the same story from a different point of view. Just when you think you understand all the motives and events in one playthrough, you learn something earth shattering in the next playthrough that recontextualizes all those things you thought you knew, to a point where it almost feels like, after the cold opening of the third playthrough, the developers are finally letting you look at the bigger picture of the narrative, which in any other game might have come across as contrived, or just as a means to drag out the game length, but Platinum Games really made this feel powerful and rewarding.
A great action RPG with an absolutely mesmerizing soundtrack to boot, Nier Automata is easily one of my favorite games. Very intuitive controls and some interesting mechanics, combined with challenging enemy types and incredibly intense boss fights makes every successful encounter feel fresh and rewarding, which helps considering a lot of the missions can boil down to one of a few formulas, either clearing out an area of enemies, escorting a character to an objective, etc.
HOWEVER, this game is a perfect example of a PC port being done as a complete afterthought, and it performs absolutely abysmally. I've tried every graphical preset in the settings, and no matter how I configure the graphical settings I get a consistent framerate of 24-32 which is absolutely inexcusable. I've also noticed weird things such as how I have my resolution set to 1920x1080, yet it looks as if it were set to something slightly lower.
All in all, an incredible game but a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor excuse for a port. I'd absolutely recommend playing the game, but make sure to get it on sale, because $60 for a game that the publishers/developers have no intention of patching is ridiculous.

NOTE: THIS POSITIVE REVIEW COMES WITH A GIANT GLOWING ASTERISK!
Saint's Row 2 is an open-world classic that set up a successful sister series to the infamous Grand Theft Auto.  It is a definite Must Have of any serious gamer's collection.
But the PC port on Steam is just awful.  Lack of proper control integration and lack of HD options and myriad other problems ruin this otherwise amazing game for the PC.
If you want to play this on PC, you've got a couple of options.  The first is to get it off GOG, as that port is more modern and many of the issues with the Steam version have been ironed out.  The other option (which I seriously recommend) is to download the Gentlemen of the Row mod, which not only fixes almost all the issues present in the Steam version but also adds a simply astonishing amount of extra content (including quite a few optional mods that do things ranging from making a "brighter" nighttime for folks with less than great eyesight to tons of extra items  and more).
tl;dr  Get this game, but either A) through GOG or B) get the Gentlemen of the Row mod ASAP.

Original review after. Re-Review of Saints Row 2:
Yes, on my first stab at Saints Row 2, I was not initially impressed with what I saw. To an extent, many of my criticisms still stand, but after making another attempt after another stiff cocktail of mods injected into the mix, I have finally beaten the game in such a fashion that I found it enjoyable. I will list the mods presently:
SR:TT style camera - makes it more familiar for the player going back to SR2 from 3.
High Quality Radio Mod. Whatever happens, you're going to be driving from end to end of Stilwater all the time, so you're going to want better quality audio for your music during these trips.
SR2 Improved vehicles. Brings their handling closer to the feel of Saints Row 3 generally. As driving didn't make me wish for death constantly after installing it, I mark it lives up to its name.
SR2 Powertools.
And last but not least, the superlative Gentlemen of the Row:
Installing all these mods together is involved and not for tha faint of heart, but certainly not the most difficult thing I've ever done either. That said, I'd consider these mods the minimum work necessary to get Saints Row 2 to enjoyably playable status, and tunes up the game's challenges from impossible, annoying and often defective to genuinely difficult.
That said, you're still going to have to relearn how to fly helicopters.
[After a whirlwind tour of Saints Row the Third, IV, and Gat Out of Hell, I decided it was finally time to give the originals their fair shake - or at least Saints Row 2, the only one of the first two games currently ported to PC. I wanted to see where it had all begun, and what I'd heard from other fans about SR2's sandbox being even more expansive than the latter sequels was also encouraging. While there were also warnings of it being a bad port, I was reassured that the superlative mod pack by IdolNinja, Gentlemen of the Row, addressed many of the issues admirably, while broadening the base content of the game considerably. Needless to say, I was excited.
However, I am finding myself disappointed with the game. Perhaps I have been spoiled by starting with the Third, but I get the sense that if I had started with Saints Row 2 I might never have glommed on to the series the way I have.
The first issue is vehicles. They're a huge part of Saints Row 2, and the game offers even greater customization of them than its sequels. None of that is enough to make up for their atrocious handling. Even with mods, there wasn't a moment when I wasn't cursing with frustration at them. Their amped up sensitivity makes any fine movement virtually impossible, which is pretty crucial if you're, say, piloting a helicopter at treetop level between buildings.
Second, are the activities. I thought that they were frustrating in SR3, but God DAMN, I didn't know what frustrating was until this.

My experience so far:
Playing FPS games:
With Kb/M - 10/10
With Steam Controller - 8/10

With Kb/M - 10/10

Playing Full gamepad support games (Such as racing or platformers):

All in All - The Steam controller is the best single option for PC gaming. Been using this thing for a while and it's... strange. But I'm getting ahead of myself.
Let's check off the standard features. Build quality is great, feels solid, no trouble with the wireless, weight is fine, suits someone like me with large hands. XYAB buttons, all present and correct. Shoulder buttons - both analog and digital, along with a third pair where your ring/little fingers sit when holding the pad, cool. Pair of analog sticks - nope, just the one. Okay, boring stuff out of the way, let's get to the touchpads.
Anyone who ever played Metroid on the Nintendo DS will immediately understand how the right-hand touchpad works. Don't be put off if you've ever tried to play an FPS on a laptop touchpad, the angle of the grip lets you naturally drop your thumb smack in the middle of the pad and breeze around it easily, while the adjustable haptic feedback really helps you keep your movement rate in check. I won't pretend it's as accurate as using a mouse - it simply isn't, but I've found it much better than using an analog stick. The click-down function is also kinda useless as it always causes a shift in your touch as you apply extra pressure, jerking your aim around.
That just leaves the left-hand touchpad. Er... no. Just... no. It's pretty much the same as the right-hand pad, but it's got a recessed D-pad texture which someone at Valve thought would let it do double duty. In reality, it's utter crap. Physical touchpads stick out and pivot in the centre, giving you plenty of feedback about where you are on the surface and allowing super-fast movement between multiple cardinal points, no thought required. This pad relies on the same click-down function the right-hand touchpad uses with no pivot point and only the very slight inverted texturing to give you any touch-based frame of reference feedback. I have never used a worse D-pad in all my life, it's atrociously bad. Forget using it for platformers, fighting games, puzzle games... well, anything really.
This leaves the Steam Controller in a bit of a problem situation. For first person shooters and anything that doesn't make heavy use of the D-pad, it's great. As soon as you reach for that D-pad as a main control, you'll need another control pad to fall back on instead.
Recommended for sofa gamers, but ONLY if you already have another good controller, like an X-Box PC controller. Otherwise, no.

The game is easily worth the money I paid for it. The main reasons for my short play time are that I frequently opt to spend my nights drunk on Xbox with my friend or enjoy some other hobby. Also, the dwindling player count. Out of the available servers, there are still enough to play, but I usually only find a handful with a playable connection or open slots.
Luckily, many viable options still have plenty of players.
With my recent shooter history being softcore like Battlefield, Rainbow Six, and Battlefront, this game is an extremely welcome change of pace from trolls, teabaggers and the like. If you're sick of being punished for playing it smart, like in console available shooters, this game will provide a much needed respite from the horrors of arcadey gameply. It's a game where you aren't shot in the head by a standing sniper with a 300 lumen flashlight for a scope whose moving side to side... while you're prone and still with a bipod. No sprinting at superhuman speeds, whipping out a machine pistol and getting headshots on players you ran/spawned behind.
The gunplay is kind of like ARMA, but with more stablization options (you can rest your gun on walls, corners, and the ground). I actually find weapon handling more realistic in ways, as your gun is very unsteady unless you do something about it, as opposed to being very steady unless you run, sprint, or get shot/shot at. I've found RS2's mechanics to be more similar to my own experiences with firearms.
Character movement feels like a clunky Battlefield. Clunky in a good way. You need adequate space to aim and assume certain stances and you move at a lower speed. The infinite sprint and its lack off affect on aim is one thing they have in common, unfortunately, but I don't care enough to complain, just point it out.
The small amount of available maps hasn't gotten to me, as I haven't played long enough, but it's getting better all the time. Modders have made playable maps, some of which look really cool and there's a free DLC coming that gets the Australians and their unique weapons involved.

Been using this thing for a while and it's... strange. But I'm getting ahead of myself.
Let's check off the standard features. Build quality is great, feels solid, no trouble with the wireless, weight is fine, suits someone like me with large hands. XYAB buttons, all present and correct. Shoulder buttons - both analog and digital, along with a third pair where your ring/little fingers sit when holding the pad, cool. Pair of analog sticks - nope, just the one. Okay, boring stuff out of the way, let's get to the touchpads.
Anyone who ever played Metroid on the Nintendo DS will immediately understand how the right-hand touchpad works. Don't be put off if you've ever tried to play an FPS on a laptop touchpad, the angle of the grip lets you naturally drop your thumb smack in the middle of the pad and breeze around it easily, while the adjustable haptic feedback really helps you keep your movement rate in check. I won't pretend it's as accurate as using a mouse - it simply isn't, but I've found it much better than using an analog stick. The click-down function is also kinda useless as it always causes a shift in your touch as you apply extra pressure, jerking your aim around.
That just leaves the left-hand touchpad. Er... no. Just... no. It's pretty much the same as the right-hand pad, but it's got a recessed D-pad texture which someone at Valve thought would let it do double duty. In reality, it's utter crap. Physical touchpads stick out and pivot in the centre, giving you plenty of feedback about where you are on the surface and allowing super-fast movement between multiple cardinal points, no thought required. This pad relies on the same click-down function the right-hand touchpad uses with no pivot point and only the very slight inverted texturing to give you any touch-based frame of reference feedback. I have never used a worse D-pad in all my life, it's atrociously bad. Forget using it for platformers, fighting games, puzzle games... well, anything really.
This leaves the Steam Controller in a bit of a problem situation. For first person shooters and anything that doesn't make heavy use of the D-pad, it's great. As soon as you reach for that D-pad as a main control, you'll need another control pad to fall back on instead.
Recommended for sofa gamers, but ONLY if you already have another good controller, like an X-Box PC controller. Otherwise, no.

A beautiful game!
Instead of putting a whole paragraph on how I love it, I'll just put some points down on what I really liked about it. I will also put some kind of not-so-great things here as well, so you can see if this is the game for you!
Pros:
1. The scenery itself is very beautiful! Each town and area has their own little thing and you can explore all of the beautiful sights!
2. The enemies are very adorable! Now this isn't much of a pro to the game since enemy style doesn't really tell how good a game is, but I thought to put it out there. I feel bad killing a lot of the enemies because of how cute they are.
3. There are 3 servers in a game. Each server is seperate so you can make 3 characters per server. In total, you can have 9 characters. I am a person that likes to try a lot of different classes, so this is great for me! If you're like that too, you'll love this! I know from my experience of different MMORPGs that a lot of games don't really allow this kind of thing. The only one I can remember was Fiesta online did this. I know there are a couple more out there that I don't remember. But this one does that kind of thing, so I think it's great!
4.  The character design for your character and the NPCs are so adorable! I really like the character customization on this game. While there isn't too much to the customization, it's enough to make nice characters, in my opionion! I wasn't expecting something like this to have PS2 Online super ultra customization, but I was surprised to how much there was in it. So overall, its a great player maker!
5. There are so many quests! Many of them are not fighting-based either, so you won't always be running around doing the same thing over and over again. You set up traps, deliver things, make things, etc. Of course, though, there will always be more fighting than, lets say, delivery quests. But, the small difference in routine gives it a little more fun! It even has a stroy questline to it as well!
6. You get an ostrich. That's right. You get to ride an ostrich. This also doesn't make a game 100% better, but I think it's pretty cool that your free mount is an ostrich.
7. Another thing I like about this game is it has such a friendly environment! Many times have I made a character and at a low-level, higher ups have me join their guild or party to help me out thinking I'm extremely new. I have not once gotten into an argument with anyone. The community is great in my opinion. I'm not sure if others would agree with me because everyone has their own experiences with other people in MMORPGs, but my experience has been good so far. I'm hoping it is like this for everyone!
8. You can get something called "loyalty points" through out the game that you can use to "buy" costumes! Loyalty points are free, but a little difficult to get a lot. But if you're determined and do a lot of easedropping on NPCs, you'll rack up those loyalty points and get that cool costume you wanted! They also have another point system that you actually have to pay money to get, but I think that it's great that the game developers let the people who don't pay money on games have a chance to get something cool!
---
Cons:
1. This game does get kind of repetitive. Even though they have different quests thats not all fighting, they are usually "get __ amount of __" kind of quests. My higher up is aroung level 36 if I remember, and it's getting a little boring aroung there. However I do sometimes continue to log on and play. They do have "fame quests" and "daily quests" that they put up if you don't feel like doing the same old quests. (<---maybe should have put that in pros?)
2. It is a point-and-click stlyled fighting game. You do have hot keys for your abilities, but for the most part, it's a point-and-click. If you're not a fan of that style of fighting in an MMORPG, then you'll probably get bored very fast.
3. Laggy a bit. This might just be for me and my dumb computer. But if you have just a general computer or laptop, you may experience some lag (not too much of it unless you're in a crowded area, but thats normal for every crowded MMORPG). The cutscenes don't work for me because of it. It may be different for you though! So don't stress over this point too much.
4. Some quests require you have a party of 3. If you are a solo player like me, that may serve a problem in trying to find and work the courage to work with people. There is a party finder so you can form parties for just the dungeon. However, for me, I like doing things alone and forming parties is awkward because then I have to figure out if I should leave the party or if they still want to work together, etc. So if you're a solo player, some of these moments might not be for you.
5. Very easy. This could be a pro as well if you like things easy. Bosses are not that hard, enemies are farley easy. (I've killed an enemy about 3 or 4 levels above me with not a problem). So if you like easy MMORPGs, this is for you. But if you like a challange, this may not be it.
---
Overall, in my opinion, I really like this game and I think, despite the cons, I will continue to play this game. It's very beautiful and the scenery and characters are very well made. Even though quests become a routine, they have daily quests and fame quests that break the routine a little bit. If there was a 10 rating, i think it would go about 8.5/10. I would reccomend people to give this a try and see if it is their cup of tea.

tl;dr: Great game plagued by horrible matchmaking and lacking features.
I'm giving this as thumbs down despite still playing it and actually liking the game. There's a reason, read further...
This is a team-based arena FPS (though 3rd person is by now also possible), similar to Overwatch.
The main draw, and there is no beating around the bush here, is that it is free to play.
However, after more than 20 hours of playing, I decided to buy the Founder's Pack for 20€ to unlock all current and future characters - well worth it as a package and support the devs.
The game is really good, the characters are surprisingly varied, the classes are clear and you have a load of options to play single characters very differently.
So all is well? No.
This game suffers from an absolutely horrible matchmaking (at least in non-ranked mode, where most are playing).
Simply put, teams are put together entirely at random. Before level 5, you will be teamed up only against bots, but after that, it is fully random.
Winning depends entirely on your team mates, and I have to say, there are just too many idiots running around. Healers not healing, tanks chasing around in the wild, damage/flank champions thinking they can tank, people not focusing on the objective and going for kills only, etc., etc. This game is not rocket science, a decent human being should be able to pull it off good enough to fulfill their job at least.
But it many cases, people just don't. I don't understand why, but it is really bad.
It wouldn't matter if matchmaking would team you up with people at a similar skill level - but it doesn't.
It wouldn't matter if there was a rating system where you could rate your team mates after each match - but there isn't.
It wouldn't matter if you could block people to not play with them again for a time - but you can't.*
It would matter less if you could see people's stats during game to tell them where to improve - but you can't.
I could go on...
* Some say this is abusable to block better players. Easy solution: Offer really good players immunity. Of course, they should still be reported if they behave toxic, etc. Too often, I was placed with the same unreasonable player match after match that never listened to advice and was just not playing his role, costing victory again and again.
But a rating system and matchmaking based on that would be the best solution, either way.
Right now, the only way for an enjoyable match experience is either finding somewhat decent people to play with and add them to friends - or hoping for luck. That's not enough.
The game is in early access still and I hope that matchmaking gets improved or we get some of the missing skills.
I'd gladly improve my rating to a thumbs up, because the base game is really good.

Very innovative piece of tech with full rebindability (except for the steam button).
If you just look at all the features, you'll see how much room for customization there is compared to a regular controller, which only has the thumbsticks, bumpers and triggers, dpad, xyba, and start buttons.
This has some regular xyba buttons, a thumbstick with obligatory clicking, and 2 buttons that can work as either more buttons OR a mouse (With all it's sensitvity + other options) OR a thumbstick AND has an extra button built inside of it.  Not to mention these two giant buttons also vibrate in a complex and beautiful way.  The triggers are dual-staged, which means you can softly pull on them to do one button, and click in hard to do another button.  AND you can even make it so that if you pull fast enough, you can skip the soft button and just do the hard button.
There are 2 buttons on the back, which is really new, but those are just regular buttons, although you don't have to move your fingers to get to them, so that's good.  There's 2 bumpers, and 2 more buttons (start and escape).
There's a gyroscope in there, so you can (theoretically) make it so you can tilt it and the controller will press virtual buttons FOR YOU.  As I mentioned before, the steam button is off limits, though.
And it has good battery life, feels sturdy and well built, and can support virtually all games in some way or form, etc. etc.
Doesn't replace mouse+keyboard for regular use, but if you want to play on a couch, this is for you.  Only problem I have with it is that it's either impossible or really, REALLY hard to use a steam controller as player 2 in a splitscreen game, even if the other person is using a controller and not mouse+keyboard

Words for Evil is a high speed version of single player Boggle.  Instead of a timer, you have adventurers that go in to battle.  There are four different types of puzzles your adventurers will face.  First is the regular battle, where you spell as many words as you can using letters that connect (just like Boggle).  The twist is that in order to progress (cause damage/use abilities), you need to incorporate highlighted letters in to your words.  A minimum of three letters are required for each word, and bigger words have a stronger effect.  Second is the trap puzzle, where you are given letters you need to incorporate in to words, regardless of their placement.  The letters can only be used once, and the key is to use as many letters as possible.  All unused letters cause damage, but a bonus is granted if all letters are used.  Third is a treasure puzzle, where you decypher a code using one of two letters available for every space in the word.  Even if you aren't sure what the word is, you are not penalized for guessing, so fit as many guesses as you can before time runs out.  The fourth puzzle is a 'saving throw' puzzle, where you have a final chance to escape death's grip.  You have a short amount of time to descramble an anagram.  Definitely not easy, but extremely rewarding as a last resort.
I am really mixed on whether or not I recommend it or not.  Some of the words you are expected to have in your vocabulary have a wide variety of national origin.  I also have run in to problems where certain common words are not in the game's vast library.  Other times, I have been faced with the problem of being given trap puzzles where the only vowel I'm given is the letter "i." The game is also so high paced that you are typically taking all focus on the puzzle itself, making the animation of your adventurers in combat more of a distraction.  I recommend this to people who love word play, and a college level grasp of the English language.  Otherwise, you might find this game overly frusturating.

oO has been developed and published by Maciej Targoni and Wojciech Wasiak. A seemingly simple game, yet it holds plenty of flexibility if not novelty from the arcade formula we’ve seen countless times already. The fact that it was created by a two-man team which has experience already with geometry-based gameplay mechanics, speaks volumes and assures that oO is more than just a shy debut onto Steam’s ever growing indie library.

While it may not necessarily impress with its looks, oO’s gameplay is most certainly its main attraction. Relatively short and few levels, that are well diversified through careful use of colors and obstacle shapes but quite difficult. Not entirely unexpected since the game has to stand out somehow. I never found it frustratingly hard but it does take some hefty time getting used to it. It uses the mouse controls to its advantage and can also provide a test for your own reaction time. For being a fast-paced game, it is surprisingly needy, when it comes to your required level of concentration. I consider it a nice break from other genres and as far as an affordable arcade game is concerned, this title hits all the right spots.

The minimal chromatic and shaping style suits the game just fine and the relaxing selection of sounds, prevents a potential attempt at rage quitting. It works as intended and you can’t complain about it at any given point.

+ Fun and challenging for the right price
+ Steam Achievements

- No Trading Cards


oO is one of those nice little games on Steam that was appropriately priced from the get-go. It features Achievements, but the inclusion of Trading Cards would have added even more sugar to this sweet deal. Does it really need more sugar to warrant a purchase? Most certainly not.

If you dug Jet Set Radio and / or Marc Ecko's Getting Up and are seeking out an urban game with a graffiti component you miiiiight wanna check this out, although Jet Set Radio is a far superior (and comparably-priced) title. For myself, despite being a fan of both hiphop (Mr. Lif and Akrobatik / the Perceptionists, who are featured on this game's soundtrack) music and graffiti I find it hard to recommend this unless you're a diehard fan of either and looking for a platformer with a unique mechanic and can tolerate some chunky framerate issues.
The game itself isn't terrible and has a fair amount of enemy variety and player skills (a slide, swing, dive kick, etc...) but the game runs choppy as♥♥♥♥♥♥and the music they use although enjoyable (I'm a big fan of the Perceptionists) it seems like the game repeats the same 2 songs over and over and over AND OVER. I like the song "People 4 Prez" and all but already being a fan of it and hearing it a ton before this to hear it again here on nearly every level gets pretty tiring. Plus while some of the graffiti art is cool (the end level tags leading to the next stage are the most complex) a lot of them are pretty simplistic and could have used a lot more refinement, particularly amongst the enemy designs as some of them appear so tiny on the screen that it's hard to even make out much of the illustrative detail that went into them.
The game is at its best (and oddly seems to run more smoothly) when you are running along quickly dodging / killing enemies and moving from one side of a building to another in rapid succession, but then you run into sections where you have to slow your rhythm completely to line up a jump, press RB to make a platform materialize, and hope you don't fall back down to the previous area. This is common in platforming games, but really kills the pace on this particular title.
This game feels half-done. A cool concept and it isn't broken, but it seems like the level designs are all pretty generic (putting aside the mechanic of running along whichever wall..) I will still play through more of it here and there, but the choppy display and especially the repetitive music are wearing thin on me already and I haven't even made it very far into the game. I'm glad I checked it out on sale but I wouldn't recommend this game to most other people.

I forgot it existed for a couple years, mostly because I was always busy playing Guild Wars 2 or some new release game.  It's now 2017.  I tried to play it yesterday and it kept giving me PhysX errors.  Dammit, PhysX.  Okay, I don't blame this game for my PhysX woes, but PhysX never seems to install correctly with the games which require it.  Anyway, I solved the PhysX errors by reinstalling the latest PhysX driver software.  Then, it played without any further problems.
The game has a unique visual style that I've only seen implemented well a couple times, once here and once in A Link Between Worlds.  I'm sure someone wants to mention Vexx or Mario or something of that nature, but in those games, it's always a small part of the game; not the whole game's style.  Anyway, I enjoy the paintings-on-walls visual style, and in this game, it actually serves to add some explorative elements to the platformer gameplay mechanic.  For example, gravity can be switched depending on how you enter a wall.  It doesn't really matter to the overall experience, though.  It's still a mostly linear platformer with small branching paths.
For $9.99, it's kinda pricey, but if you like the art style or the move-inside-walls mechanic, I recommend getting it.

You play as a teenager which is warped to another dimension in his own world in a journey to escape this world, save a missing girl and beat the master boss of this dimension. You'll soon discover that you're in a 2-dimension world running along the walls of the streets and even the roofs of the buildings. You'll need to prove your jumping and fighting skills against the environment and enemies.
The game features an immersive world with a great soundtrack, leaderboards for every levels, a local co-op and many unlockable skills and power-ups.
There is no time limit to finish a level and you have many checkpoints and infinite lives. But that doesn't mean the game isn't that challenging.
In every level there is a finite number of spray-paint can and only the best can achieve to find them all and be in the top of the leaderboards, hopefully you don't need to achieve that for an achievement.
For the achievements you have some challenging parts : beat the game, collect all secrets tags, collect all the unlockable and power-ups, finish a level without dying and complete a level without killing anyone.
In every level (except bosses) you have 5 secrets tags well-hidden to find and several unlockable and power-ups to find. In almost every normal level you'll have a question mark tag, if you collect it it will activate a limited time event in which you need to collect every bonus spray-paint cans to reward you with a secret tag.
Bosses can be easy to very challenging depending of your gaming level. And you'll unlock several skills to help you to reach some place that weren't possible before or to release powerful attacks.
Anyway this game is really awesome.

Ever since this game popped up on the main shop front page as a new game, I was curious. I love word games. Words for Evil did not disappoint at all.
It's a walker type game, and you can quit out anytime from the level and keep the progress you've made. You make your own party out of a number of unlockable heroes, including Santa Claus (who is seriously impressive in a fight)! Essentially you're given one of a number of puzzles, depending on whether you are up against a monster, a chest, or a trap, and you have to do your best at figuring them out. It stimulates the mind, and there are RPG elements as well, such as levelling up and buying gear.
I set it on the Zen difficulty and I still find it stimulating and challenging. It's the kind of game that sucks you in and, before you know it, hours have passed. It's so easy to say 'I'll just go to the next fountain' or 'I just want to do a few more battles'.
The graphics are adorable and charming, as well as in some cases quite stunning. The sense of humour in the game is welcome and pleasant. It's also noteworthy that it has a mode for those who may be colour blind or have a deficiency in distinguishing colours, so that's a really important thing.
It's a light game that doesn't take up a lot of space or demand masses of processing power, so it's the perfect game for any system. Some words you'd expect or know may not be in the game's dictionary, but that can just add a little to the challenge. Either way, it's been perfectly delightful for me, and I have no problem recommending it to anyone who likes to think as they play a game.
Charming, fun, and really absorbing, Words for Evil also has a price that can fit into most any budget. It's worth picking up and supporting. I'd love to see more games like this, and I look forward to seeing what the developer does with Words of Evil in future.

I've been waiting for something like this for ages. This game has a broken and inconsistent feel like the original Dungeon Lords by DreamCatcher did. Other than that gripe, it definitely feels like the dungeon crawlers of days gone by and even brings some interesting new enhancements to the genre. To me this seems like it could be the prototype for a revival of the genre.
Pros:
+ Very interesting genre enhancements
+ Skill, Stat, etc system varies slightly from most stale stock D20 copies
+ Main characters are fairly entertaining in a cliched self-aware way
+ Story doesn’t take itself too seriously and is also self-aware of that.
+ Nicely pokes fun at stale RPG tropes and cliches
+ Drama points can mix-up a stale situation and encourage side-questing
+ Nice tutorial dungeon
+ Balanced gameplay
Cons:
- Inconsistent art and graphics
- Lack of narration
- Lack of music variety
- Music track doesn’t loop properly
- If your going to allow free-look, why not just permanently allow it?
- No multiplayer
- Linear
- Limited to no replayability
Conclusion:
Buy it on sale if you're a fan of old dungeon crawlers, roguelikes, or obscure and different RPG titles. If you're looking for your cookie-cutter modern RPG Elder Scrolls title then this probably isn’t for you. O, and don't forget to just mute the audio entirely and play your own music.

Frayed Knights is a party-based first-person POV RPG. Similar to games such as WIzardry, Eye of the Beholder, etc. The story is decent, creating the desire to move ahead and figure out the mysteries of what is going on. One feature of the game is the witty banter between party members. The game focus on a being lighthearted and witty. The biggest negative is the graphics. They would be at home with games from 10-15 years ago. But the gameplay and story make up for that deficiency. Leveling up is rewarding, with many spells, abilities and bonuses to choose from.
Loot was sufficient, but barely. Around 95% of loot is white junk that you sell for a bit of coin. When you do find a "legendary" item, it is a big deal, so don't expect wondrous loot to rain down from the heavens. Fights start out very slow, until you get some abilities and spells under your belt. Exploration is fun. There are some decent puzzles, but nothing that is too difficult (I'm not a puzzle-man myself, so one or two here and there is fine).
One of the biggest pitfalls is load times. I have the game installed on an SSD and load time between zones is around 25-30 seconds. Fortunately, you won't be reloading or zoning very often. The game has a system where you build up stars that give great bonus abilities as long as you don't reload the game or die. Abilities like giving a character full health or resurrecting a character.  Unfortunately, my party got stuck in several places, hung up on the geomtry of the game world, unable to move, so I had to reload and lose my stars a few times, but you rebuild stars pretty fast. Other than that, the game never crashed and I ran into virtually no other bugs.
My final gripe is the mapping system. Auto-mapping is available, and it works great. However, if you zone, you lose the map to that zone. Not sure why the maps don't save, but once you explore a zone, you most likely won't need the map anyhow, so it's a minor annoyance.
All-in-all, if you like party-based rpg games and can put up with a game that feels old-school, I think this is a pretty good game. I give it a total of 6.5 out of 10, and I feel like I got my money and time's worth out of it.

I rarely write interviews for games on Steam, but I really enjoyed this one. Know what you're getting into. The price tag reflects the quality of the graphics, music and what not. Its an indie game made by a very small team and it shows. The style is cartoony, and light hearted and that's not everyone's thing. You also have a group of premade characters, though the freeform skill system still means you can "multiclass" them with few problems. For example the thief can be effective made into a combat oriented thief or a thief/cleric type character. I made my mage into an archer/mage for example. The game is a first person/party based game and it looks a lot like Wizardry 8 and feels like it too. There are random encounters, the game has a lot of party building options, and so its not really a casual game. Its a short, fun RPG if you like these kinds of games. Its not Might and Magic 10 or Wizardry 8, but if you have enjoyed those and are looking for something similar and don't mind the shorter playing time and light hearted gameplay, than I can definately recommend Frayed Knights.

This game gives me the 3-D explore feeling of Bard's Tale, the repetitive combat of Final Fantasy, and the spells, traps, and combat engines of Elder Scroll games. Oh, and then it's got the character personality of Three's Company.
Frayed Knights is clearly a labor of love done by gamer enthusiasts in their spare time. It's the genuine indie article, and the developers did a great job bringing it to life.
This review is mostly about game play. You play this game for an RPG dungeon crawler. You don't play it for graphics and looks. The graphics do their job, but the beauty is in the mechanics, the characters, the humor, and the story.
This is a dungeon exploring game, with heavy emphasis on combat encounters.  You will fight, gain xp and loot, level up, customize your character abilities, solve some light puzzles, and fight some more.  Along the way you will also fight things. After that, you'll wander through a few zones fulfilling quests while fighting things. It will be a rare 60 seconds of wandering that doesn't have an encounter... and by that I mean more fighting.
You play a party of four adventurer-wanna-bes with a loser reputation. Each character is already pre-classed, and the balance is good: A fighter, a rogue, a sorcerer, and a priest. As you level up, you can customize them in any way possible, making the rogue a magic user, for instance, but the party you're given will save you some time and calculating. Many events in the game trigger entertaining dialog among the characters. It's the kind of tabletop style banter that is snarky, while still providing exposition, and makes you feel like you know the inside jokes they're tossing around. I never laughed out loud, but I smiled a lot and I liked the characters. I think the programmers had fun with this.
There are about 4 or 5 major zones in the game, one of them being a town.  Each zone has a couple of "dungeons".  Some quick, many are optional, but there's a lot of variation. The dungeons usually aren't starkly linear either, which is refreshing. The town is really boring, though. It's Elder Scrolls Morrowind boring. I wish it had all the same characters and one-third the size, with no superfluous buildings. I'm sure it was built for immersion, but you don't run very fast in this game so it became tiresome.
Combat fatigue is the main mechanic in the game. It controls everything. As you adventure about, you will experience random encounters, ambushes, and monsters walking about. Combat is turn-based, and each action your characters take uses up endurance. At any time you can rest to recover endurance, but you never fully rest up. The more that you cycle through your endurance meter, the more fatigued your character gets, until finally, the character cannot recover any more endurance by resting until he/she sleeps at an inn. The trick of the game is maximizing your character abilities and balancing combat choices to be endurance efficient so you can stay away from town longer. Rather than cast the giant overkill of a maximized sorcerer fireball, you can cast the efficient but slow-killing disease over time while your fighters whiddle down the baddies.
The combat system throws you a few bones though. One of them is a novel game mechanic called drama stars. Your stars fill as you win battles and stuff, then you can redeem them any time for stat buffs, resurrections, healing, or my favorite, a full endurance meter top-off. These are a neat perk, keep you adventuring longer, and they're meant to be used as you get 'em.  If you load a savegame, you lose the stars. If you continue a game after quit (not the same as loading), then your stars stay intact.  It's an incentive to not reload save games every time something bad happens. An RPG first!
Combat takes time and deliberate thoughtfulness. You will never get so strong that you have a one-shot "I-Win" button. Even very powerful AE spells never really take out a whole group.  It's pretty much the essence of the game, and it's not meant to be a cakewalk. It can be hard.
There are an ample amount of potions and consumables that you can loot and buy. USE THESE. Use them all day long and do not hoard them! They let you win more battles with minimal endurance spend.
Your inventory is unlimited and this is handy. You just don't have to worry about returning to town to sell things or playing inventory tetris to make room for things. The merchants never refresh their sellables anyway, and most equipment upgrades will come from loot, treasure, and quests. Your money will be used for potions mostly.
A lot of time and energy was spent building a trap and lock mini-game. Well, it's not really a minigame, but there are endless ways to disarm traps and unlock chests. Do you want to disarm the trigger? or neutralize the trap payload? or perhaps some mechanics in the middle?  It's cool that so much thought went into such a small part of the game, and it is far better than some of the lockpicking dexterity checks I remember from Elder Scrolls games.
The spell system is probably also overkill. I felt throughout the first 5 or 6 levels that I only had small percentage of useful spells. Then suddenly after a few more levels I had too many spells to choose from, and boosters for my oldest ones so they never became obsolete. There are just a lot of spells. I played the whole game and never cast all the spells that I had. I enjoyed the spell effects for what they were, and the witty descriptions, but it became tiresome to search through spell books all the time.  A better spell interface may have helped here. There are spell casting hotkeys, but only for 3 spells. As the game needs a keyboard and mouse anyway, three hotkeys was too few. Ten would have been better.
As you level up, the game opens up in terms of character class customization. Just as with the spells and disarm options, there are a LOT of feats, skills, and abilities.  Maybe too many feats. It doesn't matter.  Pick fun things to do with your characters and do those things.  I spent a little time microgaming and trying to optimize it, then I just said screw it and picked stuff that looked fun. I'm glad I did. Maybe all the options add to replayability, or to the RPG factor, but there's just no way you'll even get most the skills and feats available on any one character. Definitely get the feat that allows you to detect random encounters. If combat gets too repetitive, that feat will possibly save your interest in the game.
The graphic user interface itself is clunky and needs polish, but it is manageable. There are buttons in weird places, and it takes too many clicks to get to spells or inventory. It's also heavily dependent on keyboard/mouse. Luckily, the most common combat functions have keyboard hotkeys. A suggestion for next time would be tiny interface buttons for each character that you can drop in consumables or spells, a la Diablo.
So try the game out. Get past the graphics and the UI, and enjoy the billions of combat options.
A final note, there's humor in this game at every turn. It's subtle, it's smart, it's the kind of humor I would use with my own gamer friends. You're supposed to have a good time with this.
Thanks for reading.

I will update this review as the development progresses. - In its current state I would not recommend it because it is practically unplayable with the glitches and server instabilities but keep checking in since the game has huge potential.
Update: (12/28/2014)
Here are my gripes:
-The Pteradon grab is way too easy now making them ridiculously more threatening than they should be.
-The fact that a T-Rex can spawn with less than 10 players makes it nearly impossible for humans to survive, there aren't enough people to provide the damage output required to take them down.
-There is currently no auto-balancing (at least not that I noticed) and we had teams of 7 humans vs 14 dinos
-My friends and I tried 4 different servers of various pings (and even hosting our own) and the rubber banding was ridiculous to the point where sniping is impossible and the trapper might as well put the net gun away. Normally I would assume this is the local machine's issue or my own network, however three different friends from three different IP addresses using three differently powered machines all had outlandish server instabilities making the game more frustrating to play than fun.
-Raptors no longer use stamina to jump allowing them to spam their jump constantly making them impossible to hit.
-I'm not sure if I just don't have the item or not, but the removal of melee attacks from the humans makes close combat impossible for the humans.
However, these are new features of the game that I enjoy and why I want to keep checking in during the development of the game:
-The loadout system is nice and allows for different classes to be tweaked for an individual need
-The sub-classes of dinosaurs are a nice touch and allows balance for the dino team vs the human team's loadouts
-The addition of a side arm adds utility for some of the classes that didn't have one (like the commando)
-The ability to get unlockables from playing grants replay value and a goal to keep playing, it is also fun to actually unlock something as you play that you can use in the game.

Out There Somewhere is not a great Steam game, but would be right at home on a Flash website.
The opening feels like a student's first Multimedia Fusion game after following a tutorial on how to make a space shooter.  Staticky sound effects, zero enemy variety, unnatural parallax scrolling, no interesting visual effects... It's pretty amateurish and gave me a poor first impression.
As the game progressed, I was pleased that it has some originality, and it's reasonably satisfying to jump around and teleport from place to place.  In the game's cleverer moments, it does a good job introducing new mechanics and ideas.
It was over in less than an hour.  I was expecting the game to go on for quite a bit longer, considering it hadn't expanded upon the teleport-gun mechanic all that much, and I was still seeing the same three enemies.  I never spent a full five minutes in any one room, and I know that because several of the Steam achievements I didn't get reward being slow.  I'm sure there were some areas that I missed out on, but I don't care to go back to them, because it would mean going back through the unchallenging samey puzzles I already solved.
I couldn't tell you what the plot of the game was, or how any of the music goes from memory, because none of it particularly stood out.  What I do remember is how irritating it was that the gun fired shots so slowly, and how enemies seemed to take more hits than necessary.  I remember discovering all the doors are needlessly one-way when I tried to check an earlier room and couldn't do it.  And I remember how closing a textbox had an awkward delayed reaction because I kept immediately reopening NPC dialog on accident.
The way I see it, Out There Somewhere feels more like a prototype than a finished game.  There's very little diversity, no thought required, not enough polish, and even the visuals feel flat and artificial.  It's not bad, per se, but it's not great, and not something I'd recommend to my friends if they had to pay money for it.

Stellaris has had a long and sometimes difficult history, but it has come quite a ways from where it was when it launched. The game systems all feel like they are starting to gel with each other a bit better with every revision, and the current version of the game (as of Synthetic Dawn DLC) has managed to flesh out and address many (but not all) of the oustanding issues with the game.
The patch due for Spring 2018 sounds like it should take a swing at fixing some of those remaining problems with war and diplomacy, which are the last two major sore spots that I encounter when playing Stellaris. The AI is a bit too predictable with how it approaches war at the moment, and the current game of doom fleet "whack a mole" is a blemish on an otherwise interesting game.
There is a lot of potential left still untapped in Stellaris, and anyone that is on the fence can easily wait until after the next major expansion to see how things have developed. I get the feeling that another year of development is going to leave Stellaris is a very good state. It's fun as it is, but it definitely slows down towards the mid to late game (both in terms of actual game speed and things for the player to do). I have faith that Paradox can find good solutions to those problems given time, however.

The graphics aren't great, but to be honest it didn't take long to get used to. Considering the game has a cyberspace theme, you wouldn't really expect top quality graphics (or at least I wouldn't, anyways...) So they certainly stood out enough to be easy on the eyes for the duration of the gameplay. I haven't tried Multiplayer so I don't actually know what the player model looks like, so in my ignorance i'll assume it has the same minimalistic appeal.
The audio for this game, I didn't really notice it. That isn't a bad thing - I knew when something happened, but it was more of a confirmation than actual sfx. It added to the feel of calm under pressure, and aided the relaxing puzzles through what could have been frustrating experiences if it wasn't for one problem...
...It was too easy. I finished the game (all data fragments) and all the bonus mission in 92 minutes. It was enjoyable, so I would recommend at a low price, but it certainly wasn't something that I had to struggle to understand the solutions. It took a few attempts to actually do some of the solutions, granted. Some of that was because of a slight issue with physics/momentum that I wasn't expecting. If you are on a moving platform, you will continue to move in that direction as you jump off it. This means that instead of jumping towards what you are looking for you have to account for a slight air drift. Which, again, wasn't difficult to understand, just wasn't as expected initially.
I don't know if this game was supposed to be for a younger audience, or if I am better at this game than others. Personally I felt like the bonus missions should have been part of the main missions, but if the game was meant to be a little easier I can understand why the difficulty would be at a mismatch in that situation. There were 22 levels (including bonus levels) for Singleplayer mode, and I assume 15 for multiplayer - given there are 3 fragments per level and 45 set to CoOp mode. All the same, I was sort of expecting more challenging puzzles, but I didn't dislike the experience up to the end goal.
I doubt this game would get a great deal of re-runs. The base price is not worth the content in my opinion. That being said, I got this game around 90% off (maybe more) and I certainly think this game would be worth it at a discounted value. I have seen this game on sale many, many times. So long as it is half price or better, I would say go for it. As it stands, however, my view is that the game should be around four times longer, with much more challenging rooms in order to justify the retail value asked. Or maybe include a level editor and allow workshop support, but that is likely above the developer's skill level judging by the content provided. Again, not a bad thing, as I in no way disliked the levels that I played, I just don't think that there is
content provided...

This is, in my opinion, the best gamepad available right now. It's not quite as good as a mouse and keyboard, but it's close-and it definitely beats out regular controllers in terms of precision, comfort, and versatility.
As compared to an Xbox One controller...
Pros:
-Heavily configurable and versatile.
-Far more precise.
-More comfortable (At least to me...)
-Better build quality (From what I can tell...)
Cons:
-Steep learning curve.
-A lot more work required to configure it (For now...)
And to address a few concerns I've been reading a lot...
-The build quality is very good. People have been saying that it's light and flimsy and shoddily built, but I have no idea where that's coming from. The only thing I've noticed is that the seem appears sharper than normal, but it hasn't bothered me.
-It is quite comfortable. I've heard quite a lot of people saying that it's so uncomfortable that they have to stop using after an hour, but I've played with it for more than 5 hours at a time with no problem. If it's uncomfortable for you, I'm pretty sure you're holding it wrong.
-It's very precise. Nearly every review out there says that it isn't quite as good as a regular controller for FPS games, which is weird, because my experience is exactly the opposite. I'm fairly certain that those conclusions are due to the fact that most people are used to regular controllers. As someone who was only used to a mouse and keyboard, I found the steam controller far superior for FPS and TPS games
-It's true that there's an occasional software glitch, but those are very quickly being weeded out. This controller is a very different product for Valve and a radically different concept for controllers, so you should expect bugs in the software- And you should also expect them to be actively repaired.
That being said, this is still pretty early. There are a lot of features that it doesn't have that I (and a lot of other people) would like to see soon, like multiple mode shifts, more expansive control over haptics, more options for the motion controls, access to the on-screen keyboard while in desktop, and even a rechargeable battery (Though there are two contacts under the back cover...)
So, overall, it's a great controller as it is with a lot of promises for future improvement. I'd pick it over any other controller (M/K excluded) any day.

I wanted to believe in this controller. My first instinct just from looking at it was, "This isn't gonna work for me." But I stowed those knee-jerk reactions and gave it a shot. Using it since I got it about a week ago, it's most disappointing. As usual, I'll start with the good things I can say about it.
Its shape is actually fairly good. Rests in the hand nicely. The concavity of the grip sorta molds to the palm of your thumbs--assuming you don't have really large hands. Fingers hook around nicely so you have a tight and secure grip on it. This's where the compliments stop.
While my index fingers are not so much an issue, nor are my middle and ring fingers, it's my thumbs that this positioning starts to fall apart. I have to re-position my thumbs downward at a wider angle in order to reach the action buttons and/or the analog stick. This is a reach for me because of the way my hands rest holding the controller. I don't think this is an appropriate design, as the action buttons are what I will use at all times, not the right track pad.
The left trackpad is an okay placement, since I would utilize it the most, if it weren't an absolutely abhorrent circle D-pad. It's worse than the 360 circle D-pad. When moving my thumb quickly,
My thumb instinctively goes for an elevated positioning on a button; but that's actually a down-left or a down-right spot on the D-pad, which will result in me moving completely the wrong way.
I might hear you asking, "Why use the D-pad when you have a perfectly good analog stick?!" My answer is because an analog stick is not the best choice for
. Most of my library consists of precision platformers, where making careful movements in either the left or right direction is paramount to my playing successfully. This is hindered the use of circular movement controls such as analog sticks or circle D-pads.
The other issue I have with the D-Pad is it's a lot like the trigger buttons in that you can apply pressure to it before it actually clicks. This is kind of not something best suited for "you hold right to go right," instead of "tilt right and go almost right".
It's not to say the controller is all bad. For a 3D environment, I can see how this sort of movement would be better. Games like Devil May Cry, or Deadpool, or Dynasty Warriors, or Starfox, modern Legend of Zeldas, maybe some adventure games or more free-roaming combat, I can see this controller working quite well--given the analog stick and action buttons switch spots with the trackpads.
Ultimately, this controller
like it was designed by committee, each aspect of it split to different teams, all going by a statistics sheet of what kind of games are most played and how to emulate what players will use when playing them. This controller was designed to compete with the attraction to mouse/keyboard. But what the designers may not have realized is that every game has a best suited control scheme. Shooters where you're moving your field of view very quickly with the need for precise clicks, mouse/keyboard are the best way to go for the most control. For a third-person fighter/shooter/adventurer, where you rely on movement and access to a variety of actions at once, a controller analog stick is better. And for sidescrolling shooters/platformers, where your total control over your movement is crucial, while not needing too many actions at your command, a controller with a solid D-pad is the best choice.
The Steam Controller tried to be the best to market and I feel that was its mistake in design. It went for popularity rather than solid functionality. It wanted to be an entertainment system control. As such, I can't really recommend this as a video game controller at a price of $50. This is all excluding the fact that as soon as I plugged it in it needed a firmware update which tells me that it was rushed.
After testing it with Deadpool, I've learned that the action buttons are not always mapped to what the game has configured. If games don't allow you to remap buttons, which is the case for many occasions, you could be pressing the D-pad in place of the action buttons. Until this is interface is addressed, I absolutely can't recommend this controller.

Graffiti comes in all shapes, sizes, and variances in quality. For every breathtaking mural there's a dozen cheap tags ranging from the generic to profane. Similarly, Sideway: New York jumps violently between an abundantly stylish and creative platformer, to a cheap, controller hurling annoying one. Unfortunately, the imbalance often shifts toward the later, and even then the good parts only serve to highlight how frustrating the rest of the game is, which no amount of personality can save.
By now you've hopefully gathered that Sideway is based around graffiti, placing you running and jumping along cluttered walls, shifting from different panes and using parts of the environment to create a makeshift path toward the end. It's a really neat idea that's pulled off with a good deal of success, even when it's more often used for style than a core gameplay mechanic.
This is fine at first when everything is new and bursting with creativity, but Sideway falls on its face about halfway through by being at least twice as long as its content can sustain (which isn't saying much when it clocks in at just around 3 hours). Level designs start to repeat, backgrounds become less interesting as the originality wears off, and the 3-4 track soundtrack just keeps cycling through over and over (it will be going around in my head for days to come I'm sure). It also back loads most of its boss fights, which are easily among the most infuriating and poorly designed of any game I've played all year. Compared to the rest of the game, they create huge roadblocks that I wouldn't be surprised caused many players to simply give up on the game (which might honestly be for the best, as at that point the challenge is only going to keep rising).
Later levels also begin to focus heavily on combat, which is clunky, boring, and by far the worst element of the game. It's hugely perplexing why the developer chose to put so much effort into this one portion of the experience, but it's clear they spent a good deal of time on it and all that's come from it is a lesser game than we might otherwise have seen.
For the first hour or so I was really digging everything about Sideway. Its style is great, the premise original, and the entire package bursting with personality. But the further I got the more it seemed to try and put me off the entire game, spoiling the experience that came before and causing me to rather despise the game by the end. I hope the developer gets a chance to make another game and learns from the mistakes made here, but I won't be disappointed if we never end up seeing a Sideway 2.

Most of the negative reviews I read were along the lines of "same as 2K17" - I haven't played a wrestling game regularly since WWF No Mercy, so I thought I would enjoy this.
Unfortunately, I was wrong.
First, the loading times are UNBEARABLE. There is literally a 10-second loading screen after nearly every single thing you do. Want to change your MyPlayer moves? Loading screen. Changed your mind and want to go back MyPlayer Menu? Loading screen. Want to go all the way back to the main menu? Loading screen. IT CAN TAKE YOU AS LONG AS 2 MINUTES TO GET BACK TO THE MAIN MENU WITH ALL THESE. Do not take this lightly - it very seriously ruins your experience.
Now, it would be one thing to have all those loading screens to get to gameplay, but once you're in the MyPlayer gameplay, there are SO MANY MORE. Seriously, the pacing in this game is atrocious. It's not just the loading - the entire experience itself is so unnecessarily bogged down by design choices.
The career mode goes like this: you play the game day by day. You get control of your character backstage, and you get to walk around. Sounds cool, BUT YOUR CHARACTER RUNS THROUGH MOLASSES. There is short hallway that serves as the main area to walk around in - in real life, it would probably take you 5-7 seconds to walk down this hall. I timed my character RUNNING down this hall, and it took 27 SECONDS.
There are characters to talk to, but instead of a dialog box popping up when talking to them, they decided to include this stupid cutscene of your character approaching, then a shot of the character talking to you, then a cutscene of you walking away from the character. WHY?! The character could say something insignificant like, "You can't pass this way," but if you sit through all those cutscenes, it takes almost 15 SECONDS. Why in the hell did anyone think that was a good idea?!
Okay, so say you skip talking to all those characters and just go where they tell you. 20 seconds to run down the hall. 15 seconds to talk to the guy that tells you what to do. 20 second loading screen so you can watch a cutscene of RAW pyros going off (which is 20 more seconds, but you can skip it). A LONGER 30 second loading screen so they can actually load your match. When you finish your match, it's another 20 second loading screen to get backstage. From there, your ONLY OBJECTIVE is to run to the garage to end the day by talking to a guy (20 seconds to run to the guy and 15 more seconds to talk to him).
Oh, and god forbid your task for the day is to do a run-in on someone's entrance, or someone runs in on yours. There is no match that follows that - it ends as soon as someone lands their signature move. WHY DOES NO MATCH FOLLOW?!
Promos as well - such a stupid mechanic with terrible writing. You are basically playing a quiz game for your day, only so you can run back to the stupid garage after. (More loading! YAY.)
So say you are tired of career mode. Let's play with friends! Oh wait - you wanna use the character you spent so much time on in career mode? Nope - sorry, you can't use them outside of career mode. No export, no nothing. All that time you spent fine tuning your character's look and face; choosing all those moves one by one; lovingly creating your entrance and pyros? Yeah, do that all over again from scratch if you wanna play against your friends.
There as so many more examples of poor design. From navigating the menus, to playing the actual game - it is such an un-fun experience. I even tried getting a refund on this after 5 hours of play (half of that was sitting through loading screens), but it was rejected due to being over 2 hours of play. Now I'm forcing myself to play it so I don't feel like I wasted my money (it's not working).
TL;DR - any fun in the game is SEVERELY overshadowed by terrible pacing issues due to loading screens and game mechanics.
UPDATE 1: There are HUNDREDS of customization options (clothing, moves, etc) for your character. 95% of them (!) are locked in MyPlayer, which requires you to purchase loot boxes for in game currency. The highest-tier lootbox costs 10,000 credits. Problem is, you earn 200-500 credits per match IF you drag the match out to get a high rating. It would take you at least 20 matches to get 1 high-tier lootbox. That lootbox contains MAYBE 3 unlockables, and some junk cards (temp match boosts). If you wanted to unlock everything for your character, you would have to play hundreds and hundreds of matches!! What does that mean? HOURS AND HOURS OF LOADING SCREENS. So I cheated. Got a trainer to give me unlimited credits. I sat at the lootbox screen, purchasing about 100 lootboxes hoping to get the 5 or so clothing options I wanted to use. I GOT NONE OF THEM. God forbid I actually played through the game to get those credits. Even with cheats, I lack the patience to sit there and purchase loot box after loot box to maybe get the one item I want. I cannot express how bad this is.
