I've been playing a lot more than it says I have on Steam, but I recently downloaded it again from Steam because I'm weird like that and I like all my games to be in Steam if possible.
Anyways, this is a real gem in an ocean of crap F2P games.
Good:
--------------------------
Awesome story that makes sense and is easy to follow
Beautiful world, amazing attention to detail and a real joy to just look around
The things you can buy from the store can also be earned (usually in several different ways) from in-game things as well or you can easily and *safely* earn free Aeria Points by installing and playing apps on your phone or watching a minute long video.
Translation is spot on.  I haven't seen any issues and usually with games like this half the quest text makes 0 sense.
As you progress you have several ways of changing and making yourself better.  From talent trees to mastering skills to adding gems, enchants and fortifying armor and weapons.
Great sense of humor.
A lot of classes to choose from which are not sex locked.
Lots of different looks without even mentioning costumes and dyes and all of that, I'm just talking about character creation.
Every day you log back in you are greeted with a free present and your Eidolon as well.
Eidolons.  These are exceptionally well done "battle pets" (bascially) with stories and personalities all of their own.  They don't just level, you help them to level and to better themselves as you progress as well.  Not only are there several to choose from or earn but they all have their own way of speaking, seeing the world and battling.  Some are healers, others plain warriors and so on.  They can be evolved at certain levels with the right items, given items to up their stats permanently, you have conversations with them on a regular basis and they give you great gifts which can help both of you a lot in the long run.  This is by far, one of the most impressive battle pets systems I have ever seen in any game, and it's free to play!
Auto-route.  I have no idea why, some people see this as a bad thing but I don't understand that at all.  You can open the map up, find a specific NPC and just run to them without having to worry.  I don't see a problem with this and with all of the other types of games I have played, I just see it as it's own game mechanic.  You don't have an "auto kill everything" feature so it isn't game breaking in the least.  If you don't like it, just don't use it.  I see this as only a plus and will not name this as a con for any reason.
The way they did quests is not only pretty clever, it's also very fun.  When you approach an NPC and click on them to start a quest a small box will take over your screen.  You can then watch the interaction between your character and the NPC as they engage in quest conversation.  It's really cute, allows you to cut off the rest of the MMO world for a moment to get into what you are doing and also lets you see the amount of emotions displayed in a really fun way.  I really like it.
I've played four different classes, all of which had spells and attacks that were very different from one another.  Battle Bow looks nothing like another class, which some of these F2P MMOs do and it is very boring.  The attacks and spells in this game are vibrant, fun, fast-paced and well thought out.  You cannot just mash buttons either, which I really appreciate.  You have a global cooldown on all abilities.  Speaking of abilities, you can do a combo with your Eidolon.  It is unique to each one and does a ton of damage.  Even the healer types have one they can do with you.  Very fun, awesome to watch.
Auto-potions.  I love this feature as well and will not say this is a con either, for any reason.  You don't like it don't use it.  I don't care, I think this is awesome.  What this does is allow you to place whatever type of potions you have in your bags in the Auto-potion slot.  You can then click it "On" and choose a percentage of health in which to have it switch to.  I have mine at 30% and it has seriously helped.  This allows you to focus on the action (you'd just be clicking it anyways, don't waste the global cooldown) while staying somewhat safe.  This does not gaurantee that you will stay alive.  This is not a 100% proof plan against death.  You can still die.  Don't kid yourself.  Some of the daily instances are just mean.  But this feature is just really awesome and I've never seen it before in any MMO.  That I remember.
Lots and lots to do.  You have cooking done in a unique fashion, bring items you find randomly around the world to special cooks in the towns and they can help you fuse up something amazing.  Sometimes it's green, sometimes it's orange and you will get an achievement and exp for doing so.  Sometimes it's purple and helps specifically with PvP!  There are thousands of hidden quests and achievements in every area of the game.  From finding green question marked items and finishing the tasks lined up with them, to gathering loyalty points that you can also use in the item mall for lots of really cool items without spending a single penny.  Or chase down the 4-6 unique monsters in each area and turn in their pots to the city/village jailer for extra goodies and more achievements/titles.
Everything on the UI can be moved anywhere you want it.
The UI itself is great looking and you can even shrink or enlarge all of the elements.
Lots of different ways of doing quests.  I have noticed some people saying it's the same as many other MMOs and there is a lot of grinding.  I don't think this is true at all.  Yes, you kill enemies and you collect items but there is a LOT more than just that going on.  Sometimes you are dodging the eyes of the bad guys trying to get through a dungeon or winning over the baddy in order to help you later on.  Planting bombs, fishing, sneaking through very dangerous areas.  There's more than just the normal amount of "kill this" and "collect that".  Plus, it actually makes 100% sense as to WHY you are doing it.  it isn't just "my farm is in danger kill 5000 beetles".  You are killing those things and collecting those items in order to help finish a much bigger picture which I think is really cool.  The kill quests and collection items aren't over done either.  At most I have been asked to kill 10 things at one time.  Not a big deal to me at all.
Auto join a guild, get benefits and never be bothered.  Or bother them and start a conversation.  It's literally up to you.  I love this feature, I wish every game had something like this.
----------------------
Bad:
Not a lot of character slots available, only three without paying.
Bots.  They aren't a huge deal and literally only sit in one place of each zone that I have noticed, but it's really annoying.  They are always the guys with the big cannon looking things, I can't remember the name of the class.  They all look the exactg same and have ridiculous names.  Just annoying.
Sometimes it is a little too easy.  You feel like you are just sweeping through everything.  This could be a good thing to some, I don't see it that way though so am only naming it as a con.  I would like there to be much more challenge.  The daily instances offer something more, but only rarely and for the most part they aren't too hard either.
Bag space.  They will give you bags and stuff from time to time and all but really there isn't much at all.  Especially your bank.  It is TINY and I really hate that.  You have a shared bank which is awesome but it is just too small.
Cooking things requires far too much money.  I don't spend my money on much else really.  I get items from dungeons and such and don't want to spend it on AH crap or personal sellers.  But fusing together some cooked chicken costs much too much.
You share Eidolons with your account.  This can be good and bad.

You choose a hero and go out and battle monsters by creating words out of a box of letters. The highlighted letters help form an attack. Lets say you create a word and two letters are highlighted in red then the hero that represents red does a level 2 attack. You will find treasure chests and in order to open them you must spell a word with the box giving starting from the left most letter box to the right most letter. If you fall in battle you are allowed an attempt to revive. To revive at full you must get the word that uses all the letters, and to revive at half you must be one letter short. Any words shorter result in that characters dying but damaging the oponent. The goal of each area is to reach the entrance to the next area while beefing up your character(s).
The game is quite a bit of fun and makes for a great brain game.
You will run into quite a few words that the system doesn't accept even though they are words or names. The graphics aren't bad, but they aren't fantastic either.
I personally love the whole concept that Words for Evil has. I hope to see more words and possibly item strategy in the future. P.S. I loved the seasonal santa hero.

Frayed Knights is a dungeon crawler in the vein of certain old school games like Might and Magic. You control a group of 4  adventurers in search of fame and fortune.
The combat is turn-based, allowing you to take your time with each move. Movement is accomplished through the keyboard, while you can also mouse-look and click on items to open or read descriptions. The majority of gameplay consists of combat and exploring dungeons, searching to solve puzzles and find loot.
The graphics in this game are also as old school as the games it harkens back to. While it may work for those games, since they are a product of their times, certainly a newer game can update the graphics. There is no voice work, which might be a plus because by looking at the graphics I feel it may have been sub par. No voice work is better than terrible voice work all the time.
The party banter may be a big selling point of the game, since it differentiates it from other games of the genre, but I found myself not particularly enjoying it. It just wasn't my type of humor. If it works for you, then this game will become infinitely more enjoyable for you. For me, I found the humor a little bland, and the gameplay a little tired.
I would not recommend Frayed Knights. I feel there are better dungeon crawlers to play at this time. It just feels a little too old school, missing some things you'd like to see in more modern games. The humor fell flat for me, which is what is supposed to set this game apart in the genre.
Grade: C-

A surprisingly deep dungeon-crawler, a-la Wizardry, with humorous writing and tons of quests. It's a bit dated, but if you're someone who likes old-school gameplay with a more modern spin, then you'll enjoy this game. Grab it when it's on sale.

Overall a good tactical party-based RPG. Funny without being corny. It not only takes itself lightly, it mocks some of the common tropes of the genre.
Graphics are mediocre, dialogue is hilarious and riveting, and quests are often surprising.
Combat is not simply about killing the enemy, it is also about resource management. The more spells or attacks you use, the more tired your characters become.
Characters start with defined roles (thief, fighter, priest, sorcerer), but with open customization you can make them whatever you want.
If you want a good RPG but aren't afraid of a little sillyness, give Frayed Knights a shot.

Let me start off by saying that this game isn't terrible. During dungeons, its graphics can pass for "dated," and it /does/ have many of the qualities that I've come to love about the CRPG genre. However, it has downsides. Granted some of these are personal dislikes and may not be the case for everyone. In fact, if you -disagree- with this review, that's cool. I think I'm going to go ahead and be the bad guy if that means pointing out the flaws in this game that so many people are intentionally blind to. If you want the cliffnotes version of this review: take the positive reviews of this game with a grain of salt, and maybe go play something else.
So... first off, I felt I had a few miscommunications going into this game. The game claims character customization, and for some reason I was thinking that meant character creation. Not so: you play the game with the same party of four characters. To be fair, there's dialogue and banter and character development with these four characters, maybe even a bit with the npcs in the game. Even so, I consider this one one of the game's downsides. Why? Well, my all-time favorite games in the CRPG genre allow for actual character creation where you can pick race, class, and skillsets. To me, that makes each of the characters feel more relevant to -me-. I've seen games pull it off without char creation (Aarklash Legacy did that very well), but I really just kind of failed to care about the main characters in Frayed Knights. If you don't have that issue, good for you.
The graphics were probably the real deal-breaker for me. I try to be open-minded with graphics, considering some of my favorite CRPGs have dated graphics. That being said, Frayed Knights was simply unplayable at times. The models, textures, and animations of monsters weren't great, with some standing out as being particularly yuck. My real sticking point here is the towns, though. You are free to walk around in towns the same as a dungeon, yet that makes my next point glaringly obvious for players who make it this far: there really was a bare minimum of effort put into the towns. The house layouts are uninspiring, sure. But the real problem is the character models. Out of the few that don't have really terrible anatomy, they probably aren't even animated. It's honestly an embarassment of a town.
So, yes. There are a lot of things this game did. There might even be a few things this game did well. I -don't- think it poured life back into the CRPG genre, I -don't- think it's what CRPG fans have been waiting for, and I hate to say it but I don't think it's worth the ten dollars you could be spending on a better CRPG. Putting zany character sprites with goofy dialogue and fantasy names like "♥♥♥♥h daon" are really kind of misplaced effort--no matter how much you polish a clod, it's still a clod. In essence, this is an unfinished game that really can't stand up to the legacy of its genre. You could probably put the ten dollars needed for this game toward something good like Aarklash Legacy or Wizardry 8.

This is a game by Jay Barnson, aka The Rampant Coyote, who does a great blog on CRPG game development. Essentially what you're getting here is a fun, humorous CRPG. The combat system is fairly complex, so you'll find much to enjoy if you like stats. You won't mistake this for Skyrim, but the graphics are pleasant enough and evoke a Might and Magic 6 vibe for me (one of my favorite CRPGs). Movement is first-person and combat is turn-based. Considering that all of this is the work of Jay and a few friends, it's really amazing what he's accomplished.

The steam controller. Sure it looks like an owl and their are a ton of reviews on YouTube that call it the next thing to impossible, but when you take at least a good week to get get to know it it's not actually the worst thing there is. First let me say that this isn't your average controller like a Xbox or a ps4 controller, the steam controller has some depth to it. And by depth I mean there is a lot to learn and know when having the controller, but that doesn't  mean it it's bad to do. When you first start using it might feel weird holding it with the handle facing up and not down and actually it's avoid thing to have since when it's place like that you can get your handle properly placed on it and it doesn't  give you much of a issue when playing games. The track pads are also very good with the ability to customize every inch of the pads to the way it functions and how it basically works. If you want the pads to work like a joystick you can do that, as a directional pad, why not? And it's not just the customization of the trackpads, it's the customization of the whole controller it self. They made sure that if you don't like a certain aspect of the functionality of the controller, your not limited to it.
But the real question stands: could you replace a mouse and key board with this controller? Well yes and no. You see even though the controller has very well configuration to it that doesn't  mean it's completely change everything a key board has. I recently played a fps game to test out the precision of the controller and I was pretty on balance with it, I actually got someone with it! But that doesn't  mean it was easy, with the controller I want able to aim as well with it then I would have with a mouse but it overall wasn't a major difference with it. And with a casual game that doesn't  require on time precision worked perfectly with the controller. And I feel that over time I use it more the better I get which I think is the same as everyone. And I feel that way because this controller is a some what border line between a regular controller and a mouse and key board and I feel that yes you can get the same feeling on the steam controller, but it's going to get time to get used too. I feel that any one who gets this controller and give the controller a good three weeks it would turn out great and you can totally get used to it and use it in a lot more than a key board. So in general:
Pros:
1. Has very good customization feature
2.the design of it is very well made and fit for the controllers needs, also it isn't as light and cheap as they say
3. It's a thing that can totally take over a regular controller
4. It's fit for every type of gamer and can use the controller for mouse heavy games (e.x Adventure Capitalist)
5.The virtual key board is amazing and very well made to use
Cons:
1.The buttons might be a little off place but it is not hard to get used too
2. There are some minor bugs but that can be fixed soon
3.This controller does require you to get to know it or in other words out some time to get used to it if you want to use it to it's full potential
Overall: 9/10
Reason: There is some things to get a custom and there are some bugs over time it will be very fun to use.  Also the buttons are a little small but it's not bad
Overall: If you have read this far then please, give it a try and you always have 30 days to try it out and trust me, you won't be disappointed with it because it's not like what those you tubers say. And if you don't like it well you can always return it within those 30 days but just remember: all it takes is time, trust me.

I just returned my Steam Controller after only a week of using it.  I really wanted to like this product.  I had high hopes for it, I have been patiently waiting to buy one for a year now and went out on release day just to pick one up.  I tried it on five different games and I just couldn't find one that I thought was the least bit playable using it (Spec Ops: The Line, Duke Nukem 3-D, Goat Simulator, Star Wars: Starfighter, & Spintires).  The positioning of the buttons was a bit awkward and I didn't care for the angle the thumbs had to work with (it actually made my carpal tunnel flare up a bit).  I also didn't care for the flapper controls on the back, they forced me to hold the controller with an uncomfortably delicate touch.
My previous complaints however are mere nitpicking compared the problems I had using the right touch pad for anything at all.  It just isn't usable, at it's best it is no where as usable as a mouse or even another analog stick for that matter.  This controller makes first person shooters unplayable.  The other genres I played weren't so bad but in the end of the day I would say that the controller had an overall detrimental effect on my gameplay experience.  The less a game needed the right touch pad the more I enjoyed using the controller, but $50 is a lot of money to spend on a controller I just barely want to use on any games at all.
I will say that the integration with the Steam big picture mode was neat, and I thought that the near endless amount a customization in the controller's settings was incredible, but all that can't save this accessory from painfully needing a second analog stick.
Overall this experience has been a big let down for me.

Galvanic Games is a Seattle-based full service creative studio that specializes in design, development, and services for games. The team led by C.J. Kimberlin have already developed two other games in Rust Belt and Moderne Artiste. Gurgamoth is the team’s debut title on Steam. It’s a local multiplayer fighter that has recently undergone a greatly appreciated update that has seen the introduction of bots into the game. This has given the game an enormous boost in playability because, obviously, those who wouldn’t have been able to enjoy the game previously are now in a position where they can play.
Before I begin to praise the bot game – the one mode that I’ve been able to play to this date – I want to pinpoint a negative. The game, for whatever reason, gave me the ability to control multiple players in each game. Given that the starting point for each round can position the characters at either side of the screen and there are deadly traps on the sides of the screen the game almost demands that you will kill off one of the characters before you begin. The only time that you score a point is if you win the round and only one character can win the game. Therefore I would have much preferred the standard ability of controlling just a single character and playing against three AI controlled players. I’m not sure whether this was the intention of the devs or not when they introduced this mode for single players but it was more than a little frustrating.
With that said I can see how this would be a wonderful game for those who have the ability to play the game in a multiplayer environment. The game has the potential to have a great competitive scene and local competitions would be an enormous amount of fun. Unfortunately that isn’t me at this current time but when we have my partner’s best friend’s family up during school holidays it will be a game that I load up for a bit of fun. There’s been a few games such as The Hauntsters and Dwarven Brawl Bros that we have already featured and that I will be endeavoring to play with them but I believe that Gurgamoth has the potential to be at the head of the list.
What I enjoyed most about Gurgamoth is the presentation. I quite enjoyed the design choices in the color palette and the sound. The game controls very well and with the fast pace of the game and the traps deaths feel very fair but also exciting and challenging. It’s a very clever mix. There are a number of different effects that can kill you, the player can use the environments to their advantage and everything seems to be in keeping with the pace of the game.
A minor disappointment is that the only differences in the characters that I can notice at this stage are cosmetic. It may have been nice to implement different strengths and weaknesses to the characters but I admit that given the environment of the game that may have altered the competitive balance of the game and players may have felt that they were at a distinct advantage/disadvantage if forced to choose one character over another.
Gurgamoth is half price for another couple of days. Therefore you will not find a better opportunity to purchase the game at a better price for some time.

I received a copy of this game through Keymailer and was excited to try it because I enjoy combative local-multiplayer games. I was very satisfied with my gameplay experience. Be advised: this game works optimally when played with a controller.
If you enjoy arena-based local-multiplayer games, killing your friends, and fast-paced gameplay, then you will enjoy Gurgamoth.
The aesthetics are good - the amount of detail in the environment, characters, and different special effects is very high. There are a number of different characters you can play as, however, this offers only a cosmetic change. The music and sound assets are appropriate for the quick playstyle of the game.
Controls are very simple and easy to learn, however, I must again stress the importance of using a controller when playing; you can use the keyboard and mouse, but Gurgamoth is optimized for gamepad use. You can also play with up to three people using the keyboard and mouse, but it can be quite clutter-some to set things up this way. There is a pop up tutorial of the controls whenever you begin a match, but the different stage hazards/items (appear in the form of asteroids) are not explained anywhere, and must be learned the hard (and fun) way. The learning curve is mostly minimal, but mastering gameplay can take some time. The most challenging part of Gurgamoth will probably be perfecting your timing - a well-executed dodge+boost combo can end with your opponent's death (or yours).
Gameplay consists of you trying to kill your opponents by boosting into them, usually pushing them into some type of environmental hazard that varies depending on stage. For example, one stage has spikes along the edges of the map, but a covering layer must first be hit before the hazard is active (you can do this by boosting into it yourself, or by pushing an enemy). Other hazards include electricity towers that periodically turn on and laser-spitting meteors. The first player to 3 rounds won takes the cake. You begin the game with 3 boosts - there is a cooldown that will slowly recover - and the game handles balancing very well because if you are losing by a lot (ex: 0-2), it will give you 4 boosts and handicap the person winning to 2 boosts.
Other asteroids will offer you temporary bonuses - like infinite boosts, a one-hit shield, slowing down time, and warping the stage perspective (ex: shrinking the map). These, along with the different hazard set up of each stage, help add a lot to the game's replayability.
Overall, the game plays really well for an arena-based local multiplayer game, so long as you have enough controllers handy. If you enjoy fast-paced gameplay, then you should definitely give this title a try.

Yes. The PC port sucks. Yes. It's still the best Saints Row, and one of the best Sandbox games I've ever played. I was never really into SR3 and 4. They just seemed too out there to me. I played those two first, and didn't really have a good enough impression to bother with the second. But when I saw all three of them in a bundle for 10 bucks on Steam, I figured I'd give it another try. I started with the second game this time, just to see what it was like... and it blew me away. The game was running slightly fast, and all the vehicles in the game had lubed tires, but that's half of what made this game so fun for me. Once you get used to it, it makes driving in other sandbox games boring.
The narrative is lightyears better than 3 and 4 as well. It's not spoiled by the stupid wackiness of the third and fourth games (I get twelve year olds might giggle at a giant purple♥♥♥♥♥♥♥for a few minutes, but it really makes it hard to take the  game seriously at all), and overall, I enjoyed every last minute of it.
I also don't really mind the whole respect/story system. You have to earn respect by killing other gang members or, the much quicker method, competing in the various activities throughout the city. Now, if this feature wasn't implemented, I'll tell you right now that I wouldn't have bothered with almost any of it. A sandbox game shouldn't completely seperate the story from the activities. After I got familiar with the game's activities, I really began to have fun doing them and raking in a bunch of respect. My favorites were the fight club and the derby
Overall, I really enjoyed this game. It allowed me to play out the fantasy of being an over-the-top gang lord without being too silly, and it did it really damn well. I would reccomend this game to any fan of sandbox games who don't really find the silliness of the third and fourth games appealing. It isn't super realistic like most games today. It isn't super wacky or goofy. It's fun... pure, grade A fun. (And I am loving Gotr so far. It just makes the second playthrough all that more worth it)

The overall presentation and aesthetic is quite pleasing to the eyes, as well as to the gamer in general. The ideas behind Sideway New York are unique and fresh, even for a platforming action game. The artwork is distinctive, cartoony, and with an air of playfulness also. The level design is what sets the game aside from others of the same genre. It is a combination of two-dimensional and three-dimensional spaces with a novel way of going about the buildings and other structures. The game screen often flips and changes angles as you progress through each level, and you must find ways to jump, skip, slide, and pounce around the environment. All of these actions are not very fast paced, but they coincide with the game adequately, and in an enjoyable manner. The storyline is short and casual, not going very far away from the usual beat the bad guys who kidnapped my girlfriend fare, but this does not get in the way of game play gratification, as you will be mostly busy platforming and appreciating the levels and environments. As you advance through the game world, you will unlock special abilities that are both fun to use and applicable within the game world. They range from special attacks, to special jumps, and even gliding through the air. There is also the option of collecting tags in the levels, but this does not reflect any changes in the storyline or game play whatsoever. It is a mere collection mechanic for your own accomplishment and bragging rights. The ability of playing with a partner in local co-op is available, but I have not personally tried this. The soundtrack seems to have only about three or four songs that loop endlessly, which makes for quite the repetitive listening experience. On the other hand, it is done entirely by renowned underground hip hop artist from Boston, Mr. Lif. This means that depending on what your musical tastes are, you will be either pleased, neutral, or annoyed. Either way, the music may be turned off or kept on. There seems to be a serious bug with the options menu, as sometimes, it will not allow you to exit it and get back to the game. The only way to fix this major problem is to end the game in Task Manager; which also means you will lose all progress if you were mid-level. There are several instances during certain levels, which involve mechanics unique to Sideway New York that are slightly unintuitive, and the game does not do a very good job of explaining clearly how to go about accomplishing certain actions. This means there will be much trial and error before you are able to figure out how to approach some situations. The last two boss battles can be a bit frustrating, as they require several precision based actions, until you are finally successful. For a short and casual cartoony game, Sideway New York gets most what it is trying to accomplish right, and for what it is, it is quite enjoyable.

Sideway New York is a basic platformer with a hip-hop theme. Its gimmick is that you're a piece of living graffiti painted onto a building, which is visually cool but only occasionally affects gameplay. One way it's used is that the direction of gravity on the surface of a roof is decided by the direction the player entered the roof. This property could have been used to create some clever puzzles or mazes, but it never was.
The player starts the game with limited movement abilities, which makes the first few levels boring. Judging from the Steam achievements, about 40% of players got bored and quit between the first level and the first boss. Things pick up later on as the game introduces some standard abilities like double-jump, gliding, and swinging from grapple points, which allowed the designers to create more interesting and challenging platforming.
A hip-hop soundtrack is provided by Mr. Lif, courtesy of Skullcandy. (Skullcandy branding is all over this game, making it feel like an advergame.) The few tracks included quickly got repetitive, leading me to turn it off entirely in favor of my own collection.
Much of Sideway feels off. Hitboxes seem to extend beyond their sprites. Jumping from a swing isn't based on momentum, instead giving a fixed vertical boost. Combat is simple button-mashing, and the game would be improved by its removal.
Sideway is a short game, and I doubt the promised sequel will ever exist. So while it's not fun, at least there's not much of it.

If you can get past the UI and occasional lack of polish you'll find one of my favorite RPGs in a long time. While the storytelling is lighthearted and fun, the core game is deep and challenging. The combat is heavy into resource management and tactics often revolve around limiting the energy you spend while still overcoming the threats. The drama star system does a great job of helping you turn things around even when crap is hitting the fan and is far more satisfying than the average Save scum victories old-school RPGs are known for. I bought the game from the dev's site when it first came out in 2011. I played through the entire game in one marathon session, which took me 20ish hours. If you like old school dungeon crawlers, you will love this game. You have a premade party, which seems like it was done to make the story work, but it's pretty open to how you develop each character's abilities. The game is very tongue-in-cheek, and the characters sometimes break the 4th wall. The dungeons are very well designed and many contain secrets, hidden areas, and puzzles(The Tower of Almost Certain Death is the best IMHO).  The game is balanced around attrition, so if you never use consumbables or make poor decisions you will be going back to town to rest or reloading a lot. Most of the mainstream reviewers complained about this, but I didn't really have a problem with it. Judicious use of "liquid nap" potions and drama stars will keep you from going back to town constantly. It's obvious that the designer has a deep love and understanding about what makes old school RPGs work, which many devs who try to make new games with older styles don't understand. The only thing I have bad to say about it is that the UI isn't great. It's not horrible, I never had any problems figuring out how to do what I needed to do, but it could have definitely been more streamlined. Still, that is a minor quibble for what was overall a great experience. I'm looking forward to FK2.

I wanted to play as friendly butterfly people.
I spawned on the border of a Xenephopic Fallen Empire. They immediately demanded the destruction of my Homeworld. I, of course, refused. The Fallen Empire immediately invaded, destroying my fleet and executing my leader as part of their terms of surrender.
Sometime later, the Fallen Empire has decided to invade every 10 years like clockwork. Every invasion I caved to the Fallen Empire's demands of humiliation. This has kept my people unhappy and inefficient at most everything. Just to survive, I have Invaded everyone around me and expanded my empire to encompass somewhere between 1/4 and 1/3 of the galaxy through sheer numbers, superior firepower and swarm tactics at the cost of every other technological avenue.
I am the least technologically advanced empire in the galaxy at this point.
With the ascension of Queen Buttercup II, the Fallen Empire decided that enough was enough and tried to cleanse the majority of my core worlds. I tried once more to cave to humilliation, but they wouldn't have it. I had to make a stand.
The majority of my industry was located far from the Fallen empire, so I set them to build a massive fleet, while my current fleet invaded the Fallen Empire's Territory to take out their mining bases. I reverse engineered weapons and ship tech from these stations and added them to my own designs. I was slowly building a fleet to rival the Fallen Empire's stupidly powerful one.
During this time, I was kiting the Fallen Empire's fleet around my core systems by taking back every planet they conquered with only a few assault armies. (The Fallen Empire didnt bother to leave an occupying force). That way, I slowed their progress against me considerably. Once my fleet was great enough to contend with the Fallen Empire's I sent them into battle over my Homeworld.
My fleet was entirely wiped out.
But I did destroy one or two of their ships, which spooked them into giving me a white peace. I took this time to study more of the empire's technology and devise an even greater fleet. And once the time came for our next battle, I was ready.
I took my newly formed fleet deep into enemy territory and tore apart their infrastructure - Spaceports in particular. This weakened their fleet greatly, so when our fleets met, mine won (albeit barely). The Fallen Empire tried to sue for peace, but I wasnt having any of it. I was taking this all the way.
The war was long and bloody, with swarm tactics beig my only real advantage as they tried to rebuild their fleet. But with their main fleet gone, I was building faster than they could destroy. They eventually capitulated to me and I claimed all their territory and colonies.
As punishment for their actions against me, I culled their population as they had wished to do to me. I was finally free and quickly became the most powerful empire in the galaxy. With the humiliation modifiers gone, my science soon surpassed every other empire (excluding Fallen Empires) and my military might was by far the strongest. And with the Fallen Empire populations nearly gone, I could move my own species in to work their powerful buildings. Now finally, I could go make friends with the rest of the galaxy.
That was when I checked my diplomacy menu and saw everyone hated my guts. Who knew genociding your eternal enemy would be frowned upon?
Oh well, I guess they're next then.

TLDR: This is an impressive piece of hardware, yet Big Picture hampers the end user experience.
I am very impressed with the capabilities of this hardware. The unique design was tough to get used to at first, but it grew on me, and became natural. The trackpads are my favorite feature, they are surprisingly responsive, up there with laptop trackpads, and to my pleasant surprise, they act most like the trackballs of the past, just digitally.
The build quality felt solid, not exceptional. If I had one gripe, it's the A-X buttons. Their placement so close to the lip of the controller can become uncomfortable if a game uses X and A to jump and interact. The raised area has a unbeveled lip, which is hard to see in the screenshots.
The best feature of the Steam Controller is how easy it is to configure on the fly, but this (as far as I know) is impossible outside of Big Picture mode. Steam will remember the last bindings you used if you minimize Big Picture, but to edit your configurations, you must enter Big Picture once again.
I would not recommend this hardware in the state it is now, not due to the Steam Controller itself, because of Big Picture's lack of functionality. To use the full functionality of the Steam Controller properly, one must be in Big Picture mode.
Steam Big Picture is the albatross around the Steam Controller's neck. Big Picture needs some serious improvements before making this device replace a mouse and keyboard for Steam as an application.
One example of Big Picture's shortcomings compared to the desktop Steam is when you want to make a group call. As far as I know, in Big Picture you can only call with one person at a time. This is one of many features which Big Picure lacks. When you have to walk back to your computer and alt tab frequently to get things done, you realize that your experience with the product is being hampered by the software it runs on.
Over time, Big Picture will improve its functionality to approach that of the regular Steam application. Until then, I cannot recommend this product.

Skyrim is probably my least favorite Elder Scrolls game. You might ask yourself, then, why I have given the game a positive review and recommended it to anybody else. In my mind, I don't like Skyrim much, but it is actually a good game. It doesn't appeal to me because of the modern streamlining of gameplay and the lack of statistical character creation. Thus, I shall be playing Arena if I ever feel like exploring Tamriel. Yet, the game has a lot going for it, especially in the eyes of a modern gamer.
The game has good graphics and this is a relief considering that the face design for characters in Oblvion was absolutely atrocious (this is avoided in the older games by allowing only for the selection of a head sprite (and hair, in Morrowind).
The game has an open world. This is especially appealing to an RPG player, but is pretty standard of most large games these days. It is a relatively large open world, for a game today, but is vastly smaller than any seen in TES: Arena, and especially TES: Daggerfall. You can explore all over it, walking among the beautiful environments as the trees wave around you or the snow lashes across your vision. There are also a good collection of towns and cities to explore. However, the detail needed to craft Skyrim's open world makes it relatively small and walking across it feels fast and breaks immersion (compared to say, daggerfall, where fast travel is essential to getting around the MASSIVE map, where even the tiniest little hamlets are at least two times the size of Whiterun!)
The game features freedom of choice for your character. Dialogue includes full sentences you can pick to react to information that you are given, though it (Character Dialogue. The NPCs are fully voiced, and done so well) is not voiced, as it is in Fallout 4. Yet, you cannot choose from a list of pretty random things from the world to ask about, and there is no way to record what an NPC says to you directly. You can choose to join any number of guilds specialized to the Skyrim environment and the lore of the 4th Era. You can buy houses or even plots of land (if you have hearthfire, which the special edition comes with), adopt a child, get married, and anything a lot more. The game presents a lot of freedom. One thing that bothers me about at least the College of Winterhold (I haven't joned any other guilds. Probably should) is that instead of just being an actual college where I can learn magic like Harry Potter, I have to do some irritating quest line that completely takes away from the experience and makes me feel like the world revolves around me. I don't know if every guild has a specialized quest based around it, but it definately can be irritating to be so special all the time.
Let's talk about the combat now. The game has a pretty simplistic combat system based on the damagfe of a weapon and one's skill with it. However, skill doesn't reflect how often you are going to hit, like it did in the first three Elder Scrolls games. Each hit within reach of an enemy will hit them and do a certain amount of damage. Power attacks (accomplished by holding down the attack button for a second or two and then releasing) do more damage but decrease your stamina (which reghenerates pretty quickly). Overall, combat is pretty unsatisfying, especially due to the fact that enemies show no real sign of taking damage until they become staggered. The combat in the earlier elder scrolls games, Arena-Morrowind, is satisfying in that you feel good every time you manage to land a hit on the opponent. It is especially satisfying in Arena and Daggerfall when you get to control the direction of a weapon swing with the mouse. Overall, the combat is lacking in style (and is not engaging) and only serves as a way to kill your enemies.
A couple side notes about the combat system: brawling can be really fun sometimes, especially when you manage to do it in a pub. However, I only think certain enemies can engage you in a real brawl, and they are over too fast. The ranged and magical combat are a bit different, however, Arrows and such will stick out of your enemies, and the fast paced spell casting system makes combat with them fun and chaotic.
Spells: you can equip spells in both hands and they can be cast relatively easily, justby clicking the mouse button asigned to the hand the spell is in. Magic itself can be engaging and deep, especially when it comes to advancing your character with magical perks and high Magicka. Crafting potions and enchanting magical items is also a fun side activity, and is really something a magical character could aspire to get better at, training each day with progressively more success, going into the dankest dungeons to collect the most interesting ingredients. However, spellcasting isn't as independant or engaging. While you can buy fancy perks that increase your skill as a wizard in certain schools of magick, the spells are not as interesting as some that have come in orevious games. In Morrowind, a starting Altmer Mage would have a managery of interesting spells to begin with, such as Water Walking and Detect Creature, spells that don't directly affect combat or buff or debuff your character, but make magic interesting and versatile. Spells like this just aren't available, especially to a starting mage, in Skyrim. Also, there is no way to fix this lack of interesting spells: no SpellMaker is present in the game (though it is in Arena and Daggerfall).
I won't go into the strory to much, as to not spouil it, but it is pretty good and features some interesting locales and difficult boss fights (though the environments are far more detailed than those in Arena, it isn't as refreshing to find an exciting location, mostly because wherever you go is going to be really interesting). The story really immerse you in the lore of Skyrim and is set with a backdrop of civil war. Each dungeon's interior is ineteresting and has a reason for being built that way. Was it made by the Nords in ages past, or perhaps it was constructed by the now-extinct Dwemer? The game features some really beatiful natural environments, especially in the more mountainous West.
Overall, this game is pretty good. I enjoyed playing it, but have come to dislike it in favor of the older, more complex Elder Scrolls games. that's just how I am. Yet, this game is a really good starting point for players of the Elder Scrolls and there is sooooo much more I could say about it that is good. So, overall, I would recommend this to anybody looking for a good computer roleplaying game that has good graphics and is enjoyable for a modern ganer. Looking for a more statistic based game, or perhaps a RPG with a little bit more deapth when it comes to creating a character: I recommend anything like Morrowind or Daggerfall (Arena is so far my favorite, though to play Arena and Daggerfall you need to get a hold of the manuals). Want an experience like this but with modern gaming conventions? Play Oblivion, it has a superb storyline!
All in all, TES: Skyrim is a success as a RPG, and I recommend at least trying it out. It is likely to be worth your time.

Minecraft: Story Mode isn't at all what I expected...  Yes, the story is alright, but that's about it.
This is a very kid-friendly title, which is to be expected. There really isn't too much available in this game for adult players, other than the story itself. In several places I found myself staring at the screen going, "That doesn't happen in Minecraft", or simply rolling my eyes at the symplicity of puzzles.  Adults will actually screw themself up expecting puzzles to be harder than they were, your brain just won't be able to initially wrap itself around the symplicity of them.
As a kid-friendly title you'll also find yourself actually doing very little in the way of "playing" the game. Most of the time when you actually get to do something it's very linear. For example, exploring an outside area that uses invisible walls to keep you from leaving the area. So you hold "W" to walk through the area, and wait for the next part of the story to kick in. Either that or it'll give you a couple things to click on so it feels that you're actually doing something. It was the same with "crafting". Your character would walk up to the crafting table and to "toss you a bone" you got to place the items on the table to craft a bow, or arrows, or sword.  The only items in your "inventory" were the items you specifically needed for that specific recipe, so if you've played any minecraft at all you didn't even need the recipe guide.
Parts of the game where you were more actively involved were parts of the game where you actually wished you could just sit back and watch the action.  In a "god of war" style, every action sequence required you to mash several keys (usually Q, E, or a direction) in order to complete the action sequence.  For example, an enemy would go to swing a sword at you and the "E" key would pop on the screen.  If you pressed it quick enough you would defend yourself from the attack, if you delayed too long or pressed a wrong key you would get hit and possibly die.
You were so busy looking at which button to press you'd actually miss the entire action sequence!  Not only that, a lot of the button presses came after long pauses of not having to press anything, so you were usually very unprepared to fire out a rapid sequence of key presses and would usually fail the first one or two that popped up.  In addition there were sequences where you were required to quickly maneuver your mouse over a box that appeared on screen and click it.  This was made difficult as the mouse cursor responded very poorly to input during these sequences.  You almost had to perform a rapid-fire mouse clicking fest in order to click your target before your "time" to do so ran out.
So yes, this is definately a "story" first and a "game" as a distant second.  That's actually one of my biggest gripes; the fact that the game is less of a game and more of a story. There is very little activity for you to do aside from choosing dialogue (which really doesn't effect the main story) and pressing the keys that pop up on screen. In actuality they probably could have completely removed any user interaction, making this just a video, and you'd still end up with the same gaming experience.
The worst, however.  The absolute worst?  That would be fact that origional purchasers of the "Season Pass" have been completely screwed.  A "Season Pass" is supposed to include all of the content for the adventure.  Apparently Telltale didn't get that memo.  At the end of the "Season Pass", which is Episode 5, we're left completely hanging.  --Spoiler Alert--  Our heroes take a portal they assume will lead them home, and they end up in a hallway full of portals.  Will they ever end up getting home?  Apparently we have to toss Telltale another $16.99 to find out, because our "Season Pass" doesn't actually give us any closure of ANY kind.  It doesn't take us to the end of an adventure.  It simply leaves us hanging.  It's absolutely ridiculous.
To use an example, say you purchased the Lord of the Rings trillogy.  You watch all three movies but at the end of the third movie, right before Frodo and Sam walk into the enterance of the volcano, it pops up on the screen.  A little box that says, "Please insert your credit card info, a fee of $16.99 will be charged".  I'd think you would be a little angry, and you'd have every right to be.  You paid for a full adventure and it's trying to get you to pay more just to finish that adventure!  I totally agree that buying the LoTR trillogy shouldn't entitle you to get A Hobbit's Tale for free, but you should at least get the entirity of the adventure you friggin paid for!
Save your money folks.  If you're that interested in this game simply go to YouTube and watch a "Let's Play" series on it.  It'll be the same experience as if you're acually playing, except you won't have to press any buttons.  That's how I'm going to experience episodes 6-8.  Telltale can shove their DLC model where the sun don't shine.  They're not getting another dime from me.

Stellaris is the first attempt by Paradox to create a space themed 4x game. And I have to admit, they've hit upon a suprisingly fun formula. Short version: it's a work in progress, but one that's extremely engaging and worth your time.
This is a space opera game, meaning it's not hard science fiction. There's faster-than-light travel, psionics, and spaceborne creatures. That said, there's tons of room to play the type of SF story you want. You form an alien race (or play one of the presets), then guide their expansion through the stars how you prefer. You can play peaceful isolationists, xenophobic purgers, cooperative federation builders, corporate enslavers, hive-minded ravagers, or AI gestalt robots. Each combination you choose has its strengths and weaknesses, altering how your game will play out.
The economy in game is relatively simple: mineral deposits are your currency for building new things, energy credits cover your upkeep, while Influence an d Unity dictate how quickly you can expand to new star systems & alter the path of your civilization's evolution. Expansions add the ability to uplift your entire species to machine bodies, psionic beings or conquer genetics to custom build your populace. Other expansions add the ability to start as AI gestalt robots, conquering or absorbing other species to improve yourselves. Or build massive megastructures like ringworlds or Dyson spheres.
Ultimately, you'll bump into your galactic neighbors. Depending on each of your civilization ethics, you may trade & negotiate or go to war. A few AI civilizations are Fallen Empires, massively powerful civs that have stagnated and isolated themselves from the galaxy. They're too powerful to confront early in the game, but later may Awaken and begin forcing other empires to bend to their whim... unless you become powerful enough to stop them.
Or, a Crisis may occur. Invasion by a powerful enemy can threaten the entire galaxy, and you must face them down. Sometimes Fallen Empires will assist you, or they may just sit back and watch the galaxy burn. The Crisis may be a devouring swarm, eating everything it can; psionic invaders from another dimension; or an awakened AI that attempts to purge all life.
The game does have its flaws. The economy takes a while to learn, and is the key to actually prospering. Your first few games will be spent learning how to build up quickly without bankrupting yourself, or falling behind so that you can't win. Plus, combat isn't fully balanced, with the ideal technique currently being to build a "doomstack" of ships and simply steamroll any opposing force you encounter.
Paradox is aware of these flaws and constantly working to improve the game. An upcoming patch is going to completely change how FTL, borders and combat works, so the game is in a state of flux. However, this itself can be fun as it means every 6 months or so, you get a fresh system to play with and learn its tricks.
Overall, I do recommend Stellaris. It's tricky to learn and constantly being updated, but it's a fun way to play out your galaxy-conquering dreams.

I really want to give this a negative review. Really bad. It's plagued with bugs. It took me 20 minutes to even get the game to launch. Tried to change some graphical settings so I can get a decent framerate on my potato PC (surprisingly I get 60fps on low settings whereas usually in modern games I get around 20-40) and it crashed. It crashed in the middle of downloading a custom map. It crashed in the middle of a match for no reason. It's crashed maybe 6 or 7 times in the 3ish hours I've played.
But I'll be damned if it isn't a fun game. It feels like RO/Rising Storm. It feels lie Vietnam. It feels fresh, not like a simple reskin of the old games. And god damn the shotguns are fun to use. In a lot of FPS games, shotguns become useless at say 5 meters. In this game, you can get a kill at 50 meters with a shotgun. It may take 2 shots, but it doesn't become useless the second you can no longer spit on your opponent. And that makes them really fun to use, unlike in a lot of other "realistic" games. They're good up close, and at medium range, and honestly I want to recommend this game based on how fun the shotguns are alone, but they aren't the only fun guns to use.
The Americans get a handheld grenade launcher. And ho ho ho boy is that thing cool. Zeroing it for distance is easy and very useful. In my second game I got 5 kills with 1 HE grenade from that thing. Plus you can load it with 40mm buckshot and turn it into a shotgun. And you already know how much I love the shotguns in this game.
So...should you buy this game? Well, ask yourself a couple of questions first, starting with "am I willing to deal with fairly regular crashes that get in the way of an otherwise great shooter?" and "do I like the kind of FPS where a single bullet can kill me?" and if the answer is yes to both of those questions, absolutely buy it, especially if you enjoyed Red Orchestra 2 and Rising Storm. At least just for the shotguns.

I have been using the controller for a bit over a week now and so far I'd have to say that it has it's fair share of flaws.  The controller is a great idea and is a good piece of hardware, however, the abundance of errors, glitches and problems lead me to not recommend this controller to anyone.
First, it has Tons of setting making it very highly customizable, which is great for the wide variety of games it can be used for, although at the same time it has a lot of trouble remembering them all and constantly resets it's own settings, needing to be reconfigured again.  Turning the thing On is always a roll of the dice as well, as 1 out of 4 times it turns on only to forget what it's even supposed to be doing and half of it's control mappings are randomized, needing a reboot for the controller.  Hopefully this will be fixed in a software patch at a later date.
On a side note, the controller also can not be configured to be anything other than Player One in any multiplayer game.  I suppose this is because half of it is emulating a keyboard and mouse but it is still a bit annoying when trying to get 4 people to game together.  Not a very big issue but it's still there.
Lastly is a bit of a nitpick but I feel that the joystick and face buttons are too far to the center of the controller.  They should have been placed a bit closer to the outside as the shape of the handles makes reaching for them feel a bit awkward compaired to other controllers.
Overall, the concept is in the right place, the trackpads work well (with a lot of practice), and the wide variety of customization is very welcome.  Though the problems listed above as well as several otehr that I haven't mentioned make me feel that this hardware is not ready and needs a bit more work.  Hopefully these problems will be ironed out in the future but for now I cannot recommend this untill then.

The steam controller makes "Mouse and Keyboard" games playable with a gamepad.  In that regards it’s a success.  Unfortunately the dual track pads are poor in comparison for games that are already optimized for dual stick controllers.  And while the M&K games are now playable with this controller from your couch, it’s a pain in the butt to set up the controller for each game. There are tons of options to configure each game, which I guess is nice if you want to spend hours setting things up, but i really wanted to be able to plug and play.  Considering this thing has been in development for years Steam should have hired people to make templates for each M&K game, or at least the 100 or so most popular, out of the box.  You can choose from other gamer’s profiles and share your own, over time this may help make the M&K games more plug and play.
Physically the controller is fairly well made, the track pads track position well once you set them correctly for each game.  The X,Y,A,B buttons are small compared to a X360 controller and don't feel as responsive.  I do really like the paddles underneath, it feels intuitive and is easy to hold down while you move your thumb on the track pad.
Bottom line, if you want to be able to play M&K games on the couch this controller allows you to do that, albeit not intuitively and requires a lot of setup work out of the box.  For games that are already gamepad enabled don't bother.  So the only people I can recommend this hardware too are those that want to play M&K games but can't/won't use a M&K,  for everyone else it’s not worth it.  Even for the anti M&K crowd $50 seems a lot to pay for a mediocre device with limited out of the box support.

My current SE game is like a version of The Long Dark with camping and survival mod, and very dark nights settings.  The long walk up High Hrothgar is a whole new experience when you treat the weather like something that can kill you.  Even with over 950+ hours in the original, I am still occassionally surprised by new dungeons or quests I never found before.
For Skyrim: The Long Dark Edition, I recommend the following mods:
Campfire
Frostfall
Wet and Cold
Hunterborn
Climates of Tamriel (Weather Mod, choose darker night and darker dungeon options)
Random Alternate Start
With Random Alternate Start, you won't begin with the Helgen scene.  You'll be thrown somewhere randomly in Skyrim.  With Frostfall, you'll be exposed to the elements and will need to find food, shelter, weapons and clothing.  Hunterborn provides a number of enhancements to skinning animals for food and clothing.
This is the Skyrim base game as it should have been.  The 64bit driver allows bigger, bolder player enhancements.  If you're someone that is really serious about pushing your graphics to photo realistic gameplay, this is the canvas on which to draw.
However, if you're someone who has never played Skyrim, or have an older video card pre DX11, you might be better off with the original version.  The player created content library from the original is a treasure.  Many of the most popular mods have been converted to the SE version, however, that is mostly due to ports from very dedicated players.  Many of the original content creators are no longer supporting or interested in investing the time for SE.  Some others are, but it will take time.
As for me, just like the original, I spend more time adding mods and tweaking the settings then I do playing the actual game.

Purchased on launch day and have played for about 50 hours (so far -- I'm not going to be putting it down any time soon).
-------------------------------
TL/DR -
If you enjoyed 2k17: Buy it. You'll probably like it (the exception being if you loved 2k17 Career Mode, because if you did, you'll hate this year's implementation),
If you're new to 2K's wrestling games: Wait for a sale. Or try it and return it. Or buy 2k16 (which is probably pretty cheap). 2K's WWE games have always been quirky, and this year is no exception. They're definitely not for everyone.
If you didn't like 2k17: Skip this year too. Really, really. I have a strong suspicion that things that they made better are not the things that cheesed you off about last year's game.
------------------------------------------
I agree with most of the reviews (both positive and negative) here. Ultimately, it's an improvement on 2k16 and a BIG improvement on 2k17, so it gets a soft recommendation from me. If you've enjoyed 2k's WWE offerings up until now, there's enough new here that you won't be disappointed. If you've been frustrated by them in the past, the things that frustrated you likely have not changed.
Pros -
UNIVERSE MODE - I'm primarily a Universe Mode player and this year's Universe Mode is a big step up from 16 and 17. The game no longer randomly scrambles your carefully orchestrated episodes. Also, rivalries got a big overhaul, with each show tracking up to four "pre-rivalries" which helps me feel immersed in the head booker role, which is what Universe Mode is all about. Not only that, but they've tweaked the balance on rivalries so that they no longer produce week after week of matches between the two rivals. You get a lot more of what you want to see, run-ins, pre and post match ambushes, etc.
SQUASH MATCHES - This is something that I've been wanting for a while. With a little luck, and an overpowered superstar, you can trigger a squash match where you get unlimited finishers and reversals against an overmatched opponent. It synergizes well with the power ranking mechanic in Universe Mode.
IN RING GRAPHICS - I'll talk about graphical flubs in a moment, but the in-ring action in this game, and the wrestler models are really well done. There are a few weird face scans of various superstars, but on the whole, the entire roster looks way better than they did in 2k17, so much so that I don't mind the rendered models on the match cards this year, which was a change that bugged me quite a bit in 2k17.
PERFORMANCE - While still not great, overall it's a big step up from 2k17. Without upgrading my rig, 2k18 performs way better than 2k17 did for me.
Cons -
CAREER MODE - While I give them credit for trying something different, Career Mode is so poorly implemented, between really poor writing and glitchy gameplay, that it was very hard for me to get into. Also, the early stages of the Career Mode are super linear (almost on rails) and see you progress from performance center recruit to NXT Champion in about 3 matches. 2k16 still sets the bar on Career Mode for me. While there are some good ideas here, 2K definitely missed on the execution.
COMMENTARY - When I hear that Corey Graves and Byron Saxton were being added to the commentary team for this edition, I was excited. Then I heard the commentary. My god, its bad. It's so bad. It's super repetitive, very obvious that Cole, Corey and Saxton were not in the same room when they recorded, and super generic (hell, when Randy Orton hits an RKO, Graves calls it a "cutter"). JoJo is a welcome addition. Her recorded introductions sound a lot more natural than Lilian's did.
NON-WRESTLER/RING GRAPHICS - As awesome as the wrestlers look, the audience and other non-wrestlers still look like they're from a PS2 game. This is a particularly acute problem in Career Mode where you get up close to some of the ugliest character models that I've seen in a very long time. There's no excuse for how bad some of the character models that you interact with look.
BUGS - Yeah, they're still here. There are fewer of them than in 2k17 (at least as far as I've noticed so far), but they still exist.
WTFs -
MATCH RATINGS - Maybe this is just me (or maybe its a bug), but it is a LOT harder to get higher than a 3.5 star match this year. Curious if anyone else is seeing the same thing.
COMMENTARY - Yeah, OK, I have to mention it again. It's just SOOOOOOO BAD.

Edit:  I'm changing my opinion of this gadget to a thumbs up. It still has all the flaws I griped about in my original review (see below), but I have found myself reaching for my Steam Roller more than my other controllers over the past week. While it continues to inhabit this awkward space in between a standard game controller and a mouse+keyboard, it is cleverly engineered for what it is, and the triggers, touch pad, and gyro controls impress me more the more that I use them. It's also fun to tinker with -- I have entertained myself over the past week messing with settings and trying different things out.
It's still not great for playing games that require precisely timed gamepad input. But I was impressed by how nice it felt to play some digital CCGs with it, or pop open a web browser and do a bit of surfing. I might change my review back to a thumbs down after a few more weeks of playing with it. But as of right now, I am not regretting my purchase. ymmv
Original review:
----------------------
I was really looking forward to this controller. But after a couple of days worth of tinkering and trying different games with different settings, I'm coming to the conclusion that it just doesn't work for me.
The controller is amazing for gyroscope aiming. You can basically take one of the best features of Splatoon and port it into any PC shooter.
Less amazing is how much force it takes to click or press any of the physical buttons. The left touchpad is *almost* an amazing dpad. But if you set it to register touch taps as button presses, you get too many unintended taps or double taps registered. And if you require a physical click, you need so much force that all of your inputs are delayed slightly, making it frustrating to use with games that require precision timing, like Crypt of the Necrodancer or a fighting game. The same goes for using the right track pad as emulated buttons: you either get unintended inputs, or slow inputs.
Of course, that very last point is why the controller comes with physical ABXY buttons. Unfortunately, the buttons are small, stiff, and placed in an awkward location on the controller, leading to almost as many unintended or delayed inputs as using the touch pads.
The right and left bumpers are similarly stiff, and the paddles require so much force to activate that they throw off my aiming when I'm using gyro aiming, negating one of the best features of the controller :-/
In short, the controller just doesn't reliably transfer my intentions to actions on a screen, and it doesn't feel like more practice or better settings will remedy the issue: the buttons will be stiff and unresponsive no matter what.
It might be that I just don't play the right mix of games for this controller: your experience might be much better if you primarily play mouse based games, and don't mind mashing buttons a bit. As for me, sadly, I think that I am going to set this controller aside.

After having about a week of time with this controller, I can honestly say that I like it alot. It has replaced the XBOX and PS4 controllers for me. It has not replaced the K+M BUT it is a fantastic alternative when playing from my couch or bed on my steamlink.
My hands are of average to slightly above average size for a man and the controller fits perfectly. The touch pads are very responsive and feel really good once your muscles get accustomed to this foreign apparatus. I actually hold the controller differently now due to the slope of the hand grips, with both my fingers on the bumper and trigger instead of just one.
Having said this, anyone  with especially large hands might feel this controller is too small.
I have used the mouse and keyboard emulation on CIV5, Devilian and Torchlight with surprisingly positive results. However, heavy customization is required or a premade setup from the wonderful steam community. The trackball like haptic pad is quite accurate and using the joystick as a camera navigator is actually more fun than a mouse and keyboard. Also, unlike others who dislike the back panel buttons, I use these for right and left mouse click instead of the more cumbersome triggers.
The two negatives that come to mind are the the bumpers do have to be pressed a little harder than other controllers and that the customization while a godsend to the hardcore can be very overwhelming to the average person who just wants to play. Again the steam community has and will continue to alleviate this.

At first I found using the controller a strange experience as it is so differant to anything I have used before.  Coming from a background of prominent keyboard and mouse gameplay with occaisional xbox one controller usage this was definately something new.
Having spent a week now with the new hardware I can definately say that I am a believer.
Something that was alien soon turned into second nature, nearly being able to match my kill efforts on battlefield 4 set with keyboard and mouse (game added as non steam shortcut)
Alot of profiles are available already for 99% of my library of 100+ games with only some minor tweaking required for my personal control tastes.  However any non steam game will require you to make your own profile ( which is a piece of cake).
Another thing I would like to state is that all of the reviews online saying that the controller  feels cheap and awkward are totally untrue and likely to be biast from people who are either console noobs or die hard pc gamers afraid of change.
It is true that the controller can never replace my razer and rat9 but it comes damn close.  Trying to go back to my xboxone for some Halo felt alien and uncomfortable.  The right analogue stick felt like swinging a sledgehammer compared to the refined accuracy of the haptic pad.  Also I must state that the xbox pad actually feels less substantial than the steam controller.  I cant comment on PS4 as I have never used one.
So in summary:
Build quality is great
Ergonomics are great
User profiles are great (may require tweaking)
Non steam compatability is great (although you need to make your own profile)
Customisation of controller is the best I have seen
Against:
It would be nice to see more developer profiles and true integration into games.  However the hardware is only a week old so this will likely come with time.
All I can say is dont be afraid of new technology.  Change is needed to prevent stagnation.  Remember the world before steam was bundled with counter strike.
The haptic pads are a nice compromise between traditional gamepads and keyboard/mouse.

Whilst I can't play on CS:GO to my full extent with a mouse this controller is much better than a regular twin analogue stick controller for other games and has worked perfectly whilst i have been playing Fallout 4, would reccomended.
Also high customisation of all buttons and features makes the Xbox One Pro Controller even more of a ludicrous rip off.

This is a great controller, but it doesn't completely replace a 360 controller.
Pros
- Highly programmable
- More accurate than a joystick
- A good controller alternative to KB&M
- More buttons than a 360 controller
Cons
- Can only be configured in Big Picture mode
- Small buttons(A, B, X, Y)
- No rumble
- No D-pad
I feel the pros heavily outweigh the cons and I will probably be using this controller to play most of my games. I haven't found a Steam game I can't use this controller with yet. I think this controller would have been better off with an actual D-pad instead of the left track pad. I can't imagine what I'd need two track pads for.

It's an interesting controller design. The ergonomic form is nice once you get used to it. The way the batteries fit make it better than a wireless Xbox 360 controller. I always used wired Xbox 360 controllers with Steam because there is no battery block underneath to interfere with the comfort of your grip.
I have yet to be convinced that the Xbox One controller has a better ergonomic form than the Xbox 360 controller. I am not convinced it would be worth the extra cost or the effort to switch from X360 wired to XBOne wireless.

But I am pleased with the feel of the Steam controller. The haptic touch pad is intesting to use. I feel like I can aim better in FPS games than I can with dual analog sticks. The feedback is nice.

It's a delicate process to update and remaster a game as beloved as RCT 1 and 2. It's so easy to just ruin it, but then, sometimes, the nail can be hit right on the head. As someone who grew up on the RCT franchise, this remastered build combining RCT1 and RCT2 surpasses the original.
The updated ui is easy to get used to and sometimes easier to find things than the original. The customization from RCT2 combined with the scenarios from RCT1 make it easier to create and imagine. The enhanced camera features give better control over viewing an area and studying a coaster.
The charm is still there. The genius of Chris Sawyer's masterpiece is still present. The fun and addictiveness of the original is surpassed. This game is the best multi-platform coaster sim available, and I couldn't recommend it more.
Unlike the original builds of the first two games on Steam (which are only on Windows,) this build actually runs trouble free; and uses almost no computer resources at that.
In conclusion, this release surpasses the original two, and for the experience of not only a classic coaster sim, but any coaster sim, this is one of the best. It's stood the test of time this long, and it's only welcoming a new generation of people to the masterpiece that is RollerCoaster Tycoon.

Le't Sing 2016 is a lot better than Let's Sing.  The song choices are mostly, but not all, British pop stars, both current and past.  The song list is in the game description, so look there before deciding to buy.  Keep in mind there's no DLC and not likely to ever be any.  Each song does have the original music video in the background.  Each song is from the original artist (no covers).
You can sing solo, pass the mic, or by heart (once you have done the song at least once).  You are graded on your performance on each song.  1 star if less than 70, 2 stars 70-89, 3 stars 90-100.  You are graded severely.  The game does keep track of your highest score.  You can also change options so that you hear an instrumental of the song only (no lead voice).  When I played the game, I encountered zero bugs or frame drops.  You can use any USB mic, but I suggest getting a good one like the Yeti.
I do recommend this game, if you like the songs.  I just wish there was an option to hear your recorded voice end product.  Also, they need to add online leaderboards for bragging rights.

It pains me to write a negative review on this game considering the many hours I have invested into this...but where do we begin?
PCE is a team deathmatch game where players choose between 2 teams, humans and dinosaurs
The humans consist of Pyro, Commando, Pathfinder, Scientist and Trapper classes
The Dinos consist of Tyrannosaurus rex, Spinosaurus, Acrocanthosaurs, Novaraptor, Oviraptor, Pteranodon, Tupandactylus, Dilophosaurus, Cryolophosaurus and Carnotaurus
The first flaw is right there, the Dinos have far more classes: 10 in total while the humans have 5..
Please note that I am aware the developers (what's left of them) and that they're in debt while struggling to keep their game alive on a financial issue. But even yet the flaw stills stands.
The second flaw is the updates, Every month or two the devs release a new update...which are excruciatingly lazy
The updates are only unnecessary nerfs and buffs along with 60+ skins to waste your money on.
PCE is entirely run by skins, since the release of the workshop that's all the updates have been around, no new gamemodes, no new game mechanics. Just SKINS. Now I'm dying for a new map or something, maybe an update to one of the maps (Island's unfinished caves) but at this rate that's highly unlikely.

Some skins in PCE fetch up to 300+ dollars like the radiated Rex, and some people actually buy it for that absurd price when they could buy a Wii U or Xbox for around that same price
Primal Carnage: Extinction's only future seeing where we are now consists of new skins that cost hundreds of dollars, free roam servers, 7-12 year old children who make their dinosaurs have sex with eachother only to please their horny 18+ roleplays (I'm a roleplayer myself but thats just wrong), unnecessary buffs and nerfs and the toxicity of T-bagging whiny players
