As much as it pains me to say bad things about A) Telltale and B) Minecraft, I just have to. This game could have been one of the greatest creations in computing history, what with two of the most popular gaming names behind it. It failed. Unlike in Telltale's Game of Thrones, where I can never wait for the next chapter and play it all the way through the day it comes out, and unlike in Minecraft, where there's always something else to do even in Vanilla, this game has neither aspect. Although it does have an interesting storyline for a non-storyline-based game, the characters are rather cliche and boring, it's extremely child-friendly with none of the tension or emotions of Telltale's previous successes and they have ruined the greates (in my opinion) enemy a sandbox game has ever seen (More later).
I'll start on the animation. Although this game is based off of something with no communication or cutscene programming whatsoever, this game is probably better off to keep it that way. The animations seem too cartoony for a supposedly dramatic storyline and it ruins the atmosphere. The mouths ingame are too simplistic and are more like something you would find in a very old, very amateur, Windows '95 era game with only different mouth shapes for each sound.
Secondly, the characters. [Spoiler Alert] You have the cliche main character=leader, brutish-looking guy is intimidating but a bit dim and actually soft on the inside, the girl is intelligent and usually/always knows the best thing to do (even if everyone ignores her), the badass side character who comes in to save the day and becomes a main character, and the bully who learns his lesson and makes friends with the main character. This makes them very predictable and extremely boring.
Thirdly, the villain/enemy/boss, whatever you want to call it. [Spoiler Alert] The Wither is supposed to be an extremely powerful, 3-headed, flying creature, which I grant, it is. It does NOT, however, consume anything to evolve and grow. The Wither Telltale have given us here, to put simply, looks ridiculous. Just the look of it ruins the whole idea of it in actual Minecraft. It looks silly, and overdone, and nothing like the Wither at all. It does not have tentacles that reach out and grab people and blocks, it is supposed to throw a toxic-like ball at the people of Minecraftia with the destruction of blocks being collateral damage. This monstrosity (the bad context) is an insult to the Wither I, and maybe we, have come to know and fear.
All in all, this game had huge potential and I was extremely excited to see what they would do, and hugely disappointed. The game is the worst it could have been, with all the negative aspects of each Telltale and Minecraft, not the greatness within each. I shall complete it, but only because I don't like leaving anything unfinished, even this, and, as said, the storyline is, albeit only just, decent.
Thanks for reading. Sorry there's so much.

The controller I recieved did not appear to be working correctly. The right side of the touchpad was much more responsive than the left. I turned on edge movement, and the right side would move quickly as expected, but the left would slow to a crawl, I could even feel it in the haptic feedback.
I cannot recommend this controller as it is now, and believe me I wanted to like it. I have returned mine, and I will late until they either fix some of the problems, or make a new version all together.
These are my main issues:
-Can only be configured through steam big picture mode. Sorry, but I hate big picture mode. I dont care what setting I am in, I do not want to use this mode!
-This controller pretty much only works with Steam games. This is basically like DRM for the controller. I buy every game I can from steam, but some games are not available, and are not compatible with steam overlay. If I'm going to buy a specialty peice of hardware like this, it needs to work for all my games, steam or otherwise.
-Technical issues. It's frustrating to get a new product that appears to be a lemon. My touchpad is not functioning properly, making the controller useless for me. Sure I could get a replacement, but why bother.
-Design issues. The back removable panel duals out as buttons? The design of the removeable panel seems suspect at best. The small latch is bound to snap eventually.
-The back panel also slowly cuts into my hand. You'd have to hold one for a while to see why, but there is a gap, and the edge is sharp.
-I never could get the touchpad to work well for both horizontal and vertical movement. Maybe it was because it's not working properly, but otherwise this was very frustrating for me. Apparently, I swipe at an angle, but my vertical movement is true, if I change the axis rotation for horizontal movement, then when I swipe vertically it moves at an angle.
TL;DR
This controller needs to go through some growth before it's ready.

The best thing about this controller is its customization options. With the ability to mode-shift the function of any button by pressing a different one, a whole new world of custom keybindings is made available.
The haptic pads took a while to get used to, but after a few hours of use, it became much more natural. Additionally, the community knowledge base is incredible. With a few quick google searches, any and all questions I had about controller usage were answered, as well as several solutions to what I thought were unavoidable problems.
The community-uploaded configuration profiles are amazing. Sometimes, other people can create button mappings much better than you could ever come up with by yourself. I highly recommend browsing several of the top-used profiles, and perhaps making one of your own that combines the best of what you've seen.
A fair warning: this is not a magic tool for those too accustomed to keyboard and mouse to suddenly play effectively using a controller. Much of the same joystick-based skills are still required. For more intense and precision-based games, I'll still definitely use keyboard and mouse. However, in my personal experience, I am still considerably better using a steam controller than an xbox 360 controller. Perhaps, with some practice, I may be able to play more games with this controller.

Dear Valve, PLEASE STOP MAKING HARDWARE. Stop now, and never look back. We can forget that this ever happened. The Steam Controller is by far the absolute worst controller I've ever put in my hands. I mean, worse than the $20 Walmart after-market Disney themed gimmick controllers by a nameless company. That bad. I mean the concept had merit, and I've used controllers that were unique with track balls and all sorts of weird gadgetry. But your implementation of the Steam Controller is quite possibly the biggest disappointment in hardware history.
Now for some details. The build quality of this controller is absolutely terrible. I feel like I can break off any part with ease. The "d-pad" is laughable. Sure, it doubles as a secondary track pad, but good lord... it can't be taken seriously as a d-pad. The thumb stick is among the worst I've used. Worse than the Wii pro controllers. Not even close to the quality found on PS4, XBox and Logitech F-series controllers. And the buttons are "plasticky" and clicky in a cheap, bad way.
What about the concept? The whole point: the track pad. This piece of the controller does indeed work. I was able to play 7th Guest (a retro mouse based puzzle game). But not as well as I could with my Logitech media keyboard (with built-in trackpad). I could not play Supreme Commander (mouse driven RTS) with any comfort at all. And playing Far Cry 4 (FPS) was embarrassing. It's not as simple as: "oh, I can get used to this". No. I can't. It's that bad.
And finally, what about ergonomics. Well, imagine if your fingers bent in the opposite directions. That is, if all of your knuckles were backwards. Then, and only then, would the design of this controller make sense. I used it for about 45 minutes, and I developed RSI in my elbow, a part of my body that isn't even touching the controller. It's THAT bad. My hands cramped up and using this thing felt like playing a game while wearing oven mitts with backwards finger knuckles.
This is a huge disappointment. I watched this development with excitement, waited years and pre-ordered. Valve: You're doing it wrong. Stop now. I am so thankful for my XBox 360 and Logitech F710 controllers. Do yourself a favor. Buy either of those instead of a Steam Controller. And also buy a simple Logitech media keyboard to play with your Steam Link or Steam Box. Otherwise, just play on your gaming PC and/or buy a PS4. Valve has failed to deliver with its hopes and dreams of dominating the living room couch. This isn't going to cut it. Not even close.

It just struck me that whenever there's a sandbox crime game, it's always the same gangs: Italians, Yakuza, or street gangsters - you’re always either going on about respect, honour, or wearing your belt around your thighs. You know what there needs to be? A sandbox crime game where you play a Batman villain. You run around doing dastardly crime equipped with freeze-rays and jetpacks, completing story missions that lead up to you building a giant, brightly-coloured doomsday machine shaped like a top hat or something. Then Batman comes along and beats you up because you forgot to strap him into your overly elaborate, slow moving deathtrap. Then you mysteriously evade capture in order to come back and do it all again next week. Sadly, mankind has yet to recognise my genius (which is, incidentally, the title I have in mind for this project).
I bring this up because Saints Row 2 came appealingly close to my vision. The level of character customisation is straight-jacket wearing, small animal tormenting insane, and after I'd gotten away into the game and kitted out my Cockney-accented psychopath with a black and red silk suit with bow tie, two-toned shoes, and matching bowler hat, then started a mission in which I drove around the suburbs hosing things down with raw sewage, I suddenly realised I was role-playing as some kind of extremely unsubtle cousin to the Riddler. I wondered if there could be a follow-up minigame in which I composed a set of elegant rhyming couplets pertaining to houses covering in poo. Sadly not.
I know I said we should drop this term, but Saints Row 2 really is a Grand Theft Auto clone without shame. You’re in a huge sandbox city (that residents of New York would find weirdly familiar), you jack cars (that is, you steal them, not masturbate them), there are silly in-game radio stations, and you do missions pertaining to rival gangs that run you through a colourful set of vehicles and gameplay modes. The only thing it doesn’t have is your ♥♥♥♥ing cousin ringing up every ten minutes to invite you on dinner dates, and that’s just one reason why Saints Row 2 is better than Grand Theft Auto IV.
If you give players a sandbox world full of guns, cars, and innocent, blood-filled, squishy people, they are going to want to ♥♥♥♥ this world’s♥♥♥♥♥♥up. This is something that GTA IV didn’t seem to grasp. When you put a child in a sandbox, you do not spend three hours explaining proper bucket and spade etiquette, devote lengthy cutscenes to explaining the child’s motivations, nor do you interrupt the child every ten minutes to make them talk to grandma on the phone. And you also don’t paint the sand brownish grey or stir in a few shovelfuls of grit.
Saints Row 2 shows a much better understanding of its audience. It is fully aware that most gamers are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, and if you give them any kind of freedom their first instinct will be to abuse it. If you give them guns, they will shoot old ladies. If you give them cars, they will run over old ladies. If you give them aircraft, they will ascend to the highest possible height and hurl themselves out onto an old lady. And if you give them customisable outfits their first instinct will be to take off all their clothes and run around the streets hip-thrusting in the faces of old ladies. If you try to stop them doing all this, they'll hate you for it. Not only does Saints Row 2 not stop you, but it keeps score! Every single one of my examples has a little mini-game attached. You’d never see Niko Bellic farming points by casting his Serbian flag-patterned underpants aside and waving his willy at someone's grandma. Or, for that matter, embarking on missions in a floral print dress and top hat. But maybe if he had it'd have least brightened up his miserable little brown life for five minutes.
GTA IV was a game that spent its entire playtime drunkenly stumbling back and forth between "wacky fun" and "gritty realism," unable to decide where it was going to set up shop. So while the funny radio stations were there, the lead character was an angsty♥♥♥♥♥♥with a selection of dowdy outfits, like the world's least stimulating G.I Joe. The cars handled realistically (i.e., like supermarket trolleys full of rocks), and when you drove into a pedestrian they just rolled realistically over your bonnet and collapsed in a screaming pile of broken hips. Run someone over in Saints Row 2, by comparison, and their rag doll will be launched into the sky Team Rocket style and end up with their spine curled around a lamp post. I found myself becoming a lot more attached to my character, because whatever personality you choose, they're in this for the same reason you are: to have some ♥♥♥♥ing fun!
I'm not so keen on the rather dictatorial gameplay mechanic in which you must play the aforementioned minigames to build up respect points before you get on with the story missions. It leads to this bizarre scenario where you can be controlling half the ♥♥♥♥ing city, with legions of misguided youngsters at your game, but you're still not respected enough to do a mission until you go and fling♥♥♥♥♥♥at someone's house. The minigames are fun, and I admit I probably wouldn't have played them if this game hadn’t folded its arms and closed off the plot until I did, but I guarantee their entertainment value will run out before the story missions do. The game's also a little too easy on the medium setting; your handgun can shoot accurately enough to pierce someone’s nipple from across town, and our old friend regenerating health makes a show-stopping appearance, essentially making you RoboCop with more flexible ethics and trousers.
Saint's Row 2 isn't the most sophisticated gaming experience. In fact, if it were a person it were wear Deely-Boppers and laugh at dead baby jokes. But it understands what it's trying to be: pure, mindless fun, like wrestling an excitable dog in a paddling pool of disembodied breasts. (Don't think too much about that simile - I certainly didn't).
The history of gaming technology has been one long quest for total realism, but now we’re on the verge of it I’m seeing that it’s probably not worth the effort. The ultra-realistic games of recent years have been one long, gritty, depressing grey-a-thon after another, and it’s up to games like Saints Row 2 to remind us that realism is an acceptable sacrifice if it means I get to throw old ladies into jet turbines.

I really wanted a game of this type, but for me this game is unusable.  I was unable to find a configuration that made it accurately score performance.
The first configuration I tried was to use Logitech wired USB microphone that I had used for Rock Band and put the sound output through my LED TV in game mode.  This produced seemingly sort of ok results, but I decided to test the setup.  I chose some songs with decent range in pitch and just made a constant tone into the microphone.  It scored me pretty well and showed my pitch going up, down, and all over the place.  The variation was despite me just producing a monotone sound.  When I tried singing along, the feedback is often very delayed such that it is hard to use the feedback.  The feedback for singing along and for just producing a completely monotone sound were hard to even distinguish visually.  I'm not a great singer, but I'm not nearly as bad as a monotone sound.
The second configuration I tried was to use a wireless headset.  I used a Logitech G930 headset which is a wireless headset which is designed to keep latency down.  My theory was maybe the scoring would be better if I removed the sound from the TV getting to the microphone.  The scoring was much, much better in this configuration.  I could see the effect of changing my pitch on the scoring, although it was still very delayed.  The feedback was very hard to do anything with though.  All I could really get out of it was on pitch, off pitch, or so far off it didn't recognize it as an attempt.  It at least didn't score a monotone sound highly.  The feedback was still very delayed a lot of the time.  The feedback seemed to be several words behind a fair amount of the time.  I found the feedback to be almost, but not quite useless.  This was a small improvement over the first configuration.  Another killer problem in this mode is that there is basically no feedback from the microphone to the speakers.  It is really hard to sing when you can't hear yourself (at least for me).  I also tried a variation of this where I had 1 ear pad off on the headset so I could hear myself.  This was the best configuration for me as I could hear the music in 1 ear and hear myself in the other.  It is sad that the game reduced me to this level to try to save it.  Even with this, the feedback wasn't good enough to make me ever want to play the game again.  I feel like I get better feedback just by listening to myself as I sing along to things.
Beyond failing at its primary function of providing feedback on your singing, the game has a bunch of other limitations.  I don't consider these other limitations to be game killers, but they do make the game feel like an alpha release.  The only imnput to the game is keyboard and it only uses 7 keys (4 arrows, enter, space, escape).  This is a very clunky interface for a PC.  It does map extremely well to a steam controller however, so once I set up the input mapping and used the controller it was pretty good.  There are very few options or controls inside the game.  You can switch which microphone you are using in the game, but sound output is controlled by Windows.  I also didn't see any volume controls inside the game.  At one point I had my headset USB dongle plugged in with the headset off and the USB mic plugged in.  This made the game switch to the duet display even though the headset was turned off and I was playing in what would normally be the single player mode.  It didn't seem to let me select how many players I wanted just assuming that number of players = number of mics.  The controls in the game are basically limited to select song, quit, and select from a few different game modes which are pretty similar.

It’s never easy to bounce back after you’ve screwed up. I’ve been there. Screwed up as badly as some people can ever screw up and get a second opportunity. Voxler Games screwed up last year with the first Steam release of Let’s Sing. For a long time the game was sitting with a negative user review status. It’s only been in the past few months that some kind souls have raised it to mixed but it still has less than a 50% positive-negative review percentage. So somewhat bravely they returned with the 2016 edition of their music game that remains popular on consoles. It appears that the developer put a lot of effort into listening to their player base over the past twelve months because the new release is a vastly superior product than the original. That’s a great thing for fans of music on a platform that is dying out for quality games in the genre.
The first thing that I did when I loaded up Let’s Sing 2016 wasn’t actually sing any of the songs. No, I wanted to ensure that the jukebox mode worked properly and I really wanted the easiest achievement in the game out of the way early. That achievement is of course the ‘insert a token’ achievement. All you need to do is to listen to ten songs in a row while in jukebox mode. Between an occasional click between working it was a nice change. That leads me to the first issue that I have with the game but it’s an understandable one. Last year’s version of Let’s Sing did not have any downloadable content – good grief if the devs catch up on that one they might make as many songs available as Rocksmith – and it appears that may be the case once again this year. So what is the issue you may ask? It’s that the game is perhaps too centered on pop songs. You’re not going to find anything too alternative in the track list (you can see the entire track list below in the Steam Description). This immediately narrows the audience for the game as much as it attempts to broaden it. It’s clear that Voxler Games have gone for the whole not appealing to everyone so appeal to the popular group as much as possible strategy.
Although I’ve been in a couple of bands and groups before – only very small groups that never went anywhere – I’m not a good singer at all. I’m much better than I was when I was younger and my partner seems to think that when I know a song and it’s in my alley that I can sing I really find it embarrassing to share my voice. It’d be a train wreck and I’d look like Gary Brolsma only there’d be a hideous sound instead of lip syncing. I think the game picks up on that as I’m not very good and show no signs of improvement. When it comes to elimination songs I quickly lose out. However, I do believe that the voice recognition software works as it should. I’ve seen people reporting that it’s broken for them so it may depend greatly on the quality of your microphone as well as your ability to hit the right notes. I believe that this is important as you need to look past the price of the game if you’re going to play it and at the price of a good quality microphone if you don’t have one. Both my Logitech webcam and my headset, I currently use a Kingston HyperX Cloud II, work consistently well.
Voxler Games can be proud of the effort they’ve made since last release. It’s a worthy purchase this year – if you have or can get a quality microphone – but I’m really excited to see next year’s edition. If the studio can make a similar improvement next year’s edition has the potential to be one of the best singing (not necessarily music as a general genre) games ever made.

Sideway New York is a cleverly conceived and well executed 2.5D platformer about a graffiti Artist getting sucked onto the walls of New York City's urban landscape in a bid to rescue his girlfriend.  Using the buildings themselves as the levels you traverse across the walls and roofs of the skyline itself collecting items, abilites, and fighting spray painted enemies along the way.
The level design is incredibly well thought out, because you platforming along the side of a building or roof, which generally have four sides to them, the perspective and orientation of the level is constantly being rotated and flipped as you slip around a corner and switching your axis. This makes the maps very dense and tight, you never get bored going through a level because you'll be attacking it from several directions in very quick succession.
The art direction is perhaps one of my favorite part of the game, a vibrant, bright world of Graffiti and spraypaint pops out from the muted, cool coloured canvas of the urban environment. The character design is eye catching and organic, with its fluid animations further complimented by the smoothness of the camera as it rotates around corners as it follows the character. Everything looks like a urbanised flash cartoon, or Adidas commercial.
The music in the game surprised me a lot. As some one who isn't in any skretch a fan of Hip Hop, I quickly came to love the rythyms and tones they set while I parkoured on the side of a high rise. The soundtrack, which was prepared by SkullCandy (headphone maker) and Hip Hop artist Mr. Lif, is unforunately reused a lot throughout the game, but they're good enough tunes for me too not mind too much. Though I wish the game developers would sell the soundtrack as a whole on itunes.
Subway New York is a great game, an fine example of how a platformer should be made. But it has one GLARING, UNEXCUSABLE FLAW. It has got to be the sloppiest, half hearted console port I've ever seen. It becomes abundently clear this was first made for the Playstation 3 with its terrible default keyboard layout, its jump right in two player coop, its "do not turn off console" while saving messages, and sometimes refering to a controller instead of a keyboard. This game was made for a joystick and it shows, you'll struggle it make jumps and get inexplicibly killed in the environment, not to mention confuse your keys in the middle of a fight and suffer a cheap death, AGAIN!!
If you grew up playing Super Mario Bros you owe it too yourself to give Sideway a try!
But be sure to use a proper controller!!

This is a great game for anyone looking to improve their typing speed, expand their vocabulary, or parents who want to give their kids a game that will give them some long term practical benefits and maybe a little education on the side. No deep rpg storyline here, but that isn't really the point.
The gameplay is fairly fast paced and while I wouldn't say it is addictive its still fun and you will find yourself coming back for just one more playthrough more times than you will probably like to admit. There are a wide variety of characters to unlock and several lengthy levels to battle through. So rest assured this will take a while to fully beat.
Overall its a good game for anyone. The Loot Chests are quite fun too and are generally easy to figure out without pausing.
EDIT: Also, what other game lets you kill a Rhino Cavalry using the word AIDS? :P

Pro:
- Core play mechanic (find words in a jumble-type grid to attack your foes) is challenging, rewarding, and fast-moving.
- Several different puzzle minigames thrown into the mix, some easy (chests), some hard (traps), and some nearly impossible (cheat death).
- Lots of heroes to experiment with and level up, each with three unique skills.
- Enough random variation that each playthrough feels fresh.
Con:
- Very few of the game mechanics are really explained in-game. It took me awhile to realize that all equipment just cumulatively adds to hero stats, that dead heroes can't be resurrected (but do retain their level if encountered/selected again), that you can only level up at fountains, or even that I could just type words rather than painfully selecting letters from the jumble. I still don't know what mana is or does.
- As with many word games, it's often less about practical or even literary vocabulary than your ability to guess very short obscure/archaic words. (This really only becomes frustrating in the "cheat death" anagram game, which often presents you with cruelly unguessable words.)
- All of the "action" happens in the upper part of the screen, whereas you have to focus on the words. As a result, it's hard to know what effect you're really having on the battle; you just find words until the monster dies (or you do). Working messaging and effects into the main grid (e.g., flashing the name of the ability you activated) would be a good improvement.
Overall: it's a fun word game with a super basic but more-or-less-serviceable RPG bolted on.  A great casual time-killer. For 3 bucks, you really can't go wrong.

-Decent graphics.
-Many maps to choose from.
-Dedicated Servers.
-A loyal community.
-For now at least they are releasing updates and a very steady pace.
-Will be part of the steam community market and will allow cosmetic skin drops.
Cons:
-Some say the game is very laggy, this may be true on lower end machines.
-Some of the controls can seem a bit awkward on the dinosaurs at first.
-Some issues with balance between Dinosaurs and Humans, however I am sure these will be ironed out.
All in all I recommend this game for all to enjoy.

Although this is only a short review for the first episode, I have to say I enjoyed playing this with my 9 year old daughter. It's a little on the short side, but to be expected really. It's not incredibly taxing given its target audience, but it's fun, engaging and for those familiar with Minecraft you will feel at home. Don't go in expecting shocking revelations, twists and coarse language (other than about 7-8 uses of the word cr@p) - this is a family friendly adventure. The only issue is really I have is the episodic nature and having to wait so long between each one.... we did the first episode in under 2 hours in one sitting and now I estimate a 3 month wait (on average based on TTG's past entries) for the next installment.

I've left my original favourable review below, but I have to change this to NOT RECOMMENDED now.
Why?  Because in a game where supposedly choices matter (albeit usually in tiny ways, but I'm ok with that), it's completely unacceptable for the game to completely forget your choices and play out a completely different scenario.  And that's exactly what this game does in Episode 3 -- completely ignoring everything I did in the prior two episodes, it changes key details such as which characters are in the party completely arbitrarily.  Yes, it's a bug.  But it's been more than three months now and the bug hasn't been fixed -- and again, in a game about choices, actually remembering them should have been a top priority.
There's a lot of mysterious hate for this game (I guess because it's not Minecraft itself?), but don't listen to it.
If you're expecting a sandbox game like Minecraft, this isn't that.  This is (at least the start of) another story-driven episodic adventure from the geniuses at Telltale Games, that simply happens to be Minecraft-themed, instead of Borderlands-themed or Walking Dead-themed like some of their earlier works.
So if you enjoyed those, you're likely to enjoy this too.  Yes, it takes some liberties with the Minecraft universe, but as a sandbox its lore is practically nonexistent, and I personally think that they've done an excellent job at capturing what little lore there was in the original game, and adding on something unique and interesting of their own.
Certainly things get quite exciting in this first episode.  And for the very first time in a Telltale adventure, you get to choose your character.  It's not full customisation -- there's only six to choose from -- but this does allow you to choose your gender, which means that Telltale have provided two completely different voice tracks for the main character (like in Mass Effect), which is pretty rare.

It's not perfect out of the box, but there's a ton of potential here. I've only had my controller for a week, and I haven't had enough time to play around with the settings too much, but so far, aside from some bad fits and starts, it's been pretty good.
Pictures don't do it justice. It's not too much bigger than an Xbox 360 controller, and it feels quite comfortable in the hand. The dual-stage triggers offer some great possibilities in control configuration, as do the gyros and the back-side buttons, however there is a learning curve to get used to them. The ABXY buttons are remarkably small compared to competitors, but I haven't found them to be too small (though in aggressive button mashers they are a little squeaky).
The analog stick is exactly what you'd expect out of a modern controller, and the touchpads, while they might seem sloppy initially, after getting used to them they are precise enough to play racing games with, no quesions asked. The haptic feedback is adjustable (thankfully) and while I might like some stronger feedback than it's strongest, it's by no means a slouch even at the lowest settings.
I like it on the desktop as a trackball, and it works great on my little 8" tablet. However not all games like it. Internally it emulates a keyboard, mouse, and controller, and while it can function as a combination of these three devices, some games are keyed to accept a keyboard/mouse OR a controller, and learning which ones accept which can be a bit annoying. Thankfully checking for community suggested controller configs goes a fair way towards simplifying things, and as more people get their hands on the controller more games should have suggestions.
I am especially displeased with how the only way to change any settings about the controller whatsoever is through Big Picture Mode. It makes sense for Steam Machines and Steam Link, but not for a desktop computer. A desktop configuration utlity would be incredibly handy.
That being said, it does a great job pretending not to be a keyboard and mouse in the hand. I played Battleblock Theater using a community suggested configuration (in keyobard emulation) you could have easily fooled me that I wasn't in controller mode. It's a fantastic fusion of hardware and software. As I get used to it, I'm finding it's easier to deal with the contorller's shortcomings.

It finally happened.  We waited for 20 years, each time a 4x came out it was perhaps decent, fun, enjoyable.  But it wasn't enough to match Master of Orion 2.  We hoped each time, and our hopes were dashed.
It happened.  Stellaris can honestly say that it does NOT stand in the shadow of MOO 2.  It's a better game.  Now that may only have been possible because of 20 years of technical and design improvements, but it's better.
And it keeps gets better.  Each expansion adds significant content improvements.
Diplomacy: Much better than MOO2, though not quite as good as the Galciv series, yet.  AI is smart and generally you always understand why there is a conflict or an alliance.  You never end up confused as to why the AI chose a diplomatic option.
Ship design: Not as good as MOO2, but better than the vast majority of other 4x games.  Far better than galciv series, though not as 'pretty'.
Expansion: Wonderful, possibly best I've seen.  Colonizing a world always has meaning, exploring unknown territory is exciting and presents all sorts of interesting events or situations.
Warfare: Combat itself is automated but tactically interesting, there is no 'slog' to combats as you saw in MOO2.  Combat has more depth than Galciv series, with ships moving in a wide range of ways to avoid and attack enemies.  War itself is fairly simple, but does not suffer from the 'eternal war' problem that many other games do.
Resources: Planets are very complex beasts which can be micro-managed to a decent degree.  They feel very valuable, and the sector system means you can delegate management of less interesting planets to the AI, giving broad orders.  You will always have some planets you want to manage by hand, and it does not feel tedious.  Unique resources are present in various parts of the galaxy which provide empire-level benefits and can be traded.  Think Civ4 style.
Society: Your civilization feels like more than a spreadsheet, stellaris does this part very right.  Your population can be of many races and have up to 8 different, sometimes competing ethos such as Spiritual or Materialist,  There are 5 different government types that interact with those ethos choices. Populations will form factions in your government which can provide benefits or maluses depending on the choices you make in-game.  A pacifist faction, for example will be angered if you choose to fight aggressive wars.  Factions react to your actual gameplay choices, rather than some detached numbers.  Policies can be chosen that limit or permit various ways to interact with the game world, such as purging aliens, enslaving or uplifting primitive species, glassing planets, or rights for AIs.  There are too many to easily list.
Technology: A very complex and interesting technology tree which allows a lot of meaningful choices.  The fact that different gameplay paths gain access to exclusive unique technologies means games can play out with very different research paths depending on your choices.  The addition of repeatable late-game 'enhancement' research means that technology advantages do not cap out in late game.  The research tree is huge and not entirely tree structured, and possesses semi-random elements.
There's a LOT more here then what I listed in detail above. There are traditions.  There are megastructures which can enclose entire stars or build ringworlds. There are horrible endgame disasters on a galaxy-wide scale that can occur.  Ancient Precursor civilizations exist that interfere with the younger races, and may even fight a galaxy-spanning war with each other should things go wrong.  Space monsters, ancient relics...so many things.
There are things that other games do better, in any one category or another, but no other 4x game does as MANY things this well.  The whole is the sum of it's parts, and while many other games have one part that is better than stellaris, none possess a better sum total.

I remember the buggy mess 2k16 and 2k17 were at launch. Guess what? Seems it's easier for companies to find bugs if they have thousands of people playing their game (that's you, guys, I'm talking about the customer) than it is for them to find bugs with the 20 to 50 people they hired for bug finding purposes. The PS4 patch is already live and fixing a whole lot of things, and this won't be the last patch, as they ALWAYS include a patch when they are uploading and unlocking the DLC characters.
Let's get to the price. If you are crying that this game isn't worth the 50 bucks it's charging then you are stupid. You are paying 20 bucks less than the console peasants do for the same game. And if that is too expensive for you: There are hundreds of key selling sites that had this game in stock for 30 bucks. Yes, even before release.
Then there are people complaining 2K did not use enough voice acting. Guess what, geniuses? This isn't 2Ks fault. Do you realize who you want to be voiced? Yes, wrestlers. So you think it would be easy for them to just fly over to 2Ks studios and put in 6 to 8 hours worth of voice acting for you whiny bit*hes to enjoy. Sure, but this are 6 to 8 hours they are not attending a house show. Someone then has to pay for the downtime. Are you willing to do it? You complain that this game isn't worth anybody's money but at the same time want quality voice acting by the wrestlers. You have to decide.

You have to grind the ingame currency for these crates to unlock. TL;DR Fun, unpresumptuous, good music, no real issues, priced appropriately.
There are two types of games. The first type is like a person who goes outside wearing a coat several sizes too big, to appear more intimidating. The second type is like a person who goes outside dressed in an appropriately-sized coat, even if they look small.
Out There Somewhere (OTS) is a fantastic example of the latter type. It is a game that doesn't attempt to be something it's not, and that give it its charming appeal. When you finish the game (which takes about 90 minutes), you KNOW you've beaten it. This isn't to say games that leave the player with questions are bad, but games shouldn't feel obligated to take that approach. OTS chooses not to do so, and definitely does not suffer for that decision.
The gameplay is solid and everything handles well. Each screen is a new puzzle - there is no level space wasted on empty 'transition screens' - and checkpoints are spaced appropriately, with the game occasionally lengthening the distance to provide for a harder-than-usual stage. These occurrences are common enough to make the player feel challenged, but rare enough to make the game possible. Respawns are instant, allowing the player to quickly jump back into the game. OTS's core mechanic is a teleportation gun that teleports the player to the point of impact, sometimes limited by red, blue, and green lightbeams (which have different effects). OTS claims to have been inspired by Portal, and I found this a fantastic adaptation of its gameplay to a 2D platformer. The game is very creative in its application of the mechanic and is careful in its introduction and combination of separate elements - mostly. Which brings me to my only issue with the game: the limiter beams feature prominently, but not so much the reflector panels and the crystal thingies. I feel like the mechanic could have benefited had these last two components been used more frequently.
Again in line with the game's inspiration, OTS's artstyle is reminiscient of Cave Story and other retro-style platformers, and does well in pulling off the 'alien planet' feel the game is going for. The soundtrack is delightful and surprisingly large for a game less than two hours long, and actually includes in one track an orchestral component, which blends well with the chiptune. (Composer is Iuri Rodrigues.)
As for the pricing, there are few games for $2 that I'd consider too high-priced. And in this case it seems perfectly adequate.
Overall a very enjoyable experience complemented by a fantastic OST.

This is an awesome little game! It is a hidden little gem i picked up for $0.21. This is a puzzle platformer that is so fun because the puzzles are very satisfying to solve. At the beginning of the game i was a confused but I quickly picked up the game mechanics due to the games perfect learning curve. In other words when the game teaches a new mechanic, it starts off easy until you are familar with the mechanic, then harder till it becomes secondhand knowledge, and THEN thats when the game shows you the next new mechanic. Of course this is not to say that you will never be stumped at some parts, after all it is what makes a puzzle game a puzzle game and takes some creative thinking BUT is never anything ridiculous to solve. The main part about this game that is kept me so hooked were all the puzzles. The harder puzzles are extreamly satisfying to solve (plenty of "OHHH!!" moments) and secrets are very rewarding to find. The puzzles in this game will never become stale, thats because even though the puzzles are essentially the same, the variations and new mechanics keep it very fun, enjoyable, and interesting to play. One more thing is that great soundtrack, props to them!

I've left my original favourable review below, but I have to change this to NOT RECOMMENDED now.
Why?  Because in a game where supposedly choices matter (albeit usually in tiny ways, but I'm ok with that), it's completely unacceptable for the game to completely forget your choices and play out a completely different scenario.  And that's exactly what this game does in Episode 3 -- completely ignoring everything I did in the prior two episodes, it changes key details such as which characters are in the party completely arbitrarily.  Yes, it's a bug.  But it's been more than three months now and the bug hasn't been fixed -- and again, in a game about choices, actually remembering them should have been a top priority.
There's a lot of mysterious hate for this game (I guess because it's not Minecraft itself?), but don't listen to it.
If you're expecting a sandbox game like Minecraft, this isn't that.  This is (at least the start of) another story-driven episodic adventure from the geniuses at Telltale Games, that simply happens to be Minecraft-themed, instead of Borderlands-themed or Walking Dead-themed like some of their earlier works.
So if you enjoyed those, you're likely to enjoy this too.  Yes, it takes some liberties with the Minecraft universe, but as a sandbox its lore is practically nonexistent, and I personally think that they've done an excellent job at capturing what little lore there was in the original game, and adding on something unique and interesting of their own.
Certainly things get quite exciting in this first episode.  And for the very first time in a Telltale adventure, you get to choose your character.  It's not full customisation -- there's only six to choose from -- but this does allow you to choose your gender, which means that Telltale have provided two completely different voice tracks for the main character (like in Mass Effect), which is pretty rare.

TL;DR: If you're a fan of tactical, objective based shooters, then you'll most likely enjoy RS2.
Rising Storm 2 is the spiritual successor to the Red Orchestra Series, and the expansion of RO2, Rising Storm. It's a unique take on modern FPS games, and can be the host of the greatest FPS matches you'll ever have the pleasure of taking part in...but also the worst.
This game's style is a double edged sword. On one hand, a good team with good squad leaders and a solid commander will reign supreme and create an atmosphere of gritty combat. There's nothing more intense than sitting behind a wall with your squad taking heavy fire, and your commander calling in the perfect support to help make that final push towards victory.
However, it can be extremely frustrating when your teammates fail to play the objective, and just run around like headless chickens with no concept of teamwork. Roleplay is a must in this game. That being said, you don't need a mic or even to comunicate with your team. Lone wolf gameplay is completely possible, and still very fun, you just have to play the objectives if you want to be successful.
I find this game to be similar to Battlefield 2. Not Bad Company 2, but the 2004 classic Battlefield 2. It's a game that doesn't necessarily appeal to the average run and gun 10 minute round FPS crowd, but rather focuses on the crowd that wants to sit down and have a 1-2 hour tooth and nail battle. Personally, I love this game, and I wish I had the time and motivation to write out everything this game does right(despite all it does wrong), because if you can find it in your heart to forgive the problems this game has, you'll have an amazing time.

If you like gamepads, this is the best gamepad. More buttons, more accuracy, incredibly useful haptic feedback, and gyroscopic controls that are actually insanely practical. It won't replace a mouse and keyboard setup for competitive shooters or RTS's, but for single player games (including shooters!) it's amazing and it can still hold up surprisingly well even in a competitive environment with the proper bindings.
The most obvious feature are the dual trackpads. They look weird, but they're damn good. The right trackpad is far superior to a joystick for just about any game out there, you're getting far more accuracy with a slimmer profile. It takes a little getting used to, but a properly configured binding profile will feel natural. It even clicks easily without messing up your aim too much, so unlike the right thumbstick in most games you can actually bind it to something important. I actually set it as my Use button, it's like the big green A on a Gamecube controller, it just begs to be The Button.
The left trackpad, on the other hand, is not at all superior to a joystick. Movement in games is very reliant on you returning to a neutral position to signify that you've stopped moving - for a joystick, a spring returns it to a neutral position, while WASD spring back up when you let up your fingers. While you can stop moving on the left trackpad by simply lifting your thumb, you have to lift your thumb. You can't just relax your thumb to stop moving, you have to actually move your thumb to stop moving. Luckily Valve saw fit to add an actual joystick, so the left pad is freed up for more interesting uses.
Typically the left pad is set up as a d-pad. It's weird, but not necessarily bad. You can tell it to activate on touch alone, allowing something akin to a joystick, or you can require a click of the joypad which feels very satisfying. You can specify whether to allow or disallow diagonals, how much preference diagonals get, and the like. This makes the pad one of the best for quickly managing inventories or activating voice commands and the like. Turn off diagonals and you'll always get the direction (and weapon) you need. Unfortunately, the pad is large and the top of the pad is far away from the joystick where your thumb will spend most of its time resting, requiring quite a bit of travel distance to reach your up binding.
That large size also makes it hard to recommend the d-pad for anything that demands a quality d-pad. While you can be sure that you're only ever getting the directions you specify, the pad is just too damn big for the job. On a 360 pad, your thumb almost entirely obscures the d-pad - you can hit any direciton at any time with no need to move your thumb very far. Same with pretty much every other d-pad in existance. On the Steam Controller, there's just too much space for it to be a reliable way to move your character, much less pull off special moves in a fighter.
That's not the only trick the left pad is capable of, though. You can set the left pad as a Touch Menu; if you touch the pad, an overlay appears on the screen and you can highlight a button and click the pad to select the button. You can have up to 16 buttons bound to the Touch Menu, enabling you to bind pretty much every keybind to your controller no matter what. The Touch Menu is too slow for anything time sensitive or twitchy like swapping weapons, but it's great for mapping shortcuts to your inventory, character sheet, quicksaving and loading, voting yes or no to map changes on a server, that sort of thing. I find myself actually getting a little more efficient in city building games as the Touch Menu is way faster than navigating the in-game menu by mouse and all the buttons are labelled with their functions.
Both trackpads owe their accuracy to clever ergonomics, a "just right" texture, and most importantly the haptic feedback.
If you're a touch typist, you know how to find home row just by feeling the keys - the F and J keys have a little nub on them that signals to your fingers that they're in the right spot. As it turns out, that same principle works for mouse movement too. When a trackpad is emulating a mouse, it feels something like a trackball - that side of the controller will very gently vibrate almost exactly like a trackmall mouse does when the slight imperfections in the ball cause a slight vibration that you can feel in the mouse. That vibration tells you when you're moving and not moving your mouse, and your brain can very quickly learn to associate that rumble with mouse movement.
It's feels sorta like you're running your thumb over the pixels on the screen, as if they were rough sand. It's not as accurate as an actual mouse that you can put your whole arm into, but if a gaming mouse were to use this sort of haptic feedback it'd probably be the most accurate mouse you could possibly buy.
The haptic feedback isn't just for the trackpads, however. Nearly all the buttons on the controller can be set to activate haptic feedback upon activation, in particular the dual stage triggers. Once you pass the activation threshhold, by default you'll feel a "clicking" sensation within the grip of the controller. This is almost addictive, you can tell at exactly what point a trigger registers a pull and then feather it for rapid input, and since this is activated by software you can set the precise point at which that happens.
The haptic feedback is probably best used for ultra precise gyro aiming.
If you've played Splatoon, imagine that except the controller is way lighter and more ergonomic and you can feel the controller slowly click with your movements. If you haven't, imagine using the right trackpad to get roughly in the neighborhood of where you want to aim and then fine-tuning it by using a lower sensitivity setting and aiming with both your wrists - this is the secret that lets it be so close to an actual mouse. You're aiming with both hands and benefitting from that haptic feedback which tells you how much you're moving. This video should give you an idea of the kind of accuracy you can expect:
They're bad. But that's OK, because there's other far superior buttons you can bind your controls to instead.
The ABXY buttons are just so tiny and recessed. They're still work just fine, but their size is a real pain as it can be a bit hard to tell you've pressed them. It feels like they should have been a bit taller like on the 360 pad.
The biggest issue, however, is their impractical placement. They're fairly far from the right trackpad where your thumb will be most of the time, and the way the handle of the controller causes you to cup your palm limits how far you can reach with your thumb. My adult sized hand can barely reach the X button.
Fortunately, the Y and B buttons are within reasonable reach and are perfectly suited for binding important things. Instead of using the X and A buttons, you can instead use the wonderful back grips.
Why are these not standard already?
So the idea is that you can use your otherwise unused pinky and ring fingers to push a couple extra buttons. You don't need to take your thumb off of the right pad to use these, making them great for functions like reloading, jumping, sprinting, or anything else you would normally have to make The Claw to pull off while moving and aiming. They're a godsend, playing without ever taking your fingers off of movement or aiming is sublime. They work wonderfully and you should always be using them.
This is the best gamepad you can buy. That said, it's still a gamepad. A keyboard and mouse will give you better aim and more buttons, even if those buttons aren't exactly laid out with gaming in mind. But the Steam Controller is a ton of fun to use and way more ergonomic. It's worth the learning curve.

In similar vein to games like Super Hexagon, 140, Gauge and Duet, oO is a minimalistic game with simple objectives and simple controls - on the surface. But while things may look easy enough at first glance, the challenge comes in mastering the sparse mechanics you are given to get past whatever sadistic obstacles oO's glowing, circular world cares to throw in your direction.
With ever more complex patterns to overcome and a faster and faster rate of play, the simple "push space to flip" mechanic might only be one button but will eventually build to challenge even the fastest of reflexes. You will die again, and again, and again
; but unlike some other punishing titles of similar ilk, the deaths here don't tend to feel cheap. You'll always know why you died, and what you need to do to avoid death next time.
oO has four main levels, with four optional "drunk" levels and two endless modes which are again normal and drunk. Minimalistic, punishing games like this aren't often to everyone's liking, but I'm a huge fan of 'em and always gun for total completion before moving on. I'm currently on the final drunk level and am slowly going insane trying to complete it - but mental stability aside, oO is a fantastic little entry to the "easy to learn, punishing to master" genre, and I hugely recommend it.
So! With all the familiarities out of the way, I guess there's only one question left to ask you:
Are you ready to die?

It is a great accesory to an already vibrant ecosystem.  The controls are a little stark and confusing at first, however, after the learning curve it's sometimes hard to want to go back to mouse/keyboard for certain games.  Combining use of the right track with the gyro-sensor capability reveals some really neat gameplay options and features - it can also make precision aiming via a controller very accessible once the learning curve is overcome.  My number one gripe, which is also a plus, is the weight of the device.  It weighs so little that you feel like it is a toy, but when using it in gyro mode this is a welcome adaptation.  The joystick is what yoiu have come to expect from any controller worth it's salt.  The D-pad (left track pad) is great and can function in many ways, as can the right track pad.  Soft trigger and full pulls can both be activated as DIFFERENT actions, such as soft press on right trigger aiming down sites then pressing hte rest of the way makes you fire is a really cool feature.  The grip buttons are intuitive, easy to press, and make a tactile click.  Bumper buttons are exactly as you have come to expect with a high end controller.  I guess another complaint would be the face buttons (a,b,x,y)... they are small and semi-lack a distinctive tactile feel that you are likely used to.  Over all I love the controller, and find it be a welcome upgrade, albeit different, over most well known pc game controllers.  <3

Includes a level, scenario, ride editor, known as the toolkit.

Works out of the box on Modern Operating Systems without the use of Hex edits, Compatibility Modes, Mods, Windowed Mode hacks.

For those who dont know Windowed mode is possible through a keybind or Alt+Enter and UI Scaling is also available through a keybind.
Ive been playing the Rollercoaster Tycoon series (Not including 3 or World) since its release in 1999. Everything an original RCT fan, or a new one, could want is here in this package. Sure, its a port of a PC game to Mobile back to PC, and it shows only when the in game tutorial asks you to "tap" a menu, but other than that, I wouldnt be able to tell, nor do I care. Its so minor compared to some other mobile ports that I dont feel it matters in this case. The Interface is fresh and more modern feeling. Simple additions like scroll zoom, and time controls are welcome.
My only complaints, and they're minor at best, would be as follows:
The addition of proper audio sliders if possible.
The Ability to delete save games from within the application.
Lack of Steam Workshop integration.

Some people joke that this a $20 fast forward button, but I defy anyone who has played through Evergreen Gardens to tell me that by the end they weren't ready to fork over $20 for a fast forward button.
In all seriousness I really like this remaster. It's smoothed out a lot of the annoying technical issues I had playing the original releases of these games on modern machines. Everything feels a lot cleaner and more intuitive even than it was, and it's a real joy having all the scenarios from 1 and 2 plus the expansions of both in one place. There have been a few changes to some scenarios, which irks me since I liked them as they were, but these are minor. It's also a little annoying that, despite all the other modernizations, there is no option to switch to WASD scrolling.
All in all you probably don't need to buy this if you have the originals, but I'm not in the least sorry I did.

A young boy must escape his insane mother’s religious delusions in The Binding of Isaac, an action rogue-like that plays like the original 2d Zelda series. In this game, you play the young protagonist (Isaac) and must delve through various dungeons defeating enemies and bosses until you reach the game’s initial final boss, with other final encounters unlockable as you play and complete the game.
Gameplay is similar to the first Zelda game in that you are in a top-down dungeon with 1-4 doors per room. Different however is that Isaac’s main weapon is his tears, a projectile that can gain different properties and enhancements depending on which power-ups you pick up. Map layout and item placement is very RNG-dependent so you might get a really good set of items on one run and get totally shafted on the next one. Many items and bosses are locked at the beginning of play and will gradually become available as you complete challenges.
Binding of Isaac is a great “pick up and go” game. It’s very easy to learn but also contains quite a bit of challenge under the hood. The bosses are total bullet sponges so you should try to get anything capable of enhancing your damage if you want to finish them in a reasonable amount of time. Also, as mentioned earlier, the RNG can be quite cruel as per a typical rogue-like, so expect to start over a lot. For the most part though, this game is fun and won’t take a whole lot of your time per playthrough. Try it!

I have never played Drakengard or the first NieR, but I can definitely say that this game is a masterpiece in its own way. The gameplay is an ARPG (Action Role-playing game) w/c features an open world, bullet-hell/hack and slash style with lots of secrets packed into 1 amazing game. The story is beautifully made, filled with lots of emotion and roller coaster rides (literally. there's an amusement park level.), One minute, you're happily doing main quests and side quests, but then the story hits you. It's not all happy moments, but there is an underlying message in the dialogue (you just have to play it so you can see why).
Overall, the gameplay is quite solid. It's neither too easy nor too hard, you just have to be, as they say, "GIT GUD" in order for you to make progress in the game. It's perfectly catered to casual gamers and hardcore gamers alike (there's an easy mode, where pretty much the AI plays it for you. But I prefer normal mode since I like quite a bit of a challenge in the games I play). It has rpg elements wherein you can make different types of builds for different playstyles or overall general farming (yes, this game can be a bit grindy because of the plug-in chips and materials to upgrade weapons and pods).
The only negative I experienced in this game is the horrible port (not optimized for PC gameplay). FPS issues (but I guess that's my own fault since I don't have a good GPU) but that was remedied by using the FAR mod located in the discussions.
Well, enough of me rambling on about this masterpiece. Play it, it's definitely worth it.

Just to start off, I played this game on normal mode using mouse and keyboard. It took me 36 hours to complete endings A B  C and D, which are sequential and make up the main storyline. Now I am going through a second playthrough on hard using a controller. There is some dislike for playing the game on keyboard which is deserved. I would say that playing with a keyboard is marginally worse for most of the game, and much worse during hacking (minigame) and flight suit (shooter/bullet hell) portions of the game, which overall makes up around 3-5% of the total playtime.
Overall it's a very interesting game that has a couple of minor flaws. The story and soundtrack are both perfect and the combat is good enough to tie the game together into a pretty pleasing experience (even on keyboard). You can chain together moves pretty nicely and it's very satisfying (and good looking) when you can pull off some chained moves on your enemies.
Main flaw is as others have probably said, normal mode feels pretty easy while hard is extremely annoying to play. Main culprit in this is 1HKO moves. I got 1 hit killed a single time on normal (getting ending C). Contrast that to hard, where the boss at the end of the opening can kill you in one hit with any of his moves and takes a good 5 minutes to kill. This is especially annoying since if you die at any point in the ~20-40 minute opening you have to start over from the beginning. Hard also changes some stuff up subtly. There were a couple more enemies, and it feels like their patterns are slightly different and your hitbox is slightly bigger, which is fine I guess.
Other flaw is the subquest system. You can have as many subquests as you like at any given time, and they're all marked the exact same way on your map (some of them even mark 3 different places or more). This means unless you finish every quest as soon as you get them, you'll end up with 10 red dots on your map and no way of knowing what each points to without pausing, looking at the full map, then mousing over each location to see what they are, and finally marking the one you actually want to do. This problem is worsened by quests like Robo Dojo and Half-Wit Inventor which stick through multiple endings and require you to be reasonably far through the game to complete.
There are a few more minor issues. Loading screens are 20 seconds. Every. Single. Time. Since it only takes a minute or two to sprint across the whole map, "fast" travel is really a joke, and helps make sidequests tedious. Cutscenes are 30fps and in worse resolution than the game itself. The game itself is capped at 60fps and sometimes you'll even lose some of those frames for no reason. The game also crashes the during the first time you enter the amusement park (happened in two separate playthroughs at the exact same spot).
TLDR:
Keyboard is good enough, makes dodge worse and ranged/shooting (5%) portions terrible
PROS:
CONS:
In conclusion 4/5. The game is very nice and has a couple minor issues. Worth playing even for the story by itself.

I'm honestly a little taken aback at how many negative reviews this is garnering thus far.  I play quite a bit of minecraft, and found this to be quite the charming little beginning. While much more light-hearted than other tell-tale series (which does not, in my opinion, mean this is the 'kids' tell-tale game), it stays true to the minecraft universe and does a great job characterizing the mains. The story was interesting, has a few neat turns for an old alpha-build minecrafter like me, and I look forward to see where the tale goes from here.
To address some of the common complaints in other reviews, I felt the voice acting was fine, and the graphics definitely fit with the source material.  Really. If you complain about minecraft's graphics, then you aren't going to like this one bit. I also found the mouth syncing to be a little off towards the end, though that might just be my computer.
The only real complaint I have is that the price point is a bit high, but that's a complaint I've always had with the tell-tale games series; one that eventually goes away when the chapters are bundled together. (Edit: episodes are bundled together, so price point is fine.)
All in all, I really enjoyed this, and I look forward to seeing the rest.

Minecraft: Story Mode has been a little shallow and frankly, dull so far, but it has the feel of a game that is gearing up for more action and adventure. So in short the first chapter of this story series has been "meh" but it ended with me finding myself engrossed and wanting the next chapter, which is a good thing.
I love the comments from some people about how the game is made of cheap graphics and flat figures and such, or how this is only for little kids. Obviously these comments are from people who have either never played Minecraft, or are oblivious to the Minecraft universe. Knock knock, there's a big following for Minecraft, and it's certainly not all children. Telltale is gearing this MSM game towards both audiences, which is good, but the adults who play Minecraft should be picking up on the more serious aspects from the Minecraft game as well.
In the end, I recommend the game only to those who have played Minecraft. If you haven't, you may still enjoy it but it probably won't go as deep for you. Also, don't expect too much whiz-bang for the first episode...it'll pick up pace.

Its not a bad game exactly, but even when all 5 episodes come out I doubt it will be worth the price. The again, that is a subjective matter, and perhaps the next episode will be longer. My verdict: the jury is out.
As an aside, I am somewhat disapointed that so many other reviews of the game are somewhat ageist.

Redoing my review for the 3rd time now after playing the latest version of the game. Keep in mind I have 300+ hours on the original game and 80 on this one. Love the developers behind the game and the community that plays it, etc.
Here's why PCE is better than the original PC:
- Still has developers devoted to it.
- Loadouts, DLC, gamemodes, and a new class.
- Plenty of class and weapon choices.
- It has an economy made up of skins and hats.
Here's why it ain't:
- Controls feel like PC did a metric ton of meth.
- Seriously, the controls are worse than if I tried playing PC blindfolded, drunk, and hung upside down.
- Some of the new mechanics I mentioned earlier don't make much a difference.
- The diverse choices of classes and weapons are either fairly similar to one another or just lazily made.
- Economy is a very bloated feature. There's plenty of it, but only a few good items belong in it. Not to mention humans get little-to-no-attention in DLC. DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME IF YOUR MAINLY INTERESTED IN THE ECONOMY. Seriously, there's a big, big chance you'll be disappointed with what you don't get.
- Servers aren't the best if you are out of the states/europe. Anywhere else in the world and your kinda burdened with lag.
- While the map design is eye-candy in this game, they really aren't balanced.
- Since release, the biggest content update is ANOTHER new Tyrant and a single gamemode containing only one map. The gamemode is fun for a while but does get repetitive and pointless after the first few minutes of playing it.
- There's only going to be one more big update for a VERY long time as the developers are going to halt any development on the game to work on PS4 port.
- Again, the controls. They're cringeworthy bad on the dinosaurs. A freaking human can circle-strife a raptor. Dilophosaurs can just barely sprint to catch a human.
- Human hit-detection is pretty poor. Aiming feels sluggish.
- The animations for humans and any other animations that aren't featured in the original game are pretty bad. The only good animations are recycled from an animator who has left the team.
I really tried to like this game and I'm going to keep on trying because the majority seem to find this game good. I want to think the game is good since I did love the original and the devs who are making this game. Maybe I'm missing something but this game is probably one of the worst I own in my library.
As of 7/28/15, I suggest you don't buy this.

Hello,
So I am one of the people who ended up buying Primal Carnage while it was on sale to get the discount on Primal Carnage: Extinction. I am simply making this post to provide some feedback for the game.
Before I give some feedback I will say that I enjoy this game and that I think it has A LOT of potential. Some people ingame tried to get me to compare this to Orion and to that I simply say that Orion is more of a Killing Floor style game where zombies were replaced with dinosaurs and the people were put in Halo suits and some vehicles tossed in. In other words comparing Orion to Primal Carnage is just silly because you can't compare player controlled dinosaurs to computer controlled.
1) Dinosaur View. The most mind boggling thing I immediately noticed when playing is that dinosaur's don't have a first person view. It hurt my insides, badly. There is another game where players are given the choice between playing as an alien creature or as a human and that game is called Natural Selection (or Natural Selection 2) that some of you may be familiar with and while I'm not comparing this games all I have to say is that the aliens in that game are first person view and that is a feeling that dwarfs 3rd person view beyond words. I need my dinosaur immersion. I need first person view as a dinosaur.
2) Communication. There is none. Humans need some form of Radio Menu where they can talk to each other in order to point out dinosaurs. This radio menu can be as simple as "I see a dinosaur over here" to let everyone know.
3) Game Modes. I tried two game modes, Team DeathMatch and Get To The Chopper. My TDM experience was as expected, a lot of killing followed by a lot more killing. GTTC consisted of all the humans standing behind this unpassable barrier as snipers shooting at an entire dinosaur team of flying dinosaurs, not the best. When I saw this game through videos and screenshots and before I blindly bought it I thought that this game would be a small scale tactical game of dinosaurs vs. humans. Perhaps a 5v5 or something where the humans would have to hold an area while dinosaurs tried to push them out or something. I hope there will be something in the future because I think this game has A LOT of potential in the competitive field.
4) Weapons. Ok so humans are hardcore dinosaur hunting and killing machines... who hipfire? We need iron sights, I feel like a small child at an arcade shooting my gun in every direction.
5) Limitation. Dinosaurs are a pretty fierce force to be reckon with from the start, now make their entire team T-Rex and it is essentially a wall of teeth coming at you and you won't be able to kill them before you reload. Default limitation should be put on larger dinosaurs such as a MAX of 2 large dinosaurs and perhaps a MAX of 3 flying dinosaurs.
6) Mobility. Rather than have humans run at the speed of The Flash it would be much more beneficial if there were climbable ladders, treehouses, more open buildings for us to maneuver through and hide inside. I feel like my only option is to run at lightning speed instead of using the enviornment to my advantage.
7) Destruction. Since my previous feedback of humans needing more enviornmental mobility such as climbing ladders and treehouses than dinosaurs would need equal footing because the only dinosaur that can reach anywhere off the ground are the flying ones. Larger dinosaurs (or even the charging one) should be able to ram trees or whatever building the human climbed up and knock them down either killing or injuring the human. This would provide a more ever changing enviornment which players have to constantly adapt to in order to win.
That is my basic feedback on what I think this game could use in order to create a true action packed experience of a real survival of the fittest.
While I also notice some balance issues such as the flying dinosaur being able to pick up players non-stop without risk and the raptors being able to pounce on humans risk-free I think that perhaps the humans should have an escape method from this pin instead of being helpless. This suggestion of course would encourage a lack of teamwork since the humans could just go solo if they were able to escape from such a pin but the flying dinosaur is able to fly away just as fast as he arrived while carrying a full grown human in his talons which makes saving the human almost impossible. The raptors are immobile while doing their pin so I can understand why you can't break out but the flying dinosaurs need a significant speed reduction after abducting a human.
Thanks for taking the time to read this, if you did.
