suggest you purchase this game if it's on sale for $5.00 or less. While I did enjoy the game, it is by no means worth their $10.00 asking price. I rate the games I play depending on if I feel it was worth what I spent. I got this game for approximately $1.50 and feel it was worth the money.
This game isn't a brain teaser. You won't spend hours and hours on difficult puzzles. The game flies by extremely fast because almost all of the puzzles are very straightforward and quick to solve. Which is good and bad, depending on the player. If you're like me, you want to be challenged and feel clever at the end of a puzzle game. You want to feel like you really accomplished something. This game doesn't give you that at all. This is more of a relax and play some easy puzzles with the SO when there's nothing on TV. In being relaxed and straightforward it does a very good job. The gameplay doesn't feel rushed and doesn't require a lot of concentration like Portal does. There are only two or three puzzles that actually require you to move quickly or decisively, the rest of the time you can just mosey your way through.
What story? I'm sorry, but that was pretty well pointless. I ended up making up my own story as I went along to make it a bit more interesting than a few lines of text at the beginning and end of the game.
I also couldn't figure out if the end goal was to finish the puzzle or collect all of the data nodes. It seemed like I could complete the puzzle just fine and then it wasn't until much later that I got a splash telling me I needed to collect X more nodes before I could go to the next level. For me, they were just the nodes on that level, so I'm not sure if it changes depending on how many I have or not. I guess collecting nodes is the end goal since it sounds like I can't progress without enough, but the game itself isn't very clear on that at the start since I finished a puzzle or two accidentally without all the nodes.
Let's start at the very beginning. The Tutorial was a little on the light side. I don't know if I missed a bit of it or not, but you can click on the spawning spots for the cubes and it will spit out another one if you accidentally throw your current one out of reach. Like I say, I don't know if I just missed the text or if it wasn't there, but it was a key aspect of the game I missed out on for a good seven or eight levels before I accidentally stumbled across it, restarting the level each time I lost my cube. Besides that I suppose it served it's purpose. Told you how to move, pick up/throw, and the primary objectives. There were no ways to check/change/reset keybindings from inside of the game and NO WAY TO CHANGE THE MOUSE SENSITIVITY! Holy cow it was WAY too high for my taste and I couldn't seem to find a way to turn it down until I went into Razer Synapse and lowered my mouse's sensitivity manually.
The keybindings for the controller were extremely awkward as well, and like I said, no way to change them from inside of the game itself. (It doesn't help that I usually don't use a controller.)
The sockets where you put the cubes are buggy as all getout. Some of them will snag the cube from half the room away, some will only grab it if you literally hit it directly, and others will grab it and then drop it or pull it toward them and then let it go to fall into the black abyss and make you walk all the way back to the spawn for the cube. They're extremely inconsistent. For instance, on one level, you have to throw the cube across the room and hit a moving socket. I must have wasted a dozen cubes trying to get it. I would get it, and then it would just bounce off of the socket and leave me raging. I managed to hit it directly two times before it finally grabbed it.
The way the cubes interact with the jump plates is also buggy. Frequently (35-40% of the time) the cube will literally just plop down on the jump plate and sit there. Then most of the time you aren't even able to get the cube back from the plate, particularly if it's a turnable jump plate, you'll just sit there spam right-clicking trying to pick up your god forsaken cube while the pad does a rendition of Dead or Alive's only good song.*
The walls are made of tar. When you strafe into them or walk perpendicular to them when using a controller (Because I guess you're always strafing with a controller?) they will stop/slow you, like getting stuck on fly paper. They do the same thing to the cube, freezing it in place and yanking it out of your hands, frequently over a pit, next to a pit, or in a pit.
This might seem minor, until you find it happening constantly. It does ware on your nerves. I assume this contributes a bit to the lack of physics when it comes to the cube bouncing/rolling. When you throw it against a wall it's as if you threw it full force into a stack of pillows.
The cubes also have a tendency to disappear randomly after hitting something hard (usually after falling a long distance.)
In the end, to play this, you need to be relaxed. You can't be taking it seriously (as I was at first), because the little bugs will drive you absolutely batshit.
Now for the good aspects of the gameplay!
Throwing is awesome and it adds a good mechanic to the game, making it less of a Portal clone.  The puzzles were diverse enough to keep me interested. They weren't all carbon copies of the last, and the introduction to new mechanics every couple of levels made for a nice little changeup once in a while (Such as the Crazy Cube Color Changer
or the rotating jump plates.) The variety (Red and Blue) of cubes added a small extra level of complexity, rather than a one cube fits all approach. If the creators were to do any more work, I would love to see green and yellow cubes implemented as well.
The footsteps and music are extremely repetative. I muted all sounds after half hour and turned on some Devildriver. If there were more variety in the music and footsteps it wouldn't have bugged me as much.
Before I get into the Co-Op. I did the co-op, all of it, by myself. I plugged in a controller and it took me about forty-five minutes. I did it mostly for the challenge and to see if Co-Op were as Co-Op as advertised. To be fair, there are four missions (If I recall correctly) that were genuinely difficult alone and designed to be done with two people playing. Most of the others were pretty well a solo run with a tagalong that would throw a block up to a high place once in a while. None of them really required any interactive coordination between the two players. Really the only time I would have needed someone were the levels where you have to avoid blocks/lasers at the same time. There were no
moments.

Stellaris excels other titles as it presents one of the best "exploration" phase among them, it offers an interesting variety among species (thanks to its genetic trait system) and civilizations (related to the ethical characterization of that empire) and the final phase of the game is quite of a challenge thanks to its "crisis".
As a Paradox game it's evolving continuosly from its release with new content and additions, both free and in DLCs. We've seen great improvements so far (Nov'17) in politics, both internal (factions) and as a "galaxy actor" (traditions), and almost every aspect of the game has been improved and received new content: planet types and colonization, ship design, buildings and space structures, etc. And warfare is expected to be revised in the next months; and if we know other games from this company like Europa Universalis or Crusader Kings, we should expect an improvement in diplomacy and economy.
Oh, and it's a really beautiful game. It's easy to keep staring at a pulsar or a black hole while your fleets are engaging a massive ship from an Awakened Empire...

Paul Heyman said, he wanted to show me his new finisher. The casting agent said to me, that I myself was already out there cutting a promo and I shouldn't interupt myself! Wrestler B is never mentioned again.
Add to that many bugs. I had match against Dash Wilder. The match started, Dash and Lilian Garcia in the ring, me at ringside. Then the game crashed. I got stuck there. Thanks 2k.
In short: Mycareer is not worth it.

So, 90% of the moves! are hidden in lootboxes. You want to go from technican to using springboard attacks? Tough luck! You can unlock the skill, but won't have any! moves, if you aren't lucky. Running attack, kick kick, running attack.

Performance:
Using a midrange i5, 16 gb of ram, NVidia 970 GT, and up to date drivers, I have suffered No Lag running this on maximum settings 1080p Resolution (I don't own a 4k monitor). My Average frame rate is between 55 and 60. People complaining about the game running poorly are running it on wooden PC's or need to update their drivers.
Bugs:
Okay... I'll admit that the game has some bugs as of release. However, I have not suffered a single crash, most of the bugs are graphical (sometimes in conversations backstage, their arms twitch a little). I have not had the experience lessened by any bugs encountered.
Gameplay:
The game is solid. It is exactly the same as the last few years but with improvements. The reversal system is unforgiving and the prompts are inconsistant but it is not game breaking at all (although it can be annoying, its still very playable. learn to predict instead of watching for prompts if it bothers you). I still win the majority of matches I have participated in, but it almost always feels like an ordeal, which is what a game should do.
Character Creation:
This is where this game SHINES above the competition. This character creation suite is the best one to date. At first I was underwhelmed because of the 'Framework' character creation in the story mode, but when I got into the story and went into Edit, I was blown away. There is an endless amount of character customization and you can modify everything from the shape of the corner of a single eye to the amount of bulk you want to appear on your butt. If RPG's had a character creation suite like this, it would be a major selling feature. Move set creation for your character is incredibly detailed, and you can get very in depth with the way your character fights in the ring. It is possible to spend 4+ hours on making a single character if you want to, and it would not be time wasted.
Story Mode:
This game did something I did not expect, it somehow made wrestling an RPG. The Story mode is very well put together and there is a lot of branching paths which overall give an indepth experience. I will admit that there are times where it is tedious (as in, there is a lot of wrestling matches, but thats why we buy a wrestling game), but I've greatly enjoyed the experience. I think that it will have a surprising amount of replayability.
Multiplayer:
Multiplayer is solid, I have played a few matches and there was not many issues outside of the usual multiplayer stuff. This is a good game to stuff around on with friends.
Universe Mode:
This mode is the same as every other year, which is a good thing. Enjoy making your own wrestling world with its own storylines. Nothing bad to say about this, its what you would expect and its good fun.
Progression:
Much of the hate that this game has recieved comes from players who don't like having to earn the 'Overly strong omega kill everything move', but feel that it should be given to them from the start. This game makes players earn the more impressive moves through random drops and spending experience (there is NO Microtransactions, so players have to play to become awesome). This actually works pretty well because it makes players who have awesome moves shine online because its clear that they have put a lot of love into their characters. Also the random nature of moves unlocked this way means that no two characters ever have the same moves. I think this is a positive thing, its a shame the majority of teenagers who want to instantly be able to throw 'Big Show' though the ring seem to disagree.
Overall:
This is a solid game, one of the best of the 2k series, and definately worth the money spent. I think that anyone who really gets into the guts of this game will find that the negative press surrounding it is not only largely unfounded, but at times outright wrong.  I suggest anyone who enjoyed any other of the 2k series to give it a try, or if you have never played a wrestling game but are interested, this game has a lot to offer.

Today, people prefer quick and easy games with a lot of positive response. Many meaningless games become so popular, while many good games are not cared by the main public. This game is full of thinking and withstand hours of reptrspection and rumination. It is open-ended, invocative, and inspiring.
In Sherryl Vint's book "Science Fiction: A Guide For the Perplexed," she purposed the science fictions should provide an imaginary perspective that readers and rethink the existence of themselve and the world. NeiR: Automata, as a game, successfuly achieves the requirement of good science fictions. In fact, the definition of science fiction has already transformed from merely novels to films. The next step is games. Yes, games are not considered serious today. Remember, however, when novels first emerged in Britain, they are also considered as an inferior style of literature. After hundreds of years of developements, novel has become an indispensible for of literature. One day, people will also analyze games as seriously as they analyze books.
Popular games are not necessarily good, and good games are not necessarily popular. A good game should not only be interesting but also be able to inspire players. I have played many games before, and I am satisfied with a few of them. I find that many game developers just want to attracted more customers and make more money. If the purpose of a company is not to make good games but just money, it can never make good games. I considered this as a result of consumerism culture. At a time the everying is getting faster and faster, we are deprieved of the time to stop and retrospect. That's a huge lost. However, NieR:Automata is different from most popular games. It provided players time to think and to introspect.
What makes up a good game is not just fancy CG, but essential ideas under it. NeiR: Automata is a game worth playing and thinking. In the torrent of stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t games that only aim at players wallets, NieR:Automata stand amid like strong statue, always reminding players the importance of deep thinking and introspection. Oneday, the statue will also fall. A single game cannot resist the power of trend. However, the most important thing is not the result but the process. The meaning of the existence of NieR:Automata is that it tells us what a good game should be like inspires future game developers to make games that worthing playing and thinking. If I am so lucky and become a member of a game development team in the future, I will told the director: I want make games as good as NieR:Automata.
For better understanding of this game, I recommend two books:
Vint, Sherryl. Science Fiction: A Guide for the Perplexed.  Bloomsbury Academic, 2015
The Wesleyan Anthology of Science Fiction, edited by Arthur B. Evans, et.al., Wesleyan University Press, 2010

Well, what I intend to do for the most part is share my experience with the overall performance of the game, which has been basically hated on for as long as I can remember. While reading the other reviews I was actually thinking of not buying the game, just based on the issues that other people were having. Though I went for the risk and I don't regret it at all. I'm playing on a laptop system (more specifically an MSI GS63VR) equipped with an i7 6700HQ and a GTX 1060 6GB graphics card. And from just the beginning I haven't had any performance issues so far. The game started up in windowed mode, but only when I first launched it, went into the settings, changed the resolution to 1080p and fullscreen mode and I was good to go. As written in other reviews, no black bars have appeared on the sides of my screen and the game runs completely fine on fullscreen mode. I'm playing on High settings with no MSAA, and have been getting stable 60 fps throughout the areas I've played in the game, except for the times, where there's a lot of vegetation (the fps drops to 55 for a couple of seconds), but there is no visible stuttering in the gameplay, so that didn't bother me at all. I haven't used any of the user-made patches for the game, as I just didn't feel the need of them. Hopefully after reading this, you might reconsider not buying this game just because you were scared of the performance issues, which as stated many times in other reviews, haven't been patched by the game's developer.
Other than that I think that this is a gorgeous game, with awesome graphics, fighting mechanics, and a pretty cool story. And if you love RPG style slasher/adventure games, I do recommend you to try it.
I hope that this review has been helpful! Cheers!

This game is such an awesome idea. It suffers from a couple of deal breakers.
Some of the words that it seems to expect you to know (or have a decent chance of knowing, i.e., treasure chests) are humorously archaic. Each chest that I came to (a dozen or so), the word they were going for was quite out-of-grasp, even with someone with a decent vocabulary and scrabble-related skillset. Here is one that comes to mind, and it wasn't even the worst example:
Dogship - The character, or individuality, of a dog.
Now, I'm sure the dozen-or-so people throughout history who have had occasion to use the word "dogship" in a meaningful way find it a perfectly good word, and I wouldn't argue with them. But it is a word that is, perhaps, unrealistic to expect to leap into mind when you only have 20 seconds to spend trying to figure out a particular 7-letter sequence.
It is a great scrabble word. For a quiz-type challenge (where there is really only a single right answer), it is a really silly word to use. Perhaps I had a run of bad luck, but almost every treasure chest or "save-your-life" challenge that I came up against, it was a word like this. Going to Zen mode didn't really get rid of that particular problem, it just seems to give you more time.
Perhaps the author used a database of words of various challenge levels for this challenge. In that case, I'd strongly recommend curating that list. It is great to use challenging words, but not necessarily archaic. Even the words that most people consider "vocab words" are possible to fit into everyday conversation. These words are on another level of obscurity.
As other folks have pointed out, it is near-impossible to pay attention to what is going on up with the fight, since most of the time you are hunting for words to use. Perhaps a mechanic more interesting than just a count-down timer would improve the overall experience. Maybe a more turn-based approach would give people time to appreciate the other aspects of what is going on.

Have you ever heard someone say a game is "deceptively simple" and wondered what that means? This game will answer that for you. I can't tell you how many times during the course of play I stopped, smiled, and thought "Huh! Clever!" The main mechanic is somewhat unique, but the implementation and level design is where this game shines. If you stop and think about what you need to accomplish, the "puzzle" solves itself with a little bit of platforming savvy. I say "puzzle" because deep down this is a puzzle game disguised as a platformer. The enemies are just obstacles to overcome as you try to get from A to B. There are plenty of secrets to warrant a second playthrough (though I haven't done that yet), and just a TINY bit of backtracking, so I guess this could loosely be classified as Metroidvania, but it has a personality all its own. This is well worth the price of admission, even though I played through it in a little over an hour.
If you have a couple of bucks you were GOING to spend on coffee, skip that and buy this. You'll thank me later.

If you don't already know, Open RCT is a free, open source project of the original RCT 2, but with innovation. It has multiplayer. I can't repeat that enough. It was multiplayer. It is both my favorite controller ever and a somewhat flawed, unintuitive controller. It has now allowed me to only need a single controller for my computer, but there's also things that are somewhat halfbaked.
The right pad is incredible. It's great! It allows for so much. But the left pad is a harder argument to make, especially at the expense of a traditional d-pad. And the left pad's attempt to emulate one, regardless of click or no click, is ultimately subpar (play a game with grid base movement that'll kill you for one false move like Lisa.)
The shoulder buttons are not as ergonomic as other modern controllers, and how it "clicks" is uncomfortable. Clicking in the pads are uncomfortable, squeezing the paddles are uncomfortable.
Feature wise the controller beats the crap out of the competition. Even a DS4 running DS4Windows can't compete. But in terms of comfort, it's pretty far down on the ladder. Hopefully Valve will continue to work on the controller and have revisions that take into consideration what critics have said about it.

Alright, so 2K18 isn't bad, it's just not a large enough jump from 2K17 to warrant a purchase, most definitely not a purchase at full price.
The good:
Creative content is at it's peak, probably in the history of SvR/WWE games. The amount of content you can create is humongous, and it looks great.
CAWs look great in the menu, a good CAW will not look out of place among other WWE superstars. This is huge for me, and I know others who like custom immersion in the game.
The bad:
Single player modes are so damn dull. MyCareer is easily one of the worst iterations in the history of the game. Their approach to go pseudo-RPG was interesting; however, long load times, the inability to truly "run" so you just briskly walk everywhere, boring promo systems that are too easy to master, and a crappy story that gets too repetitive destroys the mode.
Universe brings the "new" (to anyone who never played old school SvR games) power rankings system, but superstars goals are so limited and linear it's ridiculous. It's typically either "I WANT TO DEFEND MY BELT!", "I WANT TO WIN A BELT!", or "I DON'T WANT TO SUCK!" - it makes it so nobody stands out, I wish there were more options like "I want to turn heel!" "I want to start a rivalry" "I feel underused on the roster" - I think it was 2008's SvR that made this happen, so it's definitely possible but just not happening, which is unacceptable.
Yet another year where so much time is spent on solely improving the graphics of some characters, and the arena, fans, and ambiance is kicked under the table. I'm sure if I could see John Cena, he would look amazing on my computer, but instead all I see are the same boring crowds and choppy arenas.
OVERALL:
I can't recommend this at $60. If you are buying it this early, you're probably just in it for CAWs, go for it, it's an enjoyable system and I feel it's better this year. If you're buying this for the single player aspect, specifically MyCareer, this is a huge flop. Grab it when it's cheaper.

Just to start off, I played this game on normal mode using mouse and keyboard. It took me 36 hours to complete endings A B  C and D, which are sequential and make up the main storyline. Now I am going through a second playthrough on hard using a controller. There is some dislike for playing the game on keyboard which is deserved. I would say that playing with a keyboard is marginally worse for most of the game, and much worse during hacking (minigame) and flight suit (shooter/bullet hell) portions of the game, which overall makes up around 3-5% of the total playtime.
Overall it's a very interesting game that has a couple of minor flaws. The story and soundtrack are both perfect and the combat is good enough to tie the game together into a pretty pleasing experience (even on keyboard). You can chain together moves pretty nicely and it's very satisfying (and good looking) when you can pull off some chained moves on your enemies.
Main flaw is as others have probably said, normal mode feels pretty easy while hard is extremely annoying to play. Main culprit in this is 1HKO moves. I got 1 hit killed a single time on normal (getting ending C). Contrast that to hard, where the boss at the end of the opening can kill you in one hit with any of his moves and takes a good 5 minutes to kill. This is especially annoying since if you die at any point in the ~20-40 minute opening you have to start over from the beginning. Hard also changes some stuff up subtly. There were a couple more enemies, and it feels like their patterns are slightly different and your hitbox is slightly bigger, which is fine I guess.
Other flaw is the subquest system. You can have as many subquests as you like at any given time, and they're all marked the exact same way on your map (some of them even mark 3 different places or more). This means unless you finish every quest as soon as you get them, you'll end up with 10 red dots on your map and no way of knowing what each points to without pausing, looking at the full map, then mousing over each location to see what they are, and finally marking the one you actually want to do. This problem is worsened by quests like Robo Dojo and Half-Wit Inventor which stick through multiple endings and require you to be reasonably far through the game to complete.
There are a few more minor issues. Loading screens are 20 seconds. Every. Single. Time. Since it only takes a minute or two to sprint across the whole map, "fast" travel is really a joke, and helps make sidequests tedious. Cutscenes are 30fps and in worse resolution than the game itself. The game itself is capped at 60fps and sometimes you'll even lose some of those frames for no reason. The game also crashes the during the first time you enter the amusement park (happened in two separate playthroughs at the exact same spot).
TLDR:
Keyboard is good enough, makes dodge worse and ranged/shooting (5%) portions terrible
PROS:
CONS:
In conclusion 4/5. The game is very nice and has a couple minor issues. Worth playing even for the story by itself.

Genuinely the best controller I have ever used, hands down. It's weird going back to the Xbox or PS4 controllers.
Despite the odd look, the controller is very comfortable and all the buttons feel perfectly placed. If you are used to the Xbox or PlayStation controller the button placements and size may be off putting, but really once you have quickly adjusted to their new placement they are very easy and nice to press In fact I prefer the smaller sized buttons they have gone for the ABXY. Truthfully you won't be using them very often anyway as the grip buttons will replace the majority of uses for them. You need to press A repeatedly in a section? Map it to the grip button and it is far easier and less fatiguing to repeatedly hammer on it. Plus it leaves your thumb on top of the camera so you can still freely move.
Speaking of the camera control, the touch pads are superb. Using the right touch pad as trackball makes using the camera in any game substantially better. It reacts to every small movement you make, allowing you to track enemies better in your cross hairs far more naturally that with a joystick on controllers. Using that in conjunction with the gyroscope aiming, it's IMO better than using a mouse, you really get a feel for it and can even counteract the gun jumping around whilst barely thinking about what your hands are doing. It brings back that thing you did as a kid where you would move the controller in a certain direction as you where moving the car or aiming a gun because it feels more natural.
On top of this the triggers are also fantastic, they have a shorted travel time than the Xbox One controller, but that is also, IMO, far better. The Xbox controller feels like they should stop about 2/3 before they do, where as this feels great. Having the physical button at the end allows you to be really creative and satisfying with what you bind to each action on the controller. Adding to this the haptic feedback and you can place a second trigger on the trigger and have it do whatever, and it feels just like you're hitting an actual bump in the controller.
In fact the haptic feedback in the controller as a whole is great, the trackball mode feels just like an actual trackball and putting haptics on the analogue stick response curve also feels fantastic. The only downside you might possibly have is that they can make some noise, but you can turn that off in the software so it really shouldn't be an issue, and even if you do notice it at first it just fades into the background very quickly. The interesting thing about the haptics is that the controller now feels weird without it, as if my brain has just naturally decided that this object mores when you push it, so when you turn it off and the controller doesn't do that anymore, your brain is just like 'what that isn't how thing works' for a minute. It's kind of odd and fascinating, but it goes away after a while if you do want to play something without haptics.
For anyone worrying about the shape of the controller, please don't. I have very regular hands. Pretty much middle of the road and I have to say everything feels perfectly places. The shape of the handles fits great and naturally flow my hands into the correct position they should be in to rest right in the centre of the touch pads. From there my thumbs can happily reach all the buttons between the touch pads. With an ever so slight stretch you can reach the steam button, which I feel is how it should be, you should never be able to accidentally press the Steam/PlayStation/Xbox button on any controller. My fingers also fit perfectly into the gentle grove that is put into the triggers, making them very comfortable, with the bumpers being a short reach away, not where near being a painful reach that is can be on some controllers. The grips also have brilliant placement, my pinkie fingers nicely fits below them so I will always have one of my fingers curled around it, but really it doesn't even need that. With the general design of the controllers placing you thumbs into the centre of the touch pads you don't need to push or pull on the sides of the controller; it genuinely does just sit in your hands without any effort or strain coming to play no matter how many hours you pour into the thing.
The build quality is also great. It doesn't creak or groan at all no matter how much I try and squeeze, pull and twist on it. It has glossy parts but cleverly it is in only the places where your fingers don't press onto the controller when holding it normally. You shouldn't need to worry about those parts getting smudges unless you are holding it really strangely. The back plate that has the grips on doesn't move at all once placed, feeling like its just part of the controller, and it is simple to remove (yet practically impossible to accidentally remove). When you want to get at the batteries inside, which are also simple to remove. Speaking of the batteries, they last for ages in this controller. I've had the controller since its full release on the 10th November and now at 1AM on the 14th the batteries still say they are at 100% (and I don't believe they are lying). That's very impressive and I'm actually looking forward to them running out just to see how long they do last.
Finally, the software. The software for this product is very impressing, allowing for huge flexibility with pretty intuitive ways of editing them, as long as you read the descriptions and learn how to use it. It has a small learning curve, but in reality it isn't as big as it seems. There are some really neat tricks that you can do with it, like having one touch pad act as a massive set of virtual buttons that you can visualize on screen for MMO type games, or by having the touch pad act as an iPod style click wheel for scrolling through webpages in desktop mode. In fact using this in desktop mode is perhaps my favourite use for it. It has literally turned into my mouse, controller, keyboard and IR remote  for my everyday casual lean back content consumption, allowing me to just lean back and not be hunched over the computer desk all day every day.
If you’re interested in any of that, please buy this controller, you won’t regret it!

I thought I'd give this game a try because it wasn't terribly expensive, and I enjoy word games even though I'm not terribly great at them.
What I like about this game is that you can keep all your exp and characters so they'll progressively get stronger as you go along, but you will probably have to play over and over. There's a lot of character types to unlock and level up, and the word games are varied so that you're not really doing the same thing over and over.
It's true that when you're "fighting" with an enemy you can't really keep track of who's getting hit because you're usually too busy trying to find words. However, you can encounter things that heal you: level-up fountains (I think there's 1 per level), medicine men (heal for a fee), and potion shops. You also have characters who can heal if you can activate their skills. Even if you don't pay attention though and the character runs out of health, he enters last stand mode, where you can recover half or all of his/her health by making a big word. So, if you're really good at spelling, or just use a scrabble solver in another window you can effectively never die.
I don't know if the equipment works because I don't see their inventory, so I just click things that look nice and try to give them to my characters kind of by their job, but really this game is just about finding words and feeling good when you can recognize something longer than 3 letters.
I have fun playing it, and it's easy enough that I can even get my g/f to give it a try... and she only likes board games.

A weight, at Madras 500 pounds, at Bombay 560 pounds."

This game is not perfect, but it is definitely fun and at the price, it's worth playing if you enjoy anagram-type puzzles at all.
Video Critique:
Pros:
+Gorgeous visuals
+Excellent sound
+Gameplay mechanics work well and are quite well balanced
+The randomization of the levels is well done
+The characters are persistent, and retain their experience, stats, and upgrades from playthrough to playthrough
To use your character's abilities and deal damage, you must use the colored tiles on the board when you spell a word. Each member of your party has their own color. Using more than one tile of the same color in a single word causes your characters to use more powerful abilities. While you're hunting for words, the opponent is attacking you, slowly wearing down your health. You move from place to place in a neverending randomly generated linear landscape. Most locations will contain a monster to fight, but now and then you'll come across blacksmiths where you can upgrade your stats with weapons and armor, potion shops where you can buy up to three potions (healing, and various types of defense and offense), chests which you open by solving an anagram, traps which you disable by trying to use all the letters in a grid to spell words, and healing fountains where your characters are fully healed and level up their abilities. Eventually, you find the location that unlocks the next level, and you can choose to continue where you are or move on.
Cons:
-Mouse controls can be a little glitchy from time to time (though keyboard controls are also available)
-Gameplay can get a little repetitive, as with any word-based game
-There is no way to view your characters' equipment upgrades, and it's unclear whether they are using only the latest weapon/armor, or if the effects are cumulative; the interface could use some more transparency and better explanation
-The gameplay is so fast-paced that you never have time to look up at your characters and actually watch the battles. It's just a constant hunt for the next word. The action happening above the word box seems to be primarily for the benefit of someone watching you play the game. Would be nice if the speed were tweaked so that the action paused when you spelled a word, long enough for you to see the result.
I've found the pros to vastly outweigh the cons, and I've enjoyed all my time spent on the game. I do hope that the developer will eventually tweak it a bit to resolve some of the issues, but even if they don't, I don't regret having it.

*** BASED ON THE WIP/EARLY ACCESS TIME PERIOD ***
+ Upgraded shaders and tweaks within the Unreal Engine make the game much smoother, ensuring that older hardware can still run this at high/highest settings. This is esentially a remake or recode of the original, but one that runs 30x better.
+ Graphics are still up to par with the style and setting of the game; landscape looks lush and awesome, the models look defined and detailed.
+ DLC from Primal Carnage, their first game that this one is basically a clone of, carries over into this game, so your raptor skin, assault skin, etc etc will be carried into Primal Carnage: Extinction.
- Servers can't seem to handle the influx of new players as of this time; some games lag so badly the game is nearly unplayable, others won't let you join a team and glitch out, others kick you from a match for various reasons.
- Class balance is slightly off on this, as the Pteranodons seem to be bullet sponges and the Spinosaurus is now playable in TDM. Changes may come later as this is still a WIP game but tweaks are needed on some classes, both dino and human.
- Not free :( "Primal Carnage 2.0" as this was once interanlly known as was supposed to be a massive, free tweak of the game to weed out all the old game engine's problems. Lukewarm has since been absorbed and is now known as Circle 5 Games, who had other ideas and have since released a for-pay remake of Primal Carnage. Some may like it, others may not.
This game is shaping up to be fantastic though. It has its issues but this a WIP/Early Access review, and I'm sure by final release from now until then that many issues will be addressed and fixed. It already feels much smoother than its parent game - of which it is a re-made clone - so I have faith in the developers to continue making what I think is arguably the best dinosaur vs human FPS game to have ever been on Steam.

Tl;dr:
Quite buggy, unnecessarily hard (likely due to it's brevity... like those old NES games), but contains a good story. This game takes a little over 4 hours to complete the story. This game is in no way worth $13.99. Only consider buying when 80% off.
Upon launching, I set the game to compatibility mode so that it'd run on my Windows 10 PC.
The game cut about half of the voice narrations short, it may respawn you in areas where you immediately die again, and in some situations, after finishing one level, may throw an error that crashes the game, ends the game process, and seemingly requires a restart of Steam to fix. In this game, you will certainly die in jumping from one platform to the next, unless you already know the map layout (this is where the unnecessary difficulty appears).
Do download the OST however. Also, since it might launch the game instead of downloading the OST, you can download the free OST (with purchase of the game) by going to the game in your library, right clicking it, going to properties, DLC, and toggle the tick box so that it remains ticked. The OST should then begin to download.
This game has a great story, but this is superseded by all the bugs I encountered, therefore giving this game a negative review.

This one is a pain to watch, like seeing a young, beautiful girl lying among the squalor on the floor, absent look in the eyes from drug overdose.
A beautiful, cyberpunk universe greatly resembling cult classics like Dreamweb or Burntime, fused together with really terrible platformer that does almost everything wrong.
First of all, the animation is not smooth, but jerky and too fast - when you run on turbo (which you must on many levels, since they are timed). all you see is a stuttery blur. Compare it to the top class platformers like Strider, and your eyes will hurt. Everything is way too fast and jerky, the equipment is not interesting, combat is simplistic to absurdity (just hit'em, okay?). I can appreciate the attempts to innovate, the variation of environments and obstacles, but the core gameplay always brings it down.
I forced myself to suffer through several levels (five, I think?) just to see the bosses and the animations, but I cannot continue, the gameplay is just too painful, constant repetition and memorization of levels is simply a bad design. The characters are interesting, and everything hints to a rich universe and backstories, but there is simple too little narration. The weeby voice with forced psycho trembling is fitting, but seems over the top.
I would probably pay around 20$ for a full adventure game in this universe, provided that the story and the characters are interesting. I am a great fan of Primordia, guys, it was a masterpiece, but this game is simply a whiff. Sorry.

is a cyberpunk-themed platformer with a heavy focus on the story and atmosphere. Made by the same developer of a fantastic adventure game called Primordia. Makes me wonder why this game found no audience. Is this a hidden gem? Well, I had some really mixed feelings about it but it definitely had a lot of work put into it. The actual gameplay is designed for speedruns and that part I really did not enjoy. For me, 90% of why I liked this game was a deep story and fantastic pixel art. I don't think the gameplay is refined enough to ask $10+ for it but I would recommend it on sale.
The trailer for the game was a little over the top for me. I am curious how many people felt the same way and did not buy the game because of it. Luckily it is something that grew on me over time and I learned to appreciate what developer was trying to convey. Music and fantastic pixel art certainly made a good first impression. You can really feel the sinister mood of the cyberpunk future and in that regard the game was great. There are many cool characters including our protagonist who was well developed. The only thing that bothered me was an inconsistency when it came to voice acting. ( I could not even hear that tech lady ) Between stages, you can go back to your apartment and get more context for the story which really helped.
I thought the moving speed was kind of sluggish aside from obvious bugs that cause slowdowns in certain parts. It just one of those games where gameplay was not very fluid. I even had to play around with remapping controls for like an hour until I got comfortable. There are a lot of buttons for such a simple genre. Complexity isn't a bad thing but I found myself fighting the timing and mechanics of the game the whole 5 hours. Although the levels often have unique looking themes they are not actually unique in platforming gameplay. For the most part, it's just linear platforming where you can't see very far and die because of it. There are some really neat mechanics like time manipulation and hysteria (which is like controlling your rage). That actual platforming depth was lacking and that is a big problem. In terms of combat, you can stun-lock most enemies and that is all that needs to be said. Although boss fights had enjoyable dialogue, they were kind of one dimensional in terms of mechanics.
I kind of already touched on this but I still should acknowledge that developer really went above and beyond here. Not even sure if I can think of another speedrun game with so much going on visually. Those holograms and commercials on TV is an icing on the cake. It has so much attention to detail. Also, I really enjoyed the music that matched emotional tone of the game.
Until I Have You was a cool experience even if it has some gameplay problems. If you enjoy a story of revenge and awesome cyberpunk artwork you might be able to tolerate the game overall. It takes a specific audience to enjoy pixel gore with cybernetic parts. I would recommend it under $5 but it just one of those games that is a little rough around the edges.

(copy/pasted my review I wrote elsewhere a little while ago because this game deserved another positive review, it is possible there have been updates since I last played.)
If you're into old platformers you would like it. But also, if you're into meatboy like platformers you'd like it. You spend your time repeatedly dying in the levels until you've memorized it and do a perfect run that takes about 15-30 seconds. Similar to meatboy or hotline miami.
The most important thing with a game like this is that the controls be tight. The controls are excellent. The only thing I've had trouble with is descending from a platform. That seems a little tricky since I don't think there's a drop down command, and the guy seems to want to cling to the edge a tiny bit. So dropping from one platform to one right below is really difficult. It's not really something I want to do often though, only in the second boss fight so far. The regular levels are designed sort of like an endless runner, so it's probably a rare occurrence.
The story focus is nice. The story is cheesy and melodramatic. But with a well crafted world presenting the mega man progression type scenario (ie wipe out the enemies in the zones and the bosses of the zones until you go up against the head boss, I'm guessing). The voice work is not bad. It lags a little sometimes, but overall well above average for a project of this scope. The inter-level apartment area is very cool. I kind of wish there was more useless stuff to mess around with. But what it is is a far more engaging interface than a menu with an area for unlockables. Sure, there is a menu with an area for unlockables. But it's the tv. I wish the tv clips would glow or something if you haven't viewed them yet though since sometimes one may be added and sometimes two, it seems, maybe I'm mistaken.

I wish the emphasis was placed on spelling longer words rather than shorter ones using the said colour tiles. For what it's worth it's a cheap word game with some rogue-lite-ish elements thrown in to the mix that can be fun.

So what is oO? That's a good question...
If you're after something easy and relaxing... this AINT it ;)
In oO you play as a little Circle, and you goal is to progress from circle to circle without much trouble initially.
But the further you get, the difficult ramps up and you'll end up needing to memorise certain areas to pass them. (After failing dozens of times at least)
If the original levels aren't enough, there's a variation of each, (I call it drunk mode)
Spikes, high speed movement, memorisation of patters and MORE spikes!
Let's not forget the survival level... Want to take it slow? NOPE! You've got a big scary red wall chasing you, and it only get faster for each checkpoint you hit.
Super fun game, and super cheap too! Highly Recommended for those with quick reflexes!
You can control actions of your balls there, unlike from the real world and also it's simply the best prokrastinator simulator I've ever experienced in my life....

While it's so easy to fail with such a minimalist game, the creator of oO hasn't put a foot wrong. The game is simple, the controls are (actually, the control is) snappy, the fast gameplay leaves hardly any margin for error, and that makes the completion of the levels all the more satisfying. Very enjoyable, very much recommended.
Also, my 2c on the Kongregate topic: if you played the game on Kongregate, and you enjoyed it, I'd recommend to buy it to support the developer. Especially since It's only 1 EUR.

One late night, 'Cave Story' wandred into the house, drunk as usual. 'Portal 2' looked up from her magazine, to see the love of her life stumble in through the front door. 'You Have to Win the Game' and 'Risk of Rain' were already asleep, 'Cave Story' arived home too late to say goodnight to either of them. 'Portal 2' looked up at the love of her life and said, "Were have you been?" 'Cave Story' looked up, as if surprised to be asked a question as such. "I was... just out with some Mimigma eating some cake an' stuff... you know the usual." 'Cave Story' replied. It was the worst lie about cake that 'Portal 2' had ever heard, and even 'Cave Story' knew it. "Look, I'm sorry, its just that ever sense my fanbase went down, I've never really been the same. We both know how it is..." 'Cave Story' said, without the courage to look 'Portal 2' in the face. "Its alright." 'Portal 2' responded. at this, 'Cave Story' looked up at his wife, as if surprised that she would be so kind to him after what he had done. "I guess we've both had some screw-ups, but we always manage to pull back out of it." 'Cave Story' couldnt believe what he was hearing, afterall, 'Portal 2' was still beautiful to him. Her amazing gameplay, memorable charecters, interesting and intreging puzzles. 'Cave Story' knew he had to make this right. "Look 'Portal 2', I know I've had some screw-ups before, but, what if I make it right for you, tonight." 'Portal 2' blushed at this remark. Even after all this time, she still loved him as if it were the first day they met. 'Cave Story's' amazing gameplay and control, the soundtrack, and the story were enough to make her fall in love with him all over again. "Alright." 'Portal 2' said, "You can make it up to me tonight then. 'Cave Story' smiled and turned off the lights, both of them headed upstairs, and proceded with the game.
Nine months later, 'Out There Somewhere' was born.
THE END

The Steam Controller is a great piece of hardware and will one day be a great controller, it just isn’t there yet.
The Steam Controller has been touted as the controller sent from above to save us from crappy console controllers and to liberate us from our mouse and keyboard to enjoy PC couch gaming, even if the game wasn’t built for it.  Truth be told, the controller will do all that it has promised, it just has a long way to go.
Let’s think about this for a moment, why do console gamers like consoles?  They are convenient.  They might not offer the graphics fidelity of a high end PC or the fine precision of a mouse and keyboard, but they just tend to work.  You can pick up an Xbox controller and fire up any game and the controls just make sense.  This is the Steam Controller’s shortcoming.  It has a MASSIVE learning curve.
When you fire up your controller supported games thinking that you’re going to kick♥♥♥♥♥ you get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked.  The dual trackpads offer an unprecedented level of control as you grow accustomed to them however to begin with they offer unprecedented levels of frustration.  A few of the games that I tested the controller on were Saint’s Row IV and Payday 2 and Pillars of Eternity:
•	Saint’s Row IV being a 3rd person game didn’t require as much fine time to adapt to because it isn’t as demanding on your aiming dexterity.  It played without a hitch but controlling the camera and aiming felt awkward vs a standard keyboard and mouse or even an Xbox controller.
•	Payday 2 was far less forgiving. The default control scheme was terrible and basically unusable.  I like to think of myself as an above average play with a keyboard and mouse and an average player with an Xbox controller (how I originally played PD2) Using the Steam Controller on its default settings I could barely survive against enemies on normal let alone long higher levels of difficulty.  Trying more configurations and creating my own helped but it was very much a labor of love.
•	Pillars of Eternity is actually where the Steam Controller shined.  It took a game with no controller support and made it extremely playable, this is the experience people were set up to expect from the controller.  It felt extremely natural and frankly I was shocked at how well it worked, this is what gives me hope for the future.
While the default controls in most games tend to feel a tad awkward, they can be fixed.  This is the core strength the Steam Controller, you can customize every control.  When you find a good configuration it makes your gaming so much more enjoyable.  The problem is that half the default configurations are lackluster the community has already slowly started to become flooded with poor configurations.  This isn’t because the community isn’t trying but it’s because while the configuration software is powerful, it is a bit awkward and a bit ambiguous.

Time will fix all of the issues that I’ve mentioned especially with all the fancy hardware that Valve has crammed into this bad boy: dual-Stage triggers, dual-trackpads, excellent battery life, an analog stick, motion control sensors, haptic feedback and most importantly unparalleled customization.  But at this point in time you will experience a lot of frustration.
I am sure developers and dedicated players will start to release some amazing configurations in the future and as a result the default and recommended configurations will improve.  But at this point in time if you expect the ease of hooking up your new Steam Controller and enjoyably diving into a game, you are going to experience a lot of heart break.

THE PROBLEM with this game is the matchmaking.  Having grinded my way to Diamond status I was quite let down to see the game consistently put unranked (sometimes 2 or 3 at a time) in almost every match I play, causing consistent losses through no fault of my own.
Because this game requires that players work in a team to win, all it takes is one player that is new or that picks the wrong class to throw an otherwise winnable match.  Carrying a team is at times possible in certain circumstances, but ranking up long term cannot be achieved in this fashion.
Further complicating the issue is the fact that you can only group up with one other player.  One cannot build a team of 3 or more and go play in competition - and given that it only takes one player to lose the match for the team, progressing through the ranks comes more down to luck of the matchmaking draw.
If you are a casual f2p gamer this is a great game.  Just don't take competition too seriously.

Platforming controls are almost perfect. You can easily maneuver in the air, run and jump at different speeds, and I never fell through a platform. Even jumping on platform edges is manageable, you just have to learn to let the joystick go just before landing so you won't slide down. Enemies can push you off platforms but it happens rarely and it's a lot less annoying than in other games.
There is a lot of fighting involved. You have four weapons, each with different characteristics useful in different situations. Baseball bat/club is fast and very damaging but useful only in close combat. Pistol has long range but hits only the enemy in the front. Laser shoots through all enemies but needs some time to recharge. And flamethrower has shorter range and has a cooldown period but has high damage and can melt obstacles. You also have a shield but very soon I forgot about it and finished the game without using it. And the last ability is temporary bullet time. Good for some tough spots and bosses but it stays active for such short time it's often not that useful.
The game can be very difficult at times, thankfully it has a plenty of checkpoint so you usually don't have to replay the segments you have already beaten. One of the few problems of the game is that the difficulty of boss fights is not balanced throughout the game. Bosses from chapters 5 and 6 are insanely hard. I think it took me about 100 attempts to beat chapter 5 boss and I seriously considered abandoning the game for good. Compare to the final boss that I killed on my second try with little problems. Those two bosses could really use some changes; any small mistake means you're dead and start over. The other bosses are much more forgiving.
Anyway, this is a great action platformer. Highly recommended.

This is a fun little game for those of us who like to use our words.
It does require quite a bit of word knowledge (or you can do what I do sometimes and just guess, because you might learn a word or two!), so let's hope you can come up with words in a stress situation (like when a tree monster is beating the crap out of you while you try to find a word in a bunch of Scrabble tiles). Combat can be fustrating when you're trying to scramble to find a single word in the pile of letters that you can use to hurt your opponent (considring you can only use certain colored tiles for attacks. But don't worry! More heroes = more colored tiles!)
The graphics are adorable, the music is soothing, and the premise is fantasticly simple. You are an adventurer, go off and adventure! You start off with two different pixely heroes to choose from, and you go from there. "There" being randomly generated adventures where you come across things like loot chests (which have word puzzles), traps (which have word puzzles), shops (which you spend your gold at), and of course, monsters.
A few tips to help you along:
DON'T WORRY IF YOU DIE. You'll still have all your progress on each hero no matter what, and you don't lose heroes! Did you die as the archer? Jump right back in there with all your experience and items!
USE THE KEYBOARD. If you're a fast typist such as myself, it's FAR easier to use the keyboard to input words than trying to drag your mouse along to connect letters (because connecting letters diagonally is a pain in ye old♥♥♥♥♥with ye old mouse).
YOU CAN CHANGE THE DIFFICULTY. If it's too hard for you at first (it was for me), then you can change the difficulty in the Options menu. (You can also make the game wider if that helps you see things better!)
All in all, this is a fun, cheap game. I highly reccomend getting it, as it's one of the best (if not THE best) word game I've played to date. Really great for making your vocabulary bigger, and to kill some time. I was fully engrossed in the game, and I had a blast, and hope to continue having fun in the future.

Buying equipment, I don't see any indication of my character benefitting, the damage number may(?) have changed for the party member, but I don't see a total +x to damage from gear, for gear that has effects (+bleed effect, etc), these don't show up anywhere that I can find after purchasing and equipping them, and I certainly don't notice them in the battle animations happening up top.
Honestly, the game feels completely non-interactive, I may as well just be spelling words in the grid and the rest of the gameplay is just decoration that is not directly related.
As is, calling this "RPG gameplay" is deceptive at best.
I would like to suggest a few improvements that would make the game feel more engaging for me:
1) Combat/Word log - A log of the words you are using in a fight and which abilitie(s) and item effects are taking place, along with how much damage results. Enemy damage should also be listed in a log like this.
2) Show equipped items... anywhere in the game. I would like to see that my character has a magic katar that's adding 8 damage and causing bleeds, etc. As is, I just have to remember that I bought an item, and assume it's doing what it said it was going to... if I can even remember what it said it was going to do 10 minutes later.
3) Achievements would be nice, to mix up gameplay objectives, espcially since the main "fight" phase of the game states "find short words since they are easier to find and still deal the same damage", which seems to give no incentive to spending the time to make big words, unless you are just trying to proc a certain multi-skill-block ability.
Three hours of straight typing, worth.

First let's go over the good stuff. The puzzle mechanics are kinda interesting and will, at times, make quick use of them. The controls are as smooth as you expect from a recent game.
Now for what I didn't like. The biggest problem is that all of the puzzles revolve around finding "data." To complete a level and progess to the next one, three orbs of data need to be found. The problem with this is that the difficulty of all of the puzzles come from finding the orbs on the board. They are almost never hard to get to, just hard to find. This would be okay if the developers realized this and made each level interesting. Turn each board into a unique easter egg hunt that reveals something about the story. Show something about my mysterious empoyer. Leave notes on the wall next to an orb that shows what each piece of data is. Have comments of code that reveals something about the owner. Make each nook and cranny rewarding to explore, even if it doesn't have an orb. As is, however, each level is like an easter egg hunt where all the eggs are hidden in 4 acre egg carton: everything looks the same until you stumble upon the green orb.
For a game that is "demanding all of your wits and reflexes," this game is surprisingly easy and short. As mentioned earlier, almost all of the difficulty comes from finding all of the orbs. It's reminiscent of Knuckles' levels in Sonic Adventure, which we all know as everyone's favorite part of everyone's favorite game. What makes matters worse is that sometimes it is brutally apparent that the developers placed the orbs as an after thought just to squeeze three into each level. Each puzzle takes less than 5 minutes to complete, except one that I spent several extra minutes exploring the level looking for the last orb. Turns out it was in the exit room. Why even bother?
Minor gripes: some small steps can't be walked over, they need to be jumped. At times the physics is unpredictable. For example, a cube won't move with a moving platform when placed on it. Also, the throwing mechanic sometimes makes it feel like I accidentally skipped part of a puzzle (might just be me, though). Less than one hour of main story, maybe another with extras, and maybe another with co-op.
I like what they tried to do and the mechanics are cool, but the environment is unrewarding.
TL;DR: The game controls well and has a neat idea. The execution is sub par, unchallenging, and short. Not worth $10. If you catch it on super sale (whatever 1-2 hours is worth to you), go ahead and try it.

Don't believe the nay-sayers. The Steam controller's biggest problem isn't anything with it's hardware or software, it's that you will have to actually spend time learning, experimenting, and practicing to actually see how amazing this product is. It's not a keyboard and mouse replacement, it's not a glorified 360 controller with quirky new features, it's not something you can pick up and IMMEDIATELY be awesome at, it's a whole new kind of gamepad that's not like anything you've used before. But this is for a reason: it can do FAR more things FAR more effectively than any other controller you've used before. You only get out of the Steam controller what you put into it. It has a learning curve, but the skill ceiling is ridiculously high, and the options are near limitless. If you're not an impatient ape, the Steam Controller is for you.

Just to start off, I played this game on normal mode using mouse and keyboard. It took me 36 hours to complete endings A B  C and D, which are sequential and make up the main storyline. Now I am going through a second playthrough on hard using a controller. There is some dislike for playing the game on keyboard which is deserved. I would say that playing with a keyboard is marginally worse for most of the game, and much worse during hacking (minigame) and flight suit (shooter/bullet hell) portions of the game, which overall makes up around 3-5% of the total playtime.
Overall it's a very interesting game that has a couple of minor flaws. The story and soundtrack are both perfect and the combat is good enough to tie the game together into a pretty pleasing experience (even on keyboard). You can chain together moves pretty nicely and it's very satisfying (and good looking) when you can pull off some chained moves on your enemies.
Main flaw is as others have probably said, normal mode feels pretty easy while hard is extremely annoying to play. Main culprit in this is 1HKO moves. I got 1 hit killed a single time on normal (getting ending C). Contrast that to hard, where the boss at the end of the opening can kill you in one hit with any of his moves and takes a good 5 minutes to kill. This is especially annoying since if you die at any point in the ~20-40 minute opening you have to start over from the beginning. Hard also changes some stuff up subtly. There were a couple more enemies, and it feels like their patterns are slightly different and your hitbox is slightly bigger, which is fine I guess.
Other flaw is the subquest system. You can have as many subquests as you like at any given time, and they're all marked the exact same way on your map (some of them even mark 3 different places or more). This means unless you finish every quest as soon as you get them, you'll end up with 10 red dots on your map and no way of knowing what each points to without pausing, looking at the full map, then mousing over each location to see what they are, and finally marking the one you actually want to do. This problem is worsened by quests like Robo Dojo and Half-Wit Inventor which stick through multiple endings and require you to be reasonably far through the game to complete.
There are a few more minor issues. Loading screens are 20 seconds. Every. Single. Time. Since it only takes a minute or two to sprint across the whole map, "fast" travel is really a joke, and helps make sidequests tedious. Cutscenes are 30fps and in worse resolution than the game itself. The game itself is capped at 60fps and sometimes you'll even lose some of those frames for no reason. The game also crashes the during the first time you enter the amusement park (happened in two separate playthroughs at the exact same spot).
TLDR:
Keyboard is good enough, makes dodge worse and ranged/shooting (5%) portions terrible
PROS:
CONS:
In conclusion 4/5. The game is very nice and has a couple minor issues. Worth playing even for the story by itself.

THE PROBLEM with this game is the matchmaking.  Having grinded my way to Diamond status I was quite let down to see the game consistently put unranked (sometimes 2 or 3 at a time) in almost every match I play, causing consistent losses through no fault of my own.
Because this game requires that players work in a team to win, all it takes is one player that is new or that picks the wrong class to throw an otherwise winnable match.  Carrying a team is at times possible in certain circumstances, but ranking up long term cannot be achieved in this fashion.
Further complicating the issue is the fact that you can only group up with one other player.  One cannot build a team of 3 or more and go play in competition - and given that it only takes one player to lose the match for the team, progressing through the ranks comes more down to luck of the matchmaking draw.
If you are a casual f2p gamer this is a great game.  Just don't take competition too seriously.

Addendum: The bug mentioned below has been patched by the developer. The issue of falling through the platform after using the second wind mechanic no longer happens. :D
This is a great game with a beautiful OST. I love the story and retro cyber punk theme and cinematics. It really does feel like I am playing a William Gibson novel. However, I have found one bug that has mostly surfaced in stage 5-5 but has shown up on occasion once or twice on other stages. When in the stage five chase, if I fall and use the second wind ( a game mechanic where if you fall you can rewind time a bit to start near where you fell. It can not be used repeatedly. The next fall sets you back at the beginning of the level at full reset.) I often end up on a platform and fall through to my death. It has happened enough that I can say it is a game breaking bug. Also, when I use the second wind some times I am set well behind my chase target and some times I am set a head of her. I am not sure if it is intentional, depending on how close I am to the target when I fall, or another bug.
The following is not a bug, but an observation. The timing for this stage is fairly challenging. Particularly the stretch just before the area with the multiple window panes and the window pane stretch it self. When you jump on the plaform there are two panes with a bit of raised floor you have to jump over immediatly or do the break and jump simultaneously. Becasue of the crucialness of timing and jumping/breaking I find the second one really slows me down...often causing me to lose the round. If I make it through there to the next platform, with the 7 or so multiple panes of glass, and I dont have the breaking and jumping times just right I cant catch up with the target. This is the one area where I am happy when the second wind puts me a little ahead of the target. It has put me right towards the end of the  multiple panes, even though I fell before that stretch. This has happened maybe ten times or more.....where right at that jump to the multiple panes I fall and either end up towards the end with women behind be or at the end of the platform just before it.
Despite the one, (or two???) bugs I have encountered so far I would say this game is a must buy for fans of retro, cyber punk, tech noir, 80s and 90s genre and platformer games. Story, pixel visuals, and music  10/10. Game play level challenge and funness 8/10. Gameplay delivery/ level design are a mixed bag. Some levels are designed nicely and some need some work but it fits with cyber punk theme 7/10. Boss battles 6/10. The boss fights are easier then the levels leading up to them. They are still a challenge, but after memorizing the moves and timing I found them to be easy so far. This is all subjective of course. If they are too hard it will be a deterance to finish the game. Overall, Until i have you is a very good game with a level of challenge I rarely encounter in plaformers of late.
Until I Have You reminds me of the old Ninja Gaiden and Mega Man games for Nintendo. Those were some of the most challenging level designs and hardest boss battles. They to were all about the timing and memorization. As I play further I may change and add to the review.

overall, an  excellent game. I waited for a sale but it is well worth the asking price. You get the beautifull cyber punk sounding OST for free with the game. :D

So lets review until i have you. Before i get into that, I have been speaking with the developer of issues I had with the game and pitched ideas of that could help maintain flow of the game. Those ideas are not important to the review but i think the backstory for that with the recent updates that fixed my issues with the game I would re examine the game. I will go over things in a pro/ con style and ending with my conclusion.
pro:
Amazing story. The story is very interesting when you go back to your apartment and watch these memory shows that has key plot points in the past of our main character. Some of which are kinda sad to see the struggle that the couple face when the main character is always doing crime. While he is out she fills this jar labeled your never here with coins. That hits you hard. Other than that in the game you see how as the game continues how the main character's perception of reality is messed up and you see the world as he sees in the in the level design. Bloody with zombies or monsters.
The music is awsome. Whats crazy about the music is how it sets up the scenery. To further be more awsome the soundtrack is free so no worries about paying the equivalent of the game to buy the soundtrack. My personal favorite song would definently be Electric Ghost, it is the song played in the apartment. It is a very slow sad song which goes so well with the underlining tone of the character and fits some of the memory projector moments.
Great combat. The combat is pretty much small scaled to the platforming but is worth mentioning. You do encounter an array of enemies from thugs, cops, zombies, cathulu monsters, and more. The weapons the player uses are unique and useful agains some fights better than others.

The platforming is pretty on point. The use of a variable jump, for those who do not know what that is...its pretty much when you press the jump button you jump but the longer you hold it the higher the jump is. No you can not simply just fly over the entire map to the end because there is a jump height cap. Once you hit that cap, that is when the character will descend. Other than that the use of other neat tools help with platforming but since i wont do any spoilers, the slow mo ability. This ability will slow down time to help with those tricky jumps or help take care of a group of enemies.
Each chapter is unique. Sure sure each chapter is stared in a different location but it also adds new mechanics that are used in that chapter and for that chapter alone. So you have 12 chapters in the game and that introduces 12 new game mechanics that is cohesive to the level stye.
Con:
Some levels seem to have odd design choices such as chapter 3 which is a constant rush level where you pretty much run chasing some female who is your target. The other is chapter 8 which is a stealth mission, you dont need to stealth it but the game has had no stealth prior to this level so it feels kinda shoe horned in for the sake of unique mechanic. Both chapters are not bad but their design choices are just odd since they do not capture what made all other levels so good. The mix between combat and platforming at the players pace.
Conclusion:
I really did enjoy the game. I enjoyed sharing my two cents to help the game grow. There is not any more i can say about the game besides the story is very unique. I kinda feel a vibe of john wick when thinking of the plot that i have enxperienced. Other than story and the awsome music, the platforming is nothing short than a trip. With how the player has more control over their jump, i fall to my death less if i over shoot my jump. The slow mo does not punish the player for using it by lowering their hysteria by too much. No one likes a mechanic that is very useful in the later portion of the game be more harm than good. Gladly with the recent update i can happily reccomend the game to anyone intersted in the game or just those gamers that enjoy a good platformer.

Until I Have You is a fast-paced, energized platforming game. You control a very skilled professional thief, known as The Artist, now outfitted with a poweful exoskeleton, who's out for the blood of his former clients. With this exoskeleton, he's extremely fast, has enough strength to crush through walls and military robots, can block projectiles with a force field, and can slow his time perception to react to any threat.This, however, costs him his physical and mental health, and his time is limited, so he's got to kill all his targets as soon as possible.
The gameplay allows various approaches to the levels. You can carefully check enemy timings and pass behind them when they don't see you. You can unleash your deadly arsenal on them - and by the way, there's much more than the bat and the pistol you start with. And the most exciting option is just run as fast as you can, timing you jumps, force-field blocks and precise attacks to rush through the level in minimal time possible. This really goes on with the feeling of urgency the plot imposes on you.
Each level brings something new to the gameplay, by adding new environmental mechanics, giving you new weapons and unlocking your abilities. Some levels will require you to be either exclusively stealthy, murderous or quick, but most of the time you can use a combined approach. The game rewards the consistency of your style: for example, you get bonus points for either not killing at all or killing everything, preferably without changing your weapon.
And at the end of each chapter there's a boss - one of your targets. The boss fights are some kind of a puzzle: each boss is not like the other, and you have to do a lot of different actions to survive and kill them, for example using your exoskeleton-induced hallucinations to point out targets, or literally jumping through hoops.
For this kind of a game, controls are pretty important. I played through the whole game with an Xbox controller, which was pretty comfortable. Then, for the sake of a complete review, I played some levels using keyboard, and that was, surprisingly, also good. The default layout looks a bit chaotic (Shooting with the A button? Seriously?), but actually it's really suitable for the game and will feel natural right after the tutorial.
The plot, while managing to impose a feeling of urgency, looks sort of haphazard. You don't really understand why The Artist prioritizes killing his former clients over rescuing his wife, why would they even kidnap his wife, why does the doctor who provided him with the exoskeleton continues to help and support him, even putting herself at risk sometimes. It all comes together nicely in the ending, though, and the final cutscene is just perfect. And, as interludes between chapters, there're holo-recorded episodes from The Artist's family life (which are kinda boring) and TV news reporting his latest exploits (which are grimly hilarious).
All this is accompanied by a good soundtrack, which comes with the game freely. While retrowave music is a standard for pixel-art cyberpunk games and pixel-art fast-and-violent games, the game's composer managed to make it sound fresh by using some instruments and patterns unconventional for this genre. It is also mastered in intentional lo-fi, and that adds a nice touch and goes well with the art style, the plot's atmosphere and in-game sound effects.
Only about 2.5k people have bought this game as of today. For its price, Until I Have You is definitely worth your attention.
