I pre-ordered the deluxe edition, and I'm very satisfied with the $90 purchase. The core game is fantastic, the roster is bigger than ever, and the DLC plans sound pretty good, like not as much current roster content being added later on, like the 2K17 having an outside of the season pass $10 NXT pack for Nia Jax, Apollo, and Dillenger was lame. I really enjoy 2K18, on the first day, I played for 4 hours, just doing matches. I've heard My Career isn't very good, and what I've seen in streams, it does have some weird writting, but I mostly just play for the matches, play what sounds fun to me. With 2K17, I have the digital version on PS4, and that was going from a long break, the last one I had was 2K14 on PS3, so it was fun to learn all the new features. With 2K18, it will feel very familiar to anyone who's played the previous games, as with any yearly sports franchise. The updated graphics are the big thing for 18. They do have of course more things to do in matches, like more interactions outside of the ring, a carry system, and so on. It's not a total game changer, but it's still enough to justify a yearly release. The roster is really impressive, there are some odd absenses, but the community creations does a great job for being able to download fan creations, especially people you just won't see in a WWE game like Hulk Hogan and people from other feds like Impact, Lucha Underground, AAA, New Japan, and so on. As far as performance goes, I have not seen anything bad yet. I have the game running on max settings, it never drops bellow 59 FPS, and I have done the benchmark test to prove that. I just played about an hour with a Bitdefender virus scan running in the background, and no slowdown at all. I also like how the game has very fast load times, I don't even have it on my SSD, and it goes fast all the time. The game has never crashed on me yet, no real glitches, just standard things like his arm clipped through the ropes on a taunt, but nothing that's affected game play. I really don't know what's with the mixed reviews, because I'm not experiencing any problems like others are. Also, be happy that 2K Games released a WWE game on the same day as the consoles, that's awesome. It feels very well optimized and polished. This game is definitely better than 2K17, but it's riddled with problems. Severe problems. What kind of problems? Well lets start with the somewhat bad problems...
- In MyCareer and Road To Glory, Moves & Attires are locked behind lootboxes. This needs to disappear ASAP. I have no issue with buying these things with ingame currency (or just making them available to begin with) but locking things behind lootboxes that give you completely random abilities is awful. Do away with this in the next game please.
- Gameplay feels exactly the same as WWE 2K17. It doesn't feel very new aside from the commentary and a few new mechanics such as Carrying. Which was a very old mechanic from SVR2007. It was removed a long time ago because it's completely useless. Why bring it back?
- You immediately have to adjust the in game balance from the start. On the default Normal difficulty, the A.I has the tendency to wildly rubberband and reverse every attack you do.
- Like every wrestling game on the first month, it's riddled with bugs. Some are hilarious but others can be very annoying and you have to end up restarting the match. But this is no excuse. I'm not sure who's behind bug testing but they need to pull a finger out or leave. Because this is the eqivelant of giving someone a half cooked meal in a restaurant.
- Universe Mode is still very linear. There are some things that allow you to book things how you want to book them like in WWE12 but they're not great. Getting cutscenes out of them is still unlikely but they can happen if you're lucky. When you let the A.I book for you with the Rivalry system, it still has the insufferable tendency to book the same match over and over every week.
- MyCareer does not feel like anything special. I commend them for trying to replicate the classic Just Bring It backstage feeling but it still feels bland and nothing really special.
- Still no custom music. No excuse for this. The copyright excuse is just that. An excuse. Give people the freedon to use the music they want to use. Instead, we now have to rely on mods to intergate this when it should be in the game to begin with. They also made the excuse that PS4 and XB1's hardware doesn't allow music to be stored on the system and put into games. Well please explain to me how music on PC is not able to be put into the game?
Now for the severe, gamebreaking problems...
- Was on my 4th month in my universe mode. My female CAW won the Money In The Bank. Since then, I no longer have the ability to do any match whatsoever. Universe mode just became completely unplayable. Any time I attempt to do a match, it crashes. Worst bug in a wrestling game i've ever encountered outside of the rare data corruption bugs and the one count bug in WWE 13.
- Road To Glory's wait time in matchmaking can sometimes take a minute. And every other time. it will take 30-45 minutes to find one opponent. Really wish I was exaggerating.
- Cheesing online in this game is pathetically easy. Matches will either be impossible to win or impossible to lose. I commend the reversal system and what it's set out to do, but in an online competitive match, it causes severe unwinnable or unloseable situations.
Granted half of these issues will be patched, they really should not be in this game on release. Especially the gamebreaking ones. I was going to give this game a 6/10 because there are actually som positives to this game. It graphically looks great, the creative suite is vastly improved and Universe mode was actually pretty fun for the most part.
But now I literally cannot play it because of the bugs and I don't want to play anything else in the game. So my 6/10 drops to a 3/10. It's borderline unplayable.
If you're buying this game for Universe Mode, avoid the game all costs until it gets patched. And if you're playing it for MyCareer, wait for it to go on sale, it's not worth it at all at full price.
I think it's time for WWE, 2K and Yukes to stop being cheap and realize these games seriously need polish and they cannot be developed over the course of one year. They need 2 years or at least a year and half. This isn't 2005 anymore where it'd be easy to release these games annually. They require a lot more time and care. Stop trying to make an easy dollar and actually try please.

The Steam Controller has ruined games for me... Since I got it, I no longer care about a game's story, graphics, or mechanics. All I care about is tweaking my controller configuration for hours in search of the perfect configuration for each game. Just when I start to settle on a configuration, I remember that I can use the gyro for fine-tuned aiming, or use trigger-dampening, or bind controls to soft-pull and hard-pull of the triggers. On top of that, every single control can be mode-shifted using the grip buttons. Every game is a new experience, even games I've already put hundreds of hours into.
In short: the Steam Controller is an amazing tool for power users. I would definitely recommend it if you enjoy tweaking the settings for your games to get the experience just right, or if you are interested in trying out seemingly-bizarre control schemes that actually work.

The versatility of this controller and just the pure capabilities are mindblowing. Everything can be changed, adjusted, tweaked and tinkered. The gyro is also a very nice add, giving you a little help when aiming or controlling the camera. It takes a bit to get used to but when you dig into it there are really no limits. The haptic feedback provides a nice indication of things happening and the trackpads feel solid.
I heartily recommend this if you are ready for something new and groundbreaking.

The Steam controller is one of the most powerful gamine peripherals in recent memory,  and it's due to Valve's innovative approach to both the design of the hardware as well as how it integrates into steam.
This is the most programmable/flexible/customizable controller out there.  Is there a learning curve? Sure.  But It reminds me of the old motto for "Othello": A minute to learn, a lifetime to master.
The sheer combination of input types is staggering.  And the fact that Valve has made game-specific mappings saveable AND shareable to the rest of the ecosystem really makes it stand out and gives us a great glimpse into how our PCMR bretheren use the peripheral.
Cheers to Valve for taking a risk and creating something so innovative. I'm a fan.

is a rich sample of what good content should look like in the video game industry. It's true, not many devs dive into things like existentialism. While most titles in the past focus heavily in mechanics and gameplay to drive their popularity,
sets itself apart with a little taste of philosophy. Moreover; it’s not lacking the necessary gameplay either. No doubt, the philosophy included is icing on this cake that separates itself from others right away; or maybe it’s the spongy vanilla core.
For me, this was the cake that was on sale for thirty-five percent off in the bakery. I picked it up and said, “hmm okay, let’s give this one a try.” When you cut open a piece of
, it’s easy to appreciate the relationship between what this game offers on the inside and at face value. I can easily say that it has multiple layers for one to enjoy. When you finish the game once, it’s like you’ve just begun. There are over lapping storylines that tell different sides to the (same?) story. Instead of a linear storyline that makes character development concrete at the end.
introduces different outlooks to enhance the account of characters and forces better story telling. All in all, re-playability is crucial when enjoying what this game can offer.
At my first impression, I noticed that the soundtrack, mechanics and gameplay were top notch. The Visual art, dynamic level design, character advancement and combat are all unique and interesting to explore. For
, these aspects are captivating to use and yet, not easily picked up with simple instructions. We all can agree, “Press A to Jump” commands are extremely trite and belong in games with an ESRB rating of early childhood. In contrast,
lets you figure it out on your own for the most part, and it feels good. Similar JRPGs have done this with great success. The combat system is simple but satisfying with visuals and animations that are quite stunning. Moreover, the soundtrack to this game is out of this world amazing. Whether they belong in a videogame that you’d might like to play or not, that’s up to you. However; for me, it was enjoyable and kept me thinking just like a good movie would. Popularity in gameplay-driven games without a story is a common theme in recent. And obviously, classics like
and

Until I Have You is a decent game for its price, though it has a few problems in it that prevent the game from being a definite recommendation.
The basic gameplay is action platformer, with various weapons to defeat your enemies with. The variety in the weapons is fun for most of the experience, but starts to drag a little towards the end as you stop getting new toys to try out. Two more advanced mechanics are the ability to slow down time and rewind when you die, which are cool features that add to the experience. I feel the slow down mechanic is underutilized, as I myself never used it once, but it is nonetheless a nice addition to your repetoire.
The stages have interesting designs, but while their concepts are interesting the execution of the ideas sometimes drags and can quickly become annoying. There is what seems to be an over-reliance on pits in some of the later stages, which, combined with the somewhat slippery edges to platforms and a speed system that sometimes doesn't quite speed you up enough, can lead to a frustrating chain of falls. I won't spoil the specialized mechanics of each stage here, but I would say around 30% of them are irritating to deal with over a 4-6 stage chapter. They only get annoying toward the end of the chapters, however, so it is not so bad, as you can get through them quickly and move on to something new.
The story of the game starts out alright, and remains relatively interesting throughout, but was confusing at points, and ultimately left me feeling unfulfilled. The ending of the game was not satisfying (though that is of course subjective), and left me wanting. I am unsure if there are multiple endings based on what percentage you achieve, but the structure of the later stages makes it unnapealing to try for a higher percentage (I got a final % of 92).
To conclude, the game is fun to start, but at about chapter seven begins to drag. If you are willing to accept precision platforming over many pits, and a few awkward stage mechanics, the overall gameplay is decently fun and in some stages very rewarding. If I had to give this a score out of ten, I would give it a mid to high 7/10. I cautiously recommend this game, as some of the mechanics can be frustrating, but the game is fun in the end and has enjoyable neon/techno themed visuals.

UIHY is a gripping pixelart platformer that might challenge your patience. At least that is what it did for me many, many times. The setting is a Blade Runner-like Cyberpunk future where not everything is as shiny as the neonlights that make our town Neo-Kobe shine a lot. The player takes the role of the ARTIST, a talented Hitman, who wants to simply quit his job that has already consumed most of his private space. You might have already guessed that things did not happen according to his plan. His wife Emily gets captured, forcing the ARTIST to take any risks necessary to get her back. He gets his hands on an exoskeleton suit that gives him incredible powers whilst slowly draining his sanity. Using his new powers he wants to free Emily and take revenge for everything the both of them got into. But like I said, everything comes with a price...
What counts for nearly any other platformer doesn’t pass on UIHY either: play it with a controller. You can play via keyboard and mouse but I hardly recommended that since you have to be as precise as possible most of the time, otherwise you will die even more often. That said, I was a bit confused at first. Normally you press the direction + directional upwards + Jump to jump over a gap or obstacle but Until I have You takes it a bit different. Pressing to the left or right accelerates the ARTIST into the pressed direction and if you jump, he simply jumps as far as he can with his current speed. If you wish to stop running, you simply release the button. I found myself dying more than once because I pressed the opposite key instead just to realise that my avatar is swiftly heading into the other direction now. The longer you press, the faster he gets. Pressing boost even increases this. If a gap seems to big, you might have to rely on the ARTISTs special power. Get incredible fast or, in other words, slow everything around you.
The “Slow Mode” is one of many interesting mechanics this game uses but it is also one of the main mechanics. Use it anywhere, anytime, even in the middle of a jump - as long as your time bar is filled enough. You might use it a lot at the start but slowly stop exploiting it once you got the second main mechanic, which isn’t nearly as useful as the first one - but turns out to be impressively innovative whilst adding important pieces to the UIHY main story. The ARTIST gets “hysteric” and with that I don`t mean he starts screaming out of nowhere. No, he starts to see things, hallucinates or loses control. It is just so exciting to see how he is slowly trading sanity for power in order to release his wife but it also rises some sort of guilt I can’t fully deny.
So, besides having different mechanics for each level like alarms, hoverboards, colourtesting platforms and many more, there is always a boss at the end of each chapter. I must admit that I did not feel challenged by every single one. Some of them have been surprisingly easy to surpass, once you got the mechanics you need to beat them. I don’t think that this is bad in general. Even if you can beat some of them more easy you will still get how cool some of the mechanics were you had to use. Melting legs, chasing through walls or jumping through Fire Rings?
Graphics? Absolutely Adorable. At least if you like Pixelart and Cyberpunk. I for myself enjoyed every damn level, every boss, every cutscene. The artstyle is just perfect, leaving enough space to add your own imagination whilst making the game look dark and flashy at the same time. What`s adding up is the soundtrack I even listen to whilst writing these lines. It fits just perfect into the game but stands its own if listened separately, too. I’d love to praise graphics and sound even more but that would somehow lengthen this review to an extent even I can`t stand. Instead I’d like to mention the great dialogues and sidekicks you’ll find along the road of your tragical seeking for revenge. You get to know the ARTIST, his past, his problems, his clients and maybe their problems and sad stories and you somehow feel a bit connected to everyone of them - or at least feel sorry.
There is much to love, much to like and a bit to like less. Starting with the small negative aspects I`d like to say that the controls can be punishing at first. I think they are just unique in its way and need to be experienced to feel comfortable with. Secondly, although I liked the structure of every level in general, I still felt that I would have stopped playing after having died for the fifth time at a difficult spot with the checkpoint far away, if the story had been less interesting. But, fortunately, it wasn`t. It is a dark tale of love, revenge and sacrifice that made me feel a bit less happy and a bit more satisfied at the same time for every chapter I had finished. The artstyle is simply amazing, not to mention the amazing soundtrack. Lastly, the developer is actively taking part in steam forums and constantly updates the game to squash remaining bugs I personally didn't get confronted with.
If you are into platformers, Pixelart or Cyberpunk and you simply can’t resist a gripping story that might hurt your feelings, this is the right game for you.

A mixed bag of a game, "Until I Have You" feels like a contraption jury-rigged by a savant technomancer somewhere in the city sprawl of 2077: brilliant and horrible ideas, rough edges and state-of-the-art components, all put together with duct tape. It makes you battle against its interface, it frustrates you, it delights you.
Gameplay-wise, it tries to be a super-fast and super-violent platformer, a cross between "Canabalt" and "Hotline Miami", and the best levels do manage to achieve this high bar. The problem is, however, that "Until I Have You" tries to be fast and minimalistic, but at the same time to have lots of different features. As the result, it keeps shooting itself in the leg, slowing the gameplay down so you can try all the mechanics. Superfast running and jumping stumbles upon cover shooting, choosing the right weapon to destroy obstacles, stealth action and other legitimately cool stuff that just doesn't mix together well.
The large variety of features also makes the gameplay very incosistent. For example, in the beginning you die in one shot. Then they add Hysteria meter that punishes you for killing enemies (and makes you wait for a solid minute for it to regenerate -- so much for superfast). Then Hysteria suddenly turns into a health bar substitute: enemy attacks rise it, but killing them doesn't anymore. There's no solid mechanic, "Until I Have You" turns into something slightly different (still very enjoyable, though just as messy) with each next level. It's such a mess that sometimes I had no idea if I have played the game the way it was intended, or abused a design flaw.
The story is pretty incoherent, which is ok for the Cyberpunk genre: after all, most of the classic works have unreliable narrators, unhinged characters, lots of drugs and/or mental issues, amnesia, hallucinations and cryptic symbols. To tell the truth, I don't trust writers who make cyberpunk stories too clear: it kills the "punk" part, turning it into simply SciFi. "Until I Have You"'s story is messed up just right: enough for you to have a general idea what's going on, how it started and how it ends. The atmosphere and the characters are done very well in terms of writing, art, music and voice acting. The urban sprawl is genuine with its neon, dirt and rain, the characters are either insane or corrupt, the politics are shady, and the plot twists go as expected. In addition to the well-done cutscenes, you can watch TV between the levels to get some news about your misadventures, or see some ads that give you insights into the world's dystopian daliy life.
"Until I Have You" is a real treat for any cyberpunk fan. For a regular gamer, it's still enjoyable, though hardly above average.

Warning: Your Mileage May Vary. My results, though, were impressive!
I can see why, at this point, there are a number of negative reviews. It's not at all apparent how to set it up properly, I can't find any documentation whatsoever, the various presets give no description as to what they actually do, there are no test sounds built into the program to identify how your settings affect the output and, finally, I imagine the end result may highly depend on your headphones. I really hope the devs correct these aspects, because many users will understandably become lost and go for a refund. But then they'd miss out on what this software can do, and that'd be a shame, because this is a unique little gem.
So I opened with the negatives, but what about the positives, which I feel won out? Well, I've persisted with this software past the point of no refunds, and I've finally gotten it setup properly (I think), and the net result is that *the soundscape being played through my headphones sounds much more 3-dimensional than it did without this software*. In fact, my headphones sound more "surround" than they've ever done (in 16 years!), apart from when listening to binaural recordings. In the end, it actually does what it says on the tin, provided you can get it working.
First, my hardware setup is almost custom-tailored for good results with this program. My headphones are a very loved set of Sennheiser HD600s paired with a small Headroom headphone amplifier plugged directly into the "Line Out" (not headphone jack!) of my (meh) Realtek onboard soundcard (Windows 7 64 OS). Straight away, I experienced the "garbled sound" effect that many have complained of. On my system, as with most I assume, I had to manually select my audio output device and make sure it was in WASAPI mode. If you don't know your WASAPI from your ASIO, then maybe you didn't take audio engineering courses in university like I did... and that's why some documentation would be useful! Anyhow... this fixed my garbled sound issue. Next, I chose a preset... I have no idea what the difference between the different "city" themes are yet, but I've settled on "Dubai" for the present, chose the EQ preset for Sennheiser HD600s (very handy if you have a pair of the headphones with built-in eq presets), and then lowered the LFE (low frequency effects) knob by a fair bit (numeric values would be more useful than a knob) because the default LFE was creating audio distortion in my headphone amp.
I've tried two games with excellent surround sound to properly test everything: Portal 2 and Alien: Isolation. And the litmus test was that I could walk into an area with a clear directional sound source, close my eyes, and tell more-or-less exactly where it was at as I walked around in-game. It was much better than the built-in positional audio from the standard "headphones" audio settings of the games. And in the end, that's what counts.
Also, I spent ~£5 for this software on sale, so I think it's important to maintain a little perspective. I'm definitely going to get my fiver's worth out of it. Heck, I'd pay that just to experiment with this software and encourage developers in trying to make cool audio tech. This wasn't a snap to setup and use, and I doubt it'd be all that great with poor headphones, so you'll have to weigh your own circumstances up when considering the purchase: do you have good headphones, and are you willing to tweak and experiment to dial in your settings? If so, I reckon this gives pretty impressive results.

When considering buying this game, it is important to remember that it is not only in Early Access, it only just started a few days before I wrote this review. There are bugs, some of them bad, but they will be fixed. My main problem at the time of this writing is balance. A game built around dinosaurs and humans should be hard to balance, but the previous Primal Carnage actually pulled it off and made a pretty balanced experience. This game, on the other hand, is not so. Fixed limits of tyrant class dinosaurs (the
and
) mean you can get the maximum 3 in a game when there are only three on each team, and tyrants can be a tough to kill if there is only one human per tyrant. The game's raptors are under-powered, while the Pterasaurs are rediculously overpowered. Many human weapons are underpowered and don't do the damage they should. On to non-balance problems, the big thing is match stability and fairness. First, matches will sometimes just randomly end in the middle, which can be quite annoying. Second, you choose your team at the beginning of every match of team-death-match, meaning that if you have a slower connection than others or are just slower to click, you can be stuck on the less-popular human team for many matches to come.
The thing is though, this is Early Access and the devs care and listen to players, so these problems should all be fixed relatively soon.
Overall, it is a fun game if you can stay in a match and alive long enough to really play. Right now, I would rate it 6/10. However, once they fix the aforementioned balance and stability issues, I would easily rate the game higher, and even more so when they begin releasing new maps, dinosaurs, skins, and weapons.

Primal Carnage: Extinction is exactly the update the original Primal Carnage needed for a long while now. Although they did seperate it into an entirely new game, I do love all of the improvements on it thus far being only a BETA. The graphical difference because PC and PC:E is very different. Extinction's graphics are 10x better, as well as more optimized in my experience. Gameplay seems a lot smoother. The faster paced combat is something I still need to adjust to coming from the original game, but it's growing on me. I LOVE the fact you have to actually work hard on playing a Raptor in Extinction opposed to PC. Although I do slightly disagree with Pteras being so simple; yet I do highly appreciate and love the effert they put to simplify it's flying mechanics making it easier for Ptera fans and lovers to play as enjoyment. I never find myself getting bored of playing Extiction yet so far. Each match I find enjoyable and new ways to practice and play the game as well as help as much as possible with the development of it by providing information on bugs and possible suggestions of fixes.
If you've never played any of the Primal Carnage games, I do recommend trying out Extinction due to it being the newest and as it's still in BETA to watch it grow and develop. Overall, this is my small summary.
Pros:
~More optimized, smoother graphics
~Higher end textures
~Improved maps and lighting
~Smoother overall gameplay; although faster paced.
~New abilities/weapons for both Human and Dinosaur as well as seperate abilities for Sub-classes
~Steam Economy seems very promising in the near future
~Current combat keeps you on the edge and lookout; makes it more enjoyable
Cons:
~Combat is a tad fast at times, makes it difficult to land proper hits as a Human or Dinosaur
~Small bugs that prevents entering a server or crashing after one or a few matches
~New items in your inventory sometimes taking a while to load for use
Inbetween Opinion(s) (totally your choice whether these are good or bad):
~Fast Combat
~Raptor pounce being more difficult than the original Primal Carnage
~Jumping being more spammable
~Pteradons being more flexible, more simple to play
~Raptors being more difficult to play
~Tyrants being equally as easy to kill at times; but can also be easily over-powering depending on your playstyle
~Dilo's Stamina runs out fast and must recharge by roaring; although the the Roar meter takes a while to refill
~Tyrants not being able to heal as effectively by eating humans opposed from the original game
~Humans running faster and longer than some dinosaurs at times
~Humans possessing sometimes their own 'one-shot' attacks and methods (even to Tyrants)
Most of this review is purely just my honest opinion of the first week of release for Extinction. My opinion on the game may or may not change for the better or worse once it is developed more a few months into the future. I suggest buying and trying out the game before placing any proper judgement based off this review!
My rating for Extinction: 7.8 out of 10

Using the default controller scheme where the right trackpad acts as an analog isn't that great and using an actual controller is still preferred. Same with side scrollers since a D-Pad still feels better. It's a good addition to your setup but hardly a replacement.

It keeps getting better and better as I use it. Don't expect it to be perfect the first time you try it out in anything. That is not how this control will work for you. So after two days of use I will give my thoughts on the Steam Controller.
TLDR: Patience is required to truly appreciate the Steam Controller.
Day 1:
Upon first opening and holding the controller I was immediately disappointed. The controller feels cheaply made and very light (comparing to standard Xbox 360 wireless controller). The plastic used to make the device just takes away from the overall feel of the controller. I just placed it back in the box hoping for better outcomes when I actually started using it.
Setting up the controller was simple, exactly as I had suspected. Just plug in the extender and dongle base, set it somewhere where it can have a clear unobstructed view of the controller, place batteries in the device and power it on. Windows does all the work, steam handles the firmware updates for the controller flawlessly.
Now for the moment I had been waiting for. I went into big picture mode and started playing around. Everything feels great, it will take some time to get use to the button and joypad rearrangements but nothing too worrisome there. The typing experience was at first weird, but I was able to immediately pick up the concept and found myself typing faster with it than I can on a standard QWERTY keyboard. I booted Fallout 4 up and got ready to experience greatness.
I created my characters features without any problems, then I was dropped into the world free to move about as I saw fit. Only, I was immediately confronted with an issue, the camera movement controlled by the mouse that the right pad was suppose to emulate felt like garbage. I chalked it up to a bad default configuration, so I browsed the community for their favorite steam configurations and tested out the most popular. I was worse of now than I was with the default controls.
Disheartened and wanting nothing more than to enjoy Fallout 4 I tossed the Steam Controller to the side and went back to my faithful Xbox controller. Ah, the movement was perfect. Everything responded exactly as I was accustomed to. I continued with my Fallout experience for a few hours before calling it quits.
Day 2:
I had a good 24 hour break from the Steam Controller and since I didn't pay 50 bucks for nothing I decided to start tweaking the settings myself and seeing what I could accomplish.
I went into the configuration menu and found everything you could dream of. Dead zone settings, sensitivity, x and y-axis friction settings. There is even the ability to make the pad emulate a trackball complete with the feel of flicking the ball and the mouse continuing on as the ball rolls. After a tedious couple of hours of tweaking and testing in game I had a usable controller.
I spent a few hours using my current configuration making small adjustments to button mappings as I progressed in the game and encountered different scenarios that shed light on what best fit my play style.
After finishing up for the night I sat the controller down with a feeling of accomplishment. I looked at my trusty Xbox controller and realized that I will probably never pick it up to play another PC game ever again.
So my conclusion and recommendation for anyone interested in this device is this: If you are looking for a controller that you can just plug in and play PC games that require a K&M you are wasting your time. This controller requires dedication and tweaking to truly unlock its abilities. It will take time making minor adjustments to get that perfect feel, but once you have achieved that you will never understand how you were able to game with anything other than a Steam Controller.

Loadout is a fantastic third person arena shooter. It's biggest showcase is its weapon customization hence its name. One can change almost anything about the weapon. Do you want a sniper, machine gun, gattling gun, burst fire gun, or a beam weapon? You don't have to settle for just one make them all. The game's currency is blutonium or blutes for short. This is easy to get just through playing the game; one doesn't have to pay money for anything besides cosmetic appearances for their character. This makes Loadout a truly free to play shooter and a great one. Now on to combat, the combat is always fast paced. Players roll and jump constantly making every firefight a test of aim and quickness. Grenades add randomness to mix which can make for some interesting outcomes. On the topic of interesting Loadout's characters are the definition of interesting. Goofy taunts, dances, and clothing really add to the nature of the game. Now on to game modes. There are 4 game modes in Loadout: Blitz- A crazy control point mode, Death Snatch- Which is team deathmatch except you must pick up the fallen enemy's blutonium to count the kill, Extraction- A game mode where one person on each team is a collector and must gather blutes and put them into a bucket to score, and Jackhammer- A capture the flag game mode where the flag is actually a one-hit-kill hammer weapon. As you can tell Loadout is tons of fun and a truly free to play experience. Now that your sold on the download remember it is still in its early stages so it will only get better.

Until I Have You is an extremely atmospheric platformer that will quickly engross you in its cyberpunk, dystopian setting.  It's well worth your time and money.
Gameplay:  The gameplay is fairly unique. You scroll from left to right, navigating your way through short stages filled with platforming sections, death traps, and enemies.  Along the way you acquire a number of weapons that you can cycle through on the fly, and all of which handle a little differently.  You also a neat rechargable slow-motion ability, ala Max Payne, that you can use to handle trickier sections.  Overuse of this ability though will actually cause your character to lose touch with reality and hallucinate.
While the game emphasizes speed, it doesn't penalize you for moving at your own pace.  In that sense, it's very similar to Super Meat Boy and Hotline Miami.  Also like SMB, the platforming can occasionally be somewhat puzzle-like, so you'll find yourself dying a few times before you figure out how to advance.  These sections manage to keep the levels interesting, even though they can sometimes slow down the frenetic pace of the gameplay.
The highlight of the game for me though is definitely the boss fights.  The game has 12 chapters, and each one culminates in a unique boss fight.  I don't want to spoil any of them, but I can say that they all play very differently from each other.  This was easily my favorite aspect of the game, and at times it felt like I was playing a Blade Runner inspired version of Mega Man.
Graphics/Overall Style:  As I mentioned above, the game is incredibly stylish.  The character design matches the world perfectly, and the voice acting and cutscenes perfectly match the setting.  Also, each of the 12 chapters (each of which is comprised of multiple stages) have their own unique feel and character.  In one chapter you might be exploring the neon-drenched streets of decrepit city, while in the next you might be exploring an abandoned theme park or raiding the skyscraper of a megalomaniac obsessed with the occult.   You won't just be running through the same scenery over and over again, which is nice.
Story:  It will definitely keep you invested in the game.  While one aspect of the plot had me scratching my head at the end, it was a very enjoyable story overall, and it definitely enhances the overall game experience.
TL;DR:
Pros:
+ Great level diversity
+ 12 memorable and unique boss fights
+ Oozes style
+ Fast paced, intuitive gameplay
+ Engrossing story
Cons:
- Slightly unsatisfying conclusion
- Occasional bugs (which I'm sure will only continue to be hammered out with time)
Overall Opinion:
A must buy.  It's games like this that keep the industry from stagnating and make me happy to be a gamer.

Update: Menu navigation has been fixed, both the analogue stick and d-pad on xbox controller are fully responsive.
A unique platformer with a cyberpunk story and a great artistic style. The player has various weapons and abilities at their disposal as they can choose to either methodically kill every obstacle in their way, or make a hectic dash to the end of each stage. The game is split into several chapters which consist of several stages, the end of each stage has a percentage rank that is determined by your actions. The end of each chapter features a boss fight which become increasingly difficult and unique as you progress. It's very playable and entertaining if you enjoy platformers.
There are a few bugs within the game and very noticeable lag within the various menus. Hopefully the menu navigation will improve so the controller doesn't feel so sticky/laggy. Also I feel it is unnecessary for the end of each stage to have a ranking menu, it's jarring to be thrown into a menu instead of simply progressing to the next stage. The percentage ranking should be calculated at the end of the chapter instead so it plays more seamlessly.
My last complaint is that the soundtrack is pretty lackluster, this would be a perfect game to showcase retro synthwave artists such as Perturbator, Carpenter Brut or Daniel Deluxe for example. On a scale of 1 - 10 I'm confident that this game is a solid 7/10 as it is now. I'm sure this game will only get better as the bugs are fixed and just maybe some minor complaints of mine will be considered.

The gameplay was fluid and the fast-passed stuff was really well implemented. All in all, It was a great game indeed.

So yes, I recommend Until I Have You. A tale about revenge always gets me, but this one delivers in a way I wasn't expecting, through the price you have to pay for it and with the fact that, sometimes, it will be just a hollow victory.

tl;dr: There's nothing like it. A monument to the exceptional potential video games have as a medium.
DISCLAIMER: Let's get the elephant in the room out of the way. There's been lots of controversy over the PC version of Nier:Automata. I believe it has something to do with unsupported resolutions, occasional crashes, and fullscreen issues. I do not know the specifics because I had NO ISSUES WHATSOEVER while playing. The game functioned perfectly and ran flawlessly with only the slightest slowdown during intense moments. I installed on an SSD and played exclusively with a controller if that makes a difference. Research the issue and your hardware. Don't blindly listen to angry commenters lest they put you off from this experience any longer.
REVIEW: Now, onto the actual review. A review of a game that is truly unlike anything that has come before it. There is nothing like Nier:Automata. That is a good thing.
STORY: Exceptional. Odd. Unique. Progressive. There are 5 main endings, 26 different endings in total (including joke game over screens and the like). I say this because you need to play through the game 3 times, then the finale more than once to experience the whole package. The format is wholly original to videogames and if Yoko Taro (the game's director) is known for anything, it is taking full advantage of this amazing medium. I won't say much more, but I must admit 9S is my new favorite video game character and the absolute star of this game without a doubt.
GAMEPLAY: The gameplay is the most excellent variety of Platinum Game's hack n' slash with innumerable ways to customize your playstyle, difficulty, and abilities. The gameplay shifts perspective, genre, and direction on the fly seamlessly to fantastic thematic effect. The enemy types are wildly varied and the restrained open-world design leads to many unique combat settings. Part bullet hell, part hack n' slash, and all adventure exploring the savageness of our characters’ plight.
SOUND: The best of any video game ever. Period. There is no game that outclasses this game's sound design. In music, in environmental effects, 3D sound, it is all amazing. No sound felt too repetitive or overused. Combat sound changed based on who is hitting who with what. Sound is used properly warn the player in 3D space of charging attacks, or enemies behind you.
MUSIC: Yeah I brought up again, so what? It's perfect. There are innumerable variations of each song (of which I believe there are over 40) that play to fit the mood of each scene. Each song is altered to fit the scenario in every instance in every place throughout the entire game without fail. The composition, the mixing, the transitions are impeccable and without equal. They even give you a jukebox ingame to enjoy it. What a treat.
VOICE: Due to the nature of every character being an android/robot/machine, emotion in the voice acting is somewhat strange (and I can't tell if it was on purpose or a difficulty adhering to the writing). All the Japanese voices performed well. I played through mostly in Japanese, and parts in English. The English cast ranges from alright to exceptional. 9S's English performance was an absolute pleasure (small quirky additives like a *wipsh* sound to indicate a cracking of a whip was especially endearing). The English female voice actresses sounded slightly younger than what I felt they should have. Especially considering the battle-hardened setting. But overall it was a well done package in either language.
SETTING: A beautiful, bleak, post-post-post-apocalyptic city that shifts from ruins, to deserts, to factories, to airborne sea battles and more. All is presented with a very monochromatic aesthetic. Color is used subtly, but to great effect. I was originally not a fan of the weird grey-filter like appearance... But the presentation is done beautifully and is thematically fitting.
GRAPHICS: The character designs, world, weapons, direction, and the CUTSCENES (oh my) are all exceptional. I've kind of already said my piece on the presentation but I'd like to point out one observation. The lip-syncing and facial animations are so well done, the English dub actually resembles more of a live-action film dub (in that you can notice, despite the localizations best efforts, un-synced lips compared to the Japanese dub). I would normally consider this a negative... If I wasn't so awed by the beautiful craftsmanship.
NEGATIVES: In spite of my gushing over this game there are some nagging flaws (the game isn't perfect unfortunately). The side quests (and occasionally the main quest) largely consisted of the most run of the mill "Kill these enemies" or "Grab these things" variety. They even stooped down to including a few escort missions (unthinkable, I know). I would have been more forgiving if the side quests provided more meaningful insight into the world or characters. They all provided "some" value to the story, but as a whole I was never taken by them. I should also mention this game, despite the overall fairly brief runtime (about 35-40 hours for all playthroughs), has a fairly steep learning curve. I was familiar with this game before playing so it did not affect me, but an outsider going in may be lost.
BOTTOM LINE: With all of this said, I will simply repeat what I told my friends at the conclusion of my time with this niche, oddball, lovely, exquisite game...
"Beat all of nier. I don't know if it's my favorite game I've ever played... But I think it's the best one."

You're a tumor Garfield, but God made cancer, just like he made lasagna, except I made the lasagna. Does that make me more than a man? They call you a "bad cat" but they will never drink from the fat and rotten juices, they are unfit to be in the kingdom of Heaven and Hell Garfield. You are cut from the nape of the Earth, you little bitty cat. Don't kick Odie off the table!! Gaaarfiiieeeeld!!!! You stumble home drunk and your bits are all cut away. Did you let someone get to them? Did you snip them off yourself? You won't tell me. Instead you sit in front of the telly, sagging and staring at a sitcom. Your bits are still bleeding. Chunks soak into the upholstery. You'll be fine tomorrow Garfield You live here, Garfield. You are in between the walls and the beams but you live here. I breathe you in sometimes. It makes me remember innocence. I scream and shake outside of the shower. I try to step in but I slip on a wacky tie. I catch a glimpse of you on the way down just outside of the door frame. Your smile all pus and burn scars. Whose face will it be tomorrow? Garfield, I am your keeper. I just can't seem to get a date! A thousand shifting fever dreams couldn't molest my love for you, Garfield. It runs through the wires and the cogs and the paper cuts and the plushies. It died twenty years ago. It's pumped up again from a black river bottom and vomited onto naked little bodies. Can I remove myself from its fate? They pick at you like a great big feast. Garfield, your bulbous thoughts were always clear. I just didn't want to hear. But now it doesn't matter. Now you will see tomorrow. A thousand million living things melted for you. Rising Storm 2 isn't  the worst game out there, but the problem is that it's supposed to be carrying on the Red Orchestra legacy.  There's a severe lack of content, much of the gameplay is simplistic, and there are numerous immersion breaking game mechanics, especially the simple and unrealistic the sound effects.
The immersion was the best part of RO2/RS by far, but it is completely absent in RS2.  Even though you still have to use your ironsights, aiming feels like you're looking through a window, not down your gun.  What should be giant maps feel like tiny arenas that were mirrored a few times, and are extremely linear in terms of design.  Where in RS1 any thing that obscured you was a possible place to hunker down, in RS2, only designated spots are really safe, meaning all rounds essentially play the same.  In addition, the distance system has been scaled down as well.  In RO2, a meter was a meter.  In this game, one step apparently brings you 3 meters.  The marksman class always gets immediately picked up, so I can't tell you if ballistics were simplified to match this.
Out of everything in the Rising Storm 2, what really gets me is that the sound effects are built purely for gameplay.  I could handle lack of variety and even tiny maps if I still felt like I was in the middle of an intense battle, but in RS2, sound is built to inform the player of what's going on in terms of gameplay, not to accurately depict what's happening on the battlefield.  Your weapons sound decent enough (not that great), but enemy weapons firing in your direction sound like sharp pops regardless of distance and weapon type!  I don't think they even make noise if they aren't aimed at you.  When you hit someone, you're rewarded with an audible splat, even if it was an arm shot 150m away, and headshots get you a loud ding.  RO2 would also give you feedback when you hit an enemy, but they weren't as obvious.  Loud engine buzzing fills the map to alert you to recon planes, and although it sounds like a plane, it doesn't accurately reflect its location, the sound is more of an alert to its general presence than anything.  I don't think any of the sound in the game, except for explosions and possibly helicopters, is actually simulated.  This is a far cry from RO2, where you could hear every firefight on the map and had to take cover if an attacker was too far away to hear.  You could be pinned down by an invisible sniper and have to wait for better positioned allies to track him down.  Compare that to the RS2 experience:
Your ears are filled with bunch of pops that sound like a pistol being shot on the other side of the map, but a marker in the middle of the screen tells you they're flying your way.  Due to the simple terrain design, you can't drop to your stomach and let the uneven ground obscure you like in RS1.  You accept your fate and wait for the fatal bullet.  Maybe you'll at least be able to tell where they're sniping from and inform your team.  After the inevitable, you check the feed for the distance your killer shot from...  5m.  Yup.  Turns out it was a machine gunner in the bushes two steps away from you!  Beautiful sound design.
It's this immersion breaking gameplay that really upset me.  Sound cues are fine, but at least make them feel like part of the environment!  Make enemy shots more distinct if you want, but at least make them sound realistic!
Apart from immersion problems, the weapons are just... boring.  Aiming doesn't feel natural (which shouldn't be an issue since RS1 had amazing aiming), landing a hit doesn't feel satisfying (many body shots are no longer lethal), and automatic weapons are no longer the killing machines they were in RS1, which defeats the purpose of having them.  RS2s biggest selling point was that battles would be total choas with everyone carrying automatic weapons.  Every class does have access to automatics, but they've been balanced.  In my opinion, this goes against everything the series stands for.  There are far more refined shooters out there.  The only reason people play this series is for the intense experience where any bullet can kill you.  When a high powered assault rifle takes multiple hits to even injure someone, that just ruins it.
I want to add a disclaimer here saying that Rising Storm 2 is by no means a bad game, and some of you might enjoy it.  The gameplay is stilll better than many current shooters, the helicopters are really cool (and fun to play), I like the experience based cosmetic system, and the graphics are awesome.  It's like I said earlier, the problem is the Rising Storm name.  People play this series for immersion and unforgiving gameplay, not balanced bullets and refined scoring systems.  RS2 is a decent game, and probably the best Vietnam game out there, but if you're looking for a sequel to Red Orchestra and Rising Storm 1, you'll be sorely disappointed.
It's too bad, since I was really looking forward to Rising Storm 2.  I don't doubt it will be shaped up into a decent successor in a few years, but do yourself a favor and wait until the game is actually interesting.  You might as well be playing Battlefield right now.  I for one will be returning to RS1, but I'll be keeping an eye on this game.  I really do wish it was good.  If the developers are willing to listen to fans, make better maps, and rework certain mechanics, RS2 could be turned into a masterpiece!  Maybe someday....

When you click the mouse, you switch which side of the circle you're in.  Use this simple little ability to move from circle to circle and make a path forward.  Then you start to throw in some spikes and obstacles and the game starts to feel a bit more rewarding. Okay, let me get this out of the way first. I know I don't have a massive amount of time played on this game on PC but I have been playing this game for years.
Saints Row 2 is, in my personal opinion, the height of the Saints Row franchise. It has scores of customization, it has a fantastic radio selection, the vehicle customizability is top notch, the story is great, the characters are memorable, and it has just enough insanity that makes you realize, "Wow, this is actually really fun."
Going back to the game after many years you'll definitely see its age. The graphics feel unpolished and the physics are wonky, but that doesn't really matter. The best part about this game is the -fun-. It feels like GTA San Andreas mixed with polarized stereotypes but manages to actually have a very nice story with a lot of twists and turns. The ability to replay missions and cutscenes sounds trivial but it can create quite a bit of entertainment when you go back and experience some of the most pivotal moments of the game with a completely new character without having to replay the entire game.
The game feels unpolished, as said before, but that doesn't mean it's not a solid experience. Everything feels a bit floaty and like it doesn't have a great impact (which will become clear during things like chases and gunfights), but it doesn't detract from the sheer enjoyment factor. The game feels greatly fulfilling any time you do something like overtake another hood or kill a gang leader.
Ultimately, I can't recommend this game enough. Enjoy the underdog knock-off GTA before it got absolutely insane.

Review Update: Dec 5, 2014. Post patch.
Well, this game is now better then the original! Now that the majority of the bad bugs have been taken care of, Extinction is difinently worth playing now. The gameplay is faster-paced then the first, dinosaurs and humans control excellently, and loot drops are starting to come along in the form of a couple new dinosaur & weapon skins. Here's to hoping the human equiptable items & dinosaur cosmetic items are coming very soon.
Pros:
-Tight controls overall.
-No more abusing of terrain like in the old game! Ever since the 1.3 patch in the first PC, everyone abused rockclimbing glitches. Can't do that anymore.
-Playing as the humans is a tense, fast-paced experience. Though humans seem to move a bit fast. Maybe slowing them down a bit would fix this.
-Dinosaurs control better then in the original Primal Carnage and is extremely satisfying. Sprinting with a dinosaur actually feels faster and does not have an annoying blur effect to simulate fake speed like in the first PC.
-The enviorments are much inproved over the original. Maps are more vibrant with detail to the foliage, buildings and terrain.
-Humans have a larger variety of weapons & items at their disposal. More options are going to be added over the following weeks.
-Loot is only awarded at the end of a game, meaning players can't log on and then quit the game once they have their stuff like in TF2.
-Cosmitic skins and items can be mixed & matched, giving a better variety of customization than the first game.
-Most of the existing effects look good. The fire does looks a tad odd, but that doesn't make a flaming carnotaurus barreling straight towards your face any less scary. XD
Cons:
-Some of the animations on the humans, particularly their walking animation, could use some work.
-You can win crates in your loot, but there are no keys to unlock them yet. :(
-Some of the weapons sound pitiful compared to their counterparts in the first game, particularly the shotgun and rifle.
-The pteranodon's grab feels fantastic overall, but it seems a bit to forgiving, as humans will constently be gravitated into your grasp that should have missed. They need to decrease the grabbing zone a bit to balance how easy it is to use.
-On the other hand the raptor's pounce could have a slightly wider grab range. You can't jump if you aim past the pounce range. Having a quick-pounce option but just quickly clicking the pounce to just leap in the pointed direction would make it better.
-Could use a little more detail in a couple of the maps. One example is the Atrium C map, where the map event sets the dome to lockdown and zaps everything inside the dome to instant death. There are no electical effects when this happens. Everyone just dies. There needs to be an electical shock overlay or a flash on the screen to complete the effect, otherwise it seems a bit lazy.
-Still a few random bugs here and there. One persistent one at that at the beginning of a match, the top & bottom of the screen are cut out by black bars, block your HUD. They will eventually disappear, but its still a bit annoying. Another glitch I recently found was that after a match an error box will appear and the game crashes, however this happens after the ending screen during map transition, so it doesn't effect your loot drop.
All & all, if you are a first Primal Carnge owner, jump at the chance for the $3.00 price. If you were thinking of getting the first Primal Carnage, get this instead. It has what the first PC had and more in the near future. The first PC in its current 1.3 build is filled with unbalanced classes and glitched up terrain, and they aren't gonna update it anytime soon. Extinction however has a bright future with more fairly balancing, more maps, and customization options

If I had to describe Loadout in short, I'd just say: This game is sick.
The game is about making guns, and then destroying other players by them (yes, you are not just killing them, but actually destroying them). Fortunately, the game is not P2W, and everything that must be purchased can be bought by using "Blutes", the currency, you get for playing games. There are 4 kind of guns, but they can be customized in a hell lot of ways, to fit your playstyle, and make you feel like a total badass. The graphics may remind you of the TF2 style cartoonish-graphics, and there is no problem with it at all.
There are some game modes, but only a few of them has specific maps for themselves. These are quite fun, but you can see some differences. In this game's deathmatch, you gain score, if you collect the items, your killed enemy dropped. Or instead of capturing a flag, you've got to capture the hammer, which can also be used as a weapon. If you kill someone with it, your "Hammer Value" increases, and when you bring it back to your base, your team get additional points after every enemy, who got killed by the hammer. Personally, this "Jackhammer" is the most fun game mode for me. The last update brought you the Domination game mode, which can be familiar from the Unreal Tournament GOTY's Domination game mode. Not counting the minor difference of having to keep the points until we constantly earning points.

This game is amazing. Don't listen to the people complaining about doomstacks. While its true to some degree that a bigger number will beat a smaller number, it is very possible to beat the AI with a significantly smaller number if you are smart with your ship/fleet composition. My biggest example of this is beating a fleet of 14,000 power with my fleet of only ~10,500. A good ship design and fleet composition are far more important than having the bigger number. Not to say doomstacks are non-existent in the game, I'm sure you will pretty much always beat the AI if you have a higher fleet power, but they are not nearly as big of a deal as some people are making them out to be.

Stellaris at first glance might not appear to be too impressive, but beneath it's vanilla surface resides a wealth of content and replayability.
I have dumped a numerous amount of time into this game, and I believe it has been worth it. Even before it went on sale, I bought every form of dlc just because I felt like it would boost my experience ten-fold. This game has much to offer in terms of gameplay and empire management that has not been experienced in other grand strategy games. In fact, I'd go as far as to say that this is one of the best space strategy games of all time (exeption of Starcraft). The scale of this game is insane, and each playthrough is more different than the last.
One of the biggest positives that this game has going for it is the Devs' continued developement of the game. Each new update and dlc is dedicated to shaping Stellaris into the best game it can be. In short, they listen to their playerbase. I have no doubt that this game shall continue to evolve and grow into an even more amazing game.
Here are some things that I think would make it EVEN BETTER than it is now:
1. Ground combat needs to be a little more interesting. Current system is too bland and lacks any form of interesting playstyle. I think a few ways that the devs could improve this if they allowed us to customize our troops like we can customize our ships. It would offer more variety and less boredom to ground invasions.
2. More customizable options for your style of ships, cities and buildings.
3. Make micromanaging your empire easier. At it's current state managing your empire in the late game is very confusing and complicated. If the devs could figure out a way to ease the burden of managing your enormous empire, that'd be great!
All in all, I give this game 9/10

I've never played Metroid or Castlevania, and I never finished Mario on NES -- so this game's ultra-fast pace and insta-death mechanics so popular in the days of yore should scare me. And they DID! But I love challenges. And big pixels! In fact, though it might not be immediately obvious, it made me think od Hotline Miami -- another game that I didn't feel I stood a chance against and yet tried anyway. Lo-res and intense gameplay aside, you'll find familiar themes of extreme violence and the protagonist's slow descent into madness, including terrifying hallucinations. It's dark, it's gritty, with just the right amount of tech-noir camp and dystopian grotesque. Just like HM, Until I Have You is hard. You'll die. A LOT! By level 4 of Chapter 1 you'll think: hey, I'm getting good at this! -- and for that level 5 will kick you in the shin. Repeatedly. I think I got my 1000 deaths achievement while battling Boss #1. And it'll only get crazier from there. Chapter 4 will have you wonder if it's humanly possible to get through. But you will. You'll learn that the right moment to jump up before an incoming wave of fire is when the flames start bursting right in front of you, and not before (because otherwise they'll burn you when you fall). You'll figure that the right moment to leap over enemies crawling up from below is not when they jump, it's when they're ALMOST in your face as you dash right at them at full speed. I'm currently on level 5.3 -- and needless to say it looks IMPOSSIBLE. Climbers AND divebombers?! :O Not to mention 5.2 gave me enough adrenaline for WEEK! So... enough for now. But I'll get back to it. Tomorrow! The tempo, the rhytm is just too exhilirating to resist. Sometimes it's like I'm seeing in slo-motion (without the actual slo-mo mode on). The rush is just crazy. You'll enjoy it, whether you're a seasoned platformer maniac or a timid sudoku enthusiast like myself!, Because yes, beating your record time in sudoku is ecstasy. But this is better!

Great platformer with a great atmosphere and great artwork. The artwork and story give the game an artsy touch, which I like. The pixel-graphics fit into the art style and the story fits to the pixel-graphics.

During the two hours I have played I had two weapons. A baseball bat and a pistol. Both are requiered as some levels/parts of levels are easier to challenge with the right weapon, but if you are quick enough you can run past all of the enemys, but you need much skill for this in the later levels as the suroundings become more and more dangerous and it becomes easier to stand still, kill an enemy and look and wait until you know the movement patterns of the level (moving platforms, laser beams).
Both ways are equally fun: fast play and slow play.
And yes you will die alot, and this game might frustrate you at some point, but if you like platformers you are going to enjoy every single death as you learn from your death. You learn how to play the level step by step until you finished it and after finishing you want to try the level again just to reach a better score.

I found myself desperately wanting to play a Pirate-themed game recently. I have tried pretty much everything that has come out on PC in the past 20 years or so (not many Pirate games in two decades), and due to horrible scores and a despicable reputation, I had decided putting Vendetta off until I really needed my Pirate fix. I bought it fairly soon after launch, but just yesterday, as the gods of gaming answered my calls for digital piratey goodness, Steam notified me that a few days ago a new patch came out for this game, and people were actually enjoying it.
So I Installed it and here I am after a 12 hour gaming binge pillaging throughout the caribbean seas. I was not expecting a Skyrim-like session coming from playing such a globally hated, and I mean despised game. But dare I say it, this thing is excellent. And. Yes. I even like it more than AC Black Flag. I won't waste time explaining why, but lets just say that Black Flag needed to be its own game...away from the AC cash machine that fathered it. Where that one was rich in visuals, it was limited by the legacy of its forefathers and a bunch of stuff was included that really break the pirate experience. Vendetta on the other (poorer) side of the spectrum, has less booty, but a lot more heart, and truly scratches that itch I had for something piratey.
Open world, dynamic trading, crew hiring and management, ship upgrades and ship upgrading from sloop to galleon, awesome ship combat and boarding, great and immersive music, beautiful graphics and very stable (on high end machine), sea exploration, land exploration (treasure hunting!), cool taverns, immersively populated towns and cities (and world), decent voice acting, a story that so far has me intrigued...everything that is needed for an epic pirate experience you might think...and then there is the sword combat system. I will be blunt, if you do not invest in it seriously, and I mean flight sim level seriousness here, trying to figure out the system's complexity (and clunkiness), will lead you to believe, just as thousands of others, that the combat is worst than a french kiss with Jane Scurvae, and there is so much of it, most will give up the hunt before the treasure is even revealed. But stick with it. After a while you'll level up both in real life and in the game and it ends up making you feel like a true swashbuckler, just not at first.
But a few will brave Vendetta's murky waters, and those patient enough to do so, may actually be rewarded with one of the most complete and epic pirate games made in recent memory, that is, if Sid Meier's Pirates! has run it course in your gaming library, or if the AC part of Black Flag sunk that ship for you. If you like pirates, exploration and have the patience, give it a go. It truly is a great pirate game.
Real score: 8.5 (I will give a 10 to affect the average)

Summary:
It's a story based piraty roleplayish game with ship combat and relatively small land areas.
And would you believe it, it is actually ok now!
After the original release was an unmitigated technical disaster (check youtube!), this re-release under new name has been patched into a working game. Don't expect absolute perfection but with very limited competition, it's really worth giving it a go in a sale. The full price is a bit optimistic tbh.
Also the nasty DRM has finally been removed. Will they EVER learn? Trying it carefully, i do actually enjoy it now.
Story (so far) is ok, graphics are ok to good, the audio mess of the original game is (almost) fixed. Random NPC comments can get a bit annoying. I'd like an option to reduce them. Music is actually nice. Controls, with the exception of melee combat are ok. Only jump/loot on one button is a stupid idea. Performance is mostly ok, but some FPS drops occasionally. Could and should be better but isn't too bad..
The main character is a bit of an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sometimes, but i like that, because it makes sense. He is a pirate in rough world (And not one from a Disney Movie) on a revenge mission. He's not a sophisticated philosopher.
Also the world is dirty and kinda realistic for the time. Which also means feminists may have a  hard time, enjoying it...
Only i kinda imagined the area a bit less rainy....
In short: The actually interesting game underneath the former heap of crap is now visible and playable. No crashes, major bugs or anything so far.
____________
Worst part is the (on foot) combat system. Little feedback on hitting something and without locking on a target often you hit precisely in every direction but the enemies. Can be REALLY annoying.
The skill system implies a sophistication to the combat system, that isn't really there. It's managable but not great. There are many other skills as well though.
While the sea battles are in classic 3d action style (Black Flag, AoP), thankfully they spare us (bad) melee combat on boarding other ships. Which is the downfall of the sea part in AoP/SD
Instead Vendetta switches  to a little turn based boarding game, based on ship statistics like crew number each turn you can either send all crew to board or some board some shoot cannons or just cannons. Hull or Crew go to zero, fight  is over.
Sadly you can only board equal/smaller ships, which feels wrong (seen Master&Commander?). And only board the last remaining enemy ship unlike in BF and AoP/SD, which make sense since the other enemies don't just wait patiently (stupidly) for you to finish the 1st like in BF.
The Ship battles are a good mix of realism and action. Somewhere right between the 2 "rivals": AC Black Flag/Rogue simple arcade battles and Age of Pirates(AoP)/Sea Dogs hard and slow battles..
____________________
The Competition:
1.
Assassin's Creed Black Flag (and Rogue) is of course the superior game.  But in terms of sea battles, it's only advantage is the graphics. Otherwise it's just too simplified. It's an no depth(!) arcade action version of sea battles. Ships drive like cars, wind doesn't matter, relaoding in seconds, peoples movement on board makes absolutely no sense, cannons shoot THROUGH huge waves. And of course only one ship type.
All of the things above does Vendetta better. But without making it all as slow or complex in AoP/SD. For me it's a good way.
Only when on foot, on land or on boarding Black Flag becomes superior again since it inherited what remained of the AC games. Like the melee combat system. Graphics in Black Flag are of course better, but Vendetta doesn't look too bad either.
2.
The other competition are the Age of Pirates (AoP) games, last installation "Sea Dogs: To each his own"(SD). I'd love to like them but some great parts and mechanics are utterly ruined by horrible parts and mechanics that STILL haven't been improved for several games of that series!
Pirates of the caribbean (2006), Age of Pirates 1 and 2, Sea Dogs.
SD/AoP has the most complex and flexible (and slowest&hardest) ship combat system. Many different ships, complex mechanics depending on weather, crew number, ship equipment. Also you can fight and conquer fortresses. The managing in the ship part of the game is more complex then in the other 2 competitors. You can have and command several ships in battles. Their AI is horrible though so they always sink quickly..
And you can  take over boarded ships into your fleet or as your own. Which you sadly can't in Vendetta (can only buy new ships from certain people in certain harbours). All sounds good.
BUT!:
The melee combat, movement and control system in SD/AoP is STILL abysmally bad!!
Sadly to board ships you're forced into this horrible melee combat and movement system and in tight spaces, which makes it even worse. That almost ruins the great sea battle part.
Also it bothers you (again) with a boring and broken on land RPG story thingy before you can get a ship and play the good parts..
Also poor are graphics (almost same sincs 2006), controls, UI, Quest log. Everything BUT the actual sea battles is bad. And it doesn't work (really) in 21:9.
___________
So in short: Because Sea dogs maks it VERY hard to enjoy it and Vendetta also has the better and fleshed out world and story and skill system and is more of an story based RPG AND a has good (but less flexible)  sea battle part... it's just the better game.
Black Flag isn't really a comparable game. The arcady sea battle part is just way too simplified, to compete directly. Better for quick fun but no depth.
Btw: Try Rebel Galaxy. Is like a very good space version of these games. It's Ship fights control exactly the same way. Freelancer with Black Flag style battles.

I've been playing for about 10 hours now and think I can actually recommend this game.
The vast majority of negative reviews stems from either the previous release of this game, which was in an abysmal state - but this is a new iteration of that, so that really shouldn't count.
Or they come from people being fully unable to run this game - can't say too much about that, I had no problems - may try not running it on a toaster with WinXP?
Now, the game does still have issues, of course. Many issues, in fact. If Steam would allow a more sensible rating than just thumbs up or down, I'd probably give this a 65% or so.
Just to list a few:
- The game did crash on me twice in my 10 hours.
- The combat is clunky. REALLY clunky. More clunky than Risen. However, one CAN master it and even fight multiple enemies at once.
- Some locations invite you to explore - but there's nothing to find except for quest objectives.
- The main character is an incredible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
- The voice acting is... meh.
However, despite all of that, the game does manage to capture the Pirate & Caribbean atmosphere incredibly well. Actually close to Black Flag - some might even say better. The ship combat is also fun - and actually challenging in contrast to Black Flag.
The slight RPG system helps you define how you want to play and some of the abilities (like using the crow to steal) are just hilarious!
So, all in all, I can recommend this game. AT A SALE, though!

NieR: Automata delivers everything you'd expect coming from the derranged mind of Yoko Taro.
Set against the backdrop of a war between multiple factions of robot and all the intrigues and twists that come with it, automata uses this framework to explore a variety of philosophical and moral questions that the player might otherwise dismiss were they framed against a human element.
While Platinum Games (Creators of Bayonetta and Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance) delivers - as ever, entertaining, satisfying and larger than life action combat and visuals, which would stand up on it's own even in the absence of it's stellar storyline.
Put the two together and I cannot recommend the game highly enough. NieR: Automata is no mere "Hack and slash with a good storyline", it's the kind of game that challenges and engages the player's perceptions of how a game should play and how they interact with it's characters and world in a rare and special kind of way (Evoking games like Undertale and Majora's Mask) and will leave you thinking about it lesson's for a good time after you've finished.
After finishing the first
playthrough of the story, you also unlock a new game plus mode and chapter select to finish off quests you may have missed, replay the story, finish up achievements, seek alternative endings or just generally replay content you enjoyed, so it does offer a good amount of replay value... but, after the true ending, you might
to go back.
The only thing I can criticise is that the PC port of Automata is incredibly sloppy; with screen resolution issues needing a 3rd party fix, and one of the worst mouse/keyboard implementations I have ever laid eyes on. If you have one, a controller is advisable.
Nonetheless the game is absolutely worth your time and money.
