The Steam controller is a new kind of game pad - if it can even be called a game pad. It's so unique that it almost warrants its own classification. It is part game pad, part track pad, and has more buttons and customization than you will ever get from a standard controller. I have spent precisely one day with the device, and despite the flaws, the little quirks here and there and a steep learning curve at first, this controller gave me something that I have been looking for since we began the so called "Next gen" gaming frontier: something new and different.
The new Steam controller features a few things that anyone who has been using a 360 controller up to this point will be used to - an analog stick on the left, A, B, X, Y on the right. But then we get into some new territory as Steam has completely removed the right analog stick and traditional D-Pad in favor of two track pads. These essentially serve as a mouse (and keyboard at times), and even provide tactile feedback when used - a sensation that is difficult to explain to someone without access to the device, but provides you with a better sense of contact as you drag your thumb(s) across the pad(s). This was intended to make up for the lack of texture and centering that you would get with a traditional analog stick, and works quite well in most cases. Though certainly not in all cases.
Another new feature on the device are two extra buttons on the bottom where your hands would usually grip the sides of the battery pack. These sides can be squeezed to offer another source of input, which is fantastic for mapping the right one to the jump button as you typically do not want to remove your thumb from the right track pad to press any of the four letter buttons, ESPECIALLY in first person shooters. It's a unique way to provide an extra bit of interface as this controller is designed to work with PC specific games (Civilization V, System Shock 2, etc) that require far more buttons and a mouse interface to play effectively.
The last new feature - as stated above - is the ability to completely customize the controllers layout. You can re-map any button you like to produce any action you like. The controller is typically set to ... about as default as Valve can get it in some cases. If you want to play as if it were a traditional controller, you are good to go. If you want to remap the trigger button to taunt for some reason, that's all good too. The sky is the limit with these customizations. It also means having to play around with the settings a lot for some games to get it to be even remotely workable. I still haven't been able to pinpoint a pad sensitivity that makes Bioshock 2 even remotely playable for me, but fortunately the community is able to upload their control scheme to Steam and allow other users to use them. So if some generous soul figures out my Bioshock 2 problem (and I hope they do), that issue will cease to be.
Valve has put a lot of effort in making sure you will have every option available to you in order to play virtually any game you want without a mouse and keyboard, and to actually get my hands on something new and different in this day and age is a welcome and refreshing change. But of course, there is a learning curve, and while the controller works very well in most cases, it's definitely not ideal for any and every game you want to play. Obviously games where the right analog stick is little to never used will be largely unaffected. Games such as Rocket League, Sonic Generations and Arkham Knight functioned exactly as they did with my 360 controller. But when you're trying to play things - especially shooters - that are mouse and keyboard dependent, such as Counter-Strike and Team Fortress 2, you are hit with a very steep learning curve indeed.
As soon a game of - say - TF2 starts, you immediately realize you are at square one with the thing. All of your gaming instincts that are tied to both mouse and keyboard and traditional controllers are thrown out the window, and you basically have to start from scratch. No matter how good the track pad you are using is, trying to react to other players with a track pad just isn't the most ideal situation in an FPS. Anyone who has attempted to play TF2 on a laptop with the track pad can attest to that. And even with practice, I found my self at a distinct disadvantage every time I tried it. Now let me be clear, the Steam Controller's touch pad is far superior to a laptop track pad, and with practice you will get better. I certainly did. The problem is that without the right thumb stick, the controller simply makes the game harder than it needs to be no matter how much you work on things. With time and patience, maybe you could get your play style to match what you could do with a traditional controller, or even (Though probably not) a mouse and keyboard, but it doesn't seem worth putting your self through the hassle if you already have those two options. At least, that was my experience.
The best time I had with the controller's new functions came from playing games that I could never play without a mouse and keyboard, such as Civilization V and System Shock 2. In the later case, the touch pad's learning curve was present, but not nearly as severe. Being able to access the vast interfaces and menus of both games felt very functional and easy with the touch pad in those cases. It's still not exactly on par with a mouse and keyboard, but being able to play those types of games from the comfort of my couch for the first time was a new and interesting experience, and the controller made it very easy to pick up and play those types of games as if you were sitting at your computer.
The Steam controller is a good controller, but it's not for everything. I would even venture to say that it's not for everyone. I have the feeling that with more time and practice I will be able to play shooters on the thing with a certain sense of precision and skill, but I just can't imagine why I would want to when I have two other options that I am used to (A mouse and keyboard and/or Xbox 360 controller) sitting right there in front of me. This will of course will be a judgement call on your part, but for me, shooters are not something you want to attempt with it. Pretty much everything else functions great, and the controller is certainly interesting to use. At fifty bucks, it's not much of an investment for you to try it out your self. I recommend it pretty highly for all of the positive aspects I mentioned above. The controller isn't perfect, but few could argue that it's not at least unique.

One trick Pony.
That sums up this piece of hardware perfectly. Before reading this, know that I only tested the controller one day and that my refusal to recommend this controller doesn't mean that it's a bad device - on the contrary. I simply can not fully endorse it at the moment.
The positives:
The controller appears well manufactured, it feels good to hold, even though the middle buttons and analog stick are tiny and hard to reach for people with small hands. The rear triggers have a small range of movement but it doesn't hurt much. Customization is insane and you can waste (and sadly might have to) hours fiddling with all the options to get the controls however you want. If you spend time configuring your desktop profile accordingly you can even play non steam games with it (I tested it with Diablo 3).
I'll get the obvious outta the way first: The trackpads are amazing. I was skeptical, but they make Shooters easy to control. You will still get rekt by M+KB players, but for a quick round of deathmatch in CSGO this thing works surprisingly well. Recoil control is hard so you have to tapfire but you will hit where you want, and dont have to overcorrect awkwardly like with analog stick aiming. You can actually AWP with this thing if you are so inclined.
It REALLY shines with third person shooters. GTA V feels like it's made for this, camera control is so much better than with dual analog, yet you have all the advantages of a gamepad, IF you use one of the community profiles with mouseaim and not the standard controller mode where the right trackpad acts like an analog stick...
This brings me to the glaring negatives which prohibit me from recommending this thing: If you play a game actually meant for dual analog, the trackpad is super awkward to use. It is hard to explain, but in a way it's the reverse of how awkward analog camera aim feels to a mouse user. GTA in native controller mode felt so much inferior to the community profile with the mouse trackpad. I started up Divinity: Enhanced Edition, with its shiny new controller mode, only to find that the trackpad usage had been reduced to rotating the camera 90° at a super slow pace, requiring me to drag my thumb 5 times across the surface just to make a full rotation. As in GTA I'd have to use a mouse emulating community profile, Ironically, because while this felt better than the slow camera trackpad, it was overall still less efficient than just playing the game with a X360 controller in its new controller mode.
Essentially the Controller fits it's niche very well: Games you wanna play with a mouse for precision but a controller for ergonomy, which are mainly 3rd person shooters. The problem is that at literally any game outside that niche, be it RTS or sports game, Mouse + KB or Dual Analog have this thing beat.
If you wanna spend 55€ on a piece of hardware that enables you to play everything, but doesn't really make you want to, then go ahead, you will not be burned. You will also not see a big improvement over what you already have though,

Pros:

-Every class has a seondary of some sort now, nice desert eagles lol.

Now for the cons which most of my issues aren't from the bugs but how they changed up the classes as well as the gameplay itself
Cons:

All and all I enjoy dinos, I enjoy dino games, if they keep at it I'm sure the game will get its deserved balance. Give it time people and things will eventually come full circle.

Vendetta: Curse of Raven's Cry is a rebranding after minor bugfixes of the abysmally terrible Raven's Cry. While the developers managed to successfully make the game less shockingly horrible, they didn't manage to make it good in any way whatsoever. The ship battles are cool and remind of, yet completely lack the dynamic feeling of Assassin's Creed: Black Flag. The combat system has parrys and dodges but feels like the characters and their animations are going forward on rails... really really slow rails. It's possible to board enemy ships after they have been mostly disabled, yet there is only a minigame instead of actual combat to overtake the other vessels crew. On top of that, the minigame is horribly boring and after the dozenth time it becomes so much of a hassle that I personally just went and sunk every single ship I wasn't required to board due to the quest goal forbidding to add the wreckage to the other several hundred ships which sank into the depths of the sea over the course of my playtime.
Main and side quest design is very often bugged, doesn't register quest progress, some quest details don't update, there's no markers and the entire gameplay is highly repetitive. Animations are lackluster. The graphical quality jumps between actually quite atmospheric and an abysmally lighted scene with a plastic look several times within the same minute. The voice acting is terrible, the writing is even worse and truth be told it is so bad that it actually starts getting ridiculously funny at times again.
Then there's the ability to do other things than missions, killing random people or attacking random ships: Trading. There's literally no reason or incentive to ever buy any resources, because just boarding a single random ship will already yield more material than most ships could possible get into their hold. That is, if you still are willing to bother with the boarding minigame, although between having to walk to each individual trader on every port to be able to buy and sell wares and the boarding minigame, I'm not entirely sure which of those two is wasting more of the players time. I probably spent 50 hours alone walking through ports just to be able to sell enough wares to get the achievement for making 100.000 in trading income. It's just horrible.
As for the interface, it is minimalistic, but sufficient. The inventory works most of the time, but equipping new items often doesn't update character statistics without having to close and reopen the inventory. There's a severe lack of items and customization options in the first place, the character progression skill tree is a bad joke and I could actually ramble on for way longer but I don't think there's a point of wasting more words and time on reviewing this game.

That time probably added up to close to 75% of the entire time it took me to grind my teeth through this completion.
One of the games that really makes me question my compulsive tendencies to try to 100% every game I play. Just skip this and play Black Flag instead. Or Risen 2. Or Sid Meier's Pirates Gold. Or any other game on steam, really. Statistically speaking playting literally any other random game will most likely be a better experience than this one.

Cons:

tl;dr: There's nothing like it. A monument to the exceptional potential video games have as a medium.
DISCLAIMER: Let's get the elephant in the room out of the way. There's been lots of controversy over the PC version of Nier:Automata. I believe it has something to do with unsupported resolutions, occasional crashes, and fullscreen issues. I do not know the specifics because I had NO ISSUES WHATSOEVER while playing. The game functioned perfectly and ran flawlessly with only the slightest slowdown during intense moments. I installed on an SSD and played exclusively with a controller if that makes a difference. Research the issue and your hardware. Don't blindly listen to angry commenters lest they put you off from this experience any longer.
REVIEW: Now, onto the actual review. A review of a game that is truly unlike anything that has come before it. There is nothing like Nier:Automata. That is a good thing.
STORY: Exceptional. Odd. Unique. Progressive. There are 5 main endings, 26 different endings in total (including joke game over screens and the like). I say this because you need to play through the game 3 times, then the finale more than once to experience the whole package. The format is wholly original to videogames and if Yoko Taro (the game's director) is known for anything, it is taking full advantage of this amazing medium. I won't say much more, but I must admit 9S is my new favorite video game character and the absolute star of this game without a doubt.
GAMEPLAY: The gameplay is the most excellent variety of Platinum Game's hack n' slash with innumerable ways to customize your playstyle, difficulty, and abilities. The gameplay shifts perspective, genre, and direction on the fly seamlessly to fantastic thematic effect. The enemy types are wildly varied and the restrained open-world design leads to many unique combat settings. Part bullet hell, part hack n' slash, and all adventure exploring the savageness of our characters’ plight.
SOUND: The best of any video game ever. Period. There is no game that outclasses this game's sound design. In music, in environmental effects, 3D sound, it is all amazing. No sound felt too repetitive or overused. Combat sound changed based on who is hitting who with what. Sound is used properly warn the player in 3D space of charging attacks, or enemies behind you.
MUSIC: Yeah I brought up again, so what? It's perfect. There are innumerable variations of each song (of which I believe there are over 40) that play to fit the mood of each scene. Each song is altered to fit the scenario in every instance in every place throughout the entire game without fail. The composition, the mixing, the transitions are impeccable and without equal. They even give you a jukebox ingame to enjoy it. What a treat.
VOICE: Due to the nature of every character being an android/robot/machine, emotion in the voice acting is somewhat strange (and I can't tell if it was on purpose or a difficulty adhering to the writing). All the Japanese voices performed well. I played through mostly in Japanese, and parts in English. The English cast ranges from alright to exceptional. 9S's English performance was an absolute pleasure (small quirky additives like a *wipsh* sound to indicate a cracking of a whip was especially endearing). The English female voice actresses sounded slightly younger than what I felt they should have. Especially considering the battle-hardened setting. But overall it was a well done package in either language.
SETTING: A beautiful, bleak, post-post-post-apocalyptic city that shifts from ruins, to deserts, to factories, to airborne sea battles and more. All is presented with a very monochromatic aesthetic. Color is used subtly, but to great effect. I was originally not a fan of the weird grey-filter like appearance... But the presentation is done beautifully and is thematically fitting.
GRAPHICS: The character designs, world, weapons, direction, and the CUTSCENES (oh my) are all exceptional. I've kind of already said my piece on the presentation but I'd like to point out one observation. The lip-syncing and facial animations are so well done, the English dub actually resembles more of a live-action film dub (in that you can notice, despite the localizations best efforts, un-synced lips compared to the Japanese dub). I would normally consider this a negative... If I wasn't so awed by the beautiful craftsmanship.
NEGATIVES: In spite of my gushing over this game there are some nagging flaws (the game isn't perfect unfortunately). The side quests (and occasionally the main quest) largely consisted of the most run of the mill "Kill these enemies" or "Grab these things" variety. They even stooped down to including a few escort missions (unthinkable, I know). I would have been more forgiving if the side quests provided more meaningful insight into the world or characters. They all provided "some" value to the story, but as a whole I was never taken by them. I should also mention this game, despite the overall fairly brief runtime (about 35-40 hours for all playthroughs), has a fairly steep learning curve. I was familiar with this game before playing so it did not affect me, but an outsider going in may be lost.
BOTTOM LINE: With all of this said, I will simply repeat what I told my friends at the conclusion of my time with this niche, oddball, lovely, exquisite game...
"Beat all of nier. I don't know if it's my favorite game I've ever played... But I think it's the best one."

So, I've had the steam controller for about three and a half weeks. I've played a bunch, and used it outside a gaming space, a bunch.
The twin haptic pads are very interesting. Resting your thumbs on the pads with the forward facing grips feels good. I have large hands and the controller works great with large hands. Small hands, might prove taxing.
The grip buttons are large and effectively sit on the back, under the triggers. These work well, and can be used as modifiers. FPS games seem to be using them for duck/jump and that seems to work well.
Creative apps, such as adobe suite, and illustration/vector based users should find a lot to like with the steam controller. It's not perfect, but it makes mouse/keyboard free navigation and such reasonably simple. The most precise setting I've found emulates two trackballs for the left and right thumbs. What's nifty is that you can set up both pads to create one large virtual track/mouse space. flicking things over with one thumb to the other side of the screen (or window) back and forth.
Clicking on the pads is heavy, but feels good. The haptic feedback is on the subtle side and there is no normal controller vibration. Here is a list of what I've tested and made controller profiles for.
Space Channel 5 no. 2. A very simple set-up. I cranked the haptic sensation up to max for a musical/percussion setting. It feels good to do the up/down/left/right on the left haptic and the shouts/shots on the right haptic.
Deus Ex Revision. The new mod update is fantastic and the keyboard/mouse controls map rather fantastic to the Steam Controller.
Invisible Inc. Works great.
Alan Wake. Really good controller set-up with mouse precision. Looking around and aiming the flashlight feels great. A bit of haptic feedback gives the flashlight weight and momentum.
Unreal Tournament 2K4 and UT3. Both these work great. Feels lovely.
VR stuff. I tested the controller with the oculus rift on Mind: Path to Thalamus & InMindVR. It's a great controller for VR.
Civ: Beyond Earth and Endless Legend both feel great. I can imagine playing 4Xs with this controller may not be ideal, but it'll work just fine.
Pillars of Eternity. Worked pretty good. There are some great settings out there that give you almost complete control.
Audiosurf 2. Pretty sweet.
The two titles I probably enjoyed the most with the controller were Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, which, for an older game, feels rejuvenated on the Steam Controller, and Bulletstorm, for similar reasons.
Cave Story+ felt great. And console controls on Legend of Heroes : Trails in the Sky also click just right.
Oh. And it's a dream on Dolphin emulation. Like, perfect.﻿
My only complaint is that the presspad alpha keypad is tucked behind the steam big picture menu, when it should perhaps have the option to be mapped to a button to bring it up.
The other big thing that takes some getting used to is the high precision haptic controls in addition to rather great gyro adjustments. So Splatoon fans will be able to enjoy most their games this way, or using gyro to direct a third person camera, etc.
And Valve's own games have many great controller setups. More devs are adding their own custom configs.
Big potential for people who are into music creation and audio/video editing. Using the haptic pads to scratch feels great. You can use mouse scroll up/down on the indented pad, too. This could be a good DJ tool for a DJ who wants to leave the board for a spell.

Mode of operation: I do not use this on a TV + couch setup. This is used for my computer.
I do not care for the Xbox controller, and the Playstation controller is a pain in the butt to hook-up to a PC properly. The Steam controller feels good in your hands, with a nice shape that doesn't bother my hands like the Xbox controllers do.
The large touch sensors are nice, but not used in most of the games I play. For playing Rocket League, this controller has been excellent. Even better is the ability to fully customize the button layouts and what they do. That alone was worth the price of the controller.
There are still, sadly, some games on Steam that really just need a controller as opposed to my preferred keyboard + mouse. This controller finally lets me play those games comfortably, and more importantly, customizably.

None of the reviews I have seen has mentioned this, but the packaging for this controler is pretty spiffy.  I almost felt like I was buying an Apple product with the level care given to the packaging.  The box open and closes (kind of like a shoebox that folds open) where you can keep your controller in the styrofoam placesetting when you are not using it.
This controller has by far the best controller-typing I have ever seen using the two haptic touch pads, where the keyboard is split in half--the left side for the left haptic pad and right side for the right haptic controller.  Just like everything else with this controller, it takes some practice to get comfortable with how it works, but once you do, it feels like magic.
I have no idea why there are so many naysers for this controller.  It is a fundamental shift from analog to digital technology with using that haptic pad and gyro sensor instead of using the right joystick in a standard XBox controller.
I also love how you can configure this controller for each game, so it's possible to play games that require a keyboard and mouse with just this controller.  Sure there are already programs that do this for standard controllers, but this configuration is much more extensive and powerful.  Also, I have always found it next-to-impossible to use a controller joystick for a mouse.  It just doesn't work.  However, the haptic touchpad DOES work instead of a mouse, just like a touchpad on a laptop can be used instead of a regular mouse.  Plus you can just use one of the popular configurations created by other users, which saves a lot of time.   This is not to say this controller is a replacement for the mouse and keyboard.  Clearly, it is not, but just the fact that it can work if need be is quite impressive.

Overview: Minecraft: Story Mode is a game made by Telltale Games, a studio known for its story-driven narratives powered by player choice. This game attempts to merge the universe of Minecraft, an open-world sandbox game, with the tradintional Telltale format. It is in my opinion that the game preforms well in all factors, but has its flaws. In short: I reccomend this game to lovers of Minecraft. However, you may get bored fast if you do not like Minecraft.
Story: *NO SPOILERS* I found the story to be quite charming, although a bit cliche. Odds are you'll be able to guess what happens before it does, but there are a fair share of suprises. Although this is certaibly not vanilla Minecraft, the world does stay faithful to most of the machanices. A lot of people seemed to find the dialouge cheesy or annoying. I disagree (mostly) and found it quite charming and humorous. That being said, there is a notable difernce between the Male and Female player character voice actors. I personally found the female version of Jesse to be much more entertaining and full of personality then the male version. They say the same lines, but the WAY they say it is radically diferent.
Graphics: Faithful to Minecraft without a doubt. It does have a little polish here and there to make it look nicer, but overall it feels now Minecraft. Unfortunetely, so does the animation. I must say i expected better quality animation then what we got, the movements are stiff and at times they distract from what is going on.
Audio: Sounds are faithful to Minecraft. Voice acting is solid.
SUMMERY
Pros:
-Faithful To The Look And Feel Of Minecraft
-Charming And Unique Characters
-Humorous And Full Of References
Cons:
-Cliche Main Story
-Poor Animation
Other:
-Female Player Character Is Far Better Then Male. I'd Reccomend Playing As Her Regardless Of Your Real Life Gender
-Take Your Time And Look Around

All-in-all though, Primal Carnage: Extinction has many advantages over its predecessor and is a major upgrade.
All of the maps have been completely overhauled and now look fantastic, the design and graphical quality is far superior and contributes to a more immersive and satisfying gaming experience.
The different species of dinosaurs within each class now have slightly differing abilities which adds variety to gameplay whilst providing players with a wider range of play-styles. The human weapon system has also been revamped with all classes now having a secondary weapon as well as the addition of support roles (i.e. throwing down health or ammo packs). This, I feel, helps to make the game a lot more balanced. (Providing people utilize teamwork, of course!)
The movement and the attacks of the dinosaur classes takes some re-learning, but once you get used to it you'll have no problems. Definitely worth the purchase, especially if you enjoyed the original Primal Carnage.

If there was an "Eehhhhhh... Kinda?" option for whether or not I recommend the game, that's what I'd select.
It's hard to really say. Sport games aren't really my big thing, but I do enjoy the customization options for WWE games, it's fun to make (or download from others) a bunch of other characters and have them fight. Particular when there's the ability to swap them out with the official roster, and watch things play out on its own. I can't even begin to describe how delighted I was to see a sudden pairing of Batman and Shrek come out to ambush to tag team champions and watch that fued unfold.
But that's practically a factor of my own making, to which I'd just flat out say game of the year every year, but obviously I should be looking at what's presented.
The issue with yearly releases with sport games is they might fix and/or make things better this year compared to last, but they'll also have broken or forgotten something of last year. I can't remember the last time there was a 'perfect' sport game. And really, that's probably how they get your money. "We'll make them think 'Well maybe it's better this year.'".
For the most part, I'm personally enjoying the game. I haven't had any crashes or major graphical issues or anything... had a moment of Becky Lynch sitting on a crate, but not actually sitting on it and instead floating in the hallway, but besides that, game runs pretty awesomely. I'll thank my PC for that, so decent computers can or should be able to run the game fine.
But the main appeal factor with custom characters in MyCareer modes and such, it's... A LOT of hit and miss.
-No voices for characters
-Small and bland soundtrack
-Sloooow running around backstage
-A few too many mistakes in what the characters are saying (The Rock asked me if I was bothering myself when -MY NAME- should've been whoever I was fueding with at the time)
-Probably a little too much 'not-actual-matches' matches
Although the funny thing with that last point is as I joined RAW and was told to lose 3 matches in a row, I thought "Huh... that's like every new person that joins Raw.". Then I did a series of actions that led me to joining Smackdown instead and I proceed to have matches with Dolph Ziggler that turn into cutscenes of instant losses, and spent the next few weeks doing pretty only promos and interviews... Aaaaand I thought that's just like Smackdown a lot of the time.
So in a way... it's accurate to the shows.
Buuuut any fan can tell you the state of the WWE lately hasn't been amazing, so maybe being just like them isn't the way to go.
As for the gameplay, it's pretty much what you'd expect, although they're nice enough to provide some alternatives for some actions, such as how you do submissions. They keep some newer actions while providing former alternatives to them, which I like. Haven't really got any complaints on anything there, other than reversals sometimes not registering. I COULD just be making excuses, but I am pretty damn certain I hit that right trigger perfectly on that finisher!
At the very least, it's probably the best one 2K has given since they took the franchise, but it's a bit hard to say whether the bigger fans will enjoy it. I can't really think of why they wouldn't, but I don't think I'm looking real hard at it.
For my own personal pleasures in customization, I get a lot of good stuff, and probably the best I'd seen in the games in quite some time. The amount of customization options is massive to a point where I hope to god the game picks up enough to see how good and accurate the community can make a bunch of characters look.
Although the major downside to this is that, for some ungodly reason, a lot of them for MyCareer and such come out of Lootboxes... whyyyyyy they chose to include those, I'll never know. But at least the boxes are easy enough to acquire without a tremendous amount of effort besides regularly playing... I guess?
Really though, I'll continue supporting PC versions in hopes that they'll stick around for it, and include Steam workshop one of these years.

Main problem I have with Vendetta - Curse of Raven's Cry is the price.
I've paid less money for far better games, and had better looking games run more smoothly on my computer. If the game was a lot cheaper, I would actually recommend it, since there is a good game buried somewhere deep beneath dozens of optimization issues and bugs. I'm willing to look past many issues for any game that lets you take the helm of your own ship, be it starship or sailship, and sail to the open seas.
Basically this game is like poor man's Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag. Except you can get Black Flag cheaper. Wait for a decent sale at least, before buying. And while you do that, I'm getting a refund.

For me Vendetta: Curse Of Raven's Cry is a game that could do with a little TLC from both developer/publisher and from users/game players.
Having played Vendetta: Curse Of Raven's Cry for about 29 hours now then I think that it's a quite nice game. Surely it has crashed for me a few times and surely I have had to run it in Windows XP SP3 compatibility mode to get it to not crash (using Windows 7 , 64 bt) , but apart from that I think that it's a rather nice game and it's a game that has been put a lot of work into.
If publisher could fix the reasons for the (at least for me) blatantly obvious problem which is that game crashes especially if not run in compatibility mode then I would hope that many people would came to appreciate what this game has to offer which for me is a lot.
For me the sea battles were too difficult initially but I just used the cheat console to give the Raven all perks upgraded and fully upgraded ship. After that the sea battles were quite easy for me but still entertaining as they then have become more arcade like while still also being a rather nice and entertaining ships battle simulator and a lot better comparing to Port Royale 3 , Patrician IV and others and with better graphics than East India Company. Of course how difficult sea battles ought to be from the start depend on taste - I mean I am sure that a lot of people would like them to be very difficult until ship and captain are fully upgraded by game play advances but as I play to be entertained then I just like stuff to be solvable relatively easy I guess..
Many of the maps in the game seem to have been put a lot of work into though there are the odd minor graphic glitch here and there but I think that that's to be expected. And there are a lot to be explored though I am left with a feeling that though Curse Of Raven's Cry is the more impressive to me then Two Worlds II were the more content rich with all the houses with chests too loot but maybe it's just too long time since I played the original TWII Velvet Edition. One thing I wish though is that the current objective indicator were more clear to me in VCoRC like it was in the TWII game.
There is other stuff that I personally would have liked better or easier and there ought to be a Wiki for a walk-through but that has not been game breaking for me so far I just used Google and Youtube to find solutions to what I could not find out or understand myself and I guess that opinions always will vary - also I already had maxed out the Raven's skill tree to make sea battles easier and gotten gold to upgrade the ship(s) so I then also used that gold for buying available weapons on shore and that might have influenced game play for me other ways too....
Oh , I almost forgot , the nice music ought to be mentioned too.  What is good music of course also  is dependent on both taste and mood but I thought the music to be nice.
My verdict is that this is a nice game that deserve a much better reputation than all the negative feedback that it got.  It might need to run in compatibility mode (Win XP SP3) and one could experience the odd crash after that but game auto saves at all important points and user can save too so to me the game has been a relatively nice experience. So I would recommend the game to other people that are able to accept to play it under those conditions.  (Of course I do think that developer / publisher ought to give the game the attention it needs to be completely stable so that  no compatibility setting would be needed).

The criticisms of this game are valid, though not nearly to the point of justifying how badly recieved it is. The graphics are outdated but not horribly so, somewhere between The Witcher 1 and 2 I'd say, and the controls are clunky, making combat far more frustrating than it is fun at times. This is not a AAA game and it shows but what also shows is that the devs really wanted to make a great pirate game, something there are far too few of. It's a fun game that could benefit from some tweaks, maybe even a few mods.
On top of this the devs made an enhanced version of the game, addressing a lot of the criticism and gave it to the people who owned the original game free. That kind of pro-consumer attitude is hard to come by and I respect them for it. There was apparently a lot of complaints about racism, sexism and homophobia in this game but I haven't encountered any. Perhaps it was watered down in the rerelease, I don't know, but in any case this is a story about pirates. A few unflattering words are hardly the most egregious crimes being committed here.

Rising Storm 2: Vietnam. One of the best games of this year. Complete with great representations of the era, Character customization with a wide variety of cosmetics and grueling sound design. Not to mention very detailed and satisfying to shoot weapons. While there are still some problems with the game, and a few bugs that have yet to be ironed out, it's still a fun and engaging experience, even if you'll most likely be killed by a friendly more than an enemy.
Pros:
-Great sound design
-Awesome gun models
-Character Customization
-Very immersive at times
-Funny voice lines
-Great soundtrack
Cons:
-Still some bugs that have plagued the previous installments
-A lot of friendly fire incidents (Especially by commanders)
-Old engine (not really that bad, but some people would see that as a con)
-Can get old after a little while of playing
-Wonky hit detection sometimes
All-in-all I'd say it's a solid 7/10 and can only get better as the devs work on it. Pick it up if you have the extra cash, or if it's on sale..

None of the reviews I have seen has mentioned this, but the packaging for this controler is pretty spiffy.  I almost felt like I was buying an Apple product with the level care given to the packaging.  The box open and closes (kind of like a shoebox that folds open) where you can keep your controller in the styrofoam placesetting when you are not using it.
This controller has by far the best controller-typing I have ever seen using the two haptic touch pads, where the keyboard is split in half--the left side for the left haptic pad and right side for the right haptic controller.  Just like everything else with this controller, it takes some practice to get comfortable with how it works, but once you do, it feels like magic.
I have no idea why there are so many naysers for this controller.  It is a fundamental shift from analog to digital technology with using that haptic pad and gyro sensor instead of using the right joystick in a standard XBox controller.
I also love how you can configure this controller for each game, so it's possible to play games that require a keyboard and mouse with just this controller.  Sure there are already programs that do this for standard controllers, but this configuration is much more extensive and powerful.  Also, I have always found it next-to-impossible to use a controller joystick for a mouse.  It just doesn't work.  However, the haptic touchpad DOES work instead of a mouse, just like a touchpad on a laptop can be used instead of a regular mouse.  Plus you can just use one of the popular configurations created by other users, which saves a lot of time.   This is not to say this controller is a replacement for the mouse and keyboard.  Clearly, it is not, but just the fact that it can work if need be is quite impressive.

While it is akward to hold at first, you'll get used to it.
The Steam Controller is a full replacement for a mouse. Left Trackpad works as the scroll, RB2 is left click, LB2 is right click, and the right trackpad is the mouse portion. There are two bumpers on the back of the controller. They go back and forth through whatever page your on if you're on a browser, left and right respectively. It's nice to have the option to have basically a mouse in your lap. If you play a lot of console games, I highly suggest you get it. Very natural transition.
Unfortunately, it's a bit overprice. During the pre-order, you got a copy of Portal 2 and Rocket League, which made the controller effectively $10. If you have the cash, get it.

I really wanted to like this controller, but:
A Different Kind of Gamepad
Notice where the buttons are? If you are used to using PS or xbox controllers, your wrists are going to be parallel if you don't want to be pressing the wrong buttons. Maybe can get used to this if only have steam controllers.
Dual track pads
Notice the lack of second analogue stick, that's okay right because of the extras track pad? Try playing a dual stick shooter with this configuration, hands cramp up in no time, especially when using those buttons.
HD Haptics
Really? The haptics on my 10 year old logitech mouse are more realistic than the supposed track ball (sounds like clicking in an empty plastic shell, barely noticable feel)
Dual Stage Triggers
Yes, though I've yet to witness the benefit of this, hopefully more games will support,
Ergonomic Control
No, I've switched back to using the xbox 360 controller on my main machine.
Mac OS Support
No, well not last time I checked. As I bought this controller for my second rig, which is running Mac OS, I had hoped it would work. Did get an email from Valve apologising and offering Valve complete pack gift for my troubles, but I have not received this. Will chase them up.

I am not a controller/console player but I recently found a couple of games that recommend using one, Rocket League being one.
I tried an Xbox controller and it worked but it is older technology, tried and true. I found lack of configurability to be an issue with games other than Rocket League. It meant I was using K&M for most games and picking up the controller for a few others.
Enter the SC.
I found the form factor to be a bit larger than the Xbox; I have small hands. Holding it asymmetrically made all the difference in the world. No longer uncomfortable, it in fact became very easy to use.
In Rocket League I find it much easier to perform aerial maneuvers that were impossible with K&M and somewhat hard on the Xbox controller. Rolling about the long axis while in the air and boosted are a breeze.
Now further add in the configurable aspect of the SC. I start browsing templates put together by the community.
It is now another game altogether.
(The particular template I grabbed has Boost (B) built into the throttle by contacting the switch at full firewall)
And the templates just keep coming. People are writing configurations for just about any game you can name. And if there is no template for a particular game - make one!
The freedom that this controller allows, both where you play and how you play makes this literally a game changing piece of hardware.
132 hours out of the first set of batteries.
And each day another game I own seems to be begging for the controller.
I started with one game in mind when I bought this and now have 4 games in which this is the MUST USE form of control.
It'll only get better.
EDIT - almost a year later the 'A' button has stopped working. However after contacting support I was sent a prepaid shipping label to return the device and was told I'll get a new one when they receive the old one.
I was gifted a second controller and included was a carrying case.
The case came in a box filled with packing material while the controller came in a poly bag with no packing.
Their Quality Department needs some prodding.
I was surprised how simple adding a controller is. BPM asked me if I wanted to add the new controller to my account. I answered, 'yes' and that was it. It then told me an update was available and after I ok'ed it the update was installed.
Steam Controller Case:
A hardened case its not.
It feels like a soft injection molded form with a cloth covering, a zipper and a logo.
It is very much like a laptop case/bag. Much better than nothing but not the same as inside your suitcase.
But it will keep the controller and cable & batteries stored safely enough. It's also a nice place to put the controller when I finish playing. It is very dusty out here in the western USA, so that'll help too.
If you travel with a laptop and wanna play, I can recommend the case. If you tend to toss things around, it'll help but how much...I am not sure.
On sale, I can REALLY recommend the case.

I haven't played this series before, but Eskimo Bob reminds me what is "classic".

I backed this game on Kickstarter just because I was so excited to see a new NES game in development. Yes--you read that right--an all-new game in 2017 for the orginal Nintendo Entertainment System.
One other thing I should note is that I didn't know anything about the Eskimo Bob series on Newgrounds, so this review is from the perspective of someone with no nostalgic connection to the game's characters or story.
As with all Kickstarter game projects, you sometimes wonder if the pledge was worth it--if the game is as good as it looks on the videos. Well, I've finally gotten around to check it out, and I'm happy to say that I'm loving it!
The gameplay, like many classic NES titles, is very simple. It's your basic 2D platformer, with a few puzzle-type mechanics added in to make it interesting. The 2 playable characters, Bob and Alfonzo, have different abilities and slightly different jump arcs, which felt like a throwback to Super Mario Bros. 2 (the North American Mario 2, of course). The first few levels start out very simple, but get progressively more complex and interesting as you go along. So far, I wouldn't say this is a challenging game, but it's also not a pretty fun little game, and the level designs so far feel very carefully designed to keep things fun.
The controls themselves are very smooth and responsive--more-so than many NES games of years ago!
The presentation of the game is also very well done. The colour choices are great, the characters have cute animations, and the music is a fun throwback to the simpler days of gaming. One thing to note is that I only heard one song so far in the game. I haven't gotten tired with it yet, but I'm not sure if it will get old after a while or not.
I've been disappointed in the past with some of the games I backed on Kickstarter, but I'm not regretting this one. It's clearly a labor of love, both for the old web series and for the NES. I'm just thrilled that this game exists, and recommend it to anyone looking for some retro platforming action.

This game is the perfect example of why we need more options than just "Yes / No" on reviews.
This is a silly action puzzle platformer with tight controls. You control either Eskimo Bob or Alfonzo as they collect all the floating fish on a stage to advance to the next area. Bob can jump higher and farther, and punch blocks below him, while Alfonzo has a stick which lets him attack enemies and destroy blocks in front of him.
And you might think it can get boring, but it doesn't. The controls are super tight, better than most games on the old NES, and while most stages are straightforward and can be cleared out pretty quickly, there are a few that will take you much longer to complete because you have to plan out your moves ahead of time, or you don't have access to Alfonzo's stick to defend yourself. And there are a few stages where you can get stuck if you don't do things the right way - thankfully, the game tells you in advance by placing a warning sign at the start. There are also some stages that require you to have pin point accuracy and reflexes (I was stuck on Level 40 for a long while) but you'll get the hang of it.
The game also features a password system which saves your progress. The password is saved automatically and restored when you load the game - I imagine it's a carryover of the forthcoming NES version, which likely won't have the benefit of autoloading the password when you start up the game. You can remap your control settings and choose between windowed and fullscreen modes.
You get a boss fight every 16 stages. The first three bosses are pretty fair, you basically have to punch them three times so you can proceed to the next level. And here's the reason for this review... the final boss. Unlike the earlier bosses, he has more hits, and each hit also changes up his attack patterns. And if you even get hit once, you have to start the fight all over again. And I'm sorry, but after losing to him twenty times, I gave up.
This is the sort of design choice that made me return Ninja Gaiden II to the rental store over 20 years ago. This is the same design choice that made me shelve Sly Cooper and the Thievius Raccoonus (Sly 1) 8 years ago. And now it's made me shelve this game. I no longer have the patience nor the drive to deal with a design choice that should not even be considered in 20-friggin-17.
I beat Dark Souls 3, but I couldn't beat this game, so the creators should be proud of themselves.
Final game stats as of this writing: 3.2 Hours Played from start to finish, about 1 hour of that was spent replaying levels I couldn't beat. Over 100 deaths and multiple game over screens. Lots and lots of cursing.
Final word: Fun throwback to the NES era, including both the best and the worst design choices of the time. Kinda short, but worth a playthrough. Neutral to yes reccommended.

Pros:
1. Beautiful graphics
2. Very large and varied roster featuring stars from different eras that can be incorporated nicely into Universe Mode
3. An extensive, detailed creation suite
4. Reversal system is very well done (Depends on timing, but it works pretty much every time i press the button on time and the too early or too late is pretty accurate)
5. Lots of backstage area to take the action too with plenty of places to explore during both MyCareer and Falls Count Anywhere matches
6. The intros of the shows with the opening and the fireworks as Michael Cole introduces everyone is a nice touch that makes it seem more realistic
Cons:
1. A number of bugs/glitches (such as the wrong person appearing in a cutscene in Universe Mode instead of the person you're feuding with)
2. Animation issues (such as the referee magically jumping in the ring like Superman in super quick time if you choose to do a Break Out during an entrance and then enter the ring along with your opponent and some Superstars going through each other)
3. Universe Mode gets quite boring pretty quickly (some will love it, but many of the same issues remain such as rivals facing each other a lot on the weekly show as well as PPV and the Promo Engine is hugely flawed as all talent sounds pretty much the same and the likes of Brock Lesnar with no Paul Heyman is in the ring saying lines he'd never say in real life in long winded promos and the walk to the ring during the promos is almost always the same for everyone but a selected few and the dialogue options are never unique to the talent speaking into the mic so everyone sounds similar and nothing like they do in real life)
4. MyCareer (which can be fun at times, but can also be repetitive and the writing isn't all that great and the lack of real voices used to me anyway makes the mode decent at best, but the roaming feature is still a positive)
Overall, i would rate this a 7/10 - fix the bugs and occasional animation issues and improve Universe Mode by fixing past issues, adding more realism, depth and detail to the Promo Engine and add more cutscenes, then this would be even better.

TL;DR Nier:Automata has the potential to be one of the greatest games ever made. However, there are some design decisions and technical issues that make it not reach this potential. It is still definitely worth buying on sale, probably even for the full price.
The combat in this game is very fast paced and enjoyable. You will definitely not get tired of it as the game constantly keeps changing the playstyle that you are allowed to use. The story is simply amazing. Graphics and sound were also great.
And now, I'm gonna talk about the game's faults but before I do that, I'd like to stress out that this game is a masterpiece for the story alone, so it is definitely worth playing, even despite its faults and some technical issues.
The difficulty tuning in this game is not great. It is not terrible, but definitely not great. There is an extremely hard difficulty where you are killed by any hit, and then there are "normal" and "hard" difficulties which are just too easy because you are allowed to buy basically unlimited number of healing items which you can then constantly spam and never die. Also, there are "plug-in chips" which gives you passive buffs and if you get good combination of plug-in chips, together with the healing items, you are basically invincible.
On the other hand, there are parts of the game, when you loose access to vendors for some time and if you didn't buy enough healing items, you might run out of them! The game is extremely hard then and I was forced to play on easy for one boss fight because of that.
I think that this issue with difficulty tuning could be solved by limiting the number of healing items that you are allowed to use per battle, just like it is done in Dark Souls series. I'd like to point out though, that just the fact that I compare the combat in Nier:Automata to combat in Dark Souls is a huge compliment.
Then there are the technical issues. Oh boy, the PC ports... These technical issues are the main reason why this game doesn't have great reviews on Steam and that is quite unfortunate because these reviews do not review the game itself but only its technical aspects.
There is a weird bug with fullscreen mode, when the game doesn't really go fullscreen but leaves these black stripes on the edges. I solved this issue by using Window Borderless Gaming program and apparently there is even a mod that can solve it but just the fact, that you are forced to do such a thing, is not good, not good at all. Also, anti-aliasing is extremely demanding for some reason, so it is recommended to either turn it off or set it to lower.
I managed to get 60 FPS on my 60 Hz monitor with Window Borderless Gaming program and low anti-aliasing. If you experience any other technical issues, there is a great section in DIscussions, where you can find help.
That being said, I'd like to encourage people not to get intimated by the technical issues and give this game a chance, because it definitely is worth it.

This controller is perhaps the most unique controller experience I've had thus far in my gaming life (so, my entire life).
Other controllers for various platforms are surely different, but despite a few exceptions (such as the PS4 controller touch-pad) each controller is just a slight variation in terms of button-placement, ergonomic design, number of buttons, type of analogue stick, type of button, etc.
The Steam Controller, however, is entirely different. The dual touch-pad instantly sets the controller apart from all others. Trying its best to mimic a mouse+wasd, the controller attempts to make a very bold stance against the previous gold standard for PC gaming. Does it succeed? Here's my take:
The shape of the controller is, for the most part, nothing too wild and crazy (looking at you, N64). The controller is comfortable to hold, and the battery placement (each battery going into either side of the controller) makes the controller have a nicely distrbuted weight, so it's both comfortable to hold and isn't top or bottom heavy.
As with all controllers, a lot of this is purely subjective and totally up to personal preference. This is presented more as "Things some people may not like" as opposed to "Things that are objectively bad." First and foremost, The front buttons and analogue stick may be a bit awkward to reach to at first as they are not the primary thumb-resting-position like they are on several controllers, with that spot being dedicated to the right touch-pad.
Something else I noticed is that different games may call for different grips. I haven't tried this controller out with every possible type of game, but the standard hold of being able to press every single button (if needed) requires your index fingers to go on the top triggers, middle fingers to go on the lower trigers, and your ring and pinky fingers to rest on the lower triggers which are on the lower-back of the controller - this may be hard to get used to or require some awkward finger presses - I couldn't get used to using my ring and pinky finger to press the back button, but I suppose that will come in time. (A side note: The back buttons are well placed such that you shouldn't have to worry about accidentally pressing them.
These things are really cool. Perhaps the coolest part about using the touch pads are the faint robotic scrolling sounds the controller purs back at you when you use the touch pads for a mouse-pointer. The right side offers fainter, rapid feedback rumbles and the left side sends back slightly stronger pulses. I was able to navigate menus just fine, and I think with some practice I may be able to substitute this controller for many games.
Of course, getting used to this thing will take time. For the first few minutes of using this my mouse was flying all over the screen, and I would overshoot my targeted click-points by a mile. Just using this for a few minutes though helped my accuracy tremendously.
Clicking could be kind of awkward - for strictly using the controller as a mouse on a browser, the lower back triggers were registered for right/left click, which felt rather awkward. The good thing is that these settings can all be changed, but the defaults were a bit uncomfortable to me (imagine left-clicking with your right middle finger).
Another blatant shortcoming of the Steam Controller, if you can really call it a shortcoming, is the blaring lack of, well, a keyboard. Any game that requires you to type means you either have to be sitting at your computer anyway, or come up with your own creative keyboard solution. The Steam controller has no built-in software for calling up an on-screen keyboard, and I think it could really use one. Some demo videos for the controller showed the devs speed-typing quite effectively - perhaps an exeggeration for marketing purposes, but not having the ability to even attempt an on-screen keyboard makes this controller off-putting for games with typing.
Finally, For certain games that require extreme precision, I'm not sure how this controller will hold up. I'm trying my best to be patient and get used to it (only had it for one day), but I question for some games if it could ever match the repsonse and precision of a mouse. I play sniper type classes in most shooting games, and getting the pixel-perfect headshot precision was quite difficult with this controller. I'm sure it will improve over time, but I wonder by how much.
This controller has been incredibly pleasing to me. It is very simple to use, (USB plugs in and you're good to go) and the touchpads are truly revolutionary. I'm not sure I'll ever be able to return to a standard controller. The learning curves are definitely worthwhile, and while this controller may not replace your mouse for everything, it will certainly be quite incredible for the things that it can replace.

"Polarity" is a first-person puzzle platformer that's hugely derivitive of "Portal," except that it's:
1)  much cheaper (both in terms of price and production value)
2)  much shorter (main "campaign" takes about an hour, maybe)
3)
easier (see #2 above)
4)  much not-as-good, frankly.
Oh, and there's no jokes...  Or portals, for that matter. There
one original gameplay innovation -- you can alternate the ability to walk between red and blue force fields -- but this is so rarely incorporated into the puzzles that it's hardly worth mentioning.
"Polarity" isn't a
game so much as it's just a deeply unsatisfying one. Taken solely on its own terms as a cheap knock-off, it's made with a certain degree of underwhelming competence.  If you're desperately itching to play a first-person puzzle platformer that starts with the letter "P", and the phrase "cheap but competent knock-off" doesn't scare you away,
you've already played through both "Portal" games at least twice, then buy "Polarity" when it goes on sale for fifty cents (which seems to be every six months or so). Do not under any circumstances pay full price for it.

It's a really good game, but the port is terrible.  I was able to make it launch without crashing, but every now and then the game would still crash.  Fortunately, your progress gets saved frequently so this wasn't too much of an issue.  There is also some noticeable stuttering when driving the car and on rare occasions the sound gets staticky.   Some people have had trouble getting this game to run (especially if they have older computers) so be aware of this.
As for the game itself,  it's what many people wanted GTA IV to be, though I haven't played GTAIV so I can't make that comparison.  However, I have gone through GTA III, Vice City, and San Andreas and it's very similar to San Andreas.
Like San Andreas, you control a gang and can conquer territory that earns you money and prestige, especially if you buy up all the stores in the zone.
The prestige system is unique to the Saints Row series.  Basically, you have to earn enough prestige in order to continue the storyline missions, though this is very easy to do.  You can earn prestige in many, many ways, though the minigames are the best way to do this.  You can also buy clothing and upgrade your Cribs (various storage units and homes) to earn style points that give you a bonus to prestige.   Because it was so easy to earn prestige, this never felt like a roadblock to me.  Besides, the minigames are pretty fun.
Minigames are the best part, actually.  Most of them are pretty funny and there were only a few I didn't like, such as the Heli Assault missions, but that's because I've never liked flying vehicles in these types of games.
The storyline is pretty basic, but decent, and I liked the music stations for the cars, though I do miss the talk station from the GTA games.  The graphics aren't too bad, either.  The later Saints Row games are much sillier than this one, but since I haven't completed those yet I can't make a comparison.
Probably my favorite aspect to this game is character customization.  Unlike the GTA games, you create your own gang leader and have a ton of options.  I made mine an obese Latina and covered her in tattoos and awful makeup and ran around in a bikini and a pimp hat, so that's just a little bit of what you can do.
I've spent a lot of time on this game and have completed the main storyline, but there are still lots of things I haven't done, like collecting all the CDs and doing all the diversions.  The minigames that show up on the map, though, offer the best rewards because they upgrade your character in various ways such as giving you unlimited ammo and extra health regeneration.  These make the endgame rather trivial, so you might want to increase the difficulty for a better challenge.
There have been several GTA-type games  that I've played over the years like Destroy All Humans! and The Simpsons: Hit and Run, but this one is by far the best.

Oh well this review is going to be kind of tough. I'm a person who has seen it all (I´ve played Dr Jekyll and Mr. Hyde to the end, so I should know about bad games... right? LOL)
Sum up: It ran for me with no problems (Windows 7 x64). The game is... completable but has many annoying bugs. Clunky combat. Decent story. Chapter 3: TOO MUCH WALKING. Bad voice acting. Bad lip sync. Not worth the actual price tag. I'm giving a thumbs down because of the price - quaility ratio. I would give a positive review if the game was $15 since it kept me entertained.
Detailed review: This game actually does have its moments, it really does. Sadly its not enough to justify its pricetag. First of all, if you are a completionist or achievement hunter you'll be pist because many achievements are bugged. The reputation achievements mainly. I think the devs made a mistake there, becuase there are (supposedly) 2 achievements related to reputation per faction. I think they didn't want that. They wanted to make one rep achievement and other for completing the faction questline but somehow the programmers screwed up. Another completionist annoyance is that sometimes questmarks stay FOREVER in the map, even if the damned quest is mark as solved, speaking of which... LOTS of quests appear as finished when EVEN THE FREAKING DESCRIPTION says that you still have to go and collect your reward. Quests should end when its ALL OVER.
A.I. is random AF, sometimes they are tactical geniouses that surround you and mob you to death Dark Souls style and sometimes they just stand ther and wait for you to patiently reload your pistol (or special skills like the kkick or the hook) and beat the crap out of them one by one. You can just jump on a rock and shoot them from there: profit, they'll neve climb it.
The graphics are not horrible, though I've experienced FPS drops sometimes. Level desing seems kind of neglected and you can see that a lot on the islands. To the poor soul who wants to start exploring an island: you'll end up in glitch city if you don't follow the defined path. There are floating stones, textures you can fall through, unescapable pits, etc. The ambience is kind of good (on the defined path), the flora and fauna are not THAT accurate (Sabretooths on the Caribbean? Thanks Obama) but when it gets it right: wolves, parrots, lizards, river crocodiles, tapirs, boars, monkeys, etc. It's enjoyable. The animal sounds are accurate.
Combat: Oh my god the combat. If you master the combat in this game you can have some fun. It'll always be annoying, but you'll get used to it. "Why annoying Mr. Bison?" Oh well: AOUTO TARGETING, and a very BAD autotargeting. one expects to press a directon and hit the attack button and see your character swinging its sword to that direction. t doesn't happen. It always swings to the closest threat and even then it doesn't get it right. The most disgusting examples is the battling the animals, which is more like battling with the controls to land one FU-KING hit. If you are on a slope and they are in a lower position, you'll never hit them. Diagonal attacks? What for? LOL If they are too close your sword never hits either. You have to step away or step rightwards and then forwards+attack to make a thrust. THIS THING IS UNBALANCED. At the start of the game yeah you can feel somewhat the challenge, failing a parry can get you killed... But oh boy, on the mid-end game you can TANK your way almost through anything with the right perks and items and with a one hit kill sword: the British sword. Enemies don't level up.
Stealth: When it works its fun... but most of the time it doesn't. Silently slitting throats is very rewarding and landing throwing knives too. I don't know how does the silent close kills work. It seems that the NPCs in ehich it works must already be hostile and not fully aware of your presence.
Content: The storyline is decent enough, I enjoyed it until chapter 3, when you basically become an errand boy and OH GOD THE WALKING. Its too much. Speaking of which, you have to walk way too much on some ports to get to the trader or shipwright to sell things or repair your ship. The music is kinda good, especially the sailor songs sung on bars or streets. Naval combat is fun and challenging until you get the last ship in the game and♥♥♥♥♥♥the SHAIT out of everyone EVERYTIME.
Bugs: A lot, they don't make the game unplayable but they are annoying. Avoidable, but annoying. The steam overlay problems made the game crash 4 times in my whole playthrough.
Controversy: If you are here, you must already know this is a re-release of "Raven's Cry" and that the company took down  its Steam Store site to whipe away the bad reviews. They should've just patched it and live with it. Not much people are happy with that business move since we consider it is dishonest.
Conclusion: This game is not a bad game, but its not worth $60 in my opinion due to a poor Quality- Price ratio. When its $15 you might want to give it a try.

I got this by the applying for a free upgrade, and I was surprised I got it approved because I didn't have any proof I owned the original game and said I wanted to review it. I also mentioned I was a fan of Two Worlds...so yeah. After playing the game for roughly 4 hours. My first impressions of this game are
1.The main lead is an♥♥♥♥♥ but his deep voice and overall appearance make me like him. (plus one spin on the stereotypical pirate attire is instead of owning a pet parrot....he owns a pet raven and that makes it much cooler.)
2.The story is interesting enough to make me care, yet it's a little cliche.(Christopher's parents were murded by a group of pirates, and he finds a lead by chance, so he decides to go after them for revenge.) (It is a decently entertaining unlike Reality Pump's well known Two Worlds series where the stories aren't very good.)
3.The graphics and overall atmosphere are very good with even some tiny touches that I didn't notice. An example is when it's raining, you can literally see the drops hit the ground. You even notice water sliding down your character's clothes. It's pretty cool, yet the water shading isn't the best.(By that I mean the water in the sea.)
4.The combat is a little clunky, but I usually find ways to manage through it. The biggest issue I see is that sometimes the blocking can be unresponsive like there's a tiny delay that can make a weird difference depending on when you do use block, and you getting outnumbered is not good because anybody hitting you from behind kills the flow of the combat because it staggers you. (If I didn't have the fear skill, it would be worse, but the fear skill does allow me to kill one enemy when the bar fills up instantly with some cool execution animations.)
5.The ship combat reminds me a little bit of Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag, but it feels more down to earth. You have to manually set your aim by changing how high or low you aim the cannons and fire from either side of the ship using the left and right mouse button. You even have different keys set to move the camera to different view points to aim your shots better. The only thing I had trouble with was boarding the ships. If there are any surviving crew on the enemy ship, it becomes a weird turn based battle system where you can choose three different tatics and even have the cannons loaded. It feels a bit clunky, and I prefer the method of Black Flag where you literally board the ship with your crew and slay enemies till you take over the ship.
6.I have no idea how to get more generic crew mates. The more unique ones I can get easily, but the only way I see getting new crew members is to board ships with some of the crew still on there then pray to god you have enough of your own crew to take over the ship. You then can take some of the surviving crew as your own. If anybody knows another way, please for the love of god, let me know.
UPDATE TO #6
Oops. I found out a while ago you need to go to either the crew or ship menu (can't remember which) and use a slider to adjust how many men you want on your ship. It also automatically does it for you, but I prefer manually setting it. My bad XD.
7.The economy system has a good amount of depth. You take cargo from ships and can sell them to traders for money. The biggest pro I think is that some places have a surplus and sell/buy certain goods at lower prices but also buy supplies at higher prices that they don't have. So, it's possible to get a bunch of one supply cheap and find a trader on another island who will buy it for much more.
8.I feel the music is well composed and the tavern songs are well executed enough to be good.
9.There's a decent amount of humor in the quests that made me laugh a bit. One example early on is when Christopher has to steal a ship with his first mate Marcus, and the captain of that ship is drunk and accuses them of taking his ship. Christopher just calmly says,"Nope." So, the captain replies,"Y-You're not?" To which, Christopher replies,"No everything's good here, Lay back down. Get some sleep." He just replies with a thanks and goes back to sleep...I found it funny.
10. Animals man. There are literally monkeys that show their feces at you....yeah I chuckled a bit, but it is a decent attention to detail, but I do have one issue..some of the animals are hard to hit with your sword. The cougar..leopard...or whatever is a bit difficult to hit and what makes it worse is that these things are fast and bite. You can shoot them, but you better make sure you haven't been in the water or your pistol might not shoot because the gunpowder is wet.
That's the good and the meh, but this is going to be the bad.

Just to clear the air:
1) No I am not a young-child writing a review regarding the "Minecraftiness" of Telltale's Minecraft: Story Mode.
2) I have completed the 1st episode and KNEW BEFOREHAND that this was not a complete game at initial release, but an episodic release game
3) Yes my profile picture is of a Minecraft character, but simply because I have not updated it in quite some time.
===Now to begin the review===
* Time to Complete (Episode 1): 1-2 hours *
The first episode can easily be completed within an hour to 2 hours depending on your level of interest in the story. I have additionally begun a second campaign taking on a more "rude and aggressive" approach to completing the story and am quite enjoying the slight differences. EASILY REPLAYABLE
* Glitches: There are some minor, non-gameplay affecting ones *
I noticed a few glitches during my playthroughs, but they were not game affecting. The major one involved controlling the movement of the main character during a zombie fight that caused the zombies to back away as I moved forward. Patches are fixing these issues and so should not be worried about. NOTHING GAME BREAKING
* Story Quality: Great so far *
The story itself is quite interesting and incorporates components of the basis game (Minecraft) rather well into the plot. Though not following the iconic Minecraft figure Steve, Telltale's story is quite entertaining and already has me hooked for future episodes. The incorporation of Minecrraft components (basic crafting and tool destruction) is an added bonus for Minecraft enthusiasts looking to pick up the game simply for it involving Minecraft. Keep in mind, however, this is for minor story purposes and is not the sole focus of the story. THIS IS NOT A MINECRAFT CLONE NOR IS IT MEANT TO ACT LIKE MINECRAFT. IT IS A UNIQUE STORY THAT CAPTIVATES USERS THAT ARE OPEN TO IT.
* Recommendation: Buy *
If you are looking for yet another Telltale success, this is definitely a title I would recommend picking up. If you are a fan of Minecraft, keep in mind this game is not purely about Minecraft or how it operates. The world is simply set within Minecraft.
Thanks for reading! Hope it helps.

Game's fun, but likely not £39.99 fun for most. The vast majority of my enjoyment has actually come from the character creation options. There's a lot you can do and if customisation's your thing then it'll definitely appeal, since it's so robust. That alone will personally add a ton of replayability to the game for me. I like playing Barbie dress-up in any game that allows it. <3
The meat of the game, the actual combat, is pretty damn entertaining and fun to watch. The reversal system seems a little finicky but I think I'll get used to it eventually. Split-screen and multiplayer is probably where most people will spend their time (if they have friends unlike me) since there's a ton of laughter to be had in beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of each other. That being said; I had a lot of trouble even getting the online multiplayer to work. Game's buggy to say the least.
All of the quick play modes have held my attention and I can see myself booting this up every now and then for an hour or two of making sweaty dudes bump into each other.
However, the career mode feels entirely tacked on and is seemingly held together by a string. The amount of needless, horrendously long loading screens is beyond frustrating, as is the abysmal writing. There's also zero voice acting or even any sound at all beyond the game's soundtrack when outside of matches which lends to everything feeling soulless and empty. I understand that it'd be impossible to bring in every wrestler to voice themselves, but even some impressions would've been preferable to nothing. The lack of a career mode for female wrestlers is a huge bummer too.
Overall, it's *okay*. Okay enough that I'm cool with giving it a positive review. I'd wait until it's half price, though. Most people aren't gonna be as easily entertained by dolling people up in blue mohawks and elaborate make-up.

One of the most adorable indie platformers I've played.
Out There Somewhere gets all things right. You have to explore a weird planet in order to be able to launch your ship into space (again). The controls are very simple - you only get to use 3 buttons (teleport gun, jump and gauss gun), other than the directional ones, throughout the entire game - but that's more than enough in order to tackle the game's puzzles, enemies and areas.
Most of the areas require a bit of thinking, and in some cases, reflexes, in order to reach the "end" of the screen and get to the next one. Every screen represents an entirely different area you need to pass.
Out There Somewhere is challenging enough for gamers of all ages and levels, but at the same time, you will never feel frustrated, even if you fail to overcome a certan obstacle in several attempts. The game's atmosphere and (retro) music are just too adorable for that.
The game can be completed in ~2 hours. And while it may not be a game that will keep you coming back for more, unless you're an achievement junkie, you can rest assured that it will provide you with few hours of pure, retro platforming fun!
