I'll be comparing this to an xbox 360 controller as I believe it's the popular choice for controller PC gaming.
The "bulbed" handles makes the Steam Controller (SC) fill out my hands comfortably. If you hold your 360 controller, and imagine both sides have trackpads (in place of the analogue stick and buttons), you should be able to tell that your hands would be quite cramped together. The SC has enough space for you to move your thumb around on the pads without discomfort, allowing you you swipe, rather than "point", your thumb around.
It comes working right out of the box on your desktop as long as Steam is running. When you launch a game that has controller support, the SC is configured just like a 360 controller.
But when you get into configuring the controller to act as kb+m, you might be overwhelmed by all the features available. After about an hour of configuring my controller, I've learned the workings and non-workings of the controller fairly quickly. There's so much to customize, you'll have no problem making your perfect layout.
Do you want a 360 controller with touchpads? This can be that.
Do you want a controller that acts like a kb+m setup? This can be that.
Do you want to mix both?
With all-keys of a keyboard, all buttons of a mouse, and all buttons on a 360 controller that can be mapped to any button on the SC, you'll find that this does an amazing job at being the desk-to-couch controller (or desk
couch).
Some other things to consider:
Worth $50 if you want to play kb+m games comfortably on the couch. I personally have been looking for a solution to this problem for years now, and this is exactly what I wanted. I hope future updates give a few more features, namely keyboard functionality out-of Big Picture mode.

This game has confused controls. No, not confusing; I do in fact mean confused.
-
It would say "too early" when I'm sure I pressed to late, say "too late" when I know for a fact that I pressed too early, or give me no response at all and fail the reversal. Hell, there are even times when I would flat out NOT do anything and it would lead to a successful reversal.
-
Now, looking at the control scheme and the move set up, in theory it is actually well thought out and feels good. Ability to move from a strike to a grapple to a finisher to what have you is smooth and nothing feels like it's getting in the way of itself... That is however, if it feels like working. Often times, I'd try to perform some kind of strike, only for my character to poorly attempt a finisher or something else not even remotely close to the button combination I pressed. And the rest of the time, he would just stand there and not do anything. Very rarely would he perform the actions I input.
-
If you are a newcomer to the series, or this is the first game you played in a long time in the WWE line up, then be prepared to look at the input menu A LOT. Don't get me wrong, the tutorial prompts come up when contextually appropriate. Once you complete that tutorial successful (and sometimes not even that) that's all you get. There is no mode to walk you through the gameplay so you know you have it down. It tosses you in, gives you some pointers, and that's it.
-
I've done some digging and thankfully this is a problem that only myself and a handful of others are experiencing, but come on. It's a menu. You press up, an sometimes it might take a second to actually register. Want to make a small adjustment to some option with a slider? TOO BAD, IT'S ALL OR NOTHING!
-
This is because this game is taking a bit more of a "simulation" approach than previous titles. There's nothing wrong with that, but momentum is weird, hits feel like they don't connect as hard as they should, throws feel slower and more awkward. Again, everything just feels off. Like a little too fast, or a little too slow, or too heavy or light. It's always something.
-
Going into my Week 1 match, the fight started; I got tossed out of the ring pretty damn early; fade to black; I won?!?! I am by no means a good player at this game, so I know when I get my♥♥♥♥♥kicked. Even worse is when the match starts and I take a few steps towards my oppenent. Neither of us do anything, then suddenly fade to black. I won again.... Okay???
-
With the above problem, I just assumed it was for "story telling purposes" or some such. I got made and decided to just play a quick 1v1 from the main menu. The game loaded up, everyone had their shnazzy intros, aaaaaaand fade to black. I won........
There's a lot to have in this game. I'll give it that.
-
You have a lot of options to choose from for body, hair, clothing, behaviour, moveset, and a whole lot more. And that's before everything is even unlocked! 2k18 brings a lot of quirky goodness that everyone will love. If you want to make that freakish Smurf Danny Devito/Goku hybrid you've always dreamed of, you have the freedom.
-
I don't mean the bad kind, but all the little extra fillings that you can do in between matches. You can talk to other characters and learn more about the current events of the game, choose from multiple matches to go into, do a photo op for your Goku Devito and whatnot. It's not a lot, but it's nice.
-
Personally, I haven't played in online yet, but even so there is a lot to do in the game. There's a rather good list of matchs from the main menu as well as the TLC line within the MyPlayer tab. Don't ask much about it from me though, because I mostly just played the quick matches and MyCareer so far.
Oh boy, this is a fun one.
-
Nothing more than 1920x1080. The game likes to boot in 4k and it's not optimized for it. The graphics options are a bit thin, so good luck because the game doesn't seemed to be optimized for any resolution at all.
-
In this day in age, high quality graphics is to be expected. The problem is that it doesn't look any better than the mildly cartoonish appearance of before and opts for even more realistic textures. It all ends up looking rather off putting, especially when you notice that everyone looks wet. And no, turning down the "body oil" option for your wrestler won't make them look any less wet.
-
It's kind of jarring to see your Goku Devito sitting down and moping to suddenly (and without much transition) stand up, throwing a punch as the cloth physics of his suit start flailing about not knowing what to do.
-
Granted, it's rare.... But every so often, it's fun seeing Goku Devito's arm go through his torso as his head reenacts the characters from ME:A. I wish I had some way to have recorded them. Would've been fun to put on youtube.
-
Now, I get it. The geometry of a model won't always line up with its collission, but when I see Fandango standing inside the ref, who in turn has the ropes going through him, then I supsect something is wrong.
This game has a lot of work put into some places, but the time put in some aspects shows in the lack of time put into others. This game is confusing to play, confusing to run, and confusing to operate. I want to like this game, honest. But too much is wrong with it. I'm sorry Goku Devito, but I'm not going to recommend this.

PLEASE BE CAUTIOUS Of Fake Reviewers.
If you are considering this game based on reviews and review scores on steam, first consider looking at the accounts making the review and gauge their legitimacy for yourself.
Many seem to solely exist simply for Vendetta -Curse of Ravens cry and it's publisher (with the rest of their account games untouched and never played)
-------------------------------------
Note:  This game was already released around 10 months ago as "Raven's Cry", one of the worst rated games on Steam.   If you are new to this title, please take that as warning as the store page for "Vendetta" makes no mention of this.   If you would like to see what the original release was like, please see the video linked below (which I made for the original release which has since been Deleted).
I feel really bad for this developer.   They try so hard to fix this mess of a game, but it would have probably been better to just walk away.   Instead, they decided to re-release Raven's cry under a different name and try to pretend it's a different game.   Well, it's not.
There have been improvements made, which is great, but these could have easily been applied as a patch so it does not justify being renamed and released again.   So why try and release this as a different game?   It's simply a way for them to try and erase their past and all the extremely bad reviews the original release was bombarded with.   Now that all the old reviews are deleted and gone, they have distanced themselves from their failures and are trying again.
The game still screams "Budget title" with poor vocal talent, terrible animations and glitchy NPCS.   Quests are still boring and the only redeeming feature it has is the ship battles - Just like the original release.
Changes:
Changes have indeed been made, but nothing that warrants a new release.
* NPCS now all have full voicing and don't just go silent with missing vocal tracks.
* Quests (that I have played so far) are no longer broken and causing the game to be unfinishable.
* Islands are no longer barren and void of content, and now have random animals to fight
* Animations have been changed too, but not for the better.   In fact, it seems worse.   Instead of the characters being flat and boring when talking, they now flail their arms around like mad men, over emphasizing gestures to a laughable degree.

As an avid player of MMORPGs, this caught my eye immediately (especially when it came to Steam and I didn't have to use the Aeria Games launcher, kekeke) when I saw it.
You play as an Envoy of Gaia, and because of this you can summon creatures known as Eidolons to fight alongside you. Dragons, maidens, fairies, unicorns, golems, all sorts. To start with, I picked Grimm, and have recently unlocked Sigrun and Gigas. You can name these anything you want, so the names don't particularly matter. There are plenty of different classes to fit your playing style. I, personally, have used a Bard - a healing class - all the way to level 43 as of writing this. I chose Sorcerer as my secondary class at level 40. The stats system is a little unbalanced and there are glitches here and there, but the game as a whole completely overpowers these with its good graphics and intuitive game mechanics
The game itself is gripping and the mechanics are amazing. It's clean, tells you everything you need to know and has a deep, fleshed out story and world. The art style is also adorable, so if anime-style games are your thing, AK is for you. What I love most is the questing mechanics. Any item you need to use or make is shown in the quest tracker, and all you have to do is double click the objective and you automatically travel there on an adorable ostrich by the name of Beebis. What I love is that killstealing does not exist. So long as you contribute to the killing of an enemy, everyone gets the same amount of XP, the kill registers and everyone gets their own drops, so no need to worry about someone else stealing your kill for a quest.
It looks a little inaccessible once you see all of the different things you can do, such as fortification, equipment salvaging and feeding your Eidolons with experience crystals. However these are introduced in interactive quests, and are presented very well.
My one complaint is the abundance of jiggle physics in the female characters... but hey, it's an anime game, and it's rather unnoticeable except for the female Eidolons. If anything, it's hilarious to watch!
I would highly recommend to any fantasy RPG lover.

Another reviewer pegged this game as Portal without portals. Having played through both the single player and the co-op, I definitely have to agree.
Polarity's own tagline mentions being "one of the most fun puzzle/platforms since Portal", and I definitely agree; A lot of their mechanics are things that wouldn't feel right in the Portal universe, but feels right in Polarity.
Examples would be rotating building segments, manually throwing cubes (not dropping - throwing them), changing colors, vertical-focused and horizontal-focused puzzles without portals or shortcuts, and demanding physical movement.
Polarity can be either quick reflexes or calculating puzzle depending on the level, and sometimes a level will demand both, sometimes at the same time.
The game goes on sale quite a bit during major sales, and I would definitely recommend it to anybody who enjoyed the Portal series. They may not be the developer of Portal, but they do a great job on taking that style and making it their own.

This game has potential. It could be made into a great game like Portal and Talos Principle if it had a better story (instead of just about 5 lines of text telling you what the story is) and if it was better technically.
It is extremely buggy. You'll fall through walls, you'll have the cube you're carrying fall out of your hands for no reason. I played the coop mode with a friend and what he tells me was "it feels like a school project". And he's right, it doesn't feel like a finished product, it feels like some prototype from 2008. There are a lot of strange design choices, from the ugly menus, to some objects behaving really strangely (like the fact that in coop, at the end of every level there are two spots to exit the level, and it won't end the level until the first player is on the left spot and the second player on the right spot, switching spots won't work) (or the fact that you can walk through gun turrets instead of having to dodge their bullets).
Still, if you like puzzlers, you could still like it (I liked it, even though I don't feel ok recommanding it since it doesn't feel like a finished product). I don't think it's worth the 10$ they are normally asking, but if you can get it on a sale like I did it could still be worth it, but be ready to have your patience tested, not so much by the puzzles as by the bugs. It took me 3 hours to get through all of it (single, coop, bonus levels), but it could have easily taken me one hour less if I hadn't had to deal with all the bugs and weird design mistakes.

Three achievements away from completion at the time of writing, and in excess of 440 hours... not including time spent playing on either of my cell-phones.
I can give pros and cons, but this game doesn't really follow a standard model so I will approach the review a little differently. Do I recommend it? Yes. Not because it's super in depth or complicated or even value packed as far as things to do. But, because - in its extreme simplicity - it is arguably one of the best designed games I've come across in a *very* long time.
If you're the kind of person that watches the progress bar during a scan or a massive install - even if you know it'd take hours - then you'll get hooked fast. I keep logging on and expecting something to change (other than events). I hope for quests. A town to enter. Skills. Adventures. Yet, none of that exists. It's all about watching progress bars, lots of them, and reaching goals.
Ultimately, it is the sheer simplicity of this game that is brilliant. It takes a little bit of thought. It takes some strategy to get the best results. It takes a great deal of patience. So, if you want a time killer that you keep coming back to, then do play this game. Seriously, it's worth it because it's so cleanly made.
As an aside ~ on every single instance I've had to deal with customer relations ~ the staff are friendly and helpful. I imagine this is in part because I am polite and clear in my requests for help and I'm not a jerk about it, but also because they at Hyper Hippo are a great team. I've had 100% of my issues resolved in reasonable time, and with generous professionalism. That speaks volumes about the development team and the kind of company it is. In short, it's a company worth supporting.

Linea is a minimal reaction game where you have to dodge objects for at least 60 seconds. Main game contains 4 levels during that you listen to funky bitpop music.
There is no story in Linea and the whole gameplay consists of only dodging platforms and incoming objects to survive more than 60 seconds. The game feels smooth and reacts well to user's input. The control consist of only pressing WASD or the arrow keys to control the camera.
The challenge of level 3 and level 4 is what makes this game so much fun. The first level is only for introduction, second showing that it will get harder while the third starts to actually take few tries to get past it. The fourth level took me about an hour of total tries since you have to concentrate for 60 seconds straight and its not that easy when colours flashing all in a quick manner all the time.
The interface is absolutely simple containing only the needed buttons for starting a leve, checking achievements and high score and the settings. The graphic is containing only the needed elements to play the game, so not much to rate here.
The progress felt nice for the levels existing, but I would definetely have enjoyed more levels and a bit smoother progression. The hit from 2nd to 3rd level was quite hard and level 4 felt at the start quite impossible. After a while you get the hang of it, but still compared to 2nd level there are world between. Smoother progression in challenge would have felt much better.
The tracks were not bad, but something for bitpop fans. I turned the volume off at the fourth level since it felt like being distracted by then. The immersion happens only when you are really into playing a quick level but for such a mini-game talking about real immersion would be silly.
I would suggest to get this game if you want to try your reactions, since 3rd and 4th levels are quite hard even for a hardcore gamer. The bitpop tracks are quite fun to listen to for the first time. It gets some time getting used to the level styles and way of dodging the obstacles, but once you figure them out its fun retrying to get best highscore and compete on the ladder list.
Short playtime and lack of replayability are the biggest minuses, however since the price is not that high either, the game is still recommended.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.
~ForestWolf

I feel like this game is only hard because of unfun game design rather than actually requiring skill.
Linea, the Games is a game about dodging obstacles that are coming your way similar to Super Hexagon, a game that I do like. While doing so it removes any indication of whether you are actually going to collide with the red boxes or not; you cannot actually see when you will get hit or not.
The problem I have with this game is that it has none of the redeeming qualities that Super Hexagon has. The music in this game gets stale and repetetive quickly.
Level design isn't great either. Level 2 is beatable by just staying in either the top left or the top right corner for almost the entire 60 seconds it takes you to beat the game. Level 3 simply feels unfun to play to me.
I feel like a lot of games  nowadays are designed specifically to be hard, while forgetting to actually make the game fun. To quote Reggie: "If it's not fun, why bother?"
Yeah, maybe, but if a game isn't fun to me I don't want to spend time getting good at it either.

Look, idk. This seems like a nice minimalist student or self-study project, but I can't personally recommend Linea because I have poor depth perception, and there are essentially no visual cues to discern where objects are relative to your hitbox.  Even the tutorial took me like 100 tries to complete, because "successful dodge" and "unsuccessful dodge" looks EXACTLY THE SAME to me.
Yes, it's challenging, but it's both dull AND tiring--which seems like an oxymoron, but a game where you put numbers in alphabetical order QUICKLY would also be challenging, dull, and tiring, and I would similarly not recommend THAT game, either.  I'd sooner recommend a game like Timberman if you want a game about dodging--at least it has some personality.
Also HUGE WARNING, if you care about your game completion percentage, get the "Tutorials are for dummies!" achievement FIRST THING, because otherwise you will have to RESET YOUR ACHIEVEMENTS to get it later.  Really bad design flaw.  If you don't care, then w/e ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ Get it cheap to up your "owned games" count, I guess.

Okay, I'm going to be completely honest in this review.
This is a rogue game. It's pretty addictive. It's fun. It's challenging; I still haven't made it to the lowest level yet. But, I began to find out recently why I play this game so much.
Not to preach like the average reviewer, but in this game, there's an interesting story, and though through the midst of the came, it never really pays attention to the beginning, nor, I'm assuming, the end, it continues to interest me.
I'm Christian, and if you have any affiliation with my religion, you're going to end up in one of two places playing this game.
1. You're going to be disgusted by the opening, and take your refund and erase the idea of it from your memory.
2. You're going to wonder how it makes sense because of our religion, maybe thinking that the voice Isaac's mother heard was not God, but perhaps Satan, or some other evil presence.
I personally refuse to believe that the voice was actually God, for if it was, yeah, I'd be offended, and probably never play the game anymore.
But since I see so many negative reviews revolving around the Christian-based plot twist, I just wanted to warn fellow Jesus lovers.
The fact is this, and nothing more.
It's a fun game, well built, need design, odd but fun princible, never forgiving levels, and made for people that have time to waste on a small window when you're tired of Counter Strike.
Please acknowledge, though, what I said about the plot's basis, for it'll change a lot of minds about the credibility of value in this game.
(By the way, I'd strongly reccomend buying this on a Steam Sale in the summer or something.)
Best of luck, guys. If you have any questions before you buy, just ask.

This game isn't Minecraft. Nor is it Telltale. It doesn't feel like it anyway. There were moments when I was playing this and was thinking "This is a Minecraft game." and "This is a Telltale game.", and I just couldn't believe it.
The game begins by introducing all this new lore into Minecraft, and all these new Characters. It kind of just spits it all out and somehow expects you to take it all in somehow. It would have been easier to understand if there was a stronger link between this game and the original Minecraft, but there just isn't. It would've just been as easy as having the pickable characters at the beginning of the game being the 2 set characters we already know - Steve and Alex.
When playing the game you feel as if you are watching a poor fan animation on youtube - Like someone trying to be like Element Animation but not quite. It falls into the uncanny valley - It's close to being a good looking animation while still looking like Minecraft, but it's just not quite there. It just feels un-natural. Also, the lip syncing in this game (for me) was annoyingly... weird. Rather than smooth mouth movements, they used still mouth shapes that just jump to other mouth shapes when a different sound if pronounced. During the whole game, I was just staring at their mouths because it just didn't look like they were really speaking at all.
Finally, the game itself is clearly aimed at a younger audience, but Telltale have tried to give it the atmosphere found in their other games. In the Walking Dead you may have to save someone's life, and there is a real sense of threat as you know that if you fail they will die and you'll have to watch them get brutally murdered - Whereas in Minecraft Story Mode if you have to try and save someone you don't get a real sense of threat, you know that they aren't going to kill a character off in a kids game, and if they do it will be off-screen and clean. This means that I don't feel worried when I have to try and save someone as I know that in the end, everything will be okay. Another thing I noted was that [Spoiler Alert]
Overall, I wouldn't recommend getting this game at the current price. If you do want to play it despite what I've said then you should wait till it's at least on sale. It's not the worst thing I've ever played, but Telltale really missed the mark on this one.

Be sure to get the manual form the games website. You’re going to need all 454 pages of it. (Although it is not completely up to date with the numerous balance changes and new content the game has received over the last four years.)
The best implementation of “Turn Based Strategy” I’ve ever played. Where instead of each player taking their turn one at a time each player takes their turn at the same time, then the computer simulates the turns simultaneously. Meaning if you see an independent province and you command your troops to take it to add to your “Dominion” but unbeknownst to you an enemy also had their eyes on the province so they too try to attack the province you’ll end up in an unexpected battle with another player. Making information gathering(such as sending out scouts or using magic to “scry” unowned provinces) an actually important feature unlike most strategy games were it's just a minor thing.
[Pros]
So. Much. Magic. From simple fireballs to summoning succubi that can seduce enemy commanders to causing “natural” disasters to happen in enemy provinces(or even your own if you so desire) and many more and by many more I mean 800+.
Multiple unique nations with differing lore spread out over three “Eras” some nations have presence in all eras in some shape or form.
Many styles of play.
A strategy game you can “Role Play”(staying within your nations “lore”) without sacrificing too much efficiency or viability.
[Cons]
In single player there is no diplomacy.
The amount of “Micro” can get a little insane in the late game.
The UI can be intimidating at first, even compared to a Paradox title.
[Other]

I love this controller!  Here's why...
Touchpad:  I'm finding that the touchpad is amazing after you learn how to properly configure the many variable settings.  Haptic feedback on the pad helps you keep track of your thumb location, and it doesn't feel much different than using a mouse for aiming.
Profiles:  This reminds me a lot of the Pinnacle Profiler software.  You can view the profile that was intended for use by the developer, or you can find a community profile based upon its popularity.  I found a wonderful Fallout 4 profile and it has made a huge difference in my ability to understand how a great control scheme can improve game playability.
General Feel:  I like the feel of the controller in my hands.  It has a good weight to it.  I was worried that it may be cheaply made or feel odd, but that's not the case at all.  The buttons on the back are also really cool.  It's a great way to fill some empty (yet available) space on the controller.
I also have a Steam Link box and being able to pick up a controller, press the Steam icon button on my controller, and then start playing on a TV from my gaming PC is a dream come true.  I used a laptop + HDMI + XBox Wired controller before the Steam Link and Controller arrived.  I know the end result is very similar, but it just feels better to me.  The laptop I used was a cheap HP Stream laptop.  The Steam Link seems to encode video much better than the laptop did, and I haven't dropped a single framerate yet on a hardwired connection.

+ okayish mouse / keyboard replacement

- much less ergonomic than traditional controlers
- compatibility issues (especially with x-input (x-box layout))
- build quality
- price
- durability concerns
Some thoughts:
Compatibility with games is the most important aspect to me. The design is new and thus it's obvious that it's not as compatible as X-Box controllers (x-input) for example. However, it feels as if Valve tries to force mouse / keyboard emulation upon the player - ending up in a tinker session to hack perfectly ergonomic gamepad or mouse/KB control schemes into something that works with the Steam controller. Even on optimized games I had more fun playing with an X-Box controller. For example Portal 2 or Rocket League.
Yes, it does allow you to play without mouse / keyboard but in a much much less ergonomic way.
Further it's not as compatible with X-Input as I would have hoped. That renders many existing controller games unplayable or makes them stressful due to bad ergonomics.
Also there's durability and built quality, or rather the lack of thereof. It's built like a flower. Too many fragile parts like the latches of the "battery cover", the belly triggers (just a metal clicker overlayed by a steam controller sticker), the pads which appear to be uncleanable and prone to mechanical failure due to the mechanical feedback etc.The buttons are too small and also feel very "mushy", not clicky like x-box or playstation gamepads (or even classic controllers).
Interesting note: Design! Probably the least important part but an interesting one. The packaging looks feels and smells like a generic product - not a Valve / Steam product. No portal like in the Steam VR manuals or anything "Valve Soul". It's so generic that you wouldn't be able to tell it's a Valve / Steam product if they didn't print it on top. A minus? Probably not. But it makes it less exciting to me.

Three achievements away from completion at the time of writing, and in excess of 440 hours... not including time spent playing on either of my cell-phones.
I can give pros and cons, but this game doesn't really follow a standard model so I will approach the review a little differently. Do I recommend it? Yes. Not because it's super in depth or complicated or even value packed as far as things to do. But, because - in its extreme simplicity - it is arguably one of the best designed games I've come across in a *very* long time.
If you're the kind of person that watches the progress bar during a scan or a massive install - even if you know it'd take hours - then you'll get hooked fast. I keep logging on and expecting something to change (other than events). I hope for quests. A town to enter. Skills. Adventures. Yet, none of that exists. It's all about watching progress bars, lots of them, and reaching goals.
Ultimately, it is the sheer simplicity of this game that is brilliant. It takes a little bit of thought. It takes some strategy to get the best results. It takes a great deal of patience. So, if you want a time killer that you keep coming back to, then do play this game. Seriously, it's worth it because it's so cleanly made.
As an aside ~ on every single instance I've had to deal with customer relations ~ the staff are friendly and helpful. I imagine this is in part because I am polite and clear in my requests for help and I'm not a jerk about it, but also because they at Hyper Hippo are a great team. I've had 100% of my issues resolved in reasonable time, and with generous professionalism. That speaks volumes about the development team and the kind of company it is. In short, it's a company worth supporting.

Out There Somewhere is an absolutely charming platformer that I highly recommend as an essential addition to any Steam user's library.  Much like Shovel Knight or Momodora, this is a modern game that looks and plays like one of the classics.
The game's hero is a fighter pilot who is shot down during an epic space battle.  After crash-landing on a volcanic planet populated with friendly talking snails and strange tree-men, he ventures off, armed with a teleportation gun, to repair the ship and rejoin the battle.  Along the way, there's a few health upgrades and maybe even a weapon or two to help survive the baddies; there's also 11 hidden ship upgrades to find.
While the platforming elements and the game's retro aesthetic are both great, the real star of the show is the teleportation mechanic.  Your primary trigger fires a slow-moving bolt of energy that instantly transports your character to the point of contact when a surface is struck.  Using this competently is necessary for getting through the game.  The really exciting bit, though, is the teleportation gun conserves momentum, just like Portal; beginning a leap just before your energy bolt hits something, for instance, means you'll still be traveling upwards after being teleported.  Mastering this makes for very satisfying gameplay, and abusing this mechanic to go as high or as far as you possibly can also lead you to secret areas or shortcuts that you wouldn't otherwise find.

This game isn't very long, and while it's not a total cakewalk, the level of challenge is relatively low.  My first playthrough took about 90 minutes, and that was with a lot of optional exploration and puzzle-solving.  My second playthrough was a 100% playthrough, and took a little over an hour.  After learning the game's layout and mechanics, a speedrun will take not much more than 15 minutes.
However, while not long, this game is really quite fun, and totally worth the very reasonable asking price.  Give it a shot, you won't regret it.

NOTE: Despite the store page's description, the community claims this game is a multiplayer only title, with the singleplayer being only a very light practice mode. So, if you're looking at those positive reviews with 800 hours, don't be fooled. There's nothing to the singleplayer, just as I've described below. Maybe the multiplayer is great, but I know from experience grand strategy games like this take assigned days of your week, schedules, and planning to play. If you're looking for a single player strategy game or unwilling to give up your Friday, turn away.
As someone who's played a lot of Paradox Interactive games, I immediately got the "deep UI" of the game. How to make units, move, manage resources, research, how and why to build 'dominion', searching for relics, and understood what I needed for each spell. Beyond that, though, the game very much boils down to moving tiles of stronger armies onto weaker armies, in a Risk-like manner. Very underwhelming to my expectation, from all the heralded 'complexity' of Dominions 4.
I probably would have loved this game when I was big into randomized experiences and strategy for its own sake as a younger person. Now it just seems like a game in a series that has seen a lot of work, but fails to deliver on depth of content or gameplay. Sure, there's a lot of mythological writeups and different sprites and races. But does all that fill out to any semblance of a game world that seems enjoyable? I don't think so. Like, I boot up a game of Civ 5, and even though there's only a limited number of factions I know can be in the game, it still feels like each world I generate in those games is unique.
Dominions 4 relies so heavily on crunching numbers that the worlds it generates feel dead. Yes, I've got a god. Other people have gods. That's cool. But then my units and everything are just a series of numbers. Where's the passion behind the game's design? I don't see it. And then it's discouraging to look at Dominions 5 and see their big ideas for innovation are.. a fast forward button on the game's automated gameplay? It really shows you that the game's creators are out of ideas, even before they began. This is a cash-in on the random generation trend that's been going since Minecraft, which is just a way for developers to use less creative talent and more coding skills. Sure, that's great for them and their line of work, but I see it as symptomatic of a dying industry. Maybe Dominions 5 could add some loot boxes and multiplayer only features, to stay fully on-trend. *eyeroll*
For a 2D strategy game on a modern market, it's surprisingly lacking in early game depth. Whether it's in combat, stats, or the game board's generation. If it weren't for all the randomization options, this game is so simple it could have been released on the NES. Not what I was expecting at all.

Shooting, dodging, jump boots, and wacky custom firearms are the name of the game here. This combined with map designers leaving lots of object collision to climb over gives fans a pretty high skill ceiling to master. In some ways it reminds me of the MNC series, minus the Dota/Moba aspects. Hardcore fans of that series found plenty of advanced maneuvers that revealed almost a completely different game just under the surface. Loadout seems to have much of the same potential and will most likely evolve as players discover the small nuances to the game engine.
For anyone who doesn't care to read the previous paragraph, it's a fun shooter where you get to kill all the things in as crude a manner as possible.

I have to admit, I didn't expect this to be what it was at all.  And after the first couple of minutes, I really came to love this title.
Every decision you have to make has a time limit, and you have to weigh it all, because there's always that chance that the decision you're making is truly important.  Some of the decisions must be made in the middle of an action sequence, and I think that's where this game shines: a reflexive action can have consequences, and I'm not used to seeing that play out in games at all.
The game does a great job of balancing when you can control your character, as well as when quick time events, or other segments when you have very little time to perform an action, pop up.  This meant that I was always engaged in what was going on, and the timed nature of certain elements makes sure the game keeps flowing; if you're one of those people who is used to battling out the consequences of a single action (like me when I'm playing Tactics Ogre) before making a decision, this game forces you to go against that mindset, and keeps you on your toes.
I have to say, the way that the game's areas are planned out is really clever; there's always a general pathway that you take, but it keeps things moving instead of bottlenecking the pace, and really drives the narrative.  The only hiccup I found involved a sequence where you had to pull some levers, and the clicks didn't always select the lever I was clicking on.  Other than this one flaw, I can't think of anything I don't like about the game.
The first episode delivered a lot of satisfying content, and I was hopelessly attached to the main character's trusty pig companion.  It's elements like the pig, the camaraderie between the main group, and just the general way the characters in the world acted that brought me back to those older movies that made me feel great when I was a kid.  It has that charm, but it's all delivered in a way that both adults and younger audiences alike can thoroughly enjoy.
I haven't played a game this heartwarming or exciting in a long time, and I really can't wait to see what the future has to offer.  If you decide to buy this, I hope you find as much enjoyment out of it as I did.

* Disclaimer: I purchased this controller because a) My RSI/Carpal Tunnel pain makes playing games like Diablo, MOBAs, etc nearly impossible. b) I love supporting innovation in Human-Computer interfaces. I've purchased some strange and interesting input systems in the past. The steam controller is honestly the best of any "alternative" control setup I've ever used for games.
---
Overall the steam controller is a vast improvement in controls compared to standard gamepads for most popular PC games. It takes some getting used to, but once you adjust and get the sensitivity where you like (just like normal mouse controls in this regard) it plays very well in games, only suffering to KB/Mouse in arena shooters like Quake 3.
A touchpad for aiming sounds like a horrible idea on the surface, but what makes it great is the incredible job of haptic feedback they use to emulate a trackball. I used to play FPS with a trackball sometimes (it has certain advantages over a mouse, like quick 180 spins, etc). You can do flick-stop, slow/fast precision movements, and generally everything they promised in this regard. Stellar job addressing the biggest issue in traditional analog stick control for PC games. Theres also a ton of different options for configuring it just the way you want, including acceleration, friction, trackball emulation, sensitivity, etc.
Overall this controller is very good for FPS, RPGs, RTS and MOBAs. It's weak for traditional 2d platformers or other games that rely primarily on d-pad input.
I've tried this controller with:
Dota2
Killing Floor
Insurgency
Quake live
Xonotic
Battleblock Theater
General breakdown:
Pros
+ Great control precision for FPS aiming. The haptics and trackball emulation are spot on. I think after a few days of exclusive use, will come very close to approaching KB/M effectiveness for most PC-oriented games (FPS, RPG/MOBA, RTS)
+ Trigger and paddle button placement is great
+ Solid build. Not too heavy, not too light. Only time will tell as far as longevity/durability however.
+ Easy setup, GREAT customization options.
+ Works with non-steam games just fine (though steam must be running)
+ Analog stick works well, and can even function well as a Dpad replacement thanks to the haptics
+ Paddle buttons! Combined with the 4 shoulder buttons, this means 6 inputs your non-thumb fingers have instant access to.
+ Little to no input latency, very responsive
+ Its something new, exciting and experimental. The first real controller innovation since the PSX Dual shock!
Cons
- No real D-pad. The analog stick w/ haptics does an ok job, but the left-side touch pad is often relegated to inventory switching or other non-critical inputs. Its not servicable as a D-pad for most games despite the design they put on it
- Two AA batteries. Really for $50+shipping it should have a replaceable lipo.
- For people with short thumbs, the XABY buttons might be a bit of a stretch
- XABY buttons are a bit small, combined with the somewhat long reach needed to hit them, this exacerbates the issue.
- No bluetooth, uses a RF USB dongle. This an inconvenience for laptop users, mainly. Its just another piece that can get lost, take up a USB slot, and overall shouldn't be necessary. I wonder if the haptics made it impractical to use BT for some protocol-level reason, because I can't think of any good reason not to use it otherwise. Latency issues, etc have largely been addressed and most BT controllers perform great.
Thoughts per-game:
* Dota2
While I don't see any 'pro' gamers using this controller, it'll be great for people like myself who have RSI/Carpal Tunnel issues and make MOBAs/RTS/Diablo-style games enjoyable again! I could definitely use the steam controller as my primary/preferred control scheme, but it may not be to a 'pro' level.
* Killing Floor
Works great. Had no issues dispatching baddies and getting headshot after headshot once sensitivity was adjusted to my liking. The paddles are great for crouch/jump bindings so you don't have to stop aiming. I could definitely use the steam controller as my primary/preferred control scheme.
* Insurgency
Works great, just like Killing Floor (pretty similar controls). The paddles are great for lean left/right bindings. I could definitely use the steam controller as my primary/preferred control scheme.
* Quake Live / Xonotic
Works decent but not KB/M good. The twitch responses and high skill ceiling needed to hit such fast moving targets in an Arena FPS makes certain weapons tough to use (like the rail gun), though given enough time to adjust, it may be possible to be competitive. I was able to play pretty well in Rocket Arena modes. I'd probably stick with KB/M if I wanted to be remotely competitive in these games, however I am going to stick with the steam controller for a couple weeks to see if getting used to it improves my ability.
* Battleblock Theater
A 2D platformer exposes this controller's biggest flaws. I really hope for a revision 2.0 controller that has a sony-style Dpad and moves the standard buttons a little closer to the edge for people with shorter thumbs. Overall its playable, but its not the most comfortable, and sometimes you just end up hitting the wrong direction due. Using the analog stick w/ haptics as a Dpad is better IMO than the left-side touchpad. Ultimately this makes using the left-side touchpad for critical inputs ineffective for most game types. Stick with a 360 controller for these.

So, I'll break this down into 3 parts. 1: How it feels, 2: How its customization is/isn't good, 3: Ways to use it properly
1: So I have large hands which always kinda make the 360 controllers i've used since 2007 feel a little on the small side but my hands could always reach every button. The Steam Controller feels comfortable to me with the face buttons not feeling entirely out of place.  I'm waiting for someone else to come over with smaller hands than mine to see if its more or less awkward. The paddles in the back are very subtle and sometimes I forget they are even there.
2: So lets just get this out of the way, default settings for most games is complete♥♥♥♥♥ This is not a 360 controller and the right pad shouldn't try to emulate one. I tried a few games last night (DmC, Fallout 4, MGS: V, Killing Floor 2, and Resident Evil Revelations 2) and while they all control completely different I found community control settings which worked for me with some mild tweaking like more haptic feedback or just changing the paddle keybindings which brings me to part 3...
3: Never try to treat this as a 360 controller, this is something totally different. Take the time to tweak the settings on some games to how you think you want it, play it and tweak it some more. Just like any kind of new hardware you'll need time to adjust.
In closing, this controller is for you if you want to take time to get used to it, if you just want something to plug in and start using I'd suggest sticking with a 360 or Ps4 controller, does that mean this is better/worse? No its just something different.

Polarity is the poor man's Portal, but perhaps that's being a bit unfair to Polarity; it IS its own game in its own right. It doesn't have an incredibly engaging story to it (in fact, save for a short text introduction at the beginning of the game, there's no story to it at all), but at the same time it doesn't really need one. The objective of each level is to use colored cubes to activate corresponding gates and switches to get to the end-level warp while collecting data fragments.
HIGHS: --Gameplay is fun and engaging, albeit a bit bare-bones.
--Bonus levels and Co-op campaign add much needed replay.
--The music (or I should ambience) is soothing without becoming repetitive. Accompanied with the easy-on-the-eyes visuals, the game is actually quite calming (in the good way).
LOWS: --The levels aren't incredibly challenging. They're enough to make you think, but none will really stump you or leave you stuck.
--There's a couple important details the game neglects to inform you about. For example, later in the game you'll encounter yellow gates that, turns out, change the color of whatever cube passes through it. An attentive player would be bound to figure this out on their own eventually, but the more casual player may not be so quick to catch on (especially when the FIRST none-red/blue gate you encounter without being informed kills you).
--The game is FAR too short, especially for the asking price of $10.99 (The single player campaign can be finished in less than an hour, even if you're not the greatest at puzzle games). The game could've, and SHOULD've, been much longer; especially with the multitude of potential puzzles the aforemention yellow gates can bring to the table.
BUY or BYE: I say buy, especially if you're a big fan of the Portal series or puzzle games in general. Polaris is not worth the default $11. A good default price would be $5 (perhaps $9.99 at the most), but certainly not $11. HOWEVER, it IS a fun puzzle game that should be experienced, and for the current sales price of $0.54, you can't go wrong!

Honestly, this is my favorite fighting game of all time HOWEVER please read the end of this review to consider your purchase. It has a perfect in-between of offensive and defensive tactics. Yeah, you can do combos in like every good fighting game, (even games you don't expect have them like Mortal Kombat II), but you don't win fights solely on that (and they're not very long combos either), you have to space, evade, and use certain special moves, normals, combos at the right opportunities. NOW this sounds all generic, but it's how The King of Fighters handles this makes it even more prevalent. It's a very simple fighter to pick up, but still deep enough to make it very engaging and worth while to learn. Controls are very tight, and while the input timing is strict, it's very rewarding and I honestly feel it helps the game since you have to work harder for the more damaging special moves and supers. Of course how I can forget to mention the large variety of characters.
A lot of what I said could be applied to the vanilla version of The King of Fighters '98, and honestly, this version is only slighty better! You got retuned balance, which the original was already nicely balanced as is, and the added characters and added ex versions is of course very welcomed, making it feel more complete. You have 40+ characters to pick from, 50+ if you count the EX versions, so you'll be bound to find a favorite, let alone three.
HOWEVER, there is one major flaw with this game. The netplay isn't that great. As you may know, I'm from Florida (GEE WIZ how could anyone figure that out!?), and I played with a friend from California. Our experience was alright, we got some epic matches in, but we for sure faced several problems with lag, and at times the game would even hang awkardly for a few seconds. This game goes for about 15 US bucks, and I am recommending this because I love this game. I recommend playing the original first, you can have online matches through FightCade, and if you really like that, get this version. Right now it's about $5.09 USD (i'm writing this during the 2017 summer sale) so you can't find a better time to get this amazing game. But if you're hesitant because of the poor netplay, that's understandable, and while $15 dollar is a good deal for a game like this, with such a large roster and such a great quality of the game itself, there are however features missing from the previous UM version such as color edit mode, 3D backgrounds, and arranged soundtracks (something you can get as a mod). If this had better netplay I give it a much more confident Thumbs up, but here it's a more It's a thumbs up, BUT it's something to think about, that's for sure.

The King of FIghters series is aptly named as to date it's still my favourite fighting series. It's technical, flashy and oozes style and KoF 98 is the absolute cream of the crop. This Steam version is in my opinion the optimal version of KoF 98 as it combines many of the best elements of previous versions, my only complaint is it would have been nice to have included the arranged soundtrack as an option, but that said the original soundtrack is still spectacular.
So what makes KoF so good? For one I really like the story of these games which I realise is an unusual pro for a fighting game series, but from Fatal Fury (technically the first KoF) I found myself invested in the characters, specifically Terry Bogard's grudge match with Geese Howard and their battle across South Town and my interest has only grown from there. KoF's roster is large and loud, boasting unique personalities that all have their own reasons for entering the tournament and have interesting and sometimes comical pre fight interactions with one another. Once again as with many Neo Geo titles SNK really pushed the hardware at the time and worked within it's limitations to truly create something special, it's a delight to play and it looks fantastic. From the introduction sequence you'll instantly pick up the visual style and fantastic sound direction, intro sequences in arcade games are usually something special as they lure in punters to spend their hard earned cash and here it's no exception, the opening theme and video effects really get you in the mood for a good scrap. Starting up the game here you pick your style and three fighters to roll with, you can opt to go with the pre selected teams or mix and match to create your own unique one, this can be a little daunting for new players as it means you have to learn three characters if you want to get good and play competitively against others, but if you have the patience to put in the time it really pays off.
I'm not sure what else to say, if you're a fighting game fanatic you no doubt already have your own opinions on KoF 98, if you're a newcomer there are maybe easier places to start, but don't let that discourage you, because if you really put in the time you'll have a handle on one of the greatest fighting games of all time. So what are you waiting for, grab an arcade stick, choose your fighters and get ready for the greatest smack down of your life!

My first review.   Overall very positive for strategy gamers.
Good: Impressive variety of units/nations/gods/items/spells. Addictive turn based play for armchair generals with many strategies and tactics that can be experimented with and devised. Creative and immersive setting which needs many hours to explore.
Bad: UI is clumsy, micromanaging movement gets tedious after a while since you can only direct armies to move to adjacent provinces.  Some illogical design choices like scattering of troops after a battle which you would then like to go around picking up, you cannot disband them or its not obvious?, provincial defense always gets replenished for the next turn.  AI is also not stellar plus I wonder how it manages to increase its units during sieges out of nowhere;it doesn't seem to be playing under the same rules as the humans do.
Ugly:  Battles are automated. sprite like graphics (I am ok with this), tin sound (this could be made better) takes away from the immersion.  After playing for a while, I pine away for more complex building options, AI personalities/diplomacy, and story detail, so the game feels like it has undeveloped potential. Big learning curve. Dominions 5 is coming out soon as of this reviews writing.

Aura Kingdom. This game is a ♥♥♥♥ing gem. You play nine classess, The Guardian, Duelists, Ravager, Wizard, Sorcerer, Bard, Grenadier, Gunslinger, Brawler Ranger and Ronin. I play Duelists, personally, I love it. At a very early stage in the game, you get a mount, it's an Ostrich with a name, Beebis, he adds +30 move speed. The upgrade system is pretty, different from an avergae RPG, MMO, & MMORPG. When you level you, you open the character menu, and at first you can only choose offensive points, between DMG, CRIT, and SPD. I forgot the level, but at a certain level, the defensive menu opens up, and you can upgrade that, HP, DEF, and EVA. And I think, at least level 30, you can upgrade twice, at 50% and 100%. The game is very similar to World of Warcraft, which is also amazing, but Aura Kingdom is free, and no subscription required. I'd say, Aura Kingdom is like World of Warcraft, but Anime-ish. At the level of 40, you can get a secondary class, and you can choose one of the nine classess again. Me, I went with Duelist, Gunslinger combo. The companion system is uniqe, I'd say, I love it, you can get new companions as you go. The companions are known as, Eidolons. You can choose between four Eidolons at the beginning. Merilee, which was my first Eidolon, can heal you, with a spell known as The Power of Love. The User Interface is like, a take of the World of Warcraft add-on Dominos I'd say. In the creation, you can choose between 9-10 faces, 9-10 hairstyles, and a few hair color pallets, and eye pallets. There's a difference in the Armor and Clothing system. There
s Costume which is what controls your look, and gear control your stats, it's a different system from games I have played in the past, and it's pretty cool, and flawless. You begin to level up fast at the beginning, and whence you hit level 45, it gets hard, and at level 50, it may take even DAYS to level up. Right now I am at level 47? Yeah, 47. Each area, I've noticed it's like, report to person, kill quest, retrieve quest, defeat person quest, instance quest, new area. Each area can provide up to ten levels. PvP isn't avalible till level 20, but I don't recommend it till level 40+. Right now, the max level is level 70. There are differences in the instance/dungeon system, which I find pretty cool personally. There's solo, which is less enemies, and less area. There's party which is more challenging, more enemies, and more area to traverse. The smithing system is personally at first, confusing, but you get the hang of it, I can't really describe it in words. There's uniqe monsters which you can kill, and they get put in a urn or box, and you can collect it, via right click, and bring it to the head of town guard, and you recieve a reward for doing so, The inventory system is a small inventory, but you can get more bags. Bags contain up to Five to 20 more slots. The currency system is another confusing, yet you get the hang of it, there are AP points, which is the buy with real money currency, Loyalties, a different currency, Gold and Silver, the normal currency, the Tokens, which idk what are used for, the War Coins, which you can buy PvP gear from. There's a shop known as the Item Shop, with one tab containing AP spending, and Loyality spending. There's also Dragon Points, which you can use the Adventure Encyclopedia to spend with, said book contains the weapons and armor and other things locations through Gaia, or Terra, idk where Aura Kingdom is set, I know it's one of the two. Navea is sort of the, "Org," or Orgrammar of the game, it's the central hub, military district, cathedral district, auction house district, and teleportation district. The Auction House system is very similar to World of Warcraft's. The Guild system, again, very similar to WoW's. BUT, there's something called a Guild Hall, which is a hall made when a guild is made, it's the sorta, "hangout" for the guild. You cannot enter this location before 24 hours real time. You must wait 24 hours real time before you can enter the Guild Hangout. The fishing system is different, I can't really describe it in words. Loyalties I forgot about, are collected via Eavesdropping. You can get new Eidolons from the Eidolon Temple, or a place in the Guild Hall, I've never found :/. The questing system is hard to describe in words, but very similar to WoW. The game is non-age restricted, there are censores among swear words. The game is gender-friendly, you can be Male, and Female. The game is WASD, and Click Move friendly, so you can do both. So, get out there, and play Aura Kingdom! 9/10

This is the first time I played a game where every time I load, I get different experience. It is like being in an alternate universe rather than travelling back in time to change your choice. Why? Because the research tech is a random out of 3-5 choice, leaders you can hire too, the anomaly events and AI action is also random. Nothing is consistent so often it is a choice of whether to redo or to live with it.
Stellaris also gives you the choice to go back to their previous major updates for the game in case you are not happy with what they give you in the latest one. Instead of whining about unbalance forces, removed features etc, you can rollback to what you're happy with.
I have to point out that the space battle is the achilles heel of the game due to the power leap of research. It is like a light tank vs heavy tank before research (you can customize your space ships with weapon loadout btw). Then after research, it is like tank vs submarine vs airplane kinda situation. Totally outmatch.
The battle event is lacking some maneuvers like keeping distance, formation and flanking. It is about who has better variety of loadout when it is close in strength. It looks like battles in Last Exile (anime) for 2-3 seconds and then it goes to space dog fight which would have worked better if those are Gundams instead of ships.
Lastly, the choice comes down to between sleep or continue playing. Because like I said, loading the game will change your experiece.

Out There Somewhere is an okay little platform games with minimalistic retro pixel-based graphics and music. The game mechanics is based on jumping and a teleport gun that teleports you to whatever you shoot with it instantly. There are some blocks and beams that react differently to the teleport shot and you conserve momentum, so that if you jump before being teleported, you will be going up at your point of teleportation.
It's a simple and decent mechanic. It may be a bit hard to understand at first, but you get the hang of it quickly, and when you do get the hang of it... the game ends.
Yeah, the game is really short, I beat it in 32 minutes of game time. I didn't try to do a speed run or anything, I was just solving screens one after the other. Maybe there are optional paths I didn't check out, but it didn't feel like it. So, yeah, very short, but it is a very cheap game, so I won't complain, just adjust your expectations.

TL;DR
1. This is not only the best KOF, but IMO the best fighting game period.
2. The port is solid, works really well offline, but doesn't have the best online and is missing features from the PS2 port.
3. This game needs more exposure!
INTRO: A BRIEF HISTORY OF KOF 98
KOF 98 at its first release quickly became one of SNK's biggest blockbusters in the arcades. Having just wrapped up their first significant story arc, the Orochi Saga, in 97, SNK decided to make their first Dream Match game, where the cast was not bound by any canon restrictions. As a refinement upon gameplay concepts explored in KOF 97 and featuring characters who had died during the Orochi Saga, 98 was received with open arms.
In the years that followed, KOF 98 stood as a legend in fighting games and remained one of the pinnacles of KOF. Through new KOF entries and even SNK's own demise, 98 remained a constant in the KOF community and still has strong widespread communities today.
To celebrate the 10 year anniversary, SNK released a remake in KOF 98 Ultimate Match, where a lot of positive changes were made to the original, including the rework of the previously weak and gimmicky Extra mode, and cool new characters were added. 98UM brought back the '96 boss team (Geese Howard, Wolfgang Krauser, and Mr. Big) as well as Kasumi and Eiji. In addition to these, 4 new EX characters were added (EX Blue Mary, EX Yamazaki, EX Geese, and EX King: the former three being based on their appearances in Real Bout Fatal Fury 2, while EX King being based off her Art of Fighting appearance).
These 9 additional characters round out the cast to a whopping 59!
However, there were some significant balance problems that plagued it, the most infamous of which being Krauser's dominance: his overwhelming strength was enough for him to end up on the teams for most players. After Tougeki 2008, KOF 98UM had lost a lot of popularity. Most in the 98 community preferred the original to the Krauser fest.
A couple years later in 2010, a new revolution in the arcade industry was introduced in the form of NESiCAxLive, an online distribution service for arcade games ran by Taito. SNK Playmore chose to release 98UM and 02UM on the service. 02UM already having been an amazing success for them, they wanted 98UM to attain similar success. And here is where we get to...
KOF 98 UM [FINAL EDITION]
For KOF 98 UM's NESiCA release, SNK Playmore decided to update 98UM. This update brings about a host of balance changes (great list compiled here
to fix the problems of the first 98UM. With the exception of Krauser receiving a host of nerfs and touches to Iori's command grab and Eiji's MAX projectile super, the entire cast received buffs and/or quality of life changes, and certain system mechanics were standardized (Extra meter charge times, charge motion input times).
It's absolutely astounding how well refined the balance became. EVERYONE is strong, EVERYONE is a threat. The tier list is SUPER compressed as a result of how viable everyone in the game is. Everyone has fun and interesting tools. Honestly this may be the closest to perfection humanity may see in this lifetime.
So yeah this game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing on the gameplay end of things, but let's take a look at this port finally.
3 years of thinking we may never get this game, and it finally comes.
TECHNICAL REVIEW
This is a pretty solid port, but unfortunately not quite as incredible as the game itself is. Code Mystics ported over the 360 version of the game and implemented the Final Edition balance changes with new netcode. WHAT DOES THIS MEAN?!?!?
Well unfortunately that means this version doesn't include certain features from the PS2 version.
-No 3D stages (your mileage may vary, I don't like these very much personally)
-No arranged music (easily modded in if you look at the guides, but not having options is the slightest touch annoying)
-NO COLOR EDIT (this I'm actually really tight about. It's probably possible to mod the color palletes in the game but UUUUUUUUUUUGH)
All the other stuff is there though, and the game runs really well. The button config is also way better than the 360 version as not only can you just select the button you want to configure and hit your button, BUT YOU CAN TEST YOUR BUTTONS IN THE MENU. No more menuing through all those buttons and being utterly confused as to which buttons on your nonstandard controller/stick are which!
Code Mystics was also REALLY COOL and patched in options to see your inputs in training mode! No frame counter on it but still cool.
ONLINE
Online multiplayer is basically a requirement these days, aaaaaaaaand that 360 version's online was really really bad. How's this version? Not ideal unfortunately, but servicable enough in some cases I guess?
Despite GGPO's revolutionary rollback netcode implementation being a tried and true method, having cultivated large communities together for older games, it's unfortunately not here. Instead using the clearly outdated method of just adding input delay to compensate for lag.
This leaves me to address something that's outside the scope of this port.
THE COMMUNITY
One of things that curses 98UMFE is that the only platforms it's been released on are Steam and NESiCA. This ends up actually limiting some of the outreach this game can get as
1. NESiCA isn't the most widely spread arcade platform. A lot of KOF tournaments for older games are held on the original boards they came out on, including 02UM.
2. Steam (and PC in general honestly) isn't the most popular platform for tournaments in general. Most games utilize consoles or arcade boards where applicable.
It'd be really cool if 98UMFE was released on MORE platforms so it could hopefully get more exposure.

So, I'll break this down into 3 parts. 1: How it feels, 2: How its customization is/isn't good, 3: Ways to use it properly
1: So I have large hands which always kinda make the 360 controllers i've used since 2007 feel a little on the small side but my hands could always reach every button. The Steam Controller feels comfortable to me with the face buttons not feeling entirely out of place.  I'm waiting for someone else to come over with smaller hands than mine to see if its more or less awkward. The paddles in the back are very subtle and sometimes I forget they are even there.
2: So lets just get this out of the way, default settings for most games is complete♥♥♥♥♥ This is not a 360 controller and the right pad shouldn't try to emulate one. I tried a few games last night (DmC, Fallout 4, MGS: V, Killing Floor 2, and Resident Evil Revelations 2) and while they all control completely different I found community control settings which worked for me with some mild tweaking like more haptic feedback or just changing the paddle keybindings which brings me to part 3...
3: Never try to treat this as a 360 controller, this is something totally different. Take the time to tweak the settings on some games to how you think you want it, play it and tweak it some more. Just like any kind of new hardware you'll need time to adjust.
In closing, this controller is for you if you want to take time to get used to it, if you just want something to plug in and start using I'd suggest sticking with a 360 or Ps4 controller, does that mean this is better/worse? No its just something different.

TL;DR Quite possibly the most versatile controller known to man. Get it if you like tweaking things.
The best thing about PC gaming is that you don't have to settle for what you're given. If something's buggy you can mod it with fan patches. If you don't like the controls you can rebind keys. If you don't like the graphics you can mod them or increase your graphics settings. The Steam controller takes this idea and applies it to the living room with one of the best pieces of gaming hardware I've ever owned.
It can function like a 360 controller, like a keyboard, like a mouse, like a trackball, or any combination of them in so many ways it makes my head spin. Ever wanted to map two buttons to a single trigger, like aiming through sights on a soft press and hip fire on a quick press? You can do that now. Ever wanted to make Xbox-style joystick controls feel like you're using a mouse? You can do that now. Ever wanted to add precision through optional motion controls based on context-sensitive actions? You can do that now and so much more.
Quite possibly the only kinds of games that don't work well with the controller are games that are designed for really specific hardware to begin with. I'm speaking of fighting games (just go and buy an arcade stick) and competitive MOBA/RTS games (KB+M will always be superior) but for nearly any other kind of game it can be configured to match or even surpass other methods of control. It's the Swiss Army Knife of video game controllers and even when you barely change anything it's brilliant.
For example, Dark Souls has this problem where you can't run and adjust the camera at the same time without moving your fingers in a "claw" position on a normal controller. With the Steam controller I just map the run button to the back-left paddle and now I can run and change the camera at the same time. Or in Wolfenstein: The New Order, after mapping aiming/firing to the right trigger as a soft pull action system, I mapped the left trigger to both sprint and crouch. A light press instantly starts me sprinting, and a light press followed by a full press is an instant, one-button slide maneuver. Absolute brilliance and much more comfortable than pressing in the left stick to run (gross) and then pressing another, separate button to crouch/slide.
If any of that sounds appealing to you, just get it. It's comfortable in your hands and it might take a bit of time to get used to but once you set it up for your favorite games you probably won't ever go back (for couch play at least). This is one of the most innovative controllers ever made and then some and quite possibly the best thing to come out of Valve since Steam and HL2.

Fantastic controller! Yes it takes getting used to, but it's well worth the slight learning curve at the beginning. The community has created presets for almost every game I've tried = no need to configure manually. It replaced my xbox 360 wireless controller, except for games where an analog D-Pad is a must.
For those still skeptical, check out this guy playing CS:GO with it:

Oh this has replaced my 360 controller I've been using.  The steam controller is boss player, and easily contains more buttons than any controller on the market.  It's form factor is slim so any size hand player can use it.  The X Y B A pad buttons are slightly smaller than the current controllers allowing more compact hand movements so you aren't reaching too far with your fingers for the buttons.  The two extra trigger buttons on the bottom side of the controller REALLY help with complex movements on any FPS game if you want to play with a controller.  I'd even say you could play CoD with this and make no difference between the controller or the keyboard and mouse.
Of course, everything has strengths, but I would say the learning curve is this controller’s weakness.  Unless you are willing to learn the controllers, do not buy it.  Then again, this shouldn't be a problem as you would have to learn any new controller.  The learning curve for the Steam Controller though is just a wee bit higher than the others.  The touchpads are really innovative and are the reason for the learning curve, as the D-Pad is the left touch pad, and the left acts by default, the mouse or right stick in this case.  Another is you can't be too far from the receiver or behind anything because it uses standard RF tech which is a little baffling considering the time put into the controller and the price but, that's just me nit picking though.  It plays differently, and feels different from any game pad currently on the market.  I would definitely recommend this thing.
Pros-
Has 15 reconfigurable physical buttons and 4 digital (the left touch pad is the D-Pad in touch form, creating 4 extra buttons digitally)
Compatible with any game (it doesn't have to be steam)
Configurable for ANY game (it doesn't have to be steam)
2 touch pads completely reconfigurable
Solo joystick ideal for third-person and flying which is also one of the 15 buttons
*****No "Batteries not included" here.  IT COMES WITH DURECELL BATTERIES!  Valve is just throwing awesomeness around.  The first battery charge is on Valve, and that's just PC thinking right there.  Gabe, you rock!  Gabe Newell and Mike Harrington created one of the best video game companies to ever make a dent in this society.  It's always been for the gamers.  Stay classy Valve!
Cons-
LEARNING CURVE = HUGE
Requires RF receiver
8/10
I'd LOVE to give a full 10 but, the learning curve is really high, it seriously took some getting used to, it lost a point, and no Bluetooth connection so requiring a RF receiver which the signal can be easily interrupted!  There is a spew about it being tested but it's bull crap, RF signals are easily screwed with.  You can't go further than 7 feet from the receiver or have anything in front of it hence, the reason it loses another point.  Bluetooth is cheap as hell, and frankly I'm not sure why they chose to go with RF but, at this point it's a preference thing I suppose.
All in all, I'd purchase a second, and I definitely would recommend the controller to anyone playing in the living room or in the computer chair.  Happy gaming people!

I don't really like leaving negative reviews for games or other products in general, especially not for those which work as intended. This review must therefore be an exception - I give this game a 3/5 for a first download and play, though replayability is zero, so from then I would give it a 0/5.
The (mostly) good:
The game runs well on my old (9 year) gaming laptop, and the music is fairly catchy if a little annoying. It's quick to download and get into the game, and easy to play.
The layout and menus are well put together and everything is smooth and seemless - the sort of game you could run on most modern devices with other things going on in the background (i.e. as the game description states - whilst a proper game downloads).
It's somewhat interesting in how it works and it's humerous - notably the game managers being references to popular culture, the use of outrageous amounts of money, and the free add ons.
The bad:
Nothing really happens - the game is just a counting program which you increase the levels of counting by clicking boxes. Though it's superficially more than that, I couldn't get past the pointlessness of what it is.
To summarise - I wanted to like it, but there just isn't enough to the game for me.
It looks to me like a mobile game, not really a game I would want to play on pc.

Having been playing this game for two weeks almost non-stop, I feel as if I can finally give a good review once the "OMG, NEW GAME TO PLAY" hype wore off.
First things first, the story is no challenge. If you don't take your time, you can blow through about half the story in a day. This is both good and bad, seeing as how it's fun and easy to get into.
Pros:
Easy
Not too system heavy (In my opinion, I run a rather low-end rig)
Emphasizes teamwork, but doesn't shove it down your throat
Fun
Easy to understand and grip the story
Lots of classes to choose from, a little bit of this, a little bit of that. Melee, ranged, magic, all sorts of goodies.
KAWAII AS HELL
Nice art style
Explorable terrain
Diverse (Somewhat) creatures and races
Cons:
Very little story progression per quest, gets too meticulous, tedious and repetitive.
Emphasizes defeating creatures moreso than the actual story. ("Here, take this item, but I need you to collect 12 things that drop 1/4 times from a creature that's evenly matched to you")
The mail system is loaded with spammers, sending offers for sites that allow you to buy gold with real money.
Too many bot characters, people who aren't even playing themselves in order to get gold.
Easy, no real challenge
Central city LAGS EXCESSIVELY, and is required to pass through several times towards endgame.
PVP is unbalanced. It's unlocked at level 20, but you should wait until you're level 65 to actually participate in the arenas.

How to gain more FPS in WWE 2K18
Now, this method worked for me, I went from 10 FPS - 60 FPS using these steps.
If you have a NVDIA graphics card, than this will mostly work for you, or atleast boost your FPS a bit.
Step One: Right click on your desktop and find "NVDIA Control Panel"
Step Two: Find and click on "Manage 3D settings"
Step Three: Click on "Program Settings"
Step Four: Click on "Select a program to customize" and find WWE 2k18 and select it.
Step Five: Click on "Select the preferred graphics processor for this program" Once there, find and click on "High-performance NVIDIA processor" than select okay.
These five steps will gain you FPS in WWE 2k18 If this didnt help your game at all increase with FPS, than you're PC mostly can't handle the game at all. I know as a fact I could run this game, so seeing 10 FPS at the start I knew something was wrong with the settings. So, I fixed it by doing these steps, now I can finally play WWE 2k18 with good FPS.
Most reviews are because people can't run it, I did have a bad review at first, but then changed it due to me fixing my FPS issues. For some reason 2k18 doesn't auto set your graphics card and you need to do it.
