The game is fun for a very short while (the time required to reach the late 40's) at which point, it becomes an extremely boring grind.
PROS:
-Great art style.
As practically everyone mentioned, the art style is very nice, and if you're a fan of anime, you'll obviously be a fan.
-Nice animations.
The battle animations tie in very nice with the art style for a nice visual experience.
-Very, very nice community/player base.
The player base is great, everyone is willing to answer any question (providing they speak your tongue) and it's really easy to join a guild of other like-minded players.
-Story.
From what I saw of the story, I actually enjoyed it. Despite being a somewhat generic telling of Good vs Evil, the dialog is well written with nice humour in some parts.
-Enemy variety.
For each zone, there's a fitting bunch of enemies that suit the environment and are very well designed, it's just a shame they take no cognitive higher thought to beat.
-F2P.
You can actually 'complete' or get to the end game of Aura Kingdom without spending a single pound/dollar, which is always good to see in a game.
-Difficulty.
Aura kingdom can be played with just one hand. Leaving your other hand free to do hand-related hings. This is in part thanks to it's simplistic nature and user friendly UI (though it can be very cumbersome at times).
CONS:
-Difficulty.
The game is so. So. SO easy. It requires very minimal skill, which ties in heavily with my negative review. There's simply no challenge. Beyond occasionally being overrun (which is only really possible if you are purposefully attempting to get yourself swarmed) there's literally no tension involved in any aspect of the gameplay, there's no benefit to be gained from paying attention to battle. Pressing 1-2-3-4 will yield the same results as trying to dodge and making use of buffs/debuffs.

For example, as a lower level character, you can run straight towards the end of a zone and kill everything. I was easily taking on level 30 mobs 19, not even having to heal (when quitting my playthrough, I had over 200 potions and used collectively about 10 on the Hell mode dungeons (before quitting them, which I'll get to later)). This is countered (or at least attempted) by some mobs attacking with a power attack, indicated by a red AOE circle that you are recommended to walk out of, or a red line. But they deal so little damage that it was generally more effort than it was worth to take your fingers away from the 1-2-3-4 keys.
-Zones.
The zones (or regions as they're called here) are designed nicely enough, but they're ultimately very small and can be explored fully with barebones gear in around ten minutes (and you're going to be running across these zones for the next ten hours), as previously stated, a player in a new zone can run towards the higher level areas and destroy everything without much hassle.
-Soundtrack.
Boring. Extremely boring. There's relaxing enough songs for when you're in town, but none of the songs ever had me excited or nervous or feeling any emotion about anything because they're just... generic. You're best off muting the music and playing your own, because it ultimately adds little to the game.
-Armour/costumes.
In Aura Kingdom, the F2P model revolves around real money being spent on cosmetic items, which are very, very nicely designed, but as you can guess, ludicrously priced (costing occassionally £7 and above for a costume for only three days) which is all well and good, they need to make their money somehow, and I won't fault them for that. But the fact that any armour you pick up in game is merely a stat booster is very disappointing and leaves little feel for actual progression, as you'll be wearing the same costume for around 15 levels (around 8-15 hours depending). This is offset by some quests giving you a new costume for your effort, but these are generally terrible in comparison to the costumes that cost; meaning your fancy anime character becomes very stale, very fast.
-Quests.
The quests are as you might expect and the term 'mailman simulator' is very literal here. Kill 8 of these things, then go and get 4 of their teeth (resulting in you having to go back to kill the same thing you just killed 8 times around another 20-30). There are one or two fun quests that involve you taking over a bat and infiltrating a camp, or masquerading as a treasurer for pirates, but these are few and far between.
'Daily' and 'Guild' quests that refresh every day allow you to gain experience for your guild, but are also very repetetive and boring, recycling the same 5-6 maps with very similar objectives (namely, kill 15 of these or get 6 of these eggs).
-Bots.
I swear there's one bot for every player. And they're very easily recognizable. Working on a similar name system, with the exact same looking character, in the same area. The game has an auto path find feature built in, meaning that botters have half the job done for them anyway. Prepare to see a lot of spam about "buy 100 0 gold for $5$ at
<3<3<££". It's just daft that there's no mention about doing anything to get rid of these purple headed ♥♥♥♥♥.
-Dungeons.
In each region, there are around 3-4 dungeons that are very samey-samey, with 2-3 bosses in each. You have the option to do a dungeon in either: Party mode, Solo mode, or Hell mode. Hell mode is the polar opposite of the rest of the game, taking any form of comfort you might have taken with you inside, and throwing it at a wall. The enemies are the same level as they would be normally, but instead of being smarter, having larger agro ranges or more spells, they're simply in slightly larger numbers, with an absurd damage output and equally insane amount of health. No biggy, you can just come back at a higher level for the sweet loot they'll have, right? ...not the case. The gear you get from these Hell mode dungeons is only good for the level of the mobs inside (coming into a level 30 Hell mode dungeon at level 40 means you'll be getting terrible gear).
I don't consider myself a master or anything, but it is statistically very, very difficult to manage to complete any of these Hell mode things at the recommended level to benefit from the loots. Outta all of the people I asked in game, not one had managed to finish one of them, making their difficulty spike very pointless and unwelcome in comparison to the rest of the game.
-Gear. The gear you get from quests is very easily offset by gear you can purchase in the shops before even reaching that quest, which sucks.
I never actually tried the PvP beyond a few player duels, which are fun enough and do require some degree of skill and knowledge of the game to win. The fact that you can walk up to any one and offer them out is a pretty cool feature. It's just a shame none of the rest of the game requires this degree of thought.
Conclusion:
If you're looking for a game that requires minimal thought and that you want to multitask with, I'd highly advise this one. But if you're looking for a good MMORPG with a strong sense of progression and character development, I'd stay away from this one. Even though the artstyle kicks♥♥♥♥♥and the story is o-kay, most-everything else is just lacklustre and generic, it's like 'vanilla icecream' it's okay enough, but it doesn't do anything particularly great: except this vanillia icecream is slightly out of date and melting through a hole in the bottom of your cone.

This game is a true gem. But undeniable it is also a very niche game. I hope with this review i can help you in your decision if you should buy this game or not.
Lets start with the obvious stuff: the negative.
- the graphics are the worstest graphics i have ever seen in a game. Like in every game you get used to it, and im still happy that at least every differnet unit has their own little picture, from which you can set them apart, but besides this, the graphic is very unsatisfying.
-its very hard to get in. To play the tutorial (which is basicly a 1v1 game against a very weak AI) you have to print a 400 pages manual (or at least the tutorial part of it) so that you can follow the steps is it and have the chance to slowly understand what to do and how to play.
-The AI is not very smart and in the Single player game their is no diplomacy option which means that after the AI or you have declared war to each other, their will be war until the end.
So basicly what is the problem with the game is the very poor presentation and its very hard to get into it. Their will be no feelings of success in the first hours so i can totally understand if someone wants to give it a try, buyed it on steam and then refund it after two hours because in this short time he did not get any fun at all.
But if you can overlook the presentation here are the reasons, why in my opinion this game is such a wounderful one.
- The scale: This game offers 100 different nations, everyone with a unique backstory based on ancient tales i dont know how many hundret gods, hundret of spells 1000 of units...you name it. The scale of this game is immense and if you belong to the kind of persons who always wants to try new things out, then this game will make you happy.
-With the huge scale their also comes: tactics! While the balance of so many nations and spells+ unitcombinations may not be perfect for hard core players who wants to play the best way possibile, since their may be some nations that are just stronger if you play them right, then other nations, but for a more "casual" player the amound of possible tactics that you can develop and try to outplay the opponent are immense!
-the community: While this game is a very niche game, with only a few sells, the community is still very active, and it is way more likely to get help if you have a question in this game, then in even the most tripple A games. The community members are as far as i can say very friendly, and since they are so active you also shoudlnt get to many problems in creating or joining a Multiplayer Game.
- The Multiplayer: To be honest i have to admit, that while i like MP games, and i like strategie games...i never played a round based mulitplayer game besides Civ5 before. To long are the games, to stressfull the games, so i never enjoyed playing in Multiplayer. But in this game the multiplayer part is the true way-to-play of dominions 4...and gives me the best multiplayer experience i have ever seen in a game!
The biggest reason is: the free diplomacy. (together with the awesome community) Because while the most games have very "forced" diplomacy, which means if you make a non aggression pact you are just unable to invade the opponents lands until this contract is active, and if you give someone in a trade 500 gold for 10 magic swords you get instantly the 10 swords.
In dominions 4 the diplomacy has no strict limitations, and is very based on the trust you develop with the other players. Which means that you write real messages to them and ask them for stuff like a trade deal or a non aggression pact and they can write you one thing...and do something totally different.
So you can for example make a non aggression pact for 2 years, and all went well but then suddely, when your army is on the other side of the world, your "ally" betrays you since he have diplomacy against you which you dont know and invades your lands, you can give him 1000 gold for magic items that he dont send you and stuff like this.
So you have to figure out in the game itself how you should punish such untrustful diplomacy. Because you have to think: Can i really trust this player who have already broken a non aggression pact against his other neighbor? Do i support the other player who claimed that he was betrayed from his "ally"...or is this player just tries to trick you into a war?
From this open diplomacy so many intense "game-of-thrones" moments happens, and it really gives you the feeling of an emperor of your nation who has to find out his best way to get more power. Will you betray your weak ally to get his lands, knowing that this will hurt your reputation, and will make further diplomacy harder? Will you play honorable and dont attack a nation that has a non aggresion pact with you, while it is weakend from a war against a other nation? To risk that this nation will overcome your nation, if you give it enough time to regain its power?
This open diplomacy is of course a very risky option, since when you have the "wrong" players in your game that just dont communicate with you what so ever and start attacking you for no reason without any messages, this will really harm the fun that you get from this game, but thanks to the awesome community, most of the players i have seen so far are more then willing to "roleplay" the diplomacy which leads to the most interesting situations i have ever seen in any video game.
After a while you get really into your games, you truely begin to trust some, misstrust others, you feel great joy, if a plan works as intendet and will cry in frusttration if your masterplan gets crusht by the plans of the other players. This leads to the most immersive gaming experience i have ever seen so far in a round based strategie game.
If you love the idea of a diplomacy where like in the real world anythink can happen and a strategie game that is very hard to get into, but has so much to offer that even after thousend of hours you still have more to learn, then i really can recomment it to you.

- Very steep (and long) learning curve
- Enemy AI (while improved in the last few patches) is still pretty abysmal at playing like a human, even when given ridiculous resource advantages at higher difficulties, so it's basically a multiplayer game with not very good single-player tutorials

This is pretty much the epitome of guilty pleasure gaming. There's zero actual ability required to play, no real challenge to overcome or personal skills to improve, hell, you could walk away from the thing for a couple of days and leave it playing by itself and you're still not
going to miss anything. But you know what? I still bloody love the thing.
In AdVenture Capitalist (huh? Get the joke? Eh?... It's like VENTURE capitalist but with an AD at the front of it! Genius) the goal is to make money in order to buy and invest in new enterprises which make more money and allow you to further repeat the cycle ad nauseam. You'll start off with a humble little lemonade stand, then buy several more, before then having enough money to invest in newspaper deliveries and carwashes and pizzas, right the way up to banks and oil companies. This is done simply by clicking on an image of the desired business once you have enough cash to blow on it to purchase either 1, 10 or 100 of a selected property at a time. Once you reach certain landmarks and own a certain amount of these businesses, you'll gain a multiplier bonus to either increase the speed at which a business will accrue money, or just the overall return for a particular investment. This is also on top of upgrades you can buy for each individual business to multiply its profits as well. It may sound pretty involved or slightly complex to the uninitiated, but it really isn't. Even for someone as numerically illiterate as me, it couldn't be easier.
As your juicy, oily, pizzary empire grows, the multipliers and upgrades begin to turn things on their head and instead of oil companies accounting for the vast majority of your wealth, you'll now find things like donut shops being your main source of income... thousands and thousands of donut shops. Because why not? The only other real complication of note are angel investors. This is essentially a prestige system, whereby, the more money you make, the more angels you'll accumulate. You then have the option of resetting to start from scratch but carrying over your angel investors with you. Each one you have provides a large bonus multiplier, but these can also be used as a form of currency to buy extra upgrades as well. So a balancing act kicks in of knowing when to hold them and when to spend them as well as what purchases will provide the best returns. Again, it all sounds kind of intense or marginally intimidating if you've never laid eyes on this before, but it really,
isn't! Even for someone as angelically illiterate as me, it couldn't be easier.
There's nothing glamorous about this game at all. No fancy 3D environments or flashy animations. There are some catchy tunes and pleasing enough sounds effects, but otherwise there's no real frills to the experience. Just a single screen with some boxes to click on and some numbers rapidly running their course. That said, there is a sort of endearing charm to the basic MS Paint style art of everything. This was also expanded upon when the game decided to launch additional planets to the mix. Well, they call them planets. It's the Moon and Mars. These are whole, self-contained experiences that play similarly to the basic Earth mode, but the rate of returns and costs of specific, planet-themed purchases behave wildly differently. Mars can be completed in a couple of weeks, though, while the Moon will take several months. The Earth, on the other hand? Well... that's a bone of some contention.
As it stands right now, all signs point to it being impossible to actually "finish" the Earth game, that it would take literally thousands, if not millions of years of play before every upgrade and unlock bonus could be obtained, with many suggesting this is designed to force players to spend real world money on additional bonuses in this otherwise free to play game. The developers have responded by saying they intend for all players to be able to finish the game regardless of whether to buy their way to the end or never spend a single penny, and will continue to tweak the game throughout its life. But so far, this doesn't seem to have manifested in any considerable changes to address or balance these issues. Whether or not they ever will, remains to be seen.
To be completely honest, though, I really don't mind that either way. I've clocked up a few hundred hours on this without parting with any of my money so far, and have enjoyed the oddly satisfying, mindless pursuit of clicking on numbers to make even bigger numbers do some numbers so the numbers can be all numbery and number and stuff. And at this point, I'll happily throw them a few bucks as a token gesture of thanks for the time I've had with it. Hopefully they'll do something about the Earth game, but even without it, with what appear to now be monthly timed events with extra themes and rewards, and still all for free, I don't see myself leaving this game alone any time soon and look forward to seeing what they'll do with it next.

I don't know... maybe it's just too early for the Steam Controller to shine, but as a PC gamer I just don't see it's appeal.
Don't get me wrong, it's definitely a fine, innovative piece of hardware, and the way it works and how it works is quite impressive. But I'll explain why I don't really see myself using the Steam controller.
First, a little about my set up: I have two 24" monitors, and to the left, a 60" 1080p HDTV. I'd love to sit back and relax in my couch to play a number of my PC games, as opposed to being hunched over in my computer chair. That being said, I want to be able to seamlessly go back to my inevitably more precise method of playing via keyboard and mouse. Pretty much a shoe in for the Steam Controller and its functionality
I used Left 4 Dead 2 and Transistor as my trial games. In playing Left 4 Dead 2, there seems to be an added 'Steam Controller' menu, but when I click on it (either in Big Picture Mode on my TV or regularly on my computer monitor) it doesn't seem to actually do anything. The settings for the trackpad were far too sensitive, and it seems that in order to adjust this, I'd have to actually change the mouse settings (which I don't want to do, since they are set for optimal play on my default M+K setup). To sum up my first gripe, its that the Steam Controller settings don't seem to be 100% independent from the normal settings. And I assume that is because the Steam Controller acts as an actual mouse, and is meant to be integrated as best as possible with as many games as possible. But as an avid M+K user, it puts me in a bit of a hard place, and if I had to chose, would take the accuracy and ease of M+K over the comfort of my couch.
Ease is the second part, and it bleeds into my Transistor experience. Aside from the resolution issue Transistor has with Big Picture Mode (which I don't actually blame on the Steam Controller), for a game that wasn't meant to use the controller (as far as I know) the controls are rather cumbersome. Valve has done something awesome with the customization options that are available via the community, etc. But even if I were to get the most intuitive set (even for Left 4 Dead 2), the controller's buttons are a bit awkward to use. I have large hands (I actually owned and used the Nexus 6 phone one handed) and many of the Steam Controller functions feel great in concept (including the paddles, and including, but not so much, the trackpad click buttons), but the thumbstick and the ABXY buttons are awful to use. While there are fixes for my gripes before, I don't see how this issue is fixed, but simply put, for games that would use a traditional gamepad setup, the Steam Controller is a burden to use. And this may just be an artifact of the fact that the steam controller uses positioning that is different from just about every main controller (referring to the Big Three here).
I am not giving up on the Steam Controller. I preordered it because I see it's potential. I've never played Rocket League, and it came with the preorder, so maybe I'll try that. But as of now, I see its use for special occassions only. Very special occassions.

I have to say after being told by valve they were going to revolutionise the controller experience for PC users...I thought they were going to do it in a good way not a bad one. I despise controllers for things like FPS games, love them for racing games etc - to me the controller has its place, but being a FPS player I stick firmly with my mouse and keyboard and have the controller for fifa and my xbox itself. In comes the steam controller, and it has one place for it to go after a few days testing - the bin.
Dual trackpads are horrific...these things have no accuracy what so ever and if you remove your finger off them too fast/hard the gyro inside of it continues to roll so your cursor/head movement always wanders and there is no precision to your actions. Its also sluggish to respond and even with the sensitivity up high fails to meet the demands of an FPS by a long shot - even with the aim assist on (which I despise and should not HAVE to be on in the first place). Then theres the click inside each of them....you cannot click it with your fingers anywhere other than the center, if your at the edges you have to really press down to the point where it interupts your movement on the trackpad - and it clicks....the damn gyros click for every tick on the left pad - its annoying beyond belief.
Button placement is....allright - its not as bad as it looks. The two lower buttons are snug and unexpected but I actually like them, but as for the two shoulder buttons I dunno if I hold things wonky to other people but I feel they should be an inch higher on the shoulders....not just above the triggers. Its not uncomfortable to hold them and you can see the way it moulds a hand if you hold things where the buttons are but it just does not feel how I would GRIP a controller. Its hand shapped yes, but not how I would grip something if you follow what I mean.
All in all it doesn't even work with half the games, I expected waves of different set up on launch by them but the have lazily just left it to the community to do - hell even games just released like black ops 3 have stupid things like no bound button for your specialist feature - but the jump button was assigned to one of the lower paddles?
One place for it - bin. Sorry, nice try valve and I am sure somewhere in this is some technology that someone will take and use better, but for now its been a huge waste of your time this and - imo - a real lack of effort when it comes to game setups for it. I picked up a dual shock back in the day, used it, felt odd but used it, even the N64 controller which was a HUGE difference, I still just looked at the pictures, held it, used it - and so the trend continues. Yours is the first controller I genuinely have picked up and just flat out CANNOT EVEN USE - and I think using it was part of the plan was it not?

I usually never write reviews, but I feel like this poor controller has gotten a lot of misguided criticism. There been a lot of complaints how it's useless for playing fighting and racing games with, which is like critiquing a mouse for failing at the same things. This isn't an xbox controller, but rather an alternative to the classical  mouse and keyboard combination.
Where this controller excels is in games such as old school RPGs with click to move controls, city builders and strategy games like HoMM. Such  games have been nearly impossible to play with controllers before, but with the Steam controller it now feels easy and natural.
So I would say that it's a good controller that fills a particular hole in the market. It won't replace your xbox controller or make mouse and keyboards useless, but I don't think that was the intention either. It's a controller that functions like a mouse, and when you allow it to simply do that it does a great job.

1 Line review: It's like Portal, but without Portals. Also, it's very short. 5/10
Full Review:
There isn't much to talk about this. The story is almost non-existent and is just a bunch (~20 + 10 extras) of really short levels (5min max if you want to get everything in each level). I'd say that the concept is kinda cool: instead of Portals, you have you manipulate your own "polarity", between red or blue if you don't want to die from lasers of that color, if you want to be above platforms of those colors and even transport cubes of those colors without desintegrating them.
As a puzzle game, I didn't find it hard, only slightly on very specific segments that you have to get some items to unlock the ending. It should be more as an introdutory puzzle game to kids ages 8 and lower rather than to teens and adults used to more complex games like The Talos Principle and PQ (the psp exclusive). If you fall on the latter category, this game should be just one or two hours long.
On the other hand, this game often comes *really* cheap, like dirt cheap (some 50 cents... no pun intended), so the price/game hours ratio isn't that bad. The experience itself is bug-free and the visual is simple and a little retro, so it's nice to relax if you want something for that. Visuals are quite simple as well, but don't strain the eyes.
Overall, it is a fair game... I mean, fairly standard. Short, cheap, soothing, but nothing more. Well, it has multiplayer, but it's not that entertaining as other puzzle multiplayer games. So, just don't expect much.

Usually, one shouldn't fix what isn't broke, but sometimes it doesn't hurt to do so.  KOF98 Ultimate Match is one of those times.
An updated version of the classic Neo-Geo 3-on-3 fighting game, Ultimate Match provides players with a truly complete roster of characters from the first three KOF games.  The conspicuously absent Boss Team from 1996 joins the game roster, along with Art of Fighting's resident ninja Eiji Kisaragi (last seen in KOF95), and aikido devotee Kasumi (from KOF96's womens' team); and endboss Omega Rugal is joined by 96's infamously cheap Goenitz and a newly renovated version of Orochi, the skinny-jeans wearing snake god from KOF97.
Make no mistake; aside from the obvious exclusion of the boss characters, all the new characters in 98 UM are balanced to fit in with the rest of the cast, which itself has had some tweaks, both major and minor, to make them play just a bit differently from the original version.  WIth the Final Edition, further rebalancing attempts were made to ensure that all 59(!) characters are viable, with some underappreciated characters (such as Lucky Glauber) getting a much-needed boost in effectiveness.
If I had any complaints about this PC port, it's that I wish it had a couple of the extra features from the PS2 version of KOF98UM, like the single-player challenges and palette editor.  As it is, it's a straight port of the 2009 release on Xbox 360, with some brand new balance tweaks.  Those are pretty minor omissions, however, and for the price tag, you're getting a good deal nonetheless.

Well honestly what can I say that's really negative about this game. It's one of the best games I've ever played - and arguably one of the best games ever made. You needn't know about any of the other NieR games to experience this one's story to the fullest so worry not.
Considering it's a port from the console version (or so it seems) the game has built in keyboard support - HOWEVER this keyboard support is utter garbage and I would not recommend playing this game with a keyboard under any circumstances unless you're some masochist. It is definitely worth purchasing a controller for this if you don't have one already - there are some affordable ones somewhere on Amazon if you look hard enough. Other than that I had no problems with the game at all. It runs fine, it plays fine. I have no complaints.
---
Let's talk about the actual game experience now, starting from obviously the gameplay. The gameplay was a little bit awkward at first, not gonna lie - though that may be in part due to having started using the keyboard. Having switched to the controller I find it a lot easier to play the game since the buttons are mapped in a fairly intuitive way. There are several types of gameplay you will encounter in the game:
- Hack and Slash: Self explanatory, just kill everything with swords and guns.
- Bullet Hell: Dodge a massive amount of slow-moving bullets and destroy lighter, weaker ones. Evasion is key.
- Twin-stick Shooter: Bullet hell but you can shoot and move in all directions.
- Platformer: A visual twist, changes nothing about the combat whatsoever, only the way one moves - and as expected you can only move on a two-dimensional plane.
- Top-down Shooter (idk what to call this): Basically opposite-platformer.
These all blend into each other seamlessly throughout the game and there are rarely moments where it felt like a hinderance. They only add to the variety and make sure you never get bored of any one section.
The combat felt slightly clunky at first but after fiddling with it for a while I grew used to it. It plays fluidly for the most part and the game is fairly straightforward in teaching you how to fight. I find dodging a bit overpowered though since a good tap of the button can dodge pretty much any powerful or even lethal strike if timed properly.
---
The soundtrack, oh god I love this soundtrack. I grew up with stellar soundtracks from games like Ar tonelico and Ace Combat but this one by far outshines every single OST I have ever heard and undoubtedly many of the OSTs I will hear in the future. The way the songs are constructed throughout the world (they even build up depending on the circumstance by adding new layers like vocals or drums on top of the base melody to simulate intensity) provides such a stimulating audio-visual experience that the soundtrack alone is reason to not teleport everywhere and to just walk and take in the music.
The sound itself was pretty good - as in the clanking of swords and clenching of fists, I don't think there's much to say here. Good.
Having only played through the full game on the English voice (I will soon on the Japanese voices) I can say for certain there was no expense spared in the english voice acting department. People may say it's sub-par but I find each character's voice fit them to a T - especially 2B and A2. Shoutout (literally) to 9S's performance in the final stages of the game. There's so much raw emotion in the voice acting it was almost palpable to me as the player.
---
Graphics-wise this is easily one of the most stunning games even on the lower end of the spectrum. This game far surpasses the "it needs to look at least THIS good for me to enjoy" threshold on the lowest settings and runs at a fairly solid 40-60 FPS on a 960X + 8 gigs of RAM. The game is very resource intensive, so a very high-end PC is recommended to run the highest level of graphics.
The color palette is very.. unique. It uses bleak desaturated colors as norm and brighter vibrant colors in moments of visual emphasis. I feel like there's a thematic/figurative reason that the YoRHa Bunker is in perpetual black and white but the reason there eludes me. It doesn't take away from the experience however, in fact I feel like black and white was a good choice - it gives the area a very sterile, high-tech look.
---
The story. The story is just.. stellar, unbelievably detailed. The pace is perfect, you won't feel like it's going too fast or too slow - there are plenty of side quests to undertake to slow down the pace of the story if you feel it is progressing too fast. There are so many deep psychological questions asked and answered and so many plot twists and just aaaaaaaaaaaaaa it's such a page-turner! That coupled with the 5 different endings plus the other 20-odd joke endings just gives you so much story to go off of. It's basically guaranteed you will not get bored playing this game since there is always something to do. If you like a deep and rich intricate story, this game has got you covered way more than you think.
---
Conclusion: In my personal opinions this is up there with the best games ever created for all of these reasons. I feel like my inexperience with actually reviewing anything really undersells the game but I want to at least alleviate the somewhat plentiful negative reviews by saying this and this alone:
If you are considering buying this game - do it. It will be the best 60 bucks you've ever spent in your life and you'll have an amazing experience in return.

Trying to find all different kinds of Eidolons, armors, and weapons. I have only been lucky enough to get my second Eidolon which is mildly depressing.
Eidolons make this game very unique combining the use of your own skills while also having to depend on the skills of your "Pet". They can help you in battle in various ways. For example they can do heavy amounts of damage or heal you in a pinch.
Another beauty of this game is there are not many "Go kill me 25 of these monsters." Leaving you wondering why? Even though there are some missions that require you to kill a specific amount of monsters most are fairly easy and can be done without traveling very far.
You get your mounts very early in the game. Mounts are simliar to Eidolons except you cannot use them in battle they are only for use to get around the world faster. Which brings me to another aspect of the travel system. Most MMOs I have played recently require you to find a person which could be multiple towns away. In this you can simply click on a part of the quest you wish to complete and it will take you to the area of the task.
The World itself is very beautiful. The world is very vibrant and full of color along with the enemies you face most of the models are very well done. Some of the base models do seem to be reused quite often but nevertheless it is still quite impressive.

This game is a textbook definition of "hard to get into". It's turn based strategy game with minimum graphics and almost no animation and music. There is no tutorial, but you can read 300+ page manual that don't cover everything. The goal is simple - to wipe out other pretenders to god's throne - but the process is long and complicated, thanks to clunky UI, a lot of micromanagement and extreme list of rules. It's like playing grand D&D 3.0 campaing by the book and with a lot of expansions, as a Dungeon Master. You either memorise most important stuff, have vage understanding of the rest and energy to manage dozens of NPCs, sites and events, or you will be like a blind child in the fog in the middle of earthquake. The abundance of content does not help either, especially with hundreds of spells to choose from. A lot of patience for loading times on big maps is also needed.
But after grasping the rules the game became brilliant. You can min max in ways that almost break it. You can play as heat loving nations and then magically create more suns to boost your armies with massive bonuses. You can give your mages so much power and artifacts that they will win almost every battle singlehandedly. You can build undead legions that do not need sleep and food and then make them even bigger with every battle that you won. There are thousands of combinations of nations, spells and artifacts that in every other game would be called overpowered.
But this game wants you to feel and to be overpowered. It gives you the ability to play as a demons summoning, fireballs throwing dragon, conquering the world with the armies of beasts, horrors beyond time and space, and released from Tartarus ancient titans. It gives you the power to craft artifacts like Sun Slayer, Carcator the Pocket Lich and Fenris' Pelt and give them to your commanders. It allows you to summon fire and ice storms, create vampires, hybrids and automatons, perform blood rituals to build castles and throw bolts of god's wrath onto your enemies. It demands a lot from you, but after that it gives you a lot of tools to experiment and have a lot of fun with.
The important think is, that you do not controll combat. You also can't tinker with economy, cause there is none. You collect gold and magic gems, provinces generate resources, there is unrest, temples and fortresses, but that's it. You build armies, equip commanders, choose formations, give them simple orders and then watch. It's like late game Total War, when you just build bigger forces than enemies and click auto resolve, but this time you can watch Cthulhu spawns beating dragon raiding minotaurs and archwizards using mage slaves to boost their powers. Did I mention that you can also teleport from one side of the map to the other, move your armies under the oceans and turn whole provinces into undead filled wastelands?
If you like grand strategies with tons of options, that can be expanded through mods, this game is for you. If you like to feel powerfull and do things on monumental scale, this game is for you. If you think that battles are more important than economy and base building, this game is for you. If you don't mind somewhat unfriendly UI and have patience for micromanagement 50+ armies and provinces, this game is definitelly for you. Full price may be a bit too much considering how much time is needed to fully grasp it's rules, but with regular patches and active community creating new maps, mods and additional resources like wikis, I would say it's worth the risk.

An interesting little game that is great for those who like to really test their reaction time and hand-eye co-ordination.
I’ve never been that great at these type of games myself, so admittedly I had a little help from my bloke who enjoys these kind of games (and is insanely good at them!). I honestly think this would have taken me a hell of a lot longer to complete on my own.
Despite that, the game is fun. There are a few little things that I noticed with this game that undoubtedly makes it harder that I was actually kind of impressed with.
Usually with these types of games you’ll default to hugging the walls, pushing the joystick as far outward away from obstacles as possible to avoid contact, but this game doesn’t allow you to do that. Most levels you have to avoid the walls as well as the obstructions. I guess that could be considered good or bad, but I personally thought it was good as it makes it more challenging. There may be only 4 levels without the DLC, that you have to survive 60 seconds on each, but it really isn’t as easy as it sounds.
Onto the next thing,
You might assume that when you die in this game, the level will start again, however it doesn’t. It’ll pick up where you left off and you’ll have to try for your 60 second win from there. If you manage to get through a minute, you’ll notice the track will start again.
This is a great mechanic in my opinion because it is actually very disorientating to be thrown back onto the level at a seemingly random place. With these type of games if the level starts over from scratch you’ll eventually start to memorise the track. You’ll know what is coming and that will make it easier to complete, so this game adds that small level of difficulty by not even allowing you that.
The graphics are minimalistic, which is nice. I like it but it’s also oddly mesmerizing in places. You know when you look at an optical illusion for too long and you can feel your eyes slowly going cross-eyed? Well, I’d be lying if I said that this game didn’t do that to me on the later stages. My eyes couldn’t even handle what I was looking at, never mind having to actually complete the level! No idea how my boyfriend managed it to be honest.
The music was fun. Given how minimal this game, is the music is probably one of the key factors to it. In other reviews I noticed how many people found it one of the worthwhile parts to the game.
Achievements wise, I’ll admit I only started this to try for an easy 100%. I personally would of never gotten that on my own. It requires you to complete every level and there are 2 or 3 missable achievements that I had to go back for (one included dying 666 times, which amusingly has a higher percentage of completion than actually finishing the game).
All in all though, I like this game! I may not be very good at it, but I’d say if you like these kind of games you should give it a go. If you’re looking for an “easy” 100% though… you may want to reconsider.
TL;DR: Fun but difficult fast-paced game that can really test your reaction time. Nice graphics, good music and a few mechanics that kind of make this game stand out a little from the rest. Achievement wise, it’s not that easy of a 100%. If you like these kind of games, give it a go.

This is pretty much the epitome of guilty pleasure gaming. There's zero actual ability required to play, no real challenge to overcome or personal skills to improve, hell, you could walk away from the thing for a couple of days and leave it playing by itself and you're still not
going to miss anything. But you know what? I still bloody love the thing.
In AdVenture Capitalist (huh? Get the joke? Eh?... It's like VENTURE capitalist but with an AD at the front of it! Genius) the goal is to make money in order to buy and invest in new enterprises which make more money and allow you to further repeat the cycle ad nauseam. You'll start off with a humble little lemonade stand, then buy several more, before then having enough money to invest in newspaper deliveries and carwashes and pizzas, right the way up to banks and oil companies. This is done simply by clicking on an image of the desired business once you have enough cash to blow on it to purchase either 1, 10 or 100 of a selected property at a time. Once you reach certain landmarks and own a certain amount of these businesses, you'll gain a multiplier bonus to either increase the speed at which a business will accrue money, or just the overall return for a particular investment. This is also on top of upgrades you can buy for each individual business to multiply its profits as well. It may sound pretty involved or slightly complex to the uninitiated, but it really isn't. Even for someone as numerically illiterate as me, it couldn't be easier.
As your juicy, oily, pizzary empire grows, the multipliers and upgrades begin to turn things on their head and instead of oil companies accounting for the vast majority of your wealth, you'll now find things like donut shops being your main source of income... thousands and thousands of donut shops. Because why not? The only other real complication of note are angel investors. This is essentially a prestige system, whereby, the more money you make, the more angels you'll accumulate. You then have the option of resetting to start from scratch but carrying over your angel investors with you. Each one you have provides a large bonus multiplier, but these can also be used as a form of currency to buy extra upgrades as well. So a balancing act kicks in of knowing when to hold them and when to spend them as well as what purchases will provide the best returns. Again, it all sounds kind of intense or marginally intimidating if you've never laid eyes on this before, but it really,
isn't! Even for someone as angelically illiterate as me, it couldn't be easier.
There's nothing glamorous about this game at all. No fancy 3D environments or flashy animations. There are some catchy tunes and pleasing enough sounds effects, but otherwise there's no real frills to the experience. Just a single screen with some boxes to click on and some numbers rapidly running their course. That said, there is a sort of endearing charm to the basic MS Paint style art of everything. This was also expanded upon when the game decided to launch additional planets to the mix. Well, they call them planets. It's the Moon and Mars. These are whole, self-contained experiences that play similarly to the basic Earth mode, but the rate of returns and costs of specific, planet-themed purchases behave wildly differently. Mars can be completed in a couple of weeks, though, while the Moon will take several months. The Earth, on the other hand? Well... that's a bone of some contention.
As it stands right now, all signs point to it being impossible to actually "finish" the Earth game, that it would take literally thousands, if not millions of years of play before every upgrade and unlock bonus could be obtained, with many suggesting this is designed to force players to spend real world money on additional bonuses in this otherwise free to play game. The developers have responded by saying they intend for all players to be able to finish the game regardless of whether to buy their way to the end or never spend a single penny, and will continue to tweak the game throughout its life. But so far, this doesn't seem to have manifested in any considerable changes to address or balance these issues. Whether or not they ever will, remains to be seen.
To be completely honest, though, I really don't mind that either way. I've clocked up a few hundred hours on this without parting with any of my money so far, and have enjoyed the oddly satisfying, mindless pursuit of clicking on numbers to make even bigger numbers do some numbers so the numbers can be all numbery and number and stuff. And at this point, I'll happily throw them a few bucks as a token gesture of thanks for the time I've had with it. Hopefully they'll do something about the Earth game, but even without it, with what appear to now be monthly timed events with extra themes and rewards, and still all for free, I don't see myself leaving this game alone any time soon and look forward to seeing what they'll do with it next.

I usually never write reviews, but I feel like this poor controller has gotten a lot of misguided criticism. There been a lot of complaints how it's useless for playing fighting and racing games with, which is like critiquing a mouse for failing at the same things. This isn't an xbox controller, but rather an alternative to the classical  mouse and keyboard combination.
Where this controller excels is in games such as old school RPGs with click to move controls, city builders and strategy games like HoMM. Such  games have been nearly impossible to play with controllers before, but with the Steam controller it now feels easy and natural.
So I would say that it's a good controller that fills a particular hole in the market. It won't replace your xbox controller or make mouse and keyboards useless, but I don't think that was the intention either. It's a controller that functions like a mouse, and when you allow it to simply do that it does a great job.

I have mixed feelings on the Steam Controller, but overall it is definitely a reccomended piece of hardware for a certain demographic. I'll detail more below.
Valve's big hardware push this Autumn has obviously fallen under controversy (mainly due to the underpowered and overpriced Steam Machines) but the general consensus decides upon the Controller being the most innovative and interesting product. For the sake of brevity and focus, I'll resort to a Positives and Negatives list with bulletpoints.
So, I enjoyed using this controller. It was innovative and entertaining. I did not, however, feel like it was something that really helped me out or had a substantial impact on my gameplaying. The forcefeeding of Big Picture to allow many features to activate made me upset, as it's not practical for me to use at my computer. I get it's designed more for people with Steam Machines or Steam Links and playing on TV, but I love to have a good controller to play certain games with next to me.
I really feel that if you are a console gamer looking into PC gaming, and want to find a similar control scheme that will allow you to play any PC game, this just might be the peripheral for you. The button placement might put you off a bit, however. If you're a hardcore PC gamer looking for a new controller to use during games better enjoyed with one, you really might want to just stick with your Xbox or Playstation controller you may or may not be using.
When not in use, however, this does make a pretty fancy display item.
tl;dr
If you play consoles and want a controller for PC it's pretty nice. If you've used PC for a while and want something better than what you have, it's really not the most spectacular thing for you, especially considering some of the smaller issues I had.
EDIT: It appears that thanks to the latest firmware update, scrolling works miles better and as expected. Nice to browse webpages now.

this controller is very different, it highly requires you to use big picture mode.  thing I like about the controller is when you are playing games like Elder Scrolls 3, you can choose any controller setup that were previously inputed by other steam users who also own a controller.  Setting up games like Elsword could take some time because you have to manually input the buttons yourself, the good about this is you can make your controller setup private or local (which means you are sharing the controller setup with other people).  Some games like Agarest Zero will read the steam controller as a X-box 360 controller.  There are some games that won't need you to manually set up buttons, games like Quake, Spiral Knights and Ultra Street Fighter 4.  The 1 game I had a problem with was Streets of Rage 2 because it only read the controller as a X-box 360 controller, the bad part is, it won't let you set the buttons from inside the game's option menu, I guess you can only set up before you actually PLAY the game.
Overall, I thought I would do my own observant review because, most of the magazine articles I read, The Steam Controller was only tested on games like Team Fortress 2 or Left 4 Dead 2 and Apparently, they say the controller works perfect.  Personally, I still have alot to learn when using the steam controller because its different.  I think its a cool piece of technology, I hope Valve keeps expanding & creating more ways to play games, the Steam Controller is worth your money.

Is an introduction to this blockbuster RPG even necessary at this point? Skyrim is and has been, since 2011, the best Elder Scrolls game and one of the greatest single player RPG's ever created. A review can go on for hours upon hours talking about the positives of this game alone, while the negatives leave little to be remembered by. There is one thing that I will say I wish had a bit more diversity in this game, and that is the voice acting. Literally every male Nord is Ralof, and as much as I love Ralof, we need more voices! Aside from this minor complication, the game is simply breathtaking. The world is vast with a plethora of areas to explore. Even if you have played the game for years, you'll find that there are those few places that you have yet to explore. The combat system is amazing, and I love the diversity it brings in terms of how flexible you can be with your character(s). Speaking of diversity, the armors the game has to offer are great, but I do feel as though there could have been more. Some unique armors and weapons really didn't stand out too much for me, and I really wanted to feel a sense of accomplishment when I quested for weapons like Wuuthrad and Dawnbreaker. As I see it, these weapons and many other uniques, including armors, are easily forgotten and overshadowed by the Dragon and Daedric categories. The crafting system is flawless, and definitely brings a bitter sweet sensation to the game when you know you have to grind for a specific set in order to craft it, but feel accomplished when you adorn that new piece. Lets not forget the ability to enchant weapons and armor, as well as upgrade and name them. While there is much more that can be said about Skyrim and it's vast majority of quests and activities, I believe that the true value of the game comes from the player's perspective and not from a review. However, I do hope that from this, if you are new, you consider purchasing this game, as you will not regret it!

Nier Automata is many steps up in terms of gameplay from the original Nier. Combat is fun, beautiful and works fluidly and is by far the saving grace of this game. As a standalone game, Nier Automata is relatively decent. However, when compared with its predecessor, from my perspective, the game falls flat in terms of memorability and lacks the beauty, charm and soul of the original.
The game's soundtrack is by no means bad, but it is in no way even remotely as grand as the original Nier. It is certainly many steps backwards.
Character development seems extraordinarily rushed and while 2B and 9S are "cool", you really couldn't care too much about them. 2B has known 9S only for a terribly short amount of time and yet, it's as if they've known eachother for years and have gone through hell with eachother time again about 5 minutes after they meet.  The entire cast of the game is easily forgotten, whereas in the original you WILL remember and mourn every character in your party, and the NPCs you come across.
The story certainly isn't in the least memorable. It's bland, predictable and certainly what you'd expect from the modern day hack & slash RPG. This is especially so if you compare it to the first game, which to this day sends shivers down my spine with how haunting it is. For new players, while there are a number of references to the original, you won't miss anything too important if you haven't played it. The story has multiple endings which require multiple playthroughs, which provides a "new perspective" on the game as the developers like to put it, which is also a welcome addition and does show some level of dedication in the development of Nier Automata.
In terms of bugs, there are few that I have encountered and absolutely none that have been gamebreaking. All issues related to the gameplay and sorted themselves out without my intervention.
If you're searching for a game that will stay with you forever, you absolutely MUST play the original NieR on PS3/XBOX360. If you're looking for a fun hack & slash to pass the time and you're not interested in a great story or don't have time to be immersed into a virtual world and become involved with the characters, then this game is certainly recommended. It is by no means a bad game, just not a great one when compared with the original.

No spoilers of course. The story to Saints Row 2 follows directly on from Saints Row 1 with the main character waking in a prison hospital after being in a coma after a huge boat explosion. Now the mod GOTR includes options to show button hints for Xbox 360 controllers which were spot on and therefor playing on PC didn't feel any different for me. Car handling IMO is perfect for this game with the outrageous power slides and unrealistic but fitting handling. This game easily comes top for the greatest soundtrack of all time. Just another part of how this game makes you feel so immersed.

Dominions 4 could easily become one of the best triple A titles out there.  The game has a dense soul and is truly unique.
I can't however recommend it due to the absurd amount of micromanagement required. Mind I am used to playing strategy games like Crusader Kings, Civilization, Age of Wonders, etc. And I can say nothing compares to Dominions 4. Micromanagement here is simply unbearable.
I hope the developers will take this as a constructive criticism, for I would love one day to play Dominions 5 with a decent UI and a few ordinary features implemented, such as automovement, clear interfaces and functional commands that will help reduce the hundreds of useless clicking, and also allow for a quick and effective way of verifying the relevant game aspects.
*** My negative review doesn't necessarily mean you should not buy Dominions 4. Just be warned, though, about the micromanagement inconvenience. Fortunately, this game can be highly customizable. In my case, in order to alleviate the said burden, I have decided to play my single-player campaigns in smaller maps (around 100 provinces), adjust victory conditions to a reasonable throne of ascension percentage and set resource income to a 50% debuff.

On the surface this game doesn't look like much. However, once you get past the cover and into the meat of the game it's absolutely fantastic! Example: The game lets you create equipment and give it to the commanders in your army. Around midway through a game I was looking through all of my units when I noticed that one of my commanders no longer had the sword and shield I gave him. When I looked closer I found that somewhere in the course of many battles this guy has been in he lost both of his arms! Now his only attack was a headbutt! This absolute badass was running around the battlefield headbutting everyone and commanding the army at the same time!
Needless to say he impressed me enough that I dedicated a huge amount of time and resources to get one of my mages powerful enough to create an item that would heal his wounds. After crafting the item (basically the holy grail) and healing his wounds he was back on the front lines with some other fancy equipment I decided to make for him. From then on he just had to deal with the minor inconvenience of being radomly attacked by questing knigts looking to take the grail from him!

Let's say you have 6 provinces between your home province and your front. Moving a commander to the next province will take 1 turn. The problem is that you can't order him to go to the front by one click and wait a few turns, no you'll have to move him manually 1 province EVERY turn! So you will have to give him 6 commands within 6 turns, 1/turn.
Imagine 3 castles scattered around your empire each 6 provinces away from your front producing units and want to support the frontline, then you will have to manually move 3 seperate commanders every turn. Resulting in giving 6*3=18 commands over a period of 6 turns, 3/turn for only 3 units (you have to locate them first by selecting the province), cumbersome and tedious.
There is no total number of units view of your provinces. You need to grab the nation's overview and sum up the sizes of armies in that province by yourself. Seriously? There is no way telling from the world map how many units are occupying that particular province while there is a depiction of the total number of units in enemy provinces, doesn't make sense.
The pictures representing the type of commanders in the nation's overview table are so small that it is almost impossible to distinguish them from eachother. Overall the interface is cluncky and there are nested menu's. The game doesn't discriminate between mages and commanders with high leadership but without magic abilities (they are both registered as commanders), thus no hotkeys for selecting idle specific commanders.
The game is similar to the board game RISK added with deep tactical combat. Economy and empire development are negligible. There is zero diplomacy (for SP). Combat is auto-resolving and totally hands off. Instead you will program your battleplan. You can chop up your army in different squads and got 3 general options for each squad; Formations (box, line etc), Battle order (attack, hold and attack, keep distance while firing etc) and Target (cavalry, rearmost enemies etc).
I never thought it was possible to have auto-resolving combat with deep tactical layers, dominions 4 shows it. Spreading dominion (=religion) in this game is equivalent to spreading your sphere of influence in 4x games. Dominion affects abilities and/or environments, like turning farmland into swamps. The singleplayer is a skirmish free for all battle where you goal is to capture all the thrones on the map. The game revolves around countering builds of your opponent and since the AI does a poor job at it, it is therefore more suitable for multiplayer.

Absolutely amazing. A must buy for all gamers. I can't recommend this enough.
It is very sleek and comfortable to hold.  It feels very solid, and the batteries give it a nice heft. Despite that I found I could use it for hours without fatigue, a welcome discovery indeed.
The buttons felt fine, just like any other controller really.  The bumpers are a little stiff for my liking, but it was only mildly irritating, and only noticeable in some games.  I did really like the triggers though, they felt very smooth, and the click at the end is very satisfying.
As for the learning curve everyone is complaining about; I found it to be quite quick. After a couple of hours of fumbling about I am almost as good in my games as with a keyboard and mouse,  my usually preferred method. So while it is undeniable different,  you will quickly get used to it.
Now for the big question: how does it do in actually controlling the game? Very good in fact. It does great in controller specific games, especially thanks to the paddles on the back that allow for easy access to frequently used functions like reloading. It also does aa good job in keyboard centric,  and even keyboard only games. CSGO and Binding of Isaacwere playable,  especially with the trackball mode for aiming. The remind able keys are also great.
I did have a couple issues with games recognizing it as both a keyboard and controller, and switching prompts unexpectedly, but it wasn't the end of the world.
Now for my favorite part: the happiness feedback.  Simply put,  it is incredible. In trackball mode I could swear to God there was an actual ball spinning under the touch pad. No more crazy vibrations; the Steam controller's haptic feedback blows everything else out of the water. I also really like the subtle clicks when simulating a mouse and keyboard. It's unnecessary, but really fun anyways.

Yes this is gonna be a lengthy review of how awesome it is. No I will not put a TL;DR thing.
I was looking for a free mmorpg to play on Steam...you know something different, and this game exceeded my expectations.
Graphics:
The graphics are downright gorgeous. They put care into the designing of costumes and the characters expressing emotions. Now I know graphics can't only make the game, but I have to applaud them for the details they put into characters and the buildings. They really captured the anime feel of this game.
Customization of Character:
There are many customization options to choose from: Gender, Hairstyle, Hair Color, Eye Color, Face Style, and Skin Color. Regret your decision in the future? No problem. They sell a kit to help you change that. There are various costumes out there that you can use to customize what your character wears. You get free ones by completing the main story quest, but the rest you will have to buy with real money or loyalty points(points you earn while playing the game). Basically, your armor does not change the appearance of your character. There are costume slots such as headgear, body, and back.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is more action style and not slow turned based. The stats are allocated differently. There are three attack stats and three defense stats. The three attack stats are DMG,Crit,and SPD. The three defense ones are HP,DEF,and EVA. Each level later on, you gain one attack and one defense stat. Depending on your class and weapon, you can attack while you're turned around and while running. Did I mention you can glide in the air? Well you can! Did I mention they give you a starting mount? Well you get one! Did I mention EIGHT different classes? I know...*faint*
One key feature of the game is the game gives you a companion to use alongside your journey, more like a permanent two-person party. You have the option to summon or dismiss it whenever you like. At least you're not playing alone!
Story:
Fantasy and anime. The story is awesome so far for fantasy lovers. I could go on, but I think it's for the best to see it yourself.
List of things to do:
There are a ton of things. Hidden quests, achievements, and more where you can get different titles to boost your stats, or add some character to your character.
Economy:
Surprisingly with bots out there, the economy maintains its composure to be fair.
Customer Service:
They may ask you repetitive questions, but overall their service is kind and quick.
Overall, this game is the next big thing. This can beat all the free-to-play mmorpgs out there.

"Linea, the Game" is a cheap, platform dodging game including 4 levels the get increasingly difficult and the only thing distracting you will be the urge to look at the clock. Each level is somewhat randomly generated and the quota for finishing a level is surviving for 60 seconds. While each replay of a level is random, each does contain patterns that constantly show up to allow you to learn through trail and error to pass as those are usually ones that causes a game over.
Despite the difficulty increase, each level is possible through constant replaying, and with this often comes the feelings of excitement as you pass your last high score/ beat the level, despair when you are 1 second away, or determination while playing.
It does not show that it is controller supported, but it is and I do recommend playing with a controller. It makes it easier and faster to dodge and doesn't wear on the fingers like playing with the keyboard does.
I also do recommend looking at the achievements, as one requires you to play the first level without doing the tutorial first (locking you out from the achievement if you play the tutorial first). The dev has added a launch option to reset by demand (however this resets everything in the process).
Overall, I recommend this game, but be warned this game is harder than it looks like and be ready to die a lot.

This game has serious problems.
It's a fairly straightforward 4X at its core, but this is buried under an utterly appalling user interface that obeys no conventions of any other game anywhere.
The game mechanics are difficult to learn and find good builds for, mostly because the information is buried. I can't just look up all the units and magic paths a given race has access to, to figure out how to play that race. I don't know how useful xyz spell is going to be because I don't know what other stuff is going to be in play. I have no idea, looking at a scouting report from some province, that 20 demon monkies are going to be no match for my 30 spear chuckers (or whatever).
All the tutorials I've seen for this game are step-by-step "you should build A then B then C", and the reasons are always "because after playing for 100 hours I discovered that if you don't have B then xyz kills you" or "because C is really good in the early game". It looks like not even people who've sunk hundreds of hours into this game can tell you how to evaluate different mechanisms and elements and use them to put together a strategy yourself - only to copy stuff that has already been proven to work and you just have to take it on faith.
The manual (which you're going to have to look elsewhere to download) opens with a tutorial that hand-holds you through the interface (fair) and then explains what a ****ing dice roll is. Nothing is laid out in a useful manner. It tries to be witty and fails. It's like reading bad board games instructions (read: nearly all board games instructions).
I'm not even holding the graphics against it. My favourite game is Dwarf Fortress. And when a Dwarf Fortress fanatic says your interface is garbage...
Simply put: don't waste your money and time.
Better games you might try:
If you have a spare 500 hours to spare just memorising reams of information just to be able to play the game, maybe try Falcon 4 (in which you learn how to fly an F-16, in sufficient detail that you could operate a real one). Or perhaps actually try start your own cult in real life.

Though the game is incredibly short (the READ ME option will tell you why) - it took me 90 minutes to complete the campaign and all the bonus levels - the gameplay feels smooth, and the whole thing seems replayable. Each level filled the hole in my mind which Portal left; the whole test chamber feel sinks back in. The physics is occasionally glitchy, but otherwise, it's almost always on point.
The game is based around being a hacker, invading systems and whatnot, but the only feel for this we ever feel is in one of the bonus levels, where you have to unlock three doors to allow yourself to finish. The format feels very portal-like too, and each level has its quirks and fun solutions.
My problems are only with the length of the game, though I am yet to attempt the multiplayer, and that there was not enough variety in solutions for each level. Some of the levels felt too short, whereas some of the bonus levels had ingenious puzzles which took me minutes to get my head around. Just more, more, more! A second Polarity, or a huge dlc for this one would be recieved well.

The Castle Doctrine is a creepy and unnerving exploration of the idea of home security and more specifically, the doctrine which it is named after.
You begin with 2000 dollars, a lovely wife, two beautiful children and a wide open empty home. You have a vault that you keep your money in. Everyone else around you lives in similar houses, with lovely wives and beautiful children of their own. They also started with 2000 dollars and a wide open and empty home.
Trouble is, 2000 dollars is not enough for anyone. They're going to come for your money soon enough. And if that's not enough, they'll come for your family and take anything your wife is holding onto for you. You're the man of the house. It's up to you to protect the things that matter to you. So you build a security system.
You dream up a complicated sequence of traps, with dogs, electrified floors, pits, cats, glass, switches, doors and tight mazes. Then you build it. Nobody can get to your vault now.
But you've forgotten that your family needs to be able to get out. You redesign your traps. Now your family can escape easily, but nobody can get to your vault.
But you've fogotten that you need to be able to get to your own vault, or it's all for nothing. You redesign your traps. Now only you know how to get to your vault and your family can escape.
But you've forgotten how much it costs. You have no money. But everyone around you has money. You enter their house. Just to take a look around. You can see their vault. Just there. It's so easy. Until you realize you've just walked into a trap someone else made. You die. So you start again, a new man, a new wife, new children. You redesign your traps. Now nobody can get to your vault but you, your family can escape and you have money.
But you've forgotten how clever your neighbors are. They break into your house while you're not home. They get to your vault, kill your family and leave you with nothing. Nothing. You kill yourself. You start again. A new man, a new wife, new children. New things to protect. You redesign your house.
Your traps have become your house. Your security system is as much a part of you as your own body. And now everyone else is just a sea of people you can rob.
This is The Castle Doctrine.
Emphatically, this is an artistic game. It has very little comrpomise between vision and accesability. There is no tutorial, there is no guide. There is nothing that stops people from building near-impenetrable home security systems. If you die, you die. There is no save game. You can't stash a design for later. For some, this may be a deal-breaker. For some, this might be just what you want.
The Castle Doctrine is eerie in every aspect. The pixelated faces of your wife and children as well as your own make everything seem almost like dolls, things, mere possessions to be guarded at all costs, rather than actual people. The low music that only plays during roberies reminds you that the only wrong-doing in this game comes from other players who are motivated by the cost of their own security to destroy yours. The entire conceptual idea of robbing another player and destroying everything they have worked for is frightening. More frightening is that the game relies on this happening to actually promote any gameplay. The fact that you never actually interact with other players (you can only rob players that aren't currently building their house, whether that means they are offline or out robbing others) adds to the isolationism of the game, where you start to think more and more about yourself and your own paranoid need to secure what you own, regardless of how high the cost may go and regardless of how many lives you need to destroy to make it so.
Superficially, The Castle Doctrine is kind of like a player-generated series of dungeon puzzles. This fact means that many of them are highly unfair and require inside-knowledge to beat conventionally. Fortunately, during a robbery, it doesn't just boil down to guess-work about how to get through a house. You can bring tools along to disarm traps or cut through things. Problem is that this costs money. So you must be thoughtful about your use of these tools.
But if you're buying The Castle Doctrine purely for its superficial reasons, you are not looking at the much more intense aspects of the game. The Castle Doctrine, despite its very minimalist and at times even clunky art style, delivers a huge amount of tension with its permanent death and sometimes even emotional terror as you realize what a monster the game turns you into. Of course, it also offers fascinating social points, from the obvious comments on security and home invasion, but also on less obvious issues, such as the role of the provider and protector as a man, but simultaneously also the threat and murderer to others. It places a huge weight on the shoulder of the player; you need to consider how much you want to protect your wife compared to your vault and you need to decide if you can live with shooting another man's wife, just for the money she's carrying.
Playing the game itself is kind of fascinating. The very same paranoid and crazy attitude that the game sets out to warn against is exactly what you need to play well. But the fact that you have to tap into that is key; it shows that there is only one way to succeed if security becomes a never-ending arms race like this.
The only downfall of the game, up until the point of my review, has been a steadily dropping player-base. But as of the latest updates, this has been remedied by adding in 100 "abandoned" houses: homes where the players left nothing in their vault. Squatters, having taken up residence, have left peculiar sets of items and belongings in the unused vault. Now, they are ripe for any player. Well, except for their security systems, which, despite having been outsmarted once, often still have a kick to them. With this update, a playerbase of roughly 50+ players has returned, which makes the game quite playable, once again.
I heartily recommend this game to anyone who likes puzzles, artistic games or very difficult games. Don't be too intimidated by the price tag; this game is quite playable for a long stretch of time.

edit; Well, okay, maybe I should write a bit more than a thumbs up and a silly situation in the game.
One thing that really strikes out in a 3d action game is when it starts up as a side scrolling shmup. There are also transitions to side scrolling platformer, topview action and bullet dodging here and there. It's kinda funny to see more than one genre in a game, and it all seems to go pretty seamless.
Game looks nice, and in the first portion of the game you'll see what generally gets thrown at you.
So... yeah, there's areal combat, in the form of a sidescroll shooter. When you exit the plane the close-combat fighting action starts. Ending with a giant goliath as boss.
After that the story really kicks in. And you wake up on a space station, have to reporting for your second mission where you'll get to explore earth a bit more, meet many machine lifeforms, and uhhh... talk to them? I mean, sure you could kick all their rusty metal asses, but apparently not all of them want to fight. There's plenty of quests to do here'n there.
With a nice upgrade, you can also kick back and catch some fish using your Pod.
And yes, you can die from eating a mackerel, apparently andriod bodies aren't human bodies. lol. I rather enjoy the numerous details in the game. Running like the wind, and stumbling over a rock or uneven surface. Also the mess some of the bots make from ancient civilisation. Even the music has some nice detail to it, fading out starts with the vocals when you're near exits of areas. The music also changes to an x-bit version when you initiate a hack.
When you defeat the Eve boss, the game goes to a credit roll, but when you continue from save, you start the story again from 9S's shoes instead of 2B.
This gives a different intro, starting from his position, and there's some added scenes from the minor bosses. Gives a nice addition to the story, and a good reason to continue on.
With 9S you get the hacking ability at the cost of heavy attacks. But you can take over enemies with it, so that's even better.
Again after Eve and a credit roll later, you can continue the game again, and now the story moves on to the next part; An all out war against the machines, storywise things become quite a bit darker. And enemies become a bit harder too.
Rather than just sticking to 1 protagonist for the rest of the game, you'll switch back and forth between them.
When you finish the game entirely, you get a chapter select and a few extra's.
There's also mutliple 'bad endings' to discover, which may make it worthwhile to revist the game.
Considering some negative reviews because of technical difficulties, I should probably add that I've had zero issues on my configuration; AMD hardware with Windows 7.
Kind of sucks it doesn't have a demo to give it a good testrun, so try it as soon as you buy it, and ask for a refund if you have too much issues.
