Summary:
NieR:Automata is a master peice. Solid combat gameplay is combined with a unique story telling in which the player themselves almost self-narrate the story by finding small explanations while playing. NieR:Automata's two strengths are: sexy characters and beautifully intricate story telling. The game is best enjoyed slow and methodically.
Bought for $80 CAD. Completely worth it. A2 pls marry me.
Automata is my first game in the NieR franchise and I have to admit, it does an unbelievable job in setting the tone of story. Not only are the plot twist subtle, they are also multilayered and only get deeper the more the player looks for them. Combat was deep and well designed. Not only can it cater to the biggest noob of the hack and slash, it leaves room for theory crafting, speed running/optimizing leveling, and even a super hardcore mode in which you die in one hit.
Gameplay:
[+]Attractive Character Design
I've never been so okay with staring at my character. Both from a admiring view and a perverted one. The design of the character is detailed and elegant. Although unrealistic, 2B and A2 easily will make you fall in love (not you 9S >:( ).
[+]Combat
Gameplay is very similar to God of War, Heavenly Sword, and Vindictus. The combat is very fluid and fun as you are able to interupt your moves with movement in most cases. Additionally, the dash mechanic keeps things fast paced and feels alot like how a megaman game would've played if it was 3D.
[+]Character Customization
The 'skill tree' equivalent in this game involves a data chip optimizing game. You can only carry so many chips on your motherboard, so pick wisely. UI and Skills are tied to the chips, so if you wanted to optimize your abilities, perhaps you would need to sacrifice your information display.
[+]Story
The last time I've had this type of attachment to a world's universe was FInal Fantasy 7 and Tales of Symphonia. Although I hate post apocalyptic worlds, NieR still retains enough of nature to make me love it. The ending makes me yearn to know how the characters eventually lived out their lives, and that to me is the mark of a memorable game.
[+]Optional Content
This game has so much optional content left for the player to discover. There are full sets of weapons which particular traits, as well as four weapon types(light, heavy, spear, and fists). There are cosmetics obtained through quests (my favorite being A2's long hair). There is a large portion of lore/story descriptions within items and other areas. Finally, you can also max all your chips, fight secret bosses, and discover all the endings.
[-]Repetitiveness
On harder modes, the game becomes a grind. You will mash the button until your fingers are sore. Boss mechanics in general are pretty much the same, only the context of the battle keeps it interesting (e.g. you are trying to get revenge, it is a 1v1 duel, etc.). Particularly one of the final bosses, where the game gets a little frustrating because there is no blocking projectiles and dodging is difficult from a over-the-shoulder 3rd person perspective.
[-]Auto save locations
There are a few moments in the game where the Autosave is very far from the boss you died on (in on instance I pretty much had to redo the whole stage). Although not a big deal, it is frustrating. Try not to die :).
[-]Hacking Mechanic
I appriciate and enjoy the addition of this mechanic as it's change of pace was unexpected, but the 'mini game' quickly got tedious and annoying. It's only redeeming factor is that it saves so much time if you are doing a speed run as you do a stupidly high amount of damage compared to standard hack and slash methods. If you are having difficulty with this, try a controller, the game is designed with that in mind anyways.
Technical:
[+]Great Port
During my whole play through, the game has never crashed. Only during one boss fight has the frames every dropped and I'm pretty sure that was for artistic effect.
[-]Controller Centered
The game was designed for a controller, although it is playable via keyboard/mouse, the game gets more difficult when the hacking mechanic is introduced.

- Able to play mouse/ keyboard only games on the couch
- More accurate than a standard joystick (use right trackpad to emulate a mouse with trackball mode turned on and gyro functionality enabled)
- Extremely customizable
- able to create more keybinds compared to other gamepads
- Not familiar
- takes a good amount of time to configure to your liking
- AXBY buttons are small and slightly far to reach
I think this controller is very unique. Its for anyone who's willing to take a step into the obscure. It is certainly different from any other controller. I personally enjoy it a lot.

I hear a lot of complaints in reviews from people on YouTube to sites like IGN where they use the controller expecting it to be like any other controller.  It's so disappointing to see people barely tinker with the settings and then come to the conclusion that they don't like it.  It will take some getting used to.
Something that many people are ignoring is the gyro.  This may not sound like anything incredible, but trust me, it makes this controller even more awesome.  FPS games are now much more comfortable to play because of the combination of the gyro and also the right touch pad.  Using the right touch pad for fast aiming and the gyro for small, precise aiming is so much better than being limited to an analog stick.
One of the greatest things about this controller is that EVERYTHING in it is customizable.  Seriously, if you don't like how the A button is used for jumping, go ahead and bind that to something else.  Haptic feedback annoying you? Disable it.  Want to make the right pad act as a mouse only when you're pressing a certain button?  Mode shifting.  Want to use gyro only when pressing the left trigger?  You can.
When launching some games in big picture, games like Borderlands 2 or Fallout 4 would have the launcher window before being able to play, making me have to use my mouse to hit 'Play' and then go back to my 360 controller.  With the Steam controller, I just use the right touchpad to move my mouse over the Play button and then press the right trigger to click; no need to use my mouse.  It's fantastic - this controller solves so many problems I had before.
I've heard some complaints that it feels cheap, but I don't really agree.  The only thing that feels cheap is the removable battery cover/plate, but even that isn't that bad.  The ABXY buttons aren't really clicky, they feel a bit more like the 360 buttons.
Now onto what I don't like, or things you should know before purchasing:
The left touchpad is just that - a left touchpad.  It's not going to be a replacement d-pad, you're better off using the left analogue stick for things like platformers.
Inserting the batteries requires a lot of pressure, making me feel like I'm going to break something.  The battery placement itself is fine, it's just actually inserting them that isn't really ideal.
It can be a little time consuming configuring the controls for some games, but thankfully community-made (and official) presets can save time.
If you're going to get this controller, make sure you give it time before you decide whether you like it or not.  It's definitely different from most controllers, so it'll take some getting used to.

This is the controller I've been waiting for years! Finally, it is possible to play strategy games from a comfortable couch. I'm loving every aspect of it:
- big trackpads
- awesome haptic feedback
- size
- handy buttons
- configuration
I actually started using it as my main windows input device for browsing the web, keyboard is rarely needed if you have your favorite sites saved.
THANKS VALVE

EDIT: Dominions 5 was announced a while back, and will be coming out in November. As much as I love this game, I would recommend waiting to buy that, since they added a lot of improvements to the game. It's basically gonna be a straight upgrade to Dominions 4.
In Dominions 4, you play a pretender god who has risen up to claim the spot of Pantokrator, after the last one dissapeared for reasons unknown. There are others however who wish to take that spot, and only whoever proves themselves the most worthy will take the place as the god above all gods!
Dominions 4 is a grand strategy game with a few interesting twists. First of all, you are a god, and as gods are, you need worship to survive and become the one true god! Second of all, unlike other grand strategy games, you don't give orders to troops directly during combat. You give them a set of orders and tactics to use when combat begins, as if you were commanding an actual army of troops. Finally, magic is a ever-present necessity in any age, and a great deal of magic requires the use of magic gems. Magic gems are an incredibly compressed form of magic, and even a single one can unleash a great deal of power to an experienced mage.
Pros:
+ Customizability allows for a variety of different playstyles for each nation.
+ 75 nations to play, if you count all three ages.
+ Has a modding community supported by the devs.
+ Has a great depth of strategy, coupled with a large library of spells to bolster any tactics you choose.
+ Great deal of replayability, since only a few nations are identical to each other, and the ones that are is intentional.
Cons:
- The learning curve is quite steep, but there's a manual to help on their website. It's about 100 pages long, but the vast majority is just listing artifacts and spells.
- Can get very tedious with alotting magic gems and artifacts to units each turn.
- Games tend to be very long, and on very large maps, a turn can take upwards of 15 minutes.
Verdict: The price is a bit high, but if you're a fan of the grand strategy genre, and want some fantasy to spice up your library, this is a great game!

It's not easy to get to rewarding part but it is one of the best game when you start to get the hang of it. If you like 4X or Strategy games with a lot of depth this is a game to try.
It may be unappealing at first due to the graphics and the UI that might not look very user friendly but the amount of keyboard shortcut makes it very easy to navigate through menus and such. There are numerous Let's Play and tutorials on Youtube to get a good idea of how to approach the game.
Reading the Manual would always be useful but I would only recommand to read the nations part so you can find a nation you would like to play:
Find The nation that represent best want you want to play. Then you can quickly search for a guide (or a let's play video) to have a rough idea of how the game works and then let's dive into this world and let the lore transport your imagination as your army conquers the world. Let your mage research more and more powerful spells or let them walk in your domain to find magic sites. Claim Thrones of ascension to gain more power and increase your Influence through the world.
This game has an insane amount of replayability, it get more and more fun the more you know how it works.
You can play Solo, multiplayer, Coop or PvP online or hotseat.
You can find a good community of players on different forums to find scheduled MP games, there are tons of mods (but the game without any mod is enough, it's not mandatory) adding new content, new nations or modifying the game to your liking.
To summarize:
+ Great Strategic Game with a lot of Depth.
+ Insane amount of Nations to play (Roughly 20+ nations per age, with 3 different ages).
+ Deep lore taking root in historical nations or existing myth and legends from different cultures.
+ High fantasy world, Elves, dwarves, undead, demons, humans, etc. pretty much everything you want is here.
+ You'll never get enough of the game and you'll always try new crazy fun strategies.
+ Random generated maps for more replayability.
- Graphics and animations reduced to the lowest minimum. That's not really a Problem I think but needs to be mentioned.
- Many keyboard shortcuts need to be learnt to really improve the quality of life. The game is So much easier to navigate and manipulate when you know them but it may take a bit of time.
- A lot of information to learn the game. But once done, only the best part remains. The sweetest bits awaits you.

Overall, this game has a lot of potential.  The concept is cool and unique, and is the reason I bought it.
But the execution of this game falls way short.
1.) The A.I. is horribly broken.  On the hardest difficulty, the computer spams moves from full screen, and rarely ever blocks.  If you can knock them down, which is fairly easy, you can attack them as they wake up, and knock them back down.  Repeat forever and win.  With no online multiplayer, this is the only way to play the game aside from local co-op, and it makes the game not fun whatsoever.
2.) Controls are laggy and unresponsive.  Fighting games thrive on good execution and balance to do well, and unfortunately this game doesn't live up.  There is a parry system, but it is difficult to pull of because of input lag.  If you perform a combo, it takes several seconds to show up on the screen.
3.) I am worried about copywrite infrigement.  Not the characters themselves, as they (I believe) fall under parody law, but the blatant rip of voices from movies starring said actors.  This isn't so much of a complaint, but just a general worry.
I hope this game receives some updates that fixes the glaring problems that it has.  I absolutely LOVE the concept, being a fan of kung fu movies, but this game is a broken unenjoyable mess.  I also understand that this was made by  an indy company with a limited budget, and a failed kickstarter, but that is no excuse to put out a broken game.

If you're like me, and couldn't care less about the achievements, you may find yourself thankful that you got the game on sale and only paid $0.19 for it. I'm one of those rare idiots who did everything he could to beat the opening area, defiant of the 'no-win' sccenario. Trust me, let yourself get beaten. The real game starts the moment you fail.

Some of the toughest ones are optional, but its a fair challenge throughout. A full run will cost you little more than 2 hours, but there is a lot of little things to stumble upon, and the game is worth playing through multiple times simply for the extra challenge, and the chance to see what you might've missed. On top of all this, there is an utterly lovely soundtrack with a great sound design over all.
Rare is it that brevity can be counted in a game's favor, but Out There Somewhere knew when to take its leave. There is plenty of optional stuff to mess with too mind you, but for the cost of a chicken sandwich you can experience a truly remarkable little gem. One of the few games I truly wish I could give more money to.

The best game in Orochi Saga makes a triumphant comeback. This time on Steam.
In short: if you loved the arcade game - you'll love this.
Longer:
This is an updated port of King of Fighters 98, with some added online functions. I am aware that the PS2 port was also an updated one, but I only played the arcade and this one, so the comparisons will be made between the two.
New:
* 10 more playable characters (Including Orochi officially playable for the first time)
* Several new stages and music, mostly lifted directly from KoF 96 / 97
* Rugal is not the only available boss. Now it's either Rugal, Orochi or Goenitz and the boss team before that also changes depending on this.
* New power gauge bar (Ultimate) in addition to old Advanced / Extra setup
* Customization options for  pixel graphics (original / blurred (smoothed))
* Online features
Some changes were made as well. These include:
* Different / new special moves for certain characters
* More characters have alternate form (by holding down the start button on the select character screen)
* The fighting is more fluid. Hit detection / counters / dodges were tweaked for greater balance.
___________________________________________________________
Overall - this is one of the best 2D fighting games currently available on Steam. And at a super fair price. Hundreds of hours of fun await me. Here I go!
Missing a bunch of features from the PS2 port, buy only if you played the pirated version of the original port.

I might not be able to speak for everyone else, but KoF '98, along with this update, is what got me more into fighting games. There's such a delightfully large variety among the cast of characters, whether it's ease of use, skill cap, playstyle, or personality that it's really hard to not like at least a couple of them. There are so many ways to fine-tune your playstyle and mess around with different options, e.g. ordering your characters in different ways or hand-picking the different Advanced or Extra options, that you can really find something that works for you or use stuff way differently than it was intended and still have fun. What's really important, however, is that the game doesn't present it all up-front so as to intimidate newer players. It's all pretty smoothly integrated into the regular gameplay, with the exception of typical fighting game shenanigans like memorizing special moves and such. The game is excellent at really making you feel comfortable with the mechanics and cast and really lets you experiment until you find something that fits you just right, and it's because of this that I recommend it to anyone who might be interested in fighting games. Simple enough and with a wide enough breadth of content on a surface level to draw anyone in, fighting game player or not, yet technically complex and demanding enough to keep veterans interested for a very long time.

Linea, the Game is a minimalistic dodging action game akin to Super Hexagon. The premise of the gameplay comes from a series of red bars that move towards your screen, normally in one of the 4 directional positions (up, down, left, right). The object of the game is to dodge these red bars and survive for as long as possible. (60 seconds minimum to progress to the next level.) The gameplay is supplemented with minimialistic white and gray backgrounds, and fast-paced chiptune music.
Each stage has its own music track, so repetitive plays on the same level can cause the music to grow stale. The patterns for which objects appear don't seem too varied, so they become easier to pick up as the stage is repeated.
The difficulty ramps up as you progress through stages; the first few levels are relatively drawn out, enabling an understanding of the mechanics of the game. Once the player reaches stages 3 and 4, the tempo and difficulty increases. There is also currently a DLC pack with 3 extra stages and a bonus coin collecting stage, also with increasing the difficulty from the last stage of the game.
Overall, I was able to complete the game in one sitting. Replayability seems low, as the stages don't seem to increase in difficulty regardless of time. Those that are quite fond of these types of games are likely to have short play times as well, while newer members might find a challenge with the later stages. I was able to pick up both the game and DLC for 2 dollars, and received 1.5 hours of play time.
Will recommend for the low price of the bundle coupled with the quality of the game.

Also important is that Steam has continued to improve the functionality of the controller with firmware updates.
Most importantly is the community bindings for games. I have had to create or tweak a couple of game control schemes, but the more people use the controller and make configurations, the less I have to do anything as it just works. Fallout 4 is a great example. Fired up the game, picked the community config that had the most users, and haven't looked at that screen again!
I highly recommend you try this controller out!

I don't see myself switching from m+kb for the majority of the games that I play, but for the others I now have this.
The ergonomics have room for improvement.
Steep learning curve. But this isn't a negative because this means that the controller is truly different.
Those who hate this controller like console controllers and have no reason to buy this controller. This controller is not targeted at you. Stop being so vitriolic.

Positives:
- While the touch pads take some getting used to, they have the potential to be very accurate; somewhere between mouse and joystick, similar to a trackball.
- The triggers are lovely, with dual stage analog pull with a button at the end.
- The paddles on the back are very convenient.
- Community controller profiles are fantastic and the ability to remap any of the buttons is exactly what
- Controller mouse input can be used outside of games and all over the desktop, which is very cool and was somewhat unexpected.
Negatives:
- After extended use, my thumb started to hurt from the shape of the controller, but I imagine this will get better with time.
- Comes with batteries but they don't recharge. Claimed 80 hour life, but you will need to replace them eventually. All things considered, this seems like a bit of an oversight to not have rechargable batteries.
- While you can boot games through Steam that aren't from Steam, I've been having trouble getting some games to recognize input (mainly the GOG version of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt)

I give it 4 out of 5 if I had a choice. One of the better one's I've played, alone or with others.
Pros:
Cute and Pretty - Even the "naked" Girl Costume has pretty pink panties.
Rewarding for No Effort (Instant Gratification)
Solo Story - While this game is NOT a Single-player game/RPG it's story is setup to read like one
Solo Play - While this game has certain events that are not preformable without a Team, these are limited to dailies and such for the most part.
Buffs on Multiple Levels - In this game you can buff yourself just by using your attacks, which is nice for me because I tend to forget to use my buffs in the first place otherwise. You can have a buff for example that heals and boosts attacks along with adds a stack of "buffing" channels (UI Has upto 2 unique meters for a buff per character/class from what i've seen)
Cons:
To be fair it's alittle *too easy* for a long time, and by the time things start getting challenging they start getting impossible ( bad habit of MMOs Right? ) An Example of this is: Until level 40ish the game is pretty quest driven and fast, but after 40 things open up to "challenge" the players skill, imo these were designed for a different game than the main storyline, because as soon as you get to the first sub-boss in one of these "hell" mode dungeons (which btw I was 20 levels too high for so it should've been a cinch) as a single char you can just barely heal enough to keep you alive without doing anything else - Definitely Calls for a party, much like other MMOs.
Also it can be alittle hard to work with a "Team of friends" early on, because alot of the Mainline Quest Instances are only solo-able, and CANNOT let a party in - if you try to go in as a group you each get split into your own instance - Which is pretty annoying and kinda confusing considering the map icons for your party members show up but their characters don't.
Also the channel system may be a little different than your used to, instead of having totally seperate "Channels" the Maps are linked as a party minimap icon whether your in the same channel or not. The good news is the game displays which channel they are on if you mouse-over a party members health bar - so tracking people down outside of instances shouldn't be too much of a problem.
Also Where are the @$#@ Dyes?! - I see all these menu's and tutorials referring to dying costumes but they don't seem to be anywhere, not even in the item mall.
Overall:
Cute & Easy & Mood = WIN.
Challenge & Players & Bugs = LOSE

Dominions is a difficult game to rate, in part because it is borderline impossible to fully experiance. With nearly 100 factions divided over 3 eras a player would have to play hundreds of games to get the complete experiance of the game. Additionally multiplayer matches are  long experiances. A turn a day turns into a turn a week. Eventually you can get a feel for the magic spells, the units, the complex interactions of the many special abilities. But even then there are countless magic sites, random events that can change strategies and open new oportunities, Dozen's of alternate starting configurations that can completely change the dynamic of the game and finally randomly generated maps just in case the 20 or so hand crafted ones are becoming repetitive.
What this creates is an enigmatic, and content rich game that gives the impression of being mechanically complex. Is it balanced? pff, I only have around 500 hours on it. I barely can make it to endgame. balance and metagaming is something that should be reserved once you master the basics. I don't even know if I am there yet. Maybe I am just bad at strategy, and maybe I overestimate the complexity. But hopefully my ramblings have helped you understand the game.

I'll start with the cons.
- Bad graphisms. Actually, the sprites are really nice, but since there's no animation at all, I have to admit that the game is not a delice to the eyes.
- Lots of text, and it's all in english. The first half of this con is actually not really a con since you can play the game perfectly well without reading most of it. Also, it could even be considered as a pro, since this text is often very poetic and inspiring - it's all about myths, cultures, and metaphysics. The second half of this con, obviously, is only a con if you're bad at english, which you're probably not if you're reading this.
- Very very complex game. Actually not a con, since it also means that there's a lot to learn and do before feeling like you know this game very well. However, be aware of the fact that you'll be pretty much lost about most of the game for a long time. You'll still be able to have a lot of fun with it.
- No music. There's one on the game menu, and it's nice, but since it's the only music in the game, you'll disable it very quickly.
And that's all. Yup, that's not much. I guarantee you one thing: if you don't mind too much these points and like turn-based strategy games and mythology, you'll definitely love this.
This game is a real treasure. A true independant game, made by two people alone, and yet extremely deep and interesting. I have more than 100 hours in the game at this time, and I still consider myself a beginner. There are something like 50 playable nations. Most of them have real gameplay differences (they're not copies with slight quirks like in Age of Empires for example), some of them even bending the rules of the game. All of them are very inspired and original.
You can play a lovecraftian nation, the roman empire, the UNDEAD roman empire, byzantium, the tuatha de danann of celtic mythology, the knights of the round table, giants of jewish and mesopotamian mythology, weird and creepy beings that live under the earth with psionic olms, a greek philosopher's kingdom, a greek philosopher's kingdom-that's-undead-and-doesn't-know-it, vampires, inquisitors, egyptian lizardmen, mermaids, at least three different kinds of vikings and their giants, zoroastrian angels, japanese demons, wise sentient monkeys, etc, etc, etc. And in each case, you customize your god (you) with an incredible number of possibilities.
The amount of content in this game is tremendous. Also, it is being updated very frequently and sometimes even receives new nations. All of this for free. Yup, no DLC at all. And it's heavily modable. And once you've tried everything in solo, you still have a whole new layer of strategy to discover with multiplayer games.
As /vg/ says, "it's an autist’s wet dream of a war game". Take it as a huge compliment.

Here it is!  My follow-up review is finally ready:
Video Transcript:
Hello viewers!  Welcome to a special episode of A Bird's Eye View.  My name is Endeavor, and today we are revisiting Kings of Kung Fu.  It's been six months since I first reviewed this game, and now that it's out of Early Access, let's see how it holds up.
The story mode in Kings of Kung Fu remains largely unchanged.  The player takes control of a stunt-person looking to become an action star.  A man named Red Ronin organizes a tournament that offers the winner that very opportunity.  All you have to do is defeat the other fighters.
The playable characters are all obvious parallels to real-life actors from martial arts movies.  The roster has expanded to include fourteen characters.  Both the 2.0 and 3.0 patches added characters to the roster for free.  This bodes well for future updates considering that the New Fighter Request post in the forums is the most active thread in the community.  The diversity of the playable characters remains a strong feature, although the options for playable female characters is still fairly limited.
If one was to make a list of this games best features, the atmosphere would clearly be at the top.  The stages are homages to iconic scenes and sets from various martial arts movies.  The bright and bold colors combine with music that ranges from funk to traditional to bring the player back to the golden age of kung fu flicks.  Everything is cheesy and over-the-top, and this game revels in it.
Gameplay may be a sticking point for people used to triple-A fighters.  There are four attack buttons, and every character has a list of combos that can be strung together.  Hit-detection isn't always spot-on, and it can take some time to really get a feel for controlling your character.  Since the days of Early Access, there have been numerous fixes and tweaks to the gameplay.  Jumping attacks are much smoother now than they were in December, but they do still feel a little cumbersome.
Controller support is included, but be warned that the controls were made with a D-pad in mind.  Players used to controllers with a joystick will have difficulties consistently doing quarter-circle attacks.  There was mention of a fix for this somewhere in the future, but this update is probably a ways off.
One major complaint that users have with Kings of Kung Fu is the lack of online multiplayer.  This feature was talked about during Early Access.  At some point in time, Jae Lee Productions realized they would not be able to deliver, and all plans to include it in the final product were scrapped.  They have since apologized and pledged to work harder than ever on adding more characters and stages.
One point I made in my last video praising Jae Lee Productions on their commitment to user feedback still stands.  Even after beta testing and months of Early Access, they are just as active as ever with their community.  The new fighters they've added for free were picked largely from suggestions by the players, and gameplay fixes are uploaded regularly.
Kings of Kung Fu officially released on June 25th.  After six months, I feel that I can still recommend this game.  Despite its rough edges, there is a genuinely enjoyable product here that shows a lot of heart and commitment.  The retail price is $9.99, although the game frequently goes on sale.  It's available on Steam for Windows, Mac, and Linux.
That concludes my follow-up review for Kings of Kung Fu.  I'd like to congratulate Jae Lee Productions for getting their game through Early Access.  And, of course, thank you for watching.  Don't forget to follow us on Twitter at Rookery Gamers for let's plays and additional reviews.

A plank is a piece of timber that is flat, elongated, and rectangular with parallel faces that are higher and longer than wide. Used primarily in carpentry, planks are critical in the construction of ships, houses, bridges, and many other structures.[1] Planks also serve as supports to form shelves and tables.
Usually made from sawed timber, planks are usually more than 1 1⁄2 in (38 mm) thick, and are generally wider than 2 1⁄2 in (64 mm). In the United States, planks can be any length and are generally a minimum of 2 in (51 mm) deep by 8 in (200 mm) wide, but planks that are 2 in (51 mm) by 10 in (250 mm) and 2 in (51 mm) by 12 in (300 mm) are more commonly stocked by lumber retailers. Planks are often used as a work surface on elevated scaffolding, and need to be wide enough to provide strength without breaking when walked on. The wood is categorized as a board if its width is less than 2 1⁄2 in (64 mm), and its thickness is less than 1 1⁄2 in (38 mm).

The controller is definitely new. At first, I didn't know that scrolling is actually a circular motion on the left trackpad, so if anyone is having trouble there, that's the answer.
There are a lot of things that I already like about it.

the smoothing of mouse movement that comes with the track pad,
a crap ton of programmable buttons,
the surprisingly satisfying clicks it makes when using a trackpad,
but there are some thing that annoy me.
The distance of the ABXY buttons. For me, this is quite a big reach. It's not uncomfortable, but it's not quite natural either.
And the fact that it's not chargable like a normal controller is a bit irritating, but this can be remidied with rechargable batteries. For those who don't know, this controller requires two AA batteries.
Other than that, this is a very lovely piece of hardware.
The box that it arrived in is not bad either.

Three points to make right off the bat:
1) Yes, this is better than a gamepad for K+M-oriented titles like FPS, strategy, action rpg, etc.
2) For skill-based titles (FPS), you're going to need to invest a significant amount of time tweaking the controller and getting used to it. It's a STEEP learning curve.
3) This is not a replacement for K+M, but rather an option for folks who want want to play PC titles on their couch that would have been best on K+M
I received the controller four days ago and am still getting used to it (I'd say I've dumped more than 10 hours into it). At first I agreed with all the editorial reviews you'll see -- it's some weird device caught in the middle of a controller and mouse. But after dumping more time into it and figuring out some key tweaks (USE THE GYRO FOR FPS GAMES!!!), I see what this controller can do. I truly believe I'll be competing with K+M players (non-pro of course) in a month or so.
On the negative side, it's a bit uncomfortable for my smallish hands. Both the joystick and trackpad make my thumbs hurt sometimes. Also, the community config system needs some work -- there needs to be an ability to rank up configs or sort them in some way. Overall, it's a good start and for those willing to make the investment and are caught on the couch with a PC, take the plunge. If I was at a desk, I'd stick to K+M of course.

It's definitely a unique experience. Weight, shape and size are balanced helping to make the controller feel comfortable to hold. The trackpad is smooth and fluid (once you get the hang of it). One thing I really enjoy about this controller is the fact you can use it easily on the desktop (without the annoying setup of a third party application)!! You can search the web and navigate through your PC with ease, which is nice. The rear triggers are also pretty handy as well, (Especially with the weird layout of the trackpad and YXAB buttons). The rear triggers really help (and are almost vital) when gaming.
NOTE: There is a bit of a learning curve to this controller. It wont be as simple as plugging it in and being the top score overall in COD multiplayer. There will be several hours in the beginning learning how to play each style of game.
There are a few gripes that I do have with this controller, however, but it doesn't exactly take away from the experience.
1. There is no 3.5mm audio jack on the controller, which is something I particularly liked about the Xbox One and Playstation 4 controllers.
2. Steam Big Picture Mode has to be running in order for the controller to work properly.
3. The layout of the bottons and trackpad are interesting and most definitely takes some getting used to. I would have prefered it more if the trackpad and YXAB buttons were swapped (More like the conventional controller we are all used to.
4. Lack of rumble feature. (No vibrations in-game).
Other than that, the controller is nice, setup was fast. typing with the controller is nice as well but, like most things about this controller, takes time to get to know.
I look forward to gaming with this controller some more.
I recommend this controller if you are looking for a unique WIRELESS gaming experience without the hassle of third party applications and setup.
Controller Rating: A- (For now)

I have played about 50 hours with the Steam controller and tried the following games:
- Resident Evil Revelations
- Tales of the Borderlands
- The Witcher 3
- Rocket League
- Divinity: Original Sin
Here are my findings:
+ Games that you played with a gamepad before will work well with the Steam controller, but...
- ... it will take quite some time to get used to the trackpad and the buttons
- I'm still unsure whether to keep my thumb on the trackpad all the time or to do seperate small thumb movements... both options seem to work and seperate thumb movements are good for finetuning the precision but by doing this your muscles will get tired very quickly
- compared to a PS4 or Xbox Controller the material, buttons, button clicks and basically everything else looks and feels rather cheap
- the biggest disappointment for me are the face buttons, which are strangely positioned. Getting from the trackpad to the A button (which is used most often imo) takes a really long time because the button is so far away... and chances are you will press another button instead because the buttons are so small. It gets better once you're used to it, and of course you could change the button layout but it's still a rather perplexing design decision to put the buttons under the pad and to the left instead of the usual top/right
- based on the games I played I can't recommend the Steam controller for games that rely heavily on precision and/or speed. It just takes too long to finetune your aim with the trackpad...

Disclaimer: My first 'proper' review of a game.
After completing the singleplayer with all collectibles, and as much as I would love to recommend this game, I just can't.
Don't get me wrong, the concept for this game is amazing and the potential is there if they want to expand on it.
It's just that for €11 you aren't getting what you paid for. The length of the game, even when getting all collectibles and completing all the bonus levels (apart from co-op) is just over an hour. I would definitely recommend this if you could get it for <€3, but any more is just not worth the €/hour value.
Now for the concept, the idea and potential in the game mechanics is great, but the execution is lacking. Quite a lot.
The game reminded me a lot of Q.U.B.E. mixed with Portal. The visuals are kinda similar to these two games, and the game mechanics for the 'puzzles' have some similarities to these two games. But they just fall short in the puzzle department.
After playing through the game it's more like a platformer/cubethrow than a real puzzle game. The only real puzzle element in this was finding the place to place/throw cubes at. After you found those it was all just platforming to the end of the level and onto the next one. Occasionally you would miss a collectible that you'd have to look for, but most of those you would come across regularly, or find when you would miss a jump.
There wasn't a single moment in the game where I had to think about what to do in the level beforehand, it was all just look for the cube and the platform to put it on to advance.
My final verdict for this game would be a 4/10.
I encountered too many random bugs for it to score any higher, from me clipping through platforms to my cube just randomly resetting when I was trying to use the launch pads.

I'm sorry people... It's not for me...
I LOVE EVERYTHING out of this game. Really everything. I love its depth. I love its clear gameplay. I love that you have to take care of thousands of things. I love the fact you play a Pretender god with its mighty armies, crushing the infidels. What can be more epic than this? Nothing. I love it's music. I love its lore. I love the races... I really love everything. Even the graphics are cool. Sounds aren't (it's a pain playing with War Elephants...)
This game has the potential to be the greatest and most famous Strategy Game in all times. But it won't be...
It won't be for a very simple reason the UI is absolutely terrible. Within all the 4X / Grand strategy games I've never seen something like this...
Imagine you're playing Hearts of Iron 2 or 3 for instance. I know they are RTS but still. Imagine now that you cannot pause more than once every In-game Day.
- make sure no one invaded any region
- make sure you are not attacked anywhere
- make sure no troop is missing supply
- make sure you're not running out of ressource
- make sure your planes are not nearly destroyed
- make sure no convoy is being attacked.
- make sure you're fully making your researches etc.
- make sure any other thing you make in HOI (thousands)
Can you imagine the nightmare it would be?
Why this comparison? In Hearts of Iron, you have thousands of things to think about. In order to make your life easier you are spammed by messages that you can carefully select on: to they pause game or not, is it shown in a separate square or just in the corner as a report.
It's EXACTLY the same thing in Dominion except that you are given very few information on what is happening. And every turn LOADS of things happen and you can't make a single mistake or you will be punished like hell.
And this is something I like. I like not having the right of missing something if I want to win.
I'll give you an example of my first game:
My empire is strong, well defended. No roaming armies. Strongholds near the bridges and mountain passes. Very cool.
I'm at war with my neightbore. I gather 3 strong armies and start a grand campaign in order to invade it's major cities.
And at one point. BHAM! A general has been killed by a spy. Army scatters. Enemy armies hunt them down and consolidate to counterattack my two other armies. And I lose...
OK COOOOOOL. Next time I'll provide spies to my armies.
2 hours of gameplay later. I gather 3 strong armies. Fully equiped heroes and my pretender God commanding another; Each army is followed by several spies. Not only their are followed by spies but equally spies are ahead in order to scout the territory.
On ONE SIGNLE F****G turn I forgot to move the spy along with the general and on that very specific turn, the general is killed by an enemy spy. Distructing my entire campaign...
This is starting to be annoying. Because, as I mentionned in the comment and uphere the tools you have in hand are extremely limited in comparison to what is asked to you.
It's really like playing Civilization (way less deep than Dominions) but with almost no help at all concerning the actions you are doing:
- auto movement for example is missing
- you can see a list of heroes but you can't quickly see their gear or assess the situation in which they are. There is visually and information-wise nothing at all that allows you to do this (and I don't want to hear "use F1")
By making those very simple things, the experience would clearly be enriched.
And some other things too that do not require any further development:
- use colors instead of flags to delimit each and every one empire. Sometimes flags are too similar. It's already an overwhelming game, why not making things more userfriendly?
I mean.. Is it on purpose or what? I have the impression developers in this game said during their brainstorming meetings "So you know what? No colors!! Let's put an additional flag on a already over-filled of pixels and information region (with fate, with armies, with temples, with threes etc) so that the player needs extra focus!!!!! It will a pain for him to conceptualize the size and borders of it's empire!!! Hahahahah"
- use something nicer to provide the player with a quick look on the map of where are the heroes. Make them pop-up more clearly for god sake!!! F1 screen is useless... You anyway need to go over every single of your Hero to see: where he is on the Campaign map, what is the situation around him, what he is doing and if he is doing the good thing etc.
Wouldn't it be better for example to use Sliders for heroes and leave the arrows on the screen so that you can assess all your orders and you can quickly see the stuff? "No no no no it would be too nice to provide this to the player."
These are very small examples on how exhausting this game can be on larger scales. So imagine you need every single turn to:
- go over about 20 to 40 events (battles, regional occupation, spells casted etc)
- go over every of your hero to see: is the gear ok? Are the troops situation ok? Where he is? Where are it's spy colleagues? Are the spies doing to good thing?
- go over every of your city to see: are the heroes summoning the good creatures? Are they researching? are they iddle? etc
- go over your entire map to see: any roaming army? am I losing fate?
- I created a new army: provide orders to the general, provide formation for every troop, provide a stance to every troop.
And about 20 other things.
And do this every turn.
And a single game is counted in several hundreds of turns.
Make a single mistale, forget to do one thing once and you're nearly screwed. Another example: for the 100'th time you gave all your armies the correct plannings for the battle, but once, you forgot to say to the general to stay behind the troops. Ooooops!! Too bad for you!!! The general went in suicide mission alone because you forgot to activate the correct stance.
And this kind of mistake will happen because, I don't know about you, but I'm NOT a VBA Macro. I'm a human being that will forget something...
There are too many things to do manually all the time. And all the time the same things you'll do a countless number of times just to conceptualize the empire situation. THAT IS NOT OK!!! Empire situation, as in any other game, should be clear at the FIRST sight... And only once the situation is assessed then the player can dig into the various possibilities at hand... It's NOT OK having to do the same things over and over just to understand what the situation is... Assessing the general situation should be effortless... But it's clearly not. So if such a basic thing is already requiring an effort since you don't see s**t on the map imagine the titanesque effort needed to assess the details...
To the developpers, make something to make life easier. Still as punishing, still the same number of things you need to think about, but make it less overwhelming. Provide standard Army templates a player can save and then use after creating an army / before a battle or like a reminder: "are you ok with your battle stance?"
Another hint: it's turn based but why not, like any other 4X, during enemy turn: show the armies moving? Show a spy has been spotted? This way the player would conceptualize more quickly the situation. No no no. You don't see s**t about anything and you just have to read a bible size report of everything that happened instead...
Again: no no no!!! such things would be too helpful or what????
Things like this and this game would redefine, without improving the graphics, the 4X genre...
And to potential buyers: this was my warning. If what I wrote doesn't really bother you and you're up to this incredible challenge, then you HAVE to buy this game and you'll end up with a real gem
A REAL GEM, belive me despite my thumb down

I thought this game was about spamming units, but I learned more.
Then, I thought this game was about powering up characters, but I learned more.
Then, I thought this game was about counter-attacks, but then I learned more.
Then, I thought this game was about resource management and building, but then I learned more.
Dominions is a deceptively straight-forward strategy game which is a unique pleasure.  It involves trying to conquer the world as a Pretender God by harnessing armies, unleashing terrible magics upon unbelievers, and drawing money, resources and gems from the Earth.  Tactically it involves positioning your armies and giving each unit orders, which is surprisingly satisfying.   It is quite easy to grasp, but has a depth of alternatives and so the complexity of the game arises in how you want to play it.  I'm a strategy nut and I've not played a game like this, it's a bit like Pokemon crossed with Chess crossed with Lord of the Rings, crossed with Religious Genocide.
In big games it gets ridiculously epic as you cast spells which upset the very basis of nature, bring plague and horrors from beyond the void into your enemies' homelands.  While dated, the graphics are actually really cool, and the sound track is fitting.
It's also the only game in which you can have this conversation seriously-
"How did you win that?"
"Magic".
Anyhoo, I'm off to make a tornado of corpses which eats the souls of all those it passes.

This game is a great simulator of Vietnam. It is unfair and unrewarding. It may be a great tool to show how much of a bad time Vietnam was, but it does not make for a good video game.
I am very upset to not recommend this game. Most of my play time was during the alpha and beta. I am very thankful that I was able to participate in the development process, but unfortunately the game did not mature as I'd hoped. Upon release I played a little bit but it wasn't much different from the pre-release versions other than running into fewer crashes and physics bugs. I took a couple months off for the developers to improve things. After seeing that the game was recently updated and PBS releasing a Vietnam documentary I was motivated to give it another shot. Not much has changed. The biggest issue I have is spawning, running for 10 seconds, then getting shot in the head. The screen goes black and then you start waiting to respawn. That may be what it is like to really be shot in the head but it is not very entertaining. You miss out on all the carnage. If you try to take things slow, you take things slow until you are either taken out by a camped enemy, or you see find and kill the camped enemy, only to be killed by another.
A big part of the game the developers are depending on is the squad based combat. RO2 and RS had squad based combat, but the entire 32 player team was divided into 4 squads. This game has multiple squads with a max of 6 players per squad. Previous games only needed to have 4-5 competent players to lead the rest of the team. They built this game expecting the entire team to coordinate and cooperate, which does not happen with public games. Players that take leadership roles are not qualified and that has a negative impact on the rest of the game.
The gunplay is very satisfying. It is rewarding to take down an enemy player. The sound effects are amazing. It is intense to be in the middle of an artillery barrage or suppressive enemy fire, until you are killed. If you have a lactose intolerance then avoid the game, because the voice acting is cheesy and uninspiring.
Overall it's not a terrible game, just not a great one like its predecessors. It has enough flaws to prevent me from getting immersed inside the combat, which is a problem when most of the game is build around being immersive. I would love to see a campaign mode added to the multilayer games to add more of a sense of urgency for victory. Tripwire is currently depending on the community to add meaningful content with modding contests so there is the possibility to get better. At this moment there are several other FPS games that are much better. RS2 does not stand above the competition at its current state.

Having been both a fan of Master of Orion (the first game of this genre I played) and anything Paradox crafts, discovering the design genius of Stellaris was easy. This game has the subtle ability to drain away the hours in a day, while you blissfully journey through the 'verse with your created race and civilization.
The Pro:
- Incredible variety of racial traits, types and polities enabling the crafting of anything you can dream up...and play.
- Powerful pulls to stay in the game, from exploration with reward, to discovering innovative technologies, to upgrading ships and finally improving any race in your empire.
- Multiple ways to set and acheive your victory besides just conquor.
- Easy interface
- Delightful story elements (at the beginning and mid game)
- Not a difficult learning curve, yet rewards veteran play with the ability to fine tune almost every aspect of your empire.
- Impressive fleet battles with impressive rendering of the universe and its systems, including many variables at set up.
- Ease at modding, and a huge community of mods in the workshop.
- Continued developer support with DLC and updates, as only Paradox can do so well.
The Con:
- Poor story elements at the late game (pretty much just the end game crisis and the fallen empires resurgent).
- For huge universe players with many civilizations, the time it takes to conquer the universe far out paces the technology tree (at least new technologies).
- Space Station power and development (looks like this will be fixed in an upcoming update).
- Familial bliss… if you find yourself unable to pull away.
I would definitely recommend this game to the serious strategy player, as the reward for those who constantly tweak, design, tinker with world development, and ever seek the path of perfection...Stellaris delivers!

I've been playing loads of games in my Steam library using the controller for the past month in early access and it has been an amazing experience. It works very well with FPS games which traditionally use controllers and I find that the right trackpad (which is used as a joystick) is much more precise than my Windows controller when aiming. The haptic feedback in the left and right trackpads can be adjusted and I personally prefer them on the highest settings, so that I can get the physical feedback that I would usually get from a physical joystick, but it's easily adjustable if you want different settings. One thing which has shocked me about the Steam controller is how incredibly well it works with keyboard and mouse games like Civilization V, Democracy 3 and FTL. The recommended configurations and the community configurations are all good and it's very easy to switch between them to find the best settings for each game and how you play it.
The customisability of the controller is brilliant and if you're willing to spend a bit of time playing with different settings, it'll be easy to find what works best for you and your play style. Personally, the best thing about the Steam controller is how much it has changed the way I play my games. Instead of playing on my relatively small laptop screen, I can now play on my TV from the comfort of my sofa. The price of the controller is high, but it's definitely worth every penny and I highly recommend purchasing this brilliant product.

First, I didn't really want to give this hardware a thumbs up or thumbs down, because it's really about what you need it to do. It's a good substitute for a mouse and mouse-based games when a mouse isn't convenient. It's a bad substitute for an actual controller and controller-based games.
In a scenario where you want to play something like Cities: Skylines from your couch, the Steam controller works well (not great, but well enough). The pads are responsive and feel smooth (similar to an Apple trackpad), and after a short time you'll be pretty acclimated to using the controller. That said, it is very hard to controller FPSs with the Steam controller and you'd be advised not to take this controller into any kind of online competitive scenario because even if it can simulate the function of a mouse it is still leagues behind the speed and accuracy of a mouse.
With games that are designed for a controller (e.g. Dark Souls, Rocket League, Assassin's Creed) the controller is simply inferior to a standard XBox and PS controller. The triggers and single analog stick feel fine, but almost all other inputs are better served by the more traditional controllers. The Steam controller's face buttons are small and, for me, uncomfortable to reach (they are pushed down and to the left to accommodate the large right thumbpad). The pseudo-D-pad is much harder to accurately select directions, because it's harder to feel the lightly indented "arrows" with your thumbs. And the right thumbpad is an inferior substitute for a right thumb stick simply because many games are designed around the input of an analog stick, not a trackpad.

As someone who has been playing MMORPG's for a while, let me just say that this game is different from most other MMORPG's I've played, including F2P ones, but it won't be for everyone. While I personally enjoyed it, it's a very niche game, although arguably one that could appeal to a wider audience than most other "anime MMO's."
Pros:
1. BEAUTIFUL graphics. Cel-shaded, looks just like an anime.
2. Not difficult at all. Can get very grindy at endgame, but casual players will have an easy time getting into it.
3. Loyalty points manage to avoid the dreaded 'pay to win' label, though IRL is obviously a faster way to get item mall stuff.
4. Very friendly playerbase.
5. Never seen any particularly bad bugs, though I'm sure they're out there.
6. Eidolons are awesome. They range from being adorable to downright scary-looking, and are the best take on pets I've seen since SWTOR's companion characters. They each have their own personalities, and some of the conversations are hilarious.
7. Kill-stealing and ninja-looting is virtually impossible, since anyone who hits a monster gets credit for the kill.
Cons:
1. If anything, it could be TOO easy. Hardcore players could scoff at the global cooldown being the only real way to prevent spamming skills, since there's no mana bar.
2. "Fortune packs" earned the nickname "scam packs" for a reason. The rate of getting a good item/costume from them are abysmally low.
3. Endgame is VERY grindy. Levels 1-40 is a breeze that you can literally do in one day, but it gets painfully grindy once you hit 55.
4. Bots are everywhere, and I mean EVERYWHERE. But at least they can't actively interfere with quests/monster-killing (see pro 7). Only the gold-spammers really get on my nerves.

And I thought the first Portal game was short...
○ While this does have some nice ideas and a few puzzles took me a while to figure out, it's way too short. I 100%ed (all collectibles and achievements) the whole singleplayer part of it in less than an hour and a half.
○ It's also pretty buggy, I managed to clip out of the map through a wall once without actively trying to do so.
○ The movement feels really tedious - you can get stuck on a 1 inch step and have to jump in order to traverse it. The collision detection of jumping platforms is a pain, too, among other things.
○ Then there's the thing with some of the puzzles... You know, in a puzzle game I like the idea to be "spend some time figuring out what you have to do, then do it" whereas here it's often "see what you have to do right away, then spend 5 minutes trying to pull it off with the dodgy physics system and clunky movement".
○ Some gameplay elements don't add anything to the challenge of the puzzle itself, they merely serve as a layer of hogwash that can foil your efforts at any point (I'm mostly talking about the moving lasers).
○ A couple times I didn't get any hints on newly introduced mechanics (e.g. rotatable jump pads or cube colour changing portals) so I wondered what the hell I'm supposed to do with a blue cube and red socket.
All in all it's not an awful game but if I had paid the full price for it I'd feel robbed. For the current price of 0.21€ though it'd be a shame not to give it a try.

My review is one that may be worth your time reading. The reason I say that is because I am not a massive Minecraft enthusiast nor am I someone that dislikes the game. I'm just an individual who loves playing games and reviewing them, if the games good i'll like it but if it is not I won't. Therefore my stance is completely unbiased going into this game. This is also my first experience with TellTale which is rather new for me. I will update my post when every new episode comes out.
EPISODE 1:
The game surprised me with its focus that was primarily on voice actors and cutscenes, Both of which were absolutely outstanding. The voice acting cast for this game was talented and the effort put into every line of dialogue was full of impact. Cut scenes were graphically impressive and held a consistent frame rate, I found the lack of gameplay to be surprising though. The gameplay was most comparable to The Order:1886, sometimes it only took for you to walk from one end of a hall way to another to finish your section and then proceed to watch another 5-10 minutes of cutscenes.
The game is mostly a point and click adventure with a bit of walking, making choices and clicking on things is all you do for the most part. The choice making is very much like Until Dawn in that what you say will effect the people around you and what you do will possibly change the whole scenario for the worse. This was incredibly effective and one of the first games ive ever played where I felt my choices actually mattered compared to games like Life Is Strange or Until Dawn where sometimes you would tell the charector to do one thing and then they'd end up doing the other anyway.
Overall as a game that played out as more of a rather interactive movie rather than a video game it was quite good. If you just want to sit back and enjoy yourself this is worth your money BUT I must address the one major con to the game that goes out of it's way to beat you over the head which was the button mashing (quick time events). The placing for quick time events were frequent but incredibly awkward which sometimes lead you to cheap deaths.
Instead of hitting, collecting and creating houses and forts to live in you just bashed the "Q" button and watched the players do it themselves which was a real head scratcher concidering the franchise. I almost feel that the term "Minecraft: Story Mode" was not appropriate for this game, just because it would have been better off as a spin off game (and gotten way much less hate)
Conclusion: Effective choices, Fun and graphically impressive cutscenes, a compelling story, AMAZING voice actors but absolutely awful choices were made in regards to quick time events and taking the core element of the original games gameplay entirely out of this experience.
Episode 2:
I've been reluctant to continue doing these reviews because an obnoxious young minority who haven't even played the game have been very persistant in knocking down anything good said about this title because it is seemingly different to what they expected. I am doing them though so people don't get misinformed.
This episode homed right in on character development and also introduced a few new notable plot points but overall didnt progress the story as much as it could've. Once again the game runs beautifully and the voice acting is outstanding. This game reeled in some of the best voice actors in the industry and the pay off was brilliant. Props going mostly to the voice of Petra. Petra has one of the most unique and well fitted voices I've seen in a long time.
Besides the again suprisingly thorough choices and consequences aswell as bright, impressive visuals, this episode didn''t have as much to offer. Combat and interaction with the WASD keys were less frequent and there was alot of watching going on. This would have been more okay if the episode wasn't so alarmingly and quickly cut off (it was very short).
The times that you were constructing or in combat were really fun and I had a blast going through quick time events or hitting enemies when the time came around, but the game did a good job of leaving you wanting more.
Overall: This episode wasn't great but it certaintly wasn't bad. A short and quick run through some fresh ideas aswell as running/playing smoothly in the process.
Episode 3:
Wow, the devs certainly listened to the only lukewarm reviews for the second episode. The sophomore ep was not bad but it was a little short and the interact ability was way less frequent than in the previous episode. This episode is by far the best out of the three, being the most juicy, most exiting, most interactable and most enticing of all.
The pacing and story was executed far better than the previous 2 episodes and most episodes from any episodic game. Being longer than the second episode and just the right size, Episode 3 was capable of establishing a GREAT opening sequence, character development (LOTS OF CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT :D), a solid climax, an unexpected plot twist and a satisfying yet nail biting ending.
.
Every already introduced character had their chance at one point or another to teach you as a player a large amount about them. Their intentions, the way they think and what there is to know about them. The game left more scenarios where you could just talk to the characters not for plot progession but just for a little more insight on the individual. This made the game feel far more real and made you want to do something to help these people because you care about them. The dialogue was written exceptionally well ( more so than previous episodes ) having the characters react the way an actual person would given the situation.
The gameplay was great also, the actual gameplay has been the only seriously problematic weak link of the "Minecraft: Story Mode". Luckily, this issue has been fixed with this episode was exiting to play more so than a lot of other games I have even played this year. Using the mechanics they have established since episode 1 and using them in such an effective manner you may even want to play this episode twice in one sitting.
The story was INCREDIBLE. What they have created within this Minecraft world and what they have implemented that was already existing from the Minecraft world is mind boggling. The plot went upwards 150% in this episodes and you feel like you got every cent of your moneys worth for 5 episodes in this 1 episode alone. The only irritating part about the story is that they spent a little too long focusing on the Enderman and that broke the pacing/exitment a little as it wasn't very interesting. Oh, and again I will stress HOW AWESOME THE VOICE ACTING IS OMAGERSH IT IS AWESOME.
Overall: If you were on the fence about buying this game THIS should completely intrigue you into getting it. This was amazing.

TellTale games is well and truly into the rythm of combining puzzles + story + combat affectively. The conclusion is  box office, smash hit levels of well written and well executed.
The story is woven together so greatly that it almost feels like a waste that this wasn't saved for the MINECRAFT movie, because with a script like this, a Minecraft movie wouldn't be a bad idea at all. Very poor puzzle game with a lot of bugs, and gameplay that is likely to be more frustrating than calming.
While it looks quite nice, and the game plays fairly intuitively with just needing to place tiles adjacent to each other based on either the colour or shape, beyond that things break down quite quickly. Firstly the bugs while not gamebreaking are annoying - use the wind ability twice too quickly to remove two tiles and it messes up the tiles in your hand so you can't tell what they are. Also if you give up and retry a level before completing it, some of the tiles will not reload properly on your second attempt. Menu buttons sometimes can only be clicked from somewhere above/below the button. And so on.
More critically though is the frustrations of the gameplay itself - in the early (Spring) levels you have 4 shapes and 4 colours and to get three stars on the level you need at least one of each, this increases to 5/4 in Summer, 5/5 in Autumn and finally six of each in Winter. In the smaller Winter levels you will miss at least 1 of the colours or shapes more than half the time, meaning no matter how well you play you never had a chance of getting three stars in the first place. So as you progress the game increasing seems to become more a matter of waiting for the RNG to let you win.
Even the larger levels where there are plenty of tiles to place and getting all the colours and shapes down isn't an issue, the later levels are heavily interlinked meaning you will need (at best) one of two tile types to join things up again, in Spring this is 2/16 possibilities and given you have 6 to choose from isn't too bad odds. By winter it is down to 2/36 possibilities, so no surprise you get stuck a lot - while the ones that form one big loop aren't too bad, there are levels with four branches that will need just the right tile to merge things back together in each branch.

Finished 3/4 of the levels with 3 stars.  Gave up out of frustration.  This game can be closest described as a form of solitaire.  Some "hands" are unwinnable and impossible to get 3 stars.  If you need a blue tile and never get one, you can't get 3 stars.  Simple and frustrating as that.  First 40 levels are too easy.  Then it turns into frustration and unwinnable (3-star) games.

It could have been a good game... BUT. There's many bugs. And the 3 stars system is stupid, especially at the last season because you need to use 1 color and 1 shape of each avalable. And they are random. So you need more luck than brain...

This game appears to be attempting to be relaxing; yet it does not succeed in this, in my opion.  There is considerable focus on scoring, and as the seasons progress your score becomes much more dependant on luck than skill.  It gets increasingly frustrating, as you are denied the three-star score for either failing to use one of each colour and shape to fill the grid, or for getting stuck at any point.  This would be tolerable if it were actually always possible to 'win'.  It is not - you can fill the grid without ever being offered a shape / colour that you need.  The massive ramp up in probability of failure in Winter is especially frustrating.
This game feels at odds with itself.  If it wishes to be relaxing, it should drop the score and the achievements (and put something in their place, as the game feels a little empty as it is).  If it wants to be a puzzle game, it should eliminate the luck component.

This game is a great simulator of Vietnam. It is unfair and unrewarding. It may be a great tool to show how much of a bad time Vietnam was, but it does not make for a good video game.
I am very upset to not recommend this game. Most of my play time was during the alpha and beta. I am very thankful that I was able to participate in the development process, but unfortunately the game did not mature as I'd hoped. Upon release I played a little bit but it wasn't much different from the pre-release versions other than running into fewer crashes and physics bugs. I took a couple months off for the developers to improve things. After seeing that the game was recently updated and PBS releasing a Vietnam documentary I was motivated to give it another shot. Not much has changed. The biggest issue I have is spawning, running for 10 seconds, then getting shot in the head. The screen goes black and then you start waiting to respawn. That may be what it is like to really be shot in the head but it is not very entertaining. You miss out on all the carnage. If you try to take things slow, you take things slow until you are either taken out by a camped enemy, or you see find and kill the camped enemy, only to be killed by another.
A big part of the game the developers are depending on is the squad based combat. RO2 and RS had squad based combat, but the entire 32 player team was divided into 4 squads. This game has multiple squads with a max of 6 players per squad. Previous games only needed to have 4-5 competent players to lead the rest of the team. They built this game expecting the entire team to coordinate and cooperate, which does not happen with public games. Players that take leadership roles are not qualified and that has a negative impact on the rest of the game.
The gunplay is very satisfying. It is rewarding to take down an enemy player. The sound effects are amazing. It is intense to be in the middle of an artillery barrage or suppressive enemy fire, until you are killed. If you have a lactose intolerance then avoid the game, because the voice acting is cheesy and uninspiring.
Overall it's not a terrible game, just not a great one like its predecessors. It has enough flaws to prevent me from getting immersed inside the combat, which is a problem when most of the game is build around being immersive. I would love to see a campaign mode added to the multilayer games to add more of a sense of urgency for victory. Tripwire is currently depending on the community to add meaningful content with modding contests so there is the possibility to get better. At this moment there are several other FPS games that are much better. RS2 does not stand above the competition at its current state.

This is the final rendition of one of the best 2D fighting games of all time. The balance has been re-tweeked, several characters have been added and now there is online play (welcome to 2005).
The graphics are certainly of the nostalgic variety; if you enjoy the old school sprites of yesteryear, you will feel right at home. If you aren't a fan of that retro look, the game still moves and plays silky smooth and decently quick.
A gamepad is a minimum requirement for this game, so if you don't already have one, that extra investment is to be considered. To truly experience this game to its full potential, I strongly suggest purchasing a fightstick. This game is fully playable with a keyboard, and some actually do, but it is not recommended.
Now let's talk a bit about the online. Quite frankly, the online in this game is acceptable. I know several people lombast it, but compared to other fighting games, it certainly isn't bad. That said, I come from the old arcade culture, and I have yet to play a single fighting game online that is acceptable to me. I simply cannot abide by ANY level of input delay. I am very greatful for this game's input delay display (available in the beta version) so I at least know exactly how psychic I am going to have to be, or how early I need to prompt my inputs.
If you are a fan of fighting games, especially if you have other friends whom are as well, this game is a must buy. It, like all other fighters, excels when there are others to play with in the same room. If you are a fan of the series and are dying to find others who are of a like mind, at least the option to play online is there, and it's certainly not the worst.

Ratings:
If you are a fighting game fan: 9/10
+Tons of characters
+"Spot on", very tight gameplay
+Good balance
+Retro graphics that hearken to a better time
+One of the best and most varied soundtracks of any fighting game
If you are apathetic toward fighting games: 7/10
+Tons of  varied characters to learn
+Smooth, fast paced fighting
+/- Retro graphics, love 'em or leave 'em
+/- Retro music. Great compositions hampered by archaic sampling/synth, unless that's your bag!
- Keyboard playable, but not the optimal input device. Additional expenditures to be considered
-Couch VS play the only way to really get everything out of this game
