I've played a bit more than Steam says I have because I played before it came to steam.
Anyway, I've spent countless hours playing P2P MMORPGs over the last few years. I've played everything from Star Wars Galaxies, Everquest, Star Wars: The Old Republic, to the Elder Scrolls Online. One of the biggest parts of playing a game such as an RPG is the story and immersion, as well as fluidity. Aura KIngdom does a great job at both of these.
The game tells some interesting stories if you care to pay attention to them (there is a "Skip" option for dialogues). If you don't, you can still pick up some of what's going on around you. While most quests are "Kill X of Y and return to me," there is still meaning to what you're doing.
The second thing I mentioned was fluidity. Aura Kingdom is very simple and polished. It didn't take long to pick up on the game and it's concepts. Within a few days, I was able to explain the game to newer players like I was a vet.
Overall, it's a very good game; and it's free to play! There are countless hours you can get out of it, and it's worth your time. I've used it as a great escape from large, P2P MMOs and still play it today!

Linea is a simple, challenging and well-made game.
The objective is to avoid obstacles on your endless fall through each level. You beat a level by surviving 60 seconds, which might sound easy, but it's not.
Unlike a few other "falling" games, you can't freely roam around anywhere you want avoiding obstacles. You use the arrow keys (or WASD) to move in a direction, and as soon as you let go, you're centered.
There are 4 levels to play through, each increasingly difficult, and each with their own obstacles and music.
Speaking of the music, it's one of the best parts of the game in my opinion. I really love jamming to it, and thank goodness it doesn't restart every single time you die, or else you'd be listening to the same bit over and over again.
Although the controls might take a bit of time to get used to, when you get the hang of it and finally complete a level, you feel really good about yourself.
Overall, the game doesn't have an insane amount of variety to provide, and it's very simple, but I can see it as a fun little game to play every now and again. The replayability is decent considering the levels are more or less randomly generated, and the game is quite cheap. Most importantly, it's fun!

I've waited a long time for this glorious moment, but finally the arcade hit fighting game classic The King Of Fighters 1998 is here, with the latest arcade update - Ultimate Match Final Edition.
Honestly, this is pretty much good as fighting games get. Initially this game had a really rough day 1, with issues such as frame rate drops/frame skipping, unbearable online play and a bunch of other problems. However since I got to play the public beta version for an upcoming patch to the game, most of those problems have been addressed and I'm pretty satisifed with this game.
Also don't listen to those players crying about the lack of superficial features from the PS2 version of the game like 3D Backgrounds, Arrange Soundtracks, etc. They aren't required to enjoy the game where it matters most - the gameplay.  Most of the 3D backgrounds looked awful anyways, and while the Arrange Soundtrack is really good, I'm sure there will be a way to mod the music in the game anyways as with most PC titles.
If your first time playing The King Of Fighters series was XIII, you are in for a wild ride. This game is way different, everything hurts alot more, normals and anti-airs are much stronger, characters and movelists are far more diverse, and the action is very faced paced and unforgiving! Truly this game is one of the finest 2D fighting game classics out there, and you can even play the original '98 in all it's glory.
Last but not least, Eiji Kisaragi is the greatest. So glad to play with him again. He's a real beastly character.

Dominions 4 is last in a quartet of games curiously mixing the board game sensibilities of Risk with the epic high fantasy of spell slinging games like Heroes of Might and Magic. Players are tasked with leading one of the game's many, many factions to victory in a couple of different game modes that all boil down to "defeat all enemies and paint the map your colour".
In this way the game, like Risk, is very simple. You take over and occupy provinces that you can use to generate soldiers to build into armies. Contrary to Risk however, fights are not won with static dice, but through simulations where fights between armies plays out based on unit composition, mages on the battlefield, or the positioning of the soldiers, all available to the player to organize. After a simulation starts, players lose control of the army, and it follows any instructions its components are given. This takes some getting used to, but emphasises the planning phase of wargames that has taken a backseat to directly controlled combat popularized in the current climate of hard and fast macro oriented games, even among non turn based grand strategy titles like contemporary Total Wars or the crop of RTS available that follows the entertaining-to-watch format of Starcraft 2.
Nothing wrong with such energetic gamestyles! Variety is the spice of life, and Dominion's spice is old and venerable, slow paced and strategic to the hard and fast tactics above. Be advised though, if you are looking to command the armies in person, Dominions would fail you.
Where it will not fail however is in the lore department. As mentioned previously the game sports what many dare call the most varied set of people and factions available in any strategy game in existance! Dominions 4 sports a cast made up of mostly unaltered figures (gameifies of course, and some original faces are brought to bear) and beings stemming from the imaginative real world mythologies around the globe. This makes factions varied and plentiful, further exasperated by the sheer ammount of optional but plentiful information that has been appropriated from myth to everything from individual characters to unit types, or the factions themselves.
These factions are organized into three separated time periods, chosable at the beginning of game-setup that serves the dual purpose of varying each game in terms of playstyles and factions available, and also -cleverly enough- as the game's meta plot. The three eras are separated so as to allow for the passing of time to be implied to take place between them, meaning that descriptions of factions found in the lore, will change between eras.
Some factions will change over time, radically in some cases. Others will split or dissapear completely, being present perhaps only at the dawn of the game's timeline or emerging later on only to get snuffed out, during implied conflicts (IE the games you play!) or from internal strife. Others still remain intact from the passing of time, with blurb describing how they made it through each eras rather than how it all crumbled underneath them. It feels truly epic to read about the factions and see how they change or gets destroyed, and overall this ominous method of story telling, while as passive as the game's combat, is really what makes you fall in love with the game. It is truly unique and really does make it feel as if you are part of a vast, age long struggle between ancient civilizations and their even older gods.
You are one such god. Did i mention that?
You are represented in game by a fully customizeble borderline-divine being looking to step it up a notch and assume the right of rule over all of creation. Power is excerted through the titular "dominion" translated to domain power, spread by your followers and priests, but you can also participate (still in a non-controllable fashion) in combat as a force of nature (think movie-Sauron) a tempestuous mage, or a benevolent buffer. As with the factions, godly archetypes are taken from authentic myths both in terms of gameified kit and in game lore, and you can play both as great beasts or ambitious wizards to more conventional divinities, all of which further diversifying the way you play your faction.
Games such as this, with cluncky UIs and crappy graphics are perfect for "making your own fun" or creating interesting story threads (think Crusader Kings II or Dwarf Fortress!). And given the amount of lore and the underlying ominous note to your excursions into it, Dominions 4 tickles the imagination and succeeds in providing the fantasy of world shaking struggle between pretender gods!

Seeing this game has come out of Early Access I gave it another try just to find out none of the things I've mentioned in my original review below have been worked on. Sad to say that this remains a thumbs-down and I'm afraid it'll stay like that. Bummer.
Definitely has something going for it. Though graphics aren't state-of-the-art, I very much like the overall style the game tries to get across. Film grain, flickering, filmstrip frames, fitting background music and
from martial arts cinema (though no real names), each with their own fighting style. There's not much bells and whistles gameplay-wise and I like that simplicity. Directional controls and only left punch, right punch, left kick and right kick; that's it.
The user interface also looks dated but works, so I don't really care much.
What keeps me from giving this the thumbs-up is the overall gameplay itself: Controls are really bad (at least with a Xbox 360 controller, didn't bother playing with a keyboard) and oftentimes your character ends up doing things you didn't expect, e.g. dashing back or jumping instead of doing a ↓+←. Some combos often do not register or you need very weird timing to execute them and some simply do not work. Also, grabbing your opponent only works if you stand still. Why?
In addition, hitboxes and hit registration are really bad and need work. I understand that Ron Jones is huge and has long legs and what not. But receiving a kick in your face whilst there's at least a 1 m gap between foot and face isn't funny.
So in summary, I really want this to be good, it already provides some fun and has great style but the gameplay and controls are imho badly broken. For a fighting game this is fundamental. I hope this gets fixed.
If you don't care about the technical issues, get it while it's on sale. Still a bargain.

Stellaris is probably one of the best space 4x games out there, and manages to get the grand strategy feel of other Paradox games. You get to customize your own space-faring civilzation, allowing you to take control of the narrative of a sci-fi species looking to find (or make) its place in the galaxy.
You can genocide an entire species of starfish. 100/10, best space game. (God is a SERB, not a bloody starfish.)
As a 4x game, Stellaris succeeds on all fronts, despite a few holes that are in need of repair.

At the time of writing, Stellaris is the youngest of Paradox's grand strategy lineup, and that certainly shows. But what I commend it for is potential, creativity, and uniqueness. Stellaris takes full advantage of the galatic and futuristic setting to throw off the reigns of history that, in my opinion, have dragged back other games by this studio. It's a breath of fresh air in a cast of mostly militaristically focused games that equate history with war to see a game give peace a chance. Stellaris is truly flexible in that both militarists and pacifists will find a way to enjoy their adventures through the galaxy, destroying enemies under your imperial foot, or sharing the light of liberty with friends. Though many mechanics are still simple and in need of redesign and improvment. Combine this with a beautiful aesthetic and understandable UI, plus extroardinary soundtracks and creative modding communities, with many updates planned in the future, and Stellars is a truly cosmopolitan experience.

It's possible. Want to rule over alien planets and civilizations? You can do that. Want to create a lasting Federation to rid the galaxy of cruelty? Of course you can.

I love this game. I’m a sucker for art and story. And this game gave me both. But all started with some logic…
First challenge I have passed stroke me like a lightning!  I enjoyed a beautiful area design, but most importantly, I have noticed that objects do not just hang around in the places disconnected, apart from the surroundings. Whereas all of the games with hidden objects I have seen before would just place them everywhere, where they could not get in real life (that could be just my poor luck). That was always♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, to be frankly. You’d see a location that looks more like a disposal dump. You can’t just design a level and then spoil everything with poor thinking on where to place the quest objects. But, in this game objects coexist in harmony with the “rooms” they are in (most of the time). So you can enjoy beautiful design of every location and logic for placing the objects. You can even think of a short story of how they got there and why. But don’t think for too long, cause the clock is ticking.
Some people have complained that the objects are not well hidden. Well, they clearly didn't go far in the game.
ART. If you like art and putting up together puzzles, you might just like this game. With progress collecting all the pieces for a puzzle becomes more difficult. As a lazy person I don’t like that at all! But I can endure all the pain for the sake of art.
STORY. The story gets more and more interesting the further you progress. Some of the story turns could be a bit of a cliché. But such is the time we live in, difficult to invent something absolutely new. All and all this is a free game. Also, there are a lot of fun side quests and challenges, where you have to rely on your friends (which is not so fun, because some friends may disappoint you).  Some challenges can really go under your skin and test you. The game will try to make you feel despair and desire to spend some money on it. After all, the developers need to eat too. But you CAN  progress without paying real money. I do. Just have to be patient and give a second thought before you waste anything that you’ve gathered. Even better if you set up a plan. Remember, patience’s the main lesson of the Puppeteer ;P
With friends the progress will go much faster. Well, I say much faster because I was playing this game on VK without friends until I reached 32 level, but still was one step behind the Second Season. And that took me 2-3 years! XD With friends it didn’t take so long for me to repeat and beat my personal record.
All and all, I do recommend this game. At least you can try and find out if it suits you. I am not a fan of casual games. But this one feels deeply mine.

After 100% completing the single-player campaign (including the bonus levels) I do not recommend this game and here's why.
-The puzzle designs are lazy and linear. I wouldn't even classify them as puzzles as they don't really get you thinking.
-Even though the main mechanic of the game is that you can change your polarity, you suprisngly don't use it that often.
Not as often as you should. It felt like most of the puzzles used the cubes more than the core mechanic, and that got
boring fast.
-Cubes. The physics weren't the best and elevators were the worst. Rising platforms (Elevators) would have a circle pad
in the middle to put a cube on to raise the platform. However if you fell off the platform you could not get the cube
off, so you'd have to go back to the beginning and reset the cube back to it's orginal position, and like I said before
since the puzzles revolved around them you would have to do whole entire levels again just because you fell.
-At first I thought the data crytals were supposed to be secret, optional objects you would find in levels. But the hiding
places are so stupid. On one level there's a data crytal in a corner not being blocked by anything, just out in the open.
Another level has two of them next to each other. Because of how poorly they are hidden and that the last level requires
you to find all of them, I don't think they are optional.
-The story doesn't make sense. You're a hacker hired by a hacking company. What does that have to do with puzzles?
Does the game take place in a computer? It doesn't explain.
-At the beginning they explain some of the mechanics but later on whenever they introduce a new object they don't
bother explaining what it does. So good luck trying to find out what to do with a green laser field or a circle ramp.
-If you thought Portal 1 was short, wait till you play this. I beat all the levels and got all the data
crystals in less than 2 hours.
And it's sad because the game had so much potenial. The graphics were nice and the polarity mechanic was promising.
Really, all I have to say about this game is that it is lazy. I give it a 4/10.

Nier: Automata was on my wishlist since its announcement and I was hoping that the price would eventually drop so I could justify buying it. Personally I think that it is a cult classic and
and people will hate me for saying so but I think that most people on Steam are missing the point. Plenty of triple A games require external patching or modding in order to be 'worth' their asking price. Take Skyrim for example. On its own, it released as a mostly boring, very old looking and buggy mess (and still is). Take into account community mods that transform it into a brilliant, stable and beautiful 4K experience. Why is it so terrible that Nier:Automata requires a little bit of similar third-party love in the way of patching? Skyrim was once €60, and Skyrim devs also released DLC before patching some of the inital massive bugs, so why all the hate here? Plenty of other games that get fantastic reviews have needed similar patches, but people just like to jump on the bandwagon of bashing Square Enix any chance they get, despite publishers like Bethestda releasing far more buggy and easily exploitable messes *cough* Oblivion/Skyrim's crafting system *cough*.
Anyway in my opinion Nier: Automata has almost everything I wanted it to have. It has a huge amount of replay value and basically needs to be finished 3 times in order for you to get the full story. It has tons of side quests and little tasks to accomplish. It runs beautifully on my hardware and I don't get any slowdowns or lag at all. Controller support is fantastic and controls are responsive. I love the voice acting, and surprisingly even the English voicing is outstanding. As for the OST, it is something that I will probably listen to for years to come as there are well over 100 music tracks in the full OST due to multiple variations of each song which is also goes into how well the pacing fits the game. Like all Square Enix / Final Fantasy typed games the story is a little cliché but if that is a concern for you then honestly I'd say that this is definitely the wrong genre of gaming for you. Those of us who bought it knowing full what it is, will love it and only those who are new-ish to Square Enix's way of things will be confused and angry.
Whether you like it or not, Nier: Automata has already established itself as a cult classic, and some including myself would say that it's just short of a masterpiece. Buy the game if you don't mind using free patch called "Borderless Gaming" (can be downloaded from Google). An official patch for Nier will inevitablly be released when they get around to it. However, if it is more important to you to complain about things that you can honestly fix yourself in mere minutes with practically zero effort, be my guest. Just note that it doesn't remotely derive from what a fantastic game this is.
P.S. To those complaining about how DLC was released before a patch. The DLC was released only days after the game's initial release, before really anyone had time to document that the resolution needed a quick fix. This happens with 95% of other games so I don't see what the fuss is here. People just getting furious without knowing the facts.

Previously I have reviewed this game and decided not to recommend this game to anyone simply because for a premium price, I was still getting bombarded with crashes because this game's port is ♥♥♥♥ing awful, and you had to download something called "FixAutomataRes" to make the game somewhat playable.
However since then I have tried playing it again and I've managed to fix the crashing issues I previously had, thus I was able to play the game smoothly and at my native resolution of 1440p.
This game literally gave me goosebumps several times, especially on the opera boss fight because that's the video of NieR:Automata I first watched (my pair of grados is part of the reason too though). Other times include other bosses where one of the main reason why I had such goosebumps was because the soundtrack was so good and the scenes leading up to the boss fights were really good, plot thickening and reaching climax, like how my ex-gf would moan so hard right before she comes.
I still stand by my claim that this game is like my ex-gf from my previous review, cause it really is. The soundtrack and storyline doesn't have a happy tune to it, and when I got through all the important endings (A to E), I realize the ending is not a happy one like how my ex-gf and I ended our relationship. I would say, the storyline of this game was some of the best I've ever encountered.
The game's fight mechanics is fast paced which is totally suitable for an action RPG, the levelling system isn't really a grind fest which is a good thing for a single player game like this, the weapon and character upgrades provide a certain level of diversity though each character has their own special abilities and you kind of have to make use of it to go through the gameplay easier. The cutscene graphics isn't the best, and at times it feels like I'm watching a movie made of 2006 3D game due to the really meh'ish quality. The soundtrack is one that you have to buy (and I've bought it) simply because this game's soundtrack is just AWESOME.
It's not too hard to get a full completion of the game, and I've completed all quests and slained all the mini bosses with about 55 hours of gametime.
In terrms of CPU/GPU demands, this game's a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the optimization. At maxed out settings except AA at 2x, I'm getting on average 40-60 fps which isn't really good considering this game isn't really as detailed as some other AAA games like Rise of the Tomb Raider, heck Battlefield 1 looks better and is less GPU demanding than this game.
This time, I'd recommend trying out the game, if you encountered crashes and you can't solve it even by installing the FAR mod, there's *another alternative available to play the game* where in my experience, it was a good one and I have never experienced any crashes during the game, however sometimes the game would crash when you try to open them.
In conclusion, truly a great game. Somewhat wished they had an online version of this. And also wished SquareEnix even bothered releasing a patch of their own rather than dumping the responsibility onto Nvidia or AMD.

As others have said, this is indeed the Final Edition of King of Fighters 98UM. However, that means it's the final rebalancing. It doesn't include the features the PS2 one does because that's not the version that was ported. It's a port of the XBLA version with all the balance changes applied to it. It's about as close to arcade perfect as you'll get. I can understand why people would be disappointed by that, but all things considered this is a good port. Now let's talk about the part everybody cares about most.
The netcode itself seems to be about KoFXIII's levels of quality. So it's very playable, but not perfect. This has been my experience with player matches only with players ranging from 100ms to 200ms. Yes, it displays the ping times, thank God. When someone's connection has issues, you can definitely feel the delay, but it resyncs pretty quickly.
Single player consists of small challenges, arcade mode, 1v1 matches, etc. All the stuff you would expect from a fighter. It also includes the NeoGeo version of KoF98 if you want to play that.
So to sum it up: few SP modes, no PS2 features, only way to play FE outside of arcades, netcode is good for input delay based netcode. So you're getting an arcade faithful version of KoF98UM FE with online play. I'm happy with it, but you can't please everybody. One little thing I'm personally happy about is that everybody is unlocked from the start, too.

Pros
- Ridiculously versatile and flexible to all kinds of games and genres. Everything is customisable.
- Trackball and Gyro combo are incredible for FPS, third person and any other games demanding precise aiming
- Dpad is actually brilliant when set to a small deadzone and activating on press, allowing you to just roll your thumb as if it is a normal Dpad, but with additional feedback when you set the haptics high.
- Playing mouse driven games is amazing, using the two trackpads simultaneously for extra speed and range or using a pad as a "Touch Menu" which overlays hotkeys for quick use
- Grips are perfect. Use them as additional buttons, or use them with a feature called mode switching to change the functions of the controller when held
- New features and fixes being added regularly
- Insane battery life and wireless range
- Haptics are great and customisable
Cons
- Initial learning curve can be frustrating. Particularly with the dpad as it feels a bit alien for a while
- Frantic RTS and MOBA are still a bit of a challenge with the controller
- The controller is noisy
- Pressing the trackpads requires more force than expected, takes time to get used to
- Valve need to organise the community binding section better. Some of the best new bindings are at the bottom of the list, while the ones being used the most are often older, not using the new features that help make things even better
I've been blown away by this controller. There is quite a learning curve to it, but over the course of a few hours, I started to see improvements, and over a several days that just kept getting better. There is an insane amount of customisation to mess with and great solutions from the community.
There are some brilliant ways to use this controller. A personal favourite is the trackball mouse and Gyro combo, which is really intuitive and works perfectly for competitive FPS or third person games needing precise aim -
Also finally being able to play mouse and keyboard games in the lounge is just so good. Trackball mouse emulation is a joy and can be customised to suit almost all needs. You can even use the controller with games outside Steam or just in Windows. The controller has worked either on par of far better than the other controllers I have used. Works for fighting games, action games, rpgs, platformers, FPS, pretty much everything, although intense RTS / MOBA is not quite good enough yet.
Valve keep adding new features and fixing stuff since the controller is so software driven, recently adding some brilliant new features such as a touch menu that converts one of the pads into multiple segments represented on screen - brilliant for quick weapon selection or having hotkeys easy to access. They also added a fantastic mouse-joystick mode, where you can get mouse movement even though the game is accepting analogue input - perfect for the games that don't support both gamepad and mouse simultaneously (such as MGS V).
If you can handle having to practice for the first couple of weeks, and experimenting with the mentioned input styles, chances are you will be extremely pleased with the controller by the end. It isn't as quick and accurate as a mouse and keyboard, but it certainly comes very close while still letting you play all the games you would use a normal controller for - which is far more than I was expecting for a controller.

The Steam controller is a great piece of hardware. For mouse controlled games it's great for having the comfort of a typical controller but with little to no loss of control and precision. For other games it works great emulating a gamepad, or providing gamepad like controls for PC games without proper gamepad support. For FPS and other games demanding on mouse control precision, it will take practice, as well as tweaking some of the controls. You can customise and change almost everything, from button bindings, to sensitivity and deadzones of the trackpads, to what functions the trackpads emulate (Mouse? Buttons? Key presses? It can emulate them all).
It may look a little strange, but the controllers shape fit well in my hand, and the grips are made to support the base of your thumb over the trackpads.
Some games have also been updated with native support, which works even better. You can change the binding of in-game actions how you like and still customise sensitivity and the like. With Portal 2 for example it will update the in-game button prompts with the correct controls when you customise them. It even has seperate modes e.g. a mouse control config for when you're in the Portal 2 level editor.
As of the time of writing, the only real limitations are some rare issues with configuring it, some minor bugs in Portal 2 and the fact you have to use Big Picture to configure it, obviously aimed at Steam machines/Steam Link users.
To summarise, the controller does exactly what it intends to do. It allows you to play PC oriented, mouse and keyboard games with the comfort of a controller (especially if you want to play them in a living room setup) while still supporting traditional gamepad controls for games you're fine using them with. It will take practice to get used to it, but after a few hours, maybe even up to a week of getting used to it, it works great.

If you like trap making games (Kagero: Deception II, for example) this game is awesome.
Instead of fooling a predictable AI into falling into the traps, you're fooling actual people.

Even though this is a kind of totally different experience from most any other game on Steam, it is not particularly special except that it is within Steam's library of games, which makes it a semi active community. That is, you build a decently devious house with some dead ends and electricity for cheap death traps, with the safe behind some random door. After a day, perhaps 3-4 people will have died in your house, giving you a bounty of about 100$ or more each, which you can then spend to further extend the size of your trap er I mean house.
If you want to have fun, you have another approach to take, which actually benefits the new players. You can choose to spend your money on *gear* and go try to break/pillage houses. The reason this game is relatively dull is because, apart from its most elegant graphics and tutorial (not), it actually punishes you pretty severely when you die; you have to start completely over.
The point is, that there is no clear victory or progress. When you do rob someone, then immediately you have to secure your safe into a more safe position, upgrading your fortifications and making the way to your money more confusing and deadly. If you are idle for 5 minutes, you automatically leave the house, making it vulnerable to attack. Sometimes, you can find an easy 2,000$ by finding someone who has not built anything but instead left their house for any reason.
I could recommend it, simply based on how it is kind of logical, kind of puzzle-y, and so forth, but the absolute truth is that it just isn't your typical entertainment, and it somehow makes you wish that the general idea was carried into a more complete game, with upgradable room to build your house, a second or third story, the option to have a turn-based or real-time kind of interaction that lets you decide between buttons or reflexes, and a bunch of other really quite interesting things that simply are not done.
On the point of inspiring creativity, it does actually create a space for puzzle-craft. Where it fails is simply that it could be more visually appealing, it could offer a greater variety of tools for defense and offensive style of play, it could allow for coordination and teamwork rather than a strange list that magically "knows" exactly how much money is there, and therefore takes all the mystery out of things. Despite all of that though, with any of the things I mention, the game itself becomes something other than what it is. It feels like you should be able to put money in a hundred places rather than in the big obvious safe.

I was really excited about the idea of this game.  The author did a good job of providing a sense of "hype" to those of us that enjoy old-school looking and brutally difficult games.
However, in no way did this game deliver what I had thought it was going to be.  The author often touted how he doesn't believe in Steam sales and I thought that was respectable so I preordered to get a small discount.  Big mistake.  It's rare I regret game purchases, but this is some major buyer's remorse here.  This game is about as bare-bones as it can get.  It's esoteric, which I can enjoy (in, say, Dark Souls), but to a fault.  You have to spend time designing a trap for your home and you have to be able to pass your own trap in order to "set it".  This is sensible, since we obviously don't want people to make impossible traps.  But that doesn't really prevent the creation of "impossible" traps.  It's very easy to create a set of traps that are 100% guess work and one step in the wrong direction and it's impossible to escape.
At the end of the day, this just isn't a fun or good game.  It looks, feels and plays like a high-school project.  I absolutely do not recommend this game to anybody.

Can't say I liked this game. I'm addicted to Hidden Object games so I know there will probably be some money involved but this game really isn't worth it. Too many menus and a poorly put to together storyline to focus on and not enough searching for hidden objects.

Sure, this is a free-to-play game which means: it doesn't hurt to check it out, there will be real money transactions, and said transactions will be bombarded in your face every step of the way.  I've played quite a few of the free-to-play hidden object (or other puzzle) titles available and enjoyed quite a few of them.  This isn't one of the ones I enjoyed.
The whole game is a poorly set up, confusing mess.  Every time you click on anything some form of menu pops up trying to sell you some miscellaneous piece of junk.  There are far too many different types of collections and items to know what is actually needed to play the game.  The "quests" don't make a lot of sense and aren't introduced well.  And the actual hidden object puzzles (which should be the meat of the game) are short and just use the same 10 items over and over again in each room.
Add to that an odd horror setting, which might work in paid for Hidden Object games where you can focus on whatever is being investigated and immerse yourself into the atmosphere of the game, but it doesn't work in the short play sessions of a free-to-play dynamic.  The horror theme just comes across as ridiculous.
All in all, there is no harm in checking out a free-to-play title if you really like the look of the game, but there are much better entries on Steam and this one is just too tedious to play.

What this game lacks in complex storytelling it makes up for in charm.
What you can expect from Minecraft Storymode in brief:
-A simple rendition of the classic Heroe's Journey.
-A cast of entertaining, if a bit stereotyped, characters already showing signs of promising development.
-A tastefully silly sense of humor.
-A slow beginning pace that gradually picks up along the way.
-And for me, personally, a sense of innocent wonder I haven't felt in quite some time.
This game is simple, yes, and not like Tell Tale's recent titles, but what more can you expect from a game based on Minecraft? I urge you to check your expectations at the door, because if you're assuming it'll be like what they've previously made you'll be disappointed. That said, what they have done is taken Minecraft and successfully told the beginning of what seems to be an engaging, fun adventure about a group of diverse small town kids rising to the occasion and taking on a mission far bigger than themselves. Witty humor, good dialogue and surprisingly well done voice acting abound in a story limited in scope, but full of personality. If that sounds like your cup of tea, I do recommend.

Nier: Automata was on my wishlist since its announcement and I was hoping that the price would eventually drop so I could justify buying it. Personally I think that it is a cult classic and
and people will hate me for saying so but I think that most people on Steam are missing the point. Plenty of triple A games require external patching or modding in order to be 'worth' their asking price. Take Skyrim for example. On its own, it released as a mostly boring, very old looking and buggy mess (and still is). Take into account community mods that transform it into a brilliant, stable and beautiful 4K experience. Why is it so terrible that Nier:Automata requires a little bit of similar third-party love in the way of patching? Skyrim was once €60, and Skyrim devs also released DLC before patching some of the inital massive bugs, so why all the hate here? Plenty of other games that get fantastic reviews have needed similar patches, but people just like to jump on the bandwagon of bashing Square Enix any chance they get, despite publishers like Bethestda releasing far more buggy and easily exploitable messes *cough* Oblivion/Skyrim's crafting system *cough*.
Anyway in my opinion Nier: Automata has almost everything I wanted it to have. It has a huge amount of replay value and basically needs to be finished 3 times in order for you to get the full story. It has tons of side quests and little tasks to accomplish. It runs beautifully on my hardware and I don't get any slowdowns or lag at all. Controller support is fantastic and controls are responsive. I love the voice acting, and surprisingly even the English voicing is outstanding. As for the OST, it is something that I will probably listen to for years to come as there are well over 100 music tracks in the full OST due to multiple variations of each song which is also goes into how well the pacing fits the game. Like all Square Enix / Final Fantasy typed games the story is a little cliché but if that is a concern for you then honestly I'd say that this is definitely the wrong genre of gaming for you. Those of us who bought it knowing full what it is, will love it and only those who are new-ish to Square Enix's way of things will be confused and angry.
Whether you like it or not, Nier: Automata has already established itself as a cult classic, and some including myself would say that it's just short of a masterpiece. Buy the game if you don't mind using free patch called "Borderless Gaming" (can be downloaded from Google). An official patch for Nier will inevitablly be released when they get around to it. However, if it is more important to you to complain about things that you can honestly fix yourself in mere minutes with practically zero effort, be my guest. Just note that it doesn't remotely derive from what a fantastic game this is.
P.S. To those complaining about how DLC was released before a patch. The DLC was released only days after the game's initial release, before really anyone had time to document that the resolution needed a quick fix. This happens with 95% of other games so I don't see what the fuss is here. People just getting furious without knowing the facts.

Previously I have reviewed this game and decided not to recommend this game to anyone simply because for a premium price, I was still getting bombarded with crashes because this game's port is ♥♥♥♥ing awful, and you had to download something called "FixAutomataRes" to make the game somewhat playable.
However since then I have tried playing it again and I've managed to fix the crashing issues I previously had, thus I was able to play the game smoothly and at my native resolution of 1440p.
This game literally gave me goosebumps several times, especially on the opera boss fight because that's the video of NieR:Automata I first watched (my pair of grados is part of the reason too though). Other times include other bosses where one of the main reason why I had such goosebumps was because the soundtrack was so good and the scenes leading up to the boss fights were really good, plot thickening and reaching climax, like how my ex-gf would moan so hard right before she comes.
I still stand by my claim that this game is like my ex-gf from my previous review, cause it really is. The soundtrack and storyline doesn't have a happy tune to it, and when I got through all the important endings (A to E), I realize the ending is not a happy one like how my ex-gf and I ended our relationship. I would say, the storyline of this game was some of the best I've ever encountered.
The game's fight mechanics is fast paced which is totally suitable for an action RPG, the levelling system isn't really a grind fest which is a good thing for a single player game like this, the weapon and character upgrades provide a certain level of diversity though each character has their own special abilities and you kind of have to make use of it to go through the gameplay easier. The cutscene graphics isn't the best, and at times it feels like I'm watching a movie made of 2006 3D game due to the really meh'ish quality. The soundtrack is one that you have to buy (and I've bought it) simply because this game's soundtrack is just AWESOME.
It's not too hard to get a full completion of the game, and I've completed all quests and slained all the mini bosses with about 55 hours of gametime.
In terrms of CPU/GPU demands, this game's a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the optimization. At maxed out settings except AA at 2x, I'm getting on average 40-60 fps which isn't really good considering this game isn't really as detailed as some other AAA games like Rise of the Tomb Raider, heck Battlefield 1 looks better and is less GPU demanding than this game.
This time, I'd recommend trying out the game, if you encountered crashes and you can't solve it even by installing the FAR mod, there's *another alternative available to play the game* where in my experience, it was a good one and I have never experienced any crashes during the game, however sometimes the game would crash when you try to open them.
In conclusion, truly a great game. Somewhat wished they had an online version of this. And also wished SquareEnix even bothered releasing a patch of their own rather than dumping the responsibility onto Nvidia or AMD.

I was really excited about purchasing this game initially. I was completely sold by the trailer and the whole vibe they were obviously going for.
It has been sitting in my library for nearly a month now until had enough data to download it.
What i found upon install was less than satisfying...to put it mildly.
Visually, every thing is up to par.... Almost. I have a minor grip with the frame timing for the animations but that is linked to the controls.
The sound is buggy. Some characters are clearly much louder than others, and the sound fx seem to fluctuate at times.
Otherwise the classic look and feel of Kung Fu cinema is most certainly there. This i cannot fault the game on.
Next, the controls...
Just..AWFUL. Spongey, unreponsive, illogical at times. Murders the "fun" element the game could potentially have.
A key ingredient to a solid fighter IMO.
-There just doesnt seem to be much weight behind the attacks, and as such, most are just plain unsatisfying to execute.
The fighters also tend to fall over after attacked nearly every opportunity they get. If this is for effect...it really doesnt work. It just makes for a frustrating experience. Esspecially when you consider you can't after getting knocked over or retaliate from the ground.
-The roster is small, but quite well rounded, and the stages are diverse enough to be satisfactory.
-Hopefully the developers will attend to these issues, in particular the controls.
-My verdict ultimately is, as much as i wanted this game to be great, it just simply falls far short at this stage.
PS: A Tutorial feature would be nice.

Inspired by the Shaw Bros/ Golden Harvest Kung Fu classics of the 1970's -80's,  Kings of Kung Fu is a beautifully simple and fun fighter that will appeal to the casual fighting game fan as well as those who grew up with classic Kung Fu cinema.
While the game is still in development, the developers seem to be taking the more constructive community feedback pretty seriously, and I think there is huge potential here and tons of fun to be had for a good price.
Everything about this game from the character designs to the sound and stage designs are fun. It’s not the most complex fighter you will ever play, but it’s a wonderful tip of the hat to a golden era of martial arts films and promising endeavour that I hope picks up a ton of support.

Yes at time of this review I've only played 15 minutes but I just had to write a quick review now to counter the last 2 reviews that were negative (before that most were all positive). There was some mention of it being like a platforming game and too much jumping. Well before I bought this game I did look at some u-tube videos of it and I could see no evidence of that. On the contrary, when playing this game it has less jumping than most other martial arts fighting games that I have played. The ususal cheap trick is to somersault in kick punch and back out. That doesn't work here. In Kings of Kung Fu there is a lot of side to side punching it out and blocking more like the movies it's based on. It thus plays a lot better. The other great thing about this game was how close the contests can be, right down to the wire. Makes for some nerve racking fights. First time in on normal difficulty level and using a keyboard I won my first 2 fights (second one very close) and the third against a monk, kicked his butt in first round and then he won the next 2 in very close shaves. It was pure fun and a pleasure to play. I will definitely be going back for more. A great game and it's not even finished yet! I highly recommend this game if you like fighting games. If you love kung-fu then don't even think twice, just buy it. It plays superbly.
Edit: Now that I've played it more, there is a bit of jumping but that seems more if you put it on easy level - the AI is jumping all over the place.
Just some pros and cons that I've found but they will be cleaned up no doubt when finished:
Cons
Menu system is bad, first use mouse then use keyboard. Doesn't seem to know what it's doing. A bit frustrating. The menu system of Skyrim when first released springs to mind.
Some characters seem a bit overpowered compared to the others - Bruce Lee in particular.
No multiplayer mode yet.
At the moment same game every time you play. Same characters in certain orders mostly.
Boring repetitive music. But you can turn it off.
The AI doesn't seem any differnet between easy and normal except that on easy mode the AI jumps all over the place making the game a ridiculous mess and making it no easier then the normal level. I'd stick to normal level if I were you.
Pros:
Superb animations.
Superb sounds of the fighters.
Health system drains very slowly making for some really long kung -fu film style fights.
Excellent graphics overall.
Excellent different styles of each fighter. Each very different.
The price of £5 at the moment is a bargain for what you get.

The Castle Doctrine had a very nice thought, yet was terribly executed.
For one, the game is hyper-realistic. when trying to get to your vault by testing your traps, you can actually die by your traps. And I mean literally die, so you have to start all over again. even the smallest change to your house will make you test it again. Another thing is that you can give your wife a shotgun as a defense, and she will kill you.
Next, there is interface. While playing, I felt very, very enclosed. no real menus, you only get to see one kind of screen, and most of the time it's just black darkness. It alwas uses re-ocurring colors like grey, orange, dark cyan and black. it seems very bland and boring to just look at.
Graphics aside, we are onto gameplay. My gosh, is it hard to even take a step. you start off in house with your wife and kids and $2000. You can either use the money to build your house, or you can use it to get robbing equipment. Oh, and by the way, the main premice of the game is to rob people or steal robbers' bounty. You can go to the list of countless people and rob their houses, but you know you can't. Somehow, someway, everyone on that list has figured out the perfect way to protect thier house and get tons of ca$h. So how do you win? You can't. You'll try , but after about 5 minutes you realise that no mattter what you try to do, it's impossible to get more than your base $2000.
To sum it up, The Castle Doctrine is not worth half it's price. It's badly made, which will make you expect much more. But no, I pretty much told everything in this review. I thing the price for $16 dollars asking for waaaayy to much, so it should be down to $5. Anyways, the promotional sale was literally the only discount ever on this game.It's literally in the announcement. So if you have $16 to burn, do NOT use it here. Please use it somewhere else. Thank you.

One of my favorite games of alltime! After almost 300 hours and all achievements later, I can safely say this game is worth it if you haven't played it yet. The 3rd person is something to be desired, as is with all bathesda games, Fallout included, as they run on the same engine.
My favorite types of games are ones that you level up based on what you do, Ultima Online and oldschool FLYFF shared that quality, are you hacking and slashing with your sword? you're going to level your swordsmanship up, are you blasting people away with lightning? Your destruction magic will start to go up. There are a few ways to cheese this but the game will sort of punish you in that way by leveling up the enemies with you, if you level one thing too quickly, your other skills will lack and you'll get mowed over by the increased level all the enemies have.
This was a crazy ride to achievement hunt. I do recommend anyone try it. Although the longer you play the game, the more glitches you will find in the game. Dragons will start to fly sideways or just straight up, some quests become undoable, which is why it's important to save new save files regularly, some notable ones were the civil war questline, and getting the totems for Aela. I would have been unable to finish those had I not had a seperate save file. The unofficial patch might help here, I never used it. It's a game I love even with flaws, it can't be perfect, but it's damn well close!

Really awesome hidden object game that keeps you hooked. A mysterious mansion with untold secrets with you as a curious house guest. Each task and quest leaves you wondering. The puppeteer gives you that eerie vibe, given his name he's the master pulling the strings. Since playing this game I've grown a fondness for it because it drags me in especially at night. You don't know what to expect or what you might find.
Though It's pretty mindblowing to me that this mansion resembles a mansion near my area. In my neighborhood, there's this creepy mysterious mansion, that was built in 1896 by stone dealer Edwin Shuttleworth. Due to it's significance, NYC declared it a historical landmark so despite it's old decrepted appearance no one can destory it. Outside gives it a creepy look of hauntingness, front gates chained up, broken wooden shed garage, overall a brick-like gothic structure. No one knows what it looks like on the inside and there hasn't been much information known about past owners decades later after it was built. It just goes to show that Shuttleworth Mansion is without a doubt a mansion of untold mysteries and wonders

I got the Steam Controller early through the pre-order scheme and I've been using it for a few weeks now.  It's very well made and very responsive.  In addition to my PC, I also have a PS4 and I had purchased an Xbox1 controller for PC games.  The Steam controller is every bit as professional in terms of build and quality as the high end console controllers.  The two trackpads are very responsive and clickable, and the analogue stick and 13 buttons work exactly as expected.
The Steam controller is "application dependant" and will function differently depending on what program or game you are using.  It can be used wired through a USB port, or remotely (the cable, receiver and batteries are included - "AA" batteries slide into the left and right grips, one on each side).
The concept behind the Steam controller is clearly designed to bridge the gap between console controllers and keyboard / mouse use.  In terms of quality and button layout, Steam have got it right.  The only issues will be around "muscle memory", that is, people who have used a keyboard and mouse for thirty years (like myself) are going to have to learn how to use the new controller before they become fluent with it.  Console players will have less "muscle memory" to relearn, but may find the trackpads will take getting used to.
The Steam Controller is an excellent device which does it's job very well.  It is going to require most people to do some some "retraining" to get fully proficient with it, however once that familiarity is reached, the Steam Controller has the potential to perform at the hightest levels.  I have no doubt that Steam will support their controller and over the months ahead many gamers will make the transition.

This is just a quick review based on the gamepads singple player FPS game performance.
I bought this gamepad mostly out of curiosity, most people seem to dismiss it as it has touch controllers and touch games on phones are rubbish and laptop touch pads are generally useless. However the reasons phones and touchpads are near unusuable in complex games isn't the touch pad themselves but usually the layout or lack of any buttons and the methods used to track movement. I noticed really good 1:1 tracking in some phone fps games and saw a lot of potential so when I saw this was being made I was quite interested.
Turns out the steam controller is instantly a lot better than gamepads in FPS games when setup correct (which it is not by default)
Long story short, reconfigure the right touchpad to "mouse" mode and turn off trackball mode and you can aim exactly in a way keyboard and mouse can. However the accuracy is not that great, sniping long distance targets on serious sam 3 is not really possible, but anything medium to close range works perfect. Straight away I was doing flick shots, killing people moment they pop around corners, strafing around enemies and shooting them in the back like I would on mouse and keyboard and with no aim assist.
Some slight drawbacks however...
The surface area is smaller than your usual mouse mat movement area, and sensitivity needs to be fairly low to keep accuracy good enough, the result is a lot of lifting thumb to continue moving in a direction.  this can be countered by using track ball mode but I found it made me do a lot of unwanted movements (could maybe improve in time with use of the controller)
Still a lot less buttons than on a keyboard, I found myself havign to come to a complete stop in Serious sam 3 to change weapons by using the Dpad (left track pad)  could be fixed with custom profiles though.
Lots of software problems (usually on the game side of things) Games often arent designed to use keyboard/mouse and gamepads at the same time, the result is button prompts can flicker between keyboard and gamepad icons.  Also not sure how I can have 3 analogue axis in 6DoF games like Sublevel zero when all it seems to be able to do is emulate gamepad axis and doesn't have its own 3rd analogue bindings (this could be user error as I haven't given this much thought or time)
Overall it did exactly what I expected it to do and I'm quite pleased with it.

From the moment I received the Steam Controller in the mail on October 16th, 2015, a tidal wave of community mappings and firmware tweaks by Valve quickly evolved it from an infancy of bleeding potential to my end-all, be-all couch gaming solution for my PC.
Yearning for higher precision in console-oriented FPSs such as Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel and Call of Duty: Black Ops 3? Set the right touchpad for mouse aiming and leave every other button mapped the same. Is that specific game (namely Fallout 4, Grand Theft Auto V, etc) not very cooperative with said configuration? The Steam Controller mapping software can emulate a "mouse-like joystick" to play along with such restrictions while sacrificing little to no precision. Is reaching for A, B, X, and Y cramping your hands? The grip buttons on the back in cooperation with the hardware's dual-stage triggers and software modeshifting can assist your sayonara to that traditional layout.
While you may have seen folks such as Gamer Muscle wipe the floor with mouse and keyboard players in a CS:GO Arms Race match, don't expect this gizmo to replace your mouse and keyboard at all. However, if you're willing to sacrifice some competitive competence for a cozy couch gaming session or two, you're allowed to do that, because as Valve trumepts throughout their hardware push, PC gaming is all about options.

Sure, it's different.
Sure, it takes some getting-used-to.
Sure, it lacks a d-pad* and rumble support**.
But this thing is literally a game-changer. I can play mouse-driven games, such as Icewind Dale Enhanced Edition, Pillars of Eternity, Card City Nights and the like, from the comfort of my couch. I can play FPS games with much more precise aiming thanks to a combination of trackpad and gyroscope aiming. I can remap games to play exactly how I want, even games that didn't include any gamepad support whatsoever - no need for external third-party software such as AntiMicro - and I can manage those configurations WITH the gamepad! I can also share my configurations with the Steam community easily, and they're applied automatically by Steam on the fly. Oh yeah, and it all works identically and seamlessly on Linux, Windows, and OSX.
Valve have pushed out several firmware updates for the Controller, as well as many beta Steam client updates which not only fixed some bugs, but also added, expanded, and improved upon the ways we can configure this thing. They're listening to our feedback emails, as I've seen several additions which I specifically requested, myself. Even how it is now, it's virtually infinitely configurable, and once you get used to creating and tweaking configs, you'll figure out what you like and become a pro at setting up configs for your favorite games in no time.
Battery life seems to be quite good. The included batteries endured daily use from the day my Controller arrived on October 16th, until I finally had to replace them on the morning of November 16th. It doesn't compete with my Logitech F710 experience, but I still can't complain about that, considering what I typically got out of my DualShock 3.
This is only the first retail iteration, but I think they nailed it. I now have no need for any of the other gamepads I've invested in over the years, and I no longer need a keyboard or mouse for the games that don't support gamepads natively.
Thank you, Valve!
Sincerely,
A long-time gamepad user who has longed for something better.
PS: now you gotta figure out a way to make fonts readable in all games in a ten-foot setup.
* - seriously, STOP calling the left trackpad a d-pad. IT'S NOT A D-PAD! It's a trackpad! It's far more useful than a d-pad will ever be, and touch-to-move is the best thing since sliced analog stick.
** - each trackpad has haptic feedback, but this is not yet being used in any games that I'm aware of to emulate traditional rumble support or anything of the like. And really, do you even care about rumble support? A lot of games don't support that anyhow, and it's not like you get it in your standard keyboard and mouse either.

I stumbled upon this game as was searching through Steam for something to play - and I'm *so* glad I did. The art grabbed my attention, as did the very positive reviews, so I checked it out. Here's what I think:
PROS
--------------------------------------------
- Excellent gameplay (it's so cool that people are *still* finding new things to do with platformers. I love it! ^_^ )
- Tight controls. I never felt overwhelmed, and that's a good thing.
- Great art! (though I'm not sure why the backgrounds were moving underground - maybe to keep things visually interesting >_< )
- The tone, feel and setting are all really good.
- The pacing is just incredible. I started playing it saying, 'I'll just play it for a little while', and the game moves at such a pace that I found myself playing for far longer than I thought. I beat the game in two sittings! I love games that can grab your attention and keep it like that.
- The characters and puzzles kept me glued to my chair. I tell ya - there's something great about this game. Once you start - you don't want to put the game down!
- Frequent checkpoints that enforce the fact that you're always making progress.
- I also really like the fact that the last boss, while challenging is not SUPER-HARD-OH-MY-GOSH-YOU'LL NEVER-BEAT-THIS that so many platformers end with. While challenging, the game is more fun than hard - and I like that a lot.
CONS
----------------------------------------
- The music, while good, never really connected with me. I still listen to the 'Shovel Knight' and 'Super Mario 3D World' soundtracks, for example. But here, nothing really jumped out. The music is not bad - it just didn't stand out to me.
- While the controls felt fair, there were a few parts that I thought the difficulty curve was a bit steep. Reflecting back on it, I think it's because the devs wanted to put in as many different puzzles in as small a time frame as possible. I never got stuck or had to look solutions up online (which is great!), but smoothly transitioning from one puzzle to another sometimes felt a little weird. Maybe that's a nitpick. Just thought I'd mention it.
- At a little over two hours, the game is *short*. What it lacks in length, it more than make up for in variety and fun, though.
OVERALL
----------------------------------------
I was really pleasantly surprised with 'Out There Somewhere'. The pacing was excellent, the art was really fun and quirky and the platforming action kept me coming back for more (and kept showing me things I'd never seen before - so I loved that). I loved the fact that I went into this 'blind', so everything it showed me was a surprise. Love it! I had a great time and I look forward to seeing what else the devs have made. Bring on more great games! :)
FINAL SCORE
---------------------------------------
8.5 out of 10

Nier:Automata was instantly on my wish list the moment I heard about it, since Platinum is one of my favourite developers. I kept away from spoilers, because what's the point? I always knew I would play the game. If you want some idea of whether or not this game is for you without spoilers, keep reading.
Game play:
The majority of the time you will be running around hacking up enemies in a traditional third person perspective. However, the game will from time to time shift to being a sidescroller, top down brawler, scrolling shmup, twin stick shmup, and Starfox-esque on rails shooter.
Regarding the various shmup sections, they are not the top tier of shmup action, but they don't appear all that often and they are done well enough to not tarnish the rest of the game. They also don't overstay their welcome.
As for the meat, the third person hack'n'slash action, it's great. If you have played other Platinum games, you will know what to expect, though it does a few things to mix things up. There is a nice assortment of weapons, with their own combos and various special features (such as absorbing health from cutting bullets or detonating combo finishers).
Sound:
This is easy. The sound effects all fit. The music is a really nice mix of orchestral, pop, cute/funny and electronic styles. I had to get the soundtrack before I even finished the game. The game has English and Japanese voices. Usually I would default to Japanese (assuming that's it's source country), but since English was selected by default, I decided to give it a go. I was pleasantly surprised at how good the English dub was (given how terrible they can be).
Graphics/Art:
Overall really pretty. There are a few issues, like the occasional muddy texture or detail levels popping in and out, but nothing to really break the overall presentation. The art design (for my tastes) is spot on and a breath of fresh air compared to a lot of games that aim for pure realism. The style is somewhat "realistic", but stylised enough to have it's own identity and not take you to uncanny valley.
Story (no spoilers, I promise):
I came in completely blind and if possible, I suggest you do the same. I knew there would be robots, and didn't expect much more than that. I was completely happy to play an action game with that backdrop. I was very (VERY) pleasantly surprised. The story has depth I didn't think would be here. I am not ashamed to admit that I got "hit in the feels" multiple times. I honestly can't remember the last time a games story and characters had this much of an impact on me.
Conclusion:
If you want an action game with a decent story, nice graphics and a great soundtrack, it doesn't get much better than this. Honestly, this is one of the best games I've ever played.
Caveat:
There are a whole bunch of issues with certain PC hardware, though I didn't experience any myself (using a laptop with a GTX1060, i7 CPU, Win10). Check the forums and definitely download the FAR mod. This can help increase performance and fixes some issues. Having read up in advance, I installed the FAR mod before I even started playing the game. The only issue I ran into was it displaying on the wrong monitor and the game resetting my camera config (ONLY the camera config, nothing else for some reason). Annoying for sure, but easily fixable and hardly a deal breaker.

I want to make a note before I start my review that I play Skyrim fully vanilla. I do not use mods, cheat codes, or anything of that sort. If you're looking for a review about anything relating to the new Creation Club, mods, or anything like that, this review will not help you.
I'm still rather new to the Skyrim series, having gotten this game (and ESO) a few months back but just recently sitting down and playing my way through everything. This is the best unbiased review you're going to get, as I have no dedication to the series or the developers.
I assume most people who are browsing the reviews for a game as popular as Skyrim are the ones who have heard of it but want to decide if it's for them, so that is who my review is geared toward. I've had multiple friends over the years who have played Skyrim and I always found myself saying "it's overrated, it's not my genre, I'll never play it". After actually watching some gameplay, I decided to give it a shot.
Personally, I find myself really enjoying this game genre when I thought I wouldn't. Don't get me wrong, I really, really enjoy open-ended games, but I'm not usually someone who enjoys combat in my open-ended games. Skyrim's combat system was so well done that I found myself easily able to learn what I needed to do and how to quickly switch my weapons/spells where I needed them, which I was not expecting. Skyrim opened up a whole new door for me, and I found myself enjoying singleplayer RPGs more than I ever did, which had me really impressed.
The graphics are immersive, and this game plays better with sound. Usually when I play games where I'm not in a heavy storyline I put music on in the background but I've yet to do that with Skyrim. Speaking of storyline, I do appreciate how much work went into each individual quest line. The quests feel unique, different, and sometimes difficult but not to the point of rage-inducement. I've yet to have to repeatedly replay a quest because I couldn't finish it, if anything I would die accidentally from not paying attention to my health bar or trying to rush down a boss's health bar and get the losing end of the stick.
The only things I've found that bother me are the horse physics, which is easily overlookable. It extremely bothers me as someone who used to ride horses when I was younger, how the riding animation for the horses looks. It feels very unnatural and clipped instead of realistic and smooth. My only other issue is that with an Xbox controller, the sensitivity is not changeable. I find my camera jerking a little too fast for my taste and it makes aiming very difficult. If you're someone who plays most of your games with a controller, this may be a huge turn off for you.
If you were like me and are debating back and forth about getting Skyrim, get it, try it for yourself. Even if it is on a sale, the game is very much worth it. The replayability is immense and it's the ultimate sandbox for any kind of RPG player.

This game is a remaster of game that was released in 2011. This game is 100% a single player game and now, in 2017, it has micro-transactions tacked on. Why? Because Bethesda isn't rich enough I guess. With that out of the way, let's get on with the rest of the review.
This game is the same game as it was 2011 - that's obviously not a suprise. It's just a remaster - nothing really special going on in that department. However, it does add a updated version of the Creation Engine which adds DX11 support and is 64-bit. This is a big deal for those that want a generally more stable game - and enjoy throwing large amounts of mods into their games. Load times are significanlty faster. On my SSD, loading into taverns (a small cell) is lightning fast. The same applies to pretty much all loading screens.
In addition to that, graphically it is very slightly improved. Lighting has been tweaked, and God Rays have been added. The grass density has universally been increased (which makes the whole game look nicer). The water flows correctly now, and rain occlusion is an offical feature. The mod that added that was faking it, this implementation is legit. Shadows are actually good looking in this version - they were an eyesore in the original no matter what settings you used. LOD's have slightly been improved, and Z-fighting has been completely fixed. Overall, this version is more complete visually. Mods can touch up some of the things I've mentioned - but not all of them. Having them be good out of the box is pretty seet though.
Why do I not recommend this game?
1. Microtransactions have been randomly thrown into a re-relase of a game from 2011.
2. It's a remaster of a game from 2011 and it currently costs $39.99 USD and released at a price tag of $60 USD. Way too high of a price for a game this old.
3. The modding scene is constantly being sabatoged by the seemingly unending updates for the Creation Club, the microtransactions service added by Bethesda. Every time they update the game the .exe changes. When the .exe gets changed then SKSE64 needs to be updated. That screws up any mods that may use it until it gets updated. This isn't a big deal right now as SKSE64 is in its infancy, but for such an old game modding is the only thing keeping it alive.
Why do I recommend this game?
1. The modding platform/potential this version of the game provides is very good. It is the technologically superior version of the game, but as mentioned already, that potential is being soiled by Bethesda's own lust for more money.
2. As a Vanilla expirience (as in no mods) then this is without a doubt the version to buy. Wait for a big sale, as in under $19.99 USD, and grab this. It will run better on newer hardware and look better out of the box. For a no mod kind of person - this is a good deal when it's on a big sale. Never buy it at a high price. Never.
I'm very conflicted on this game. I love Skyrim, and I like what this game offers from a modding perspective. However, due to the microtransactions and the constat updaets screwing up modding - I also dislike it. I chose to "Not Recommend" it because I can't stand the fact that Bethesda thougtht further monetization through microtransactions is acceptable for such an old game. In reality, it's closer to a mixed review. I recommend it and I don't at the same time. Know what you're getting into when looking at this title, and make the best choice for you.

The positives are: Hidden Object Game, great storyline (so far), available on multiple platforms (but you're locked to the one you've started the game on, non-transferable to i0S/Facebook), good music, lots of different puzzles, additional themed quests, interesting modes.  The negatives are: like MMORPGs there are some performance issues with updates, microtransactions are available, sometimes badly translated from Russian (as in "hard to read occasionally").  Play for the story; it's an interesting one!
I started playing this game on Facebook, before I upgraded to Windows 10 last year which started a LOT of issues playing for me.  When I heard that they were going to put this on Steam, I waited patiently until June of this year. I am now level 35 and enjoying it just as much as I was on Facebook.
Hidden Object Puzzle Games (known as HOPs or HOGs) are games that I like, providing that they're good.  I've played a lot of them via Big Fish Games, of which a good 60% were major duds.  This one is not a dud; it is a gem among the genre.
Basically, you wake up in a house you can't leave and don't know how you got there.  You have a choice to follow the Puppeteer and find out his story and that of the house as a Follower (symbolised by the Crow), or you can choose to buck against the system and fight against him any which way you can to get the heck out of the "prison" as a member of the Underground (symbolised by the Rat).  I personally chose to be a Follower because I was fascinated by the house and the story behind the Puppeteer, but judging by the event mutual jars, there are a lot more Underground members on Steam than Followers...
There are times when the point and click fails to actually "pick up" the item (stupid horseshoe); it could be my mouse settings.  What I like about the items in the rooms is the fact that there are a good FIVE places that they can be hidden, while other MMOHOGs only have two.  Some of them are hidden so well that I run out of time trying to find them because they blend in, or are made smaller (damn spider, grrrr...) There are penalties to overclicking in lost time and lost health; this gets worse the higher the level of the room and which mode you are in.
There are some amazing room modes so far, with the Mirror Mode being the most interesting.  You go through the rooms as they are, but once you reach a certain level, you unlock this mode that can completely mess your mind up.  The room can be flipped upside down, it could be flipped side to side, or it could be a combination of both!  Time also runs much, MUCH faster in this mode which makes it even
challenging.  There are items that can turn the mode off, but they're hard to come by unless you do microtransactions to get more.  The downside to turning off the mode is that you cannot win specific items that are only available in that particular mode.
Every month, there are new events that happen.  In July, it was the American Independence Day, and this month seems to be turbo-charged mechanical rats and crows to catch.  These help you get decorations for your room that help with gaining coins, or freedom points (read: experience points), or gaining more items to combine.  The thing is, you need a lot of friends in the game to trade stuff around, or else the events just aren't worth it.  They're extremely difficult to do as a solo player unless you have a lot of money to burn.
But, like all games, there has to be some bad with the good.  Some of the quests are frustrating because the items you need to combine the collections
and it takes forever to get them.  Or you have to be level 45 for them to show up (blue tape, I'm glaring at you).  Distracting people/things in the courtyard is a crapshoot; more often then not, they won't give you what you need.
Like most online games that involve a lot of people, there are microtransactions.  There is no getting out of it.  The company needs to make money, and I need chronometres in order to beat some of the Puppeteer challenges ("finish [room] in less than 30 seconds" kind of thing) and mirror mode.  VIP mode helps to restore your life much faster, but the cost can be prohibitive.  Wait until you can get a magnetic charm which doubles up the number of coins you get from the  purchase for the regular price.
And on the theme of online games, there can be issues with updates.  Sometimes it's minor, as in "text description missing", or they didn't complete the "user name" code when the characters are talking to you. Other times, the update can revert you to level one (serious panic mode for a lot of us there, but the issue was fixed within 24 hours), or cause the Bank to not work.  Their support is great; they reply to you within 48 hours, and restored an item I was supposed to have received and never did.
One of the things about the updates is that they tell you on Facebook in their local time, which is usually around 14h00-15h00 UTC
.  Type the time into Google as "[time] UTC" and you will get your local time.  You don't know how much whining there is on the Panic Room Facebook page about update times, lost freshly used amulets and how they assume the makers of the game are in the US...
Speaking of Russian, the translation can be very iffy sometimes.  It's not Engrish, but there are times when the grammar is all over the place and hard to read.  You get the gist, don't get me wrong, but sometimes the "all your base are belong to us" can take some puzzling out.
On the whole, I recommend this game. For me, it's a fresh take on the HOP with a great story that will end in Season 3; they've already said that
to the game planned out which has made me give them a lot of respect points.  There are some annoying parts, like not getting the items you need and then in frustration just paying for the gold coins to get the stuff to move the story, or slightly botched updates.  But, they take care of the problems quickly, their customer service is great and they give out gifts...to Facebook and iOS players (Steam, not yet).
Give it a shot; it's free to play, and you don't
to do any microtransactions.
