The Castle Doctrine is a game by Jason Rohrer that I bought the alpha version of last year—it subsequently occupied me for a couple of weeks and resulted in many sheets of graph paper filled with strange diagrams and schematics…
A game about protecting your stuff while trying to steal everybody else's, with drastic consequences if you make any mistakes. It just recently had its full release, so I went back to see how it had changed since the point in its development when I was playing it—disappointingly, it failed to capture my interest a second time like I was hoping it would.

It's neat, but incredibly frustrating. You build a complex fortress to hide your cash and keep your family safe. But if you die you lose all your progress. So the more time you put into your base the less incentive there is to go and test other people's bases. A cool idea, that could have benefitted from some fleshing out. Simply wasn't what I want in a game.
If you like uber roguelikes, where you put in hours of work and die before you can achieve anything. Then it's for you.

I'd like to start by saying I heard about this game via YouTube and the series i watched was incredible enjoyable. I decided to give the game a shot since it looked at the very least decent. I picked it up while it was on sale and using some tips from the series I watched and reddit I made a simple house with a commitment trap and a electric floor lock out type trap as well as gave my wife a shot gun. I went out and got lucky with a few houses that had been broken into but not robbed... this is where I noticed one of the first major problems, if your wife is alive and you have a decent amount of money her death is enough for some people since they'll get half and any damage they have done to your house will remain (whereas if they die it gets fixed). Death of the wife seems to be higher up on some peoples lists if they can afford a gun, (guns have a range of 2 spaces whereas your wife's shot gun has a range of 1) and as such people will "dance" near the entrance or search for your family to get them to make their way to the door. I've also noticed that people will occasionally just enter someone's house to mess it up and kill a family member, probably in revenge for stealing their money. So, after I had some decent cash and upgraded my home significatly I let it sit for a while to see how many people I'd kill, and what I'd get with my house. for the most part I'd have people entering the house, taking 2~5 steps then backing out once they saw a commitment trap or a dog, or even just a door... the only time I'd see someone stay longer is if they had a full bag of tools that usually cost more than my savings, and even then most people wouldn't stay in very long and even would back out before they robbed my house. When someone finally successfully robbed my house they also killed my wife, leaving me with a broken home and absolutely no money. At this point it was virtually impossible for me to "recover" as most houses that I would go to rob had only a few dollars in them and were too risky, I ended up just starting over, which leads me to another major flaw... the prices of just about everything. All robbery tools cost hundreds of dollars, most effective house defense stratagies cost thousands in total, and the most effective are also incredibly cheap feeling as they are mostly combo locks after a commitment trap and the wrong combo permenantly locks you in the house while locking off the safe forever causing you to have to suicide. I feel if you were given some materials to build and rob with at the beginning of a "fresh start" and you kept your materials after surviving a hosue 2000 wouldn't be a bad starting point but as it stands it's barely enough to protect anything. Also normal doors can't be locked... which is just silly to me, the game lets you buy an electric locking thick metal door for a few hundred dollars, but we can't find a simple lock for a door. the purpose a lock on a normal door could hold would be to waste a "movement turn" breaking the lock(no tools, just slamming into it with your shoulder or something) and causing everything/everyone within a certain radius to notice someone's in the house. It could also act as a way to block off your family (they'd have keys) so that they don't need a very very obvious escape route, as mentioned int he video they need an escape route that's 100% obsticle free (aside from dogs).
Originally there was a "salary" that your character and your wife(if your wife died it was just your salary) would earn while you where away from the game (more the more time you where not playing) to suppliment stealing and house defense, it also made more sense that you where out of the house when you where getting robbed that way. But they took it out I assume to controll the money flow of the game and as a balancing attempt... but I think it unbalanced the game more than it helped and it made it so that there is truely no recovery from having your wife killed and your house robbed (barring getting lucky as hell while robbing someone with more than $50 and a broken home...
Some commonly used traps/deturants that can be considered "cheap tactics" include:
"leaps of faith" where they have an open trap door that you're supposed to assume a cat/dog will activate and close as you step onto it
"Commitment traps" such as an electric grill flooring or an electric door that locks/turns on as you pass it so there is no turning back and it's pretty much get the money or die trying scenario.
"death traps" there are many of these that are usually hidden behind commitment traps and literally force you to die, a simple one is to hide a cat around a corner behind some glass and cover the floor in grills so it looks like a simple commitment trap, but once they turn the corner they scare the cat and it hits a switch frying the person on the plates, another variant is the same thing but uses a small dog to run towards you.
"Dog traps" basically dogs behind doors that lead to no where, again when paired with a commitment trap this can be deadly...
So many ways to trap people in this game, some are super easy to make, some are very expensive and most are not effective by them selves and require at least a few to protect your money.
Overall this game has a great concept and a decent execution, but it has some major flaws and some major balancing issues.
As it stands I would not reccomend this game. I think it needs to be improved in many ways before I'd say give it a shot, especially for the $16 asked for it, if it was maybe $5  I'd say give it a shot and if you don't like it... hell at least it'd only be $5 spent.

This game -- It is a brilliant idea and extremely addicting. It is not for everyone, so please read the following before you decide to buy the game.
Firstly I want to state that all the critics giving this game a bad review should not be allowed to even rate a game like The Castle Doctrine. I mean this with no hate but if your job is to quickly play a game and write a report about it, day in day out, then you will NOT be able to appreciate a game that involves thinking/learning such as this.
Short summery: You are given a house with some money and you build traps to keep other players out. Afterwards you have the choice of either logging off and waiting for people to die(get money) or break into your vault, or invading someone elses house. Once someone breaks into your house you can actually watch footage of how they do so. The amount of people in the game is very active. Once I build my house, people normally bite within minutes.
If you have played Minecraft and enjoy the 'engineering' aspect of the game where you build and wire items together, you will enjoy this game. At first the amount of items may seem overwhelming but the learning curve is small. Once you have given the game a chance, and come to appreciate that every single house you enter is the fabrication of someone elses individual imagination, you will LOVE the game. The amount of traps and mazes that people create is AMAZING. It makes no difference how long you have played, you will always be a student in this game. You cannot ever master this game because there will likely be someone that will figure your design out -- that's the point of the game!
The game lacks a tutorial for good reason -- this game is for people that like to think/innovate. If you enjoy games that are linear, hand things out, or have safety nets, then you will not enjoy this game. The punishment of failure is very large and you will die a lot at first, however you are given all the tools to test your designs at will. If you dare to copy someone elses design, expect people to have already seen it(you better add a new spin onto it).
Recommendations: Play around with all the different types of items, or watch a quick youtube video on how they work. Then go into other peoples houses to explore, and die, and die, and die, and die, and die again. You lose nothing as a newbie so check out how some other people are creating houses. Then create a simple house and watch how someone robs you. If you fail, recreate it and improve on the design -- simple as that.
Personal tactic: I fill up my backpack with saws in order to try and rob someone as a complete newbie. I break into a house that is worth more than the starting amount of money and try to saw my way through as much as possible, minding traps. If I reach a vault then I will likely double my cash, and then create a house from scratch with more money then I originally had. If I die, I respawn and repeat the above until I crack someone's house. Along the way I see cool looking traps and try to replicate them. ONCE I build a house, I never rob anyone. I logout and wait for people to die to my traps, and then build more and more.

I actually quite like this game, but am giving it a negative with how they are conducting business.
As highlighted by some of the other negative posts, the issue is that the devs have made a core part of the game impossible. Partially to try to trick people into spending money (don't do this, you can spend all the money ever created since the beginning of time, and still won't beat it), and partially to try to keep people playing while they predictably roll out more monetization schemes. There is a promised fix, and there are no problems rolling out special events every 6-8 weeks, but no progress on this particular issue. I suspect it will never be "fixed" because it is by design.
Besides that big issue, I think the game is actually pretty good. One of the few 'idling' games where you can actually make significant headway while idling. You can just play a couple minutes each day and still make decent progress - just don't expect to beat it unless you expect to live a couple trillion years.
Edit: Version 3.3 update (May 2016)
From the update notes: "The ability to upgrade the Platinum Boost multiplier should be considered the way to effectively beat Earth and Moon in a reasonable amount of time." After playing for a couple weeks, it is apparent that the devs are again lying - Earth is still impossible even with the 7,777x multiplier (which shows how impossible it was before). Instead of waiting for our sun to go supernova a million times now you only need to wait a thousand times.
Edit: Version 4.0 update (July 2016)
Changing my review to 'positive' after this latest patch. With a small investment of gold (around 100, which you can earn playing a couple events) and the 7,777x multiplier, Earth is now beatable. Kudos to the devs by making the change. I still load up this game occasionally, and will make a purchase to support further development even though I have technically "beat it" already.

Incredibly fun, fast, customizable game play coupled with insanity and a toon shader, Loadout is undoubtedly a great experience for the first couple of runs. Upon last play, I ran into the wall of lacking parts to extend the experience and lost interest, but with v2.0 Domination I hope to reap in the chaos once more.
The content's direction pushes toward the more adult audience but invites the immature younger crowd, similar to what one expects of Xbox Live, which may come across as a downside to some. I feel as though the community is a potent mix, however, of great sports and imaturity; the clashing of which makes for a grand spectacle of name-calling and internet politics, without which no online game would be complete.
The game engine is in-house according to one of the developers I met during a match. It is very nicely optimized: clean frame rates excluding massive explosion barrages, no context grabbing issues (black screens) on minimizing to the taskbar, and multitasking such as weapon customization while waiting on the matchmaker to pair you with your soul mates.
Overall this is a good game. The mechanics are sound. Game modes could detail the objectives a little more clearly. Bots could be toned down to a more human level where they don't always know perfectly how to roll to grab objectives. A few other tweaks wouldn't hurt either, but that is true of any game. (NOTE: My experience comes pre-Domination patch, so many of my issues may have been addressed)
Pros and cons aside, I feel like this is a very niche game. One in which I feel like I fit into in many ways.
The only way to know whether you'll enjoy playing is to try it yourself! It's free and definitely worth a shot.

Don't get me wrong. I love this game. King of Fighters is my favorite video game franchise and I have been playing it for years now. even though I have the PS2 version of this already, I was psyched when this was coming to Steam. I'm happy to support SNK because they deserve it. They make quality games. BUT, this particular version of the game is terrible. It honestly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off pretty bad. Allow me to explain the reasons.
1. True full-screen mode is not optional.
What is with this? In the PS2 version of '98 Ultimate Match, the game is in full screen like it should be.  I get that this is an arcade version, but this really could not be stretched for the steam release. The sidebars are distracting and I don't like playing my games in a tiny window in the middle of the screen. It's a good idea to have the sidebars if you're setting up an arcade cabinet with this game. But, it should be optional. Boo to them on that.
2. No arranged music option.
WHY? The PS2 version had it. Why not this? Would it have been so hard to include it? I think not. This is a big let down. I like both the OST and AST. But, the option should have been there.
3. No color editing.
Once again, WHY NOT? The PS2 version had this too! This would have added even more depth into the game if they had included it. It's fun to create your own unique color palettes for your characters. Very bad decision not to include this.
4. The online.
Oh boy. As much as I love KOF, I have to say that the online in KOF titles has always been terrible (At least XIII on steam is a little better). This is no exception. The online is awful. It's extremely laggy. The first match I played had about 3 second late input delay. I'm not kidding. I see why the online is dead already. It's a shame.
All in all, the KOF '98 Ultimate Match is a good game. But the Steam version is not. These fatal flaws just make the game much less enjoyable and souless. If you have a PS2 or a backwards compatible PS3, get the PS2 version. It feels much more complete and joyful than this. Or, if you don't have KOF XIII on Steam or console yet, get that instead. You'll enjoy yourself a lot more. I was hoping to be able to give this a positive review. But, I can't. These stupid mistakes have ruined this version of the game for me. Let's just hope they'll do better with KOF 2002 UM when in comes to Steam. (And hopfully KOF: Maximum Impact: Regulation A)
By the way, the 3D backgrounds from the PS2 version are missing. WTF?

If you can't get the PS2, or any CD version of this game, here's the best next alternative honestly. At least there's online to make up for it...but beware of the high ping spikes. Don't just match with anyone. Make sure you check their ping and that it's around 100 and below before you go into a match. I've had very laggy matches due to ignoring the ping at first, and then very awesome matches because I paid attention to the ping.
If you are getting the game to play online with friends...hopefully you won't experience ping problems with them. Otherwise, search for a player you could rival up against, friend them, and play away! A great experience and good training!
Now as for the game itself. King of Fighters 98 is a much more simplified game than what it became with XIII and even 2002. You'll be using more basic combos, some juggles, and technical gameplay strategies to outwit your opponents with mix-ups and what not.
There's a great selection of characters and they all play very unique from one another. Not to mention, there are even second versions of some characters usually based on previous renditions of them whether it's referenced to older KoF games or their origin (such as Fatal Fury or Art of Fighting.)
Unfortunately, why I reccommend to get the a CD based version, (Neo geo cd, PS2, etc) is for its incredible arranged soundtrack, color edit (I enjoy this since it allows me to personalize my main team), and actually functional graphic filters.
Let's just hope they patch a whatever they can with the netcode, and maybe that someone will make a mod to add in the Arranged sountrack.
Otherwise, I'd still reccommend the game to anyone who wants a taste of King of Fighters' origins beign that people claim this is the most balanced KoF game. Definitely worth it for Fighting gamers!

The Castle Doctrine is for lack of a better way of explaining it, a massively mutiplayer puzzle game. Your goal is to concoct a house that will kill anyone foolish enough to enter attempting to get to your vault. If you desire, you have the option being the fiendish buglar perhaps stealing all the wealth your neighbors have worked hard to conseal.
You will either love it this game or hate it. Everything you do is a risk and you could loose everything with one misclick of your keyboard, you'll find this exhilarating or utterly frustrating. Personally I love this game for one reason, it forces you to improve, unforgivingly so. Although I enjoy this game I couldn't recommend this for the same reason I like it, it has a very steep learning curve if you die at any point in this game you will loose everything you've worked for starting fresh giving you either more resolve or a deeper hatred of yourself for spending 15.99. Bottom line unless you have an iron will, save your money.

As far as games go, this one has a seriously steep learning curve. Understanding how things work, that's one thing. The real challenge, however, is trying to put it all together, because a good portion of how well your traps function is based on psychology, and on that note, there's no way it hell you can know who's gonna break in, or when.
Highly recommended game, 10/10.

Stay far away from this.  It's really hard for me to call it a game, to be honest.  I could write about how broken the progression is, or how buggy it is, how awfully coded and designed it is, and how people are hacking it to pieces essentially destroying the entire purpose of it being an MMO, but I feel those subjects have already been covered enough by plenty of other people.
What I would rather discuss is the price and its relation to what the product is actually worth.
Everything here feels like an experiment, from the "game" itself, to the pricing, to even the developer's lifestyle, and really in the end the customer as well as the health of the community are the ones paying the price.  The developer's "anti-sales" stance means the community will only die over time and never flourish.  For a "game" that trys to promote itself as an MMO, it means a unsustainable fanbase.  Anyone joining at this time will surely find only the super hardcore players and an even smaller window of opporotunity to learn the mechanics and to get better, from an already overly harsh learning curve.
Want to suggest anything at all and provide feedback?  Well, apparently unless you've put in hundreds of hours of gametime, the community and the developer want nothing to do with you, and will freely attack you and assume even the tiniest suggestion means you want to turn the entire game inside out.  Ask to streamline the learning curve in anyway and you'll be accused by players that you are a terrible gamer and can't handle the (bad) design, or that you're just wanting permadeath removed (Like I was accused of).  It doesn't matter that a large majority of games I play and love most are brutally challenging games with permadeath as their prime feature (games like Spelunky, Binding of Isaac, FTL, etc), in their eyes I wanted permadeath removed.  I even saw the developer personally tell his players that were hoping for more from it that "the game's not for you", which just seemed rude and completely self-sabotaging.
One could argue that this "game" is okay in the end, just like how you could squint your eyes hard enough to make a whale into a supermodel, its a neat experiment concept in theory but really what brings this down is the price.  There are players who do enjoy the game so it is possible that you will also.  But it's just a question of whether or not you're willing to put down the $16 to find out whether or not this experiment fits you, which is a big pricetag for a "probably not".  The game is nowhere NEAR worth $16, there are $1-2 iPhone/Android games that are almost twice or more what this game offers.  I love experiemental games, I love when developers push the boundries of what defines a game, but usually the price is adjusted and recognized for what it's actually worth.
I read the developer first tell new players to "put more time into it before judging it" which is fair, but then I saw him say to another who did put the time into it and still didn't like the game that because he had all those hours that he should consider it being worth the price.  I also read a statement from him saying that there are players who put hundreds of hours into his game, and therefore that justifies the pricetag.  But I could play with my own rectal filth for a thousand hours, and that wouldn't make it worth anything more then what it actually is.

How do I put this without making all of you nostalgia-lovers hate me on the spot due to the thumbs down...hopefully like this. This is the WORST port of the BEST game I have ever seen.
Saint's row is a game most of us have come to know fitting the genre with games like GTA, Mafia, Batman Arkham, and even Just Cause. Saints Row 2 takes a serious approach to gang violence as you play the leader of "The Saints". Your goal is essentially to defeat all opposition to your gang so you can rule the city. To do so you need to so many side-activities to earn "respect", as each main mission requires one full bar of respect to play. Sounds fun in essence, but why does it not cut the bill on PC?
-The main character turns like an elephant trying to find a pimple on its butt. I hold A to go left, and my guy runs forward off of a cliff and I die and mission failed. Thanks SR2, thanks.
-The Co-op is just horrible (Note, it can only be played through LAN). The two players are consistently out of sync with each other. So Player 1 is constantly speeding ahead of Player 2. Player 1 may not even notice if he rams Player 2's car, sending him flying off a cliff. Player 2 can't shoot out of a car worth♥♥♥♥♥♥because the enemies are teleporting around, syncing to Player 1 and then desyncing to player 2. It has to have been the worst co-op experience I have ever played through. The host of the sessions always seemed to crash after an hour or two (we switched to test if it was maybe just one of us, but no this is a LAN bug.)
-The AI isn't worth mentioning. They're extremely buggy in some missions. IE: Rocketeers that spawn directly in your face and blow you up instantly. Groups of enemies spawning right next to you while you are already fighting.
-The Driving mechanics are the worst driving mechanics I have seen in any game in my life. Getting over the fact that you can't drive in a straight line down the street to save your life unless you get a lucky angle. The AI drivers have no sense of how driving actually works and are constantly causing accidents, tend to forget you even exist and simply ram you out of the blue. Note the driving is much worse in co-op once you add in all the desync. OH, and not to forget how many times I've held "W" to go forward and my guy just straight up stopped moving for no reason until I pressed W again.
-Some weapons are very unresponsive to when you shoot them. Especially the Deagles. I have to click 4 times just to get one of them to shoot when I'm dual-wielding.
-Many of the side-activites have glitches. For example in the "brawling" side activity, there's a bug my friend and I ran into where we kept falling over onto the ground for no discernable reason every couple of minutes.
-The graphics are dated. While that means nothing to me, I know plenty of gamers are willing to pass right over a game if it doesn't have beautiful modern graphics. If you're one of them, avoid this game. The draw distance is sub-par due to the age of this game, the character models are on par with "The First Templar", and the textures are pathetic by today's standards.
-The sounds aren't all that great, and they're buggy on top of that. There are many times where the sound glitches out and you hear a loud repeating gunshot for the next 20 minutes or until you exit the game.
+Luckily, the story of the game really still holds up, so if you can get past all the many problems this has, you still have a well written story awaiting you in this game.
+The dialogue is also well written and entertaining to hear and read.
+The voice acting is done well, but it's nothing to brag about.

When it comes to developing a game franchise, the most common approach is to improve every aspect of the game, with a strong attention given to UI and graphics. For Dominions however, Illwinter Games took a different turn. They piled up content and added extra features over a very old engine. They have done so for many years now.
So yes, this game is an ugly mess if you compare it to, say, the latest Civ. The barrier of entry is immense : Even if you've gotten your hands on some of the most complex 4X games of old such as Imperialism 2, or for a more recent exemple, Distant Worlds, you are not ready. I have played many of these games in my time, and boy I was not ready.
The amount of micro management and planning required to make you a "decent" Dominions 4 player is insane. Recruiting the right troops, managing a good income, and agressive expansion won't get you very far. You will need a sound understanding of the Magic Paths (hundreds of spells), your God design will determine if you're an early game nation with a Dragon rampaging through hordes of unprepared half-naked barbarians, or a late game nation with an old but powerful Crone biding his time in his cell, carefully planning research and assembling around you some of the most powerful magic users in the land.
I must warn you : If you come aboard, there's no turning back. Civ now feels shallow, when I boot up Total War I get flashbacks of the toy soldiers of my youth. Even my first 4X crush Master of Orion 2 has left me for good.
I used to be a nostalgic of the old 4X games, but that was before Dominions 4. I regret nothing.

Steam kept recommending this game to me based on other games I played, and for a long time I ignored it because I expected better graphics from a game this expensive.  Then it went on sale one day and I took the plunge, and I haven't looked back since.
Dominions 4 is a turn-based strategy game about warring nations each ruled by a mythological entity (titan, monster, wizard, etc) that is trying to become a god.  In the most commonly played game mode, this is accomplished by capturing a certain number of Thrones which are scattered around the map.  In addition to granting victory points, each throne also gives some kind of bonus to your nation when you claim it.
There are dozens of different nations to choose from, and while the diversity keeps things interesting, balance seems to have unfortunately been a secondary consideration, and some nations are really better than others.  Once a nation is chosen, the next step is to create your pretender, the previously mentioned creature that's trying to become a god.  Each nation has a dozen or more pretender options to choose from that fit that nation's theme.  So nations with a Norse theme can choose pretenders like frost giants or giant serpents, while Greco-Roman nations get a variety of different titans and monsters like the Manticore.  Each pretender is also highly customizable, and how you build your pretender can have an enormous impact on how you play the game.
Once the game actually starts, turns consist of recruiting units from the territories you control and sending them out to conquer more territory.  Which sounds simple, and even seems simple when you first start playing.  But soon you realize there's a TON of strategic depth to this game.  When you tell your units to attack a province, you don't control the battle directly.  Instead, you issue the orders that you want your units to follow during the battle before the battle starts.  So you might tell your frontline sword-and-shield infantry to take up a line formation at the front of the battlefield, hold position for the first two turns of combat, and then advance on the enemy, while your archers stay behind with orders to fire on any flying enemies that appear, for example.
You also recruit mages to perform your research and cast all your spells.  There are literally hundreds of spells to research, which creates untold opportunities for play and counterplay - like I said, strategic depth.  Again, balance doesn't seem to have been a primary focus here, and the fact is that many spells are rarely if ever actually used in competitive games, but it's always interesting to encounter spells you haven't seen before, or familiar spells used in new ways.
Bottom line: if you're a fan of complex turn-based strategy games and don't mind a steep learning curve, Dominions is as good as it gets.  I started out playing single player exclusively, which is fine if that's what you're into or just looking to learn the ropes, but multiplayer is where this game really shines in my opinion.  I would be remiss if I didn't point out the game's flaws as well, which include the general lack of balance I've mentioned before, the frankly unimpressive graphics, and a UI that often leaves much to be desired.  That said, the good outweighs the bad here, and while the normal price point might be a little high given the lack of polish, I highly recommend grabbing this game when it's on sale.

If you are just looking to solve hidden object puzzles for 5 minutes each day, you'd find this game to be a pretty good choice. It is pretty well laid out and challenges could be interesting; most quests are BS though, very weak and fragmented, with bad translation. But this isn't an actual game for PC. It is microtransactions moneysqueezer.
This game is very manipulative in its attempt to squeeze as much real money out of you as possible. At start it gives you a decent amount of store items for free, kind of like 'first time it is free' drug, to get you get used to them. But in-game currency you buy such items with is _extremely_ stingy and prices are high. Copper tokens (in-game free currency) are even more useless, with absurdly high prices, and you can't buy anything decent with it anyway .
The game has idea of 'levels' – not only of the character, to unlock certain rooms, but also levels of mastery through each room. Each such level of mastery will give you less and less time to complete the particular room; some modes (there are multiple mods) are built in a such way that eventually you won't have enough time to go through the room on higher mastery unless you use store items.
Why can you play only for 5 minutes each day? Because the game uses 'health' system which regenerates extremely slowly (about 1 point of 'health' per 3 minutes, and below 'critical level' even slower). Your 'health' grow up with each level but stamina regeneration doesn't speed up, and with cost of 'health' for rooms also going up in the same rate as it grows with level, eventually you'd hit a point when 24 hours is not enough to regenerate all your 'health'.
Even full 'health' gives you just a couple of rooms per try, as 'health cost' climbs up quickly and some mods increase it even more; unless you want to go through first kitchen room again and again, you'd find the rising cost of each new room equal to no feel of progress at all.
The game continuously urges you to buy medkits, the only way to regenerate 'health' fast. You get some freebies, but they are drop in the ocean.
Like a slowly boiling frog, game almost entirely shifts its focus on microtransactions after about first 5 levels. It does it pretty slowly but at level 20 it almost entirely all about the store (and level 20 isn't even half way up). Just some examples:
– more and more quests require items you get from shop. I currently have 18 open and only 2 of them don't rely on something available from store
– more and more quests/collections require items you get from catching animals (with traps you get from shop or, extremely rarely, from rooms)
– amount of traps to catch animals _grows up_ with your level, but drop rate of such traps from game remains very small and random;
– collectable puzzle pieces can be doubles of what you already have, so it might take you extremely long time to get all 24 pieces for each puzzle even if you go just through the same room again and again.
– early rooms are all opened by your progress but eventually you'd hit areas where you'd have either to rely on stingy random drops (of multi level variety, i.e. get stingy random traps to catch animals, get a stingy random items from animals) or get the stuff from the shop.
– there are chests with keys. I have had more than 100 chests (it caps at 100) and I only even got 1 free key. I believe some keys are store-only. Drops from each chest are randomized.
– quests will make you either to find 1 uncertain item/person in uncertain room in certain modes (and even if the room/mode is known, item might not drop until many tries later) or, as you guessed it, get the stuff from the shop.
– into-your-face special events that rely on very random rare drops or on items from shop
– the further you go into 'levels of mastery' in each room, the more pixel-hunt it becomes. While it might look like a challenge (and until certain point it is) eventually items became so small, that combined with decreased time to go through level, it turns into pixel-hunt under pressure but quess what? Everything can be bought in the store.
– free drops of stuff you need to progress or finish quests are very rare, the needed number of such items grows with level but the drop rate is not; again, the game always mentions you can get stuff from store.
– the game relies on double random drops with small chances of useful stuff; say, you need an item you can only get from trapped animal (or a store) but traps drop very rarely and what you get from an animal is very random as well
If not for BS store mechanic and _numerous_ gameplay distortions it forces onto game it would be a solid hidden object game with quite good challenges and maybe a decent, if poorly translated, story. But the greed of developers fragments and mutilates the whole experience.

Nier:Automata was instantly on my wish list the moment I heard about it, since Platinum is one of my favourite developers. I kept away from spoilers, because what's the point? I always knew I would play the game. If you want some idea of whether or not this game is for you without spoilers, keep reading.
Game play:
The majority of the time you will be running around hacking up enemies in a traditional third person perspective. However, the game will from time to time shift to being a sidescroller, top down brawler, scrolling shmup, twin stick shmup, and Starfox-esque on rails shooter.
Regarding the various shmup sections, they are not the top tier of shmup action, but they don't appear all that often and they are done well enough to not tarnish the rest of the game. They also don't overstay their welcome.
As for the meat, the third person hack'n'slash action, it's great. If you have played other Platinum games, you will know what to expect, though it does a few things to mix things up. There is a nice assortment of weapons, with their own combos and various special features (such as absorbing health from cutting bullets or detonating combo finishers).
Sound:
This is easy. The sound effects all fit. The music is a really nice mix of orchestral, pop, cute/funny and electronic styles. I had to get the soundtrack before I even finished the game. The game has English and Japanese voices. Usually I would default to Japanese (assuming that's it's source country), but since English was selected by default, I decided to give it a go. I was pleasantly surprised at how good the English dub was (given how terrible they can be).
Graphics/Art:
Overall really pretty. There are a few issues, like the occasional muddy texture or detail levels popping in and out, but nothing to really break the overall presentation. The art design (for my tastes) is spot on and a breath of fresh air compared to a lot of games that aim for pure realism. The style is somewhat "realistic", but stylised enough to have it's own identity and not take you to uncanny valley.
Story (no spoilers, I promise):
I came in completely blind and if possible, I suggest you do the same. I knew there would be robots, and didn't expect much more than that. I was completely happy to play an action game with that backdrop. I was very (VERY) pleasantly surprised. The story has depth I didn't think would be here. I am not ashamed to admit that I got "hit in the feels" multiple times. I honestly can't remember the last time a games story and characters had this much of an impact on me.
Conclusion:
If you want an action game with a decent story, nice graphics and a great soundtrack, it doesn't get much better than this. Honestly, this is one of the best games I've ever played.
Caveat:
There are a whole bunch of issues with certain PC hardware, though I didn't experience any myself (using a laptop with a GTX1060, i7 CPU, Win10). Check the forums and definitely download the FAR mod. This can help increase performance and fixes some issues. Having read up in advance, I installed the FAR mod before I even started playing the game. The only issue I ran into was it displaying on the wrong monitor and the game resetting my camera config (ONLY the camera config, nothing else for some reason). Annoying for sure, but easily fixable and hardly a deal breaker.

Loadout is exactlywhat it looks like; a frenetic, over-the-top-violent, twitch shooter. I normally don't dig twitch shooters. I wanted to like Teamfortress 2 so much, but I just couldn't. It was just too "twitchy." But for some reason I like Loadout. It has a very similar visual asthetic to Teamfortress 2 (which I love), just with more crass. The concept where all players build their own guns is a fun one, and it's a great carrot for players to chase as they earn points to buy that next great gun upgrade. It's not a perfect game. I still wish it wasn't so twitchy, and the cash shop, while being very good at offering no "pay to win" options, seems overly expensive. I'd love to customize the look of my character, but I'm not going to pay 50 bucks to do so. And there are no cosmetic options available to be earned whatsoever. For what it is, this game is great for being completely free. I'd happily throw down $20 for this on Xbox Live Arcade and not have to worry about any micro transactions whatsoever, but here I feel like $20 wouldn't give me much of anything. It wouldn't buy me all the cloths options I want, and that certainly would leave no money for XP bonuses or things of that nature. Because of that I won't drop a dime on this game, and I'll just have to be content with the generic character. It doesn't make the game less fun, but it does seem to prevent it from being "more" fun (if you get what I mean). The fact that it's free means you have nothing to lose by trying it out. It really is worth a look if the trailer even halfway looks appealing to you.

Still though, it’s a shame they couldn’t find (or haven't, in case you want to go into the forums and keep insisting) a way to add the extras from the PS2 version (Color Edit mode, Arrange Soundtrack and the 3D backgrounds). I know it’s because this port is based around the XBOX Live Arcade version, but still... Overall, this game is a must-buy if you like fighting games, The King of Fighters series, old-school games, or all of those combined.

This review is obsolete. It describes what the game was like when the community was vivid and bustling (it was a very fun game back then). Nowadays almost no one plays this game and the few houses that remain are very much unbreakable.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
In order to enjoy this game you need to accept it's rules:
, you're supposed to learn how to play the game by trial-and-failure. Some of the best experiences from this game come from experimenting by your own initiative and gradually learning better methods to build and destroy trap systems. Tutorials would only ruin all the fun of learning by dying or getting robbed.
Don't come in with any illusions that you are going to be able to simply figure out the solutions to other players houses by using your smarts. Efficient homes are designed in such a way that their solution cannot be seen and if you try to take a guess the odds will be staggeringly against you. In order to defeat a home what you really need is to make the best use of your available tools in order to disable the houseowner's traps.
There is no 'leveling up' or gaining 'experience' for killing enemies here, the only thing that separates the veterans from the noobs is the very things that The Castle Doctrine is all about; tactics and deception. The players who are up in the top are there solely because they know how to manage their risks and have figured out techniques to build houses that are very hard to penetrate. You won't stand a chance against the home of a top player before you have learned how to scout and hold a sizable wealth of your own.
You start with only $2000 and that will not be enough money to build a house that will make you reasonably safe from other players. In order to build a decent house you need use your starting 2k to buy tools and rob richer players, in this process of trying your luck against the rich you will die (a lot), but you need to keep trying because eventually you will succeed. Then, after your success, it's time to stop dying and start seeing other players die in the deathtrap that you have built for them.
Due to the permadeath mechanic you can lose everything that you have worked on due to one single wrong step. This rather harsh rule actually makes the game far more interesting and tense, it means that every time you defeat another player you get the knowledge that he has been completely ruined and additionally it means that you become afraid of your own house because every time you make a modification to it you are supposed to go into your own deathtrap and reach your safe in order to prove that what you have created is solvable, during these 'self-tests' you can die. You will feel in your own skin how this machine that you have created to kill other players can be extremely dangerous even to yourself.
Just like in real life, eh? In this game you play the role of the father of a stereotypical white american nuclear family in the 90's, you have the duty and responsibility of protecting them. Other players will try to kill your wife and kids because they are a weakness and killing them can make your home more vulnerable.
There are really no overarching goals in this game other than trying to survive and rising above other players in the charts. However, all homes eventually fall. I'm a fan of difficult, tense games that don't try to hold your hand. Sadly, this isn't so much a difficult game as a discouraging game. Don't get me wrong, I like the premise a lot, and I enjoy the idea of playing this game with friends, trying to guess whose house belongs to who, with all of that kind of fun social dynamic attached when you finally penetrate a house's defenses. Sadly, playing the game as presented on the public server is an exercise in pointlessness.
To begin with, the game has extremely far beyond frustrating game flow that actively discourages experimentation to a degree I can't really explain very well using words. Despite really wanting to like the game, I was done after the second day of ownership. Experimentation of any type, with your own house's design or with exploring those of others, is 'rewarded' by completely losing the house's entire design if you make any mistakes whatsoever anywhere, either in its wiring or in negotiating the house's solution. Despite well-matching the game's design philosophy, the fundamental reality of this situation is that you will spend over 95% of your game time rebuilding nearly identical houses with the almost no money you're forced to start with.
The ease of death is really overstated, it's very easy to avoid dying provided no one with an entire inventory full of guns and saws really wants your money. That said, after rebuilding the same house for the fourth time, I lost pretty much all desire to look at anyone else's houses. And, of course, if you make a mistake wiring your own house and end up in your own trap, well. It's time to start over. Unlike a 'roguelike', instead of being able to pick the game up immediately when you die and try again doing something fun like exploring an unknown cavern and collecting loot or what have you, you're forced to rebuild your entire house once again from literally nothing. If this review is starting to seem repetitive, that's because that's what the game is like.
In conclusion, one gets the feeling that the game was primarily designed for people who are unemployed, don't have kids, and probably can't be bothered to cook for themselves, or generally do any of the other things that people value their time for. Like writing reviews.

Red Rope is an amazing game that made me feel like my brain was expanding while playing it. It takes an amazing puzzle game to accomplish the feat of actually making you feel slowly smarter instead of just making you feel like you put the square peg in the square hole.
I played it solo. I actually do not recommend playing it with another player unless you have a friend that you would risk your life for. I feel like there is so much co-ordination needed between the two parties in this game that it would take under an hour of gameplay to want to wring a noose around your friend's neck. Solo is perfectly doable, but it has a high learning curve. But it feels amazing once you grasp onto it- after a while it just gets automatic and you can control the two characters flawlessly without even thinking about it. It totally makes up for the beginning being rough with you making all sorts of dumb mistakes.
There are a lot of weird confusing mechanics here, but all of them took a very short amount of time to learn. It's offbeat nature of scoring mechanics (or "morality" if you want to go with the tacked on art game premise this game apparently has according to the advertising, even though it's completely absent in game) and gameplay tricks lead to a very zen and tense experience at the same time. You are limited in lives, but you also know that enemies don't respawn when you die in this game except a certain type so you can suicide to clear a room if need be. It creates this balance of knowing when dying is worth it and when to take the bullet to clear a tricky situation.
Like most games though, it turns out the things you like most are easiest to criticize. There are a lot of issues with this game. The music sucks. I like the droning odd style of it, but it gets easily repetitive and sounds underproduced. There is also only a total of like 9 songs, so no matter what dungeon you go into if it's the same "level" dungeon (there are 4 per level) it will always have the same song. Some dungeons are also clear wastes of time or lives because of how much harder they are in comparison to the rest of the dungeons. Particularly, the
dungeons are so tricky that you might as well go through literally anything else. Luckily it's like the developers anticipated this, and you only need a total of two dungeons on each level to make it to the final boss. So you can effectively skip half the game. Also, a small handful of rooms are balanced for longer ropes. This is terrible, because every time you die your rope gets reset. So if you screw up in these rooms, you will likely have to pixel hunt with your characters just to stay alive. There was one room in particular in the rightmost silver key dungeon where you have to travel across moving platforms with buttons on them, and I swear you have to land on the exact pixel if you have the smallest rope size. It doesn't feel like a challenge or a smart puzzle, just frustrating tedium.
All that aside, I highly recommend the game. The developers are great as they fix bugs quick and even have a promotion where the first 50 people to beat the game get pixel art done of them to put into the game. The game isn't impossible, so if that interests you and you have 10 hours aside to spare, maybe it's worth setting that up as a goal?
It's been a long, long, long while since I've played a puzzle game this good. As unpolished as it is in some aspects, it makes up for it with pure genius in other parts.

It's an ftp Hidden Object game with an interesting story.
Story is, you're lured into a house (hahaaa - I'm trying just that here too!) and can't get out. There are other people, one even acts as an npc friend. You need to find stuff to collect points of freedom, and there are additional quests like assembling collections or jigsaws.

You can only play a bit at a time, as in the typical ftp game manner, you need to wait for something to regenerate, that you need to do HO scenes. (The choice here is something that fits well with the story too!)
There's also stuff you can do when Steam friends play it. Like, breaking or improving their decoration (doesn't harm you, gets you both something, and next day interaction may just only offer the opposite; fixing or degrading). You can even send each other free gifts (one per day per friend), as well as other things they may need, from your inventory. Need more of my friends playing this! :)
The english is somewhat amusing in parts (a bit eh, not native), and some objects are a bit very small, but well... they can be found anyway, and there are tools to help. And the story is really rather interesting.

Edit: With the 6/20/16 update, I, and many others, lost all of our progress in the game. I'm just starting over (since there's really nothing else I can do about it), but if you get impatient and upset with losing progress due to system updates, I would not recommend the game for you. Otherwise, it is a very nice game to play, albeit with flaws.
I also wish to elaborate on some of my earlier statements: I think one of the major issues with this game is the "waiting" aspect. If I could play through it straight away, or if I had a way to consistently replenish my health without having to give up gameplay time for it, I would enjoy it more. At present, you can get (maybe) about 5-10 minutes of playtime, depending on how much health you have, and whether or not you have any food/health kits/pills to replenish it with.
It would be much better if I felt that I could get more playtime out of it. I love puzzles, but it's taking me too long to navigate each of the rooms and quests when I can only do about five or six rooms at a time (depending on the room, as some take more of your health than others).
I really do like this game, but these flaws are enough to frustrate me into considering not playing it. The only reason I still have it is because it's free to play. (Though, not if you want gold tokens; you either have to level up, which takes a very long time, or pay for those...)

I would rather not have to choose a thumbs-up or thumbs-down... But here we go:
Pros:
- Beautiful graphics
- Good story
- Opportunity for choice (karma, Firewoods)
- Puzzles and collections
- Always have something to do (multiple quests)
- Multiple search modes
- Many, many rooms to explore
Cons:
- Gold tokens run out too quickly; NO way to replenish them without using real money (which I will NEVER do)
- Health takes forever to regenerate
- Modes cost gold tokens to change (consider changing to copper tokens)
- Requires internet to play (this one is neither a pro, nor a con, but presents its own sets of troubles for game availability)
- Grammar can be confusing and detrimental to the aesthetic of the game (for instance, some rooms need to you to find a knight chess piece, but it is written as "pawn," which is incorrect; they need to hire someone whose first language is English to correct these sorts of errors)
The main concern is that gold tokens are too big a part of the game to not have them. Either they must MAKE a way to gain gold tokens for quests and such as well, or they must change the dynamic of purchasing food and room modes to use regular tokens instead. Otherwise, the game requires you to wait too long and you basically end up bored and not playing it (personal experience). You have to waste blood cycling through the room modes for the one you need, and you run out of health before you can complete the quest in the mode they actually need.
So my suggestion is that they fix the money and health mechanics: health needs to regenerate faster, and either you must be able to get gold tokens in-game, or you can use regular tokens for food and room modes.

TL;DR: Become a god. Crush other would-be gods with your armies, one turn at a time. Ignore the graphics.
Long version:
Dominions 4 has come a loooooong way.
The Dominions series has evolved, and its forth iteration boils down to the exact same core mechanics as each of its predecessors. This is not a bad thing.
Let me elaborate:
As for the Background and story: The former ÜBER-God, called the "Pantocrator", is dead. And now the position is up for grabs by the rising gods, like You! But, lots of "Pretender Gods" claim godhod for themselfes and like you, they have marshalled a whole Nation to do their bidding.
Traditionally, you recruit armies, and supplement that with powerful combat magics to decimate enemey armies and conquer their provinces. Add to that that your mages may also perform powerful rituals out of combat to do anything from summoning strong monsters to make everyone in the world age at the rate of a year a month. Watch them wither and die.
Dominions 4 has other Victory options to supplement the traditional "Conquer all" approach. Several strategies are possible for most Victory conditions.
Breaking down the Game in Pro's and Con's
PRO: Depth
The amount of material to go through is amazing. There are, literally, hundreds of different spells and rituals that can be researched and wielded by your mages. The amount of different troops availible to you ranges typically a dozen and more, not including summonend monsters. And the number of Factions you can choose is currently about 60, I think.
PRO: Replayability
Not only are there a ton of factions you can play, and they all play differently, but also many factions allow for different strategies. "Hmm, Marignon focused on troops was good, but what if I use fire magic instead..."
Also, Depending on the size of the map used, the game plays totally different.
PRO: Multiplayer
Multiple variants are supported. From traditional "Play by mail" and hotseat to direct connection to a server.
Single player can be considered "training wheels" for multiplayer, since this is where you will find the challenging plays.
CON: Graphics
They are bad. Old-timey at best. They also have evolved a lot and look way better than Dominions 3, but are not on par with current releases of major triple A titles.
PRO: Mods.
So many. So many. Toooooo many. Simple mods can tweak a Faction or a few troops. But total conversion mods exist too. And they add variety to NO END.
CON: User Interface
The user interface is subject to current optimization. Playing the game without keyboard shortcuts is feasible, but it gets tedious. You will be thinking "Why can't I order my mage to forge the same magic item every turn?", you can, but only if you know or look up the keyboard shortcut.
My conclusion is: As a hardcore strategy game fan, you should give it a try. If you consider yourself a "casual" gamer, this game probably will not be for you.

First flaw is graphics, obviously, if you want to see beautiful picture, Dominions is not an eye-candy game. Second flaw is micromanagement, it may be quite tedious to play on huge map with a lot of provinces and opponents. Well, it is always hard to control a vast empire, is not it?
And what is good in this game? Well... everything else. Dominions offers a huge amount of content and deep, well-designed and balanced mechanics. By other side, it is not hard to learn basics, Dominions is one of these games that "easy to learn but hard to master". You may gather an army and send it to conquer neighbours in just a couple of clicks... and then realise, that you need to think about strategy.
I absolutely loved all playable nations, they are not typical boring "elves, dwarves and orcs", but thoroughly developed groups, based on myths and cultures from all around the world - from celtic myths to slavic folklore, from african stories to chinese legends. Game offers wonderful lore, and it was really interesting for me to explore it.
Customization offers a lot of choices, it has a huge impact and also provides wide capabilities to roleplay, if you want to. Do you want to rule a scorched land of sloth and misfortune? Maybe you prefer frozen realm full of magic and mineral resources? Or lush green paradise with rich fields and bountiful harvests? And how about your avatar, will it be a huge dormant dragon, or ancient powerful lich, or even a marble statue smeared with blood of sacrificed virgins? And all this customization is not just cosmetic changes, it has a huge impact on gameplay and, in fact, determines your possible ways to victory.
Economic system is simple and effective. You need to manage three types of resources: gold, production and gems, used for most powerful spells, troops and creation of artifacts. There is no penalties for territorial expansion, so Dominions is true heaven for conquerors. The more provinces you control - the more resources you will have, so expansion is absolutely necessary for victory.
Battles are interesting and quite unusual. You can not control your troops directly, but you may plan, how your squads must act and what you expect from them to do. Planning the battle, placing troops and choosing what spells your wizards may cast, is vital part of game, and you really need to think and develop your tactic and strategy. And when it comes to magic... game really shines there, lots of schools and tons of spells, and again you really need to think, what and when you need to use. Easy to learn, hard to master, as I mentioned before.
AI is decent. For me it was interesting enough to play on medium difficulty, of course AI can not be compared with human, but he actively resists, collects armies and punishes player for mistakes. And if you want challenge, you can always try hard difficulty or, maybe, join multiplayer... if you can find another players.
Main thing that Dominions can offer is huge replayability. So many combinations, I am sure that you will not get bored soon. So. You love turn-based strategic games and still did not tried Dominions? I sincerely recommend this game for you then. Excellent stuff, high quality. I mean it, man!
I would write a longer review here, but that would require being away from Dominions. Wonderful game, although I reccomend waiting for a sale.

Overall, this game is a lot of fun.  I have only really played it as single player, but I find that it offers a heck of a lot of replay and depth to it.  Don't let the old style of graphics turn you from this game, it is incredible.  While the AI is far from perfect, it is still solid and the depth of strategy is beyond basic explanation.  Take combat, for example.
You build up an army, you can tell the men what squad they are in, and where that squad will start.  From there, you can give a SINGLE basic order to the squad and that is it.  The order can be Fire (target type, which does NOT include leaders), Hold and Attack (wait two turns then attack target type), and similar.  But that is it, the rest is out of your hand.  Your leader you have slightly more control over, able to give orders for the first five turns through script like commands set up with the armuy (such as cast a certain spell, hold or cast, etc.).  And since it is required to be done before you go into combat, once combat starts, you can only watch it play out, no Total War controls here.
There is NO diplomacy in single player, that is a big downside for me.  The computer though does seem to recognize when you are at war with them, which is nice.  You attack their lands and they will fight and attack you, otherwise they seem to leave you alone (until you are their next target).  Kill their pretender and they won't stop attacking until they are destroyed.  No trading, no NAPs, nothing of that nature, but still, it is a remake of an old game.
Replayability is incredibly high.  There are three ages (High Magic, High Human, and inbetween) each with their own races avaliable.  Each race, unlike some games that are simple reskins, are very different in play.  Some are high magic focused, even for the high magic age, while others rely on mythical creatures or humans blessed by their god.  No matter how you look at it though, each race fights their own way, takes their own different tactics, and offers plenty of replayability because of it.  Even the same race over the different ages play differently, and some races simply don't exist in certain ages, just to show the type of race they are.
Overall, its an incredibly addicting game, active community, and lots of fun.  Go for it, especially when on sale.

It's a great game although the asking price of 32€ is too expensive. I waited for a special to buy it and at 60% off it's definitely worth the money.
I wouldn't compare it to Civ. It feels more like Rome Total War during the grand campaign mode but it gives me some Warlords 2 nostalgia feel too. There's a lot of depth to it and the different factions do handle very differently, which is great. The differences go beyond just combat and units and there's a LOT of factions so we're spoilt for choice in this game.
All conflicts are automatically resolved for you, but you get to organise your troops into batallions and tell each batallion how it's meant to behave. For example, you can organise a line of infantry which is meant to advance towards the enemy, a line of archers that follows behind and shoots, and cavalry on the sides which flank. Morale is a big deal and if your troops rout then the battle is certainly lost.
So unlike in Total War where you have to micromanage everything, there's no micromanagement in this. You have to plan in advance and hope for the best.
I think if you enjoy Total War's grand campaigns then you're probably going to enjoy this.
Edit: After more time with this game, I would buy it at full price. The trouble is that to give this game an honest go, it's going to take you several hours to figure it out and by then your refund opportunity is definitely gone. I can't see many people wanting to refund this though, especially not after experiencing multiplayer.

Pros: The game itself plays perfectly fine. The control feels a bit wonky on a pad and some people have reported issues with sticks, plus poor keyboard support. But there's no lag / pausing problems when playing single player. There's 30 challenges in the game too but I don't believe you get anything for clearing them, since all the secret characters are unlocked by default. Classic NeoGeo mode is also available, which is a nice plus, but it doesn't have any of the extra characters.
Cons: No arranged music, no 3D stages, and only twelve achievements, two of which are wasted on the typical "beat 5 / 10 players in a row". Plus some of the music sounds off, like Billy's theme, which has a bit that sounds like they had the wrong settings in their YM2610 emulator, but it's still not nearly as bad as Metal Slug 3's. And the netcode is horribly broken as of launch.
Is it worth it? HELL YEAH IT IS. I wasn't expecting the game to be this good out of the gate, and it's a shame that we didn't get the arranged music as an option, but this is a fine offering, so hopefully SNK Playmore hires Code Mystics to handle their future PC ports instead of the idiots at DotEmu.

I’ve started a project where I’m gonna try to review every game in my steam library. I do this in the alphabetical order, and the next game on the list is Bionic Commando. Instead of playing that though, I’ve been playing a lot, and I mean A LOT of Skyrim. So, I’ve decided to review that instead.
When someone asks what my favorite game genre is, I always say it’s Role playing Games. Almost all of the games on my top 10 games list are rpgs, and when it comes to Western rpgs, I find Bethesda to make some of the best ones. With The Elder Scrolls and Fallout, they’ve made tons of memorable experiences that any rpg fan should play. I hold Skyrim in a very special place in my heart, since it was the first rpg I ever played. well, if you don’t count JRPGs like Pokemon. Yeah, I haven’t been around for very long. I’ve put over 100 hours into skyrim, and recently came back to play more of it. Does it still hold up? Yes. It definitely does.
There’s a civil war going on in Skyrim, between the Imperials and the Stormcloaks. From what I understand, the imperials owns pretty much all of Tamriel, including Skyrim, until some nords decided they wanted Skyrim to be independent from the rest of Tamriel and started a war. You’ll pick your side in the war yourself, and it’s actually a pretty hard choice! While it is tempting to choose the stormcloaks since they didn’t try to chop your head off in the first ten minutes, the stormcloaks aren’t exactly clean themselves. On top of that, the dragons, whose been dead for hundreds of years, are coming back to life! Their leader Alduin is trying to end the world!
You play as the dragonborn, who has the power to kill dragons, and shout people of cliffs. Your job is to kill Alduin and save the world. I love how the main story and the war are their own separate questlines! You can choose what you want to do. If you want to, you can just completely ignore the main story and go explore. Almost all the sidequest have a fun story to follow. There’s tons of side missions and guilds for you to do! there’s also a ton of books. I don’t know how many words there are, but I think that if you were to read all the books in this game, it would probably be longer than something like Lord Of The Rings. I love to dig deeper into the lore, and it really makes me want to play the rest of the series!
The vanilla version of the game does show its age. Don’t get me wrong, it’s still beautiful, but you can see that it’s a six year old game. The special edition however, is one of the prettiest games I’ve ever played! The graphics are much better than the original! You can mod the game to make it look even better, but the special edition looks good enough for me. The snowy mountains and the green forests feels good to walk around in. All the cities have it’s own style, and almost none of them feels the same. You could argue that the world gets a bit repetitive after a while, since there’s only snowy mountains and forests. But since they look as good as they do, I don’t really mind.
Skyrim has one of the best themes in all of video games. That is a well known fact. While the main theme kicks♥♥♥♥♥and steal the show, that doesn’t mean the rest of the music isn’t good. Skyrims soundtrack is great! When fighting, the battle theme will appear and makes the fight much more intense. When walking through a town, there’s a relaxing song in the background. When in a tavern, you can hear bards playing or singing. Overall, the music is really good!
I’ve been only talking positive about this game so far, but the one thing about it I don’t like, is the gameplay. Let’s start with the combat. You do get a lot of variety in how to fight, but the fights themselves never really turn out very interesting. I often tell myself that the Ebony Blade is my favorite weapon in the game. While the weapon is really good, and the quest to get it is fun, when using it, you basically just spam your left mouse button and wait for the enemy to die. It isn’t very engaging. What might be fun for a while is using a bow. But once the enemies rush into your face, you’re pretty much forced to pull up a melee weapon and kill them that way. The most fun way to play the game is being a mage. There’s a lot of variety in the spells, and I find all the magic schools to be useful. Some more than others. When using magic to conjure a sword out of thin air and resurrecting dead bodies to fight for me, while making enemies who were alive attack each other I was actually having quite fun! If you’re looking into having fun with this game, I recommend using magic.
I love the leveling system in this game. You level up by doing stuff. If you use two-handed weapons a lot, you’ll level up your two-handed skill. If you pickpocket a lot, you’ll level up your pickpocket skill. Once you’ve leveled up enough skills, your main level will increase. You’ll get to put 10 point into either Health, Magicka or Stamina and you’ll also get a perk point to put into a skill. Some perks cannot be chosen if you skill level isn’t high enough. If you want to make dragon armor, you’ll need to get your Smithing level up to 100, then put a perk point into dragon armor. I love this concept. The problem comes when you can exploit the game until you’re in a much higher level than you’re supposed to be! I don’t really mind this though. I have actually used some of these exploits myself. If you don’t want to cheat, just don’t do it.
The exploration part of the game is pretty cool, but gets really repetitive after a while. There’s a lot of caves and bandit camps for you to explore. The first ten or so dungeons you explore might be fun, but after that they just get tedious. I ended up only exploring caves if there were quests for doing so. When I found a cave, I just ignored it and walked to my destination. In the late game you won’t really find cool stuff in dungeons. The best thing you’ll get is usually a small amount of money.
I love Skyrim. Everybody loves Skyrim. The amount of content they have put in this game is breathtaking, and it will take you a lifetime to complete it 100%. You can’t really go wrong with Skyrim. It has something for everyone. The only reason why you might not like this game is if you only care about combat in your games. With that, I’ll give this game a:
The game could easily earn a 10/10 if they’d just made the combat more enjoyable. Let’s hope that they’ll improve that with  The Elder Scrolls VI. I would love to see the Dark Souls combat in a big rpg like The Elder Scrolls. Get on it Bethesda!

Red rope is one of if not the best co-op experience I've ever had...
It's also the most communication heavy co-op I've ever experienced. Do not play with a partner you are not ready to forgive. I may have blamed mistakes on my partner, I may have got mad at myself. Few times I was ready to give up... but at the same time our communication and collaboration got better. Clearing a room after room felt good. Opening a new door gave a rush of excitement and fear for the worst.
When the final boss died after around 80 tries, I felt excellent... and at the same time sad, because I'm most likely to compare all my future co-op experiences to Red Rope. I hope some devs will take heed and serve as fantastic experiences aimed for two players.
The mysterious labyrinth can feel relentless and confusing at first, but the creepy atmosphere and diverse enemies kept me hooked. As the game itself suggest, I would mainly recommend it as a co-op experience with a good friend or significant other.

If a game had the power to strengthen the relationship you share with a loved one, wouldn't you play it? For me and the one I chose to play with, my ex-husband and one of my best friends in the world, I genuinely think it did just that.
Red Rope is an immensely stylish two-player action-adventure enigma that represents for me the single most difficult game I've ever played. Immediately you will be thrown into a world lacking clear explanation of anything from your goal to the mechanics, though you'll quickly figure it out: basically, get the hell out of this labyrinth together or die trying. And die you will. A lot.
Yet part of the beauty about Red Rope is that you don't have to be some expert gamer to play. The controls are very simple: you can move around. That's it. There are no buttons to press in combat, because the only weapon you and your partner have is the rope tied between your waists. Using this rope, you'll slice through, surround, or avoid ghosts, zombies, flames and any other of the game's threats. It felt great on Steam controllers, but playing on a single keyboard is an option as well.
Even though Caleb and I are apparently two of only a handful of people in the world who's beaten the game so far, I am really not joking when I say I think you could give the controls to anyone who has basic game familiarity and go through it with them, with enough patience. (Had we not been recording it, we would have taken it slower - 2 hours a day, maybe.) The game's challenges are difficult, but fair. Very rarely did we feel like any of our 100's of deaths couldn't have been avoided if we hadn't made a mistake.
The game teaches its lessons without feeling punishing, starting you out with 100 lives and with a gradual incline in difficulty that felt fair after figuring out what can and can't kill you in the first few rooms. I was impressed at how the challenges in each area were roughly equal in difficulty to the current tier (there are 3 tiers of difficulty in the game - the seasons, the elements, and the plagues). Yet, the challenges were genuinely different from each other, too. As we played, there were areas I was significantly better at than my partner, though more often vice versa, and therefore leadership exchanged hands depending on the area.
And that's the trick to this game: it's not surviving the labyrinth, it's surviving each other. During our first try, the worst of us came out. Whether it was him blaming too many of the deaths on me, or me not paying enough attention, we really got frustrated. We had to learn to communicate and trust each other in ways life had rarely asked of us, much less a game. But by the end of it, we had improved our own behavior for the sake of each other. I was staying alert, he was accepting his own mistakes, and most importantly, we were communicating constantly.
Realize like we did, as quickly as you can, that blaming the other person will only detract from both your fun. You must accept that you are not equals, learn each other's strengths and weaknesses, and accept your own failures. If one method isn't working, try talking it through. Let the person who has the best understanding of the current situation call the shots - and realize that it isn't always going to be you, even if you think you're awesome at games. And if you don't feel that way? Know that your ideas are worthy and you should keep presenting them to your partner even if you're wrong a lot. You need each other to survive!
Given Red Rope's emphasis on simple controls and communication with your partner, you could play this with just about anyone: a coworker, your best friend, a parent, a sibling, a date, an ex. Even if the two of you only got through a few levels, you'll have learned something valuable about each other. But if you manage to make it all the way through, you'll have been through a genuinely harrowing experience with another human being, which is the stuff legendary friendships are made of. That felt really satisfying.
I highly recommend entering the labyrinth today. And while you're at it, look for me, Caleb, and the other folks who have been put into the game after beating it! (Hint: look for white belts.) I will leave you with our Let's Play below, and one cryptic word of advice: sometimes, a short rope can free you; others, a long rope can kill you.
